sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Unresponsive patient with absent or abnormal breathing, including agonal gasps.
• No definite pulse within 10 seconds in a healthcare professional assessment.
• Pulseless electrical activity (PEA), asystole, ventricular fibrillation (VF), or pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT).
• Begin CPR immediately if cardiac arrest is suspected and no definite pulse is detected.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate the resuscitation team and obtain a defibrillator.
• Start high-quality CPR: Compression rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, allow complete recoil, minimize interruptions.
• Change compressor approximately every 2 minutes.
• Attach monitor/defibrillator and identify the rhythm.
• Defibrillate immediately for VF or pVT.
• Establish IV access; use IO access if IV access cannot be obtained promptly.
• Provide bag-mask ventilation with oxygen; avoid excessive ventilation.

sections.heading: 03 — RESUSCITATION ALGORITHM
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Shockable Rhythm: VF / Pulseless VT[/color]
• Deliver an unsynchronized shock.
• Immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes without checking the pulse immediately after the shock.
• Reassess rhythm every 2 minutes and shock again if VF/pVT persists.
• Give epinephrine after initial defibrillation attempts according to the current ACLS algorithm.
• Give amiodarone or lidocaine for refractory VF/pVT.

[color=#1E3A8A]Non-Shockable Rhythm: PEA / Asystole[/color]
• Continue high-quality CPR. Give epinephrine as soon as feasible.
• Reassess rhythm every 2 minutes. Do not defibrillate PEA or asystole unless the rhythm changes to VF/pVT.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]High-Quality CPR[/color]
• Compression rate: 100–120/min. Depth: 5–6 cm. Ratio: 30:2 (without advanced airway), continuous compressions with 1 breath every 6 seconds (with advanced airway).

[color=#1E3A8A]Defibrillation[/color]
• Biphasic: manufacturer's recommended energy (commonly 120–200 J). Monophasic: 360 J.

[color=#1E3A8A]Epinephrine[/color]
• 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes. Concentration: 0.1 mg/mL (10 mL contains 1 mg).

[color=#1E3A8A]Amiodarone (Refractory VF/pVT)[/color]
• First dose: 300 mg IV/IO bolus. Second dose: 150 mg IV/IO.

sections.heading: 05 — REVERSIBLE CAUSES (Hs & Ts)
sections.content:
• Hypovolemia. Hypoxia. Hydrogen ion excess (acidosis). Hypokalemia/Hyperkalemia.
• Hypothermia. Tension pneumothorax. Cardiac tamponade. Toxins. Pulmonary thrombosis. Coronary thrombosis.

sections.heading: 06 — POST-ROSC CARE
sections.content:
• Secure oxygenation and ventilation; avoid hypoxemia and hyperoxia (target SpO2 ~92-98%).
• Avoid hypotension and support perfusion.
• Obtain 12-lead ECG and evaluate for acute coronary occlusion.
• Check glucose, blood gas, electrolytes, renal function.
• Provide temperature control and post-arrest critical care.

sections.heading: 07 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay compressions while obtaining equipment or IV access.
• Do not perform prolonged pulse checks.
• Ensure nobody is touching the patient during shock delivery.
• Do not confuse the cardiac-arrest epinephrine concentration (0.1 mg/mL) with 1 mg/mL.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA Adult Advanced Life Support; AHA Adult Basic Life Support.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Central chest pressure, heaviness, squeezing, or pain radiating to the arm, jaw, back, or shoulder.
• Dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, or unexplained weakness.
• Atypical presentations are common in older adults, diabetes, kidney disease.
• STEMI may require immediate reperfusion; do not wait for troponin results when ECG and presentation establish the diagnosis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, vital signs, hemodynamic stability.
• Obtain 12-lead ECG as soon as possible (within 10 minutes).
• Establish IV access and cardiac monitoring. Obtain high-sensitivity troponin.
• Give aspirin unless contraindicated.
• Activate local reperfusion pathway for STEMI.
• Assess for alternative life-threatening diagnoses (aortic dissection, PE, tension pneumothorax).

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• 12-lead ECG; repeat when indicated.
• Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin.
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, glucose, coagulation.
• Echocardiography for shock, mechanical complications, or diagnostic uncertainty.
• Risk assessment using GRACE pathway.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Aspirin[/color]
• 162–325 mg orally, chewed once, unless contraindicated. Subsequent maintenance 75–100 mg daily.

[color=#1E3A8A]Nitroglycerin[/color]
• 0.4 mg sublingually, repeated every 5 minutes up to 3 doses while reassessing BP.

[color=#1E3A8A]Anticoagulation and P2Y12 Inhibition[/color]
• Selection depends on STEMI vs NSTE-ACS, reperfusion strategy, bleeding risk, renal function.

[color=#1E3A8A]Reperfusion for STEMI[/color]
• Primary PCI preferred when delivered within guideline time.
• If timely PCI unavailable, fibrinolysis may be considered according to local STEMI protocol.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid aspirin in true severe allergy or active major bleeding.
• Avoid nitroglycerin with hypotension, suspected RV infarction, or recent PDE-5 inhibitor use (sildenafil/vardenafil within 24h, tadalafil within 48h).
• Fibrinolysis is not appropriate for NSTEMI or unstable angina.
• Do not delay primary PCI for nonessential tests.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• STEMI: immediate reperfusion pathway and admission to monitored cardiac unit.
• NSTEMI/unstable angina: risk-stratified admission and cardiology management.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/ACC ACS Guidelines; ESC ACS Guidelines.

Cardiovascular.title: Acute Heart Failure and Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Acute dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
• Tachypnea, hypoxemia, crackles, increased work of breathing.
• Elevated JVP, peripheral edema, pulmonary congestion.
• Severe: diaphoresis, exhaustion, cyanosis, altered mental status, frothy sputum.
• Precipitants: ACS, arrhythmia, hypertensive emergency, infection, renal dysfunction, medication nonadherence, PE.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, SpO2, BP, mental status. Sit patient upright.
• Continuous ECG and SpO2 monitoring. Give oxygen if hypoxemic.
• Consider early noninvasive ventilation (CPAP/BiPAP) for significant distress.
• Obtain IV access and 12-lead ECG.
• Treat precipitating cause (ACS, arrhythmia, severe hypertension).
• If shock/severe hypotension, avoid routine nitrates.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• ECG and serial troponin if ACS possible. Chest X-ray.
• BNP or NT-proBNP if diagnosis uncertain.
• CBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, liver function, glucose, blood gas.
• Bedside ultrasound/echocardiography.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Oxygen and Noninvasive Ventilation[/color]
• Titrate oxygen to target (commonly 92–96%). CPAP/BiPAP per protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV Loop Diuretic — Furosemide[/color]
• Diuretic-naive: 20–40 mg IV. Already on loop diuretics: initial IV dose often ≥ usual total daily oral dose.
• Monitor urine output, BP, renal function, K+, Mg2+.

[color=#1E3A8A]Nitroglycerin for Hypertensive Pulmonary Edema[/color]
• IV infusion 5–10 mcg/min, titrated rapidly according to BP and symptoms.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Noninvasive ventilation may be unsuitable in severe hemodynamic instability or inability to protect airway. Do not delay intubation in a deteriorating patient.
• Avoid reflexively giving large diuretic doses without reassessment.
• Avoid nitrates in hypotension, suspected RV infarction, recent PDE-5 inhibitor use.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for new acute heart failure, significant pulmonary edema, oxygen requirement, or IV diuretic requirement.
• ICU/high-dependency for NIV failure, severe distress, shock, or significant arrhythmia.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ESC Acute and Chronic Heart Failure Guidelines; AHA/ACC/HFSA Heart Failure Guideline.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Persistent hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg) or need for vasopressors to maintain perfusion.
• Tissue hypoperfusion: confusion, cool extremities, delayed cap refill, oliguria, elevated lactate.
• May occur with acute MI, severe heart failure, myocarditis, acute valvular disease, or mechanical complications.
• Pulmonary congestion may coexist with low systemic perfusion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate critical care and cardiology teams.
• Assess ABCs, perfusion. Continuous ECG and frequent BP monitoring.
• Obtain IV access; prepare vasoactive support.
• Urgent ECG and bedside echocardiography.
• Blood gas, lactate, CBC, electrolytes, renal function, troponin.
• Avoid indiscriminate fluid loading when pulmonary congestion is present.
• Arrange urgent coronary angiography/revascularization if ACS-related.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Norepinephrine — Vasopressor Support[/color]
• Initial infusion: 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min IV, titrated to perfusion and BP (MAP target ~65 mmHg).
• Formula: mL/hour = dose (mcg/kg/min) × weight (kg) × 60 ÷ concentration (mcg/mL).

[color=#1E3A8A]Dobutamine — Low Cardiac Output[/color]
• Starting range: 2–5 mcg/kg/min IV, titrated to cardiac output, perfusion, BP, rhythm.

[color=#1E3A8A]Fluid Strategy[/color]
• Do not give routine large fluid boluses. If preload deficiency, cautious 250 mL isotonic crystalloid challenge followed by immediate reassessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Treatment[/color]
• ACS: urgent revascularization. Arrhythmia: rhythm-specific treatment. Tamponade: specialist intervention.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Extravasation of norepinephrine may cause tissue injury; follow local guidance.
• Do not use blood pressure alone to judge response; assess organ perfusion.
• Dobutamine can cause tachyarrhythmias and hypotension.
• Excess fluid can worsen pulmonary edema.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Cardiogenic shock requires ICU or cardiac intensive care admission.
• Transfer early to a center capable of definitive cardiac intervention.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/ACC ACS and Cardiogenic Shock guidance; ESC ACS Guidelines; SCAI Shock Classification.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• HR typically < 50/min may be clinically significant, but symptoms and perfusion determine urgency.
• Compromise signs: Hypotension, acute altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure, syncope.
• Identify sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, AV block, medication-related bradycardia.
• High-grade AV block may deteriorate rapidly.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, mental status, BP. Continuous ECG and SpO2 monitoring.
• Obtain IV access and 12-lead ECG.
• Identify and treat reversible causes.
• If causing cardiopulmonary compromise: give atropine and prepare for pacing.
• Do not delay transcutaneous pacing in unstable high-grade AV block.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Atropine[/color]
• 1 mg IV bolus, repeated every 3–5 minutes if required. Maximum total dose: 3 mg.

[color=#1E3A8A]Transcutaneous Pacing[/color]
• Apply pads, select pacing mode, increase current until electrical capture, confirm mechanical capture.

[color=#1E3A8A]Epinephrine Infusion[/color]
• ACLS infusion range: 2–10 mcg/min IV, titrated to response.

[color=#1E3A8A]Dopamine Infusion[/color]
• ACLS infusion range: 5–20 mcg/kg/min IV, titrated to response.

[color=#1E3A8A]Treat Reversible Causes[/color]
• Hypoxia, hyperkalemia, medication toxicity, acute coronary ischemia, hypothermia.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Atropine may be ineffective in infranodal high-grade AV block or transplanted heart. Do not delay pacing.
• Electrical capture does not guarantee effective mechanical perfusion.
• Pacing may be painful; provide analgesia/sedation when condition allows.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Unstable symptomatic bradycardia requires emergency resuscitation and monitored admission.
• High-grade AV block, recurrent syncope, or need for pacing requires urgent cardiology assessment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA Adult Bradycardia With a Pulse Algorithm; ESC Cardiac Pacing Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Tachycardia with a pulse (often ≥150/min). Assess for hypotension, shock, altered mental status, ischemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure.
• Classify rhythm:
  - Narrow-complex regular: SVT.
  - Narrow-complex irregular: AF or atrial flutter.
  - Wide-complex regular: VT until proven otherwise.
  - Wide-complex irregular: Polymorphic VT (including torsades) or AF with pre-excitation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and hemodynamic stability. Apply ECG, SpO2, BP monitoring.
• Obtain IV access and 12-lead ECG.
• Treat unstable tachyarrhythmia with immediate electrical therapy.
• For stable patients, identify rhythm before choosing medication.
• Correct reversible causes (hypoxia, electrolytes, ischemia, fever, toxicity).

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Unstable Tachyarrhythmia — Synchronized Cardioversion[/color]
• AF: 200 J biphasic. Atrial flutter: 200 J. Regular narrow-complex: 100 J. Monomorphic VT with pulse: 100 J.
• Escalate energy if unsuccessful. Confirm synchronization markers.

[color=#1E3A8A]Regular Narrow-Complex SVT — Adenosine[/color]
• 1st dose: 6 mg rapid IV push + rapid saline flush. If unsuccessful: 12 mg rapid IV push.

[color=#1E3A8A]Stable Regular Monomorphic Wide-Complex Tachycardia[/color]
• Treat as VT. Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes, followed by infusion if indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]Atrial Fibrillation With Rapid Ventricular Response[/color]
• Selected stable patients: IV diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg IV over 2 minutes, followed by titrated infusion. Beta-blockers are an alternative.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay cardioversion for sedation, ECG printing, or IV access in a critically unstable patient.
• Polymorphic VT cannot be reliably synchronized; treat with unsynchronized high-energy shock.
• Do not use adenosine for irregular wide-complex tachycardia or polymorphic VT.
• Avoid verapamil or diltiazem to an undifferentiated wide-complex tachycardia.
• Avoid IV diltiazem/verapamil in significant systolic dysfunction or pre-excited AF/WPW.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit unstable arrhythmia, sustained VT, syncope, ischemia, heart failure, or significant structural heart disease.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA Adult Tachyarrhythmia With a Pulse Algorithm (2025); ESC AF Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Severe BP elevation with acute target-organ damage. A high BP reading alone does not establish the diagnosis.
• Hypertensive encephalopathy (confusion, seizures, visual disturbance).
• Acute pulmonary edema/heart failure. ACS. Aortic dissection. AKI.
• Intracranial hemorrhage/ischemic stroke. Severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, neurologic status, symptoms.
• Repeat BP using appropriate cuff, consider both arms if aortic pathology suspected.
• Establish IV access, continuous monitoring.
• Identify specific target-organ injury.
• Select titratable IV agent appropriate for the condition.
• Avoid rapid, uncontrolled BP reduction unless condition-specific protocol requires.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]General BP Reduction Strategy[/color]
• Reduce MAP by no more than ~20–25% in first hour, then gradually toward ~160/100–110 mmHg over 2–6 hours.
• Targets vary by diagnosis (aortic dissection, stroke, pregnancy require specific protocols).

[color=#1E3A8A]Nicardipine IV[/color]
• Starting infusion: 5 mg/hour. Increase by 2.5 mg/hour at defined intervals; usual max 15 mg/hour.

[color=#1E3A8A]Labetalol IV[/color]
• 10–20 mg IV over 1–2 minutes, followed by additional doses or titrated infusion.

[color=#1E3A8A]Condition-Specific Management[/color]
• Aortic dissection: IV beta-blockade first. Pulmonary edema: avoid beta-blockade. Stroke/ICH: specific neurocritical protocols.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Excessively rapid BP reduction can cause cerebral, coronary, or renal ischemia.
• Do not treat asymptomatic elevated BP with rapid IV reduction solely to normalize the number.
• Avoid labetalol in severe bradycardia, heart block, cardiogenic shock, or active bronchospasm.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit hypertensive emergencies to ICU or high-dependency care.
• Document target-organ injury, BP target, selected drug, titration plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA Management of Elevated BP in Acute Care (2024); ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Sudden severe chest, back, or abdominal pain (tearing/ripping).
• Syncope, neurologic deficit, limb ischemia, abdominal organ ischemia.
• Pulse deficit or substantial BP difference between arms.
• New aortic regurgitation murmur, hypotension, tamponade, shock.
• Type A involves ascending aorta; Type B does not.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Treat as life-threatening vascular emergency. Activate cardiothoracic/vascular surgery and critical care.
• Monitor ECG and BP; obtain IV access and arterial BP monitoring.
• Provide analgesia. Urgent CT angiography in stable patient.
• Begin anti-impulse therapy to reduce aortic wall stress.
• Avoid anticoagulation/fibrinolysis for presumed ACS until dissection excluded.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Esmolol — Heart Rate Control[/color]
• IV loading dose 500 mcg/kg over 1 minute, followed by infusion starting around 50 mcg/kg/min, titrated to response.
• Target HR 60–80/min. Aim for systolic BP < 120 mmHg (or lowest level maintaining organ perfusion).

[color=#1E3A8A]Alternative IV Beta-Blocker[/color]
• Labetalol may be used according to institutional aortic-dissection protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Additional Vasodilator[/color]
• If BP remains above target after adequate HR control, add IV vasodilator (e.g., nicardipine).

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Treatment[/color]
• Type A: emergency cardiothoracic surgery. Complicated Type B: urgent vascular/endovascular assessment.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not initiate vasodilator therapy before adequate heart-rate control (reflex tachycardia may increase aortic wall stress).
• Avoid esmolol in severe bradycardia, high-grade AV block, cardiogenic shock.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit all suspected/confirmed acute aortic dissection to critical care.
• Transfer immediately to center with aortic intervention capability if needed.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline; ACC Acute Aortic Syndrome Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Cardiac tamponade occurs when pericardial pressure impairs cardiac filling and causes reduced cardiac output.
• Hypotension, tachycardia, dyspnea, raised JVP. Pulsus paradoxus. Muffled heart sounds (not always present).
• Obstructive shock, oliguria, altered consciousness, cardiac arrest.
• Causes: Malignancy, TB/infection, trauma/iatrogenic, aortic dissection, uremia, inflammatory.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, BP, perfusion, oxygenation.
• Obtain urgent bedside echocardiography.
• Activate cardiology/cardiothoracic surgery/emergency procedural team.
• Prepare for urgent pericardial drainage if hemodynamic compromise.
• Use cautious IV fluid administration as a temporary bridge if preload responsive.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Urgent pericardial drainage[/color]
• Hemodynamic instability/shock requires urgent drainage. Echo-guided pericardiocentesis. Surgical drainage for traumatic bleeding, purulent effusion, clotted hemopericardium.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Temporary hemodynamic support[/color]
• Cautious isotonic crystalloid bolus (e.g., 250 mL) if hypotensive and awaiting drainage, then immediate reassessment.
• Fluids are only a temporary bridge, not definitive treatment. Avoid routine diuretics.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Pericardiocentesis is high-risk; do not attempt by untrained operator.
• Do not delay life-saving drainage for CT or nonessential investigations.
• Avoid positive-pressure ventilation when possible in severe tamponade (can reduce venous return and precipitate collapse).

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Emergency admission and definitive drainage.
• ICU or cardiac critical-care monitoring after drainage.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ESC 2025 Guidelines for Myocarditis and Pericarditis; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Irregularly irregular rhythm with absent consistent P waves.
• Rapid ventricular rate, often > 100–110 beats/min.
• Symptoms: Palpitations, dyspnea, chest discomfort, dizziness, fatigue.
• Assess for hemodynamic instability, acute HF, myocardial ischemia, sepsis, PE.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, BP, perfusion, mental status, chest pain. 12-lead ECG and continuous monitoring.
• If hemodynamically unstable: urgent synchronized electrical cardioversion.
• If stable: determine rate vs rhythm control. Identify/treat reversible triggers (infection, hypovolemia, hypoxia, ischemia, electrolytes).
• Assess stroke risk and anticoagulation needs after stabilization.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Unstable AF: Synchronized Cardioversion[/color]
• Indications: Hypotension/shock, ongoing ischemia, acute pulmonary edema, altered consciousness.
• Biphasic energy (e.g., 200 J). Sedation if feasible without delaying.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Stable AF: Diltiazem[/color]
• IV 0.25 mg/kg over 2 mins. Second dose 0.35 mg/kg after 15 mins if needed. Infusion 5–10 mg/hour.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Stable AF: Metoprolol[/color]
• IV 2.5–5 mg over 2 mins. Repeat every 5 mins to max 15 mg.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Alternative rate control[/color]
• Digoxin (selected HF), IV amiodarone (critically ill/decompensated HF).

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Anticoagulation[/color]
• Assess CHA2DS2-VASc. Elective cardioversion requires appropriate anticoagulation or imaging. Emergency cardioversion must NOT be delayed for anticoagulation.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid IV diltiazem in moderate-to-severe LV systolic dysfunction or decompensated heart failure.
• Avoid AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF/WPW.
• Do not combine multiple AV-nodal blockers casually (bradycardia/hypotension risk).

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit instability, acute HF, ischemia, major precipitating illness, or inadequate rate control.
• Discharge only after stability and appropriate plan for anticoagulation and rate/rhythm management.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF Guideline; AHA Tachyarrhythmia Algorithm.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Suspect deterioration in a patient with STEMI/NSTEMI when:
• Persistent/recurrent chest pain despite treatment.
• New hypotension (SBP < 90), cold extremities, oliguria, confusion, rising lactate (cardiogenic shock).
• Acute pulmonary edema, increasing oxygen requirement, respiratory failure.
• Sustained VT, VF, severe bradycardia, high-grade AV block.
• New loud systolic murmur, sudden pulmonary edema, or shock (mechanical complication: papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free-wall rupture).
• Sudden collapse, JVD, PEA (tamponade/rupture).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate emergency response and contact interventional cardiology immediately.
• Assess ABCs, perfusion. Attach continuous ECG monitoring and defibrillator pads. 12-lead ECG immediately.
• Establish 2 IV lines. Bedside echocardiography urgently if shock, new murmur, or unexplained deterioration.
• Check glucose, blood gas, lactate, electrolytes, CBC, renal function, coagulation, serial troponin.
• Arrange emergency coronary angiography/revascularization when indicated.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Recurrent ischemia or cardiogenic shock[/color]
• Aspirin 162–325 mg chewed if not already given. Do not delay emergency revascularization.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Cardiogenic shock[/color]
• Norepinephrine infusion 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min IV, titrated to MAP ≥ 65 mmHg.
• Do not routinely administer large fluid boluses if pulmonary congestion is present.
• Revascularization of culprit vessel is the priority. Mechanical circulatory support decisions require specialist assessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Life-threatening arrhythmias[/color]
• Pulseless VF/pVT: immediate unsynchronized defibrillation.
• Unstable tachyarrhythmia with pulse: synchronized cardioversion.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Mechanical complications[/color]
• Emergency echocardiography. Contact cardiac surgery/interventional cardiology immediately. Consider temporary mechanical circulatory support as bridge.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay emergency revascularization while waiting for serial biomarkers.
• Do not use synchronized cardioversion for VF or pulseless VT.
• Mechanical complications can deteriorate rapidly; medical stabilization alone is not definitive.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to cardiac ICU or equivalent monitored critical-care setting.
• Immediate transfer to PCI-capable center if emergency revascularization/surgery unavailable locally.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: 2025 ACC/AHA ACS Guideline; AHA ACLS Guidelines.

Cardiovascular.title: Acute RV Failure and Obstructive Shock

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute right ventricular (RV) failure occurs when the RV cannot deliver adequate blood through the pulmonary circulation. Obstructive shock may result from massive PE, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax.
• Hypotension, tachycardia, cool extremities, confusion, oliguria.
• Elevated JVP. Clear lungs despite severe hypotension (though varies with cause).
• Bedside echo: RV dilatation/dysfunction, septal flattening, or pericardial effusion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate emergency/critical-care teams. Assess ABCs.
• Give oxygen for hypoxemia and support ventilation if necessary.
• Continuous ECG, SpO2, frequent BP monitoring. Obtain bedside echocardiography ASAP.
• Identify obstructive cause urgently; treat the cause rather than hypotension alone.
• Avoid indiscriminate fluid loading (can worsen RV dilatation and reduce LV filling).

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Fluid management[/color]
• If hypovolemia suspected and no significant RV overdistension: cautious 250 mL IV bolus, reassess immediately.
• Stop fluid loading if RV dilatation, venous congestion, or oxygenation worsens.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Vasopressor support[/color]
• Norepinephrine 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min IV, titrated to adequate systemic pressure and organ perfusion.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Suspected high-risk PE[/color]
• Activate PE response team. Urgent reperfusion (systemic thrombolysis, surgical embolectomy, catheter-based treatment).

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Suspected cardiac tamponade[/color]
• Urgent image-guided pericardial drainage. Small fluid boluses only as temporary bridge.

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Tension pneumothorax[/color]
• Immediate decompression according to local protocol, followed by definitive pleural drainage.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Large empiric fluid boluses can worsen RV failure. Do not assume every hypotensive patient needs more fluid.
• Excessive vasoconstriction can impair peripheral perfusion.
• Diuretics and unnecessary positive-pressure ventilation can worsen preload-dependent tamponade physiology.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to ICU for persistent hypotension, RV failure, vasopressor use, or reperfusion treatment.
• Transfer urgently to a center with required cardiology/interventional/surgical capability.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: 2026 AHA/ACC PE Guideline; ESC/ERS PE Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Infection of endocardial surface, usually heart valve. May cause sepsis, acute valve failure, embolic events, conduction abnormalities.
• Fever + new/changing murmur. Persistent bacteremia/unexplained sepsis.
• Prosthetic valves/intracardiac devices. Previous endocarditis. Injection drug use.
• Embolic stroke, splenic infarction, systemic emboli. New heart failure or conduction abnormalities.

[color=#1E3A8A]Life-Threatening Complications:[/color] Acute severe mitral/aortic regurgitation, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, perivalvular abscess/new AV block, stroke/ICH, persistent bacteremia/septic shock.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess sepsis, hemodynamic status, heart failure, neurological deficits.
• Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible without delaying urgent treatment.
• Urgent echocardiography (TEE when indicated).
• Involve cardiology, infectious disease, microbiology, cardiac surgery early for severe disease.
• Avoid delaying surgery assessment in acute valve failure.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Empiric Antibiotics[/color]
• Choose based on native vs prosthetic valve, community vs healthcare-associated, prior antibiotics, likely pathogens, renal function, local resistance.
• In severe sepsis, administer promptly after cultures.
• Narrow when cultures/susceptibilities available.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Acute Heart Failure / Cardiogenic Shock[/color]
• Oxygen/ventilatory support. Cautious hemodynamic support tailored to valve lesion/shock phenotype.
• Avoid indiscriminate fluid boluses in severe acute valve regurgitation/pulmonary edema.
• Immediate cardiothoracic surgical assessment for acute severe valve dysfunction.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Embolic/Neurological Complications[/color]
• Activate appropriate stroke/neuro pathway. Urgently assess ICH/infectious aneurysm.
• Anticoagulation is NOT routinely initiated solely to prevent septic emboli.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Surgical Assessment[/color]
• Urgent for HF from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection, large vegetations with embolic risk, prosthetic valve/device infection.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• There is no single empiric regimen appropriate for every endocarditis presentation.
• Do not delay life-saving treatment in unstable patients while awaiting cultures.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Suspected IE requires hospital assessment/admission. Shock, acute HF, conduction block, neuro complications, or persistent bacteremia require urgent specialist management/ICU.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the Management of Endocarditis.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Myocarditis is inflammation of the myocardium that may present with chest pain, arrhythmias, heart failure, or cardiogenic shock.
• Chest pain resembling ACS. Dyspnea, fatigue, or new heart failure.
• Palpitations, syncope, or ventricular arrhythmias. Recent viral/systemic illness.
• Elevated troponin with or without ECG changes.

[color=#991B1B]High-Risk Features:[/color] Hypotension/cardiogenic shock, sustained VT/VF, high-grade AV block, rapidly declining ventricular function, severe hypoxemia/pulmonary edema.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, perfusion, mental status. Obtain ECG, cardiac biomarkers, bedside echocardiography.
• Monitor continuously for arrhythmias/conduction abnormalities.
• Treat shock according to hemodynamic phenotype.
• Avoid strenuous physical activity.
• Obtain urgent cardiology/critical care consultation if dysfunction, arrhythmias, or shock.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Hemodynamic Support[/color]
• Treat hypoxemia/respiratory failure. Assess fluid responsiveness carefully; avoid indiscriminate fluid loading.
• Use vasopressors/inotropes for shock. Consider temporary mechanical circulatory support for refractory cardiogenic shock.
• Fulminant myocarditis can be reversible; early escalation to an advanced cardiac center may be lifesaving.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Arrhythmias and Conduction Disease[/color]
• Treat unstable tachyarrhythmias per ACLS. Correct K+/Mg2+. Manage high-grade heart block with pacing as indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Disease-Specific Treatment[/color]
• Standard HF treatment when tolerated. Avoid routine immunosuppression for presumed viral myocarditis without specific indication.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• A normal initial echocardiogram does not exclude myocarditis.
• Avoid indiscriminate fluid loading in ventricular dysfunction.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with suspected clinically significant myocarditis for cardiac assessment.
• ICU for shock, sustained ventricular arrhythmias, high-grade heart block, or rapidly deteriorating ventricular function.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: 2025 ESC Guidelines for the Management of Myocarditis and Pericarditis.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute limb ischemia is a sudden reduction in arterial perfusion that threatens limb viability. Causes: embolism, thrombosis, graft occlusion, trauma.
• The Six Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia (cold limb).
• Viable limb: no sensory/motor deficit. Threatened limb: sensory loss and weakness. Irreversible: profound anesthesia, paralysis, absent arterial and venous Doppler signals.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Obtain immediate vascular surgery consultation.
• Document symptom onset and last known normal limb function.
• Examine both limbs and compare temperature, color, sensation, motor power, pulses.
• Use handheld Doppler if available. Establish IV access, provide analgesia, keep NPO.
• Begin IV unfractionated heparin promptly unless contraindicated, per protocol.
• Do not delay vascular intervention for imaging when limb is immediately threatened.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Anticoagulation[/color]
• Unfractionated heparin: Use institutional weight-based IV bolus and infusion protocol. Monitor aPTT/anti-Xa. Avoid in active major bleeding.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Pain Management[/color]
• Titrated IV analgesia according to severity and hemodynamic status.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Revascularization[/color]
• Options: Catheter-directed thrombolysis, surgical embolectomy/thrombectomy, endovascular thrombectomy/angioplasty, bypass surgery, amputation if irreversibly ischemic.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Reperfusion Injury[/color]
• After restoration: monitor for hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis/AKI, compartment syndrome, arrhythmias, hemodynamic instability.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Heparin prevents thrombus propagation but does not independently restore adequate blood flow.
• Thrombolysis is inappropriate in several bleeding-risk situations.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Immediate vascular admission. Threatened limb requires emergency intervention; irreversible ischemia requires urgent specialist assessment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ESVS Acute Limb Ischaemia Guidelines (2020); SVS guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, unexplained hypoxemia.
• Syncope, hypotension, shock, or cardiac arrest (high-risk PE).
• Hemoptysis may occur but is not required.
• Risk factors: recent surgery, immobilization, previous VTE, active cancer, pregnancy/postpartum, estrogen, thrombophilia.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, oxygenation, hemodynamic stability. Give oxygen for hypoxemia.
• Obtain ECG (cannot exclude PE). Use validated clinical probability pathway (Wells).
• Stable: arrange D-dimer or imaging according to pretest probability.
• Unstable: bedside echo and urgent specialist decisions if CT unsafe.
• Begin anticoagulation when PE is sufficiently likely and bleeding risk acceptable.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Anticoagulation — Enoxaparin[/color]
• 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours (adjust for renal impairment).

[color=#1E3A8A]Unfractionated Heparin[/color]
• IV bolus followed by weight-based infusion per institutional nomogram. Preferred if rapid titration/reversal or urgent procedures anticipated.

[color=#1E3A8A]Systemic Thrombolysis for High-Risk PE[/color]
• Persistent hypotension or cardiopulmonary failure with acceptable bleeding risk.
• Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours (subject to protocol).

[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive Care[/color]
• Oxygen, cautious fluids (excessive worsens RV failure), vasopressors if shock.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Check for active bleeding, recent major surgery, severe thrombocytopenia, history of HIT.
• Review thrombolysis contraindications carefully (previous ICH, active major bleeding, recent major surgery).
• Do not use an unverified heparin infusion rate.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Shock, persistent hypotension, severe hypoxemia, or RV failure requires ICU-level care.
• RV dysfunction, elevated biomarkers, or increased severity require admission and close observation.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/ACC 2026 PE Guideline; ESC PE Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Severe dyspnea, wheeze, chest tightness, cough.
• Inability to speak full sentences, accessory muscle use, tachypnea, tachycardia.
• PEF markedly reduced from predicted/personal best.
• Life-threatening: exhaustion, confusion, cyanosis, silent chest, poor respiratory effort, hypotension, normal/rising PaCO2.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, mental status, SpO2. Give controlled oxygen (target 93–95%).
• Start repeated inhaled SABA therapy promptly. Add inhaled ipratropium for severe.
• Give systemic corticosteroids early.
• Reassess work of breathing, speech, oxygenation, PEF.
• Consider IV magnesium sulfate for selected severe cases.
• Call ICU/anesthesia early for exhaustion, altered consciousness, silent chest, or poor response.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Salbutamol (Albuterol)[/color]
• Nebulized: 2.5–5 mg repeated every 20 minutes during first hour, then titrated.
• MDI with spacer: 4–10 puffs every 20 minutes during first hour.

[color=#1E3A8A]Ipratropium Bromide[/color]
• 0.5 mg nebulized every 20 minutes for first 3 doses alongside salbutamol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Systemic Corticosteroid[/color]
• Prednisolone 40–50 mg orally once daily for 5–7 days. IV corticosteroid if oral not possible.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV Magnesium Sulfate[/color]
• 2 g IV over ~20 minutes when severe symptoms persist despite initial intensive therapy.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Tachycardia, tremor, hypokalemia, lactic acidosis can occur with intensive SABA.
• Worsening fatigue or reduced air entry is not reassuring even if wheeze becomes quieter.
• Noninvasive ventilation is not a substitute for timely intubation in a tiring/confused patient.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for persistent severe symptoms, poor response, hypoxemia, or life-threatening features.
• ICU for respiratory failure, altered consciousness, or need for ventilatory support.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: GINA 2025 Strategy Report; AHA Adult Emergency Cardiovascular Care Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Acute worsening of dyspnea, cough, sputum volume, or sputum purulence.
• Increased respiratory rate and work of breathing. Wheezing, reduced air entry.
• Hypoxemia; severe cases may present with confusion, exhaustion, cyanosis.
• Hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis may develop.
• Consider alternative/additional diagnoses: pneumonia, PE, pneumothorax, acute heart failure, ACS.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, mental status, respiratory effort. Position upright.
• Give controlled oxygen, generally targeting SpO2 88–92% while assessing blood gases.
• Start inhaled SABA. Add ipratropium for significant exacerbations.
• Administer systemic corticosteroids early.
• Obtain blood gas in severe illness or suspected hypercapnia.
• Consider antibiotics if bacterial infection likely (increased sputum purulence/volume).
• Consider NIV for persistent hypercapnic respiratory acidosis despite initial therapy.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Pulse oximetry and repeated respiratory assessment. Arterial or venous blood gas.
• Chest X-ray to assess pneumonia, pneumothorax, edema.
• ECG and troponin if ischemia or arrhythmia suspected.
• CBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, glucose. Sputum culture in selected cases.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Salbutamol[/color]
• Nebulized: 2.5–5 mg, repeated every 20 minutes during first hour, then titrate.

[color=#1E3A8A]Ipratropium[/color]
• 0.5 mg nebulized, repeated according to local protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Systemic Corticosteroid[/color]
• Prednisolone 40 mg orally once daily for 5 days. IV if oral not possible.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics (If Indicated)[/color]
• Increased sputum purulence with volume/dyspnea. Common option: Doxycycline 200 mg day 1, then 100 mg daily. Amoxicillin/clavulanate alternative.

[color=#1E3A8A]Noninvasive Ventilation (NIV)[/color]
• Persistent hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH ≤7.35 with elevated PaCO2) despite initial treatment.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Worsening exhaustion or decreasing air entry may indicate respiratory failure rather than improvement.
• Reassess if symptoms persist; corticosteroids do not replace bronchodilation, antibiotics, or ventilatory support.
• NIV must not delay intubation when respiratory failure is worsening.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for persistent hypoxemia, hypercapnia/acidosis, poor response, or need for NIV.
• ICU assessment for deteriorating consciousness, severe acidosis, shock, or NIV failure.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: GOLD 2026 Report; British Thoracic Society Emergency Oxygen Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: Significant hypoxemia despite room air/supplemental oxygen. (Pneumonia, edema, ARDS, PE, asthma).
• Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure: Elevated PaCO2 with respiratory acidosis. (COPD, severe asthma with fatigue, neuromuscular weakness, opioid toxicity).
• Danger Signs: Exhaustion, confusion, reduced consciousness, cyanosis, weak respiratory effort, silent chest, hemodynamic instability.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for senior emergency, respiratory, and critical care support.
• Assess airway, respiratory effort, circulation, mental status. Clear secretions.
• Administer oxygen and titrate to appropriate target.
• Use high-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) or NIV in selected patients.
• Prepare for intubation if airway protection, oxygenation, or ventilation is failing.
• Treat the underlying cause without delay.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Oxygen Therapy[/color]
• Most acutely ill adults: target SpO2 94–98%.
• At risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (e.g., COPD): target SpO2 88–92% pending blood gas results.

[color=#1E3A8A]High-Flow Nasal Oxygen (HFNO)[/color]
• Flow and FiO2 titrated according to distress, oxygenation, tolerance. Flows up to ~60 L/min.

[color=#1E3A8A]Noninvasive Ventilation[/color]
• Particularly useful for COPD-related hypercapnic acidosis and acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

[color=#1E3A8A]Endotracheal Intubation and Invasive Ventilation[/color]
• Inability to protect airway, refractory hypoxemia/hypercapnia, severe exhaustion, apnea, or impending arrest.
• Use lung-protective ventilation when indicated (especially ARDS).

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not withhold oxygen from a severely hypoxemic patient because of concern about CO2 retention; provide controlled oxygen and monitor.
• Avoid unnecessary hyperoxia.
• Do not allow a trial of HFNO/NIV to delay intubation in a deteriorating patient.
• Intubation can precipitate hypotension or cardiac arrest in critically ill patients.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Acute respiratory failure generally requires hospital admission.
• ICU admission for invasive ventilation, worsening gas exchange, shock, severe acidosis, or rapidly deteriorating mental status.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: British Thoracic Society; GOLD 2026; ARDS Network.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Pneumothorax[/color]
• Sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Reduced breath sounds and chest expansion. Hyperresonance.

[color=#1E3A8A]Tension Pneumothorax[/color]
• Severe respiratory distress, rapidly worsening hypoxemia.
• Hypotension, tachycardia, obstructive shock, peri-arrest.
• Positive-pressure ventilation may precipitate or worsen tension.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, hemodynamic stability. Provide oxygen.
• If tension pneumothorax is strongly suspected in an unstable patient, decompress immediately without waiting for imaging.
• Prepare for definitive pleural drainage after emergency decompression.
• In a stable patient, confirm diagnosis with lung ultrasound or chest imaging.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Emergency Decompression for Tension[/color]
• Needle/catheter decompression at an approved site (e.g., 2nd ICS mid-clavicular or 5th ICS anterior axillary) or finger thoracostomy in trained hands.

[color=#1E3A8A]Chest Drainage[/color]
• Persistent/large pneumothorax, secondary spontaneous, traumatic, or associated with mechanical ventilation.
• Confirm drain function, monitor for persistent air leak, bleeding, infection.

[color=#1E3A8A]Stable Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax[/color]
• Conservative management, needle aspiration, or ambulatory management in selected minimally symptomatic patients.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Needle decompression may fail due to inadequate catheter length, kinking, or incorrect placement.
• Do not clamp a bubbling chest drain routinely unless directed by a specific specialist protocol.
• A small pneumothorax can be clinically important in a patient with underlying lung disease.
• Tension physiology is a clinical emergency and must not be managed by observation alone.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Tension pneumothorax requires immediate decompression and hospital-level care.
• Admit for significant symptoms, secondary pneumothorax, trauma, persistent air leak, or need for drainage.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Sudden onset of airway, breathing, or circulatory compromise after allergen exposure.
• Urticaria, flushing, angioedema (may be absent).
• Wheeze, stridor, throat tightness, hoarseness, difficulty swallowing.
• Hypotension, collapse, syncope, shock. GI symptoms (cramps/vomiting).
• Triggers: foods, medications, insect stings, latex.
• [color=#991B1B]Do not delay epinephrine while waiting for rash or tests.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for emergency resuscitation support. Stop exposure.
• Lay flat with legs elevated (position of comfort if severe respiratory distress). Do not allow standing/walking suddenly.
• Give IM epinephrine immediately.
• Provide oxygen, monitoring, IV access. Give isotonic crystalloid for hypotension/shock.
• Prepare for early airway intervention if progressive edema.
• Repeat IM epinephrine if symptoms persist (every 5–15 minutes).

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Epinephrine (Adrenaline) — First-Line[/color]
• 0.5 mg IM for an adult using 1 mg/mL solution (0.5 mL). Inject mid-anterolateral thigh.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV Crystalloid[/color]
• Initial 500–1,000 mL isotonic crystalloid bolus for significant hypotension, reassess and repeat.

[color=#1E3A8A]Bronchodilator[/color]
• Nebulized salbutamol 2.5–5 mg for persistent wheeze (adjunct after epinephrine).

[color=#1E3A8A]Adjuncts[/color]
• Antihistamines: Only for persistent skin symptoms after stabilization.
• Corticosteroids: Not routine first-line; delayed onset; do not delay epinephrine.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not use IV epinephrine bolus as routine initial treatment for anaphylaxis.
• Salbutamol does not treat upper-airway edema or shock and must never replace epinephrine.
• Antihistamines do not treat airway obstruction or hypotension.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Observe after stabilization according to severity and risk of biphasic reaction.
• Admit for severe reactions, recurrent symptoms, airway involvement, or need for repeated epinephrine.
• Provide epinephrine auto-injector, action plan, and allergy follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: World Allergy Organization; AAAAI/ACAAI; Resuscitation Council UK.

Respiratory.title: Acute Severe Asthma and Near-Fatal Asthma

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Severe: Marked breathlessness, inability to complete sentences, RR >30, tachycardia, accessory muscle use. PEF substantially reduced.
• Life-threatening: Silent chest, exhaustion, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, confusion, reduced consciousness, hypotension, bradycardia.
• Normal/rising PaCO2 in severe distress indicates impending respiratory failure.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and call for senior emergency/critical-care support. Sit upright.
• Controlled oxygen (target 93–95%).
• Start repeated inhaled bronchodilator therapy immediately.
• Add inhaled ipratropium for severe exacerbations.
• Give systemic corticosteroids early.
• Consider IV magnesium sulfate for severe disease with inadequate response.
• Arrange early airway support if deterioration/exhaustion.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Salbutamol[/color]
• 2.5–5 mg nebulized, repeated every 20 mins during first hour. Continuous nebulization in selected severe cases.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Ipratropium[/color]
• 0.5 mg nebulized every 20 mins for up to 3 doses in first hour.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Systemic Corticosteroids[/color]
• Prednisolone 40–50 mg orally daily for 5–7 days. IV if oral impossible.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. IV Magnesium Sulfate[/color]
• 2 g IV over ~20 mins in selected severe exacerbations with poor response.

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Near-fatal asthma[/color]
• Involve experienced airway/critical-care team early. NIV should not delay intubation. Intubation for exhaustion, worsening consciousness, refractory hypoxemia.
• Ventilator settings designed to minimize dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• High-dose beta2-agonists can cause tachycardia, hypokalemia, and lactic acidosis.
• Persistent tachypnea may reflect lactic acidosis or fatigue rather than bronchospasm.
• Positive-pressure ventilation can precipitate hypotension and barotrauma.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit life-threatening features, persistent severe symptoms, poor response, or significant comorbidity.
• ICU for respiratory failure, ventilatory support, altered consciousness, or impending arrest.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: GINA 2026 Strategy Report; Local emergency asthma protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Life-threatening hemoptysis is bleeding into the respiratory tract that threatens airway patency, gas exchange, or circulation.
• Inability to clear blood/clots from airway. Hypoxemia, respiratory distress, rapidly increasing O2 requirement.
• Hemodynamic instability. Large or recurrent episodes of fresh blood. Reduced consciousness.
• Causes: Bronchiectasis, TB, malignancy, pulmonary infection, fungal disease, PE, vascular abnormalities.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate emergency, anesthesia/airway, respiratory, and interventional radiology teams early.
• Assess ABCs. Provide oxygen and suction blood/clots.
• If bleeding side known, position bleeding lung dependent to reduce contamination of unaffected lung.
• Establish large-bore IV access; send CBC, coagulation, renal function, crossmatch.
• Review/reverse anticoagulants. Prepare for urgent airway protection if unable to maintain oxygenation/airway clearance.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Airway and respiratory support[/color]
• Oxygen titrated to needs. Prepare suction, airway equipment, large-bore ETT.
• Intubation with experienced airway clinician (plan for blood/clot obstruction). Bronchoscopy for clot removal/localization.
• Danger is airway flooding and asphyxiation rather than exsanguination alone.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Tranexamic acid (selected cases)[/color]
• Nebulized TXA (e.g., 500 mg TID) has been used in selected non-massive/persistent hemoptysis. Do not substitute for airway management/definitive control.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Definitive control[/color]
• Bronchial artery embolization (BAE) is key definitive treatment for life-threatening/recurrent hemoptysis after stabilization and CT angiography.
• Surgical management if embolization fails or underlying lesion requires surgery.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• The major immediate danger is often airway flooding and asphyxiation.
• Avoid unnecessary delays for diagnostic imaging when airway protection is urgently required.
• BAE requires careful identification of vessels supplying spinal cord, brain, or heart to avoid catastrophic non-target embolization.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Life-threatening hemoptysis requires admission to ICU or equivalent critical-care setting.
• Arrange urgent transfer to facility with airway expertise, bronchoscopy, CT angiography, and IR if unavailable locally.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: CIRSE Standards of Practice; Society of Chest Imaging and Interventions Consensus Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is a potentially fatal complication of sickle cell disease, characterized by a new pulmonary infiltrate + fever and/or respiratory symptoms.
• Chest pain, cough, fever, dyspnea. Hypoxemia/increasing O2 requirement.
• Tachypnea, increased work of breathing. Falling hemoglobin or rapidly worsening respiratory status.
• Mechanisms: infection, pulmonary vaso-occlusion, fat embolism, hypoventilation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Admit, assess respiratory distress and oxygenation.
• Give supplemental oxygen if hypoxemic. Obtain chest radiography, CBC with reticulocytes.
• Assess for pneumonia, PE, other causes of deterioration.
• Provide prompt analgesia while avoiding excessive sedation.
• Involve hematology/critical care early for progressive hypoxemia/severe disease.
• Encourage incentive spirometry in appropriate patients.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Oxygen/Respiratory Support[/color]
• Correct hypoxemia. Escalate to high-flow O2, NIV, or invasive ventilation if indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Antibiotics[/color]
• Empiric regimen covering typical/atypical respiratory pathogens per local guidelines.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Analgesia/Pulmonary Care[/color]
• Appropriate analgesia (opioids if needed) with careful respiratory monitoring.
• Avoid excessive sedation/hypoventilation. Incentive spirometry, mobilization.
• Cautious fluid management (avoid dehydration but prevent fluid overload).

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Red Cell Transfusion[/color]
• Simple transfusion: clinically significant anemia or worsening oxygenation.
• Exchange transfusion: urgently for severe/rapidly progressive ACS, increasing O2 requirement, multilobar disease.
• Discuss with hematology/transfusion service. Avoid excessive post-transfusion hemoglobin elevation (hyperviscosity risk).

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• All suspected ACS cases require hospital admission.
• Transfusion decisions depend on severity and baseline hemoglobin; do not use a single threshold in isolation.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • ICU care for progressive hypoxemia, increasing respiratory support, hemodynamic instability, or other organ failure.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ASH transfusion guidelines; BSH guidance; CDC ACS in SCD.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Angioedema is sudden swelling of the deeper skin or mucosa. It may be histamine-mediated or bradykinin-mediated.
• Triggers: ACE inhibitors, foods, insect stings, medications, hereditary/acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency.

[color=#991B1B]Features Suggesting Airway Threat:[/color]
• Tongue, floor-of-mouth, or pharyngeal swelling.
• Hoarse voice, voice change. Stridor, drooling, difficulty swallowing secretions.
• Progressive swelling or respiratory distress.
• Swelling of tongue/larynx can threaten airway even without urticaria or hypotension.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call airway, anesthesia, and critical care teams early.
• Assess voice, tongue, oropharynx, respiratory effort, ability to handle secretions.
• Prepare for early definitive airway management if swelling is progressing.
• Give IM epinephrine immediately if anaphylaxis or histamine-mediated airway involvement is suspected.
• Stop a suspected causative medication (especially ACE inhibitor).
• Establish IV access and continuously monitor SpO2, ECG, BP.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical.
• Flexible nasolaryngoscopy by experienced clinician may help assess laryngeal involvement if stable.
• C4 and C1-inhibitor concentration/function may help investigate hereditary/acquired angioedema after stabilization.
• Serum tryptase may support suspected anaphylaxis, but treatment must not wait for result.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Suspected Histamine-Mediated Angioedema/Anaphylaxis[/color]
• Epinephrine: 0.3–0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL preparation) into mid-anterolateral thigh. Repeat every 5–15 minutes if symptoms persist.
• Provide oxygen and IV isotonic crystalloid if indicated.
• Do NOT delay IM epinephrine for antihistamines or corticosteroids.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Suspected Bradykinin-Mediated Angioedema[/color]
• Features: No urticaria/itching, ACE-inhibitor exposure, recurrent episodes, poor response to allergy meds.
• Prioritize airway protection. Stop ACE inhibitor permanently when implicated.
• For hereditary angioedema: C1-inhibitor concentrate or icatibant according to availability/protocol.
• Epinephrine, antihistamines, and corticosteroids may be ineffective in bradykinin-mediated angioedema.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• If mechanism is uncertain and anaphylaxis remains plausible, treat anaphylaxis while managing the airway.
• IV epinephrine boluses are not routine treatment for anaphylaxis.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit to ICU or closely monitored setting for laryngeal involvement, progressive tongue swelling, respiratory compromise, or airway intervention.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: World Allergy Organization; International Hereditary Angioedema Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute epiglottitis is a potentially fatal infection and inflammation of the epiglottis and adjacent supraglottic structures. Can rapidly cause complete upper-airway obstruction.
• Severe sore throat and painful swallowing. Drooling or inability to swallow saliva.
• Muffled voice. Fever and toxic appearance. Inspiratory stridor or respiratory distress.
• Tripod positioning and reluctance to lie flat.
• [color=#991B1B]Symptoms may be severe despite a relatively normal-looking oral cavity. Stridor can be a late sign of critical obstruction.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway patency, breathing, oxygenation, mental status.
• Call anesthesia, ENT, and critical care teams immediately if airway compromise suspected.
• Keep patient calm and in preferred position. Provide supplemental oxygen if tolerated.
• Keep patient nil by mouth.
• Prepare for controlled airway management in operating room or equivalent high-acuity setting.
• Do NOT force patient to lie down or perform unnecessary throat examinations.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Airway Protection[/color]
• Early expert airway management for progressive respiratory distress, stridor, hypoxemia, exhaustion, or inability to handle secretions.
• Difficult-airway strategy and immediate surgical-airway backup. Avoid repeated intubation attempts.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Antibiotics[/color]
• Ceftriaxone: Adults 2 g IV every 24 hours (commonly used for severe bacterial epiglottitis). Pediatric dosing weight-based.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Supportive Care[/color]
• IV fluids when oral intake unsafe/inadequate. Analgesia and antipyretics. Monitor SpO2, respiratory effort, fatigue continuously.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Sedation or airway manipulation without an appropriate rescue plan may precipitate complete obstruction.
• Do not delay airway protection for imaging or routine laboratory tests.
• Antibiotics do not replace airway management.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit for specialist assessment and monitored treatment. Airway compromise requires ICU or equivalent critical care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: IDSA Guidance; Local ENT/Airway protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Hematemesis, coffee-ground vomitus, melena, or occasionally hematochezia.
• Tachycardia, hypotension, syncope, pallor, confusion, shock.
• Common causes: Peptic ulcer disease, erosive gastritis, esophagitis, varices, Mallory–Weiss tears.
• Risk factors: NSAIDs, anticoagulants, previous ulcer, liver disease, heavy alcohol use.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs; protect airway if massive hematemesis.
• Obtain two large-bore IV lines. Send CBC, urea/creatinine, electrolytes, liver tests, coagulation, type & crossmatch.
• Resuscitate shock with crystalloid while arranging blood products.
• Stop/review anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents.
• Contact gastroenterology/endoscopy and critical care early.
• Arrange endoscopy after initial stabilization (generally within 24 hours).

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Resuscitation and blood transfusion[/color]
• Restrictive red-cell transfusion threshold (~7 g/dL) in many hospitalized patients; individualize in massive bleeding or myocardial ischemia.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Suspected non-variceal bleeding[/color]
• IV pantoprazole: 80 mg IV loading dose followed by 8 mg/hour infusion for high-risk ulcer bleeding after endoscopic hemostasis.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Suspected variceal bleeding[/color]
• Octreotide: 50 mcg IV bolus, followed by 50 mcg/hour continuous IV infusion (for 2–5 days).
• Antibiotic prophylaxis: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours (often for up to 7 days).

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Erythromycin before endoscopy[/color]
• 250 mg IV ~30–120 mins before endoscopy in selected patients with severe bleeding to improve gastric visualization.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay resuscitation in a patient with shock while waiting for hemoglobin.
• PPI treatment does not replace resuscitation or endoscopic control of active bleeding.
• Use erythromycin cautiously in patients with significant QT prolongation.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU or high-dependency for shock, ongoing major hemorrhage, airway compromise, or severe comorbidity.
• Very-low-risk patients (e.g., Glasgow-Blatchford Score 0–1) may be suitable for outpatient management.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACG Upper GI Bleeding Guideline; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Diagnosis requires at least 2 of 3:
• Characteristic acute, persistent epigastric pain radiating to back.
• Serum lipase/amylase ≥ 3 times upper limit of normal.
• Imaging findings consistent with acute pancreatitis.

• Common causes: Gallstones, alcohol, hypertriglyceridemia.
• Severe features: Persistent organ failure, hypotension, hypoxemia, AKI, altered consciousness.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, hemodynamics, pain, oxygenation, urine output.
• Establish IV access and obtain blood tests.
• Provide analgesia and antiemetics.
• Start isotonic crystalloid resuscitation when needed.
• Identify and treat cause (biliary obstruction, cholangitis, hypertriglyceridemia).

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IV fluids[/color]
• Moderately aggressive, individualized isotonic crystalloid. Initial approach: 1–1.5 mL/kg/hour, with a 10 mL/kg bolus if hypovolemic, followed by reassessment. Lactated Ringer's commonly preferred.
• Avoid indiscriminate large-volume fluid administration (fluid overload worsens outcomes).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Analgesia[/color]
• Opioid or non-opioid according to severity. Adjust for renal impairment.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Nutrition[/color]
• Start oral feeding early as tolerated in mild cases. Enteral nutrition preferred if oral not possible.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Antibiotics and biliary intervention[/color]
• Do NOT give prophylactic antibiotics for sterile acute pancreatitis or sterile necrosis.
• Urgent ERCP for pancreatitis complicated by cholangitis.
• Cholecystectomy during same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid indiscriminate large-volume fluid administration.
• NSAIDs may be unsuitable in AKI, dehydration, or GI bleeding.
• Do not keep every patient fasting until enzymes normalize.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for significant pain, dehydration, persistent vomiting, organ dysfunction, or diagnostic uncertainty.
• ICU for shock, respiratory failure, persistent organ failure, or severe metabolic complications.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACG Guidelines: Management of Acute Pancreatitis (2024); Local protocols.

Gastrointestinal.title: Acute Liver Failure and Hepatic Encephalopathy

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute liver failure (ALF) is acute liver injury with coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing cirrhosis.
• Jaundice, nausea, vomiting, RUQ discomfort.
• Confusion, agitation, drowsiness, coma.
• Hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, coagulopathy, AKI, cerebral edema.
• Causes: Paracetamol toxicity, viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, autoimmune hepatitis, ischemic hepatitis, Wilson disease, pregnancy-related.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, GCS, bedside glucose, oxygenation, hemodynamic status.
• Check INR, liver enzymes, bilirubin, renal function, electrolytes, blood gas, glucose urgently.
• Identify all medications and toxic exposures (especially paracetamol).
• Start N-acetylcysteine promptly when paracetamol toxicity possible; consider in early-stage non-paracetamol ALF under specialist guidance.
• Contact a liver-transplant center urgently. Do not wait for advanced encephalopathy.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) for suspected paracetamol toxicity[/color]
• 150 mg/kg IV over 1 hour.
• 50 mg/kg IV over 4 hours.
• 100 mg/kg IV over 16 hours.
• Do not automatically stop NAC at 21 hours if persistent liver injury.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Hypoglycemia[/color]
• IV glucose if hypoglycemic. Consider continuous glucose infusion if recurrent.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Hepatic encephalopathy and cerebral edema[/color]
• Elevate head ~30 degrees. Maintain oxygenation, avoid hypotension, fever, severe hypercapnia.
• Consider early airway protection. Hypertonic saline or mannitol for suspected intracranial hypertension under specialist protocol.
• Lactulose is not a substitute for specialist management of cerebral edema in ALF.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Coagulopathy[/color]
• Monitor INR. Use blood products for clinically significant bleeding or procedure-specific indications. INR elevation alone does not necessarily mean prophylactic plasma is beneficial.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not automatically stop NAC at 21 hours if persistent liver injury.
• Hypoglycemia may recur because hepatic glycogen stores are impaired.
• Unnecessary plasma may cause fluid overload and obscure progression of liver failure.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent admission and early transfer discussion with a liver-transplant center.
• ICU for encephalopathy, hypoglycemia, shock, severe acidosis, AKI, or organ failure.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AASLD Management of Acute Liver Failure; Local protocols.

Gastrointestinal.title: Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding and Variceal Hemorrhage

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) originates proximal to the ligament of Treitz.
• Hematemesis or coffee-ground vomitus. Melena; occasionally hematochezia with massive upper GI bleeding.
• Tachycardia, hypotension, syncope, pallor, or shock.
• History of peptic ulcer disease, NSAID use, anticoagulation, cirrhosis, or portal hypertension.
• Non-variceal bleeding: peptic ulcer, erosive gastritis, esophagitis, or Mallory–Weiss tear.
• Variceal bleeding: esophageal or gastric varices in portal hypertension.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and activate major hemorrhage protocol if bleeding is severe.
• Consider early airway protection if ongoing massive hematemesis or impaired consciousness.
• Insert two large-bore IV cannulas.
• Send CBC, urea, creatinine, electrolytes, liver tests, coagulation profile, and group-and-crossmatch.
• Resuscitate with blood products and appropriate IV fluids.
• Review anticoagulants/antiplatelet agents; plan reversal when indicated.
• Contact gastroenterology/endoscopy urgently.
• If variceal bleeding is suspected, start vasoactive medication and antibiotic prophylaxis promptly.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Resuscitation and blood transfusion[/color]
• Initial 250–500 mL IV crystalloid bolus if hypotensive while arranging blood.
• Restrictive transfusion threshold around Hb 7 g/dL in hospitalized UGIB (individualize in shock/ischemia).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Suspected non-variceal ulcer bleeding[/color]
• Pantoprazole 80 mg IV loading dose followed by 8 mg/hour IV infusion for 72 hours after endoscopic hemostasis of high-risk ulcer.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Suspected variceal hemorrhage[/color]
• Octreotide: 50 mcg IV bolus, followed by continuous infusion at 25–50 mcg/hour for 2–5 days.
• Ceftriaxone: 1 g IV every 24 hours for up to 5–7 days.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Endoscopy[/color]
• Generally within 24 hours for hospitalized UGIB; suspected acute variceal bleeding generally requires endoscopy within 12 hours.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not wait for Hb to fall before treating hemorrhagic shock.
• Avoid over-transfusion in portal hypertensive bleeding (increases portal pressure).
• Do not use epinephrine injection alone as definitive endoscopic treatment for a bleeding ulcer.
• Vasoactive therapy is a bridge to definitive endoscopic treatment.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU for shock, ongoing massive bleeding, airway compromise, or severe organ dysfunction.
• Low-risk discharge only after formal risk assessment (Glasgow-Blatchford Score 0–1) and reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACG Upper GI Bleeding Guideline; Baveno VII; AASLD guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Diagnosis requires at least 2 of 3:
• Characteristic acute upper abdominal pain radiating to back.
• Serum lipase/amylase ≥ 3 times upper limit of normal.
• Imaging findings consistent with acute pancreatitis.
• Assess for persistent vomiting, dehydration, tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxemia, AKI, altered mental status.
• Severe pancreatitis = persistent organ failure lasting > 48 hours.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, hemodynamic stability, oxygenation, pain.
• Establish IV access. Obtain lipase, CBC, electrolytes, renal function, liver tests, glucose, calcium, triglycerides.
• Perform transabdominal ultrasound for gallstones/biliary dilation.
• Begin moderately aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with frequent reassessment.
• Provide analgesia and antiemetics.
• Do not routinely prescribe prophylactic antibiotics for uncomplicated pancreatitis.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IV fluids[/color]
• Lactated Ringer's: ~1.5 mL/kg/hour, adjusted to volume status.
• If hypovolemic, consider 10 mL/kg bolus over 1–2 hours, then reassess.
• Avoid overly aggressive fluid administration (worsens respiratory failure).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Analgesia[/color]
• IV opioid titrated to severity (e.g., morphine 2–4 mg IV).

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Nutrition and cause-specific treatment[/color]
• Oral feeding early as tolerated (low-fat solid diet). Enteral nutrition if oral not possible.
• Urgent biliary drainage (ERCP) if cholangitis.
• Cholecystectomy during same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis.
• Do not routinely perform early ERCP without cholangitis/obstruction.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid overly aggressive fluid administration in cardiac/renal impairment.
• Analgesia should not delay evaluation of shock or other causes of abdominal pain.
• Antibiotics not indicated for sterile pancreatic necrosis.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU for persistent organ failure, shock, respiratory failure, or severe metabolic abnormalities.
• Monitor closely during first 48 hours because severity can evolve.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACG Guidelines: Management of Acute Pancreatitis (2024).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute cholangitis is an infection of the biliary tree, commonly caused by obstruction of the common bile duct.
• Fever or rigors. RUQ or epigastric pain. Jaundice.
• Severe disease: hypotension, confusion, renal dysfunction, organ failure.
• Classic triad (fever, pain, jaundice) is not always present. Suspect in biliary obstruction + sepsis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and identify septic shock or organ dysfunction.
• Obtain IV access, blood cultures, CBC, liver tests, renal function, electrolytes, lactate, coagulation.
• Start appropriate IV antibiotics promptly. Give IV fluids according to perfusion.
• Arrange urgent gastroenterology and surgical consultation.
• Organize biliary drainage, usually by ERCP, according to severity.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Antibiotics[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours (for selected community-acquired cases).
• Broader therapy for severe sepsis/resistant organisms.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Sepsis resuscitation[/color]
• For sepsis-induced hypoperfusion: up to 30 mL/kg IV within first 3 hours, with frequent reassessment.
• Norepinephrine if hypotension persists despite fluids.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Biliary decompression[/color]
• ERCP with biliary drainage is generally preferred. Severe cholangitis with shock requires urgent drainage after initial stabilization.
• Percutaneous or surgical drainage if ERCP unavailable/unsuccessful.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Antibiotics alone may not control infection when biliary obstruction persists.
• Do not delay source control while repeatedly administering fluids to a patient who remains in shock.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU for septic shock, altered consciousness, respiratory failure, or other organ dysfunction.
• Admit all suspected acute cholangitis for IV treatment and assessment for drainage.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Tokyo Guidelines 2018; ACG Guidelines (2024).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute mesenteric ischemia is a life-threatening reduction in intestinal blood flow that may rapidly progress to bowel infarction, perforation, and death.
• Causes: Arterial embolism (AF), arterial thrombosis (atherosclerosis), non-occlusive ischemia (shock), venous thrombosis.
• Sudden severe abdominal pain (often disproportionate to exam). Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.
• GI bleeding in advanced disease. Abdominal tenderness, guarding, rigidity when infarction develops.
• Shock, metabolic acidosis, altered mental status in advanced disease.
• [color=#991B1B]A normal early abdominal exam or normal lactate does NOT exclude acute mesenteric ischemia.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and signs of shock.
• Keep patient nil by mouth. Establish two large-bore IV lines.
• Start isotonic crystalloid resuscitation when indicated, reassessing frequently.
• Provide IV analgesia and antiemetics.
• Obtain urgent surgical and vascular surgery consultation.
• Arrange emergency CT angiography of abdomen and pelvis.
• Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering enteric gram-negative organisms and anaerobes.
• Do not delay definitive intervention for lab results if deteriorating.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Resuscitation[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid boluses according to perfusion, BP, volume status; reassess after each.
• Monitor BP, HR, urine output, lactate, respiratory status.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics[/color]
• Example: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 hours (adjust for renal function).

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Anticoagulation[/color]
