• IV unfractionated heparin commonly initiated when arterial/venous thrombosis suspected, unless contraindicated. Use institutional weight-based protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Definitive Management[/color]
• Endovascular or open revascularization may be required.
• Urgent surgical exploration for peritonitis, bowel necrosis, perforation, or deterioration.
• Resect nonviable bowel and preserve viable bowel whenever possible.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Excessive fluid administration can worsen bowel edema and respiratory status.
• Antibiotics do not replace revascularization or surgery.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit urgently under surgical and vascular team. Shock, peritonitis, bowel infarction, or organ failure require ICU care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidelines 2022; ESVS guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Major cause of upper GI bleeding in patients with portal hypertension, commonly due to cirrhosis.
• Hematemesis (fresh blood or coffee-ground). Melena or hematochezia in massive bleeding.
• Tachycardia, hypotension, or shock.
• Known cirrhosis, ascites, splenomegaly, or prior variceal bleeding.
• Hepatic encephalopathy in advanced liver disease.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, mental status. Activate major hemorrhage protocol if indicated.
• Obtain two large-bore IV lines. Send CBC, coagulation studies, renal/liver function, type and crossmatch.
• Resuscitate carefully; avoid unnecessary over-transfusion.
• Start vasoactive agent (terlipressin or octreotide) promptly when variceal bleeding suspected.
• Start IV antibiotic prophylaxis per local cirrhosis/GI bleeding protocol.
• Arrange urgent endoscopy after initial stabilization.
• Consider early airway protection for massive ongoing hematemesis or inability to protect airway.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Blood Product Resuscitation[/color]
• Restrictive transfusion strategy (Hb threshold ~7 g/dL) in most stabilized patients; individualize for massive hemorrhage or cardiovascular disease.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Vasoactive Therapy[/color]
• Terlipressin: 2 mg IV initially, then 1–2 mg IV every 4–6 hours per protocol (commonly 2–5 days). Monitor BP, HR, Na+, ischemia.
• Alternative: Octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus, then 50 mcg/hour infusion.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Antibiotic Prophylaxis[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours is commonly used.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Endoscopic Treatment[/color]
• Urgent upper endoscopy. Endoscopic variceal band ligation is preferred.
• If uncontrolled: rescue endoscopic treatment, temporary bridging devices, or TIPS in selected patients.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Over-transfusion can increase portal pressure and worsen bleeding.
• Use caution with terlipressin in ischemic cardiovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease, and respiratory compromise.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit to monitored setting. Shock, ongoing massive bleeding, airway compromise, or advanced liver failure require ICU care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Baveno VII (2022); AASLD guidance.

Renal.title: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) and Uremic Emergencies

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute kidney injury is an abrupt decline in kidney function.

[color=#1E3A8A]KDIGO diagnostic criteria (any one):[/color]
• Increase in serum creatinine by at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours.
• Increase in serum creatinine to at least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days.
• Urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for at least 6 hours.

[color=#1E3A8A]Dangerous complications:[/color] Hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, severe metabolic acidosis, uremic encephalopathy/pericarditis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, BP, perfusion, oxygen saturation, and volume status.
• Measure urine output; insert catheter if clinically indicated.
• Obtain urgent electrolytes, urea, creatinine, bicarbonate, glucose, and ECG.
• Stop or review nephrotoxic drugs and medications.
• Treat shock, sepsis, dehydration, obstruction, or other reversible causes.
• Contact nephrology early for severe AKI or dialysis indications.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Fluid resuscitation for hypovolemia[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid bolus (commonly 250–500 mL in adults), then reassess.
• Do not give repeated fluid boluses to a patient who is already fluid overloaded. Oliguria alone does not prove that more fluid is needed.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Medication review[/color]
• Stop NSAIDs. Review ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, aminoglycosides, contrast exposure. Adjust doses of renally cleared medications.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Urinary obstruction[/color]
• Check for catheter blockage. Bladder catheterization for acute retention.
• Urgent urological assessment for upper urinary tract obstruction (especially with infection, solitary kidney, or worsening renal function).

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Dialysis and renal replacement therapy[/color]
• Urgent indications: Refractory hyperkalemia, severe metabolic acidosis, pulmonary edema/fluid overload, uremic complications (encephalopathy/pericarditis), selected dialyzable poisonings.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not give repeated fluid boluses to a patient who is already fluid overloaded.
• Infected obstructed urinary systems require urgent drainage and antimicrobial treatment.
• Do not initiate or defer dialysis based on a single creatinine or urea value alone.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for severe AKI, significant electrolyte/acid-base abnormalities, oliguria/anuria, suspected obstruction, sepsis, or uncertain cause.
• ICU/high-dependency for shock, refractory hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, or multiorgan failure.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury; Local protocols.

Renal.title: Severe Hyperkalemia and Life-Threatening Electrolyte Disorders

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Hyperkalemia[/color]
• Mild: 5.5–5.9 mmol/L. Moderate: 6.0–6.4 mmol/L. Severe: ≥ 6.5 mmol/L.
• ECG changes: Tall peaked T waves, PR prolongation, flattened/absent P waves, QRS widening, bradyarrhythmia, sine-wave pattern.

[color=#1E3A8A]Other emergencies:[/color] Severe symptomatic hyponatremia, severe hypernatremia, symptomatic hypocalcemia, severe hypomagnesemia.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Obtain urgent 12-lead ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring.
• Establish IV access. Review renal function, medications, urine output.
• Stop potassium supplements and contributing drugs.
• For severe symptomatic sodium or calcium disorders, avoid rapid unmonitored correction.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Stabilize myocardium: IV Calcium[/color]
• Calcium gluconate 10%: 30 mL IV over ~10 mins (or Calcium chloride 10%: 10 mL IV via central access).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Shift potassium: Insulin/Glucose[/color]
• Regular insulin 10 units IV with 25 g glucose. Monitor glucose for at least 4–6 hours (delayed hypoglycemia risk).

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Nebulized Salbutamol[/color]
• 10–20 mg nebulized as an adjunct.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Remove potassium[/color]
• Potassium-binding agents (e.g., sodium zirconium cyclosilicate). Loop diuretics (if renal function/urine output adequate). Hemodialysis for refractory/life-threatening cases.

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Severe symptomatic hyponatremia[/color]
• 3% hypertonic saline: 100 mL IV over 10 mins, repeated up to two additional times if severe symptoms persist. Goal is small initial sodium rise to reduce cerebral edema.

[color=#1E3A8A]F. Severe hypernatremia[/color]
• Restore circulation first if in shock. Then replace free water (oral/enteral or IV hypotonic fluid). Controlled correction to reduce cerebral edema risk.

[color=#1E3A8A]G. Symptomatic hypocalcemia[/color]
• Calcium gluconate 10%: 10–20 mL IV over ~10 mins.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane but does not lower serum potassium.
• Do not confuse calcium gluconate with calcium chloride (not equivalent volume-for-volume).
• Insulin shifts potassium temporarily; it does not remove potassium from the body.
• Avoid overly rapid correction of sodium (osmotic demyelination risk).

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Severe hyperkalemia, ECG abnormalities, severe symptomatic sodium disturbance, or significant arrhythmia requires urgent monitored care.
• ICU and urgent nephrology referral for refractory electrolyte abnormalities.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: UK Kidney Association Guidelines; Local protocols.

Renal.title: Acute Severe Hyponatremia and Sodium Disorders

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Hyponatremia: Serum sodium < 135 mmol/L.
• Mild: 130–134. Moderate: 125–129. Profound: < 125 mmol/L.
• Severe neuro symptoms: Seizures, coma, marked reduction in consciousness, severe confusion, cerebral edema.
• Causes: Hypovolemic (GI losses, diuretics, adrenal insufficiency), Euvolemic (SIADH, hypothyroidism, excess water), Hypervolemic (HF, cirrhosis, CKD).
• Hyperglycemia may cause translocational hyponatremia.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, GCS, seizures, bedside glucose.
• Obtain urgent serum sodium, K+, glucose, renal function, serum osmolality.
• If severe neuro symptoms, give 3% hypertonic saline promptly.
• Identify duration: acute (<48h) vs chronic/unknown.
• Stop contributing medications. Monitor sodium frequently.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Severe symptomatic hyponatremia[/color]
• 3% NaCl 100 mL IV over 10 mins. Repeat up to 2 additional times if severe symptoms persist.
• Goal: Initial rise of ~4–6 mmol/L to reduce severe symptoms.
• Do not aim to normalize sodium rapidly. Avoid rise > 10 mmol/L in first 24h, > 8 mmol/L per 24h thereafter.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Hypovolemic hyponatremia[/color]
• 0.9% NaCl IV when volume depletion present. Monitor for sudden urine output increase (may cause rapid Na+ rise).

[color=#1E3A8A]C. SIADH/Euvolemic[/color]
• Treat cause. Fluid restriction in stable chronic SIADH. Severe symptoms require hypertonic saline.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Overcorrection[/color]
• If sodium rises too quickly: desmopressin + electrolyte-free water (D5W) under specialist guidance to halt/reverse.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• High-risk for osmotic demyelination: severe malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, advanced liver disease, hypokalemia, very low initial sodium.
• Do not apply fluid restriction indiscriminately to hypovolemic patients.
• Do not attempt rapid sodium relowering without a monitored protocol.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit severe symptomatic hyponatremia, profound reduction, rapidly changing sodium, or serious underlying cause.
• ICU for seizures, coma, respiratory compromise, or hypertonic saline requiring intensive monitoring.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: European clinical practice guideline on hyponatraemia; Society for Endocrinology.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Metabolic acidosis is a primary reduction in serum bicarbonate, generally accompanied by acidemia.
• Deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul). Altered mental status, weakness, hypotension, shock.
• Arrhythmias/ECG changes from electrolyte disturbances.
• Causes: Lactic acidosis (shock, sepsis), DKA, renal failure, toxic alcohols, salicylates, diarrhea/RTA.
• Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3). Low albumin can mask elevated gap.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, mental status. Treat shock, hypoxemia, sepsis, DKA, poisoning immediately.
• Obtain blood gas, electrolytes, glucose, renal function, lactate, ketones. Calculate anion gap.
• Check potassium urgently before initiating insulin in suspected DKA.
• Contact critical care/nephrology/toxicology early for severe or refractory acidemia.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Treat the underlying cause[/color]
• DKA: Isotonic IV fluids, IV insulin (after checking K+), K+ replacement, add dextrose when glucose falls.
• Lactic acidosis (shock/sepsis): Restore oxygen delivery/perfusion, treat infection, fluids/vasopressors.
• Toxic ingestion: Specific antidotes, dialysis when indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Sodium bicarbonate[/color]
• No single routine dose. Consider selectively in severe acidemia with defined indication (e.g., severe AKI, specific toxicologic emergencies).
• In DKA: routine bicarbonate not recommended; only exceptional severe acidemia (pH < 7.0) under senior supervision.
• Ensure adequate ventilation (bicarbonate generates CO2).

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Renal replacement therapy[/color]
• Discuss urgently for severe/refractory acidemia, significant AKI, or dialyzable toxins.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• If potassium severely low in DKA, delay insulin while replacing potassium.
• A normal/mildly elevated glucose does not exclude DKA (especially with SGLT2 inhibitors).
• Bicarbonate can cause hypernatremia, hypokalemia, reduced ionized calcium, volume overload, and increased CO2 generation.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Severe acidemia, hemodynamic instability, altered mental status, respiratory fatigue, or serious electrolyte abnormalities require ICU-level care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ADA Standards of Care 2026; EXTRIP recommendations; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Hyperkalemia can cause fatal conduction abnormalities and cardiac arrest. Severe hyperkalemia is generally defined as serum potassium ≥6.5 mmol/L.
• Muscle weakness, paresthesia, or flaccid paralysis.
• Bradycardia, palpitations, syncope, or cardiac arrest.
• ECG changes: Tall peaked T waves, PR prolongation, flattening or loss of P waves, QRS widening, bradyarrhythmias, or a sine-wave pattern.
• Risk factors: AKI, advanced CKD, missed dialysis, potassium supplements, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, MRAs, and tissue breakdown.
• [color=#991B1B]A normal ECG does not exclude dangerous hyperkalemia.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and attach continuous cardiac monitoring.
• Obtain a 12-lead ECG immediately.
• Establish IV access and repeat potassium urgently if a hemolyzed sample is suspected; do not delay treatment if severe hyperkalemia is likely.
• Stop potassium-containing fluids and contributing medications.
• Check glucose, renal function, blood gas, bicarbonate, calcium, and magnesium.
• Contact nephrology early if advanced renal failure, missed dialysis, or refractory hyperkalemia.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Stabilize the cardiac membrane[/color]
• Calcium gluconate 10%: 30 mL IV over ~10 minutes for severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes. Reassess ECG; further dose may be required.
• Alternative: Calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV over ~5 minutes (central access preferred).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Shift potassium into cells[/color]
• Regular insulin 10 units IV plus 25 g glucose IV (e.g., 250 mL of 10% dextrose). Monitor glucose for at least 4–6 hours.
• Nebulized salbutamol 10–20 mg as an adjunct. Do not use as sole therapy.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Remove potassium from the body[/color]
• Urgent hemodialysis for severe/refractory hyperkalemia, especially in advanced renal failure.
• Potassium binders (e.g., sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) as adjuncts.
• Loop diuretics if renal function and urine output permit.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Calcium stabilizes the myocardium but does not lower serum potassium.
• Do not delay calcium in a patient with dangerous ECG changes while preparing insulin.
• Insulin can cause delayed, severe hypoglycemia, especially in kidney failure.
• Response to salbutamol may be variable, particularly in patients taking beta-blockers.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU or high-dependency care for ECG changes, severe hyperkalemia, arrhythmia, or hemodynamic instability.
• Discharge only after potassium is safely controlled, cause is addressed, and monitoring/follow-up plan is in place.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: UK Kidney Association Guidelines (2026); Resuscitation Council UK (2025).

Renal.title: Acute Kidney Injury and Emergency Dialysis Indications

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an acute reduction in kidney function.
• Oliguria or anuria. Dehydration, hypotension, or shock.
• Peripheral edema, pulmonary edema, or hypertension.
• Nausea, vomiting, confusion, pericarditic chest pain, or bleeding.
• Hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, or other electrolyte abnormalities.
• Causes: Prerenal (hypovolemia, sepsis, low CO), Intrinsic (ATN, GN, rhabdomyolysis), Postrenal (obstruction).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, perfusion, volume status, and urine output.
• Obtain IV access and treat shock or sepsis promptly.
• Check potassium and ECG urgently if severe AKI is suspected.
• Stop/review nephrotoxic medications and adjust renally cleared drugs.
• Insert urinary catheter when clinically indicated. Bladder scanning and renal US when obstruction suspected.
• Contact nephrology urgently if there are dialysis indications or rapidly worsening renal function.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Correct reversible hemodynamic causes[/color]
• If hypovolemic, initial 250–500 mL IV isotonic crystalloid bolus, followed by reassessment.
• Do not give repeated fluid boluses to an already overloaded or anuric patient.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Medication and nephrotoxin review[/color]
• Stop/temporarily hold contributory medications (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs, diuretics, contrast, aminoglycosides).

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Emergency dialysis / renal replacement therapy[/color]
• Urgent indications: Refractory/life-threatening hyperkalemia, severe metabolic acidosis refractory to medical treatment, pulmonary edema/fluid overload causing severe hypoxemia, uremic complications (encephalopathy/pericarditis/bleeding), selected severe poisonings.
• Do not delay dialysis for an arbitrary creatinine/urea threshold when a life-threatening indication is present.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Diuretics do not treat AKI itself; use them for volume overload when appropriate.
• Do not automatically discontinue every chronic cardiovascular medication in every patient.
• Dialysis decisions should be based on the overall clinical picture and complications, not creatinine alone.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU for shock, severe hyperkalemia, refractory acidosis, pulmonary edema with respiratory compromise, or uremic complications.
• Ensure repeat renal function and electrolyte testing and a clear medication review before discharge.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: KDIGO AKI Guidelines (2026); Local nephrology protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Hypernatremia is a serum sodium concentration above 145 mmol/L and usually reflects a deficit of water relative to sodium.
• Intense thirst, weakness, dehydration.
• Confusion, irritability, lethargy, or seizures in severe cases.
• Hypotension, tachycardia, and oliguria if intravascular volume depleted.
• Causes: Inadequate water intake, GI losses, excessive sweating, osmotic diuresis, diabetes insipidus.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, circulation, mental status, volume status.
• Check bedside glucose and serum electrolytes immediately.
• If shock/severe hypovolemia: restore circulation first with isotonic crystalloid.
• Determine if hypernatremia is acute or chronic.
• Measure urine output. Begin controlled free-water replacement after initial stabilization.
• Monitor sodium frequently to prevent overly rapid correction.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Initial circulatory resuscitation[/color]
• If hypotensive/shock: 0.9% NaCl in reassessed boluses (e.g., 250–500 mL).
• Do not use hypotonic fluid as the sole initial resuscitation fluid in shock.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Free-water replacement[/color]
• Estimate water deficit: Total body water × [(serum Na / 140) − 1].
• Oral/enteral free water preferred when safe. IV 5% dextrose provides free water. 0.45% NaCl may be appropriate.
• For chronic/unknown duration: lower sodium by no more than ~10–12 mmol/L in 24 hours.
• Check sodium every 4–6 hours during active correction.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Treat the cause[/color]
• Replace GI losses, address inadequate intake, treat diabetes insipidus, manage hyperglycemia.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid unmonitored correction.
• Do not rely on a calculated water deficit alone: ongoing urine and GI losses must also be replaced.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU or high-dependency care for severe neurologic symptoms, shock, very high sodium, or rapidly changing sodium.
• Admit patients requiring IV correction or frequent laboratory monitoring.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: UpToDate (2026); NHS guidance; Local electrolyte protocols.

Renal.title: Pulmonary–Renal Syndrome and Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Pulmonary–renal syndrome is a life-threatening combination of pulmonary capillary injury (often causing diffuse alveolar hemorrhage) and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
• Causes: ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-GBM disease, SLE, infections, drug reactions.
• Dyspnea, cough, hypoxemia, or hemoptysis. Falling hemoglobin. Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.
• AKI, hematuria, proteinuria. Red cell casts on urine microscopy.
• [color=#991B1B]Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage can occur without obvious hemoptysis.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess respiratory failure, hemodynamic stability, degree of bleeding.
• Provide oxygen and escalate respiratory support as required.
• Obtain urgent nephrology, respiratory, and critical care consultation.
• Check CBC, renal function, coagulation, urinalysis, blood gas.
• Send autoimmune testing and microbiological samples promptly.
• Consider early intubation for worsening hypoxemia, exhaustion, or inability to protect airway.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Respiratory Support[/color]
• Oxygen, high-flow oxygen, or mechanical ventilation as required. Use lung-protective ventilation if ARDS develops.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Suspected Severe Immune-Mediated Disease[/color]
• Organ-threatening ANCA-associated vasculitis or anti-GBM disease: urgent induction may include IV glucocorticoids + rituximab or cyclophosphamide.
• Anti-GBM disease generally requires urgent specialist assessment for plasma exchange alongside immunosuppression.
• Monitor glucose, BP, CBC, renal function, and infection.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Acute Kidney Injury[/color]
• Monitor fluid balance, K+, acid-base, urine output. Treat hyperkalemia. Arrange RRT for standard indications.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not start high-dose immunosuppression indiscriminately in undifferentiated pulmonary infiltrates; infection and other causes of hemorrhage must be evaluated urgently.
• Plasma exchange is not routinely indicated for every patient with ANCA-associated vasculitis.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit to ICU for severe hypoxemia, rapidly progressive pulmonary hemorrhage, shock, or severe metabolic complications.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: KDIGO Guidelines for ANCA-Associated Vasculitis and anti-GBM disease.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute urinary retention is the sudden inability to pass urine despite a full bladder.
• Common causes: BPH, urethral stricture/stones, medications (anticholinergics, opioids), constipation, neurological disease (spinal cord/cauda equina), postoperative.
• Suprapubic pain and palpable bladder. Urgency with inability to void. Overflow dribbling.
• Reduced urine output or rising creatinine. Fever/systemic illness if infection present.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs, pain, and evidence of sepsis.
• Examine abdomen and assess bladder distension. Ask about back pain, leg weakness, saddle numbness, bowel dysfunction.
• Perform bladder ultrasound when available.
• Insert urinary catheter promptly unless urethral injury or another contraindication suspected.
• If urethral injury possible, seek urgent urological advice and avoid repeated blind catheter attempts.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Bladder Decompression[/color]
• Aseptic urethral catheterization using appropriate catheter size and technique. Record volume drained and urine appearance.
• If urethral injury suspected, do NOT proceed with routine blind catheterization.
• Monitor urine output, pain relief, hematuria, BP, renal function.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Suspected Prostatic Obstruction[/color]
• Tamsulosin 0.4 mg PO once daily when appropriate. Monitor for dizziness/orthostatic hypotension.
• Arrange trial without catheter after a short period of treatment.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Post-Obstructive Diuresis[/color]
• Measure urine output frequently. Monitor Na+, K+, Mg2+, creatinine, fluid balance.
• Replace fluid losses according to hemodynamics, electrolytes, urine output. Avoid automatic replacement of every milliliter.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Infection or Renal Impairment[/color]
• Treat documented/strongly suspected infection per local guidance. Urgent urological assessment for infected obstruction, renal impairment, persistent obstruction, or failed catheterization.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Routine gradual clamping of the catheter is generally unnecessary.
• If resistance is encountered, do not force the catheter; obtain experienced assistance.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Discharge may be appropriate after uncomplicated retention when stable, drainage adequate, renal function and infection risks assessed, and reliable urological follow-up arranged.
• Admit for sepsis, AKI, significant electrolyte abnormalities, suspected neurological compression, or unresolved obstruction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE LUTS Guidance; EAU Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Severe hyperphosphatemia may cause symptomatic hypocalcemia, calcium-phosphate deposition, acute kidney injury, and cardiac complications. Causes: advanced renal failure, tumor lysis syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, phosphate-containing preparations, severe tissue breakdown.
• Muscle cramps, paresthesia, tetany due to hypocalcemia.
• Seizures or altered mental status. Arrhythmias when significant calcium/electrolyte abnormalities coexist.
• Oliguria or renal failure. History of tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis, or phosphate ingestion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, neurological status. Obtain ECG if significant calcium disturbance or cardiac symptoms.
• Check phosphate, calcium, magnesium, potassium, renal function, glucose.
• Stop phosphate-containing medications, supplements, enemas, or infusions.
• Treat symptomatic hypocalcemia and life-threatening associated electrolyte abnormalities.
• Involve nephrology early if severe hyperphosphatemia with renal failure or refractory abnormalities.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Remove the Phosphate Source[/color]
• Stop exogenous phosphate. Treat underlying cause (TLS, rhabdomyolysis).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Hydration[/color]
• Isotonic IV fluid when volume depletion present and patient can tolerate. Avoid aggressive hydration in anuria, severe renal failure, or fluid overload.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Phosphate Binders[/color]
• In selected patients who can take enteral medication, a phosphate binder (e.g., sevelamer) may be used under specialist guidance. Dosing depends on phosphate, formulation, dialysis status.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Symptomatic Hypocalcemia[/color]
• IV calcium may be required for tetany, seizures, significant QT prolongation, or hemodynamic instability. Use local IV calcium protocol and monitor ECG and ionized calcium. (Caution: calcium-phosphate precipitation in severe hyperphosphatemia).

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Dialysis[/color]
• Urgent nephrology assessment for dialysis when severe hyperphosphatemia with significant renal failure, refractory/dangerous electrolyte disturbances, severe symptomatic hypocalcemia, or other established indications.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Oral binders are not a substitute for emergency treatment in severe symptomatic cases or significant renal failure.
• Administer calcium only when clinically indicated and with close monitoring.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit for severe symptomatic abnormalities, AKI, TLS, or associated dangerous electrolyte disturbances. ICU for seizures, arrhythmias, shock, or multiorgan failure.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: KDIGO CKD-MBD; ASCO TLS protocols; Local nephrology guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Hypoglycemia[/color]
• < 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) alert threshold; < 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L) clinically significant.
• Severe = need for assistance due to altered mental/physical status.
• Sweating, tremor, palpitations, confusion, seizures, coma.

[color=#1E3A8A]DKA / HHS[/color]
• DKA: Hyperglycemia, ketosis, metabolic acidosis. May occur with normal-ish glucose (SGLT2i, pregnancy).
• HHS: Severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, dehydration, minimal ketosis/acidosis.
• Mixed presentations occur.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, mental status, hydration, bedside glucose. Obtain IV access and ECG.
• If hypoglycemic, treat immediately (do not wait for lab).
• If DKA/HHS, obtain electrolytes, VBG, ketones, renal function, osmolality.
• Identify precipitant: infection, missed insulin, MI, stroke, pancreatitis, new-onset diabetes.
• Monitored area for DKA/HHS with frequent glucose, K+, fluid, and neuro reassessment.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Hypoglycemia (Cannot Swallow)[/color]
• IV glucose 10–25 g (e.g., 100 mL of 10% dextrose). Recheck in 10–15 mins. Glucagon 1 mg IM if no IV.

[color=#1E3A8A]Initial Fluids for DKA/HHS[/color]
• Isotonic saline/balanced crystalloid at 500–1,000 mL/hour for first 2–4 hours (adjust for heart/kidney).

[color=#1E3A8A]IV Insulin for DKA[/color]
• Regular insulin IV infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour.
• Do not start if K+ < 3.5 mmol/L; replace K+ first.
• Add dextrose when glucose < ~250 mg/dL to allow ketone clearance.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV Insulin for HHS[/color]
• Regular insulin IV at 0.05 units/kg/hour (if no significant ketosis).

[color=#1E3A8A]Potassium Replacement[/color]
• If K+ < 3.5, start replacement and defer insulin.
• If 3.5–5.0, add K+ to IV fluids.
• If > 5.0, withhold initially.

[color=#1E3A8A]Bicarbonate[/color]
• Not routinely recommended. Consider only if pH < 7.0 under specialist protocol.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Sulfonylurea-related hypoglycemia may recur and require prolonged observation.
• Avoid rapid uncontrolled correction of hyperosmolality (especially HHS).
• Insulin can rapidly lower potassium and precipitate life-threatening arrhythmias.
• Do not stop insulin solely because glucose normalized if ketoacidosis persists.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Severe DKA, HHS, shock, altered mental status, severe electrolyte abnormalities require ICU/high-dependency care.
• Establish cause, treatment plan, sick-day rules, and follow-up before discharge.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Umpierrez GE, et al. Diabetes Care 2024; Local DKA/HHS protocols.

Endocrinology.title: Adrenal Crisis and Acute Adrenal Insufficiency

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Hypotension or shock responding poorly to initial fluids.
• Vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, fever, altered consciousness.
• Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, unexplained volume depletion.
• Known adrenal insufficiency, recent withdrawal of chronic corticosteroids, or pituitary/adrenal disease.
• Triggers: Infection, surgery, trauma, severe illness, missed glucocorticoid replacement, bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Treat as life-threatening endocrine emergency.
• Assess ABCs, BP, perfusion, glucose, electrolytes, mental status.
• Obtain IV access and blood samples for cortisol/ACTH if feasible, but do NOT delay hydrocortisone.
• Give IV/IM hydrocortisone immediately.
• Start isotonic saline resuscitation and treat hypoglycemia.
• Search for and treat precipitating infection.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Hydrocortisone[/color]
• 100 mg IV or IM immediately.
• Then 200 mg over 24 hours by continuous IV infusion, or 50 mg IV/IM every 6 hours.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. IV fluid resuscitation[/color]
• 1 litre of 0.9% sodium chloride IV over ~30 mins, subsequent fluid guided by clinical response.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Hypoglycemia[/color]
• IV glucose if hypoglycemic and cannot swallow safely.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Hyperkalemia[/color]
• Treat severe hyperkalemia per protocol. (May improve with hydrocortisone and volume restoration, but do not rely on steroid alone if ECG toxicity is present).

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Treat the precipitating cause[/color]
• Empiric antibiotics promptly if bacterial infection suspected. Investigate adrenal hemorrhage.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay the initial dose for laboratory confirmation.
• There is no meaningful risk of overdose from the emergency initial hydrocortisone dose when adrenal crisis is suspected.
• Patients receiving chronic glucocorticoids may have HPA suppression even without known adrenal disease.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• All suspected adrenal crises require urgent hospital treatment.
• ICU/high-dependency for refractory shock, severe electrolyte disturbance, or multiorgan dysfunction.
• Arrange endocrinology review, sick-day rules, and emergency steroid education.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE NG243; Society for Endocrinology.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Hypoglycemia after insulin administration or missed meals.
• Repeated low glucose during renal/hepatic impairment.
• Insulin pump failure or interruption of basal insulin.
• Accidental insulin overdose or wrong insulin type.
• Marked hyperglycemia after missed insulin/pump interruption.
• Risk factors: Reduced food intake, vomiting, exercise, alcohol, renal impairment, medication errors.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Check bedside glucose immediately.
• Assess ABCs, consciousness, seizure activity, ability to swallow.
• If conscious and can swallow safely, give rapid-acting oral glucose.
• If unable to swallow safely, give IV glucose; use glucagon if IV access unavailable.
• Review insulin type, concentration, dose, timing, food intake.
• Consult toxicology/poison services for major overdose. Assess for ketosis/DKA if pump failure suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Conscious patient with mild-to-moderate hypoglycemia[/color]
• 15–20 g rapid-acting oral glucose. Recheck in 15 mins. Repeat if low. Provide longer-acting carbohydrate once corrected.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Severe hypoglycemia: IV glucose[/color]
• 10–25 g IV glucose (e.g., 100 mL of 10% dextrose). Recheck within 10–15 mins. Consider continuous glucose infusion if recurrent.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Glucagon (No IV access)[/color]
• 1 mg IM in adults. Recheck glucose and provide oral carbohydrate once awake.
• May be less effective after prolonged fasting or severe liver disease.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Suspected insulin overdose[/color]
• Correct hypoglycemia with IV glucose. May require titrated continuous glucose infusion. Obtain toxicology advice for large/long-acting exposures.

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Insulin pump interruption[/color]
• Check glucose and blood ketones. Assess for DKA. Restore insulin delivery or use alternative regimen.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not give oral food/drink to a patient with impaired consciousness or unsafe swallowing.
• Long-acting insulin overdoses may cause recurrent hypoglycemia for many hours.
• Patients with type 1 diabetes must not be left without basal insulin coverage.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit/observe for recurrent hypoglycemia, insulin overdose, persistent neurological symptoms, or unstable comorbidities.
• ICU/high-dependency for prolonged severe hypoglycemia, seizures, airway compromise, or major overdose.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ADA Standards of Care 2026; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Thyroid storm[/color] (life-threatening thyrotoxicosis, precipitated by infection/surgery/trauma):
• Fever, marked tachycardia, AF, HF. Agitation, delirium, psychosis, coma. Vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice. Shock.

[color=#1E3A8A]Myxedema coma[/color] (severe decompensated hypothyroidism):
• Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation. Altered mental status, stupor, coma. Hyponatremia, hypoglycemia.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and obtain ICU support for organ dysfunction.
• Continuous ECG, SpO2, temperature, BP monitoring. Obtain glucose and correct hypoglycemia.
• Send TSH, free T4, T3, but do NOT delay treatment while awaiting results.
• Check CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function, cortisol, cultures if infection suspected.
• Identify and treat precipitating cause.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Thyroid Storm[/color]
• Beta-blockade: Propranolol 60–80 mg PO every 4–6 hours (IV reserved for monitored settings).
• Thionamide: PTU 500–1,000 mg PO/NG loading, then 250 mg every 4 hours (or Methimazole).
• Iodine therapy: Give at least 1 hour after thionamide (do not give iodine first).
• Glucocorticoid: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 hours.
• Supportive: External cooling, acetaminophen (avoid aspirin).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Myxedema Coma[/color]
• IV Levothyroxine: Loading dose 200–400 mcg IV once (lower in older/cardiac disease).
• Empiric Glucocorticoids: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 hours.
• Supportive: Controlled rewarming, respiratory support, cautious fluid/electrolyte correction, treat hypoglycemia.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Beta-blockers can precipitate cardiovascular collapse in severe low-output HF or shock.
• PTU can cause severe hepatotoxicity.
• Rapid thyroid hormone replacement in myxedema can provoke ischemia or arrhythmias.
• Avoid sedatives and opioids in myxedema coma where possible.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Both conditions generally require ICU or high-dependency care when severe or associated with organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: 2026 Joint Consensus Statement (ETA/BTA/SfE/WEDS).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening deficiency of cortisol, sometimes with aldosterone deficiency.
• Triggers: Infection, sepsis, surgery, trauma, abrupt cessation of long-term glucocorticoids, bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.
• Hypotension/shock responding poorly to initial fluids.
• Weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration.
• Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, fever.
• Confusion, reduced consciousness, collapse.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Treat suspected adrenal crisis immediately; do not wait for cortisol results.
• Assess ABCs, attach monitoring, establish IV access.
• Check bedside glucose and treat hypoglycemia promptly.
• Send electrolytes, glucose, renal function, CBC, cortisol, and ACTH if feasible.
• Start IV hydrocortisone and isotonic saline.
• Identify and treat precipitating cause (e.g., infection).

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Immediate glucocorticoid replacement[/color]
• Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately (or IM if no IV access).
• Continue 200 mg over 24 hours by continuous IV infusion, or 50 mg IV/IM every 6 hours.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Fluid resuscitation[/color]
• 0.9% sodium chloride: 1 L IV over 30 minutes in adults (if no contraindication).
• Reassess BP, pulse, capillary refill, urine output, lung findings.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Hypoglycemia[/color]
• IV dextrose per protocol if severe hypoglycemia present.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Treat the precipitating cause[/color]
• Cultures, appropriate antimicrobials, correct electrolyte abnormalities.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Short-term emergency hydrocortisone should not be withheld because of concern about a high dose.
• Failure to treat adrenal crisis promptly can be fatal.
• Avoid unmonitored fluid loading in patients at risk of pulmonary edema.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit; ICU for persistent shock, severe electrolyte abnormalities, altered consciousness, or vasopressor need.
• Before discharge, ensure patient understands sick-day rules and has access to emergency steroid treatment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Society for Endocrinology; NICE NG243.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
HHS is a life-threatening hyperglycemic emergency characterized by severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and profound dehydration, typically with little or no significant ketoacidosis.
• Polyuria, polydipsia, progressive dehydration.
• Weakness, tachycardia, hypotension, reduced skin turgor.
• Confusion, lethargy, seizures, or coma.
• Often in older adults with type 2 diabetes.
• Triggers: Infection, missed meds, stroke, MI, drugs.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, mental status, perfusion, degree of dehydration.
• Check bedside glucose immediately.
• Establish IV access; obtain electrolytes, renal function, blood gas, ketones, serum osmolality.
• Start IV fluid replacement promptly, tailored to cardiac/renal status.
• Measure potassium before insulin and correct significant hypokalemia first.
• Identify and treat precipitating cause.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IV fluid replacement[/color]
• 0.9% NaCl or balanced crystalloid: initial rate 500–1,000 mL/hour for first 2–4 hours in adults without significant cardiac/renal compromise.
• In older adults/HF/CKD: use smaller boluses (e.g., 250 mL) and reassess frequently.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Potassium management[/color]
• If < 3.5 mmol/L: replace and delay insulin until > 3.5.
• If 3.5–5.0: add K+ to IV fluids.
• If > 5.0: do not add initially; recheck frequently.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Insulin therapy[/color]
• Regular insulin IV at 0.05 units/kg/hour (for HHS without significant ketoacidosis).
• If mixed DKA/HHS, use DKA pathway (0.1 units/kg/hour).
• Add 5–10% dextrose when glucose < ~250 mg/dL.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Treat the precipitating cause[/color]
• Treat infection, evaluate for MI/stroke, review meds. Provide thrombosis prevention.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Excessively rapid osmotic shifts may cause neurologic complications.
• Do not start insulin before addressing significant hypokalemia.
• Mixed DKA/HHS requires a different insulin strategy.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • ICU or equivalent high-dependency care for severe HHS, shock, altered consciousness, seizures, significant electrolyte disturbances, or critical illness.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Umpierrez et al., Diabetes Care 2024; ADA Standards of Care 2026.

Endocrinology.title: Severe Calcium Disorders: Hypercalcemia and Hypocalcemia

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Severe hypercalcemia[/color]
• Total serum calcium commonly ≥14 mg/dL (3.5 mmol/L), especially when symptomatic.
• Confusion, lethargy, coma, muscle weakness. Polyuria, dehydration, nausea, vomiting, constipation.
• AKI, shortened QT interval, arrhythmias. Causes: malignancy, primary hyperparathyroidism.

[color=#1E3A8A]Severe hypocalcemia[/color]
• Perioral numbness, paresthesia, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm.
• Tetany, seizures, laryngospasm, altered mental status. Prolonged QT interval.
• Causes: hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, severe hypomagnesemia, pancreatitis, massive transfusion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and attach ECG monitoring if severe symptoms.
• Check calcium, albumin, magnesium, phosphate, renal function, glucose.
• Measure ionized calcium in critically ill patients or when albumin/pH makes total calcium difficult to interpret.
• Obtain ECG and assess QT interval. Establish IV access.
• Treat symptomatic severe hypocalcemia immediately.
• For severe hypercalcemia, begin appropriate hydration if tolerated and identify cause.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia[/color]
• Calcium gluconate 10%: 10–20 mL IV diluted in 50–100 mL of 0.9% NaCl or D5W over ~10 mins.
• Repeat if severe symptoms/ECG abnormalities persist. Continuous infusion may be required.
• Correct hypomagnesemia (can make hypocalcemia refractory).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Severe hypercalcemia[/color]
• Isotonic IV crystalloid: 100–200 mL/hour after initial assessment (if hypovolemic).
• Calcitonin: 4 international units/kg SC or IM every 12 hours (rapid, short-term adjunct).
• Definitive: IV bisphosphonate or denosumab (especially malignancy-associated). Treat underlying cause.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Rapid calcium administration may cause hypotension, bradycardia, or arrhythmias.
• Calcium chloride contains more elemental calcium and is more damaging if extravasation occurs.
• Do not force high-volume hydration in patients with pulmonary edema or severe heart failure.
• Calcitonin effect is temporary (tachyphylaxis develops within 48–72 hours).

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • ICU or monitored admission for severe symptoms, arrhythmias, seizures, marked calcium abnormalities, or organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance.

Endocrinology.title: Acute Adrenal Incidental Hemorrhage with Adrenal Crisis

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Adrenal hemorrhage can cause acute primary adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis, especially when bilateral. Risk factors: anticoagulation, severe sepsis, trauma, major surgery, underlying adrenal disease.
• Hypotension or shock responding poorly to initial fluids.
• Abdominal, flank, or back pain. Nausea, vomiting, profound weakness.
• Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, or hypoglycemia. Fever or altered mental status.
• History of anticoagulation, trauma, or severe systemic illness.
• [color=#991B1B]Normal potassium or sodium does NOT exclude adrenal crisis.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Treat suspected adrenal crisis immediately; do NOT wait for laboratory confirmation.
• Assess ABCs, glucose, mental status.
• Obtain IV access and blood samples for cortisol/ACTH before steroids only if no treatment delay.
• Check glucose and electrolytes promptly.
• Give IV hydrocortisone and isotonic fluid resuscitation.
• Correct hypoglycemia immediately.
• Investigate and treat precipitating cause (sepsis, hemorrhage).

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Immediate Glucocorticoid Replacement[/color]
• Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately. Follow with 200 mg over 24 hours by continuous IV infusion, or 50 mg IV every 6 hours.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• 0.9% NaCl: 1 L IV during first hour (adjusted for hemodynamics/comorbidities). Further fluid individualized.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Hypoglycemia[/color]
• IV dextrose per protocol if hypoglycemia present. Recheck and monitor.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Hyperkalemia[/color]
• If significant hyperkalemia or ECG changes, initiate emergency hyperkalemia protocol. Do not assume hydrocortisone alone will correct immediately dangerous hyperkalemia.

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Identify and Treat the Cause[/color]
• Assess for sepsis, trauma, anticoagulant-associated bleeding. Review anticoagulants with specialist. Arrange endocrinology and surgical consultation.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay hydrocortisone while waiting for cortisol results.
• Use more cautious fluid replacement in patients at risk of fluid overload.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit all patients with suspected adrenal crisis. Shock, severe electrolyte disturbance, hypoglycemia, or ongoing hemorrhage requires ICU-level monitoring.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Society for Endocrinology; Endocrine Society Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Sudden focal neurologic deficit: Facial droop, arm/leg weakness, speech disturbance, visual loss, ataxia, neglect.
• Posterior circulation: vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, reduced consciousness.
• Establish exact last-known-well time.
• Consider mimics: hypoglycemia, seizure, migraine.
• Time-sensitive reperfusion assessment is essential.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate stroke pathway immediately. Record last-known-well time.
• Assess ABCs, glucose, oxygenation, neurologic deficit.
• Establish IV access and obtain ECG without delaying brain imaging.
• Obtain urgent non-contrast CT brain to exclude hemorrhage. Add CTA when LVO suspected.
• Assess eligibility for IV thrombolysis and endovascular thrombectomy.
• Keep patient NPO until swallowing safety assessed.
• Avoid unnecessary delays from routine tests.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]IV Thrombolysis — Tenecteplase[/color]
• 0.25 mg/kg IV single bolus (max 25 mg) for eligible adults.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV Thrombolysis — Alteplase[/color]
• 0.9 mg/kg IV (max 90 mg). 10% as initial bolus over 1 min, remaining 90% over 60 mins.

[color=#1E3A8A]Blood Pressure Management[/color]
• Before thrombolysis: BP < 185/110 mmHg.
• After thrombolysis: maintain < 180/105 mmHg for first 24 hours.
• Use titratable IV antihypertensive (labetalol/nicardipine).

[color=#1E3A8A]Endovascular Thrombectomy[/color]
• Eligible patients with confirmed LVO, within 6 hours or up to 24 hours based on imaging criteria.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antiplatelet[/color]
• Aspirin within 24–48 hours after hemorrhage excluded (not treated with thrombolysis).
• After thrombolysis: wait 24 hours and obtain follow-up imaging before starting.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Only administer thrombolysis after hemorrhage excluded and eligibility confirmed.
• Do not give routine antiplatelets/anticoagulants during first 24 hours after IV thrombolysis.
• Do not delay eligible thrombolysis for nonessential advanced imaging.
• Do not use a single BP target for every stroke patient.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to stroke unit or monitored setting.
• ICU for airway compromise, severe deficits, malignant edema, hemorrhagic transformation, or instability.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/ASA 2026 Acute Ischemic Stroke Guideline; NICE NG128.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Sudden focal neurological deficit, severe headache, vomiting, reduced consciousness, or seizure.
• Risk factors: chronic hypertension, anticoagulant use, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, vascular malformations, coagulopathy.
• Consider raised ICP: declining consciousness, pupillary asymmetry, abnormal posturing.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate stroke/emergency response and document exact last-known-well time.
• Assess ABCs, GCS, pupils, capillary glucose.
• Provide oxygen if hypoxemic; avoid hypoxemia and hypotension.
• Establish IV access, cardiac monitoring, frequent neuro observations.
• Obtain urgent non-contrast CT brain. Add CTA when indicated.
• Stop anticoagulants/antiplatelet agents initially.
• Contact stroke, neurosurgical, and critical-care services early.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Blood Pressure Control[/color]
• Mild-to-moderate spontaneous ICH with SBP 150–220: target SBP ~140 mmHg (range 130–150).
• Nicardipine: Start 5 mg/hour, increase by 2.5 mg/hour every 5-15 mins (max 15 mg/hour).

[color=#1E3A8A]Reversal of Anticoagulation[/color]
• Warfarin: 4F-PCC (dose per INR) + Vitamin K 10 mg IV slowly.
• Dabigatran: Idarucizumab 5 g IV.
• Factor Xa inhibitor: Andexanet alfa or 4F-PCC per protocol.
• Heparin: Protamine per type/dose/timing.

[color=#1E3A8A]Raised ICP / Herniation[/color]
• Hypertonic saline or mannitol (e.g., 0.5–1 g/kg IV) under neurocritical care protocol.
• Elevate head ~30 degrees if tolerated. Maintain neutral neck.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid abrupt BP reduction and hypotension. Do not target SBP below 130 routinely.
• Avoid routine corticosteroids for ICH-related edema.
• Avoid prophylactic platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated ICH unless specific indication (e.g., emergency neurosurgery).

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to stroke unit, neurocritical care, or ICU depending on severity.
• Urgent neurosurgical review for cerebellar hemorrhage with deterioration, hydrocephalus, or significant mass effect.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/ASA 2022 Spontaneous ICH Guideline; Local reversal protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Continuous convulsive seizure ≥ 5 minutes.
• Recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness between episodes.
• Causes: missed meds, hypoglycemia, electrolytes, stroke, CNS infection, toxic, alcohol withdrawal, eclampsia.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for emergency assistance, record onset.
• Protect from injury, position safely, suction, provide oxygen.
• Assess airway/breathing, check bedside glucose, establish IV access.
• Give benzodiazepine promptly at 5 minutes.
• If seizures continue after 2 benzodiazepine doses, proceed to second-line.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]First-line: Lorazepam IV[/color]
• 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg). May repeat once after 3–5 mins.

[color=#1E3A8A]Alternative (No IV): Midazolam[/color]
• IM midazolam 10 mg (for >40 kg) per protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Second-line: Levetiracetam[/color]
• 60 mg/kg IV (max 4,500 mg) over 10–15 mins.

[color=#1E3A8A]Alternatives[/color]
• Fosphenytoin/phenytoin (20 mg/kg IV max 50 mg/min, monitor ECG/BP) or sodium valproate.

[color=#1E3A8A]Refractory[/color]
• Continuous anesthetic infusions (midazolam/propofol) in ICU. Secure airway. Continuous EEG.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Benzodiazepines can cause respiratory depression/hypotension. Have airway equipment ready.
• Do not delay treatment while waiting for IV access (use IM/buccal/intranasal).
• A loading dose is not the same as a maintenance dose (e.g., levetiracetam).

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU for refractory seizures, respiratory compromise, or persistent depressed consciousness.
• Admit for first seizure, persistent deficit, suspected CNS infection, or significant metabolic abnormalities.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE NG217 (2025); Local status epilepticus protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute confusion, delirium, agitation, drowsiness, stupor, or coma.
• Reversible/life-threatening causes: Hypoglycemia, hypoxia, hypercapnia, shock, sepsis, stroke, ICH, seizure, CNS infection, drug toxicity, opioid overdose, alcohol withdrawal, electrolyte disturbances, renal/hepatic failure, endocrine emergencies, trauma, temperature extremes.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCDE. Check capillary glucose immediately.
• Assess SpO2, temp, BP, pulse, RR, GCS, pupils.
• Treat hypoxia, hypoglycemia, shock, seizures immediately.
• Obtain collateral history.
• Consider C-spine protection if trauma possible.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Hypoglycemia[/color]
• Unable to swallow: IV dextrose (10–25 g). E.g., 100 mL of 10% dextrose. Glucagon 1 mg IM if no IV.

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected Opioid Toxicity[/color]
• Naloxone 0.04–0.1 mg IV (titrate carefully). 0.4–2 mg IV/IM for severe respiratory compromise.
• Goal is adequate ventilation, not complete wakefulness. Repeat every 2–3 mins.

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected Wernicke Encephalopathy[/color]
• Thiamine 200–500 mg IV three times daily (give before/with glucose).

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected Sepsis/CNS Infection[/color]
• Cultures, empiric antibiotics promptly.

[color=#1E3A8A]Agitation/Delirium[/color]
• Treat underlying cause, pain, urinary retention. Verbal de-escalation. Avoid routine sedation that obscures reassessment.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not give oral fluids/food to a patient with impaired consciousness.
• Naloxone may precipitate acute withdrawal, agitation, vomiting. Duration may be shorter than opioid.
• Do not delay life-saving glucose in hypoglycemia while waiting for thiamine.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit/transfer for unexplained, persistent, recurrent altered mental status or serious underlying cause.
• ICU for airway compromise, severe coma, shock, or need for organ support.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE guidance on delirium; Local emergency protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy causing rapidly progressive weakness, autonomic instability, respiratory failure.
• Progressive, usually symmetric limb weakness. Reduced/absent deep tendon reflexes.
• Paresthesia/neuropathic pain. Recent respiratory/GI infection. Facial weakness, dysphagia.

[color=#991B1B]Red Flags:[/color] Rapidly ascending weakness. Weak cough/difficulty clearing secretions. Dysphagia/dysarthria/aspiration. Neck flexor weakness. Declining FVC. Marked BP fluctuations/arrhythmias.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Admit for close monitoring.
• Assess airway protection, swallowing, cough strength, limb power, cranial nerves.
• Measure FVC and inspiratory pressure. Repeat every 4 hours if rapidly progressing.
• Obtain ECG, monitor BP/rhythm.
• Early neurology/ICU consult for progression, bulbar dysfunction, respiratory compromise.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Respiratory/Autonomic Monitoring[/color]
• Serial FVC, respiratory effort, cough, bulbar function. Continuous ECG/BP in severe cases.
• Consider early elective intubation when respiratory function deteriorates (FVC ~20 mL/kg or lower, or rapidly falling).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. IVIG[/color]
• 0.4 g/kg/day IV for 5 days (total 2 g/kg). Infuse slowly, monitor renal function/thrombotic risk.
• IVIG and plasma exchange are alternative disease-modifying treatments. Do NOT routinely do plasma exchange immediately followed by IVIG.
• Corticosteroids are NOT recommended as routine treatment.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Plasma Exchange[/color]
• 4–5 exchanges over 1–2 weeks under specialist supervision.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Supportive Care[/color]
• VTE prophylaxis, pressure injury prevention, nutritional support, aspiration precautions, pain management, rehab.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not wait for hypoxemia or respiratory arrest before escalating care.
• CSF protein may be normal early. Normal early CSF does not exclude GBS.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Generally require hospital admission. ICU for declining respiratory function, bulbar dysfunction, rapidly progressive weakness, or severe autonomic instability.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAN/PNS GBS Guideline (2023).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Severe worsening of myasthenia gravis causing respiratory muscle weakness and impending/established respiratory failure.
• Fluctuating muscle weakness. Ptosis, diplopia.
• Dysarthria, dysphagia, weak cough. Neck flexor weakness.
• Difficulty counting in one breath/speaking full sentences. Shallow breathing, orthopnea, inability to clear secretions.
• Precipitants: Respiratory infection, aspiration, surgery, medication changes, drugs impairing neuromuscular transmission.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Admit to monitored setting, involve ICU/neurology early.
• Assess respiratory effort, bulbar function, cough strength, secretion handling.
• Measure FVC and inspiratory pressure serially.
• Prepare for intubation if respiratory function deteriorating.
• Identify/treat triggers (infection). Review meds for exacerbating agents.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Airway and Ventilation[/color]
• Intubate for progressive respiratory fatigue, severe bulbar dysfunction, inability to protect airway, or inadequate ventilation.
• Noninvasive ventilation only in selected patients who can protect airway; must not delay intubation.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. IVIG[/color]
• 0.4 g/kg/day IV for 5 days (total 2 g/kg). Monitor for infusion reactions, thrombosis, renal injury.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Plasma Exchange[/color]
• Alternative rapid immunomodulatory treatment (several exchanges over 1–2 weeks).

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Pyridostigmine / Other Meds[/color]
• May be temporarily withheld/adjusted during intubated crisis (can increase secretions).
• Corticosteroid initiation/escalation requires specialist planning (early transient worsening risk).

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid waiting for hypercapnia, severe hypoxemia, or respiratory arrest.
• Succinylcholine and nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers may have unpredictable effects in myasthenia.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Impending/established myasthenic crisis requires ICU or equivalent high-dependency monitoring.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: International/Regional Consensus Guidelines for Myasthenia Gravis (2023, 2025).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute spinal cord compression is a time-critical emergency caused by pressure on the spinal cord (metastatic tumors, epidural abscess, hematoma, trauma).
• Severe/progressive neck or back pain. Radicular pain radiating to limbs.
• Limb weakness or progressive paralysis. Sensory loss, sensory level, paresthesia.
• Hyperreflexia/pathological reflexes. New bladder/bowel dysfunction. Gait disturbance.

[color=#991B1B]Red Flags:[/color] Known cancer with new severe back pain, fever/bacteremia/immunosuppression with spinal pain, recent spinal procedure/trauma, rapidly progressive deficits, new urinary retention/saddle sensory disturbance.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, neurological status. Document limb power, sensation, reflexes, bladder function.
• Maintain spinal precautions if traumatic instability suspected.
• Arrange emergency MRI of relevant spine.
• Obtain urgent neurosurgical/spinal surgical consultation.
• If metastatic cord compression suspected with neuro signs, initiate specialist-directed emergency management without waiting for deterioration.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Suspected Metastatic Spinal Cord Compression[/color]
• Dexamethasone 16 mg PO or IV promptly, followed by 16 mg daily while awaiting definitive treatment per protocol.
• Monitor glucose, mental status, infection risk, GI effects. Arrange urgent MRI and definitive oncology/surgical assessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Suspected Spinal Epidural Abscess[/color]
• Blood cultures promptly. Start empiric IV antibiotics covering Staph aureus per local resistance. Arrange emergency surgical assessment for neuro deficits/compression.
• Do not delay antibiotics in septic/unstable patient.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Traumatic Compression or Spinal Hematoma[/color]
• Maintain spinal precautions. Reverse anticoagulation if indicated. Arrange urgent spinal surgical evaluation.
• Avoid routine high-dose methylprednisolone unless specialist protocol supports.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Dexamethasone regimen applies to suspected metastatic cord compression, not every cause of spinal pain.
• Do not delay surgery/radiotherapy assessment while administering steroids.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit urgently. Progressive weakness, respiratory involvement, severe compression, or suspected epidural abscess requires emergency specialist management and often ICU.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE NG234; NICE Spinal Injury; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Cauda equina syndrome (CES) results from compression of lumbosacral nerve roots (commonly large lumbar disc herniation). May cause permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, and lower-limb dysfunction.
• New urinary retention, difficulty initiating urination, loss of awareness of bladder filling.
• New urinary/fecal incontinence. Saddle/perineal numbness. Bilateral sciatica or leg weakness.
• Reduced anal sensation. New sexual dysfunction.
• [color=#991B1B]No single symptom or exam finding reliably excludes CES.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Treat suspected CES as a time-critical neurological emergency.
• Document onset/progression of urinary, bowel, sensory, motor symptoms.
• Perform focused lower-limb neuro exam. Assess perineal sensation when appropriate with consent.
• Measure post-void residual bladder volume (low residual does NOT reliably exclude CES).
• Arrange emergency lumbar MRI and urgent spinal surgical consultation. Do NOT delay MRI.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Confirmed Compressive CES[/color]
• Arrange urgent decompression by spinal surgical team. Goal is to relieve compression as quickly as safely possible.
• Document neurological status before and after intervention.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Bladder Management[/color]
• Catheterize for acute urinary retention when indicated. Monitor renal function/urine output. Avoid assuming catheterization treats the emergency.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Supportive Care[/color]
• Analgesia, safe mobility/fall precautions, bowel function/pressure injury risk assessment. Arrange rehab/bladder/bowel follow-up.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not postpone surgical consultation while trying analgesics, physiotherapy, or outpatient investigations.
• There is no universally safe delay that can be applied to every patient.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • All suspected CES require emergency assessment and usually emergency MRI. Confirmed compression requires urgent spinal surgical management and inpatient care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: HSE National Clinical Guideline (2025); NHS England Pathway (2025).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Meningitis[/color]
• Fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, altered mental status.
• Petechial/purpuric rash may suggest meningococcal infection.

[color=#1E3A8A]Encephalitis[/color]
• Altered behavior/consciousness, fever, seizures, focal deficits, memory disturbance. HSV encephalitis suspicion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Treat as medical emergency. Assess ABCs, GCS, bedside glucose.
• Droplet precautions for suspected meningococcal disease.
• Obtain blood cultures promptly if no delay.
• Start empiric IV antibiotics immediately for bacterial meningitis.
• Give empiric IV acyclovir if encephalitis (especially HSV) suspected.
• Do not delay treatment for CT or LP when they cause significant delay.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric Antibiotics (Bacterial Meningitis)[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours.
• Add Vancomycin (if resistant pneumococcus concern).
• Add Ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours (if Listeria coverage needed: >50y, pregnancy, immunocompromised).

[color=#1E3A8A]Dexamethasone[/color]
• 10 mg IV every 6 hours for up to 4 days. Give before/with first antibiotic dose if pneumococcal suspected.

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected HSV Encephalitis: Acyclovir[/color]
• 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours (adjust for renal function). Infuse slowly; ensure hydration.

[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive Care[/color]
• Treat seizures. Maintain oxygenation. Manage ICP with specialist guidance. Isolation/public-health notification.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay antibiotics to administer dexamethasone.
• Acyclovir can cause crystal-associated kidney injury (dehydration, rapid infusion, renal impairment).
• Severe beta-lactam allergy requires an individualized alternative regimen.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit urgently; ICU for shock, severe encephalopathy, airway compromise, recurrent seizures, or raised ICP.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Guidelines on Meningitis (2025, 2026); Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
• Altered mental status. Hypotension/poor peripheral perfusion.
• Tachypnea, hypoxemia, respiratory failure. Oliguria/AKI.
• Elevated lactate, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy.
• Septic shock: Need for vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and initiate resuscitation immediately.
• Measure lactate. Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics if no significant delay.
• Start empiric IV antibiotics promptly (especially in septic shock).
• Give IV crystalloid for hypoperfusion/shock with frequent reassessment.
• Start norepinephrine if hypotension persists during/after fluid resuscitation.
• Identify and control the infection source (drainage, device removal).

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Empiric antibiotics[/color]
• Select regimen based on likely source, severity, local resistance, allergies, renal function.
• Examples: Ceftriaxone (community-acquired) or Piperacillin-tazobactam / Cefepime (severe hospital-associated).
• Add MRSA or anaerobic coverage only when indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Initial IV fluids[/color]
• Initial crystalloid volume around 30 mL/kg within first 3 hours (suggested, not inflexible). Use smaller boluses with reassessment if heart failure/kidney disease.
• Stop/reduce fluids when signs of fluid overload develop.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Norepinephrine[/color]
• First-line vasopressor. Titrate to MAP target ~65 mmHg.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Additional vasopressors[/color]
• Add vasopressin when norepinephrine requirements escalate. Consider epinephrine if MAP remains inadequate.

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Hydrocortisone[/color]
• 200 mg/day IV (50 mg every 6 hours or continuous infusion) in vasopressor-dependent shock.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• In septic shock, do not delay treatment for imaging or culture collection.
• Persistent hypotension after fluid administration requires vasopressor assessment, not endless fluid boluses.
• Steroids do not replace appropriate antibiotics, source control, fluids, or vasopressors.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • ICU/high-dependency for vasopressor-dependent shock, respiratory failure, altered consciousness, or progressive organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; Local antimicrobial protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection that may progress from a febrile illness to plasma leakage, shock, severe bleeding, or organ failure.
• Fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia.
• Nausea, vomiting, maculopapular rash, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia.

[color=#991B1B]Warning Signs:[/color]
• Severe/persistent abdominal pain. Persistent vomiting. Mucosal bleeding.
• Lethargy, restlessness, altered mental status. Fluid accumulation (ascites/pleural effusion).
• Hepatomegaly. Rising hematocrit with falling platelet count. Reduced urine output/narrowing pulse pressure.

[color=#1E3A8A]Severe Dengue:[/color] Severe plasma leakage (shock/respiratory distress), severe bleeding, or severe organ impairment (hepatitis, encephalopathy, myocarditis, AKI).
• Deterioration may occur as fever subsides (days 3–8).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, perfusion, urine output.
• Record BP, pulse pressure, cap refill, temperature, SpO2, weight.
• Establish IV access if warning signs, shock, bleeding, or poor oral intake.
• Obtain CBC with hematocrit/platelets. Assess for bleeding/fluid leakage.
• Avoid unnecessary IM injections and invasive procedures if bleeding risk is high.
• Activate resuscitation team for shock, respiratory distress, severe bleeding.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Without Warning Signs[/color]
• Oral fluids/ORS. Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours (max daily limit).
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid aspirin, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, prophylactic platelets.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. With Warning Signs[/color]
• Admit for observation. Monitor vitals, pulse pressure, fluid balance, urine output.
• IV isotonic crystalloid (0.9% NaCl or Ringer's lactate) at ~5–7 mL/kg/hour for 1–2 hours, then reassess and reduce.
• Avoid excessive IV fluids (risk of life-threatening pulmonary edema).

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Severe Dengue / Shock[/color]
• Initial crystalloid bolus 10–20 mL/kg over ~15–30 minutes depending on shock degree.
• Reassess perfusion, pulse pressure, cap refill, mental status, urine output, lactate, hematocrit after each bolus.
• If hematocrit falls while unstable, suspect significant bleeding. Do NOT repeat boluses automatically without reassessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Bleeding / Organ Failure[/color]
• Transfuse PRBCs/whole blood for significant hemorrhage. Do NOT transfuse platelets solely for low count.
• Treat AKI, hepatitis, encephalopathy, myocarditis per organ-support protocols.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Excessive IV fluid administration can cause life-threatening pulmonary edema, particularly during recovery.
• Deterioration may occur as fever subsides (days 3–8).
• Do not use NSAIDs due to bleeding and renal risks.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for warning signs, significant comorbidities, pregnancy, inability to maintain oral hydration.
• ICU for shock, respiratory distress, severe bleeding, altered consciousness, or severe organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Guidelines for Clinical Management of Arboviral Diseases (2025); CDC Dengue (2026).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Mosquito-borne viral illness characterized by abrupt fever and often severe, symmetric polyarthralgia.
• Sudden high fever.
• Severe pain in multiple joints (wrists, hands, ankles, feet). Joint swelling, difficulty walking/using hands.
• Myalgia, headache, rash, fatigue. Persistent/recurrent joint symptoms for weeks/months.

[color=#991B1B]Red Flags:[/color] Altered mental status, seizures, focal deficits. Chest pain, arrhythmia, myocarditis. Dyspnea, hypoxemia. Hypotension, AKI, severe dehydration, significant bleeding.
• Dengue and chikungunya can present similarly. Do not assume severe arthralgia excludes dengue.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vitals, hydration, perfusion, mental status.
• Evaluate for dengue, malaria, sepsis, leptospirosis.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid NSAIDs until dengue is reasonably excluded.[/color]
• Admit for organ dysfunction, hemodynamic instability, severe dehydration, or inability to care for self.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Fever and Pain[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours (within daily max).
• Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs while dengue remains possible.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Hydration[/color]
• Oral fluids/ORS. IV isotonic crystalloid for inadequate oral hydration or significant dehydration.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Persistent Joint Pain[/color]
• After dengue excluded: Consider limited course of NSAID (lowest effective dose). Avoid in active bleeding, renal impairment, dehydration, peptic ulcer disease.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Severe Disease[/color]
• Organ-specific supportive care for shock, myocarditis, encephalitis, AKI, respiratory failure.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not routinely prescribe systemic corticosteroids during acute uncomplicated infection.
• Persistent symptoms should prompt reassessment for alternative diagnoses and post-viral inflammatory arthritis.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Outpatient for stable patients who can maintain hydration and have reliable follow-up.
• Consider admission for neonates, older adults with comorbidities, pregnancy, severe pain preventing mobility, or organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Guidelines for Clinical Management of Arboviral Diseases (2025).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Potentially fatal parasitic infection. Maintain a low threshold for testing in patients with fever and relevant exposure.
• Fever, chills, sweating, headache, myalgia. Nausea, vomiting, weakness, abdominal discomfort.
• Anemia, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly.

[color=#1E3A8A]Severe Malaria Features:[/color] Impaired consciousness/coma, repeated seizures, severe anemia, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, shock/bleeding, AKI/hemoglobinuria, pulmonary edema.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, consciousness, glucose immediately.
• Perform malaria RDT and/or thick/thin films urgently.
• Obtain IV access, CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function, blood gas/lactate if severe.
• Treat hypoglycemia immediately.
• Do not delay treatment for suspected severe malaria while awaiting confirmatory results if suspicion is high.
• Assess for bacterial sepsis/coinfections.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Severe Malaria[/color]
• IV Artesunate: Adults/children ≥20 kg: 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 hours, then every 24 hours.
• Children < 20 kg: 3 mg/kg per dose.
• Continue parenteral until oral meds tolerated (min 24 hours). Complete with full course of oral ACT.
• Arrange follow-up for delayed hemolytic anemia.
