[color=#1E3A8A]B. Uncomplicated Falciparum Malaria[/color]
• Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), e.g., Artemether-lumefantrine (4 tablets per dose for ≥35 kg; 6 doses over 3 days). Administer with food/milk to improve absorption.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Hypoglycemia[/color]
• Check bedside glucose immediately and repeat frequently. IV dextrose per protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Fluids and Organ Support[/color]
• Cautious, individualized fluid management (risk of pulmonary edema).
• Treat seizures, acidosis, renal failure, anemia, respiratory failure per standard protocols.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Severe malaria is a medical emergency requiring admission and close monitoring.
• Do not use oral therapy alone for severe malaria.
• Do not treat suspected malaria with an incomplete or unverified antimalarial regimen.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• All severe malaria requires admission, urgent parenteral treatment, close monitoring (ICU).
• Uncomplicated malaria outpatient only if tolerating oral therapy, no severe features, reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Guidelines for Malaria (2026); National Malaria Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Systemic infection caused by Salmonella enterica serovars Typhi or Paratyphi.
• Sustained fever, headache, malaise, anorexia. Abdominal pain, constipation, or diarrhea.
• Hepatosplenomegaly. Relative bradycardia (not sensitive/specific).
• Severe: encephalopathy, GI bleeding, intestinal perforation, shock.
• Consider malaria, dengue, brucellosis, leptospirosis, bacterial sepsis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess hemodynamic stability and screen for sepsis.
• Look for peritonitis, GI bleeding, altered mental status, dehydration.
• Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when possible.
• Review recent antibiotic exposure, travel, local resistance.
• Start empiric treatment promptly in severe illness after cultures.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Antibiotic Therapy[/color]
• Ceftriaxone: Adults 2 g IV every 24 hours (for hospitalized uncomplicated). Severe/complicated may require specialist-directed treatment.
• Adjust according to culture/susceptibility.
• Fluoroquinolones not used empirically where resistance is prevalent.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Supportive Care[/color]
• Oral fluids if tolerated. IV isotonic crystalloid for significant dehydration/shock.
• Correct electrolytes/glucose. Paracetamol for fever.
• Avoid antimotility drugs in severe inflammatory diarrhea.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Perforation / Hemorrhage[/color]
• Urgent surgical assessment, resuscitation, crossmatch, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering enteric organisms + anaerobes.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Widal testing alone is not reliable to establish acute enteric fever.
• A negative blood culture does not completely exclude the diagnosis (especially after prior antibiotics).

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for shock, severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding, suspected perforation, encephalopathy, inability to take oral therapy.
• Outpatient only for stable patients with reliable follow-up and suitable oral regimen.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO guidance on enteric fever; CDC Typhoid guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute intestinal infection causing profuse watery diarrhea, rapid dehydration, hypovolemic shock, and death if fluids not replaced.
• Sudden profuse watery diarrhea. Vomiting, muscle cramps.
• Thirst, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor.
• Tachycardia, weak pulse, hypotension, delayed cap refill, oliguria/anuria.
• Do NOT wait for laboratory confirmation before rehydrating.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess circulation, mental status, pulse, BP, cap refill, urine output.
• Estimate dehydration degree. Start immediate rehydration.
• Use ORS as soon as patient can drink safely.
• Implement infection-prevention measures and outbreak notification.
• Obtain electrolytes/renal function in severe dehydration when available.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Severe Dehydration / Shock[/color]
• Ringer's lactate preferred (or appropriate isotonic crystalloid).
• WHO Plan C: 100 mL/kg total over 3 hours (≥1 year) or 6 hours (<1 year), with first 30 mL/kg delivered more rapidly.
• Replace ongoing stool/vomit losses. Start ORS as soon as safe.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)[/color]
• Frequent small amounts as tolerated. Replace ongoing stool losses.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Antibiotics[/color]
• Adjunct for severe cholera (never replace rehydration). Doxycycline or azithromycin (if susceptible/appropriate).

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Additional Care[/color]
• Continue feeding/breastfeeding. Correct electrolyte abnormalities. Monitor for AKI/hypoglycemia. Zinc in children.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid hypotonic solutions as initial resuscitation fluid for hypovolemic shock.
• Reassess frequently in patients with heart failure or renal impairment.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for severe dehydration, shock, persistent vomiting, electrolyte disturbance, AKI.
• Mild/no dehydration may be treated with ORS and return precautions.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO cholera treatment and outbreak management guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Deep neck space infections can spread rapidly and cause airway obstruction, sepsis, mediastinitis, or vascular complications.
• Fever and severe sore throat. Neck pain, stiffness, restricted neck movement.
• Dysphagia, odynophagia, or drooling. Muffled voice or trismus. Neck swelling or asymmetry.
• Stridor, respiratory distress, toxic appearance in severe cases.
• Retropharyngeal abscess particularly important in young children; parapharyngeal in both children and adults.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and signs of sepsis.
• Obtain urgent ENT and anesthesia consultation if airway compromise possible.
• Keep patient nil by mouth. Establish IV access and obtain relevant blood tests.
• Start IV antibiotics promptly in suspected severe infection.
• Arrange contrast-enhanced CT of neck in stable patients when needed to define extent.
• Do not delay airway protection or surgical assessment for imaging in an unstable patient.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Empiric IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Select according to age, allergy, local resistance, severity.
• Example: Ampicillin–sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours (adults), adjusted for renal function.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Airway Management[/color]
• Early expert airway intervention for progressive obstruction, distress, inability to manage secretions, rapidly worsening swelling.
• Difficult-airway and surgical-airway backup plan.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Drainage[/color]
• Urgent surgical drainage for significant drainable abscesses, airway compromise, complications, or failure to improve with medical therapy. Small collections may be managed medically under close supervision.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Supportive Care[/color]
• IV fluids, analgesia, antipyretics. Monitor for sepsis, mediastinal extension, vascular complications.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Broader coverage (including MRSA) may be required based on risk factors and local epidemiology.
• Avoid unnecessary sedation and repeated airway manipulation.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit for IV treatment and ENT assessment. Airway compromise, sepsis, extensive infection, or need for airway intervention requires ICU-level care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: IDSA antimicrobial principles; Local ENT protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Unexplained altered consciousness, seizures, respiratory depression, arrhythmia, metabolic acidosis, abnormal pupils, unusual secretions, or history of exposure.

[color=#1E3A8A]Important toxidromes:[/color]
• Opioid: Reduced consciousness, slow breathing, pinpoint pupils.
• Sympathomimetic: Agitation, sweating, hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia.
• Anticholinergic: Agitation, hot dry skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention.
• Cholinergic: Salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, diarrhea, bradycardia, seizures.
• Sedative-hypnotic: Drowsiness, ataxia, slurred speech, respiratory depression.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Protect staff and patient from ongoing contamination.
• Assess ABCs, glucose, temperature, ECG, vital signs.
• Remove contaminated clothing and irrigate exposed skin/eyes.
• Support ventilation and circulation. Identify agent, amount, route, time.
• Contact a poison center or clinical toxicologist.
• Do NOT induce vomiting. Avoid routine antidote use without indication.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Activated charcoal[/color]
• 50 g orally or via gastric tube in selected poisonings. Consider only for selected substances when ingestion recent (within ~1 hour) and benefit outweighs risks. Protect airway.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Opioid toxicity: Naloxone[/color]
• Titrate IV naloxone to restore adequate ventilation (e.g., 0.04–0.1 mg IV initially). Larger doses may be required in severe respiratory depression.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Acetaminophen/Paracetamol toxicity: NAC[/color]
• Start NAC according to established protocol. Assess timing, concentration, LFTs, INR, renal function.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Cholinergic poisoning[/color]
• Atropine IV, repeat rapidly and escalate doses according to clinical response. Endpoint is improvement in bronchial secretions, oxygenation, ventilation, circulation.

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Benzodiazepines for toxicological seizures[/color]
• Use appropriate benzodiazepine regimen. Monitor respiratory status, oxygenation, BP, consciousness.

[color=#1E3A8A]F. General management[/color]
• Treat hypoglycemia, hypoxia, shock, hyperthermia, arrhythmias. Agent-specific antidotes when indicated. Consider hemodialysis for selected severe poisonings.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not give charcoal to patients with unprotected airway or for caustics, alcohols, metals (e.g., iron).
• The aim of naloxone is adequate ventilation, not necessarily complete awakening.
• Flumazenil is not routinely recommended in undifferentiated overdose.
• Do not delay life-saving supportive care while waiting for toxicology test results.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for persistent symptoms, significant ECG abnormalities, metabolic acidosis, seizures, respiratory depression, or exposure to potentially lethal substance.
• ICU for severe poisoning requiring airway support, vasopressors, or management of life-threatening arrhythmia.
• Intentional poisoning requires mental-health assessment once medically stable.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO clinical protocols for poisoning; Local toxicology guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Consider specific toxic exposures when history, toxidrome, ECG, or labs suggest:
• Paracetamol, Salicylates, Methanol/Ethylene glycol, Tricyclic antidepressants (TCA), Beta-blockers/Calcium channel blockers (CCB), Digoxin, Isoniazid.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stabilize ABCs, glucose, temperature. Obtain ECG, electrolytes, renal function, blood gas, targeted drug concentrations.
• Contact poison center/toxicologist early.
• Do not delay life-saving antidotes when indication is clear.
• Assess need for hemodialysis in severe toxic alcohol, salicylate, lithium poisonings.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Salicylate poisoning[/color]
• Sodium bicarbonate IV to alkalinize serum/urine (e.g., 150 mEq in 1 L D5W). Goal urine pH 7.5–8.0. Monitor K+.
• Hemodialysis for severe neuro toxicity, pulmonary edema, renal failure, refractory acid-base disturbances.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Methanol/Ethylene glycol[/color]
• Fomepizole: 15 mg/kg IV initial dose, subsequent doses per protocol. Urgent toxicology/nephrology for possible dialysis.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA)[/color]
• Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg IV for significant QRS widening, ventricular dysrhythmia, or hypotension. Repeat per ECG/hemodynamics.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Beta-blocker/CCB overdose[/color]
• High-dose insulin euglycemia therapy. IV calcium (for CCB). Vasopressors. Glucagon (for beta-blocker). Consult toxicology early.

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Digoxin toxicity[/color]
• Digoxin immune Fab (dosing based on level/dose/severity). Monitor K+ closely (may change rapidly).

[color=#1E3A8A]F. Isoniazid-associated seizures[/color]
• Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6): Gram-for-gram with INH ingested. If unknown in severe presentation, 5 g IV initial.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not use flumazenil routinely in undifferentiated overdose.
• Do not induce vomiting.
• Avoid intubation in salicylate poisoning if possible (loss of compensatory hyperventilation can worsen acidemia).
• Do not use physostigmine in suspected TCA poisoning.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit significant toxicity, abnormal ECG, metabolic acidosis, persistent symptoms, or dangerous exposures.
• ICU for refractory seizures, shock, severe acid-base disturbances, or antidote infusions.
• Intentional overdose requires psychosocial assessment after stabilization.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EXTRIP Workgroup; ACMT Guidance; Local poison-center protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
CO is a colorless, odorless gas causing tissue hypoxia/cellular toxicity.
• Sources: Generators/heaters indoors, charcoal, fires/smoke, vehicle exhaust.
• Headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, vomiting, confusion, impaired coordination.
• Chest pain, arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia. Seizures, syncope, coma, cardiac arrest.
• Suspect when several people in same environment develop symptoms.
• [color=#991B1B]A normal conventional pulse oximeter does NOT exclude CO poisoning.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Remove from exposure without endangering rescuers.
• Administer 100% oxygen immediately.
• Assess ABCs, mental status, glucose. Obtain IV access and continuous ECG monitoring.
• Contact poison center/hyperbaric service for severe poisoning.
• Assess for concurrent burns, smoke inhalation, cyanide toxicity.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. High-Concentration Oxygen[/color]
• 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask. If airway inadequate, assist ventilation/intubate.
• Continue oxygen until symptoms resolve and assessment supports stopping (often ~4–5 hours).
• Do not withhold oxygen while waiting for lab results.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Hyperbaric Oxygen (HBO) Assessment[/color]
• Consider for COHb ~25–30%+, LOC/neurological impairment, cardiac ischemia, severe acidosis, pregnancy.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Severe Poisoning[/color]
• Manage seizures, shock, myocardial ischemia per protocols. Intubate for coma/airway compromise.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Conventional pulse oximetry cannot reliably distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin.
• COHb may be deceptively low if oxygen was administered before sampling.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for LOC, persistent neuro abnormalities, cardiac injury, severe acidosis, ongoing symptoms.
• Discharged patients need clear instructions about delayed neurological symptoms.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: CDC CO Poisoning Guidance (2026); UHMS Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Serotonin syndrome is a potentially life-threatening drug-induced toxidrome caused by excessive serotonergic activity. May develop after overdose, drug interaction, or increased dose.
• Triggers: SSRIs/SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, linezolid, combinations of serotonergic drugs, certain recreational substances.
• Agitation, confusion, restlessness. Diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension.
• Tremor, hyperreflexia, inducible/spontaneous clonus. Ocular clonus.
• Hyperthermia and muscle rigidity in severe cases.
• [color=#991B1B]Clonus and hyperreflexia strongly support serotonin toxicity.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stop suspected serotonergic agents immediately.
• Assess ABCs, temperature, mental status. Establish IV access and continuous monitoring in moderate/severe cases.
• Check glucose, electrolytes, renal function, CK, blood gas when severe.
• Begin active cooling for significant hyperthermia.
• Contact toxicology/poison center for severe cases.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Discontinue Causative Agents[/color]
• Stop serotonergic drugs. Review all prescribed/OTC/recreational substances.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Benzodiazepines[/color]
• Lorazepam 1–2 mg IV for significant agitation, tremor, or muscle activity. Repeat titrated doses per protocol. Monitor respiratory rate, SpO2, BP, consciousness.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Hyperthermia and Severe Toxicity[/color]
• Active external cooling for significant hyperthermia. IV isotonic fluid if indicated. Severe cases require ICU assessment (intubation, deep sedation, neuromuscular paralysis may be required).
• Antipyretics are NOT effective for serotonin-related hyperthermia. Avoid physical restraints (increase exertion/heat).

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Cyproheptadine (Adjunct)[/color]
• Consider only as adjunct in selected patients with persistent moderate/severe symptoms after supportive treatment, with toxicology advice.
• 12 mg initial PO, followed by 2 mg every 2 hours until improvement, then 8 mg every 6 hours if needed. Follow local toxicology guidance.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• There is no confirmatory serum serotonin test; diagnosis is clinical.
• Cyproheptadine must not delay airway management, cooling, or sedation.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Mild symptoms: observe until resolution and stable vitals per toxicology guidance.
• Admit for persistent autonomic instability, significant clonus, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, or organ dysfunction. Severe cases require ICU.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Irish Association for Emergency Medicine (2024); Chiew & Isbister (2025); Local toxicology protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Opioid toxicity can cause life-threatening respiratory depression. May follow therapeutic use, accidental ingestion, intentional overdose, or illicit opioid exposure.
• Reduced respiratory rate or shallow breathing.
• Reduced consciousness. Pinpoint pupils (may be absent).
• Hypoxemia, cyanosis, or hypercapnia. Bradycardia and hypotension in severe cases.
• Aspiration or pulmonary edema in complicated presentations.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, level of consciousness. Call for emergency airway/resuscitation support.
• Open airway and provide assisted ventilation when breathing inadequate.
• Administer oxygen and use bag-mask ventilation when indicated.
• Give naloxone promptly for suspected opioid-induced respiratory depression.
• Check blood glucose. Consider co-ingestants and alternative causes of reduced consciousness.
• Do NOT delay ventilation while preparing naloxone.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Naloxone[/color]
• If IV access available: 0.04 mg IV initially (if opioid dependence possible and not in immediate life-threatening apnea).
• Escalate to 0.1–0.2 mg, 0.4 mg, then larger doses as needed per protocol.
• In apnea or severe life-threatening respiratory depression: do NOT delay effective treatment for cautious low-dose titration; use appropriate initial dose (commonly 0.4–2 mg IV/IM/IN).
• Repeat doses may be necessary.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Recurrent Respiratory Depression[/color]
• Repeat naloxone per clinical response.
• Consider naloxone infusion when repeated boluses required or long-acting opioid toxicity suspected (starting ~two-thirds of effective reversal bolus dose per hour).

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Supportive Care[/color]
• Maintain airway and ventilation. Treat hypoglycemia and other reversible causes. Assess for aspiration, trauma, co-ingestion. Avoid flumazenil as routine treatment.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Naloxone may precipitate acute withdrawal, agitation, vomiting, aspiration in opioid-dependent patients.
• Its duration may be shorter than that of the opioid (especially methadone or extended-release preparations).

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Observe until respiratory function and consciousness remain stable without repeated naloxone and risk from suspected opioid assessed.
• Admit for recurrent respiratory depression, long-acting opioid exposure, aspiration, pulmonary complications, significant co-ingestion, or ongoing oxygen/ventilatory requirements.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA Opioid-Associated Emergencies; WHO Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Life-threatening complication of local anesthetic exposure, commonly following inadvertent intravascular injection or excessive dosing. Can cause seizures, cardiovascular collapse, malignant arrhythmias.
• Early neuro: Circumoral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, agitation, confusion, dizziness, seizures.
• Severe: Reduced consciousness, hypotension, bradycardia/conduction abnormalities, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiac arrest.
• Presentation may be atypical or delayed, especially after infiltration or long-acting local anesthetics.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stop local anesthetic administration immediately.
• Call for resuscitation assistance and LAST rescue kit.
• Provide 100% oxygen and support ventilation.
• Treat seizures promptly with benzodiazepines.
• Start standard resuscitation while recognizing LAST requires modifications to routine ACLS.
• Administer 20% IV lipid emulsion promptly for serious LAST.
• Arrange ICU-level monitoring and expert consultation.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Seizure Control[/color]
• Midazolam 1–2 mg IV increments, titrated to seizure control per protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. 20% Lipid Emulsion[/color]
• If weight <70 kg: 1.5 mL/kg IV over 2–3 mins, then 0.25 mL/kg/min.
• If weight ≥70 kg: 100 mL IV over 2–3 mins, then ~250 mL over 15–20 mins.
• May repeat bolus and increase infusion if instability persists. Maximum cumulative dose ~12 mL/kg.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Modified Resuscitation[/color]
• Follow ASRA LAST checklist.
• Avoid vasopressin, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, and additional local anesthetic drugs when protocol advises.
• Epinephrine: smaller-than-standard doses (initially <1 mcg/kg).

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Monitoring After Stabilization[/color]
• Observe for recurrent neuro/cardiovascular toxicity. Prolonged monitored observation (at least 4–6 hours after stabilization; longer after cardiac arrest).

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not confuse 20% lipid emulsion with propofol.
• Lipid emulsion is a rescue treatment for serious LAST, not routine treatment for minor local anesthetic symptoms.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit patients with seizures, significant neurological symptoms, cardiovascular instability, or lipid rescue treatment for monitored care. Cardiac arrest or persistent instability requires ICU admission.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ASRA LAST Checklist (2020 and updates).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Heat stroke[/color]
• Severe heat illness with CNS dysfunction (confusion, seizures, coma) associated with heat exposure/exertion.
• Core temperature often > 40°C.
• Complications: Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, liver injury, coagulopathy, shock.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hypothermia[/color]
• Core temperature < 35°C.
• Shivering, confusion, bradycardia, poor coordination, reduced consciousness, dysrhythmias.
• Severe hypothermia may produce profound bradycardia or apparent death.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Heat stroke[/color]
• Move patient away from heat, remove excess clothing.
• Assess ABCs, glucose, core temperature, neurological status.
• Begin active cooling immediately. Establish IV access.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hypothermia[/color]
• Move to warm environment. Remove wet clothing, insulate from ground.
• Handle gently. Assess circulation/breathing carefully.
• Begin appropriate rewarming and continuous cardiac monitoring.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Heat stroke: rapid active cooling[/color]
• Whole-body cold-water immersion is preferred for exertional heat stroke. If impractical, use cold wet towels, ice sheets, evaporative cooling.
• Aim to reduce core temp rapidly to ~39°C, then stop intensive cooling to avoid overcooling.
• Antipyretics are NOT effective for heat stroke and may worsen hepatic/renal injury.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Heat stroke with shock[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid boluses guided by perfusion and response.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Seizures during heat illness[/color]
• Treat with benzodiazepine regimen. Continue rapid cooling.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Hypothermia: rewarming[/color]
• Mild: Insulation, dry clothing, passive rewarming.
• Moderate/Severe: Active external rewarming and warmed IV fluids. Forced-air warming or approved devices.

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Cardiac arrest in severe hypothermia[/color]
• Follow ALS protocol adapted for hypothermia. Consider extracorporeal life support where available.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay cooling while waiting for laboratory results.
• Avoid uncontrolled overcooling.
• Avoid direct high heat on insensate skin and rough handling in hypothermia.
• Do not conclude death solely from profound cooling without following appropriate resuscitation protocols.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Heat stroke requires emergency hospital assessment and usually admission; ICU for organ dysfunction, shock, seizures, or persistent encephalopathy.
• Moderate-to-severe hypothermia, dysrhythmias, reduced consciousness, or hemodynamic instability requires monitored hospital care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/Red Cross 2024 First Aid Guidelines; AHA 2024 Hypothermia Update.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
HAPE is a potentially fatal form of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema that occurs after rapid ascent to high altitude without adequate acclimatization (generally > 2,500–3,000 m).
• Early: Reduced exercise tolerance, exaggerated breathlessness on exertion, dry cough, chest tightness, unusual fatigue.
• Progressive: Dyspnea at rest, marked tachypnea/tachycardia, cough with pink/blood-stained sputum, crackles, hypoxemia, cyanosis, confusion.
• Consider pneumonia, PE, asthma, cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stop ascent and minimize exertion.
• Give supplemental oxygen immediately.
• [color=#991B1B]Arrange descent to a lower altitude as soon as safely possible.[/color]
• Keep the patient warm and avoid unnecessary exertion.
• Use a portable hyperbaric chamber if descent is impossible and available.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Oxygen and Descent[/color]
• Give supplemental O2 sufficient to improve oxygenation and symptoms (aim SpO2 > 90%).
• Descend promptly (generally at least 1,000 m or until substantial clinical improvement).
• Descent and oxygen are the primary treatments; do not delay them for imaging/labs.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Nifedipine[/color]
• Consider only when descent is delayed/impossible and oxygen/HBO unavailable/inadequate.
• Extended-release nifedipine 30 mg PO every 12 hours (or 20 mg every 8 hours) per protocol.
• Avoid rapid-release sublingual nifedipine. Use caution in hypotension/shock.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Respiratory Support[/color]
• Escalate to high-flow O2 or positive-pressure ventilation when necessary. Transfer severe cases to critical care.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Nifedipine is not a substitute for descent and oxygen.
• Do not delay descent and oxygen while obtaining imaging or laboratory results.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• All suspected HAPE cases require urgent medical assessment and descent.
• Severe hypoxemia, respiratory distress, confusion, or failure to improve requires emergency evacuation and hospital admission.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: CDC Yellow Book; Wilderness Medical Society Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) results from rapid release of intracellular contents after cancer cell breakdown (spontaneously or after treatment).
• Associated with high-grade lymphomas, acute leukemias, large tumor burden, elevated baseline uric acid, renal impairment.
• Typical biochemical abnormalities: Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, secondary hypocalcemia.
• AKI, arrhythmias, seizures, or sudden death.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, cardiac rhythm, renal function, neurologic status.
• Attach ECG monitoring if significant potassium abnormalities or severe TLS suspected.
• Obtain urgent electrolytes, calcium, phosphate, uric acid, creatinine, urea, LDH, glucose.
• Start appropriate IV hydration if not contraindicated.
• Treat dangerous hyperkalemia immediately.
• Involve hematology and nephrology urgently.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IV hydration[/color]
• Preventive approach in high-risk patients: ~2–3 L/m²/day (individualized).
• Established TLS requires individualized fluid management. Do not force hydration in oliguria/pulmonary edema.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Allopurinol (Prevention)[/color]
• 100 mg/m² orally every 8 hours (max 800 mg/day) adjusted for renal function.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Rasburicase (Established hyperuricemia)[/color]
• 0.15–0.2 mg/kg IV once, repeat per uric acid response/protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (risk of hemolysis/methemoglobinemia).[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Manage dangerous electrolyte abnormalities[/color]
• Hyperkalemia: Emergency protocol (Calcium, Insulin/Glucose, definitive removal).
• Hyperphosphatemia: Restrict intake, phosphate binders. Nephrology input for severe/refractory.
• Hypocalcemia: Treat only if symptomatic or specific indication. Avoid unnecessary calcium (worsens calcium-phosphate precipitation).

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Routine urine alkalinization with bicarbonate is not recommended for TLS prevention (worsens calcium-phosphate precipitation).
• Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
• Severe TLS may require urgent renal replacement therapy.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit patients with established TLS to a monitored inpatient setting; ICU for severe electrolyte abnormalities, arrhythmias, seizures, shock, or significant renal failure.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: British Society for Haematology (2025); Local oncology protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
An acute hemolytic transfusion reaction may occur when transfused red cells are destroyed rapidly, commonly because of ABO incompatibility.
• Fever, chills, or rigors. Back, flank, chest, or infusion-site pain.
• Hypotension, tachycardia, or dyspnea. Dark urine or hemoglobinuria.
• Unexpected bleeding or oozing. Rapid deterioration or unexplained shock.
• Consider other reactions (bacterial contamination, anaphylaxis, TRALI).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• [color=#991B1B]STOP the transfusion immediately.[/color]
• Maintain IV access using new tubing and compatible isotonic fluid per protocol.
• Assess ABCs. Recheck patient identity and blood product details.
• Notify blood bank and treating senior clinician immediately.
• Send blood bag and tubing for investigation. Do NOT restart the implicated blood unit.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Repeat patient/blood-product identity checks. Direct antiglobulin test (DAT).
• CBC and serial hemoglobin. Plasma free hemoglobin, bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin.
• Renal function, potassium, urinalysis. PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, platelets if DIC suspected.
• Blood cultures from patient and product if bacterial contamination suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Supportive Resuscitation[/color]
• Oxygen, careful IV crystalloid, and vasopressors for hypotension. Monitor ECG, BP, SpO2, urine output, renal function.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Kidney Protection[/color]
• Monitor urine output, creatinine, K+, acid-base. Maintain renal perfusion while avoiding fluid overload. Treat hyperkalemia promptly. Arrange dialysis for standard indications.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation[/color]
• Monitor platelets, coagulation, fibrinogen. Treat underlying reaction and support circulation. Use blood components per active bleeding/procedures.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Reporting and Prevention[/color]
• Document suspected reaction. Preserve implicated product/samples. Formally report and investigate.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not give fluids without reassessment in patients with heart failure or pulmonary edema.
• Diuretics are not a substitute for adequate resuscitation.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit patients with suspected acute hemolysis, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, renal injury, coagulopathy, or other systemic complications.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AABB Transfusion-Reaction Guidance; BSH Transfusion Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute angle-closure glaucoma is a sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency caused by sudden increase in intraocular pressure due to impaired aqueous humor drainage.
• Severe unilateral eye pain. Blurred vision or colored halos.
• Headache, nausea, vomiting. Red eye with hazy cornea.
• Mid-dilated, poorly reactive pupil. Markedly elevated IOP.
• May be mistaken for migraine, GI illness, or other headache causes.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Arrange immediate ophthalmology consultation.
• Assess visual acuity in both eyes. Measure IOP if trained/equipped.
• Check pupil, cornea, degree of redness. Provide analgesia/antiemetic.
• Start appropriate pressure-lowering treatment while arranging definitive ophthalmic care.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Lower Intraocular Pressure[/color]
• Acetazolamide: 500 mg IV or PO initial dose. Monitor response, renal function, K+, bicarbonate.
• Topical: Timolol 0.5% one drop, Brimonidine 0.2% one drop (if appropriate). Monitor for systemic beta-blocker effects.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Pilocarpine[/color]
• 1–2% eye drops may be used under ophthalmology guidance once IOP has begun to fall and iris likely to respond. May be ineffective at extremely high pressure.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Refractory Severe Pressure Elevation[/color]
• IV mannitol may be considered by ophthalmology for very high pressure/inadequate response. Assess cardiac/renal status first.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Definitive Treatment[/color]
• Laser peripheral iridotomy is commonly used for pupillary-block angle closure. Fellow eye must be assessed.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid or use only with specialist direction in significant renal/hepatic disease, severe electrolyte abnormalities, or relevant drug hypersensitivity.
• Do not use pilocarpine automatically in every red eye; inappropriate in some secondary angle-closure mechanisms.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Immediate ophthalmology management is required. Do not discharge before urgent specialist assessment and documented treatment plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Primary Angle-Closure Disease PPP (2025); RCOphth Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is acute retinal ischemia and is managed as an eye stroke. It may cause permanent monocular visual loss and indicates possible systemic vascular disease.
• Sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye. Markedly reduced visual acuity.
• Relative afferent pupillary defect. Retinal whitening or cherry-red spot on funduscopy.
• Consider giant cell arteritis in patients > 50 years with new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Establish exact time patient was last known to have normal vision.
• Arrange immediate transfer to ED or stroke center with ophthalmology support.
• Perform focused neuro and cardiovascular assessment. Check glucose and BP.
• Activate acute stroke pathway where appropriate.
• Do not delay referral for outpatient eye investigations.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Acute Stroke-Center Assessment[/color]
• Immediate stroke and ophthalmology consultation. Evaluate eligibility for time-sensitive reperfusion under receiving center protocol.
• IV thrombolysis may be considered in selected patients with disabling visual loss who meet criteria; evidence is evolving.
• Ocular massage and anterior chamber paracentesis have not demonstrated reliable benefit and may cause harm; should not delay stroke-center referral.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Suspected Giant Cell Arteritis[/color]
• If strongly suspected, arrange immediate specialist assessment and systemic corticosteroid treatment to protect the other eye. Do not delay treatment while awaiting temporal artery imaging/biopsy.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Secondary Prevention[/color]
• Investigate carotid disease, AF, other embolic sources. Manage HTN, diabetes, dyslipidemia, smoking.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content: • Do not assume an intervention is beneficial simply because it is traditionally used for retinal artery occlusion.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Immediate transfer to a stroke-capable center is required. Sudden monocular visual loss should never be managed as a routine outpatient eye complaint.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA Scientific Statement on CRAO (2021); AAO Guidance (2025–2026).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Wheezing, cough, breathlessness, chest tightness, and prolonged expiration.
• Assess speech, feeding, respiratory rate, accessory muscle use, air entry, oxygen saturation, and mental status.
• Severe signs include marked work of breathing, inability to speak or feed normally, exhaustion, cyanosis, or poor air entry.
• A silent chest, altered consciousness, or respiratory exhaustion indicates impending respiratory failure.
• Consider anaphylaxis, foreign-body aspiration, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and other causes of wheeze.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and oxygen saturation.
• Position the child comfortably and minimize distress.
• Give inhaled salbutamol promptly.
• Add ipratropium for moderate-to-severe exacerbations according to the local protocol.
• Give systemic corticosteroids early for moderate-to-severe attacks.
• Escalate immediately for poor air entry, exhaustion, altered mental status, or inadequate response.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Salbutamol (albuterol)[/color]
• MDI with spacer: 4–10 puffs (100 mcg/puff), one puff at a time, repeated every 20 minutes during the first hour.
• Nebulized: 2.5 mg (smaller children) or 5 mg (larger children), repeated according to protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Ipratropium bromide[/color]
• Nebulized: 250 mcg (smaller children) or 500 mcg (larger children), repeated during initial treatment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Systemic corticosteroid[/color]
• Prednisolone orally: 1–2 mg/kg once daily (max local dose) for 3–5 days.

[color=#1E3A8A]Magnesium sulfate (severe refractory)[/color]
• IV: 25–50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over ~20 minutes.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Excessive beta-agonist exposure may cause tachycardia, tremor, hypokalemia, and lactic acidosis.
• Deterioration or poor air entry despite treatment requires urgent escalation.
• Steroids do not provide immediate bronchodilation; continue inhaled bronchodilator treatment as indicated.
• Rapid IV magnesium administration can cause hypotension.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Discharge only after sustained clinical improvement, stable oxygenation, and an appropriate home treatment and follow-up plan.
• Admit for persistent distress, frequent bronchodilator requirement, hypoxemia, or significant risk factors.
• ICU referral is indicated for impending respiratory failure.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO; Children's Acute Transport Service (CATS).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Usually affects infants under 2 years, especially those under 12 months.
• Coryza followed by cough, tachypnea, crackles, wheeze, and increased work of breathing.
• Feeding difficulty, dehydration, apnea, or hypoxemia may occur.
• Severe disease is more likely in very young infants, premature infants, and children with significant cardiopulmonary disease or immunodeficiency.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, respiratory effort, oxygen saturation, feeding, hydration, and apnea history.
• Clear nasal secretions gently when they interfere with breathing or feeding.
• Provide oxygen for persistent hypoxemia according to age and local guideline thresholds.
• Support feeding with small frequent feeds if safe.
• Use nasogastric or IV fluids if oral intake is inadequate.
• Escalate urgently for apnea, exhaustion, severe respiratory distress, or altered consciousness.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Oxygen therapy[/color]
• Give supplemental oxygen for persistent hypoxemia according to local policy.
• Do not use oxygen saturation alone to determine severity; work of breathing, apnea, and feeding are also important.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hydration and feeding[/color]
• Continue breastfeeding and age-appropriate feeds when safe.
• If oral intake is inadequate, use nasogastric or IV fluids.
• Avoid forcing oral feeds in a child with significant respiratory distress.

[color=#1E3A8A]Nasal secretion management[/color]
• Use gentle superficial nasal suction when secretions impair breathing or feeding.
• Avoid routine deep suctioning because it can cause trauma.

[color=#1E3A8A]Treatments generally NOT recommended routinely[/color]
• Salbutamol, corticosteroids, antibiotics (unless bacterial infection suspected), nebulized adrenaline, or chest physiotherapy.

sections.heading: 04 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Discharge when breathing is stable, oxygenation meets local criteria, feeding and hydration are adequate, and caregivers understand warning signs.
• Admit for apnea, persistent hypoxemia, significant respiratory distress, dehydration, or inability to feed.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO; NICE. Bronchiolitis in children.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Fever, cough, tachypnea, chest indrawing, crackles, or reduced air entry.
• Hypoxemia, grunting, cyanosis, inability to drink, lethargy, or exhaustion suggest severe disease.
• Consider viral pneumonia, bacterial pneumonia, aspiration, pleural effusion, and tuberculosis where relevant.
• Infants may present with poor feeding, apnea, temperature instability, or nonspecific deterioration.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, work of breathing, hydration, and mental status.
• Give oxygen for hypoxemia according to the local protocol.
• Check bedside glucose in severely ill infants.
• Obtain IV access if shock, severe dehydration, or inability to tolerate oral treatment.
• If sepsis is suspected, obtain cultures when feasible and start appropriate antibiotics promptly.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotic treatment[/color]
• Uncomplicated outpatient: Oral amoxicillin 40–45 mg/kg per dose every 12 hours (subject to local guideline).
• Severe pneumonia requiring admission: IV ampicillin, benzylpenicillin, or ceftriaxone according to severity and local guidance.
• Do not give antibiotics routinely for clearly viral illness.

[color=#1E3A8A]Fever and pain control[/color]
• Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg orally every 4–6 hours (within local max).
• Ibuprofen may be considered in age-eligible, adequately hydrated children.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Persistent hypoxemia, exhaustion, apnea, or altered consciousness requires urgent escalation.
• Neonates and young infants require age-specific sepsis/pneumonia protocols.
• Suspected empyema or necrotizing pneumonia requires specialist review.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Outpatient care may be appropriate when the child is clinically stable and caregivers can provide safe follow-up.
• Admit for hypoxemia, severe respiratory distress, dehydration, or complications.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO; NICE. Pneumonia: diagnosis and management.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Usually affects children aged 6 months to 6 years.
• Barking cough, hoarseness, inspiratory stridor, symptoms often worse at night.
• Assess stridor at rest, chest retractions, air entry, oxygen saturation, agitation, and mental status.
• Severe features: marked retractions, persistent stridor at rest, reduced air entry, exhaustion, cyanosis.
• Consider epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, foreign-body aspiration, and anaphylaxis if atypical or toxic.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Keep the child calm with a caregiver; minimize distress and unnecessary examination.
• Assess airway, breathing, oxygen saturation, and mental status.
• Give dexamethasone for symptomatic croup.
• Give nebulized epinephrine for moderate-to-severe croup.
• Call an experienced airway clinician early if severe obstruction is suspected.
• If respiratory failure is imminent, move to a resuscitation area and prepare for controlled airway management.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Dexamethasone[/color]
• 0.15–0.6 mg/kg orally as a single dose (max local limit). Many protocols use 0.6 mg/kg for severe croup.
• IM/IV administration may be used when oral route is not feasible.

[color=#1E3A8A]Nebulized epinephrine (adrenaline)[/color]
• Epinephrine 1 mg/mL: 0.5 mL/kg by nebulization (max 5 mL).
• OR Racemic epinephrine 2.25%: 0.5 mL nebulized, diluted with normal saline according to protocol.
• Observe for at least 2–3 hours after the last dose because symptoms may recur.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay nebulized epinephrine or airway support in severe obstruction while waiting for the corticosteroid effect.
• Never administer the nebulized croup dose by IV or IM injection.
• A child with decreasing stridor but worsening air entry or consciousness may be deteriorating.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Discharge only when there is no stridor at rest, minimal work of breathing, adequate oral intake, and no recurrence during observation.
• Admit for recurrent symptoms after epinephrine, persistent stridor at rest, oxygen requirement, or poor access to emergency care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Canadian Paediatric Society; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Severe wheezing or respiratory distress with marked retractions, poor air entry, inability to speak or feed, cyanosis, exhaustion, or altered consciousness.
• A silent chest or decreasing respiratory effort in a distressed child may indicate impending respiratory arrest.
• Normal or rising carbon dioxide in a previously hyperventilating child may indicate fatigue and ventilatory failure.
• Do not assume all wheezing is asthma, particularly during a first episode.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Move the child to a resuscitation area and call senior pediatric and airway support.
• Assess ABCs, oxygen saturation, mental status, and air entry.
• Give oxygen for hypoxemia and initiate inhaled bronchodilator therapy if bronchospasm is likely.
• If anaphylaxis is suspected, give IM epinephrine immediately rather than treating with bronchodilators alone.
• Prepare bag-mask ventilation and advanced airway equipment if exhaustion develops.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Inhaled salbutamol[/color]
• MDI with spacer: 4–10 puffs, repeated every 20 minutes.
• Nebulized: 2.5 mg (smaller children) or 5 mg (larger children).

[color=#1E3A8A]Ipratropium bromide[/color]
• 250 mcg (smaller) or 500 mcg (larger), repeated according to protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Systemic corticosteroid[/color]
• Prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg once daily or IV equivalent.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV magnesium sulfate[/color]
• 25–50 mg/kg IV (max 2 g) over 20 minutes for severe refractory asthma.

[color=#1E3A8A]Respiratory support[/color]
• Bag-mask ventilation if inadequate ventilation. Intubation by experienced clinician when indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• A silent chest, worsening exhaustion, or altered consciousness is not an indication to simply continue repeated nebulization without escalation.
• Rapid IV magnesium infusion can cause hypotension.
• Positive-pressure ventilation and intubation in severe asthma carry risks (air trapping/hypotension); use experienced support.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• All children with impending respiratory failure require emergency admission and pediatric critical-care assessment.
• Admit severe attacks requiring frequent bronchodilators, oxygen, IV magnesium, or ongoing respiratory support.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: GINA; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; CATS.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Sudden coughing, choking, gagging, or respiratory distress during eating or play.
• Persistent cough, unilateral wheeze, asymmetric air entry, or unexplained respiratory symptoms.
• Complete obstruction may cause inability to cry, speak, cough effectively, or breathe.
• Cyanosis, reduced consciousness, and collapse are late signs.
• A normal chest X-ray does not exclude aspiration.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway patency, breathing, circulation, mental status, and SpO2.
• If effective cough, encourage coughing and observe closely. Do not perform blind finger sweeps.
• Infants < 1 year (severe obstruction): 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts.
• Children > 1 year (severe obstruction): Abdominal thrusts per age-appropriate algorithm.
• If unresponsive, begin pediatric CPR. Remove object only if clearly visible and safe.
• Arrange urgent airway specialist assessment if aspiration is suspected, even if symptoms improve.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
• Follow the age-specific pediatric basic life support choking algorithm.
• Do not use abdominal thrusts in infants < 1 year.
• Keep the child under observation and obtain urgent pediatric, ENT, or respiratory specialist review.
• Rigid bronchoscopy is commonly used for removal of airway foreign bodies by an experienced team.
• Provide oxygen and respiratory support. Do not delay airway management for imaging in an unstable child.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Persistent cough or unilateral wheeze after a choking event requires further evaluation, even if the child appears well.
• Do not discharge a child with significant suspicion of a retained foreign body without a specialist plan.
• Deterioration requires immediate airway support and emergency escalation.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or transfer urgently for suspected retained airway foreign body, ongoing symptoms, hypoxemia, or distress.
• Discharge only when a retained foreign body is considered unlikely and appropriate follow-up is arranged.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Resuscitation Council UK; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Epiglottitis:[/color] Sudden fever, severe sore throat, toxic appearance, drooling, muffled voice, tripod positioning, respiratory distress, stridor (critical obstruction).
[color=#1E3A8A]Bacterial Tracheitis:[/color] High fever, toxic, cough, stridor, distress. May follow viral URI/croup. Thick purulent secretions. Poor response to usual croup therapy is a warning.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call most experienced airway clinician, anesthetist, and pediatric/ENT team immediately.
• Keep child calm, in position of comfort. Provide oxygen minimizing distress.
• Do NOT force child to lie flat or open mouth for exam.
• Avoid tongue-depressor exam, throat swabs, IV attempts, or imaging that may agitate before safe airway plan.
• Prepare for controlled airway management.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Prioritize clinical assessment and airway safety over diagnostic tests.
• Once airway is secure: CBC, inflammatory markers, blood cultures, airway cultures.
• Imaging only if it will not delay or jeopardize airway management.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Airway Management[/color]
• Airway meds/induction agents selected by experienced airway team. Secure airway in controlled setting.
• Plan for difficult ventilation and emergency surgical-airway contingencies.

[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Suspected epiglottitis: IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (e.g., Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV every 24 hours).
• Add anti-staphylococcal coverage for tracheitis/MRSA suspected.

[color=#1E3A8A]Adjunctive[/color]
• Nebulized epinephrine may temporarily reduce edema (do not delay airway management). Corticosteroids per team protocol.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Sedation or examination that causes agitation can precipitate complete airway obstruction.
• Antibiotics do not replace airway stabilization.
• Do not delay treatment for imaging or cultures in a critically ill child.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Suspected epiglottitis requires emergency specialist assessment and usually hospital admission.
• Airway compromise/tracheitis/intubation requires ICU-level monitoring.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; CDC Haemophilus influenzae.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Sudden onset of illness with airway, breathing, or circulation compromise, usually after exposure to a potential allergen.
• Findings may include urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, stridor, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypotension, collapse, or altered consciousness.
• Skin signs may be absent in severe anaphylaxis.
• Do not wait for a rash or laboratory confirmation when anaphylaxis is clinically suspected.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for emergency assistance and assess ABCs.
• Give IM epinephrine immediately into the mid-anterolateral thigh.
• Lay the child flat with legs elevated when tolerated; allow position of comfort if severe respiratory distress. Do not allow standing or walking suddenly.
• Give high-flow oxygen for significant respiratory or circulatory compromise.
• Repeat IM epinephrine after 5 minutes if problems persist.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]IM epinephrine (First-line)[/color]
• 0.01 mg/kg IM (1 mg/mL solution). Max single dose usually 0.3 mg (smaller children) to 0.5 mg (adolescents).
• Repeat every 5 minutes if needed.

[color=#1E3A8A]Oxygen and IV crystalloid[/color]
• Give oxygen for compromise.
• For shock: isotonic crystalloid 10–20 mL/kg IV/IO, then reassess.

[color=#1E3A8A]Refractory anaphylaxis[/color]
• Titrated IV epinephrine infusion under pediatric resuscitation protocol and experienced supervision.

[color=#1E3A8A]Adjuncts[/color]
• H1 antihistamine for skin symptoms after stabilization.
• Inhaled bronchodilator for persistent wheeze after epinephrine.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay epinephrine while giving antihistamines, corticosteroids, or IV fluids.
• Do not give IV epinephrine boluses for routine anaphylaxis; infusion is reserved for refractory cases.
• Corticosteroids are not first-line treatment and have no established immediate lifesaving effect.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Observe after stabilization according to severity and risk of biphasic reaction.
• Prolonged observation or admission is appropriate after severe reactions, repeated epinephrine, or hypotension.
• Arrange an epinephrine auto-injector, caregiver education, and allergy specialist follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: World Allergy Organization; Resuscitation Council UK.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Suspect in a child with possible infection and acute organ dysfunction.
• Early findings: tachycardia, tachypnea, fever/hypothermia, altered behavior, poor feeding, reduced urine output, delayed capillary refill.
• Shock may present with weak pulses, cool/mottled extremities, altered consciousness, or hypotension (late sign).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and activate the pediatric sepsis pathway.
• Give oxygen and support ventilation as needed.
• Check bedside glucose and obtain IV/IO access.
• Obtain blood cultures if this does not meaningfully delay antibiotics.
• Give prompt IV antibiotics for suspected septic shock (ideally within 1 hour).
• Assess perfusion and decide on fluid boluses.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]IV fluid resuscitation[/color]
• In a setting with ICU capability: isotonic crystalloid 10–20 mL/kg IV/IO over a short period, then reassess.
• Further boluses up to 40–60 mL/kg in the first hour in selected children.
• In settings without ICU capability: use a more conservative protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric IV antibiotics[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 50–75 mg/kg IV every 24 hours (for many children beyond neonatal period) under local guidance.
• Neonates require a dedicated neonatal sepsis regimen.

[color=#1E3A8A]Vasoactive support[/color]
• If shock persists despite initial treatment: start epinephrine or norepinephrine infusion under critical-care guidance.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not automatically administer maximum fluid volume to every child.
• Children with myocarditis, severe anemia, or signs of fluid overload require modified management.
• Avoid delaying antibiotics for imaging or difficult sampling in a deteriorating child.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Suspected septic shock requires immediate resuscitation and admission to a high-acuity setting.
• ICU referral is indicated for persistent shock, respiratory failure, or need for vasoactive support.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; WHO.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Frequently preceded by respiratory failure or shock.
• Unresponsive, not breathing normally/gasping, no definite pulse (check ≤ 10 sec).
• If pulse present but HR < 60/min with poor perfusion despite oxygenation/ventilation → start compressions.

sections.heading: 02 — HIGH-QUALITY CPR
sections.content:
• Rate: 100–120/min.
• Depth: ≥ 1/3 AP diameter (~4 cm infant, 5 cm child). Allow full recoil, minimize interruptions.
• Infants: 2-thumb encircling or 1-hand heel (avoid 2-finger).
• Single rescuer: 30:2. Two rescuers: 15:2 (before advanced airway).
• Advanced airway: Continuous compressions + 20–30 breaths/min. Use capnography.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Epinephrine[/color]
• IV/IO: 0.01 mg/kg (0.1 mg/mL concentration / 1:10,000) = 0.1 mL/kg. Max 1 mg.
• Repeat every 3–5 minutes.

[color=#1E3A8A]Defibrillation (VF/pVT)[/color]
• 1st: 2 J/kg. 2nd: 4 J/kg. Subsequent: ≥ 4 J/kg (max 10 J/kg or adult dose).
• Resume CPR immediately after shock.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antiarrhythmics[/color]
• Amiodarone 5 mg/kg IV/IO bolus (or Lidocaine) for refractory VF/pVT.

[color=#1E3A8A]Bradycardia with poor perfusion[/color]
• Support airway/oxygen/ventilation. If HR < 60 with compromise, start CPR. Consider epinephrine/atropine.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Incorrect epinephrine concentration can cause fatal dosing errors. (0.1 mg/mL vs 1 mg/mL).
• Avoid excessive ventilation and long pauses in compressions.
• Routine sodium bicarbonate and calcium are NOT recommended unless specific indication (e.g., hyperkalemia).

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • All children with ROSC require urgent pediatric critical care and cause evaluation.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/AAP PALS 2025; AHA/AAP BLS 2025.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Inadequate tissue perfusion. Children maintain BP until late deterioration; hypotension is a late sign.
• Types: Hypovolemic (dehydration, hemorrhage), Distributive (sepsis, anaphylaxis), Cardiogenic (myocarditis, arrhythmia), Obstructive (tension pneumothorax, tamponade).
• Features: Tachycardia, prolonged cap refill, cool/mottled extremities, weak pulses, altered mental status, reduced UO, acidosis. Warm/bounding pulses in distributive.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call senior/critical care. ABCDE, oxygen.
• IV access (IO if delayed). Check glucose, treat hypoglycemia.
• Identify shock type and treat cause in parallel.
• Isotonic crystalloid in carefully reassessed aliquots when indicated.
• Start vasoactive support early if shock persists or fluids are unsafe.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• Initial bolus: 10 mL/kg IV isotonic crystalloid, then reassess.
• Septic shock: repeated 10–20 mL/kg aliquots per protocol.
• Hemorrhagic: blood products early; avoid large crystalloid.
• Stop boluses if signs of overload (pulmonary edema, hepatomegaly).

[color=#1E3A8A]Vasoactive Support[/color]
• Epinephrine or Norepinephrine infusion: start 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min, titrate to response.
• Use standardized concentrations and pump library.

[color=#1E3A8A]Treat underlying cause[/color]
• Septic: Cultures (if no delay), broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, source control.
• Anaphylactic: IM epinephrine.
• Hemorrhagic: Control bleeding, activate hemorrhage pathway.
• Cardiogenic: Cardiology consult, avoid repeated fluid boluses, use inotropes.
• Obstructive: Urgent relief (e.g., needle decompression for pneumothorax).

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• A normal blood pressure does not exclude shock in children.
• Reassess after every intervention. Shock evolves rapidly.
• Do not treat every shock state identically (e.g., fluid loading can worsen cardiogenic/obstructive shock).

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Shock requires emergency resuscitation, admission, and usually critical care.
• Transfer urgently if child needs ventilation, vasoactive infusions, blood products, or monitoring beyond local capacity.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/AAP PALS 2025; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; NICE NG254.

Cardiovascular & Shock.title: Acute Rheumatic Fever and Rheumatic Carditis

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Usually school-aged. Develops 1–5 weeks after GAS pharyngitis.
• Migratory polyarthritis (large joints).
• Carditis: Tachycardia out of proportion, new murmur, cardiomegaly, heart failure, pericardial involvement.
• Sydenham chorea (involuntary movements, emotional lability).
• Erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, perfusion, signs of heart failure.
• Obtain ECG and urgent echocardiography.
• Treat acute heart failure per pediatric protocol.
• Seek pediatric and cardiology consultation.
• Consider infective endocarditis, septic arthritis, JIA, myocarditis.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, ESR, CRP.
• ECG (PR interval). Echocardiography with Doppler.
• Evidence of preceding strep: throat culture, ASO or anti-DNase B.
• Apply revised Jones criteria (taking local risk into account).

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Eradication of GAS[/color]
• Benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM single dose: < 27 kg = 600,000 units IM; ≥ 27 kg = 1.2 million units IM.
• [color=#991B1B]Never administer IV.[/color] Clarify penicillin allergy.

[color=#1E3A8A]Anti-inflammatory (Arthritis)[/color]
• Aspirin or other anti-inflammatory under specialist supervision.

[color=#1E3A8A]Carditis/Heart Failure[/color]
• Admit. Manage pulmonary edema/heart failure per pediatric cardiac protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Secondary Prophylaxis[/color]
• Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis required to reduce recurrence.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Benzathine penicillin G must never be administered intravenously.
• Do not assume resolution of joint symptoms means carditis has resolved.
• Avoid unsupervised aspirin in suspected viral illness (Reye syndrome).

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for suspected carditis, heart failure, severe arthritis, chorea, or diagnostic uncertainty.
• Establish documented secondary prophylaxis plan before discharge.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Guideline; CDC Acute Rheumatic Fever.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Usually occurs in children aged 6 months to 5 years with fever and no evidence of CNS infection.
• Simple: generalized, lasts < 15 minutes, occurs only once in 24 hours.
• Complex features: focal onset, duration ≥ 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours.
• A seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer should be treated as an emergency.
• Consider meningitis, encephalitis, hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbance, poisoning, and epilepsy.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Protect the child from injury and place in a safe lateral position.
• Do not restrain the child or place objects in the mouth.
• Assess ABCs, oxygen saturation, and bedside glucose.
• If the seizure continues for 5 minutes or longer, administer a first-line benzodiazepine.
• Obtain urgent senior pediatric assessment for prolonged seizures, focal features, or persistent altered consciousness.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]First-line for ongoing seizure[/color]
• IV lorazepam: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg per dose); may repeat once if seizure continues.
• If IV access unavailable: buccal/intranasal midazolam or rectal diazepam using validated protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hypoglycemia treatment[/color]
• If hypoglycemia is confirmed/suspected: IV dextrose (e.g., 10% dextrose 2.5 mL/kg IV), followed by reassessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Treat the underlying cause of fever[/color]
• Use paracetamol for discomfort (not to prevent febrile seizure recurrence).
• Routine long-term antiepileptic medication is NOT recommended after a typical simple febrile seizure.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Repeated benzodiazepine doses increase the risk of respiratory depression.
• Do not delay treatment of an ongoing prolonged seizure while attempting difficult IV access.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• A child with a simple febrile seizure may be discharged after full recovery and assessment of the fever source.
• Admit or obtain specialist review for complex seizures, prolonged postictal state, or suspected CNS infection.
• Explain seizure first aid and provide clear return precautions.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO ETAT; Children's Acute Transport Service (CATS).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• A convulsive seizure lasting ≥ 5 minutes, or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness.
• Assess airway, respiratory effort, SpO2, circulation, temperature, and consciousness.
• Consider hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbance, CNS infection, trauma, poisoning, and epilepsy.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for help and start the pediatric resuscitation pathway.
• Protect from injury; do not restrain or place objects in the mouth.
• Position safely, provide oxygen, prepare suction and bag-mask ventilation.
• Check bedside glucose immediately and treat hypoglycemia if present.
• Give a benzodiazepine promptly for an ongoing seizure ≥ 5 minutes.
• Avoid giving > 2 appropriately timed benzodiazepine doses in total before escalation to second-line treatment.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]First-line: IV lorazepam[/color]
• 0.1 mg/kg IV per dose; maximum 4 mg per dose. May repeat once.
• If no IV access: buccal/intranasal midazolam or rectal diazepam (weight-based).

[color=#1E3A8A]Second-line antiseizure treatment[/color]
• If seizures persist: Levetiracetam 40–60 mg/kg IV (max 4.5 g).
• Alternatives: Fosphenytoin/phenytoin or valproate (selected per contraindications).

[color=#1E3A8A]Refractory status epilepticus[/color]
• Call pediatric critical care and neurology. May require anesthetic infusions and airway control.

[color=#1E3A8A]Treat underlying cause[/color]
• IV dextrose for hypoglycemia. Correct electrolyte abnormalities. Treat CNS infection.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay first-line treatment for IV access; use an appropriate non-IV route.
• Repeated benzodiazepine doses increase the risk of respiratory depression.
• Phenytoin/fosphenytoin can cause hypotension and arrhythmias.
• Persistent altered consciousness after apparent seizure cessation requires urgent reassessment.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Ongoing status epilepticus requires resuscitation-level care and urgent critical-care involvement.
• Admit children with prolonged seizures, recurrent seizures, or respiratory compromise.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: American Epilepsy Society; Local pediatric protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, or altered mental status.
• Infants: poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, temperature instability, apnea, bulging fontanelle.
• Seizures, focal deficits, or behavioral change raise concern for encephalitis or complicated CNS infection.
• A non-blanching rash with fever may indicate meningococcal disease (emergency).
• Absence of neck stiffness does not exclude meningitis, especially in infants.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, perfusion, mental status, temperature, and bedside glucose.
• Activate sepsis pathway if shock is suspected.
• Start empiric IV antibiotics urgently when bacterial meningitis is suspected.
• Do not wait for imaging or lumbar puncture in an unstable child.
• Use infection-control precautions if meningococcal disease is suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Blood cultures, CBC, inflammatory markers, glucose, electrolytes, renal function.
• Lumbar puncture (LP) for CSF studies when clinically safe. Check serum glucose near time of LP.
• Do not routinely delay LP for CT; imaging is reserved for focal signs, reduced consciousness, or suspected mass effect.
• Consider MRI, EEG, and pathogen-specific testing if encephalitis is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric IV antibiotics (Bacterial meningitis)[/color]
• Selection/dosing depend on age and local resistance.
• Often Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin for children beyond neonatal period (if resistant pneumococcus is a concern).
• Neonates require a dedicated neonatal regimen.

[color=#1E3A8A]Possible encephalitis[/color]
• Start IV acyclovir promptly when HSV encephalitis is suspected. Adjust for renal function.

[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive management[/color]
• Support airway, ventilation, perfusion, and glucose. Treat seizures promptly.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Suspected bacterial meningitis is a time-critical emergency; do not delay antibiotics for CT or LP.
• Do not perform LP in an unstable child or when signs suggest significant risk.
• Ceftriaxone has important restrictions in neonates (hyperbilirubinemia/calcium).
• A normal early examination or absence of rash does not reliably exclude serious CNS infection.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit all children with suspected bacterial meningitis or encephalitis for urgent inpatient treatment.
• Obtain critical-care support for shock, airway compromise, or markedly reduced consciousness.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE. Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease; WHO.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Head injury ranges from minor scalp trauma to traumatic brain injury (TBI), intracranial hemorrhage, skull fracture, and secondary brain injury caused by hypoxia or hypotension.

[color=#1E3A8A]Assess for:[/color]
• Loss of consciousness, confusion, amnesia, or abnormal behavior.
• Persistent or worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure.
• Reduced GCS, abnormal pupils, or focal neurological deficit.
• Signs of skull fracture: palpable depression, hemotympanum, periorbital bruising, Battle sign, or CSF leakage.
• Scalp hematoma (large or non-frontal in an infant).
• Possible non-accidental injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Apply an ABCDE approach and assess the pediatric GCS.
• Protect the cervical spine.
• Prevent secondary brain injury: Correct hypoxemia immediately, treat hypotension promptly, avoid hypoglycemia, maintain normothermia.
• Check bedside blood glucose in altered consciousness or seizures.
• Seek urgent neurosurgical or pediatric critical-care advice for deteriorating consciousness, suspected intracranial bleeding, or signs of raised ICP.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]CT head without contrast[/color]
• NICE recommends CT within 1 hour for high-risk features (suspected NAI, post-traumatic seizure, GCS < 14 on initial or < 15 at 2 hours, suspected skull fracture, focal deficit, large scalp injury in < 1yo).
• Intermediate-risk factors may require urgent CT or structured observation (≥ 4 hours).

[color=#1E3A8A]Other tests[/color]
• Blood glucose immediately. CBC, coagulation, crossmatch if significant trauma.
• Do not use skull radiographs as a substitute for CT.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Airway and breathing[/color]
• Oxygen: titrate to age-appropriate SpO2. Avoid hypoxia and hypotension.
• Aim for normocapnia. Do not routinely hyperventilate.

[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally every 4–6 hours. Opioids may be needed for severe pain (titrate carefully).

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected raised ICP / herniation[/color]
• Elevate head ~30 degrees, keep neck midline.
• Prevent hypoxia, hypotension, fever, and seizures.
• Hyperosmolar therapy may be required under critical-care protocol.
• Avoid routine corticosteroids for TBI.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• A normal initial appearance does not exclude intracranial injury.
• Infants may deteriorate without clear verbal symptoms.
• Any neurological deterioration, new seizure, repeated vomiting, unequal pupils, or falling GCS requires immediate reassessment.
• Consider safeguarding assessment if abuse is possible.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Discharge only if returned to normal state, no concerning features, tolerating oral intake, reliable supervision, and written head-injury precautions given.
• Admit or transfer for abnormal imaging, persistent symptoms, reduced GCS, or suspected abuse.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE NG232; NICE NG41.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Acute diarrhea, with or without vomiting, abdominal cramps, and fever.
• Assess hydration using mental status, thirst, mucous membranes, tears, eyes, skin turgor, capillary refill, pulse quality, and urine output.
• Severe dehydration or shock may present with lethargy, weak pulses, prolonged capillary refill, cool extremities, and reduced urine output.
• Consider sepsis, surgical abdomen, DKA, and other causes if the presentation is atypical.
• Bloody diarrhea, bilious vomiting, severe localized abdominal pain, or abdominal distension requires further assessment.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and bedside glucose if the child is severely ill.
• Determine weight, hydration status, duration of symptoms, urine output, and ability to drink.
• Start oral rehydration solution (ORS) if the child is alert and can drink.
• Establish IV or intraosseous access if shock is present or oral/enteral rehydration is unsafe or unsuccessful.
• Continue breastfeeding.
• Avoid routine antibiotics and antidiarrheal drugs.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• No routine laboratory tests are needed in uncomplicated gastroenteritis with no significant dehydration.
• Check glucose, electrolytes, urea, and creatinine if severe dehydration, shock, altered mental status, or IV therapy is required.
• Blood gas and lactate may be appropriate in severe shock or suspected metabolic acidosis.
• Stool testing is indicated selectively for bloody diarrhea, suspected outbreaks, immunocompromise, persistent symptoms, or when results will change management.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Oral rehydration therapy[/color]
• For some dehydration, give ORS approximately 75 mL/kg over 4 hours, then reassess and replace ongoing losses.
• Give small, frequent amounts using a spoon, cup, or oral syringe.
• Replace ongoing watery stool losses with additional ORS.
• Do not use plain water alone to replace substantial gastrointestinal losses.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV fluid resuscitation for shock[/color]
• If shock is present, give isotonic crystalloid, commonly 10–20 mL/kg IV, then reassess immediately.
• Repeat only when clinically indicated and according to the pediatric shock protocol.
• Do not automatically give repeated large boluses without reassessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Zinc supplementation[/color]
• < 6 months: 10 mg orally once daily.
• ≥ 6 months: 20 mg orally once daily.
• Duration: 10–14 days.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics and antiemetics[/color]
• Antibiotics are not routinely indicated for uncomplicated watery diarrhea.
