• Ondansetron may be considered in selected children with vomiting that prevents ORS.
• Avoid routine loperamide in children.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Discharge only when hydration is adequate, oral intake is tolerated, and caregivers understand ORS use and warning signs.
• Admit children with shock, severe dehydration, significant electrolyte abnormalities, altered mental status, failed rehydration, or a concerning alternative diagnosis.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO. Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children; WHO. Diarrhoeal disease.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Abdominal pain migrating to the right lower quadrant. Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, fever.
• Right lower quadrant tenderness, guarding, rebound tenderness.
• Younger children may have nonspecific symptoms, diffuse pain, or delayed presentation.
• Perforation may present with generalized tenderness, rigidity, or shock.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, vital signs, hydration, pain severity.
• Keep the child nil by mouth when strongly suspected.
• Establish IV access if dehydrated, systemically unwell, or likely to require surgery.
• Provide appropriate analgesia and antiemetic treatment.
• Request early pediatric surgical assessment.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC and inflammatory markers (cannot independently exclude appendicitis).
• Urinalysis (to rule out urinary causes).
• Abdominal ultrasound is generally the preferred initial imaging in children.
• MRI or CT may be considered if ultrasound is inconclusive.
• Imaging must not delay urgent surgical assessment in a child with peritonitis.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg orally/IV. IV opioid for severe pain using pediatric weight-based protocol.
• Adequate analgesia should not be withheld because appendicitis is suspected.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV fluid therapy[/color]
• If hypovolemic/shock: isotonic crystalloid 10–20 mL/kg IV, followed by reassessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics[/color]
• For suspected complicated appendicitis/perforation: IV antibiotics covering enteric gram-negatives and anaerobes per local guidance.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Severe or increasing pain, generalized guarding, or signs of shock require immediate surgical reassessment.
• Antibiotics do not replace urgent surgical assessment when source control is required.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Refer urgently to pediatric surgery.
• Admit for confirmed appendicitis, peritonitis, perforation, or systemic illness.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: IDSA 2024 Guidelines; Local pediatric surgical guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Most common in infants/young children (3 months to 2 years).
• Intermittent episodes of severe colicky abdominal pain/distress, often with pallor.
• Vomiting, poor feeding, or unexplained lethargy may be the main presentation.
• Child may appear well between painful episodes. Sausage-shaped mass occasionally palpable.
• Bloody/mucus-containing stool (red currant jelly) is a late sign.
• Classic triad (pain, mass, bloody stool) is often absent.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, perfusion, hydration, abdominal tenderness, mental status.
• Establish IV access, keep the child nil by mouth.
• Provide appropriate analgesia and antiemetic treatment.
• If shock: pediatric resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid boluses.
• Request urgent pediatric surgical and radiology consultation.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Abdominal ultrasound is the preferred initial investigation (target/doughnut sign).
• A normal X-ray does not exclude intussusception. X-ray is useful if obstruction/perforation suspected.
• Check glucose, electrolytes, renal function, CBC, blood gas if significantly unwell.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Fluid resuscitation[/color]
• For shock: isotonic crystalloid 10–20 mL/kg IV, with reassessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Enema reduction[/color]
• Pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction may be attempted in an equipped center when stable and no perforation/peritonitis.
• Monitor closely during and after. Surgical reduction may be required if nonoperative fails.
• Contraindicated in suspected bowel perforation, peritonitis, or unstable child.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Enema reduction is contraindicated in suspected bowel perforation, peritonitis, or an unstable child.
• Recurrent abdominal pain, vomiting, pallor, or lethargy after reduction requires immediate reassessment (recurrence can occur).

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• All suspected cases require urgent pediatric surgical discussion.
• Admit or transfer urgently when confirmed or strongly suspected.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; Perth Children's Hospital.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Foreign-body: May be asymptomatic or cause drooling, dysphagia, vomiting, chest/abdominal pain, or respiratory distress.
• [color=#991B1B]High-risk:[/color] Button batteries (especially esophagus), multiple magnets, sharp objects, large objects, objects causing airway symptoms.
• [color=#991B1B]Caustic ingestion:[/color] Strong acids/alkalis. Drooling, painful swallowing, oral burns, vomiting, stridor. Absence of oral burns does NOT exclude esophageal injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation. Follow choking algorithm if complete obstruction.
• Keep NPO if urgent endoscopy/airway intervention may be required.
• Identify object/product, time, amount, symptoms. Bring packaging.
• Contact pediatric surgery/gastro/ENT/toxicology early.
• Do NOT induce vomiting. Do NOT give activated charcoal or attempt chemical neutralization for caustics.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Foreign body[/color]
• X-rays (neck, chest, abdomen) to locate radiopaque objects.
• Button batteries: double-rim/halo appearance.
• Normal X-rays do not exclude radiolucent objects.

[color=#1E3A8A]Caustic ingestion[/color]
• Assess airway and signs of perforation.
• Chest/abdominal imaging if perforation suspected.
• Endoscopy timing determined urgently with specialists.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Esophageal button battery[/color]
• Time-critical emergency. Urgent specialist consult and emergent removal.
• Honey may be considered (≥12 months) under poison-center protocol while arranging transport (do not delay definitive care).

[color=#1E3A8A]Magnets and sharp objects[/color]
• Multiple magnets/magnet + metal = urgent specialist assessment (risk of necrosis/fistula).
• Sharp objects in esophagus/stomach = urgent endoscopic evaluation.

[color=#1E3A8A]Caustic ingestion[/color]
• Protect airway, assess for progressive edema/stridor.
• Do not induce vomiting, perform blind lavage, or attempt neutralization.
• No universal antidote; supportive care and early specialist assessment.
• Avoid blind NG tube placement.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Any esophageal button battery is an emergency.
• Multiple magnets are high risk even if initially well.
• Persistent drooling, inability to swallow, stridor, severe pain, or peritonitis requires emergency escalation.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit/transfer for esophageal batteries, multiple magnets, sharp objects, symptomatic caustic ingestion, or suspected perforation.
• Discharge after low-risk blunt object only if no symptoms and safe follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NASPGHAN; National Capital Poison Center; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Infants: fever, poor feeding, vomiting, irritability, lethargy.
• Older children: dysuria, frequency, urgency, new incontinence, suprapubic pain, hematuria.
• Fever with flank pain or systemic illness suggests upper UTI or pyelonephritis.
• Consider sepsis in an unwell child, especially infants.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, temperature, perfusion, hydration, urine output, and mental status.
• Obtain a properly collected urine sample for urinalysis and culture before antibiotics when feasible.
• Do not delay antibiotics in a septic or unstable child while attempting urine collection.
• Establish IV access and initiate sepsis management if shock is suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urinalysis: leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and microscopy.
• Urine culture before treatment. Avoid relying on bag specimens to confirm UTI (contamination).
• CBC, renal function, electrolytes, blood culture, and inflammatory markers if systemically ill.
• Renal/bladder ultrasound in selected children (age < 6 months, atypical, recurrent).

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Oral antibiotics (Stable children)[/color]
• Cephalexin 25 mg/kg per dose orally every 8 hours (subject to local max).
• For febrile UTI/pyelonephritis: choose an agent with appropriate renal tissue penetration.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV antibiotics (Severe illness)[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV every 24 hours (for children beyond neonatal period) per local guidance.
• Neonates require a separate neonatal infection regimen.
• Switch to oral therapy when improving and tolerating oral meds.

[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive care[/color]
• Encourage oral fluids. Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg orally every 4–6 hours as needed.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Infants < 3 months with suspected UTI and fever require urgent hospital assessment.
• Suspected urosepsis requires prompt resuscitation and empiric antibiotics.
• Persistent fever or failure to improve may indicate obstruction, renal abscess, or resistance.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for young infants, sepsis, dehydration, persistent vomiting, or suspected obstruction.
• Outpatient care may be suitable for a stable child who tolerates oral therapy with reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE. Urinary tract infection in under 16s.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Abrupt decline in kidney function leading to fluid overload, electrolyte disturbances, acidosis, uremia.
• Causes: Prerenal (dehydration, hemorrhage, sepsis), Intrinsic (ATN, glomerulonephritis, HUS), Postrenal (obstruction).
• Features: Reduced urine output/anuria, dehydration/poor perfusion, edema, hypertension, vomiting, lethargy, hyperkalemia, acidosis.
• KDIGO criteria: Creatinine ↑ ≥ 0.3 mg/dL in 48h, or ↑ to ≥ 1.5x baseline in 7 days, or UO < 0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥ 6h.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• ABCDE, perfusion, BP, hydration. Record strict fluid intake/output, weigh child.
• Check glucose, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, blood gas.
• Stop/withhold nephrotoxic meds, review doses.
• Treat cause: shock, sepsis, dehydration, obstruction.
• Urgent nephrology consult for severe AKI, anuria, refractory electrolyte abnormalities, or overload.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Fluid management[/color]
• If hypovolemic/shock: Isotonic crystalloid 10 mL/kg IV, reassess.
• Once perfused, calculate maintenance carefully.
• In oliguric/anuric AKI, avoid routine fluid loading (risk of pulmonary edema).

[color=#1E3A8A]Medications[/color]
• Adjust renal doses. Avoid NSAIDs.
• Loop diuretics (e.g., Furosemide 1 mg/kg IV) for fluid overload (do not use just to convert oliguria).

[color=#1E3A8A]Renal Replacement Therapy (RRT)[/color]
• Indications: Refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, fluid overload with respiratory compromise, uremic complications.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Repeated fluid boluses can cause pulmonary edema in oliguric AKI.
• A normal initial creatinine does not exclude evolving AKI.
• Investigate urinary obstruction promptly.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for significant AKI, persistent oliguria, electrolyte/acid-base abnormalities, fluid overload, or suspected intrinsic renal disease.
• Transfer to center with pediatric critical care/RRT if refractory complications.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE NG148; KDIGO.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Can cause fatal conduction abnormalities, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest.
• Thresholds: Mild 5.5–6.0, Moderate 6.1–7.0, Severe > 7.0 mmol/L (Neonates have different ranges). Treat clinical context and ECG.
• ECG: Tall peaked T waves, PR prolongation, loss of P waves, QRS widening, sine wave.
• Causes: AKI, dehydration, acidosis, tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis, adrenal insufficiency, pseudohyperkalemia (hemolysis).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• ABCDE, immediate 12-lead ECG, continuous cardiac monitoring.
• IV access, urgent labs (K+, glucose, renal, blood gas).
• If severe/ECG changes, start emergency treatment without waiting for repeat labs.
• Stop K+ administration and review medications.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Stabilize cardiac membrane (if ECG changes)[/color]
• Calcium gluconate 10%: 0.5 mL/kg IV (max 20 mL) over 5–10 min under ECG monitoring. (Calcium chloride 10% may be preferred in arrest, but is more injurious if extravasated).

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Shift K+ into cells[/color]
• Insulin/Glucose: Regular insulin 0.1 unit/kg IV (max 10 units) + Glucose 0.5 g/kg IV. Monitor glucose closely for ≥ 4–6 hours.
• Nebulized Salbutamol: 2.5 mg (smaller) or 5 mg (larger) as adjunct.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Remove K+ from body[/color]
• Treat cause (AKI, shock, acidosis). Consider potassium binders or urgent dialysis for refractory cases.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Severe hyperkalemia is an emergency even if child appears well.
• Do not delay treatment for repeat testing when ECG is abnormal or K+ is critically high.
• Calcium does not lower K+. Insulin/glucose shifts K+ temporarily. Watch for rebound and hypoglycemia.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for moderate/severe hyperkalemia, ECG abnormalities, AKI, or acidosis.
• Transfer urgently for refractory hyperkalemia or need for dialysis.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; AHA PALS 2025.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Testicular torsion is a time-critical surgical emergency caused by twisting of the spermatic cord, compromising testicular blood supply. Salvage is most likely with rapid detorsion, ideally within 4–6 hours.
• Sudden unilateral scrotal/testicular pain. Nausea/vomiting.
• Swelling, erythema, high-riding or horizontal testis.
• Absent/abnormal cremasteric reflex (presence does not exclude).
• In neonates: painless swelling, discoloration, or firm testis.
• [color=#1E3A8A]Differential:[/color] Torsion of appendix testis, epididymitis, incarcerated hernia, trauma.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess pain, vital signs, onset/duration.
• Contact surgery/urology immediately if torsion suspected.
• Keep NPO, establish IV access if surgery likely.
• Provide analgesia and antiemetic.
• Do not delay surgical consultation or transfer for imaging when suspicion is high.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Doppler ultrasound: May help if diagnosis uncertain and immediately available. Preserved flow does NOT completely exclude torsion. Imaging must NOT delay surgery.
• Urinalysis/culture: May help if infection suspected but do not exclude torsion.
• Blood tests: Not routinely required, should not delay surgery.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally every 4–6 hours.
• Severe pain: titrated IV morphine 0.05–0.1 mg/kg slowly.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive management[/color]
• Urgent surgical exploration and detorsion + fixation (affected and contralateral testes).
• Manual detorsion: May be attempted by experienced clinician while arranging surgery. Temporizing only; does NOT remove need for surgery.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Time to detorsion is critical. Do not wait for next morning or delayed ultrasound.
• Abdominal pain/vomiting may be main presentation in younger children.
• A delayed presentation still requires urgent assessment.
• Intermittent pain may indicate intermittent torsion.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• All suspected cases require emergency surgical assessment.
• Discharge only after torsion and other urgent causes are excluded with clear follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; EAU Paediatric Urology Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration.
• Kussmaul breathing, fruity/acetone breath odor. Severe disease: reduced consciousness, shock, coma.
• Criteria: hyperglycemia (>11 mmol/L), venous pH <7.3 or bicarb <18, beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥3 mmol/L or significant ketonuria.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, perfusion, hydration, respiratory pattern, neurological status.
• Measure bedside glucose and blood ketones immediately.
• Obtain IV access, send venous blood gas, electrolytes, urea, creatinine.
• Start carefully calculated IV fluid therapy according to pediatric DKA protocol.
• Perform frequent neurological assessments (cerebral injury is a critical complication).

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]IV fluid replacement[/color]
• Begin with isotonic crystalloid 10–20 mL/kg over 20–30 min if indicated, followed by reassessment.
• Calculate maintenance and deficit using the pediatric DKA pathway. Do not use unmonitored adult regimens.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV insulin infusion[/color]
• Regular insulin 0.05–0.1 units/kg/hour according to protocol.
• Begin insulin typically at least 1 hour after fluids have started.
• Never give an IV insulin bolus for routine pediatric DKA.
• Add dextrose-containing fluid as glucose falls, while continuing insulin to suppress ketogenesis.

[color=#1E3A8A]Potassium replacement[/color]
• Depends on serum K+, renal function, urine output. Never give concentrated KCl IV push.

[color=#1E3A8A]Sodium bicarbonate[/color]
• Routine use is NOT recommended. Consider exceptional use only under specialist direction.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Cerebral injury is a potentially fatal complication. Headache, worsening irritability, decreasing consciousness, bradycardia, or new neurological signs require immediate escalation.
• Do not start insulin if potassium is dangerously low.
• Children with DKA have total-body potassium depletion even if initial serum K+ is normal/elevated.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• All children with DKA require hospital admission and protocol-based monitoring.
• Severe DKA, altered consciousness, or shock requires urgent pediatric intensive care assessment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ISPAD Guidelines; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; CPS.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Sweating, tremor, pallor, tachycardia, irritability, hunger, behavioral change.
• Severe: confusion, seizures, reduced consciousness, coma.
• Infants: poor feeding, lethargy, apnea, hypothermia, or seizures.
• Confirm low glucose promptly, but do not delay emergency treatment in a symptomatic child.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, mental status, circulation, and bedside glucose.
• Conscious and can swallow safely: rapid-acting oral glucose.
• Seizures, reduced consciousness, or cannot swallow: IV dextrose.
• Recheck glucose promptly after treatment and repeat if hypoglycemia persists.
• Identify and treat the underlying cause (consider critical sample before glucose if recurrent/unexplained, without delaying treatment).

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Oral glucose (Conscious child)[/color]
• ~0.3 g/kg of rapid-acting oral glucose (commonly up to 15 g per treatment).
• Recheck glucose after 10–15 min. Repeat if low. Provide meal/longer-acting carb once corrected.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV dextrose (Severe/Symptomatic)[/color]
• 10% dextrose 2.5 mL/kg IV (equivalent to 0.25 g/kg glucose).
• Recheck glucose after 10–15 min. If recurrent, commence controlled dextrose infusion.

[color=#1E3A8A]Glucagon (If IV unavailable)[/color]
• Use age/weight-appropriate glucagon per product labeling. Give carbohydrate once awake.
• May be less effective if hepatic glycogen stores are depleted (e.g., prolonged fasting).

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Never give oral glucose, drinks, or food to a child who cannot protect their airway.
• Avoid unnecessary concentrated dextrose through a peripheral line (extravasation injury).

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or observe severe, recurrent, unexplained, or treatment-resistant hypoglycemia.
• Admission indicated if ongoing dextrose infusion is required or serious underlying illness suspected.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ISPAD Guidelines; Local pediatric protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Fever in a young infant may be the only sign of a serious bacterial infection.
• A documented temperature ≥ 38.0°C in an infant < 3 months requires urgent clinical assessment.
• Look for poor feeding, lethargy, irritability, apnea, temperature instability, respiratory distress.
• Serious causes include bacteremia, UTI, meningitis, and neonatal sepsis.
• A well appearance does not exclude serious bacterial infection, especially in neonates.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, perfusion, feeding, and mental status.
• Check bedside glucose if unwell.
• Obtain weight and establish IV access if unwell.
• Obtain urine testing and cultures using an appropriate collection method.
• Give prompt empiric parenteral antibiotics when indicated; do not delay in an unstable infant.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Stabilization[/color]
• Treat hypoglycemia using the neonatal/young-infant glucose protocol.
• If shock is present: carefully reassessed isotonic crystalloid boluses (commonly 10 mL/kg initially).

[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric parenteral antibiotics[/color]
• Select regimen by exact age, gestational age, clinical appearance, and local protocol.
• Neonatal regimens commonly use ampicillin + gentamicin for selected presentations.
• Ceftriaxone has important restrictions in neonates (hyperbilirubinemia/calcium interactions).

[color=#1E3A8A]Lumbar puncture[/color]
• Perform when indicated and safe. If unstable, stabilize and begin antibiotics before LP.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Young infants can deteriorate rapidly and may not show typical signs of infection.
• Avoid routine large-volume boluses without reassessment.
• Do not delay antibiotics in an unstable infant while attempting lumbar puncture.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Neonates with fever generally require hospital admission and a neonatal sepsis evaluation.
• Infants aged 29–90 days require risk stratification under a validated local pathway.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE. Fever in under 5s; AAP.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Acute otitis media: ear pain, fever, irritability, bulging tympanic membrane.
• Mastoiditis: postauricular pain, erythema, swelling, tenderness, or outward displacement of the pinna.
• Severe headache, neck stiffness, facial weakness, vertigo, or altered mental status raises concern for complications.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess temperature, hydration, pain severity, and signs of systemic illness.
• Examine both ears and the mastoid region. Perform neurological exam if complications suspected.
• Provide appropriate analgesia early.
• If mastoiditis or an intracranial complication is suspected, arrange urgent hospital assessment and ENT review.
• Do not delay emergency referral for imaging in an unstable child.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Pain and fever control[/color]
• Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg orally every 4–6 hours as needed.
• Ibuprofen may be used in age-eligible, adequately hydrated children.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics for acute otitis media[/color]
• Many uncomplicated cases can be managed with observation/delayed prescription.
• When indicated: Amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day orally divided into 2 doses (subject to local max).

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected mastoiditis[/color]
• Admit urgently and start IV antibiotics according to local ENT guidance.
• Urgent ENT consultation; drainage or mastoid surgery may be required.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Postauricular swelling or erythema with displacement of the pinna is a red flag for mastoiditis.
• Facial palsy, severe headache, meningism, persistent vomiting, or altered consciousness requires emergency escalation.
• Reassess children who worsen or fail to improve within 48–72 hours.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Uncomplicated cases may be treated as outpatients with pain control and safety-net advice.
• Admit urgently for suspected mastoiditis, intracranial complications, or severe systemic illness.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE. Otitis media (acute); Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Children may develop severe systemic toxicity from a smaller venom dose relative to body weight.
• [color=#1E3A8A]Snakebite:[/color] Fang marks, swelling, bruising, spontaneous bleeding, ptosis, weakness, shock, dark urine.
• [color=#1E3A8A]Scorpion sting:[/color] Severe local pain, agitation, sweating, salivation, abnormal eye movements, tachycardia/bradycardia, muscle jerking, pulmonary edema.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Ensure scene safety. Move away from animal.
• Assess ABCs, provide respiratory/circulatory support.
• Keep child calm, immobilize affected limb. Remove rings/constricting items.
• Mark edge of swelling and record time.
• Contact poison center/toxicology. Arrange urgent transfer for systemic symptoms.
• Do not delay transfer for home remedies.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Snakebite: CBC, platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, renal function, urinalysis, crossmatch if bleeding.
• Scorpion: Continuous ECG, glucose, electrolytes, blood gas, cardiac biomarkers, chest imaging/echo if severe.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]First Aid[/color]
• Immobilize limb, minimize movement. Clean wound, provide tetanus prophylaxis.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT:[/color] Apply tight tourniquet, cut/suck wound, apply ice, burn, or use electric shock.

[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 15 mg/kg. Avoid NSAIDs if coagulopathy/bleeding/renal injury.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antivenom[/color]
• Indications: Systemic envenomation, significant coagulopathy, neurotoxicity, shock.
• Children often require the SAME dose as adults (venom dose not proportional to weight). Follow product instructions and regional toxicology guidance.
• Administer in a setting capable of treating anaphylaxis. Monitor for hypersensitivity.

[color=#1E3A8A]Severe Scorpion[/color]
• Supportive respiratory/cardiovascular care. Contact regional toxicology for species-specific antivenom.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Children can deteriorate rapidly. Progressive weakness, ptosis, respiratory distress, bleeding, or shock requires urgent escalation.
• Do not rely on fang marks or local pain severity to predict systemic toxicity.
• Antivenom can cause severe acute hypersensitivity reactions. Be prepared to manage anaphylaxis.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit children with systemic symptoms, abnormal coagulation, progressive swelling, neurotoxicity, or antivenom treatment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Snakebite Guidelines; WHO Scorpion Stings.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Kawasaki Disease (KD):[/color] Usually < 5 years. Persistent fever ≥ 5 days, bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, red/cracked lips/strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, redness/swelling of hands/feet (later peeling), cervical lymphadenopathy. Major concern: coronary artery aneurysm.
[color=#1E3A8A]MIS-C:[/color] Persistent fever + systemic inflammation + multisystem involvement (abdominal pain, rash, conjunctivitis, hypotension/shock, cardiac dysfunction). Consider recent SARS-CoV-2.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, perfusion. Continuous monitoring (ECG, SpO2, BP).
• Obtain urgent pediatric and cardiology consultation.
• If shock: carefully reassessed fluid boluses, early vasoactive support.
• Obtain cultures and start empiric antibiotics promptly if bacterial sepsis cannot be excluded.
• Arrange echocardiography.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, CRP, ESR, electrolytes, renal/liver function, albumin, urinalysis.
• Blood cultures. ECG and echocardiography.
• Troponin and BNP/NT-proBNP if myocarditis suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Kawasaki Disease[/color]
• IVIG 2 g/kg IV as single infusion (standard initial). Do not delay for day 5 if strongly suspected.
• Aspirin: Used with IVIG under specialist direction (acute phase varies). Low-dose antiplatelet continued after acute phase when indicated. (Avoid unsupervised aspirin in viral illness - Reye syndrome).

[color=#1E3A8A]MIS-C[/color]
• IVIG commonly 2 g/kg. Corticosteroids commonly used (e.g., Methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day IV).
• Monitor BP, fluid balance, cardiac function, thrombosis risk.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay KD treatment while waiting for day 5 of fever when strongly suspected.
• Exclude or treat dangerous infectious mimics (sepsis, toxic shock).
• Avoid excessive IVIG volume in myocardial dysfunction.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit for specialist assessment and cardiac evaluation. ICU for shock, significant dysfunction, or rapid deterioration.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: CDC Kawasaki Disease; CDC MIS-C.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Fever in child living in/returning from endemic area + any of:
• Altered consciousness/coma, repeated seizures.
• Respiratory distress, deep breathing, acidosis.
• Shock, poor perfusion. Severe anemia/hemoglobinuria. Hypoglycemia. AKI. Jaundice. Bleeding.
• [color=#991B1B]Important:[/color] A negative rapid diagnostic test does not always exclude malaria if suspicion is high.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCDE. Check bedside glucose immediately; correct hypoglycemia.
• Obtain IV/IO access. Monitor ECG, SpO2, temp, BP, mental status, urine output.
• Obtain urgent malaria testing (thick/thin films).
• Treat seizures/respiratory failure promptly.
• Avoid routine large fluid boluses (vulnerable to fluid overload). Give fluids according to perfusion/losses.
• Contact pediatric/infectious disease team urgently.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Rapid test and thick/thin smear (parasite density).
• CBC, bedside glucose, electrolytes, renal/liver function, bilirubin.
• Blood gas/lactate. Blood group/crossmatch if severe anemia. Blood cultures if sepsis possible.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]IV Artesunate (First-Line)[/color]
• WHO: < 20 kg = 3 mg/kg/dose; ≥ 20 kg = 2.4 mg/kg/dose. Give at 0, 12, 24 hours, then daily.
• Once tolerating oral meds, complete with full oral ACT (Artemisinin-based combination therapy).
• Artesunate alone is NOT the complete treatment course.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hypoglycemia[/color]
• 10% dextrose 2.5 mL/kg IV. Recheck glucose promptly and frequently.

[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive[/color]
• Treat seizures (status epilepticus protocol). Support ventilation. Manage severe anemia/AKI.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay antimalarial treatment while awaiting nonessential tests.
• Do not use oral treatment alone for severe malaria.
• Hypoglycemia may recur, particularly during quinine treatment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• All children with severe malaria require hospital admission and close monitoring.
• ICU-level care for coma, recurrent seizures, shock, respiratory failure, or major organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Guidelines for Malaria; CDC Treatment of Severe Malaria.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Consider poisoning in a child with unexplained altered consciousness, vomiting, seizures, abnormal behavior, respiratory depression, or metabolic acidosis.
• Obtain history: substance, amount, time, route, co-ingestants.
• Examine for toxidromes (opioid, anticholinergic, sympathomimetic, sedative, cholinergic).
• A normal initial exam does not exclude delayed toxicity.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and treat airway obstruction, respiratory failure, shock, and seizures immediately.
• Check bedside glucose in every child with altered consciousness.
• Remove contaminated clothing and irrigate exposed skin/eyes.
• Identify substance and contact a poison information service/toxicology.
• Do not induce vomiting. Do not administer activated charcoal routinely without assessing airway safety and timing.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Bedside glucose, ECG, vital signs, neurological assessment.
• Electrolytes, renal function, blood gas, lactate when indicated.
• Targeted tests: paracetamol level, salicylate level, ethanol level, etc.
• Consider anion gap, osmolal gap for toxic alcohols.
• Urine drug screens have limitations; do not use to exclude poisoning.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Stabilization[/color]
• Treatment depends on substance. Correct hypoglycemia, treat seizures, support airway/shock.

[color=#1E3A8A]Activated charcoal[/color]
• Single dose 1 g/kg orally (up to local max). Consider only after toxicology consult.
• Most useful for adsorbable substances early (usually within 1 hour).
• Do not use in unprotected airway, bowel obstruction, or corrosives/alcohols.

[color=#1E3A8A]Naloxone (Opioid toxicity)[/color]
• Pediatric weight-based regimen. Priority is reversal of respiratory depression, not necessarily full awakening.

[color=#1E3A8A]Substance-specific antidotes[/color]
• Paracetamol: N-acetylcysteine per nomogram.
• Organophosphate: Atropine and oxime.
• Methanol/Ethylene glycol: Fomepizole/ethanol, possible dialysis.
• Iron: Chelation if indicated.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Respiratory depression, seizures, hypotension, severe metabolic acidosis, arrhythmias, or reduced consciousness require resuscitation-level care.
• Some substances cause delayed deterioration despite an initially normal exam.
• Consider safeguarding assessment when intentional ingestion, neglect, or inconsistent history is suspected.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit significant symptoms, abnormal ECG, altered consciousness, or high-risk substances.
• Discharge only when substance-appropriate observation is complete and child is clinically stable.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; WHO; Local poison service.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Assess burn mechanism, time, depth, total body surface area (TBSA), and associated trauma.
• Superficial: red, painful, dry (not included in TBSA fluid calc).
• Partial-thickness: blistering, moist, significant pain.
• Full-thickness: leathery, pale/brown/charred, reduced sensation.
• Inhalation injury: facial/neck burns, hoarseness, stridor, soot, respiratory distress.
• Circumferential burns: may compromise perfusion/chest expansion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stop burning process and remove from source.
• ABCDE assessment; treat associated trauma first.
• Cool thermal burn with cool running water for 20 minutes (ideally within 3 hours).
• Remove clothing/jewelry unless adherent. Prevent hypothermia (cool the burn, not the child).
• Cover loosely with clean non-adherent dressing or clean film (lengthwise, never circumferentially).
• Give early analgesia and obtain IV/IO access for major burns.
• Arrange early specialist consult for inhalation, major, electrical, chemical, or special-area burns.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally every 4–6 hours. IV morphine 0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV slowly for severe pain.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV fluid resuscitation[/color]
• Indicated for burns > 10% TBSA (or earlier if shock).
• Modified Parkland: 3 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA over 24 hours (half in first 8 hours from injury).
• Add maintenance fluids (with glucose as appropriate).
• Monitor urine output (target ~1 mL/kg/hour).
• Avoid excessive fluids (worsens edema).

[color=#1E3A8A]Airway / inhalation[/color]
• High-concentration oxygen. Early expert airway assessment; consider early intubation if progressive edema or stridor.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Children are vulnerable to hypothermia and fluid overload.
• Do not calculate TBSA using superficial erythema alone.
• Chemical eye burns require immediate prolonged irrigation.
• Electrical injuries may cause deep tissue damage despite small skin lesions.
• Consider non-accidental injury if history/pattern is concerning.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Refer/transfer urgently for airway injury, major/full-thickness burns, circumferential burns, electrical/chemical burns, special areas, or suspected abuse.
• Small uncomplicated burns may be outpatient after assessment, pain control, dressing, tetanus review, and follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; NICE NG39.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Trauma may involve isolated limb injury or multisystem injury. Children can mask significant blood loss until deterioration.
• High-energy mechanism, airway compromise, chest/abdominal tenderness, altered consciousness.
• Deformity, swelling, open wound, severe pain, inability to use limb.
• Distal neurovascular compromise: absent/weak pulse, delayed cap refill, cool limb, numbness.
• Compartment syndrome: escalating pain, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling.
• Possible non-accidental injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Structured pediatric trauma primary survey (ABCDE with cervical spine protection).
• Control external hemorrhage. Tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding.
• Treat shock promptly. Judicious isotonic crystalloid while arranging blood products.
• Immobilize fractures in position found (unless reduction needed for perfusion).
• Document neurovascular findings before/after splinting.
• Urgent orthopedic/trauma consult for open fractures, neurovascular compromise, or suspected compartment syndrome.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Pain control[/color]
• Paracetamol 15 mg/kg, Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg (if appropriate).
• Severe pain: IV morphine 0.05–0.1 mg/kg slowly.

[color=#1E3A8A]Open fracture[/color]
• Sterile dressing. Do not probe or push bone back in.
• IV antibiotics as early as possible. Check tetanus status.

[color=#1E3A8A]Neurovascular compromise / Compartment syndrome[/color]
• Remove constricting items, reassess splints.
• Urgent reduction if displaced fracture compromises perfusion.
• Suspected compartment syndrome = surgical emergency. Keep limb at heart level, remove constrictions. Do not delay for pressure measurements if clinically convincing.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hemorrhagic shock[/color]
• Control bleeding, activate major hemorrhage pathway. Blood products early. Avoid large crystalloid boluses.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Children maintain BP until late shock; do not rely on hypotension alone.
• Preserved pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome.
• Severe pain, pain on passive stretch, or rapidly increasing swelling requires immediate evaluation.
• Do not discharge with unresolved neurovascular abnormalities.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit/transfer for open/unstable fractures, neurovascular compromise, compartment syndrome, significant trauma, or suspected abuse.
• Discharge only after adequate assessment, satisfactory neurovascular findings, and clear follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE NG39; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Respiratory impairment from submersion/immersion. May result in hypoxemia, respiratory failure, cardiac arrest, brain injury.
• Cough, tachypnea, distress, hypoxemia. Altered consciousness, seizures, arrest. Hypothermia.
• Prognosis depends on submersion duration, need for CPR, neuro state, oxygenation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Ensure rescuer safety. Remove from water.
• If unresponsive/not breathing normally: Activate emergency support, begin CPR (including rescue breaths). Use AED as soon as available.
• Provide oxygen/ventilation for hypoxemia.
• If trauma suspected, use spinal precautions (do not delay airway/resus).
• Remove wet clothing, dry, prevent heat loss.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Oxygenation/Ventilation[/color]
• Supplemental oxygen. Bag-mask if inadequate breathing. Intubation/mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure.
• Lung-protective ventilation strategies.
• Do not delay ventilation to drain water. Abdominal thrusts not recommended for water removal.

[color=#1E3A8A]CPR / Hypothermia[/color]
• High-quality pediatric CPR, AED. Treat hypoxia as major reversible cause.
• Remove wet clothing, insulate, active rewarming per protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics/Steroids[/color]
• Do NOT prescribe prophylactic antibiotics routinely.
• Corticosteroids NOT routinely recommended.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Respiratory deterioration can occur after initial event.
• Do not assume safe because child coughed up water or initially appeared well.
• Consider hypothermia, trauma, intoxication, seizure, or underlying event.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for persistent cough, distress, abnormal SpO2, altered mental status, hypothermia, or need for resus.
• Discharge after observation ONLY if completely asymptomatic, normal vitals/SpO2, reassuring exam.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA BLS 2025; Resuscitation Council UK 2025.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
External skin lesions may underestimate internal damage.
• Risk factors: High-voltage exposure, lightning strike, LOC/arrest, chest-crossing current, tetany, deep burns, dark urine, associated trauma.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Ensure source is disconnected before touching patient. Do not approach downed lines.
• Activate emergency services, use scene safety.
• Assess responsiveness, breathing, pulse. Begin CPR/AED if arrest.
• Oxygen/ventilation when indicated.
• Assess burns, trauma, spinal injury. Obtain IV access.
• Arrange urgent transfer for high-voltage, lightning, cardiac symptoms, LOC, or major burns.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• 12-lead ECG for significant injury, cardiac symptoms, LOC, high-voltage, lightning.
• Continuous cardiac monitoring for abnormal ECG or significant symptoms.
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, blood gas, CK, urinalysis (rhabdomyolysis).
• Imaging for fractures/head injury based on mechanism.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Cardiac arrest/arrhythmia[/color]
• Follow pediatric BLS/PALS. Defibrillate shockable rhythms.

[color=#1E3A8A]Burns/Soft-tissue[/color]
• Cover burns, prevent hypothermia. Assess entry/exit wounds. Early surgical consult.

[color=#1E3A8A]Rhabdomyolysis/Renal protection[/color]
• IV isotonic fluids individualized to perfusion/urine output. Monitor CK, electrolytes, renal function. Treat hyperkalemia.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• High-voltage/lightning can cause serious internal injury despite minimal external burns.
• Delayed weakness, numbness, compartment syndrome, or renal injury may develop.
• Do not touch patient until source is safe.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit/transfer for high-voltage, lightning, arrest, abnormal ECG, LOC, significant burns, rhabdomyolysis, or major trauma.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; AHA BLS.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• [color=#1E3A8A]Vaso-occlusive crisis:[/color] Acute pain (bones, limbs, back, chest, abdomen). Assess for fever, hypoxemia, focal neuro symptoms, abdominal enlargement.
• [color=#1E3A8A]Acute chest syndrome (ACS):[/color] New pulmonary infiltrate + fever and/or respiratory symptoms. May deteriorate rapidly.
• [color=#1E3A8A]Other:[/color] Stroke, splenic sequestration (sudden splenomegaly, pallor, shock), aplastic crisis, sepsis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• ABCDE, vital signs, pain severity, SpO2, hydration, neuro status.
• Treat fever urgently; do not assume uncomplicated crisis.
• Prompt analgesia for severe pain (within 30–60 min).
• Give oxygen for hypoxemia (not routine if normoxic).
• Contact hematology/pediatric team early for ACS, stroke, sequestration, sepsis.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Vaso-occlusive pain[/color]
• Paracetamol 15 mg/kg, Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg (if appropriate).
• Severe pain: IV morphine 0.05–0.1 mg/kg slowly, reassess and titrate.
• Encourage oral fluids. IV fluid only if needed (avoid overload).

[color=#1E3A8A]Acute chest syndrome[/color]
• Admit, oxygen, monitor closely, analgesia without excessive sedation.
• Incentive spirometry when awake.
• Empiric antibiotics: Ceftriaxone 50–75 mg/kg IV every 24 hours + Azithromycin per local protocol.
• Discuss transfusion with hematology for hypoxemia or deterioration.

[color=#1E3A8A]Fever/Sepsis[/color]
• Obtain cultures, but start IV antibiotics promptly per sickle cell fever pathway.

[color=#1E3A8A]Stroke / Sequestration[/color]
• Stroke: Activate stroke pathway, urgent imaging, specialist-directed exchange transfusion.
• Sequestration: Urgent CBC/crossmatch, treat shock, urgent transfusion (careful of hyperviscosity).

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Fever, respiratory symptoms, hypoxemia, neurological deficit, rapidly enlarging spleen, or severe pallor are NOT uncomplicated pain crises.
• ACS can progress rapidly.
• Avoid dehydration and excessive IV fluid.
• Do not transfuse routinely for uncomplicated pain crisis.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit urgently for ACS, stroke, sequestration, aplastic crisis, sepsis, hypoxemia, uncontrolled pain, or inability to maintain intake.
• Outpatient only if clinically stable, serious complications excluded, pain controlled, and reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO 2026; CDC; NHLBI.

Hematology & Oncology.title: Severe Anemia and Acute Hemolytic Crisis

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Marked pallor, fatigue, weakness, dizziness, syncope.
• Tachycardia, tachypnea, flow murmur. Severe: altered consciousness, shock, distress, heart failure.
• Acute hemolysis: jaundice, dark urine, sudden fall in Hb.
• Splenic sequestration: sudden pallor, abdominal distension, splenomegaly, shock.
• Consider malaria, nutritional deficiency, hemoglobinopathies, G6PD, autoimmune hemolysis, marrow suppression, acute blood loss.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, perfusion, mental status. Continuous monitoring in unstable patients.
• Check bedside glucose. Obtain urgent CBC.
• Assess for bleeding, jaundice, splenomegaly, heart failure.
• Send blood group and crossmatch early.
• Treat shock according to cause (avoid indiscriminate fluid boluses due to overload risk).
• Investigate/treat malaria promptly. Contact hematology for suspected hemolytic crisis.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC with indices/platelets. Reticulocyte count, blood film.
• Blood group, antibody screen, crossmatch.
• Bilirubin, LDH, renal function, electrolytes, urinalysis. DAT if immune hemolysis.
• Malaria test/smear. Iron studies, Hb electrophoresis, G6PD testing based on timing/cause.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Packed Red Blood Cell Transfusion[/color]
• Guided by Hb, symptoms, hemodynamics, ongoing loss.
• Initial PRBC volume commonly 10 mL/kg, followed by reassessment. Use local protocol.
• Children with chronic severe anemia are vulnerable to overload. Avoid rapid/excessive transfusion.

[color=#1E3A8A]Treat Underlying Cause[/color]
• Iron deficiency: Oral iron 3–6 mg/kg/day elemental iron after stabilization.
• Malaria: Prompt antimalarial testing/treatment.
• Acute hemolysis: Stop suspected causative med. Maintain renal perfusion.
• Splenic sequestration: Emergency hematology assessment and carefully managed transfusion.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Stop transfusion immediately and initiate transfusion-reaction protocol if serious reaction suspected.
• Do not delay lifesaving transfusion in a child with life-threatening anemia and instability.
• In sickle cell disease, avoid excessive hemoglobin elevation; consult protocol.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit for instability, respiratory distress, heart failure, acute hemolysis, sequestration, active bleeding, severe malaria, or need for urgent transfusion.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAP Iron Deficiency; WHO Manual for Health Care of Children; WHO Malaria.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Neonatal resuscitation is required when a newborn fails to establish effective spontaneous breathing or has persistent bradycardia after birth.
• Assess: Gestational age, muscle tone, spontaneous breathing/crying, heart rate, respiratory effort.
• Apnea or gasping. Heart rate < 100 bpm. Persistent cyanosis/hypoxemia. Poor respiratory effort.
• Heart rate < 60 bpm despite effective ventilation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for neonatal resuscitation assistance.
• Provide warmth and maintain temperature.
• Position head in neutral/slightly extended position. Dry and provide gentle tactile stimulation.
• Clear airway only if obstruction is suspected; routine suctioning not recommended.
• Assess heart rate and breathing promptly.
• Begin positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) within first 60 seconds if apnea, gasping, or HR < 100/min.
• Attach preductal pulse oximeter (right hand/wrist) and ECG monitoring.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT: PPV
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Indication:[/color] Apnea, gasping, or HR < 100/min despite initial steps.
• Provide 30–60 inflations/min. Initial peak inflation pressure commonly 20–30 cm H2O.
• Assess heart rate response and chest movement.
• If HR does not improve, correct mask seal, head position, airway obstruction, and ventilation technique.
• [color=#991B1B]Effective ventilation is the most important intervention. Do NOT proceed to chest compressions before ensuring ventilation is effective.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT: Oxygen
sections.content:
• Term/late-preterm: begin with 21% oxygen.
• Preterm: select initial concentration per gestational age and protocol.
• Titrate using preductal pulse oximetry.
• Target preductal SpO2: 1 min (60-65%), 2 min (65-70%), 3 min (70-75%), 4 min (75-80%), 5 min (80-85%), 10 min (85-95%).
• Avoid unnecessary hyperoxia.

sections.heading: 05 — TREATMENT: Compressions & Epinephrine
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Chest Compressions[/color]
• Indication: HR < 60/min after at least 30 seconds of effective ventilation.
• Two-thumb encircling-hands technique. Lower third of sternum.
• 3:1 ratio (90 compressions, 30 ventilations/min). Increase O2 to 100%.

[color=#1E3A8A]Epinephrine[/color]
• Indication: HR < 60/min despite optimized ventilation and compressions.
• IV/Umbilical dose: 0.01–0.03 mg/kg (0.1–0.3 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL solution).
• Endotracheal route (if vascular access pending): 0.05–0.1 mg/kg.
• Repeat every 3–5 minutes if HR < 60/min.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT confuse 0.1 mg/mL with 1 mg/mL epinephrine (tenfold error).[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Volume Expansion[/color]
• Suspected blood loss/hypovolemia: 0.9% NaCl or blood products, 10 mL/kg cautiously.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Newborns requiring prolonged ventilation, chest compressions, epinephrine, or advanced resuscitation require close post-resuscitation monitoring and NICU care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/AAP Neonatal Resuscitation Guidelines (2025).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
May result from RDS, TTN, pneumonia, meconium aspiration, pneumothorax, CHD, or PPHN.
• RR > 60/min. Grunting. Nasal flaring. Chest retractions. Central cyanosis. Apnea.
• Persistent hypoxemia. Poor feeding, lethargy, temperature instability.
• Impending failure: Apnea/gasping, worsening hypoxemia, exhaustion, bradycardia, altered consciousness.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and temperature. Position airway appropriately.
• Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiorespiratory monitoring. Check bedside glucose.
• Provide oxygen when indicated, titrate to target.
• Initiate CPAP in a spontaneously breathing infant with appropriate indications.
• Begin assisted ventilation for apnea, gasping, or inadequate ventilation.
• Consider pneumothorax, sepsis, CHD, metabolic disease if deteriorating.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Supplemental Oxygen[/color]
• Use lowest concentration to achieve target (e.g., 90–94% in many preterm infants post-stabilization).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. CPAP[/color]
• Starting pressure ~5–6 cm H2O. Appropriately fitted interface. Monitor work of breathing, O2 requirement, blood gas, abdominal distension.
• Not appropriate as sole support for apneic infant or severe failure.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Positive-Pressure Ventilation[/color]
• For apnea, gasping, or inadequate effort. Monitor chest movement, HR, SpO2.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Surfactant Therapy[/color]
• For preterm RDS. Administer via approved airway technique by trained personnel.

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Investigate and Treat Cause[/color]
• Suspected infection: cultures and empiric antibiotics. Pneumothorax: urgent decompression if tension. CHD: urgent cardiac assessment.

sections.heading: 04 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit infants with persistent distress, O2 requirement, apnea, suspected infection, or need for CPAP/ventilation to NICU.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Recommendations; AHA/AAP Guidelines (2025).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Inadequate tissue perfusion. Hypotension is a late finding.
• Causes: Sepsis, hypovolemia/blood loss, myocardial dysfunction, PPHN, duct-dependent CHD, pneumothorax.
• Prolonged cap refill. Weak pulses. Cool/mottled extremities. Tachycardia/bradycardia.
• Reduced urine output. Lethargy/poor feeding. Metabolic acidosis/elevated lactate. Hypotension (late).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for neonatal/critical care assistance. Assess ABCs, temperature.
• Provide respiratory support and oxygen. Obtain IV/umbilical venous access.
• Check glucose immediately. Obtain blood gas, lactate, cultures, relevant labs.
• Start empiric antibiotics promptly if sepsis suspected.
• Assess shock type (hypovolemia, sepsis, cardiac, obstructive) before repeated fluid boluses.
• Arrange urgent echocardiography if cardiac dysfunction/duct-dependent disease possible.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• Suspected hypovolemic shock: cautious initial bolus 10 mL/kg, immediate reassessment.
• Repeat only if evidence of ongoing fluid-responsive shock and no fluid overload/cardiac failure.
• [color=#991B1B]Repeated boluses may worsen respiratory failure or myocardial dysfunction.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Suspected Septic Shock[/color]
• Blood cultures if no delay. Appropriate IV antibiotics per local guidance. Do NOT delay in unstable infant.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Vasoactive Support[/color]
• If perfusion inadequate after initial management, initiate specialist-directed vasoactive therapy (Epinephrine, Dopamine, etc., per shock phenotype and local protocol).
• Monitor ECG, BP, perfusion, urine output, glucose, lactate, extravasation risk.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Correct Reversible Causes[/color]
• Hypoglycemia, blood loss/anemia, pneumothorax, duct-dependent CHD.

sections.heading: 04 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • All suspected shock require urgent hospital management. Persistent shock, vasoactive support, severe acidosis, or organ dysfunction requires NICU.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Guidance; Local NICU Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Neonates (especially preterm/LBW) lose heat rapidly.
• Normal: 36.5–37.5°C. Cold stress: < 36.5°C. Moderate: 32.0–35.9°C. Severe: < 32.0°C.
• Cold skin/low temp. Poor feeding. Lethargy/weak cry. Respiratory distress/apnea. Hypoglycemia. Bradycardia. Poor perfusion/acidosis.
• Temperature instability may be a sign of sepsis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Confirm temperature with neonatal thermometer. Assess ABCs and glucose.
• Remove wet clothing, dry infant. Begin controlled rewarming.
• Use radiant warmer or incubator. Monitor temperature frequently.
• Investigate for infection, hypoglycemia, respiratory disease.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Thermal Support[/color]
• Target 36.5–37.5°C. Radiant warmer for rapid access; incubator for ongoing control.
• Preterm immediately after birth: plastic wrap/bag without prior drying + head cover per protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use direct high-temperature heat sources, hot-water bottles, or uncontrolled heating.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Glucose Management[/color]
• Check glucose promptly, treat hypoglycemia per protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Evaluate for Sepsis[/color]
• Consider infection with hypothermia + poor feeding/respiratory distress/lethargy/apnea. Obtain cultures, start empiric antibiotics if indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Rewarming in Severe Hypothermia[/color]
• Controlled rewarming with continuous monitoring. Manage apnea, bradycardia, hypoglycemia, shock. Requires specialist neonatal care.

sections.heading: 04 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit for persistent hypothermia, hypoglycemia, respiratory symptoms, poor feeding, suspected infection, or abnormal perfusion. Preterm/LBW may need ongoing incubator care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Recommendations for Newborn Thermal Care.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Neonatal bradycardia may result from hypoxia, hypothermia, respiratory failure, sepsis, metabolic abnormalities, CHD, or medications.
• HR below expected range. Apnea/inadequate breathing. Cyanosis/hypoxemia. Poor perfusion/weak pulses.
• Altered responsiveness. Cardiac arrest with absent effective circulation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for resuscitation assistance. Assess ABCs and temperature.
• Provide effective ventilation for apnea/inadequate breathing. Attach ECG and SpO2.
• Check glucose and consider reversible causes.
• Follow appropriate neonatal resuscitation or pediatric life support algorithm based on age and setting.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Bradycardia During Resuscitation at Birth[/color]
• Apnea/gasping/HR < 100: Provide effective PPV.
• HR < 60 despite 30s effective ventilation: Initiate coordinated chest compressions.
• HR < 60 after ~60s of compressions + ventilation: Administer epinephrine per neonatal algorithm (0.01–0.03 mg/kg IV/umbilical of 0.1 mg/mL solution).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Bradycardia After Initial Birth Transition[/color]
• Support oxygenation/ventilation. Treat hypoxemia, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, sepsis, electrolytes.
• Urgent neonatal/pediatric critical care support.
• Cardiopulmonary arrest/persistent severe bradycardia with poor perfusion: Use age-appropriate resuscitation algorithm.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT automatically apply delivery-room 3:1 algorithm to an older neonate who deteriorated later. Follow appropriate protocol.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Treat Underlying Cause[/color]
• Hypoxemia, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia, CHD, sepsis.

sections.heading: 04 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Persistent bradycardia, cardiac arrest, significant O2 requirement, or hemodynamic instability requires NICU/appropriate critical care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/AAP Neonatal Resuscitation Guidelines (2025).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Potentially life-threatening systemic infection. Signs may be subtle/nonspecific.
• EOS: First 72 hours (some use 48h). Risk factors: maternal GBS, intra-amniotic infection, maternal fever, prolonged ROM, prematurity.
• LOS: After early period. Risk factors: prematurity, prolonged hospitalization, central lines, mechanical ventilation, parenteral nutrition.
• Indicators: Temp instability, poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, apnea, grunting, tachypnea, tachycardia/bradycardia, poor perfusion, abdominal distension, jaundice, seizures, hypo/hyperglycemia.
• [color=#991B1B]Normal temp, CBC, or initial CRP does NOT exclude neonatal sepsis.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, temperature, neuro status. Provide O2/respiratory support.
• Establish IV access (IO if urgent). Check bedside glucose, correct hypoglycemia.
• Obtain blood culture before antibiotics if no meaningful delay.
• Obtain CBC, CRP/PCT per protocol, blood gas, lactate, glucose, electrolytes, renal function.
• Start empiric IV antibiotics promptly (ideally within 1 hour).
• Assess for meningitis, pneumonia, UTI, omphalitis, NEC. Monitor vitals, perfusion, urine output.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric Antibiotics: EOS[/color]
• Common regimen: IV benzylpenicillin + gentamicin (or ampicillin + gentamicin).
• Benzylpenicillin sodium: 25 mg/kg IV every 12 hours (NICE; interval shortened if severely ill).
• Gentamicin: 5 mg/kg IV starting dose (NICE); subsequent intervals based on GA, postnatal age, renal function, TDM.
• [color=#991B1B]Confirm exact penicillin formulation/units. Do not confuse benzylpenicillin with benzathine penicillin. Never assume same gentamicin interval for all neonates.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric Antibiotics: LOS[/color]
• Hospital-acquired: Base on unit antibiogram, previous cultures, device exposure (e.g., flucloxacillin + gentamicin). Modify for MRSA/resistant Gram-negatives.
• Community-presenting: Use locally recommended regimen (may differ from hospital-acquired).
• Meningitis/NEC: Use regimen covering suspected diagnosis (additional anaerobic coverage for NEC).

[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive Treatment[/color]
• Normothermia, correct glucose/electrolytes, respiratory support, cautious fluids, vasoactive support if shock persists.
• Review cultures daily; narrow/adjust/stop antibiotics when justified.

sections.heading: 04 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit any neonate with suspected systemic infection for urgent assessment/monitored treatment.
• Transfer to NICU for apnea, respiratory failure, shock, seizures, significant metabolic abnormalities.
• Antibiotic duration depends on cultures, course, site. Do not use single duration for every case.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE NG195 (2026); Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Emergency because deterioration can be rapid and long-term neuro complications possible.
• Poor feeding, lethargy, irritability, reduced responsiveness. Temp instability.
• Apnea, respiratory distress, unexplained bradycardia. Seizures/abnormal movements.
• Bulging fontanelle (not always present). Abnormal tone, weak cry, persistent vomiting.
• Signs of sepsis/shock. Organisms: GBS, E. coli, Listeria, healthcare-associated. Consider HSV.
• Consider neonatal HSV when seizures, vesicular lesions, hepatitis, encephalitis, or compatible maternal history.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stabilize ABCs. Check glucose immediately, treat hypoglycemia.
• Obtain blood culture and appropriate blood tests.
• Perform lumbar puncture if safe and no delay to antibiotics.
• Start empiric IV antibiotics urgently.
• Treat seizures promptly (neonatal protocol).
• Consider HSV investigations and empiric acyclovir when indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT perform LP immediately if uncontrolled seizures, significant cardiorespiratory instability, shock requiring stabilization. Stabilize first, do NOT delay antibiotics.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Must cover likely neonatal pathogens and achieve adequate CSF penetration.
• NICE recommends IV amoxicillin + cefotaxime for suspected meningitis in neonatal-unit patients when pathogen unknown.
• Use meningitis-specific doses from local formulary (do NOT substitute routine sepsis dose).
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use ceftriaxone routinely in neonates without checking contraindications (hyperbilirubinemia, IV calcium exposure). Cefotaxime often preferred.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Organism-Directed Treatment[/color]
• Adjust antibiotics when CSF/blood cultures identify pathogen. Obtain microbiology advice for resistant organisms. Treatment usually prolonged.

[color=#1E3A8A]Seizures and Raised ICP[/color]
• Treat seizures (neonatal protocol). Maintain oxygenation, glucose, temp, electrolytes. Avoid routine fluid restriction without assessment. Seek urgent advice for raised ICP.

sections.heading: 04 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to neonatal unit; intensive care for seizures, shock, apnea, respiratory failure, reduced consciousness.
• Arrange hearing assessment and neurodevelopmental follow-up after confirmed meningitis.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE NG195; NICE NG240.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
May occur early after birth or later (hospital/community). Can coexist with neonatal sepsis.
• Tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, chest recession. Apnea/cyanosis. Increasing O2 requirement.
• Poor feeding, lethargy, temp instability. Crackles/reduced air entry.
• Poor perfusion/hypotension in severe infection.
• Differentials: RDS, TTN, meconium aspiration, pneumothorax, PPHN, CHD.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, temperature. Monitor SpO2 and cardiorespiratory status.
• Provide O2, CPAP, or ventilation per severity and local guidance.
• Check glucose, obtain blood gas if significant distress.
• Obtain blood culture before antibiotics if feasible without delay.
• Start empiric IV antibiotics per EOS/LOS guidance.
• Assess for pneumothorax and other causes of sudden deterioration.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Respiratory Support[/color]
• Oxygen: Titrate to target saturation specified by neonatal unit. Avoid hypoxemia/hyperoxia.
• CPAP/Ventilation: Settings per gestation, weight, lung mechanics, oxygenation, blood gas. Monitor SpO2, effort, apnea, blood gas, hemodynamics.
• [color=#991B1B]Sudden deterioration requires immediate assessment for pneumothorax, tube displacement, or equipment failure.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotic Treatment[/color]
• Use local neonatal sepsis regimen (EOS vs LOS, local resistance).
• EOS example: benzylpenicillin + gentamicin. LOS: base on unit antibiogram.
• Review cultures/clinical response to avoid unnecessarily broad/prolonged treatment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive Care[/color]
• Maintain normothermia, glucose, fluids/nutrition. Treat associated sepsis/shock. Consider surfactant only for appropriate indication (e.g., coexisting RDS).

sections.heading: 04 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for monitored neonatal care. Escalate to intensive care for increasing respiratory support, recurrent apnea, severe acidosis, shock, or persistent hypoxemia.
• Determine antibiotic duration from cultures/clinical progress, not radiographic findings alone.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE NG195; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Infection of umbilical stump and surrounding tissues. May progress rapidly to bacteremia, septic shock, or necrotizing soft-tissue infection.
• Redness extending onto surrounding abdominal skin. Warmth, swelling, tenderness around umbilicus.
• Purulent/foul-smelling discharge. Induration, skin discoloration, blistering, necrosis.
• Fever/hypothermia, poor feeding, lethargy, respiratory instability.
• [color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Rapidly spreading erythema, severe swelling/pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae, dusky skin, necrosis, abdominal distension, poor perfusion, altered responsiveness. Requires urgent surgical assessment.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, temp, perfusion, glucose. Inspect umbilicus/surrounding skin carefully.
• Obtain blood culture before antibiotics if no delay. Obtain sample of purulent discharge for culture.
• Start IV antibiotics promptly.
• Assess for systemic sepsis, abdominal wall involvement, abscess, necrotizing infection.
• Obtain urgent surgical consult for rapid progression, necrosis, crepitus, or suspected deep infection.
• Monitor closely for deterioration.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]IV Antibiotic Therapy[/color]
• Cover Staph aureus, streptococci, relevant Gram-negatives. Select per severity, local resistance, formulary.
• Add MRSA-active treatment if risk factors/local epidemiology warrant.
• Modify based on culture/clinical response.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use topical treatment or oral antibiotics alone for clinically significant omphalitis.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Local Care[/color]
• Clean technique, keep area clean/dry. Avoid unprescribed powders, herbal preparations, caustic substances.
• Do NOT squeeze or probe stump. Follow neonatal unit infection-control protocol.

sections.heading: 04 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit neonates with suspected omphalitis for urgent medical assessment and usually parenteral antibiotics.
• Intensive care may be required for shock, organ dysfunction, or rapidly progressive infection.
• Obtain surgical review for suspected abscess, necrotizing infection, or deep extension.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Botswana Neonatal Guidelines; NICE NG195.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Circulatory and cellular dysfunction due to infection. Hypotension may be late.
• Prolonged cap refill. Cool/mottled extremities or warm vasodilated extremities. Weak pulses.
• Tachycardia/bradycardia. Reduced urine output. Lethargy/altered responsiveness/seizures.
• Metabolic acidosis/elevated lactate. Hypotension (advanced).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call NICU team and activate local sepsis/shock pathway.
• Assess airway/breathing; provide O2/respiratory support.
• Establish IV/emergency IO access. Check glucose, blood gas, lactate, electrolytes, perfusion.
• Obtain blood culture if no delay.
• Give empiric IV antibiotics urgently (ideally within 1 hour).
• Assess fluid responsiveness/cardiac dysfunction/pulmonary edema.
• Administer carefully titrated isotonic crystalloid boluses only when indicated, reassess after each.
• Start vasoactive support promptly when shock persists or fluids unsafe/ineffective.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Select per suspected source, EOS/LOS, local antibiogram, previous cultures. Use meningitis-specific treatment if suspected. Reassess/tailor when microbiology available.
• [color=#991B1B]Shock is not a reason to use unverified doses. Confirm high-risk medication calculations with another clinician.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• If hypovolemia/fluid responsiveness suspected: cautious 10 mL/kg bolus under specialist guidance. Reassess after every bolus.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT automatically give repeated large-volume boluses. Preterm and myocardial dysfunction particularly vulnerable to overload.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Vasoactive Support[/color]
• Persistent poor perfusion/hypotension despite initial treatment. Early treatment may be required if further fluid unsafe.
• Epinephrine or norepinephrine per shock phenotype and specialist guidance. Use neonatal weight-based infusion protocol.
• Monitor ECG, BP, cap refill, pulses, lactate, urine output, glucose, perfusion. Titrate per protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Never administer continuous vasoactive infusion without verified concentration and pump calculation.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Additional Supportive Care[/color]
• Correct glucose/electrolytes, maintain temp, treat respiratory failure/apnea. Consider hydrocortisone only for refractory shock after specialist assessment.
• Identify/control source (infected catheters, surgical pathology).

sections.heading: 04 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• All neonates with septic shock require immediate NICU and continuous monitoring.
• Urgent transfer to higher-level NICU if advanced support unavailable.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE NG195; Local NICU Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Jitteriness, tremors, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, apnea, cyanosis, seizures, or altered consciousness.
• Risk factors: prematurity, small/large for gestational age, infant of diabetic mother, hypothermia, sepsis, perinatal stress.
• Symptoms may be absent despite low glucose.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and check bedside blood glucose immediately.
• Treat symptomatic or severely low glucose without waiting for lab confirmation.
• Obtain lab confirmation when feasible, but do NOT delay treatment.
• Check temperature and assess for sepsis or other causes.
• Recheck glucose after treatment according to neonatal protocol.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Asymptomatic infant who can feed[/color]
• Feed promptly with breast milk or appropriate alternative per local pathway.
• Buccal 40% dextrose gel, 0.5 mL/kg (200 mg/kg), may be used in eligible infants.
• Recheck glucose at protocol-defined interval (commonly ~30 minutes after intervention).

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Symptomatic or severe hypoglycemia[/color]
• 10% dextrose IV, 2 mL/kg (200 mg/kg) as initial bolus when indicated by neonatal protocol.
• Start continuous glucose infusion (initial GIR ~5–8 mg/kg/min; individual requirements vary).
• Recheck glucose ~30 minutes after treatment or as directed. Adjust GIR per serial measurements.
• Monitor IV access, fluid volume, electrolytes.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not rely on feeding or gel alone for an infant with seizures, apnea, impaired consciousness, or other severe symptoms.
• Avoid excessive or repeated dextrose boluses without reassessment.
• Persistent/recurrent hypoglycemia requires investigation for hyperinsulinism, endocrine disease, or inborn error of metabolism.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit infants requiring IV glucose or with recurrent, severe, or symptomatic hypoglycemia.
• Ensure stable glucose during an appropriate feeding interval before discharge.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: British Association of Perinatal Medicine; Local neonatal hypoglycemia protocol.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Repetitive focal clonic movements, tonic posturing, abnormal eye deviation, oral automatisms, or stereotyped autonomic changes.
• Many neonatal seizures are subtle or electrographic-only.
• Common causes: HIE, stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, infection, hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbances, or metabolic disease.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stabilize airway, breathing, circulation. Check glucose immediately and correct hypoglycemia.
• Monitor ECG, SpO2, temperature, BP. Obtain IV access.
• Treat prolonged or recurrent seizures promptly.
• Arrange continuous EEG monitoring when available. Investigate underlying cause.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Correct Reversible Causes[/color]
• Correct glucose and clinically significant calcium, sodium, or magnesium abnormalities per neonatal protocols.
• Treat suspected meningitis/sepsis promptly. Consider pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy in refractory seizures under specialist supervision.

[color=#1E3A8A]Phenobarbital (First-Line)[/color]
• Loading dose: 20 mg/kg IV.
• Additional loading doses may be considered under specialist direction if seizures persist.
• Administer slowly by IV infusion. Monitor respiratory rate, SpO2, BP, cardiac status.
• Prepare for respiratory support (respiratory depression/hypotension may occur).

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Confirm total loading dose before giving additional doses.
• Persistent seizures require reassessment and specialist-directed second-line treatment.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent NICU assessment. Monitor for recurrent seizures and medication-related respiratory depression.
• Arrange neurological follow-up for infants with significant seizures or brain injury.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ILAE Neonatal Seizure Recommendations; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until evaluated.
• Rapidly increasing jaundice, extending to legs, poor feeding, lethargy, abnormal tone.
• Risk factors: prematurity, hemolysis, G6PD deficiency, bruising, inadequate milk intake, infection.
• Severe bilirubin elevation can cause acute bilirubin encephalopathy and permanent neurological injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
