• Measure total serum bilirubin urgently; do NOT rely on visual assessment alone.
• Record exact age in hours, gestational age, and neurotoxicity risk factors.
• Check maternal/infant blood groups and DAT when indicated.
• Assess feeding, hydration, temperature, neurological status.
• Start intensive phototherapy when age/gestation-specific threshold reached.
• Obtain urgent neonatal specialist advice if bilirubin approaches exchange threshold or neuro signs present.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Intensive Phototherapy[/color]
• Use intensive blue-light phototherapy with irradiance and exposed surface area meeting local standard.
• Treatment threshold must be selected using applicable guideline chart for gestational age, postnatal age in hours, and risk factors.
• Maximize skin exposure while protecting eyes. Monitor temp, hydration, feeding, serial bilirubin.
• Continue breastfeeding or provide appropriate feeding support.

[color=#1E3A8A]Exchange Transfusion[/color]
• Indication: Bilirubin at/above applicable exchange threshold, or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy requiring emergency management.
• Urgent NICU/experienced neonatal team involvement. Prepare compatible blood products. Monitor cardiorespiratory status, glucose, electrolytes, calcium, bilirubin per protocol.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not use one bilirubin cutoff for all newborns. Treatment thresholds vary substantially with age in hours, gestational age, and risk factors.
• Do not delay escalation when severe bilirubin encephalopathy is suspected.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for intensive phototherapy or exchange transfusion.
• Arrange follow-up bilirubin testing and developmental/hearing assessment when clinically indicated.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline (2022); Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Apnea commonly defined as cessation of breathing for ~20 seconds, or shorter pause with bradycardia, cyanosis, or desaturation.
• Grunting, nasal flaring, chest recession, tachypnea, poor air entry, increasing O2 requirement.
• Causes: prematurity, infection, hypoglycemia, temperature instability, RDS, airway obstruction, seizures, pneumothorax.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway position, breathing, HR, SpO2. Position airway and provide gentle stimulation.
• If apnea/ineffective breathing persists, provide effective PPV.
• Reassess HR and chest movement; correct mask leak/airway obstruction.
• Check glucose and temperature. Investigate infection and other reversible causes.
• Escalate to CPAP or mechanical ventilation when indicated.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Positive-Pressure Ventilation[/color]
• Indication: Apnea, gasping, ineffective breathing with clinical deterioration.
• Use neonatal ventilation device/mask. Confirm effective chest movement and rising HR.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Caffeine for Apnea of Prematurity[/color]
• Caffeine citrate: Loading dose 20 mg/kg, followed by 5–10 mg/kg once daily per protocol.
• Verify dose is expressed as caffeine citrate, not caffeine base.
• Administer by IV or enteral route. Monitor apnea frequency, HR, feeding tolerance.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Oxygen alone does not correct apnea when ventilation is inadequate.
• Caffeine does not replace urgent ventilation in an infant with ongoing apnea or respiratory failure.
• Dosing/monitoring may differ in extremely premature or critically ill infants.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Recurrent apnea, bradycardia, or desaturation requires monitored neonatal care.
• Respiratory failure, need for ventilation, or suspected sepsis requires urgent NICU assessment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/AAP Neonatal Resuscitation Guidelines (2025); Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Abdominal distension, feeding intolerance, bilious vomiting, or bloody stools.
• Lethargy, temperature instability, apnea, bradycardia, poor perfusion.
• Abdominal tenderness, discoloration, palpable mass. Most common in premature/VLBW infants.
• [color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Rapid abdominal enlargement, abdominal wall erythema, shock, severe metabolic acidosis, thrombocytopenia, persistent deterioration.
• Pneumoperitoneum suggests intestinal perforation and is a surgical emergency.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stop enteral feeds immediately. Obtain urgent neonatal and pediatric surgical consultation.
• Establish IV access, assess ABCs/perfusion. Insert orogastric/nasogastric tube for decompression.
• Obtain blood cultures and lab investigations.
• Start IV antibiotics covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and (when indicated) anaerobic organisms.
• Correct hypoglycemia, electrolyte abnormalities, and shock. Monitor abdominal findings closely.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Bowel Rest and Decompression[/color]
• Keep infant NPO. Decompress stomach with correctly placed OGT/NGT.
• Provide IV fluids and nutritional support per neonatal/surgical guidance.
• Monitor abdominal girth, tenderness, stool, urine output, glucose, electrolytes, perfusion.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Use neonatal NEC antibiotic protocol; selection/duration depend on disease stage, local resistance, cultures, surgical findings.
• [color=#991B1B]Do not use adult intra-abdominal infection regimen without neonatal dose verification.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Surgical Management[/color]
• Indications: Pneumoperitoneum or suspected perforation, progressive deterioration despite medical treatment, abdominal wall discoloration, peritonitis, necrotic bowel.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• A normal initial radiograph does not exclude evolving NEC.
• Suspected perforation or clinical deterioration requires immediate surgical reassessment.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to NICU. Continue close neonatal and surgical reassessment.
• Restart feeds only after clinical improvement and individualized neonatal/surgical plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: APSA NEC Resources; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Poor feeding, excessive weight loss, reduced urine output, lethargy, irritability, weak cry.
• Dry mucous membranes, fever, tachycardia, poor perfusion.
• Severe: seizures, altered consciousness, intracranial hemorrhage, shock.
• Causes: inadequate milk intake, ineffective breastfeeding, excessive insensible water loss, GI fluid loss.
• Hypernatremia defined as serum sodium > 145 mmol/L.
• [color=#991B1B]Clinical signs may underestimate degree of water deficit in neonatal hypernatremia.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, neuro status, temperature. Check bedside glucose immediately.
• Obtain weight and compare with birth/previous weights.
• Establish IV access if significant dehydration/instability. Obtain serum sodium, K+, Cl-, HCO3-, urea, creatinine, glucose, osmolality.
• Assess urine output and ongoing losses.
• If shock present, restore circulation cautiously with isotonic crystalloid and reassess frequently.
• Correct sodium abnormality gradually with neonatal specialist-directed fluid plan.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Initial Circulatory Stabilization[/color]
• If shock/severe intravascular depletion: 0.9% NaCl in cautious 10 mL/kg aliquots under specialist supervision. Reassess perfusion after each.
• Once circulation restored, calculate remaining deficit and maintenance requirements.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Controlled Sodium Correction[/color]
• Usual maximum sodium reduction ~0.5 mmol/L/hour and 10–12 mmol/L in 24 hours.
• Calculate maintenance fluid, estimated deficit, and ongoing losses separately.
• Check sodium frequently (every 2–4 hours initially in severe cases or during active correction).
• Monitor glucose, K+, renal function, urine output, weight, neuro status.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid rapid correction of hypernatremia (can cause cerebral edema and seizures).
• Do not attempt to normalize sodium rapidly.
• Seizures or neurological deterioration during correction require urgent reassessment.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit infants with significant hypernatremia for monitored treatment.
• Severe hypernatremia, shock, seizures, or renal impairment requires urgent NICU.
• Assess feeding technique and establish safe feeding plan before discharge.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Neonatal Fluid/Electrolyte Guidance; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Sudden deterioration in SpO2 or ventilation. Increasing respiratory distress, cyanosis, apnea.
• Reduced/absent breath sounds on one side may be present. Unequal chest movement or sudden cardiovascular compromise.
• Tension pneumothorax: severe hypoxemia, bradycardia, hypotension, cardiac arrest.
• Risk factors: PPV, RDS, meconium aspiration, underlying lung disease.
• [color=#991B1B]A critically unstable infant with suspected tension pneumothorax requires immediate treatment; do NOT wait for radiographic confirmation.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for neonatal resuscitation and senior assistance. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, ventilation equipment.
• Give oxygen and provide effective ventilation if needed.
• If tension pneumothorax strongly suspected with cardiovascular/respiratory collapse: perform emergency decompression per neonatal emergency protocol.
• Arrange definitive pleural drainage when indicated.
• Obtain chest imaging after stabilization if no delay. Reassess for recurrence and underlying cause.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Emergency Decompression for Tension[/color]
• Indication: Suspected tension pneumothorax with severe respiratory/cardiovascular compromise.
• Appropriately trained clinician should immediately decompress affected hemithorax using approved neonatal technique/equipment.
• Follow local protocol for anatomical site, catheter/needle selection, decompression method. Arrange chest drain insertion when indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Stable Pneumothorax[/color]
• Small, clinically stable pneumothoraces may be managed with close observation and respiratory support per specialist advice.
• Larger pneumothoraces, worsening distress, or persistent air leaks may require pleural drainage.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay emergency decompression for imaging in a collapsing infant.
• Incorrect placement can injure lung, heart, or blood vessels. Requires appropriate training.
• Avoid unnecessary positive-pressure escalation without assessing for worsening air leak.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Tension pneumothorax or any infant requiring pleural drainage requires intensive neonatal monitoring.
• Transfer to higher-level unit if drainage, ventilation, or continuous monitoring unavailable.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/AAP Neonatal Resuscitation Guidelines (2025); Local protocols.

Neonatal Emergencies.title: Critical Congenital Heart Disease and Duct-Dependent Shock

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Duct-dependent congenital heart disease may become life-threatening as ductus arteriosus constricts during first days of life.
• Cyanosis not improving as expected with oxygen. Poor feeding, tachypnea, lethargy, diaphoresis during feeding.
• Weak femoral pulses or difference between upper/lower-limb pulses. Poor perfusion, metabolic acidosis, oliguria, shock.
• Differential preductal and postductal SpO2 may occur.
• Duct-dependent systemic: HLHS, critical aortic stenosis, interrupted aortic arch. Duct-dependent pulmonary: pulmonary atresia, critical pulmonary stenosis. TGA may cause profound cyanosis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, perfusion, BP, temperature.
• Measure preductal SpO2 (right hand) and postductal SpO2 (foot).
• Obtain IV access; check glucose, blood gas, lactate, electrolytes, renal function.
• Contact NICU and pediatric cardiology urgently. Obtain urgent echocardiography when available.
• If duct-dependent circulation strongly suspected in deteriorating neonate: initiate PGE1 under emergency specialist guidance without waiting for echo when delay dangerous.
• Treat shock cautiously; avoid indiscriminate fluid boluses. Arrange urgent transfer to cardiac-capable center.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Prostaglandin E1 (Alprostadil)[/color]
• Indication: Suspected duct-dependent CHD when maintaining ductal patency essential.
• Initial infusion range: 0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min IV. Titrate per neonatal/cardiology team and protocol.
• Give as continuous IV infusion using syringe pump. Monitor HR, BP, SpO2, respiratory effort, temperature, perfusion continuously.
• Prepare for assisted ventilation and transfer to intensive care.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT give as IV bolus. Do NOT stop abruptly in neonate dependent on ductal patency without specialist direction.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Shock Management[/color]
• If significant hypovolemia suspected: cautious isotonic crystalloid 10 mL/kg aliquots with immediate reassessment.
• Avoid repeated boluses when myocardial dysfunction/fluid overload suspected. Use vasoactive support per shock phenotype.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Apnea, hypotension, flushing, and fever may occur with PGE1.
• Oxygen alone does not correct duct-dependent systemic obstruction and may not correct cyanosis from complex cardiac physiology.
• Avoid delaying prostaglandin or cardiology assessment.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent NICU admission. Transfer to pediatric cardiac center ASAP.
• Continue PGE1 infusion and cardiorespiratory monitoring during transfer with personnel capable of managing apnea and deterioration.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA Neonatal Cyanosis/CHD Management; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
HIE results from impaired oxygen delivery and blood flow around birth and may cause acute brain injury.
• Difficult resuscitation or significant perinatal hypoxic event.
• Altered consciousness, lethargy, reduced spontaneous activity. Abnormal tone, weak suck, impaired primitive reflexes.
• Clinical or electrographic seizures. Respiratory depression, poor perfusion, metabolic acidosis, multiorgan dysfunction.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stabilize ABCs. Review resuscitation history, cord gases, Apgar scores, evidence of perinatal hypoxia.
• Check glucose, blood gas, lactate, electrolytes, renal/liver function, coagulation.
• Perform structured neuro exam and assess eligibility for therapeutic hypothermia.
• Contact NICU urgently. Treat seizures and correct reversible physiological abnormalities.
• Arrange EEG/aEEG when available. Do NOT delay specialist consultation while waiting for neuroimaging.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Therapeutic Hypothermia[/color]
• Eligibility: Consider for eligible infants (generally ≥36 weeks gestation) with evidence of significant perinatal hypoxia-ischemia and moderate-to-severe encephalopathy. Initiation time-critical, generally within 6 hours after birth.
• Target: Core temperature near 33.5°C for 72 hours, followed by controlled rewarming. Use only approved device and protocol in unit capable of continuous monitoring.
• Monitor core temperature continuously. Monitor HR, BP, oxygenation, glucose, electrolytes, coagulation, urine output, neuro status. Rewarm slowly per protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT initiate uncontrolled cooling with ice packs or improvised methods.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Seizure Management[/color]
• Treat confirmed/strongly suspected neonatal seizures per protocol. Check/correct glucose, calcium, sodium, magnesium.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Multiorgan Support[/color]
• Maintain adequate oxygenation/ventilation (avoid hyperoxia/hypocapnia). Maintain glucose/electrolyte stability. Monitor renal, liver, coagulation, hemodynamics.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not initiate uncontrolled cooling with ice packs or improvised methods.
• Do not delay referral of an eligible infant while arranging nonessential tests.
• Therapeutic hypothermia not routinely recommended for every infant with mild encephalopathy or outside eligibility criteria; obtain specialist advice.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to NICU.
• Arrange neurodevelopmental follow-up, hearing assessment, and early-intervention services per findings and local pathway.
• Counsel family using serial examinations, EEG, imaging, and overall clinical course rather than single early finding.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAP Therapeutic Hypothermia for HIE; Local protocols.

Neonatal Emergencies.title: Neonatal Bilious Vomiting and Intestinal Obstruction

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency until intestinal obstruction has been excluded.
• Green, bile-stained vomiting. Abdominal distension or tenderness.
• Failure to pass meconium or abnormal stool passage. Poor feeding, dehydration, lethargy, shock.
• Blood in stool, abdominal discoloration, systemic deterioration may indicate bowel ischemia or NEC.
• Causes: Malrotation with midgut volvulus, intestinal atresia/stenosis, Hirschsprung, meconium ileus, NEC, other congenital/acquired obstruction.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Treat green bilious vomiting as emergency; obtain immediate pediatric surgical consultation.
• Stop all oral/enteral feeds. Assess ABCs, perfusion, hydration, glucose.
• Establish IV access, obtain blood tests. Insert orogastric/nasogastric tube for decompression per protocol.
• Provide isotonic IV fluids when indicated, with reassessment.
• Obtain urgent abdominal imaging guided by surgical team.
• Start antibiotics if ischemia, perforation, NEC, or sepsis suspected. Arrange urgent transfer to pediatric surgical center if required.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Stabilization and Gastric Decompression[/color]
• Keep infant NPO. Use appropriately sized OGT/NGT for decompression.
• Provide IV maintenance fluid and replace deficits/ongoing losses per neonatal guidance.
• Correct hypoglycemia and clinically important electrolyte abnormalities.
• Monitor abdominal girth, vomiting, tube output, perfusion, urine output, glucose, serial blood gases when indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Antibiotics[/color]
• Indication: Suspected bowel ischemia, perforation, NEC, or systemic infection.
• Use neonatal intra-abdominal infection or NEC protocol selected by treating team.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Definitive Management[/color]
• Malrotation with suspected volvulus: urgent surgical evaluation and often emergency operation.
• Atresia and other mechanical obstructions: pediatric surgical management.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not give feeds, oral fluids, or laxatives while obstruction suspected.
• Do not delay surgical consultation while waiting for complete investigation panel.
• Antibiotics do not correct mechanical obstruction or replace urgent surgery when volvulus or ischemic bowel suspected.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to neonatal unit with immediate pediatric surgical involvement.
• Transfer urgently to center with neonatal surgery if unavailable locally.
• Document color of vomit, onset, abdominal findings, meconium passage, fluid management, surgical communication.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; APSA Resources; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Excessive bleeding after childbirth or any bleeding causing hemodynamic instability.

• Warning signs: tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, altered mental status, oliguria, cold extremities.
• Do not wait for a specific measured blood-loss threshold if the patient is deteriorating.
• Consider uterine atony, retained placental tissue, genital tract trauma, and coagulopathy.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call the obstetric, anesthesia, blood bank, and senior emergency teams.
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and mental status.
• Give high-flow oxygen if hypoxemic or critically unstable.
• Establish two large-bore IV lines; send CBC, blood group/crossmatch, coagulation profile, fibrinogen, electrolytes, and blood gas/lactate.
• Begin warmed isotonic crystalloid while arranging blood products for significant ongoing hemorrhage.
• Activate the massive hemorrhage protocol when indicated.
• Quantify blood loss and monitor vital signs frequently.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Uterine atony[/color]
• Perform uterine massage and assess uterine tone.
• Administer oxytocin according to the local PPH protocol.
• Inspect for retained tissue and genital tract trauma; do not assume atony is the only cause.

[color=#1E3A8A]Oxytocin[/color]
• Dose: 10 IU IM or a slow IV dose, followed when needed by an infusion according to local protocol.
• Administration: Avoid rapid IV bolus because severe hypotension and cardiovascular effects may occur.

[color=#1E3A8A]Tranexamic acid (TXA)[/color]
• Dose: 1 g IV over 10 minutes as soon as possible and within 3 hours of birth. A second 1 g dose may be given if bleeding continues after 30 minutes.
• Administration: Give early alongside standard PPH treatment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Additional measures[/color]
• Consider additional uterotonics according to contraindications (Ergometrine avoided in hypertension; Carboprost avoided in asthma).
• Consider uterine balloon tamponade, operative intervention, embolization, and blood component therapy if bleeding persists.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Persistent hemorrhage or shock requires urgent escalation; do not delay surgery while repeatedly trying medications.
• Consider coagulopathy, retained placenta, uterine rupture, and genital tract lacerations.
• Do not delay definitive hemorrhage control while administering TXA.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for monitoring after significant PPH.
• Escalate to operating theatre, higher-level care, or ICU according to hemodynamic status and ongoing blood loss.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO PPH Guidelines, 2025; FIGO recommendations.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall.
• May present with painful vaginal bleeding, abdominal or back pain, uterine tenderness, frequent contractions, or fetal compromise.
• Bleeding may be concealed; visible blood loss may underestimate severity.
• Consider coagulopathy in severe cases.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call obstetrics, anesthesia, and neonatal teams.
• Assess maternal ABCs and hemodynamic status.
• Establish IV access; send CBC, blood group/crossmatch, coagulation profile, and fibrinogen.
• Monitor maternal vital signs and fetal heart rate when permitted.
• Arrange ultrasound, but remember that a normal scan does not exclude abruption.
• Avoid digital vaginal examination until placenta previa has been excluded.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
• Stabilize the mother and treat hemorrhagic shock promptly.
• Use blood products and activate the major hemorrhage protocol when indicated.
• Delivery urgency and mode depend on maternal stability, fetal status, gestational age, and obstetric findings.
• Continuous fetal monitoring is indicated when appropriate.
• If disseminated intravascular coagulation is suspected, involve senior obstetrics, anesthesia, hematology, and critical care.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not estimate severity solely from visible vaginal bleeding.
• Maternal shock, persistent abdominal pain, uterine rigidity, fetal bradycardia, or coagulopathy requires urgent escalation.
• Do not delay necessary delivery in a deteriorating mother or fetus.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Hospital admission and obstetric-led monitoring are required for suspected significant abruption.
• Severe hemorrhage or instability requires emergency delivery planning and possible ICU care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: RCOG; NICE guidance on intrapartum care.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy.
• May cause maternal shock or fetal compromise.
• Placenta previa is diagnosed by ultrasound.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call obstetrics, anesthesia, and neonatal teams.
• Assess maternal circulation and quantify bleeding.
• Establish IV access; obtain CBC, blood group/crossmatch, and coagulation studies.
• Monitor maternal vital signs and fetal status.
• Arrange ultrasound to determine placental location.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
• Stabilize maternal circulation and prepare blood products for major bleeding.
• Delivery is required when bleeding is severe, maternal/fetal status is compromised, or obstetric assessment indicates it.
• Cesarean delivery is usually required when the placenta covers the cervical os.
• Give antenatal corticosteroids when indicated by gestational age, without delaying emergency delivery.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do NOT perform a digital vaginal examination until placenta previa has been excluded.
• Do not delay resuscitation or delivery in an unstable patient.
• Consider placenta accreta spectrum in patients with relevant risk factors.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Significant bleeding requires hospital admission and obstetric management.
• Arrange delivery in a facility with blood products, anesthesia, and neonatal support.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: RCOG; NICE guidance on intrapartum care.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Sudden severe abdominal pain, abnormal fetal heart rate, vaginal bleeding, maternal shock, loss of fetal station, or cessation of contractions.
• Risk is increased with a uterine scar, but rupture can occur without a known scar.
• Fetal heart rate abnormality may be the earliest sign.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call obstetrics, anesthesia, operating theatre, blood bank, and neonatal teams immediately.
• Begin ABC resuscitation and establish large-bore IV access.
• Send CBC, coagulation profile, and blood group/crossmatch.
• Prepare for emergency laparotomy and delivery.
• Monitor fetal heart rate if feasible without delaying surgery.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
• Definitive treatment is urgent surgical exploration and delivery.
• Resuscitate with blood products and other fluids according to the degree of hemorrhage.
• Surgical repair versus hysterectomy depends on the extent of rupture, bleeding, maternal condition, and fertility considerations.
• Administer antibiotics according to surgical and obstetric protocol.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay surgery for imaging when clinical suspicion is high and the patient is unstable.
• Maternal shock can progress rapidly; concealed intra-abdominal bleeding may be substantial.
• Ensure neonatal resuscitation support is available.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Emergency operative management followed by close postoperative monitoring; ICU care may be required.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACOG; RCOG guidance on birth after previous cesarean.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Placenta has not been delivered within the expected third-stage timeframe.
• Prolonged third stage is commonly >30 minutes with active management or >60 minutes with physiological management.
• Earlier intervention is required if significant bleeding or maternal instability occurs.
• Consider placenta accreta spectrum when the placenta does not separate.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call the obstetric team and assess maternal vital signs and blood loss.
• Establish IV access and obtain CBC and blood group/crossmatch if bleeding is significant.
• Empty the bladder if appropriate.
• Assess for postpartum hemorrhage and initiate the PPH protocol if indicated.
• Prepare analgesia/anesthesia and an appropriate setting for manual removal.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Controlled cord traction[/color]
• Perform only by a trained clinician, with appropriate uterine countertraction.
• Do not pull forcefully on the cord.

[color=#1E3A8A]Manual removal[/color]
• Indication: retained placenta requiring removal, particularly with bleeding.
• Must be performed by a trained obstetric clinician with adequate anesthesia/analgesia.
• Provide prophylactic antibiotics according to local protocol.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not perform uterine exploration or manual removal without appropriate anesthesia and trained personnel.
• Avoid forceful traction because it can cause uterine inversion or cord rupture.
• Suspected placenta accreta requires senior obstetric involvement; forcible separation can cause catastrophic hemorrhage.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Continue postpartum monitoring for bleeding, uterine tone, and infection.
• Escalate to theatre and blood product support when necessary.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO PPH Guidelines 2025; NICE NG235.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Rare, sudden, life-threatening syndrome during labor, delivery, or shortly after birth.
• Abrupt hypoxemia, hypotension, cardiac arrest, altered consciousness, or severe coagulopathy.
• DIC and massive hemorrhage may develop rapidly.
• AFE is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion; no single definitive diagnostic test.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate maternal cardiac arrest or emergency response.
• Call obstetrics, anesthesia, critical care, blood bank, and neonatal teams.
• Provide high-quality CPR immediately if cardiac arrest occurs.
• Give oxygen, secure airway, establish IV/IO access.
• Send CBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, blood gas, crossmatch.
• Activate massive transfusion protocol for severe hemorrhage/coagulopathy.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Cardiorespiratory support[/color]
• Standard advanced life support algorithms. For arrest in pregnancy, use manual left uterine displacement.
• Pregnancy is not a reason to withhold defibrillation.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hemodynamic support[/color]
• IV fluids judiciously. Vasopressors or inotropes per shock phenotype.
• Consider echocardiography to assess ventricular function.

[color=#1E3A8A]Coagulopathy and hemorrhage[/color]
• Activate major hemorrhage protocol. Replace blood components based on clinical bleeding and tests.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay resuscitation while attempting to confirm AFE.
• AFE may cause both cardiovascular collapse and profound coagulopathy.
• Avoid indiscriminate fluid loading when cardiac dysfunction is present.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate critical-care management.
• Monitor for recurrent shock, DIC, renal injury, and PPH.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA Guidelines; SMFM guidance; Standard major obstetric hemorrhage protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Persistent vaginal bleeding after vaginal birth, miscarriage, instrumentation, or pelvic trauma.
• Bleeding may be brisk despite a firm, well-contracted uterus.
• Cervical or upper vaginal lacerations can cause severe concealed or ongoing blood loss.
• Assess for perineal injury, expanding vulvovaginal hematoma, urinary tract injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call senior obstetric/gynecologic help and anesthesia if bleeding is significant.
• Assess ABCs, vital signs, mental status, and estimated blood loss.
• Establish two large-bore IV lines; send CBC, coagulation profile, fibrinogen, and blood group/crossmatch.
• Assess uterine tone and placental completeness; do not assume atony is the cause.
• If the source cannot be adequately visualized, move promptly to an operating theatre for examination under anesthesia.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Hemorrhage resuscitation[/color]
• If hypotensive, give reassessed 250–500 mL adult boluses of isotonic crystalloid while arranging blood products.
• For major blood loss, transfuse blood components according to the local obstetric major hemorrhage protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Repair of cervical or vaginal laceration[/color]
• Use local anesthetic or regional/general anesthesia according to injury extent.
• Repair under direct visualization, securing bleeding vessels and closing the laceration with appropriate absorbable sutures.
• Deep cervical or upper vaginal injuries may require an operating theatre and experienced surgeon.
• Reassess hemostasis after repair; inspect for expanding hematoma.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not place blind deep sutures where the bladder, ureters, or rectum may be injured.
• Persistent bleeding after repair requires immediate reassessment for an unrecognized higher injury, hematoma, or coagulopathy.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit and observe patients with significant lacerations, substantial blood loss, operative repair, or suspected associated injury.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACOG; WHO; NICE.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Significant bleeding during pregnancy, delivery, or the postpartum period.
• Tachycardia, pallor, cold extremities, delayed capillary refill, altered mental status, oliguria, or hypotension.
• Hypotension can be a late sign; do not wait for it before initiating treatment.
• Consider concealed bleeding when visible blood loss appears insufficient to explain the patient's condition.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate the obstetric major hemorrhage protocol and call senior obstetrics, anesthesia, blood bank, and theatre teams.
• Perform ABC assessment and provide oxygen for hypoxemia.
• Establish two large-bore IV lines; send CBC, blood group/crossmatch, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, blood gas, lactate, and ionized calcium.
• Start rapid hemorrhage resuscitation and identify the bleeding source simultaneously.
• Keep the patient warm and prepare for definitive hemorrhage control.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Blood products and resuscitation[/color]
• Activate the local massive transfusion protocol.
• Give emergency-release blood or crossmatched red cells and balanced blood components.
• Use isotonic crystalloid only as a bridge while blood products and hemorrhage control are arranged.

[color=#1E3A8A]Tranexamic acid for postpartum hemorrhage[/color]
• If postpartum hemorrhage is diagnosed, give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes as soon as possible and within 3 hours of birth.
• If bleeding continues after 30 minutes, a second 1 g IV dose may be given.

[color=#1E3A8A]Cause-directed hemorrhage control[/color]
• Uterine atony: uterine massage, oxytocin, and additional uterotonics.
• Retained placental tissue: urgent obstetric assessment and removal.
• Genital tract trauma: prompt inspection and repair.
• Uterine rupture or uncontrolled intra-abdominal bleeding: emergency surgery.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not rely on a single initial hemoglobin to estimate acute blood loss.
• Excessive crystalloid can worsen dilutional coagulopathy and tissue edema.
• Do not delay standard postpartum hemorrhage measures while giving tranexamic acid.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• All patients with hemorrhagic shock require resuscitation in a monitored setting and urgent definitive treatment.
• Transfer to ICU or high-dependency care when ongoing organ support is present.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO; FIGO; RCOG.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• New hypertension after 20 weeks of pregnancy with proteinuria or evidence of maternal organ dysfunction.
• Severe-range blood pressure: systolic ≥160 mmHg or diastolic ≥110 mmHg.
• Severe features: persistent headache, visual disturbance, epigastric/RUQ pain, pulmonary edema, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, or elevated liver enzymes.
• Eclampsia is a new-onset seizure associated with preeclampsia when another cause is not more likely.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call obstetrics, anesthesia, and neonatal teams as appropriate.
• Position laterally during a seizure; protect from injury and maintain the airway.
• Do not restrain the patient or place objects in the mouth.
• Assess oxygenation, circulation, blood pressure, and neurological status.
• Establish IV access; obtain CBC/platelets, renal and liver function, urine protein assessment.
• Assess fetal status when maternal stabilization permits.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Magnesium sulfate for eclampsia/seizure prophylaxis[/color]
• Dose: 4–6 g loading dose over 15–30 minutes, followed by 1–2 g/hour.
• Monitoring: Monitor respiratory rate, SpO2, deep tendon reflexes, urine output, and consciousness. Keep calcium gluconate available.

[color=#1E3A8A]Acute severe hypertension[/color]
• Treat persistent BP ≥160 systolic or ≥110 diastolic urgently.
• Options: IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or immediate-release oral nifedipine.
• Recheck BP frequently and avoid uncontrolled, excessive reduction.
• Do not administer nifedipine sublingually.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Stabilize the mother first.
• Delivery is the definitive treatment. Timing and mode depend on gestational age, maternal/fetal condition.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Magnesium toxicity can cause loss of reflexes, respiratory depression, and cardiac arrest. Use particular caution in renal impairment.
• Persistent severe hypertension, recurrent seizures, pulmonary edema, altered consciousness, or suspected stroke requires immediate senior and critical-care involvement.
• Do not delay treatment of severe hypertension while waiting for laboratory results.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to an obstetric unit with appropriate monitoring; ICU/high-dependency care may be required.
• Arrange maternal and fetal surveillance and delivery planning.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACOG guidance; NICE guideline NG133.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• HELLP refers to: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelet count.
• Clinical features: epigastric or RUQ pain, nausea, vomiting, malaise, headache, hypertension, and proteinuria. Hypertension or proteinuria may occasionally be absent.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Urgent obstetric, anesthesia, and senior medical review.
• Assess ABCs, blood pressure, neurological status, bleeding, and fetal condition.
• Obtain CBC with platelets, blood film, LDH, bilirubin, AST/ALT, creatinine, coagulation profile, and blood group/crossmatch.
• Assess for DIC, liver hematoma, renal injury, and pulmonary edema.
• Monitor fetal status according to gestational age.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Maternal stabilization[/color]
• Treat severe hypertension urgently using a pregnancy-appropriate protocol.
• Give magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis when indicated.
• Monitor fluid balance carefully and avoid unnecessary fluid loading.
• Correct significant blood loss or coagulopathy with appropriate blood components.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive management[/color]
• Delivery is the definitive treatment.
• Do not delay necessary delivery solely to complete corticosteroids when maternal/fetal condition requires urgent intervention.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• HELLP can progress rapidly to DIC, hepatic hematoma or rupture, renal failure, placental abruption, and maternal death.
• Persistent right upper quadrant pain, hypotension, falling hemoglobin, or worsening coagulopathy requires immediate escalation.
• Continue monitoring after delivery because complications may persist or worsen.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Manage in a hospital with obstetric, anesthesia, blood bank, and neonatal support.
• ICU or high-dependency care may be required.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACOG; NICE NG133.

Hypertensive Disorders.title: Postpartum Headache: Stroke, CVST, and Hemorrhage

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Postpartum headache may result from primary headache, post-dural puncture, preeclampsia, CVST, ischemic stroke, ICH, RCVS, or pituitary apoplexy.
• [color=#991B1B]Red flags: thunderclap onset, severe/progressive headache, seizure, focal deficit, altered consciousness, fever, visual disturbance, severe hypertension.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, BP, temperature, SpO2, glucose, neurological status.
• Perform focused neurological examination.
• Activate stroke pathway immediately for focal deficits.
• Treat seizures and severe hypertension according to protocols.
• Do not attribute severe/atypical headache to epidural/spinal procedure without excluding dangerous causes.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, platelets, electrolytes, renal function, LFTs, urine protein.
• Urgent noncontrast CT head for suspected ICH.
• MRI brain and MR venography for suspected CVST.
• Lumbar puncture only after appropriate assessment and exclusion of contraindications.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected postpartum preeclampsia/eclampsia[/color]
• Treat severe BP (≥160/110) urgently.
• Magnesium sulfate for eclampsia/seizure prophylaxis (4–6 g load, then 1–2 g/hr).

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected stroke or ICH[/color]
• Activate stroke/neurosurgical pathway.
• Maintain oxygenation, avoid hypotension, control BP per protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected CVST[/color]
• Urgent neuroimaging with venous imaging. Therapeutic heparin is generally standard for confirmed CVST.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Thunderclap headache, focal deficit, seizure, altered consciousness, or severe hypertension is an emergency.
• A normal initial examination does not reliably exclude CVST.
• Do not delay emergency neuroimaging in a patient with red flags.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit suspected stroke, CVST, ICH, eclampsia, or other serious secondary headache.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/ASA guidance; ACOG guidance on postpartum preeclampsia.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Pregnancy with abdominal or pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, syncope, shoulder-tip pain, or hemodynamic instability.
• Risk of rupture exists even when the pregnancy test or initial ultrasound findings are inconclusive.
• Consider ectopic pregnancy in any reproductive-age patient with possible pregnancy and abdominal pain or bleeding.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and hemodynamic status; call gynecology and anesthesia urgently if rupture is suspected.
• Establish two large-bore IV lines in an unstable patient.
• Send CBC, blood group/crossmatch, quantitative beta-hCG.
• Perform urgent pelvic ultrasound when available, but do not delay resuscitation or surgery in an unstable patient.
• Arrange blood products and urgent operative assessment when internal bleeding is suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
• Hemodynamic instability or suspected rupture: urgent surgical management is generally required.
• Provide blood products and resuscitation according to the hemorrhage protocol.
• Provide appropriate analgesia and antiemetics while avoiding delays to definitive care.

[color=#1E3A8A]Methotrexate[/color]
• Reserved for carefully selected, stable, unruptured ectopic pregnancies with appropriate follow-up and no contraindications.
• NOT appropriate for suspected rupture or hemodynamic instability.
• Selection, dose, beta-hCG monitoring, and follow-up must follow a gynecology protocol.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• A normal or nondiagnostic early ultrasound does not exclude ectopic pregnancy.
• Do not discharge a patient with concerning symptoms without a safe, documented follow-up plan.
• Syncope, shock, peritoneal signs, or significant free fluid require emergency escalation.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Suspected rupture: emergency gynecological surgical management.
• Stable confirmed ectopic pregnancy: specialist-led decision between expectant, medical, and surgical management.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: RCOG; NICE guidance on ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Early pregnancy bleeding with abdominal cramps and passage of tissue.
• Severe bleeding may cause tachycardia, hypotension, syncope, or shock.
• Confirm pregnancy location when possible; ectopic pregnancy must be considered.
• Assess for incomplete miscarriage and retained products.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, vital signs, bleeding severity, and mental status.
• Establish IV access and obtain CBC, blood group/Rh status, and crossmatch if bleeding is significant.
• Perform pregnancy testing and ultrasound when appropriate.
• Provide analgesia and resuscitation as indicated.
• Seek urgent gynecological review for hemodynamic instability or heavy bleeding.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
• Hemodynamic instability or uncontrolled bleeding requires emergency resuscitation and urgent gynecological intervention.
• Options for stable patients may include expectant, medical, or surgical management.
• Surgical evacuation may be necessary for persistent heavy bleeding, infection, or retained tissue.
• Provide anti-D prophylaxis when indicated by local Rh-negative guidance.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not assume all early pregnancy bleeding represents miscarriage; exclude ectopic pregnancy.
• Fever, foul discharge, severe pain, syncope, or persistent heavy bleeding requires urgent reassessment.
• Ensure follow-up confirms resolution.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Unstable patients require emergency hospital management.
• Stable patients may be managed according to a documented gynecology plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE; RCOG guidance on early pregnancy loss.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Pregnancy loss or attempted termination accompanied by fever, pelvic pain, uterine tenderness, foul discharge, or systemic illness.
• May progress rapidly to septic shock, DIC, renal failure, and multiorgan dysfunction.
• Consider retained infected products of conception.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Treat as a time-critical emergency.
• Call gynecology, anesthesia/critical care, and the operating theatre team.
• Assess ABCs, mental status, vital signs, urine output, and perfusion.
• Obtain CBC, renal/liver function, coagulation profile, lactate, blood cultures, and crossmatch.
• Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly.
• Arrange urgent assessment for uterine evacuation.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics[/color]
• Start broad-spectrum IV coverage against gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms (e.g., clindamycin + gentamicin).
• Adjust antibiotic selection for allergy history, renal function, and microbiology.

[color=#1E3A8A]Source control[/color]
• Urgent uterine evacuation is generally required for infected retained products.
• Perform under appropriate specialist supervision with resuscitation support.

[color=#1E3A8A]Septic shock[/color]
• Give IV fluids with frequent reassessment.
• If hypotension persists, use vasopressors in a monitored setting.
• Treat DIC and organ dysfunction with specialist support.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay antibiotics or source control in a critically ill patient.
• Consider uterine perforation, hemorrhage, and toxic shock in severe cases.
• Avoid managing septic miscarriage as uncomplicated miscarriage.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Hospital admission is required.
• Shock, DIC, organ dysfunction, or severe infection requires critical-care management.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO; Surviving Sepsis Campaign.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Severe nausea and vomiting during pregnancy with inability to maintain adequate oral intake.
• Dehydration, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, oliguria, electrolyte disturbances, weight loss.
• Assess for hypokalemia, hyponatremia, metabolic alkalosis or acidosis, and AKI.
• Consider alternatives: gastroenteritis, pancreatitis, hepatitis, DKA, UTI, bowel obstruction.
• Prolonged vomiting increases the risk of thiamine deficiency and Wernicke encephalopathy.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, mental status, hydration, and urine output.
• Record vital signs, weight, and fluid balance.
• Obtain CBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, glucose, and LFTs.
• Check urinalysis/urine culture, blood gas, ketones.
• Admit severe dehydration, significant electrolyte abnormalities, inability to tolerate oral fluids, or renal impairment.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]IV fluid replacement[/color]
• Isotonic saline (0.9% NaCl) for initial volume replacement.
• Replace potassium carefully after checking renal function and urine output. Never give concentrated KCl IV push.

[color=#1E3A8A]Thiamine[/color]
• Give thiamine (e.g., 100 mg IV daily) before dextrose-containing fluids in patients with prolonged vomiting/malnutrition.
• Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy requires higher-dose IV treatment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antiemetic therapy[/color]
• Pregnancy-appropriate antiemetics (doxylamine/pyridoxine, cyclizine, promethazine, metoclopramide, or ondansetron).
• Caution: Metoclopramide (extrapyramidal reactions), Ondansetron (QT prolongation).

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Dextrose given to a thiamine-deficient patient may precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
• Confusion, ataxia, abnormal eye movements, or altered consciousness may indicate Wernicke's.
• Persistent tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, or rising creatinine requires urgent escalation.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Discharge only when symptoms are controlled and oral fluids tolerated.
• Admit severe or complicated cases.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 69; NICE guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Sudden severe unilateral pelvic or lower abdominal pain, often with nausea and vomiting.
• Pain may be intermittent if torsion is partial or intermittent.
• Adnexal tenderness or a known ovarian/adnexal mass may be present.
• Ovarian torsion is a time-critical surgical emergency because delayed treatment can cause ovarian ischemia and loss.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Urgent OB/GYN consultation.
• Assess hemodynamic stability and perform abdominal examination.
• Keep nil by mouth; establish IV access and provide pregnancy-appropriate analgesia.
• Confirm gestational age and assess fetal status when appropriate.
• Arrange urgent pelvic ultrasound; do not delay surgery when clinical suspicion remains high.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Transvaginal or transabdominal ultrasound with Doppler.
• Preserved Doppler blood flow does not exclude torsion.
• Definitive diagnosis may be made at surgery.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia and stabilization[/color]
• Paracetamol 1 g orally or IV every 6–8 hours as needed; maximum 4 g/day.
• For severe pain, use carefully titrated IV opioid analgesia under monitoring.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive treatment[/color]
• Urgent laparoscopy is generally preferred when feasible; laparotomy may be required depending on gestational age, anatomy, or instability.
• Detorsion and ovarian preservation are preferred when technically feasible, even when the ovary initially appears dark or congested.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content: • Analgesia and imaging must not delay urgent gynecologic intervention when torsion is strongly suspected.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit and arrange urgent operative evaluation.
• Monitor postoperative pain, bleeding, infection, and pregnancy status.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACOG. Evaluation and Management of Adnexal Masses.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• The umbilical cord descends through the cervix alongside or ahead of the presenting fetal part after membrane rupture.
• Suspect when sudden fetal bradycardia or severe variable decelerations occur after rupture of membranes.
• The cord may be visible or palpable on vaginal examination.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for an immediate obstetric emergency response and prepare for urgent birth.
• Confirm fetal heart rate.
• If the cord is felt or seen, elevate the presenting fetal part manually to relieve cord compression.
• Position the mother knee-chest or in a head-down lateral position.
• Minimize handling of the exposed cord; do not attempt to push it back into the uterus.
• Maintain elevation of the presenting part during transfer to theatre.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
• Expedite delivery, usually by emergency cesarean section unless vaginal birth is immediately achievable and safer.
• Consider bladder filling or other decompression maneuvers under trained obstetric direction.
• Tocolysis may be considered by the obstetric team in selected cases if delay is unavoidable.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay delivery for nonessential investigations.
• Avoid excessive manipulation of the cord because vasospasm may worsen fetal compromise.
• If fetal death has been confirmed, the senior obstetric team should guide management.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Immediate obstetric-led emergency delivery and neonatal resuscitation readiness.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: RCOG; NICE guidance on intrapartum care.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• The fetal head delivers but the shoulders do not deliver with routine gentle traction.
• May be indicated by the 'turtle sign' (head retracts against the perineum).
• This is an obstetric emergency requiring coordinated action.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Declare shoulder dystocia clearly and call for help.
• Note the time of head delivery.
• Ask the mother to stop pushing briefly while the team prepares maneuvers.
• Do not apply fundal pressure.
• Avoid excessive traction on the fetal head or neck.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
• First-line maneuver: McRoberts position (maternal hips flexed toward the abdomen).
• Apply suprapubic pressure as directed by a trained clinician.
• If unresolved, proceed through the institutional algorithm (internal rotational maneuvers or delivery of the posterior arm).
• Consider all-fours positioning when clinically feasible.
• Prepare neonatal resuscitation and assess the mother for PPH and genital tract injury.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Fundal pressure is contraindicated because it may worsen impaction and cause injury.
• Do not use excessive traction.
• Record the sequence and timing of maneuvers and the personnel involved.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate neonatal assessment for brachial plexus injury, fracture, or hypoxia.
• Maternal assessment for postpartum hemorrhage and perineal trauma.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACOG Practice Bulletin; RCOG guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Rupture of membranes before labor and before 37 weeks of gestation.
• Presentation: gush or persistent leakage of fluid.
• Major complications include ascending infection, cord prolapse, placental abruption, and preterm birth.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Establish gestational age and assess maternal and fetal condition.
• Check maternal temperature, pulse, blood pressure, uterine tenderness, and fetal heart rate.
• Perform a sterile speculum examination to look for pooling of amniotic fluid.
• Avoid routine digital vaginal examinations.
• Assess for labor, bleeding, cord prolapse, and signs of intra-amniotic infection.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Expectant management[/color]
• If mother and fetus are stable and there is no infection, expectant management may be appropriate.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics[/color]
• RCOG recommends erythromycin for up to 10 days or until established labor.
• Avoid amoxicillin-clavulanate for latency prophylaxis.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antenatal corticosteroids[/color]
• Betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses, or dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses.

[color=#1E3A8A]Magnesium sulfate[/color]
• Consider fetal neuroprotection when early preterm birth is imminent.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Suspected intra-amniotic infection, maternal sepsis, significant abruption, cord prolapse, or fetal compromise may require prompt delivery.
• Tocolysis is not routinely recommended in PPROM.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Obstetric assessment and a documented plan for inpatient or selected outpatient care are required.
• Arrange neonatal consultation when preterm delivery is possible.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 73; NICE NG25.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Regular uterine contractions with cervical change before 37 completed weeks.
• Symptoms: pelvic pressure, backache, menstrual-like cramps, or increased vaginal discharge.
• Exclude PPROM, infection, placental abruption, and other causes.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Establish gestational age and assess maternal vital signs.
• Assess fetal heart rate and uterine contractions.
• Evaluate membrane status and signs of infection or bleeding.
• Use sterile speculum examination and appropriate cervical assessment.
• Avoid digital examination when PPROM or placenta previa is suspected.
• Consult obstetrics and neonatal services if early delivery is possible.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Antenatal corticosteroids[/color]
• Betamethasone 12 mg IM, repeated after 24 hours (2 doses); or dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses.

[color=#1E3A8A]Tocolysis[/color]
• Nifedipine may be used in selected patients to delay birth briefly.
• Avoid tocolysis when delivery is required for maternal/fetal indications.

[color=#1E3A8A]Magnesium sulfate[/color]
• Consider for fetal neuroprotection when preterm birth is imminent.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics[/color]
• Do not give antibiotics routinely unless there is a specific indication.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay necessary delivery for corticosteroids or transfer when the mother or fetus is deteriorating.
• Assess for infection, abruption, and fetal compromise before attempting to delay labor.
• Nifedipine may cause hypotension; monitor blood pressure.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit or transfer according to gestational age, cervical findings, and neonatal capability.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE NG25; WHO recommendations.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
The fetal buttocks or feet present first instead of the head.
• Complications: cord prolapse, head entrapment, fetal hypoxia, birth trauma.
• Assess presentation, gestational age, labor progress, membrane status, and fetal heart rate.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Obtain urgent obstetric review when breech is identified in labor.
• Confirm presentation by ultrasound if it does not delay management.
• Prepare an experienced obstetric clinician, anesthesia, neonatal resuscitation, and theatre.
• Assess for cord prolapse following membrane rupture.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Delivery planning[/color]
• Cesarean is often recommended for term breech unless criteria for safe vaginal birth are met.
• Planned vaginal breech birth requires an established protocol and expertise.

[color=#1E3A8A]Complicated vaginal breech delivery[/color]
• Call for senior obstetric assistance immediately.
• Avoid pulling on the fetus or uncontrolled traction.
• If aftercoming head is delayed, use the locally approved maneuver promptly.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Footling breech carries an increased risk of cord prolapse.
• Do not use routine traction to deliver the fetal trunk or head.
• Avoid attempting an unfamiliar breech maneuver without training.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Refer to an obstetric unit with surgical, anesthesia, and neonatal support.
• Assess newborn for hypoxia or trauma.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: RCOG; NICE guidance on intrapartum care.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Twins or higher-order multiples complicated by labor, fetal distress, malpresentation, cord prolapse, or delayed delivery of subsequent baby.
• The second twin may change presentation after delivery of the first.
• Risks: PPH, prematurity, intertwin delivery complications.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call senior obstetric, anesthesia, and neonatal teams.
• Confirm number of fetuses, presentations, and placental configuration.
• Establish IV access and assess hemorrhage risk.
• Prepare for delivery in a setting with immediate cesarean capability.
• Ensure neonatal resuscitation equipment for each newborn.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Delivery of the first twin[/color]
• Manage according to presentation and fetal condition.
• Reassess the lie, presentation, and heart rate of the remaining fetus.

[color=#1E3A8A]Complications involving the second twin[/color]
• Internal podalic version, breech extraction, or emergency cesarean may be needed by trained clinicians.

[color=#1E3A8A]PPH prevention[/color]
• Assess uterine tone and blood loss after delivery. Use institutional PPH protocol.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not assume the second twin will remain in the same presentation.
• Avoid delays when fetal heart rate abnormalities persist.
• Multiple pregnancy increases PPH risk; maintain readiness for active management.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Delivery should occur in a facility with appropriate obstetric, anesthesia, and neonatal support.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE guidance on twin and triplet pregnancy.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Suspect infection in a pregnant or recently postpartum patient with deterioration, fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria, or elevated lactate.
• Sources: endometritis, retained products, urinary infection, pyelonephritis, wound infection, pneumonia, septic abortion.
• Sepsis may occur without fever.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Recognize and treat suspected maternal sepsis as an emergency.
• Call obstetrics, anesthesia/critical care, and microbiology support.
• Obtain cultures before antibiotics if this causes no meaningful delay.
• Measure lactate and assess renal function, CBC, coagulation.
• Give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly, ideally within 1 hour.
• Give IV crystalloid for hypoperfusion, reassessing frequently.
• Identify and control the source urgently.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics[/color]
• Select broad-spectrum IV therapy according to the suspected source, severity, allergies, and local resistance.
• Do not delay antibiotics in a critically ill patient while waiting for cultures.

[color=#1E3A8A]Fluids and vasopressors[/color]
• Use isotonic crystalloid with repeated reassessment of perfusion.
• If hypotension persists despite fluids, initiate vasopressor therapy (norepinephrine is commonly first-line).
• Monitor for pulmonary edema, particularly in patients with preeclampsia or cardiac disease.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not rely on fever or a single screening score to exclude sepsis.
• Persistent hypotension, rising lactate, oliguria, altered consciousness, or respiratory failure requires urgent critical-care escalation.
• Source control is essential; antibiotics alone may not be sufficient.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to hospital; shock or organ dysfunction requires high-dependency or ICU care.
• Continue reassessment and narrow antibiotics when clinically appropriate.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine; Surviving Sepsis Campaign.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Unresponsive patient with absent normal breathing and no signs of circulation.
• In pregnancy, aortocaval compression may reduce venous return and resuscitation effectiveness.
• Consider reversible causes: hemorrhage, thromboembolism, eclampsia, sepsis, amniotic fluid embolism, cardiac disease.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate the maternal cardiac arrest response and call resuscitation, obstetric, anesthesia, and neonatal teams.
• Start high-quality CPR immediately.
• Use standard adult cardiac arrest algorithms, including prompt defibrillation.
• Manually displace the uterus to the patient's left.
• Ensure IV/IO access and standard resuscitation medications.
• Identify and treat reversible causes.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]CPR and defibrillation[/color]
• Perform chest compressions at standard adult depth and rate.
• Pregnancy is not a reason to delay defibrillation.
• Do not withhold indicated resuscitation medications solely because the patient is pregnant.

[color=#1E3A8A]Resuscitative delivery[/color]
• If the uterus is large enough to cause aortocaval compression and ROSC is not achieved promptly, prepare for resuscitative delivery.
• Preparation should begin immediately; do not wait for prolonged unsuccessful CPR.
• Follow the current institutional maternal cardiac arrest algorithm.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay CPR, defibrillation, or resuscitative delivery while waiting for ultrasound.
• Standard adult resuscitation medications and defibrillation protocols remain applicable.
• Consider hemorrhage and pulmonary embolism as important reversible causes.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• After ROSC, transfer to an appropriate critical-care setting.
• Continue evaluation and treatment of the cause of arrest.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: American Heart Association (AHA) guidance.

Maternal Critical Care.title: Pulmonary Embolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Suspect PE with sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, unexplained hypoxemia, syncope, hemoptysis, or hypotension.
• Risk is increased during pregnancy and especially postpartum.
• Hemodynamic instability may indicate high-risk PE.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, SpO2, BP, HR, and mental status.
• Give oxygen and ventilatory support if required.
• Obtain ECG and chest radiography.
• Use a validated pregnancy-adapted diagnostic pathway.
• If unstable, prioritize resuscitation and urgent senior assessment.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Compression ultrasonography for suspected DVT.
• CTPA or V/Q imaging for suspected PE.
• D-dimer only within a validated pregnancy pathway; not alone to exclude PE.
• Echocardiography may help assess right ventricular dysfunction in unstable patients.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Anticoagulation[/color]
• LMWH is commonly preferred (e.g., Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC every 12 hours).
• Coordinate with labor, delivery, and neuraxial anesthesia.

[color=#1E3A8A]High-risk PE with shock[/color]
• Activate multidisciplinary emergency response.
• Consider systemic thrombolysis or catheter-based/surgical reperfusion for life-threatening PE.
• Use unfractionated heparin when rapid adjustment or reversal is needed.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay life-saving resuscitation in an unstable patient for imaging.
• Consider postpartum hemorrhage and recent surgery when selecting anticoagulation/thrombolysis.
• Do not exclude PE solely because the patient is young or has no leg symptoms.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Confirmed PE requires hospital management and a pregnancy/postpartum-specific plan.
• Hemodynamic instability requires urgent higher-level care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: 2025 ESC Guidelines; Local pregnancy-associated VTE protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Trauma from RTC, falls, assault, or penetrating injuries.
• Maternal injuries can cause placental abruption, fetomaternal hemorrhage, uterine rupture, preterm labor.
• Maternal shock may be present before obvious hypotension (increased blood volume).
• Significant abruption may occur without visible vaginal bleeding.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Primary survey[/color]
• Activate trauma team and involve obstetrics early. Assess ABCDE.
• Protect cervical spine. Control external hemorrhage and establish large-bore IV access.
• Send CBC, crossmatch, coagulation, fibrinogen, blood gas.

[color=#1E3A8A]Positioning[/color]
• Avoid prolonged supine positioning. Use manual left uterine displacement.

[color=#1E3A8A]Obstetric assessment[/color]
• Establish gestational age, assess fetal heart rate, abdominal pain, contractions, bleeding.
• Do not use a normal scan to exclude placental abruption.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Perform indicated trauma imaging (X-ray/CT); do not withhold necessary imaging due to pregnancy.
• Consider fetomaternal hemorrhage testing (especially in Rh-negative patients).

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Hemorrhage and shock[/color]
• Control bleeding source and use blood products.
• Give isotonic crystalloid judiciously.

[color=#1E3A8A]Rh-negative patients[/color]
• Assess need for anti-D immunoglobulin after abdominal trauma.

[color=#1E3A8A]Delivery[/color]
• Delivery is not automatically indicated solely because trauma occurred.
• If maternal cardiac arrest occurs, follow the maternal cardiac arrest algorithm.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Maternal resuscitation takes priority over fetal investigations.
• Do not delay indicated CT or surgery because of pregnancy.
• Absence of vaginal bleeding does not exclude placental abruption.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit significant trauma, abnormal maternal observations, or abnormal fetal assessment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAST Guidelines; ACOG guidance on diagnostic imaging.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Pregnancy and postpartum increase VTE risk.
• DVT: unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth.
• PE: sudden dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, syncope, shock.
• Risk factors: previous VTE, thrombophilia, cesarean, immobility, obesity, infection, hemorrhage.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, vital signs, SpO2, and hemodynamic stability.
• If PE suspected, assess severity immediately.
• If DVT suspected, arrange urgent compression ultrasonography.
• Check medication history, recent delivery details, neuraxial anesthesia timing, and bleeding risk.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Compression duplex ultrasonography for DVT.
• CTPA or V/Q imaging for PE.
• D-dimer should not be used in isolation to exclude postpartum VTE.
• Consider pelvic venous imaging for suspected iliac/pelvic vein thrombosis.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Therapeutic anticoagulation[/color]
• Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC every 12 hours (adjust for renal function).
• Unfractionated heparin preferred in unstable patients or severe renal impairment.
• Coordinate with recent neuraxial anesthesia and postpartum hemorrhage risk.

[color=#1E3A8A]Duration[/color]
• Generally at least 3 months total and at least 6 weeks postpartum.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not start anticoagulation without assessing active bleeding.
• Suspected PE with shock requires emergency resuscitation and consideration of reperfusion.
• Direct oral anticoagulants are generally not preferred during breastfeeding.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Confirmed VTE requires a documented anticoagulation and follow-up plan.
• PE with hemodynamic instability requires urgent higher-level care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: RCOG Green-top Guidelines 37a and 37b; ASH guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Heart failure due to LV systolic dysfunction occurring toward the end of pregnancy or in months following delivery.
• Symptoms: progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, cough, fatigue, edema.
• Severe cases: pulmonary edema, hypotension, arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock.
• Distinguish from common pregnancy-related breathlessness and edema.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, SpO2, respiratory effort, BP, perfusion, and mental status.
• Sit upright, give oxygen, provide ventilatory support if required.
• Obtain ECG, CBC, electrolytes, renal function, troponin, BNP/NT-proBNP.
• Arrange urgent echocardiography.
• Involve cardiology, obstetrics, and critical care early.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring.
• Echocardiography (LVEF, chamber size, RV function, valvular disease).
• Chest radiography when indicated.
• Consider PE, ACS, preeclampsia-associated pulmonary edema, myocarditis.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Acute pulmonary edema (adequate BP)[/color]
• Oxygen, noninvasive ventilation for distress.
• IV loop diuretic for congestion (monitor renal function/electrolytes).

[color=#1E3A8A]Cardiogenic shock[/color]
• Activate critical-care and cardiology support.
• Use vasopressors or inotropes per shock phenotype.

[color=#1E3A8A]Long-term treatment[/color]
• During pregnancy: avoid ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNIs, and MRAs.
• After delivery: optimize guideline-directed therapy per hemodynamics and breastfeeding.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• New orthopnea, hypoxemia, pulmonary crackles, or rapid deterioration requires urgent evaluation.
• Do not assume dyspnea or edema is physiological in late pregnancy/postpartum.
• Excessive fluid administration may worsen pulmonary edema.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit suspected acute heart failure for urgent evaluation.
• ICU or coronary care for pulmonary edema, shock, or severe ventricular dysfunction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ESC Guidelines; AHA scientific guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Rare, potentially life-threatening pregnancy-associated liver disease, usually in the third trimester or early postpartum.
• Symptoms: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise, jaundice, polydipsia, altered mental status.
• Severe: hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, renal impairment, encephalopathy, multiorgan failure.
• Differentiate from HELLP, viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Urgent obstetric, hepatology, anesthesia, and critical-care review.
• Assess ABCs, consciousness, BP, perfusion, glucose, and bleeding signs.
• Check bedside glucose immediately and repeat frequently.
• Obtain CBC, LFTs, bilirubin, renal function, coagulation, fibrinogen, blood gas, lactate, crossmatch.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Maternal stabilization[/color]
• Correct hypoglycemia promptly using IV glucose.
• Correct dehydration and electrolytes cautiously.
• Treat coagulopathy with blood components when indicated.
• Manage encephalopathy, renal failure, and other organ dysfunction with critical-care support.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive management[/color]
• Prompt delivery is the definitive treatment once AFLP is diagnosed/suspected.
• Do not delay delivery solely to normalize all lab values if deteriorating.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• AFLP can progress rapidly to acute liver failure, severe hypoglycemia, DIC, and maternal death.
• A single normal glucose or coagulation result does not exclude evolving disease.
• Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures when coagulopathy is present.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Manage in a hospital with obstetric, anesthesia, blood bank, and critical-care support.
• ICU care often required. Continue close postpartum monitoring.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EASL Guidelines; FIGO guidance on liver disease in pregnancy.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Sudden severe chest, back, neck, or abdominal pain, sometimes described as tearing or ripping.
• Syncope, collapse, hypotension, pulse deficit, unequal arm blood pressures, new aortic regurgitation murmur, or focal neurological deficit.
• May mimic pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome, or musculoskeletal pain.
• Pregnancy and the early postpartum period increase risk, especially with hypertension or connective tissue disorders.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate emergency, cardiothoracic/vascular surgery, anesthesia, and obstetric teams immediately.
