• Assess ABCs, continuous ECG, blood pressure, SpO2, and neurological status.
• Measure blood pressure in both arms when feasible without delaying treatment.
• Obtain urgent definitive aortic imaging; CT angiography is commonly used when appropriate.
• Do not delay specialist management for a normal ECG or troponin.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Anti-impulse therapy[/color]
• IV esmolol: 500 microgram/kg loading dose over 1 minute, followed by 50 microgram/kg/min infusion; titrate to response.
• If beta-blockers are contraindicated, IV diltiazem may be considered.
• A vasodilator such as nicardipine may be added if BP remains elevated after adequate heart-rate control.
• Target: HR 60-80/min and systolic BP <120 mmHg (or lowest pressure maintaining organ perfusion).

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive management[/color]
• Type A dissection generally requires emergency cardiac surgery.
• Type B dissection requires urgent specialist management.
• Delivery timing and mode must be coordinated with cardiothoracic surgery, obstetrics, and anesthesia.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not initiate aggressive blood-pressure reduction in profound hypotension or shock without specialist direction.
• Avoid vasodilator monotherapy before adequate heart-rate control because reflex tachycardia may increase aortic wall stress.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to ICU or an equivalent high-acuity setting.
• Immediate transfer to a center with cardiothoracic/vascular surgery capability when needed.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for Aortic Disease; ESC Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Rising serum creatinine, oliguria, or anuria during pregnancy or postpartum.
• Causes include hypovolemia, hemorrhage, sepsis, preeclampsia/HELLP, AFLP, thrombotic microangiopathy, urinary obstruction, and drug toxicity.
• Pregnancy normally lowers serum creatinine; a value that appears only mildly elevated by nonpregnant reference ranges may be clinically important.
• Evaluate for life-threatening hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, severe acidosis, and uremic complications.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, vital signs, volume status, and urine output.
• Review pregnancy/postpartum status, bleeding, sepsis, hypertension, medications, and nephrotoxic exposures.
• Establish IV access and obtain CBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, bicarbonate, liver function, urinalysis.
• Perform ECG urgently if hyperkalemia is suspected or confirmed.
• Involve obstetrics and nephrology early for severe, rapidly progressive, or unexplained AKI.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Volume and perfusion management[/color]
• If hypovolemia is likely, give isotonic crystalloid in carefully reassessed 250–500 mL adult boluses.
• If the patient is euvolemic or fluid overloaded, do not give repeated fluid boluses without evidence of fluid responsiveness.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hyperkalemia with ECG changes or severe elevation[/color]
• IV calcium gluconate 10% solution, commonly 10 mL IV over 5–10 minutes, for cardiac membrane stabilization.
• Insulin with glucose, nebulized salbutamol, and other potassium-lowering measures should follow the emergency hyperkalemia protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Treat the underlying cause[/color]
• Hemorrhage: control bleeding and restore perfusion.
• Sepsis: early appropriate antibiotics and source control.
• Preeclampsia/HELLP: urgent obstetric management and delivery when indicated.
• Obstruction: urgent relief of urinary tract obstruction.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Oliguria alone does not prove that more fluid is needed.
• Pulmonary edema and severe preeclampsia require careful fluid management.
• IV calcium stabilizes the myocardium but does not lower serum potassium.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with significant, progressive, or unexplained AKI.
• ICU care is indicated for severe electrolyte disturbance, pulmonary edema, shock, or severe acidosis.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE. Acute kidney injury; KDIGO Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• [color=#991B1B]Severe hypoglycemia:[/color] Blood glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) is low; below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L) is clinically significant. Severe means cognitive impairment requiring assistance.
• Symptoms: sweating, tremor, palpitations, confusion, seizures, or coma.
• [color=#991B1B]DKA in pregnancy:[/color] Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, tachypnea, and altered mental status.
• DKA may occur at lower glucose concentrations in pregnancy than outside pregnancy (euglycemic DKA).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Check bedside glucose immediately and assess ABCs.
• If unconscious or seizing, protect the airway and obtain IV access.
• For suspected DKA, obtain blood gas, electrolytes, bicarbonate, renal function, blood ketones, glucose, CBC.
• Start maternal resuscitation and urgent obstetric, medical, and critical-care consultation.
• Identify and treat the precipitating cause.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Severe hypoglycemia[/color]
• Conscious and can swallow: give 15–20 g fast-acting oral glucose, then recheck glucose after 15 minutes.
• Cannot swallow/impaired consciousness: Give 10% dextrose 150–200 mL IV over 10–15 minutes, then reassess.
• If IV access unavailable, glucagon 1 mg IM may be used.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Diabetic ketoacidosis in pregnancy[/color]
• Begin IV isotonic crystalloid, often 500–1,000 mL in the first hour in adults if not fluid overloaded.
• Start IV regular insulin according to local DKA protocol, commonly 0.1 unit/kg/hour after assessing potassium.
• Add IV dextrose when glucose falls to ~200–250 mg/dL (11.1–13.9 mmol/L).
• Potassium replacement must be individualized; withhold insulin temporarily if K+ is severely low.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not give oral fluids or food to a patient with impaired consciousness or unsafe swallowing.
• DKA in pregnancy can be severe at relatively modest glucose levels.
• Avoid insulin if potassium is dangerously low until potassium replacement has made treatment safer.
• Avoid routine bicarbonate; reserve it for exceptional circumstances.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Severe hypoglycemia with loss of consciousness, seizures, or prolonged drug effect requires monitored care.
• DKA in pregnancy requires hospital admission and usually high-dependency or ICU-level monitoring.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ADA Standards of Care; JBDS; NICE.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Sudden unilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain, often with nausea and vomiting.
• Pain may be intermittent if torsion twists and untwists.
• Risk factors include an ovarian mass or enlarged ovary, but torsion can occur without a known mass.
• Normal Doppler flow does not reliably exclude torsion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs, abdominal findings, and severity of pain.
• Consider pregnancy testing in reproductive-age patients.
• Obtain CBC, urinalysis, and other investigations guided by the differential.
• Arrange urgent gynecological review and pelvic ultrasound.
• Provide appropriate analgesia and antiemetics.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
• Suspected ovarian torsion requires urgent gynecological assessment.
• Definitive treatment is usually urgent laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian preservation when feasible.
• The decision to remove an ovary depends on specialist intraoperative assessment.
• Do not delay specialist assessment solely to obtain additional imaging when clinical suspicion is high.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Normal Doppler flow does not rule out torsion.
• Delay may result in ovarian ischemia and loss of ovarian function.
• Consider other emergencies, including ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, and ruptured ovarian cyst.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Urgent gynecological evaluation; suspected torsion generally requires hospital-based surgical assessment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACOG guidance on adnexal torsion in adolescents.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Excessive uterine bleeding requiring immediate intervention to prevent hemodynamic compromise.
• Consider pregnancy-related bleeding first in anyone who could be pregnant.
• Causes in nonpregnant patients: anovulation, fibroids, adenomyosis, coagulopathy, medication effects, endometrial pathology.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, vital signs, bleeding rate, and symptoms of anemia or shock.
• Establish IV access and obtain CBC, pregnancy test, blood group/crossmatch if severe, and coagulation tests.
• Assess medication history, including anticoagulants.
• Arrange pelvic examination and ultrasound according to clinical stability.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Hemodynamic instability[/color]
• Begin resuscitation and arrange urgent gynecological assessment.
• Use blood products when clinically indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]Medical treatment (Stable patients)[/color]
• Tranexamic acid may be considered when not contraindicated.
• Hormonal treatment (combined oral contraceptives or progestin therapy) may be appropriate.
• IV estrogen is reserved for selected patients under specialist protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Procedural treatment[/color]
• If bleeding remains uncontrolled, consider uterine tamponade or surgical management.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Exclude pregnancy and pregnancy-related complications before treating as nonpregnant abnormal uterine bleeding.
• Estrogen-containing treatment may be contraindicated in patients with thromboembolic risks.
• Persistent bleeding requires investigation for structural disease, coagulopathy, and malignancy.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit unstable patients or those with severe ongoing bleeding or significant anemia.
• Stable patients require a documented treatment and follow-up plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACOG; NICE guidance on heavy menstrual bleeding.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Lower abdominal or pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, uterine/adnexal tenderness, fever, or abnormal vaginal discharge.
• Severe disease may be associated with tubo-ovarian abscess, peritonitis, or sepsis.
• Consider ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, ovarian torsion, and other surgical emergencies.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, vital signs, pain severity, and signs of peritonitis or shock.
• Perform pregnancy testing.
• Obtain CBC, renal function, inflammatory markers, and cultures.
• Collect gonorrhea/chlamydia nucleic acid amplification tests.
• Arrange pelvic ultrasound when abscess, ectopic pregnancy, or torsion is suspected.
• Initiate sepsis management promptly if systemic illness is present.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics[/color]
• Hospitalize patients with severe illness, sepsis, suspected tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, or inability to tolerate oral therapy.
• Use broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering gonorrhea, chlamydia, anaerobes (e.g., ceftriaxone plus doxycycline and metronidazole).
• Modify treatment according to cultures and clinical response.

[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive care and source control[/color]
• Give IV fluids if hypoperfusion is present.
• Provide analgesia and antiemetics.
• A tubo-ovarian abscess may require image-guided drainage or surgery if rupture is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay surgical assessment when appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, torsion, or abscess rupture is possible.
• Suspected sepsis requires immediate treatment and source assessment.
• Arrange partner evaluation and treatment to reduce reinfection.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit severe cases and reassess frequently.
• Ensure clinical improvement before transition to oral therapy.
• Arrange follow-up and completion of the recommended antibiotic course.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines; Surviving Sepsis Campaign.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Sudden unilateral pelvic or lower abdominal pain.
• Pain may occur during exercise or intercourse.
• Guarding, rebound tenderness, dizziness, syncope, or shoulder-tip pain if significant intraperitoneal bleeding occurs.
• Tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, or falling hemoglobin suggest major hemorrhage.
• Always exclude ectopic pregnancy in any reproductive-age patient with pelvic pain or bleeding.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and vital signs.
• Obtain two large-bore IV lines if significant bleeding or instability is suspected.
• Keep the patient nil by mouth and urgently involve gynecology.
• Send CBC, blood group and crossmatch, coagulation profile, renal function, and serum or urine β-hCG.
• Perform bedside ultrasound if available; do not delay surgery for imaging in a patient with suspected life-threatening intra-abdominal hemorrhage.
• Activate the major hemorrhage protocol if indicated.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound: ovarian cyst, free pelvic fluid, and possible hemoperitoneum.
• Serial hemoglobin/hematocrit; an initial normal hemoglobin does not exclude acute blood loss.
• Quantitative β-hCG to help exclude ectopic pregnancy.
• CT is generally not the first-line investigation when pregnancy is possible.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 1 g orally or IV every 6–8 hours as needed; maximum 4 g/day in a healthy adult.
• If severe pain persists, titrated IV opioid analgesia may be used according to local protocols.
• Avoid NSAIDs when significant bleeding, renal impairment, or a bleeding disorder is suspected.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV fluids and blood products[/color]
• If hypotensive, give isotonic crystalloid in reassessed boluses, commonly 250–500 mL in adults.
• If major hemorrhage is suspected, use emergency-release blood or crossmatched blood according to the institutional major hemorrhage protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive management[/color]
• Stable, improving patient: monitored observation, serial vital signs and hemoglobin.
• Hemodynamic instability, ongoing bleeding, worsening hemoperitoneum: urgent laparoscopy or laparotomy.
• Aim for ovarian-sparing cyst treatment when feasible and safe.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Analgesia must not delay evaluation for ectopic pregnancy, torsion, or hemorrhagic shock.
• Persistent instability requires urgent operative hemorrhage control; fluids alone do not treat the bleeding source.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit if significant hemoperitoneum, falling hemoglobin, uncontrolled pain, or diagnostic uncertainty is present.
• Discharge only after adequate reassessment, stable vital signs, controlled pain, and a safe follow-up plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACOG; NICE. Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Lower abdominal or pelvic pain, fever, and cervical motion or adnexal tenderness.
• Vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, nausea, or vomiting may occur.
• A pelvic mass or complex adnexal collection on ultrasound supports the diagnosis.
• Rupture may cause generalized peritonitis, sepsis, and shock.
• Differential diagnoses include ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, ovarian torsion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess for sepsis, shock, peritonitis, and pregnancy.
• Obtain IV access; send CBC, renal and liver function, lactate if severely ill, blood cultures if sepsis is suspected, and β-hCG.
• Obtain vaginal/cervical testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia when appropriate.
• Perform pelvic ultrasound and involve gynecology.
• Hospitalize patients with suspected TOA; pregnancy, severe illness, inability to tolerate oral treatment, or inability to exclude a surgical emergency are additional reasons for inpatient care.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Transvaginal ultrasound, usually with Doppler when indicated.
• CBC, CRP, renal function, pregnancy test, and microbiological testing.
• CT or MRI may be considered when the diagnosis remains uncertain.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]First-line inpatient antimicrobial regimen[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours.
• PLUS doxycycline 100 mg orally or IV every 12 hours.
• PLUS metronidazole 500 mg orally or IV every 12 hours.
• Continue IV therapy until clinical improvement, then transition to oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus metronidazole 500 mg twice daily to complete 14 days.

[color=#1E3A8A]Alternative inpatient regimens[/color]
• Option A: Ampicillin–sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours PLUS doxycycline 100 mg.
• Option B: Clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours PLUS gentamicin.

[color=#1E3A8A]Drainage or surgery[/color]
• Consider image-guided drainage or operative drainage if the abscess is large, ruptured, associated with sepsis, or not improving with appropriate antibiotics.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Doxycycline is generally avoided during pregnancy; if pregnancy is possible or confirmed, obtain urgent specialist advice and select a pregnancy-appropriate regimen.
• Suspected rupture, generalized peritonitis, or hemodynamic instability requires urgent surgical assessment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for inpatient treatment and observation for more than 24 hours.
• Lack of clinical improvement within 48–72 hours requires reassessment of the diagnosis and need for drainage.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: CDC. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease: STI Treatment Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Usually occurs after ovarian stimulation during fertility treatment.
• Abdominal distension, pelvic pain, nausea, vomiting, and rapid weight gain.
• Severe disease may cause ascites, pleural effusion, oliguria, hemoconcentration, electrolyte abnormalities, AKI, and VTE.
• Red flags: dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, severe abdominal pain, reduced urine output, or unilateral leg swelling.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, SpO2, and hemodynamic status.
• Determine severity and involve the fertility specialist and gynecology team.
• Measure weight, abdominal girth, fluid intake/output, and urine output.
• Evaluate for pregnancy, ectopic, ovarian torsion, hemorrhage, and PE when clinically indicated.
• Admit patients with severe symptoms, significant ascites, respiratory compromise, oliguria, or suspected thrombosis.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC and hematocrit.
• Electrolytes, urea, creatinine, liver function, albumin, and coagulation studies.
• Pregnancy test or quantitative β-hCG.
• Pelvic ultrasound to assess ovarian enlargement and ascites.
• Chest imaging and PE investigations if respiratory symptoms.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Fluid management[/color]
• For clinically significant intravascular depletion, give isotonic crystalloid in small, reassessed boluses.
• Avoid automatic large-volume fluid administration in patients with substantial ascites or pleural effusion.

[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia and antiemetics[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed.
• For persistent vomiting, use a pregnancy-appropriate antiemetic.
• Avoid NSAIDs when renal impairment, dehydration, or significant intravascular depletion is present.

[color=#1E3A8A]Thromboprophylaxis[/color]
• In hospitalized patients with severe OHSS, consider LMWH prophylaxis according to body weight, renal function, and bleeding risk.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• OHSS causes fluid shift into third spaces; excessive IV fluid may worsen ascites and respiratory compromise.
• Severe or increasing pain requires assessment for ovarian torsion, cyst rupture, or another acute abdomen.
• Suspected PE or DVT requires urgent diagnostic evaluation and treatment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Mild disease: outpatient care only if oral intake, pain control, urine output, and follow-up are adequate.
• Moderate or severe disease: specialist review and often admission.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: RCOG; ASRM.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
• Postpartum fever, uterine tenderness, lower abdominal pain, and foul-smelling lochia.
• May occur after vaginal birth or cesarean delivery.
• Severe disease may progress to sepsis and septic shock.
• Consider retained products, wound infection, urinary infection, and other causes.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, temperature, blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, mental status, and urine output.
• Obtain CBC, renal function, and lactate if systemic illness is suspected.
• Obtain blood cultures in severe illness before antibiotics if this does not delay treatment.
• Perform abdominal and pelvic examination; assess the cesarean wound.
• Consider pelvic ultrasound if retained products or an abscess is suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric IV antibiotics[/color]
• Commonly used regimen: clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours plus gentamicin (weight-based).
• Alternative regimens may be appropriate depending on local resistance patterns.

[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive care[/color]
• Give IV fluids if hypovolemic, with repeated reassessment.
• Provide analgesia and antipyretics.
• Investigate and manage retained products, abscess, or another source requiring source control.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Suspected sepsis or shock requires immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and escalation.
• Failure to improve should prompt reassessment for retained products, pelvic abscess, or resistant organisms.
• Antibiotic selection must account for renal function and local resistance patterns.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for IV treatment and reassessment.
• Consider higher-level care for organ dysfunction, shock, or failure to improve.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO; NICE guidance on sepsis and postpartum care.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute abdomen is a sudden or rapidly progressive abdominal condition that may require urgent surgical evaluation or intervention.
Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum, commonly caused by perforation, leakage of GI contents, ischemia, or intra-abdominal infection.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color]
• Severe, sudden-onset, or rapidly worsening abdominal pain.
• Involuntary guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness.
• Abdominal distension with persistent vomiting or inability to pass stool/flatus.
• Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status, or oliguria.
• GI bleeding or signs of bowel ischemia.
• Pain out of proportion to physical examination.

[color=#1E3A8A]Differential:[/color] Perforated peptic ulcer, appendicitis, obstruction/strangulation, mesenteric ischemia, pancreatitis, cholecystitis/cholangitis, ruptured AAA, ectopic pregnancy, trauma, gastroenteritis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• ABCDE assessment: identify shock, respiratory compromise, altered consciousness, sepsis.
• Provide supplemental oxygen for hypoxemia.
• Call the surgical team early for generalized peritonitis, suspected perforation, bowel ischemia, strangulation, or hemodynamic instability.
• Do not delay surgical consultation while waiting for imaging or labs.
• Keep patient nil by mouth (NPO).
• Establish two large-bore IV cannulas in shock, major bleeding, or suspected laparotomy.
• Fluid resuscitation: isotonic crystalloid (e.g., Lactated Ringer's or 0.9% NaCl). In hypoperfusion, give 500 mL bolus and reassess.
• Provide timely analgesia (opioids titrated).
• Start IV antibiotics promptly when peritonitis, perforation, complicated intra-abdominal infection, or sepsis is suspected.
• Consider urinary catheter (shock/critically ill) and NG tube (persistent vomiting, distension, obstruction).

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Bedside:[/color] Vital signs, glucose, ECG (if indicated), pregnancy test, bedside ultrasound.

[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, LFTs/bilirubin, lipase, blood gas/lactate, CRP, coagulation, group & screen/crossmatch, blood cultures (if sepsis), urinalysis.

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color]
• CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast: preferred in many stable adults when diagnosis uncertain or serious cause suspected.
• Ultrasound: useful for biliary disease, AAA, free fluid, pelvic/pregnancy conditions.
• Plain radiographs: may show obstruction/free air, but normal does not exclude surgical emergency.
• [color=#991B1B]In unstable patient with peritonitis or time-critical emergency, resuscitation and urgent surgery take priority over CT.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. IV Crystalloid Fluids[/color]
• Adult hypoperfusion: 500 mL IV isotonic crystalloid initial bolus, then reassess.
• Monitor BP, pulse, capillary refill, mental status, lung exam, urine output. Avoid repeated large-volume boluses without reassessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Analgesia: Fentanyl[/color]
• Adult: 25–50 mcg IV slowly, titrated to pain and response. Use lower doses in frail/elderly/unstable.
• Monitor respiratory rate, SpO2, BP, consciousness.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Alternative Analgesia: Paracetamol[/color]
• Adult: 1 g IV over ~15 min. Adjust for low body weight, liver disease, malnutrition.

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Empiric Antibiotics (Example)[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours (for selected community-acquired infections).
• Broader coverage may be needed for septic shock, healthcare-associated infection, or resistant organisms.

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
Urgent operative assessment indicated for:
• Generalized peritonitis.
• GI perforation with contamination.
• Strangulated/ischemic bowel, necrosis, suspected mesenteric ischemia.
• Uncontrolled intra-abdominal bleeding.
• Intra-abdominal infection requiring urgent source control.

Procedures: laparotomy or laparoscopy, repair of perforation, bowel resection, drainage, control of bleeding.
Consider damage-control surgery in profoundly deranged patients.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate OR/emergency surgical pathway: generalized peritonitis, suspected perforation, bowel ischemia, strangulation, uncontrolled bleeding, clinical deterioration.
• ICU/high-dependency: persistent shock, vasopressor requirement, respiratory failure, severe sepsis, major organ dysfunction.
• Admit for observation, further investigations, or specialist review.
• Discharge only when dangerous cause excluded, symptoms controlled, stable, and clear follow-up arranged.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidelines on intra-abdominal emergencies; Surviving Sepsis Campaign; ACR Appropriateness Criteria; NICE Sepsis Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute appendicitis is inflammation of the vermiform appendix. Delayed treatment may lead to perforation, abscess, peritonitis, and sepsis.
• Periumbilical pain migrating to right lower quadrant.
• Anorexia, nausea, vomiting.
• RLQ tenderness, sometimes guarding. Fever, tachycardia. Pain aggravated by movement/coughing.

[color=#991B1B]Complicated appendicitis:[/color] Generalized tenderness/rigidity, persistent fever/systemic toxicity, hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria, imaging evidence of perforation/abscess.

[color=#1E3A8A]Differential:[/color] Ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, PID, mesenteric adenitis, gastroenteritis, terminal ileitis/Crohn's, ureteric stone/UTI, Meckel's diverticulitis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• ABCDE assessment; identify shock or sepsis.
• Keep NPO. Establish IV access and obtain blood samples.
• Provide appropriate analgesia and antiemetics.
• Give isotonic IV fluids if dehydrated or hypoperfused.
• Request early general surgical assessment.
• Obtain pregnancy test when pregnancy is possible.
• Start appropriate antibiotics when complicated appendicitis is suspected or surgery is planned.
• In generalized peritonitis or septic shock, initiate resuscitation and antibiotics promptly while arranging urgent source control.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC with differential, CRP, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, LFTs (if indicated), urinalysis, pregnancy test, venous blood gas/lactate (if sepsis/hypoperfusion), blood cultures (if severe sepsis, without delaying antibiotics).

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color]
• Ultrasound: useful in children, pregnancy, selected patients.
• CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast: commonly preferred in nonpregnant adults when diagnosis uncertain or complications suspected.
• MRI: option during pregnancy when ultrasound inconclusive.
• [color=#991B1B]Normal early WBC/CRP does not exclude appendicitis.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. IV Fluids[/color]
• If hypoperfusion: initial 500 mL isotonic crystalloid bolus, then reassess. Repeat per response, comorbidities, losses.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Analgesia: Paracetamol[/color]
• Adult: 1 g IV or orally. Adjust for low body weight, liver disease, malnutrition.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia: Fentanyl[/color]
• Adult: 25–50 mcg IV slowly, titrated in monitored setting.

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Antibiotics for Appendicitis Requiring Surgery[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours.
• Administer before incision. Review allergies, renal/hepatic function, local resistance.
• After uncomplicated appendectomy with adequate source control, postoperative antibiotics generally not required.
• Complicated appendicitis requires antibiotics after source control; duration per clinical response and local guidance.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Uncomplicated Appendicitis[/color]
• Laparoscopic appendectomy is standard definitive treatment where available.
• Selected patients may be offered antibiotics-first treatment after surgical assessment (when imaging confirms uncomplicated disease, no appendicolith, no perforation). Explain risk of failure/recurrence.

[color=#1E3A8A]Perforated Appendicitis[/color]
• Generalized peritonitis or uncontrolled sepsis: urgent operative assessment and source control.
• Localized abscess/phlegmon: antibiotics, with image-guided drainage when appropriate. Interval appendectomy considered selectively.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Confirmed appendicitis suitable for operative management.
• Perforation with generalized peritonitis.
• Clinical deterioration or uncontrolled infection.
• Failure of nonoperative management.
• Complications requiring source control.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for surgery, IV antibiotics, or observation for complications.
• ICU for septic shock or organ failure.
• Discharge only when safe nonoperative plan established, symptoms controlled, and follow-up/return precautions clear.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Jerusalem Guidelines; SAGES Guidelines; NICE Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute intestinal obstruction is partial or complete blockage of small or large bowel. Strangulation, ischemia, and perforation are life-threatening.
• Causes: Postoperative adhesions, incarcerated/strangulated hernia, colorectal cancer, volvulus, intussusception, inflammatory strictures, fecal impaction.
• Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting (early/prominent in small bowel), distension, constipation/inability to pass flatus.
• High-pitched bowel sounds early, reduced in advanced disease.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags for strangulation/ischemia:[/color] Continuous severe pain, localized/generalized peritonitis, fever/tachycardia/hypotension/acidosis, bloody stool, elevated lactate (early normal does not exclude), CT findings of closed-loop/reduced enhancement/pneumatosis/free air.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• ABCDE assessment and treatment of shock.
• Keep NPO. Insert IV access and begin isotonic fluids as indicated.
• Request urgent surgical assessment.
• Correct electrolyte disturbances.
• Consider NG tube for persistent vomiting, marked distension, or significant obstruction.
• Monitor urine output in seriously ill or requiring substantial fluid resuscitation.
• Provide analgesia and antiemetics.
• Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics when strangulation, ischemia, perforation, or sepsis suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT administer laxatives or bowel preparations when mechanical obstruction or perforation suspected.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, venous blood gas/lactate (if ischemia/shock), CRP, LFTs (if indicated), group & screen/crossmatch (if surgery likely), coagulation (severe illness/pre-op).

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color]
• CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast: preferred in many adults to identify transition point, cause, closed-loop, ischemia, perforation. Do not delay surgery if clear peritonitis or profound instability.
• Abdominal radiography: may show dilated loops/air-fluid levels. Normal does not exclude obstruction.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. IV Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• Adult hypoperfusion: 500 mL isotonic crystalloid, then reassess. Further replacement depends on BP, perfusion, vomiting, NG losses, urine output, comorbidities.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Electrolyte Replacement[/color]
• Replace potassium, magnesium, etc. per measured values and protocols. Check renal function and urine output before K+ replacement. Never give concentrated KCl IV push.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Antiemetic: Ondansetron[/color]
• Adult: 4 mg IV slowly. Caution with prolonged QT, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia.

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Antibiotics for Suspected Strangulation/Perforation[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours (selected community-acquired). Broader for healthcare-associated or septic shock.

sections.heading: 05 — NONOPERATIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
Trial of nonoperative treatment may be appropriate for selected adhesive SBO without peritonitis, strangulation, ischemia, or perforation.
• NPO, IV fluids/electrolytes, NG decompression, repeated abdominal exams/vitals, surgical reassessment if worsening.
• Water-soluble contrast protocols may assist assessment in selected adhesive obstructions under local protocol.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Peritonitis or suspected perforation.
• Strangulation, ischemia, or closed-loop obstruction.
• Incarcerated hernia causing obstruction.
• Clinical deterioration despite resuscitation.
• Failure of appropriate nonoperative trial.
• Obstruction caused by lesion requiring operative treatment.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with confirmed mechanical obstruction.
• ICU for shock, severe sepsis, or organ failure.
• Discharge only when obstruction excluded or safe resolution and follow-up plan established.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Bologna Guidelines; ACR Appropriateness Criteria; WSES Bowel Ischemia Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Incarcerated hernia contains tissue that cannot be reduced. Strangulated hernia has compromised blood supply, may progress to bowel necrosis, perforation, septic shock.
• Types: Inguinal, femoral, umbilical, incisional, other abdominal wall hernias.
• Painful, tender, irreducible swelling. Increasing pain/swelling. Nausea, vomiting, distension, obstipation. Skin erythema/discoloration.
• Fever, tachycardia, systemic toxicity.

[color=#991B1B]Features suggesting strangulation:[/color] Severe continuous pain, marked tenderness/skin changes, peritonitis, obstruction with systemic deterioration, elevated lactate or CT evidence of compromised bowel perfusion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• ABCDE assessment. Keep NPO.
• Establish IV access and obtain blood samples.
• Provide analgesia and IV fluids when indicated.
• Request urgent surgical assessment.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT repeatedly attempt forceful manual reduction.[/color]
• If strangulation, peritonitis, or bowel ischemia suspected: proceed toward urgent operative management without delaying for unnecessary imaging.
• Give antibiotics when bowel compromise, perforation, or operative contamination suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, venous blood gas/lactate (if ischemia/shock), group & screen/crossmatch (if emergency surgery likely).
• CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast in selected stable patients when diagnosis or extent of obstruction unclear.
• Ultrasound may help assess selected hernias when expertise available.
• [color=#991B1B]Imaging is not required before surgery when strangulation is clinically evident and delay would be dangerous.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Analgesia: Fentanyl[/color]
• Adult: 25–50 mcg IV slowly, titrated in monitored environment.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluids[/color]
• Adult hypoperfusion: initial 500 mL isotonic crystalloid bolus, reassess. Tailor to cardiac/renal function.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Perioperative Antibiotics[/color]
• Cefazolin 2 g IV before incision for clean hernia repair (3 g if ≥120 kg per prophylaxis protocol).
• If strangulation with suspected bowel necrosis/contamination: use therapeutic antibiotic regimen for intra-abdominal infection.

sections.heading: 05 — MANUAL REDUCTION
sections.content:
Consider only in selected patients with acutely irreducible hernia when there are NO clinical features of strangulation, ischemia, or peritonitis, and an experienced clinician judges it appropriate.
• Provide monitored analgesia. Use gentle, sustained pressure (not forceful).
• Stop immediately if pain worsens or reduction unsuccessful.
• Arrange surgical assessment after reduction (complications can persist despite apparent disappearance).
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT attempt manual reduction when strangulation suspected (may return nonviable bowel to abdomen and mask continuing ischemia).[/color]

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
Urgent surgery indicated for:
• Suspected strangulation.
• Peritonitis or bowel ischemia.
• Obstruction caused by irreducible hernia.
• Failed or inappropriate manual reduction.
• Clinical deterioration.

Operative management: reduction, assessment of bowel viability, bowel resection if necessary, hernia repair. Choice of mesh/technique depends on contamination, tissue condition, operative findings.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with suspected strangulation, obstruction, or emergency operative repair.
• Monitor closely after successful manual reduction and obtain surgical review.
• ICU care may be needed after bowel resection, severe sepsis, or hemodynamic instability.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidelines for emergency repair of complicated abdominal wall hernias; HerniaSurge Guidelines; Surgical Infection Society Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Perforated peptic ulcer is a full-thickness defect in the stomach or duodenal wall that allows GI contents to enter the peritoneal cavity, causing chemical peritonitis followed by bacterial contamination and potentially septic shock.
• Sudden severe epigastric pain that may rapidly become generalized.
• Abdominal guarding, rigidity, and rebound tenderness. Reduced or absent bowel sounds.
• Tachycardia, fever, hypotension, or altered mental status in advanced disease.
• Risk factors: NSAIDs, aspirin, previous PUD, H. pylori, older age, comorbidities.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment and identify shock.
• Keep the patient nil by mouth.
• Establish two large-bore IV lines in patients with shock or likely emergency surgery.
• Begin isotonic crystalloid resuscitation with frequent reassessment.
• Request immediate general surgical review.
• Administer IV broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly.
• Start IV proton pump inhibitor therapy according to local protocol.
• Provide analgesia and antiemetics.
• Consider nasogastric decompression in significant vomiting or gastric distension.
• Prepare for emergency operative source control.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, LFTs, lipase, venous blood gas/lactate, coagulation, group & crossmatch, blood cultures.

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color]
• CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast: preferred in many stable patients when perforation suspected. May show free air, fluid, site of perforation.
• Erect chest radiograph: may show free subdiaphragmatic air when CT unavailable. Normal does not exclude perforation.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay urgent surgical management for imaging in an unstable patient with convincing generalized peritonitis.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. IV Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• Adult hypoperfusion: initial 500 mL isotonic crystalloid bolus, then reassess. Repeat per response and comorbidities.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Antibiotics[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours (selected adults).
• Severe sepsis, healthcare-associated infection, or resistant organisms may require broader coverage.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. IV Proton Pump Inhibitor[/color]
• Pantoprazole 40 mg IV every 24 hours (commonly used initial regimen). Higher-dose regimens may be selected by the treating team.
• [color=#991B1B]PPI therapy does not close a perforation and must not delay surgery.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Analgesia[/color]
• Titrated IV analgesia appropriate to severity and hemodynamic status. [color=#991B1B]Avoid NSAIDs.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
Urgent operative repair is generally required for perforation with peritonitis or ongoing leakage.
• Laparoscopic or open exploration.
• Closure of the perforation, often with an omental patch.
• Peritoneal lavage and source control.
• More extensive surgery in selected cases.
• Nonoperative management reserved for highly selected patients with sealed perforation and no generalized peritonitis under close surgical supervision.

sections.heading: 06 — POSTOPERATIVE CARE
sections.content:
• Continue antibiotics according to source-control adequacy and clinical response.
• Provide PPI therapy.
• Test for H. pylori and eradicate if present.
• Avoid NSAIDs where possible and review ulcerogenic medications.
• Monitor for leakage, abscess, sepsis, and postoperative ileus.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Emergency surgical admission.
• ICU care for shock, organ dysfunction, or major postoperative complications.
• Discharge only after clinical stabilization, adequate recovery, and documented ulcer-prevention plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidelines for perforated/bleeding peptic ulcer; ACG Guidance; NICE Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute GI bleeding may arise from upper or lower GI tract. Severe bleeding can cause hemorrhagic shock and death.

[color=#1E3A8A]Upper GI bleeding:[/color] Hematemesis or coffee-ground vomitus, melena, hematochezia (massive upper GI). Causes: PUD, varices, erosive gastritis, Mallory-Weiss tears.

[color=#1E3A8A]Lower GI bleeding:[/color] Bright red or maroon rectal bleeding. Causes: diverticular bleeding, angiodysplasia, colorectal lesions, ischemic colitis, IBD.

[color=#991B1B]Severe bleeding:[/color] Hypotension, tachycardia, syncope, altered mental status, cold extremities, poor perfusion, oliguria, ongoing large-volume bleeding.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment. Assess airway protection (massive hematemesis/reduced consciousness).
• Establish two large-bore IV lines in significant bleeding.
• Send CBC, coagulation, renal function, LFTs, type & crossmatch.
• Begin resuscitation and activate major hemorrhage protocol when indicated.
• Hold anticoagulants/antiplatelet drugs temporarily when clinically appropriate; assess need for reversal.
• Arrange urgent gastroenterology or surgical consultation.
• Consider IV PPI for suspected upper GI bleeding.
• In suspected variceal bleeding: initiate vasoactive therapy and antibiotics promptly.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC and serial Hb, platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, urea/creatinine/electrolytes, LFTs, group & crossmatch, lactate/blood gas, medication review.

[color=#1E3A8A]Risk Assessment:[/color] Glasgow-Blatchford Score (assists but must not override clinical evidence of shock/ongoing bleeding).

[color=#1E3A8A]Endoscopy/Imaging:[/color]
• Upper GI endoscopy after initial resuscitation (urgently in unstable severe bleeding; generally within 24 hours for admitted patients).
• CT angiography for ongoing significant lower GI bleeding when actively bleeding.
• Colonoscopy per clinical stability and suspected source.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Blood Component Therapy[/color]
• Restrictive red-cell transfusion threshold around Hb 7 g/dL in many hemodynamically stable adults. Higher threshold may be appropriate for cardiovascular disease or ongoing ischemia.
• In exsanguinating hemorrhage or shock, do NOT wait for Hb to fall below a numerical threshold before initiating blood resuscitation.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Proton Pump Inhibitor[/color]
• IV pantoprazole for suspected nonvariceal upper GI bleeding per local protocol. High-dose PPI particularly relevant after endoscopic treatment of high-risk ulcer bleeding.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Suspected Variceal Bleeding: Octreotide[/color]
• Adult: 50 mcg IV bolus, followed by 50 mcg/hour IV infusion when variceal hemorrhage suspected.
• Adjunct, not a substitute for urgent endoscopic management.

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Antibiotics for Suspected Variceal Bleeding in Cirrhosis[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours (commonly used in selected patients with cirrhosis and acute variceal hemorrhage).

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Nonvariceal Upper GI Bleeding[/color]
• Endoscopic hemostasis for high-risk bleeding lesions. PPI therapy after appropriate endoscopic management. IR or surgery when bleeding cannot be controlled endoscopically.

[color=#1E3A8A]Variceal Bleeding[/color]
• Vasoactive therapy and antibiotics. Urgent endoscopy with appropriate variceal therapy. Specialist escalation for uncontrolled bleeding.

[color=#1E3A8A]Severe Lower GI Bleeding[/color]
• CT angiography and possible angiographic embolization in appropriate patients. Colonoscopy or surgery according to source, clinical stability, and treatment response.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL/INTERVENTIONAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Persistent bleeding despite endoscopic treatment.
• Hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation.
• Bleeding requiring embolization or operative control.
• Perforation or another associated surgical pathology.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for significant bleeding, anemia, comorbidity, or need for intervention.
• ICU for shock, airway compromise, massive transfusion, or organ dysfunction.
• Outpatient management only for carefully selected low-risk patients after formal assessment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACG Guidelines (upper & lower GI bleeding); Baveno VII; NICE Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute mesenteric ischemia is an abrupt reduction in intestinal blood supply that may progress to bowel infarction, perforation, sepsis, and death.
• Causes: Arterial embolism (AF), acute arterial thrombosis (atherosclerosis), mesenteric venous thrombosis, nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia (shock/vasoconstriction).
• Sudden severe abdominal pain (often out of proportion to early physical findings). Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.
• Occult/overt GI bleeding. Later guarding, rigidity, peritonitis.
• Shock or multiorgan dysfunction in advanced disease.
• [color=#991B1B]A normal early lactate does not exclude mesenteric ischemia.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment and resuscitate shock.
• Request immediate surgical and vascular/interventional specialist assessment.
• Keep the patient NPO.
• Establish large-bore IV access and obtain urgent laboratory samples.
• Arrange urgent CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis when feasible.
• Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (bowel ischemia can rapidly lead to bacterial translocation and sepsis).
• Consider IV unfractionated heparin when arterial/venous thrombosis suspected and no contraindication, following urgent specialist assessment.
• Do not delay intervention in a patient with peritonitis or strong evidence of bowel necrosis.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, venous/arterial blood gas and lactate, coagulation, group & crossmatch, LFTs, glucose, blood cultures (sepsis, without delaying antibiotics).

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color]
• CT angiography: preferred urgent investigation in suspected acute mesenteric ischemia. Identifies arterial/venous occlusion, bowel-wall abnormalities, associated complications.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT rely on plain abdominal radiographs or a normal early lactate to exclude the diagnosis.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. IV Resuscitation[/color]
• Adult hypoperfusion: begin with 500 mL isotonic crystalloid and reassess. Further fluid guided by perfusion, losses, cardiac function, clinical response.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics[/color]
• Example: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV, with subsequent dosing/interval determined by renal function, severity, and institutional protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Anticoagulation: Unfractionated Heparin[/color]
• When indicated for suspected arterial/venous thrombosis: use institution's therapeutic IV heparin nomogram. Monitor aPTT or anti-Xa. Monitor CBC, platelets, bleeding.
• Coordinate with surgical team if emergency laparotomy required.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Arterial Occlusion[/color]
• Endovascular revascularization or open embolectomy/thrombectomy. Resect nonviable bowel. Reassess viability and consider planned second-look operation.

[color=#1E3A8A]Mesenteric Venous Thrombosis[/color]
• Therapeutic anticoagulation is a mainstay when no contraindication. Surgery if peritonitis or bowel infarction develops.

[color=#1E3A8A]Nonocclusive Mesenteric Ischemia[/color]
• Correct precipitating low-flow state. Optimize cardiac output and perfusion. Reduce precipitating vasoconstrictors when feasible. Consider targeted intra-arterial vasodilator therapy in selected cases. Operate if bowel necrosis or peritonitis develops.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Peritonitis.
• Suspected bowel infarction or perforation.
• Clinical deterioration despite resuscitation.
• Need for operative revascularization or bowel resection.
• Uncertain bowel viability requiring direct assessment.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Emergency admission to a center capable of urgent vascular, endovascular, and abdominal surgical intervention.
• ICU care for shock, metabolic acidosis, bowel resection, or organ failure.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidelines for acute mesenteric ischemia; ESVS Guidance; ACR Appropriateness Criteria.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Volvulus is twisting of a bowel segment around its mesentery, causing obstruction and potentially compromising blood supply. Can progress to bowel ischemia, necrosis, perforation, and septic shock.
• Types: Sigmoid volvulus, cecal volvulus.
• Risk factors: Chronic constipation, older age/institutionalization, neurological disease/impaired mobility, previous abdominal surgery/adhesions, anatomical predisposition (redundant sigmoid).
• Abdominal distension. Colicky or persistent abdominal pain. Constipation and inability to pass flatus. Nausea/vomiting. Tympanitic abdomen.
• Fever, peritonitis, or shock when ischemia/perforation develops.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment. Keep patient NPO.
• Establish IV access and correct dehydration/electrolyte disturbances.
• Request urgent surgical assessment.
• Consider NG decompression for persistent vomiting or significant distension.
• Start broad-spectrum antibiotics when ischemia, perforation, or sepsis suspected.
• Arrange urgent imaging in stable patients.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT attempt endoscopic decompression when there are signs of peritonitis, perforation, or suspected bowel necrosis.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, lactate/blood gas (ischemia/shock), CRP, group & crossmatch (if surgery likely).

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color]
• CT abdomen/pelvis: helps identify transition point, twisted mesentery, bowel dilation, ischemia, perforation.
• Abdominal radiograph: may show characteristic bowel dilation (coffee-bean appearance in sigmoid volvulus). Cannot reliably exclude ischemia/perforation.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. IV Fluids[/color]
• Adult hypoperfusion: initial 500 mL isotonic crystalloid bolus, then reassess. Replace ongoing vomiting/decompression losses.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Antibiotics when Ischemia/Perforation Suspected[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours (selected adults).
• Broader for severe healthcare-associated infection or septic shock.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Sigmoid Volvulus without Ischemia/Perforation[/color]
• Endoscopic detorsion and decompression may be attempted by experienced team. Observe for clinical improvement and bowel viability.
• Definitive sigmoid colectomy generally recommended because recurrence after decompression alone is common.

[color=#1E3A8A]Cecal Volvulus[/color]
• Operative management generally recommended. Procedure depends on bowel viability and operative findings; may include resection of affected segment.
• Endoscopic decompression generally NOT recommended (limited success, significant perforation risk).

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Peritonitis.
• Suspected ischemia or necrosis.
• Perforation.
• Failed endoscopic detorsion.
• Cecal volvulus requiring definitive treatment.
• Recurrent sigmoid volvulus requiring definitive surgery.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit all patients with confirmed volvulus.
• ICU care for shock, bowel necrosis, perforation, or major postoperative complications.
• Ensure definitive recurrence-prevention plan after successful decompression.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidance on Sigmoid Volvulus; ASGE Guidance; WSES Emergency Colorectal Surgery Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) is marked colonic dilation without a mechanical obstructing lesion. Often occurs in hospitalized, postoperative, or severely ill patients.
• Risk factors: Major surgery/trauma/severe medical illness, electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia), opioids/anticholinergics, neurological disorders/immobility, severe infection/critical illness.
• Progressive abdominal distension. Abdominal discomfort/pain. Nausea/vomiting. Constipation/reduced passage of stool/flatus.
• Fever, localized tenderness, guarding, or shock may indicate ischemia or perforation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCDE and identify peritonitis or shock.
• Keep patient NPO initially if significant distension, vomiting, or procedural intervention likely.
• Review medications and discontinue contributing agents where possible.
• Correct potassium, magnesium, and other electrolyte abnormalities. Provide IV fluids per volume status.
• Obtain urgent surgical assessment.
• Evaluate for mechanical obstruction, ischemia, and perforation before pharmacological decompression.
• Monitor abdominal findings and vital signs serially.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, magnesium/potassium, lactate/blood gas (ischemia/deterioration), CRP.

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color]
• Abdominal radiograph to assess colonic dilation and follow progression.
• CT abdomen/pelvis (often with IV contrast) to exclude mechanical obstruction and identify complications.
• Assess cecal diameter and duration of dilation. Risk rises with marked dilation (particularly ≥12 cm) and prolonged distension.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Conservative Management[/color]
• Indications: Hemodynamically stable without peritonitis, ischemia, or perforation.
• Bowel rest, IV fluids/electrolyte correction, stop/reduce opioids/anticholinergics, mobilization, NG decompression (significant vomiting), rectal tube decompression (selected).
• Serial abdominal examination and imaging as indicated. Track abdominal circumference/distension, pain, stool/flatus, vitals, urine output, cecal diameter.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT continue conservative management when patient deteriorates or bowel ischemia/perforation suspected.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Neostigmine[/color]
• Indications: Persistent clinically significant pseudo-obstruction despite appropriate conservative therapy, after mechanical obstruction and perforation excluded. Requires specialist decision and continuous monitoring.
• Dose: Neostigmine 2 mg IV administered slowly over ~3–5 minutes. Repeat dosing depends on response and local protocol.
• Continuous ECG and SpO2 monitoring. Frequent BP and HR assessment. Have atropine immediately available for clinically significant bradycardia. Ensure staff/equipment for resuscitation.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid in significant bradycardia, uncontrolled asthma/bronchospasm, suspected mechanical obstruction, and suspected bowel perforation.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Colonoscopic Decompression[/color]
• Indications: Failure/contraindication to neostigmine, or when specialist assessment favors endoscopic decompression.
• Performed by experienced endoscopy team. Decompression tube placement may reduce recurrence. Monitor for perforation and clinical recurrence.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid or use extreme caution when perforation or bowel ischemia suspected.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Perforation or bowel necrosis.
• Peritonitis.
• Clinical deterioration despite appropriate treatment.
• Failure of nonoperative and endoscopic management in a patient requiring operative intervention.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for monitoring and treatment.
• Escalate to ICU for shock, respiratory compromise from massive distension, or major complications.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ASGE Guidance; ASCRS Clinical Practice Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Toxic megacolon is acute colonic dilation associated with severe colitis and systemic toxicity. Can cause perforation, hemorrhage, shock, and multiorgan failure.
• Causes: Severe ulcerative colitis, Crohn colitis, C. difficile infection, other infectious colitides, ischemic/drug-associated colitis.
• Severe diarrhea (may be bloody). Abdominal pain and distension. Fever, tachycardia, dehydration. Hypotension/altered mental status. Reduced bowel sounds, guarding, rebound tenderness in advanced disease.
• Diagnostic concern: Colonic dilation (commonly >6 cm on imaging) combined with systemic toxicity and severe colitis. Diagnosis requires clinical and radiological assessment.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment and assess for shock.
• Call general surgery and gastroenterology urgently.
• Keep patient NPO initially if severe disease or surgery possible.
• Establish IV access and begin appropriate fluid resuscitation.
• Obtain CBC, electrolytes, renal function, inflammatory markers, lactate when indicated.
• Send stool testing for C. difficile and other pathogens as appropriate.
• Stop antidiarrheal agents, opioids, anticholinergics, and other drugs that impair colonic motility when clinically feasible.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid colonoscopy and bowel preparation in suspected toxic megacolon because of perforation risk.[/color]
• Perform serial abdominal examinations and monitor for deterioration.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC and differential.
• Electrolytes, urea, and creatinine.
• CRP and albumin.
• Lactate and blood gas if severe illness suspected.
• Stool testing for C. difficile and relevant enteric pathogens.
• Blood cultures in systemic toxicity or suspected sepsis.
• Abdominal radiograph or CT to evaluate dilation and complications.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid delaying surgery for imaging when perforation or peritonitis is clinically evident.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. IV Fluid and Electrolyte Replacement[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid, with boluses guided by perfusion and repeated reassessment.
• Monitor BP, pulse, urine output, electrolytes, renal function, respiratory status.
• Tailor fluids to cardiac/renal function; avoid unmonitored fluid loading.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Suspected C. difficile-Associated Fulminant Colitis[/color]
• Vancomycin 500 mg orally or via NG tube every 6 hours.
• Add Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours.
• If ileus present, rectal vancomycin may be required under specialist direction.
• [color=#991B1B]Treatment must follow current local infectious disease guidance. Fulminant disease requires early surgical consultation; antibiotics must NOT delay surgery when indicated.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Severe IBD-Associated Colitis[/color]
• IV corticosteroids may be indicated for acute severe ulcerative colitis after appropriate specialist assessment and evaluation for infection.
• Infectious causes (particularly C. difficile) should be investigated and treated when present.
• Rescue therapy and colectomy decisions require urgent gastroenterology and surgical coordination.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT start immunosuppression indiscriminately before considering infection and perforation.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
Urgent operative management may be required for:
• Perforation or generalized peritonitis.
• Uncontrolled hemorrhage.
• Worsening systemic toxicity or shock.
• Progressive colonic dilation or clinical deterioration despite appropriate medical treatment.
• Failure of intensive medical treatment in severe colitis.

The operation depends on underlying cause and condition of the colon; subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy is commonly considered in fulminant ulcerative colitis with life-threatening complications.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit to hospital; ICU care often required in severe systemic toxicity.
• Conduct frequent multidisciplinary reassessment.
• Do NOT delay operative intervention when complications or failure of treatment are evident.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACG Clinical Guidelines on C. difficile; ASCRS Clinical Practice Guidelines on Ulcerative Colitis; BSG Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
An intra-abdominal abscess is a localized collection of infected fluid or pus. May occur after appendicitis, diverticulitis, bowel perforation, pancreatitis, trauma, or abdominal surgery.
• Risk factors: Recent abdominal surgery, anastomotic leak, perforated viscus, inadequate source control during previous procedure, immunosuppression/diabetes, complicated appendicitis/diverticulitis.
• Persistent/recurrent fever. Abdominal pain or localized tenderness. Tachycardia and malaise. Ileus, nausea, poor oral intake. Leukocytosis/raised inflammatory markers.
• Hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria, elevated lactate in severe sepsis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment and identify sepsis or shock.
• Obtain IV access and assess perfusion. Send lab tests and blood cultures when indicated.
• Begin appropriate IV antibiotics promptly in sepsis or when serious intra-abdominal infection suspected.
• Obtain urgent surgical assessment. Arrange imaging to identify collection and potential source.
• Plan drainage or surgery when source control needed.
• [color=#991B1B]Reassess frequently; do not rely on antibiotics alone for a drainable collection.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, LFTs when indicated, CRP, lactate/blood gas in severe illness, blood cultures in sepsis, culture of drained pus/intra-abdominal specimens.

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color]
• CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast: often preferred in stable adult to locate abscess, identify leak, guide drainage.
• Ultrasound: useful for selected superficial/accessible collections and when CT unsuitable.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Empiric IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours (selected community-acquired).
• Piperacillin–tazobactam may be appropriate for more severe infection or broader coverage.
• Start promptly in sepsis. Adjust to renal function, allergy, source, cultures, local resistance. Review daily and narrow when possible.
• [color=#991B1B]These are example adult regimens, not universal prescriptions. Healthcare-associated infection, resistant organisms, severe allergy, or renal impairment may require a different regimen. Antibiotic duration depends on adequacy of source control and clinical response.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid for hypoperfusion, with repeated reassessment.
• In adult sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, initial fluid resuscitation may approach 30 mL/kg within first 3 hours, but must be individualized and reassessed frequently.
• Avoid automatic large-volume fluid administration without reassessment, particularly in cardiac/renal dysfunction.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Percutaneous Drainage[/color]
• Indications: Well-defined collection safely accessible by interventional radiology or appropriately trained specialist.
• Obtain specimens for culture. Monitor drain output, fever, pain, inflammatory markers, clinical response. Re-image/reassess if improvement does not occur.
• [color=#991B1B]Not every collection is safely drainable percutaneously. Persistent sepsis may indicate undrained collection, ongoing leakage, resistant infection, or inadequate source control.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Generalized peritonitis.
• Free perforation or ongoing gastrointestinal leakage.
• Collections unsuitable for percutaneous drainage.
• Failed drainage or persistent infection.
• Hemodynamic instability or clinical deterioration requiring urgent source control.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with significant intra-abdominal infection.
• ICU care for septic shock or organ dysfunction.
• Document a source-control plan and reassess need for further drainage or surgery.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Surgical Infection Society Guidelines; WSES Guidance on Intra-abdominal Infections; Surviving Sepsis Campaign.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Esophageal perforation is a life-threatening emergency that can cause mediastinitis, pleural infection, sepsis, and shock.
• Causes: Forceful vomiting (Boerhaave syndrome), iatrogenic injury during endoscopy/instrumentation, foreign body ingestion, trauma, caustic injury/underlying esophageal disease.
• Sudden severe chest, neck, or upper abdominal pain. Pain after forceful vomiting. Dysphagia/odynophagia.
• Fever, tachycardia, respiratory distress. Subcutaneous emphysema/crepitus. Pleural effusion, pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax. Shock/sepsis in advanced cases.
• [color=#991B1B]The classic triad of vomiting, chest pain, and subcutaneous emphysema is not always present.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment and treat respiratory/circulatory compromise.
• Keep patient strictly NPO.
• Obtain urgent thoracic or upper GI surgical consultation.
• Establish IV access and begin resuscitation when indicated.
• Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering oral flora and anaerobes.
• Consider IV PPI therapy as directed by specialist team.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid blind nasogastric tube insertion; placement should be directed by treating specialist when needed.[/color]
• Arrange urgent imaging and definitive source control.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, CRP, lactate, blood gas as clinically indicated.
• Blood cultures if sepsis suspected.
• CT chest and upper abdomen with appropriate contrast protocol.
• Water-soluble contrast esophagography may be used when appropriate.
• Endoscopy may be useful in selected cases but should be planned by experienced specialist (instrumentation can worsen injury).

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Example: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV per severe-infection protocol.
• Alternative regimens depend on allergy history, renal function, likely organisms, local resistance.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics alone are insufficient when ongoing leakage or uncontrolled contamination requires source control.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluids and Shock Management[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid in boluses guided by hemodynamic status and reassessment.
• Monitor BP, HR, urine output, lactate, respiratory status. Escalate to vasopressors and critical care when shock persists.
• Avoid excessive fluid in patients with respiratory compromise or cardiac dysfunction.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
Management depends on site, cause, time since perforation, contamination, and clinical stability. Options:
• Endoscopic closure or stenting in selected cases.
• Surgical repair and drainage.
• Drainage of mediastinal or pleural collections.
• Resection or diversion in selected severe injuries.
• Carefully selected nonoperative management only when specialist criteria met and close monitoring available.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Free leak with significant contamination.
• Hemodynamic instability or uncontrolled sepsis.
• Large or non-contained perforation.
• Failed endoscopic or conservative management.
• Necrotic esophageal tissue or associated major injury.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent admission to a center with appropriate thoracic or upper GI surgical expertise.
• ICU care for shock, respiratory failure, or severe mediastinal/pleural contamination.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidance on Esophageal Emergencies; ESGE Guidance on Iatrogenic Perforation; STS/Specialist Thoracic Surgery Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Esophageal food bolus impaction occurs when food becomes lodged in the esophagus. Complete obstruction can prevent patient from swallowing saliva and may cause aspiration.
• Sudden dysphagia during a meal. Sensation of food stuck in chest/throat. Regurgitation of liquids/food.
• Drooling or inability to swallow saliva. Gagging, coughing, aspiration. Retrosternal discomfort/pain.

[color=#991B1B]Red Flags:[/color] Inability to handle secretions, respiratory distress/suspected aspiration, sharp foreign body/bone ingestion, severe chest/neck pain, fever, crepitus, signs of perforation, suspected caustic ingestion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation.
• If respiratory distress or airway compromise present, initiate emergency airway management as appropriate.
• Keep patient NPO. Sit upright when clinically appropriate and keep suction available if secretions cannot be managed.
• Request urgent gastroenterology/endoscopy consultation.
• [color=#991B1B]Complete obstruction with inability to swallow saliva requires emergent endoscopic management.[/color]
• Do NOT force oral fluids, food, or tablets. Do NOT induce vomiting. Avoid blind attempts to push bolus down.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Clinical assessment of airway and ability to handle secretions.
• Chest/neck radiographs when radiopaque foreign body or complication suspected.
• CT when perforation, sharp foreign body injury, or another complication suspected.
• Endoscopy is main diagnostic and therapeutic procedure for persistent impaction.
• Investigate underlying cause after resolution (esophageal stricture, Schatzki ring, eosinophilic esophagitis, malignancy when appropriate).

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Endoscopic Removal or Advancement[/color]
• Indications: Complete obstruction or inability to handle secretions = emergent intervention. Other persistent food bolus impactions: urgent endoscopic treatment per specialist assessment.
• Procedure: Flexible endoscopy by trained clinician. Removal or careful advancement of bolus. Evaluate for mucosal injury, stricture, or underlying lesion.
• Airway protection and sedation planning depend on aspiration risk and patient stability.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay emergent endoscopy in complete obstruction. Avoid forceful advancement and blind instrumentation.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Pharmacological Measures[/color]
• Selected agents (e.g., IV glucagon) have sometimes been used while arranging definitive care, but efficacy is inconsistent.
• If specialist/local protocol elects glucagon: commonly cited adult dose 1 mg IV once.
• Monitor nausea, vomiting, glucose, airway status.
• [color=#991B1B]Glucagon must NOT delay endoscopy. Avoid relying on it in complete obstruction or when patient cannot handle secretions. Do NOT administer oral effervescent agents/fluids to patient with complete obstruction (aspiration risk).[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — AFTER RESOLUTION
sections.content:
• Assess for mucosal injury or perforation.
• Arrange evaluation for underlying esophageal disorder.
• Biopsy for eosinophilic esophagitis when appropriate and safe.
• Provide follow-up for recurrent dysphagia or food impaction.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or observe patients with complications, persistent symptoms, significant mucosal injury, aspiration, or suspected perforation.
• Discharge only after successful resolution, adequate swallowing assessment, and clear follow-up plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ASGE Guidance on Ingested Foreign Bodies and Food Impactions; ESGE Clinical Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Testicular torsion occurs when the spermatic cord twists, compromising testicular blood flow. It is a time-critical surgical emergency.
• Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain. Nausea or vomiting.
• High-riding or horizontal testicular position. Scrotal swelling and tenderness.
• Absent cremasteric reflex may support diagnosis but is not sufficiently reliable to exclude torsion when present.
• Abdominal or groin pain may occur, particularly in children.
• Differential: Epididymitis/orchitis, torsion of testicular appendage, incarcerated hernia, trauma, tumor with hemorrhage/infarction.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess pain, onset, and associated symptoms immediately.
• Request urgent urological or surgical consultation.
• Keep patient NPO. Provide analgesia and antiemetics.
• Arrange urgent surgical exploration when torsion is strongly suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay surgery for ultrasound when clinical suspicion is high.[/color]
• Consider Doppler ultrasound when diagnosis is uncertain and imaging immediately available without delaying specialist assessment.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Clinical assessment is central.
• Urinalysis may help identify alternative diagnoses but does not exclude torsion.
• Doppler ultrasound can assess testicular perfusion in uncertain cases.
• Laboratory tests should not delay definitive management.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Select appropriate analgesia according to age, weight, pain severity, and hemodynamic status.
• Analgesia must NOT delay emergency surgical assessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Manual Detorsion[/color]
• May be attempted by trained clinician while arranging urgent surgery if immediate operative treatment not available.
• Continue to arrange emergency surgical exploration even if pain improves.
• [color=#991B1B]Manual detorsion may be incomplete/fail. Symptom relief does not prove perfusion restored. Not a substitute for definitive surgical management.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Emergency scrotal exploration.
• Detorsion and assessment of testicular viability.
• Orchidopexy when appropriate.
• Management of nonviable testis according to operative findings and specialist judgment.
• Fixation of contralateral testis commonly performed (risk of bilateral anatomical predisposition).

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate emergency surgical/urological management.
• Do NOT discharge a patient with unresolved suspicion of torsion.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology and Acute Scrotum; AUA Educational Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
