Acute urinary retention is the sudden inability to pass urine despite a full bladder. May cause severe pain and can be associated with obstruction, infection, renal impairment, or neurological disease.
• Causes: Benign prostatic enlargement, urethral stricture, medication effects (anticholinergics, sympathomimetics), constipation, prostatitis/UTI, blood clots obstructing outflow, neurological disorders (including spinal cord compression).
• Painful suprapubic distension. Inability to pass urine. Frequent small-volume voiding or overflow incontinence. Agitation/discomfort. Renal impairment in prolonged obstruction.

[color=#991B1B]Red Flags:[/color] Fever/hypotension/urosepsis, AKI, hematuria with clots, new leg weakness/saddle anesthesia/bowel dysfunction (cauda equina), suspected urethral injury after pelvic trauma.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCDE and identify sepsis or hemodynamic instability.
• Examine abdomen and assess bladder distension. Obtain bladder ultrasound/scanning when available.
• Establish IV access and obtain lab tests if systemically unwell or renal impairment suspected.
• Provide appropriate analgesia.
• Arrange urinary drainage when indicated and safe.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT attempt blind urethral catheterization when urethral injury is suspected.[/color]
• Request urgent urological assessment for difficult catheterization, suspected urethral injury, clot retention, or associated complications.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Bladder scan or bedside ultrasound.
• Urinalysis and urine culture when infection suspected.
• Creatinine, urea, and electrolytes.
• CBC and blood cultures in suspected sepsis.
• Renal ultrasound when hydronephrosis or upper urinary tract obstruction suspected.
• Additional neurological assessment and imaging if spinal cord/cauda equina pathology suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Bladder Decompression[/color]
• Urethral catheterization is commonly used when no suspicion of urethral injury and no contraindication. Use appropriate catheter size and aseptic technique.
• If catheterization difficult/unsuccessful, stop repeated traumatic attempts and seek specialist assistance.
• Record drained volume. Monitor urine output, pain relief, hematuria, renal function, electrolytes. Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis.
• [color=#991B1B]Blood at urethral meatus, pelvic trauma, perineal bruising, or suspected urethral disruption requires specialist evaluation before urethral catheterization. Do NOT force a catheter against resistance.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Alpha Blocker (When Appropriate)[/color]
• Selected adults with suspected BPO: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg orally once daily per local protocol.
• Review BP, dizziness, falls risk, concurrent antihypertensives.
• [color=#991B1B]Tamsulosin does NOT replace urgent bladder drainage. Not appropriate for every cause of urinary retention.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Antibiotics[/color]
• Do NOT prescribe antibiotics routinely for uncomplicated urinary retention without evidence of infection.
• If UTI/urosepsis suspected, choose antibiotic per severity, culture, renal function, local resistance.

sections.heading: 05 — COMPLICATIONS
sections.content:
• Post-obstructive diuresis.
• Hematuria.
• Acute kidney injury.
• Electrolyte disturbances.
• Urosepsis.
• Recurrent retention.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with renal impairment, sepsis, significant hematuria, major electrolyte disturbances, or neurological red flags.
• Arrange urgent specialist review when catheterization fails or a dangerous underlying cause suspected.
• Discharge only when drainage adequate, patient clinically stable, and clear catheter-care/follow-up plan arranged.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Guidelines on Non-neurogenic Male LUTS; NICE Guidance; EAU Urological Infections Guidance.

General Surgery - Acute Abdomen.title: Acute Gastric Dilatation and Gastric Ischemia

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute gastric dilatation is marked enlargement of the stomach due to retained gas, fluid, or food. Severe distension can impair gastric blood flow, cause necrosis or perforation, and compromise ventilation.
• Causes: Gastric outlet obstruction, postoperative ileus, severe eating disorders/binge eating, neurological impairment/critical illness, medications impairing GI motility, gastric volvulus/mechanical obstruction.
• Marked upper abdominal distension. Epigastric pain/pressure. Nausea/vomiting (may be absent if outlet obstructed). Respiratory distress from diaphragmatic elevation.
• Tachycardia, hypotension, shock in severe cases. Hematemesis, peritonitis, or severe persistent pain may indicate ischemia/perforation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment. Assess respiratory compromise, shock, peritonitis.
• Keep patient NPO. Establish IV access and obtain urgent surgical assessment.
• Insert NG tube for decompression when appropriate and safe.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT force NG tube insertion if gastric volvulus, esophageal injury, or another contraindication suspected.[/color]
• Correct fluid/electrolyte abnormalities. Arrange urgent imaging in stable patient.
• Escalate immediately if decompression fails or ischemia/perforation suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, lactate/blood gas (ischemia/shock), LFTs/lipase when indicated.
• Abdominal radiograph as initial assessment.
• CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast when appropriate to identify obstruction, volvulus, ischemia, or perforation.
• Endoscopy or contrast studies in selected patients after specialist assessment.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Gastric Decompression[/color]
• NG decompression commonly first intervention. Record volume/character of aspirated contents. Confirm tube position per policy.
• Monitor distension, pain, vomiting, respiratory status, fluid balance, electrolyte losses. Replace significant ongoing losses.
• [color=#991B1B]Failure to decompress, worsening pain, bloody aspirate, peritonitis, or hemodynamic instability requires urgent reassessment for ischemia, volvulus, or perforation.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluids[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid guided by volume status/response. Boluses for hypoperfusion, reassess frequently.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Antibiotics when Ischemia/Perforation Suspected[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics do NOT replace urgent operative source control.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Gastric ischemia or necrosis.
• Perforation or peritonitis.
• Gastric volvulus requiring intervention.
• Persistent mechanical obstruction.
• Failure of decompression with clinical deterioration.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for monitoring and treatment.
• ICU for shock, respiratory compromise, gastric necrosis, or major surgery.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidance; ACR Guidance; Local Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute ischemic colitis occurs when colonic blood flow becomes insufficient to meet tissue requirements. Often affects watershed areas (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid junction).
• Risk factors: Older age, atherosclerotic vascular disease, hypotension/shock/dehydration/blood loss, heart failure/arrhythmias, vasoconstrictor exposure, recent vascular/major abdominal surgery.
• Typical presentation: Sudden crampy abdominal pain. Urgent defecation followed by bloody diarrhea or hematochezia. Abdominal tenderness (usually without severe peritonitis in uncomplicated disease).

[color=#991B1B]Warning signs of advanced ischemia:[/color] Persistent severe pain, guarding, rebound tenderness, fever, metabolic acidosis, rising lactate, shock, perforation/pneumatosis/portal venous gas on imaging.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and hemodynamic stability.
• Keep patient NPO. Establish IV access and begin appropriate isotonic crystalloid resuscitation if hypovolemic.
• Obtain CBC, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation, blood gas, lactate.
• Perform urgent abdominal examination and involve surgery early if severe disease suspected.
• Obtain contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis when appropriate.
• Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for moderate/severe disease, systemic toxicity, or suspected transmural injury.
• Avoid vasoconstrictors where possible and correct precipitating cause of low perfusion.
• Arrange urgent operative assessment for peritonitis, perforation, gangrene, or deterioration.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, LFTs, coagulation, lactate.
• Blood gas when severe illness or metabolic acidosis suspected.
• Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis to assess colonic wall thickening, edema, pneumatosis, or complications.
• CT angiography if acute mesenteric arterial occlusion or another vascular cause suspected.
• Colonoscopy with cautious insufflation may help confirm diagnosis in selected stable patients (usually within 48 hours).
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid colonoscopy when peritonitis, perforation, or suspected gangrenous bowel makes procedure unsafe.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]IV Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid in reassessed boluses according to hemodynamics and fluid tolerance.
• Monitor BP, urine output, abdominal findings, renal function, lactate. Correct dehydration/hypotension while avoiding fluid overload.
• [color=#991B1B]Persistent pain or worsening acidosis despite resuscitation may indicate ongoing bowel ischemia requiring urgent surgical assessment.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics[/color]
• In moderate/severe ischemic colitis, use IV antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negative organisms and anaerobes per local protocols.
• One possible adult regimen: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 hours (adjust for renal function).
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics do NOT restore blood flow or replace surgery when transmural necrosis is present.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
Urgent surgery is indicated when there is:
• Generalized peritonitis.
• Perforation or gangrenous bowel.
• Persistent hemodynamic instability attributable to bowel injury.
• Clinical deterioration despite appropriate resuscitation/treatment.
• Strong evidence of transmural necrosis.

Surgical management may involve resection of nonviable colon, with anastomosis or stoma formation depending on stability, contamination, tissue viability.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with clinically significant ischemic colitis for monitoring and treatment.
• ICU care for shock, severe acidosis, or organ failure.
• Repeat abdominal examinations and laboratory assessment according to severity.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACG Clinical Guideline on Colon Ischemia; WSES Guidelines on Acute Mesenteric Ischemia.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute pancreatitis is acute inflammation of the pancreas. Common causes: gallstones, alcohol; others: hypertriglyceridemia, medications, metabolic/procedural.
• Severe epigastric pain radiating to back. Nausea, vomiting. Epigastric tenderness. Distension/ileus. Tachycardia, dehydration.
• Severe: hypoxemia, hypotension, AKI, shock.

[color=#991B1B]Features of severe disease:[/color] Persistent organ failure, hypotension/shock, hypoxemia/respiratory failure, oliguria/AKI, altered mental status, infected necrosis/complication.

sections.heading: 02 — DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA
sections.content:
Diagnosis requires at least 2 of 3:
• Characteristic abdominal pain.
• Serum lipase or amylase ≥ 3 times upper limit of normal.
• Characteristic imaging findings.
• Serum lipase generally preferred to amylase.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• ABCDE assessment. Identify shock, respiratory failure, organ dysfunction.
• Establish IV access and obtain labs.
• Give appropriately monitored isotonic crystalloid resuscitation.
• Provide adequate analgesia and antiemetics.
• Assess severity and arrange admission when indicated.
• Start oral feeding early as tolerated in mild disease (do not keep every patient NPO for prolonged periods).
• Investigate cause: gallstones, alcohol, hypertriglyceridemia.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT prescribe prophylactic antibiotics for uncomplicated acute pancreatitis or sterile pancreatic necrosis.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, lipase, LFTs/bilirubin, glucose, calcium, triglycerides, CRP, blood gas/lactate (severe illness).

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color]
• RUQ ultrasound: first-line for gallstones/biliary dilatation.
• CT abdomen with IV contrast: not routinely immediately when diagnosis clear and improving. Consider when diagnosis uncertain, deteriorating, or complications suspected. Contrast-enhanced CT more informative for necrosis after early phase.
• MRCP or EUS: when CBD stone suspected but not demonstrated on initial imaging.

sections.heading: 05 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Lactated Ringer's Solution[/color]
• Moderately aggressive, individualized fluid therapy.
• If hypovolemia: initial bolus ~10 mL/kg, then reassess. In patients without shock, lower initial rate may be appropriate; avoid routine large-volume resuscitation without frequent reassessment.
• Monitor BP, pulse, urine output, BUN, creatinine, hematocrit, oxygenation, signs of overload.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Analgesia: Fentanyl[/color]
• Adult: 25–50 mcg IV slowly, titrated to pain in monitored setting.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Antiemetic: Ondansetron[/color]
• Adult: 4 mg IV slowly or orally.

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Antibiotics[/color]
• Do NOT use prophylactic antibiotics in uncomplicated pancreatitis or sterile necrosis.
• When infection suspected: obtain cultures, assess for cholangitis/infected necrosis, select antibiotics per source/severity/local resistance. Antibiotics do not treat sterile inflammation.

sections.heading: 06 — NUTRITION & COMPLICATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Nutrition[/color]
• Mild: begin oral feeding early as tolerated (low-fat solid diet when tolerated; prolonged clear-liquid progression not essential).
• Unable to eat: enteral nutrition preferred over parenteral when feasible.

[color=#1E3A8A]Gallstone Pancreatitis[/color]
• Arrange biliary assessment. Urgent ERCP if cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction requiring intervention. Routine urgent ERCP not indicated without cholangitis/ongoing obstruction.
• Cholecystectomy during same admission generally recommended for mild gallstone pancreatitis when fit for surgery. Severe disease/collections may require delayed surgery.

[color=#1E3A8A]Infected Pancreatic Necrosis[/color]
• Suspect with clinical deterioration, sepsis, compatible imaging. Use antibiotics when infection suspected/established.
• Drainage/debridement may be required; delayed, step-up approach preferred when feasible. Immediate surgery not routinely required for every case of necrosis.

sections.heading: 07 — SURGICAL/INTERVENTIONAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Gallstone pancreatitis requiring definitive cholecystectomy.
• Cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction requiring ERCP/drainage.
• Infected necrosis requiring drainage/debridement.
• Complications requiring intervention (symptomatic/infected collections).
• Abdominal compartment syndrome or other life-threatening complication requiring specialist management.

sections.heading: 08 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for significant pain, vomiting, dehydration, systemic inflammation, or diagnostic uncertainty.
• ICU for persistent organ failure, shock, respiratory failure, or severe metabolic disturbance.
• Discharge after clinical improvement, adequate oral intake, controlled pain, and safe plan for underlying cause.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACG Clinical Guideline; AGA Guidance; Revised Atlanta Classification; WSES Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Acute Cholecystitis[/color]
• Inflammation of gallbladder, most commonly cystic duct obstruction by gallstone.
• Persistent RUQ pain, tenderness, positive Murphy's sign, fever, nausea, vomiting, leukocytosis.
• Complicated: Gangrene/perforation, pericholecystic abscess, emphysematous cholecystitis, generalized peritonitis/sepsis.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Acute Cholangitis[/color]
• Infection of biliary tree, usually with biliary obstruction. Can rapidly progress to sepsis/septic shock.
• RUQ pain, fever/chills, jaundice (Charcot's triad; absence does not exclude).
• Severe: hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria/AKI, respiratory failure, coagulopathy, organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• ABCDE assessment. Identify sepsis, shock, organ dysfunction.
• Keep NPO initially when urgent intervention likely.
• Establish IV access and obtain labs.
• Provide analgesia, antiemetics, fluids per clinical need.
• Request early surgical assessment for acute cholecystitis.
• Request urgent gastroenterology/endoscopy support for suspected cholangitis and biliary obstruction.
• Start IV antibiotics promptly when cholangitis, complicated cholecystitis, or sepsis suspected.
• In septic shock: initiate sepsis management and arrange urgent source control without waiting for all investigations.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, CRP, bilirubin, ALT/AST/ALP/GGT, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, lipase (gallstone pancreatitis), blood cultures (suspected cholangitis/severe infection), lactate/blood gas (shock/hypoperfusion), coagulation (severe illness/pre-intervention).

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color]
• RUQ ultrasound: first-line for acute cholecystitis (gallstones, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's, duct dilatation).
• MRCP or EUS: when CBD stone suspected and ultrasound inconclusive.
• CT abdomen: complications or alternative diagnoses.
• HIDA scan: when diagnosis uncertain after initial imaging and available.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. IV Fluids[/color]
• Adult hypoperfusion: initial 500 mL isotonic crystalloid bolus, then reassess. Further fluid per hemodynamics, losses, renal function, comorbidities.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Analgesia: Paracetamol[/color]
• Adult: 1 g IV or orally. Adjust for liver disease, low body weight, malnutrition, total daily exposure.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia: Fentanyl[/color]
• Adult: 25–50 mcg IV slowly, titrated in monitored setting.

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Antibiotics (Community-Acquired Biliary Infection)[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours (when additional anaerobic coverage indicated).
• Start promptly for suspected cholangitis or complicated cholecystitis.
• Narrow/adjust when microbiology and source-control status known.
• Severe cholangitis, healthcare-associated infection, septic shock, resistant organisms may require broader regimen. Antibiotics do not replace drainage of obstructed infected biliary system.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Acute Cholecystitis[/color]
• Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy preferred for most suitable patients. Perioperative antibiotics per severity/local guidance.
• If not fit for surgery and gallbladder remains uncontrolled source: consider gallbladder drainage and specialist review.

[color=#1E3A8A]Acute Cholangitis[/color]
• Resuscitation and antibiotics essential, but biliary decompression often decisive.
• ERCP generally preferred method of drainage when available/appropriate.
• If ERCP unavailable/unsuccessful: alternative drainage or surgical options per local expertise.
• Severe cholangitis with shock requires urgent drainage after initial resuscitation; do not delay source control unnecessarily.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL/INTERVENTIONAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Acute cholecystitis suitable for early cholecystectomy.
• Gallbladder gangrene, perforation, or abscess.
• Failure of conservative treatment.
• Acute cholangitis requiring biliary decompression.
• Persistent CBD obstruction or stones requiring intervention.
• Uncontrolled sepsis requiring source control.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit: confirmed acute cholecystitis requiring IV treatment/surgery, suspected cholangitis, persistent pain/vomiting/jaundice/systemic inflammation.
• ICU/high-dependency: septic shock, persistent hypotension, respiratory failure, AKI, other organ dysfunction.
• Discharge only selected stable patients after appropriate assessment and documented definitive treatment/follow-up plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Tokyo Guidelines; WSES Guidelines for Acute Calculous Cholecystitis; ASGE Guidance; ACG Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Gallbladder perforation is a complication of acute cholecystitis that can cause localized abscess, biliary peritonitis, or generalized sepsis.
• Risk factors: Delayed treatment of acute cholecystitis, older age, diabetes, immunosuppression, severe systemic illness, gangrenous cholecystitis.
• RUQ pain/tenderness. Fever and leukocytosis. Persistent/worsening pain despite treatment.
• Generalized abdominal tenderness/guarding. Hypotension, confusion, other signs of sepsis.
• Localized mass may suggest pericholecystic abscess.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment. Keep patient NPO.
• Obtain IV access and lab tests. Start appropriate IV fluids if hypovolemia/hypoperfusion.
• Request urgent general surgical assessment.
• Start IV antibiotics when complicated cholecystitis or sepsis suspected.
• Arrange urgent imaging without delaying surgery in patient with generalized peritonitis or instability.
• Assess for biliary obstruction and cholangitis.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, bilirubin/ALT/AST/ALP/GGT, CRP, lactate/blood gas in severe illness, blood cultures in sepsis.

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color] Ultrasound (initial test for gallbladder inflammation/gallstones). CT abdomen (perforation, abscess, gas, adjacent inflammatory changes). HIDA/MRCP in selected uncertain cases.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours.
• Broader (e.g., piperacillin–tazobactam) for severe infection, healthcare-associated infection, or selected high-risk patients.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics alone are insufficient when perforation or uncontrolled biliary contamination requires source control.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluids[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid according to perfusion/volume status, reassessing after each bolus.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia[/color]
• Appropriate titrated analgesic based on severity/contraindications/hemodynamic status.
• [color=#991B1B]Analgesia must NOT delay surgical source control.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Urgent cholecystectomy when appropriate and feasible.
• Percutaneous gallbladder drainage may be considered for selected high-risk patients who cannot safely undergo immediate surgery.
• Drainage of pericholecystic or intra-abdominal abscess when indicated.
• Bile duct evaluation and drainage if concomitant obstruction/cholangitis suspected.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Free perforation with biliary peritonitis.
• Gangrenous cholecystitis.
• Uncontrolled sepsis.
• Persistent infection despite appropriate treatment.
• Abscess or another complication requiring source control.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with suspected perforation or complicated cholecystitis.
• ICU care for shock or organ dysfunction.
• Reassess source control and antibiotic response frequently.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Tokyo Guidelines; WSES Guidelines for Acute Calculous Cholecystitis; Surgical Infection Society Guidance.

Hepatobiliary & Pancreatic.title: Infected Pancreatic Necrosis and Pancreatic Abscess

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute pancreatitis can cause pancreatic or peripancreatic necrosis. Infection of necrotic tissue may lead to sepsis, persistent organ failure, and death.
• Severe persistent epigastric pain (radiating to back). Nausea/vomiting. Fever/worsening systemic inflammatory response.
• Persistent organ dysfunction. Deterioration after initial improvement.
• Gas within pancreatic/peripancreatic collection on CT can suggest infection, although its absence does not exclude infection.
• Risk factors: Severe acute pancreatitis, extensive pancreatic necrosis, prolonged critical illness, delayed/inadequate management of complications.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCDE and identify shock or organ failure.
• Involve general surgery, gastroenterology, interventional radiology, and ICU teams early.
• Establish IV access and obtain lab tests. Provide goal-directed fluid therapy.
• Provide analgesia and nutritional support as appropriate.
• Evaluate for infected necrosis, other sources of infection, alternative causes of deterioration.
• Obtain blood cultures when sepsis suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT prescribe prophylactic antibiotics solely because sterile pancreatic necrosis is present.[/color]
• Plan drainage or debridement with specialist teams when indicated.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, LFTs, glucose/calcium, CRP, lactate/blood gas in severe illness, blood cultures if infection/sepsis suspected.
• Contrast-enhanced CT when clinically appropriate to define necrosis and collections. Interpret in relation to time course and clinical findings.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Antibiotics for Suspected/Confirmed Infected Necrosis[/color]
• Indicated when infected necrosis or another bacterial infection suspected/confirmed. Choose agents that penetrate pancreatic necrotic tissue and cover likely organisms per local guidance.
• Example: Piperacillin–tazobactam may be appropriate in selected patients.
• [color=#991B1B]Routine prophylactic antibiotics NOT recommended for sterile necrosis. Antibiotics do NOT replace drainage or debridement when source control required.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluid Therapy[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid with frequent reassessment. Avoid indiscriminate aggressive fluid loading (particularly after early resuscitation or with respiratory/cardiac/renal dysfunction).

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia and Nutritional Support[/color]
• Appropriate analgesia. Enteral nutrition generally preferred when oral intake not adequate. Use NG/NJ feeding when appropriate.
• Avoid unnecessary prolonged fasting when enteral feeding feasible and safe.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Step-Up Approach[/color]
• Initial antibiotics and supportive care when infection suspected.
• Endoscopic or percutaneous drainage when intervention required and anatomically feasible.
• Minimally invasive necrosectomy for patients who do not improve after drainage when indicated.
• Open surgery reserved for selected cases (failure of less invasive methods or other surgical emergencies).
• When stable, intervention often delayed until necrosis better organized (commonly ~4 weeks). Earlier intervention may be necessary in selected deteriorating patients.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL/INTERVENTIONAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Confirmed or strongly suspected infected necrosis with clinical deterioration.
• Persistent sepsis despite appropriate medical management.
• Symptomatic or enlarging collections causing obstruction or other complications.
• Abdominal compartment syndrome or another associated surgical emergency.
• Failure of a less invasive step-up strategy.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit severe or complicated cases to a specialist center.
• ICU care for persistent organ failure or shock.
• Multidisciplinary follow-up is essential.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ACG Guidelines on Acute Pancreatitis; AGA Guidance on Pancreatic Necrosis; WSES Guidelines on Severe Acute Pancreatitis.

Hepatobiliary & Pancreatic.title: Acute Liver Failure Requiring Emergency Transplant Evaluation

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute liver failure is a rapidly developing severe liver injury with impaired synthetic function and hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without established cirrhosis. Can cause cerebral edema, hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, renal failure, multiorgan dysfunction.
• Causes: Paracetamol toxicity, viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, autoimmune hepatitis, ischemic hepatitis, metabolic/toxin-related disorders, pregnancy-associated liver disease.
• Jaundice. Confusion/drowsiness/altered mental status. Hypoglycemia. Coagulopathy (elevated INR). Nausea/vomiting/RUQ discomfort. Renal dysfunction. Lactic acidosis/hemodynamic instability in severe disease.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment and check bedside glucose immediately.
• Contact hepatology and a liver-transplant center urgently when acute liver failure suspected.
• Establish IV access and obtain comprehensive lab investigations.
• Correct hypoglycemia promptly. Assess airway protection and encephalopathy severity.
• Identify and treat possible paracetamol toxicity without waiting for all confirmatory results when clinically indicated.
• Stop potentially hepatotoxic drugs and review recent medications/exposures.
• Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures (coagulopathy). Monitor for cerebral edema, renal failure, infection, shock.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay transfer to a specialist center while awaiting progression of encephalopathy or worsening INR.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, glucose, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, AST/ALT/bilirubin/ALP/albumin, PT/INR and fibrinogen, blood gas/lactate.
• Paracetamol level when relevant. Viral hepatitis studies. Autoimmune markers and other etiological investigations as indicated.
• Blood cultures if infection suspected. Ammonia may help in selected cases but should not replace clinical assessment.
• Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler to assess hepatic/portal vasculature when appropriate.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) for Suspected Paracetamol Toxicity[/color]
• Use validated IV NAC protocol, commonly three-infusion regimen delivering total 300 mg/kg over ~21 hours. Continue/extend according to paracetamol concentration, INR, liver tests, clinical status, specialist advice.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay NAC in clinically significant suspected paracetamol overdose while awaiting test results. Dosing protocols may differ by product/jurisdiction; use local validated protocol.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Dextrose for Hypoglycemia[/color]
• Treat per institutional adult hypoglycemia protocol and bedside glucose. Recheck promptly and provide ongoing support if recurrent.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid relying on a single corrected glucose measurement; recurrent hypoglycemia can occur in severe liver failure.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Vitamin K when Deficiency Possible[/color]
• Consider when deficiency or impaired absorption is plausible, as directed by treating team. Failure of INR to improve does not exclude severe hepatic synthetic failure.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT assume all coagulopathy in acute liver failure is caused by vitamin K deficiency.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]4. General Critical Care[/color]
• Maintain oxygenation/hemodynamic stability. Avoid hypoglycemia, treat electrolyte abnormalities. Assess RRT needs when indicated. Avoid sedatives/meds that obscure neuro assessment when possible. Manage suspected cerebral edema and severe encephalopathy with specialist ICU guidance.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT routinely correct INR with plasma solely to normalize lab value in absence of bleeding/planned invasive procedure; use specialist guidance.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Immediate specialist hepatology and transplant-center evaluation.
• Cause-specific therapy, including NAC where indicated.
• ICU monitoring for encephalopathy, cerebral edema risk, shock, renal failure, severe metabolic abnormalities.
• Liver transplantation assessment when spontaneous recovery is unlikely.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL/TRANSPLANT INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Fulminant hepatic failure with poor prognostic features.
• Progressive encephalopathy or worsening synthetic dysfunction.
• Severe metabolic instability or multiorgan failure.
• Fulfillment of specialist transplant criteria.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Acute liver failure requires urgent hospital admission and early discussion with a transplant-capable center.
• Do NOT manage established acute liver failure as a routine outpatient condition.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AASLD Guidance; EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines; ACMT Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute cholangitis is infection of biliary tree, usually associated with obstruction.
• Common causes: CBD stones, malignant obstruction, biliary strictures, obstructed biliary stents.
• Clinical features: Fever/chills. RUQ/epigastric pain. Jaundice. Hypotension/altered mental status in severe disease.
• [color=#991B1B]The classic Charcot triad is not always present. Severe cholangitis may cause septic shock, AKI, coagulopathy, multiorgan dysfunction.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and signs of septic shock. Obtain IV access and continuous monitoring.
• Send CBC, renal/liver function, bilirubin, coagulation, blood gas, lactate.
• Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when no delay to treatment.
• Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly.
• Begin appropriate fluid resuscitation and vasopressor support if required.
• Arrange urgent biliary decompression; severe cholangitis with shock requires emergency specialist intervention.
• Contact gastroenterology for ERCP; involve surgery/interventional radiology if ERCP unavailable/unsuccessful.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay drainage for complete diagnostic work-up in a patient with ongoing shock and confirmed/strongly suspected obstructed cholangitis.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, LFTs, bilirubin, coagulation, lactate.
• Blood cultures. Ultrasound for biliary dilation/gallstones.
• MRCP or CT in selected stable patients when diagnosis/cause unclear.
• ERCP may provide both diagnosis and definitive treatment.
• Assess for pancreatitis, hepatic abscess, other associated complications when indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Select therapy based on severity, prior biliary procedures, local resistance, allergies, renal function. One possible adult regimen for severe biliary infection: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 hours, adjusted per local guidance. Broader/alternative therapy may be needed for resistant organisms/healthcare-associated infection.
• Review blood cultures and bile cultures after drainage. Narrow treatment when microbiology/clinical response permit.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics alone are often inadequate when an obstructed biliary system remains infected.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]IV Crystalloid[/color]
• Reassessed boluses according to perfusion and fluid tolerance. In sepsis-induced hypoperfusion, initial target near 30 mL/kg within 3 hours may be considered, individualized for cardiac/renal function.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid unmonitored fluid loading in patients developing pulmonary edema/fluid intolerance.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Norepinephrine for Persistent Shock[/color]
• Start/titrate per local vasopressor protocol; typical initial range 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min. Common initial MAP target ~65 mmHg.
• Monitor BP continuously/very frequently. Inspect IV site and arrange central access when appropriate.
• [color=#991B1B]Vasopressors support circulation but do NOT replace urgent biliary drainage.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE BILIARY DRAINAGE
sections.content:
• ERCP usually preferred when available/technically feasible. Procedures may include sphincterotomy, stone extraction, biliary stent placement.
• If ERCP unavailable/unsuccessful: consider percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage or operative drainage according to anatomy, expertise, patient condition.
• Definitive gallstone management should be planned after stabilization.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Severe cholangitis or septic shock generally requires ICU-level care.
• Monitor for renal injury, coagulopathy, persistent obstruction, liver abscess, ongoing sepsis.
• Review cultures and antibiotic duration after successful source control.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Tokyo Guidelines 2018; ASGE Cholangitis Endoscopy Guideline; Surviving Sepsis Campaign.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (rAAA) is a life-threatening vascular emergency involving rupture of a dilated abdominal aorta with potentially massive internal hemorrhage.
• Sudden severe abdominal, back, flank, or groin pain. Syncope or collapse. Hypotension or shock.
• A pulsatile abdominal mass may be present but is not required for diagnosis.
• Older age, smoking, hypertension, known aneurysm increase suspicion.
• [color=#991B1B]The classic triad of abdominal pain, hypotension, and pulsatile mass is often incomplete.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate the emergency vascular surgery pathway immediately.
• Perform ABCDE assessment and establish large-bore IV access.
• Keep the patient NPO. Obtain blood samples and activate major hemorrhage protocol when indicated.
• Prioritize blood products and avoid excessive crystalloid administration.
• Use bedside aortic ultrasound if immediately available and it does not delay definitive care.
• Do NOT transport a profoundly unstable patient to CT when clinical picture strongly supports rupture and vascular team is ready to intervene.
• Prepare for emergency endovascular or open repair.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Bedside:[/color] Continuous ECG, SpO2, BP monitoring. Bedside aortic ultrasound (can identify aneurysm but cannot reliably exclude rupture). Focused ultrasound may identify free fluid.

[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, blood group & crossmatch, coagulation, electrolytes/renal function, blood gas/lactate, fibrinogen.

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color] CT angiography: appropriate for patients sufficiently stable for scanning when it will guide repair. Defines aneurysm anatomy and suitability for EVAR.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Blood Product Resuscitation[/color]
• Activate institutional major hemorrhage protocol for significant shock.
• Transfuse blood components according to clinical status, ongoing blood loss, and protocol rather than waiting for a specific Hb threshold.
• Monitor BP, perfusion, temperature, calcium, coagulation, fibrinogen, transfusion reactions. Use active warming.
• [color=#991B1B]Excessive crystalloid can worsen dilutional coagulopathy and tissue edema.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Permissive Hypotension (Selected Patients)[/color]
• In selected patients without TBI or another condition requiring higher perfusion pressure, a restricted resuscitation strategy may be used to avoid increasing hemorrhage before aortic control.
• Target determined by vascular and anesthesia teams.
• [color=#991B1B]Not appropriate for every patient. Significant coronary, cerebral, or other organ ischemia may alter the target.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia[/color]
• Carefully titrated IV analgesia according to hemodynamic condition and institutional emergency protocol.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Endovascular Aneurysm Repair (EVAR)[/color]
• Preferred when anatomy is suitable and an experienced team and equipment are immediately available. Requires rapid coordination among vascular surgery, anesthesia, imaging, and operating team.

[color=#1E3A8A]Open Repair[/color]
• Required when EVAR is unsuitable, unavailable, or cannot be delivered quickly enough.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate transfer to a vascular operating or endovascular suite.
• Postoperative ICU care usually required.
• Do NOT manage suspected rupture as an outpatient condition.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ESVS Guidelines on abdominal aorto-iliac aneurysms; SVS Practice Guidelines; NICE Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute limb ischemia (ALI) is a sudden reduction in limb perfusion that threatens tissue viability. Most commonly caused by arterial embolism or thrombosis.
• Causes: Cardiac embolism (AF), acute thrombosis of atherosclerotic artery, thrombosis of stent/graft, arterial trauma/dissection, hypercoagulable states.
• The six Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia (cold limb).
• Threatened limb features: Sensory loss (especially beyond toes/fingers), new muscle weakness/paralysis, absent arterial Doppler signals, severe pain with cold pale limb.
• [color=#991B1B]Motor weakness indicates an immediately threatened limb and requires emergency revascularization assessment.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment and identify shock or associated trauma.
• Obtain immediate vascular surgical consultation.
• Document time of onset, pain, sensory function, motor function, temperature, capillary refill, and Doppler signals.
• Establish IV access and provide appropriate analgesia.
• Start IV unfractionated heparin promptly when ALI is suspected unless contraindicated, per protocol.
• Obtain urgent vascular imaging when it will guide treatment without delaying revascularization.
• Keep patient NPO when intervention likely.
• Do NOT apply compression, elevate limb excessively, or expose to direct heat.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC and platelets, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, coagulation profile, group & crossmatch (if intervention likely), CK/potassium/renal function (if muscle ischemia or reperfusion injury suspected), lactate/blood gas (severe ischemia).

[color=#1E3A8A]Vascular Assessment:[/color] Handheld arterial and venous Doppler signals. Duplex ultrasound when immediately available. CT angiography for anatomical planning in suitable patients. Catheter angiography in selected patients undergoing endovascular intervention.

[color=#991B1B]Imaging must NOT delay revascularization when the limb is immediately threatened.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. IV Unfractionated Heparin[/color]
• Commonly used initial regimen: IV bolus of 70–80 units/kg, followed by infusion of approximately 15–18 units/kg/hour. Use institution's therapeutic anticoagulation protocol; some patients require modified dosing.
• Monitor aPTT or anti-Xa per protocol. Check platelet count and assess for bleeding.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid or modify anticoagulation when there is active major bleeding or another contraindication.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Analgesia[/color]
• Titrated analgesia appropriate to pain severity and hemodynamic status.
• Pain relief must NOT delay vascular assessment or revascularization.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Reperfusion and Metabolic Management[/color]
• Prepare for urgent revascularization. Monitor potassium, acid-base status, renal function, and CK in patients with significant ischemia.
• [color=#991B1B]Reperfusion can cause hyperkalemia, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, renal injury, and compartment syndrome.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
Depending on anatomy, limb viability, and local expertise:
• Surgical embolectomy or thrombectomy.
• Endovascular thrombectomy or thrombolysis in selected patients.
• Angioplasty or stenting.
• Bypass surgery.
• Amputation when the limb is irreversibly ischemic and nonviable.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate vascular surgical admission.
• ICU or high-dependency care for severe ischemia, reperfusion injury, major intervention, or organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ESVS Clinical Practice Guidelines on Acute Limb Ischaemia; ACC/AHA PAD Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Mesenteric venous thrombosis causes impaired venous drainage, bowel wall edema, congestion, and potentially intestinal infarction.
• Risk factors: Inherited/acquired thrombophilia, malignancy, cirrhosis/portal hypertension, pancreatitis/intra-abdominal inflammation, recent abdominal surgery, estrogen exposure, prior VTE.
• Presentation: Abdominal pain (initially exceeds physical exam findings). Nausea/vomiting/diarrhea. GI bleeding in advanced disease. Abdominal distension, peritonitis, or shock when bowel infarction develops.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess hemodynamic stability and signs of bowel ischemia.
• Keep patient NPO. Establish IV access and correct dehydration/shock.
• Obtain CBC, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation, blood gas, lactate.
• Request urgent contrast-enhanced CT with mesenteric venous phase or CT angiography as appropriate.
• Involve general surgery and vascular/interventional specialists early.
• Start therapeutic anticoagulation promptly when diagnosis established and no contraindication, under treating team's direction.
• Start broad-spectrum antibiotics if bowel infarction, perforation, or systemic infection suspected.
• Arrange urgent surgery for peritonitis or suspected necrotic bowel.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, coagulation, lactate.
• Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrating thrombus in superior mesenteric vein or tributaries, bowel edema, mesenteric congestion, or associated portal venous thrombosis.
• Assess for bowel hypoenhancement, pneumatosis, portal venous gas, free air.
• Thrombophilia evaluation may be considered after stabilization.
• [color=#991B1B]A normal lactate does NOT exclude early intestinal ischemia.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Unfractionated Heparin[/color]
• Common therapeutic IV regimen in adults: initial bolus 80 units/kg followed by 18 units/kg/hour, adjusted using institutional aPTT or anti-Xa protocol. Bolus dosing may need modification/omission when bleeding risk high or urgent surgery anticipated.
• Monitor aPTT/anti-Xa per local protocol, platelet count, hemoglobin, signs of bleeding.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT start anticoagulation without assessing active bleeding and contraindications. Suspected HIT requires alternative anticoagulant and specialist management.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]IV Fluids and Supportive Care[/color]
• Reassessed isotonic crystalloid boluses according to perfusion and fluid tolerance. Monitor hemodynamics, urine output, lactate, renal function, serial abdominal findings.
• [color=#991B1B]Resuscitation must NOT delay surgery when bowel necrosis or perforation suspected.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics when Bowel Injury Suspected[/color]
• Broad-spectrum IV coverage for enteric Gram-negative organisms and anaerobes per local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics are NOT routinely a substitute for anticoagulation in uncomplicated venous thrombosis.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL/INTERVENTIONAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Anticoagulation is first-line treatment in many patients without peritonitis or established bowel necrosis.
• Urgent laparotomy indicated for peritonitis, perforation, or suspected infarcted bowel.
• Resect clearly nonviable intestine while preserving viable bowel where possible.
• Endovascular treatment may be considered in selected patients who deteriorate despite anticoagulation but have no indication for immediate laparotomy.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for monitored treatment and serial abdominal examinations.
• ICU care for shock, severe bowel ischemia, or organ dysfunction.
• Determine duration/long-term choice of anticoagulation according to cause, bleeding risk, specialist advice.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Acute Mesenteric Ischemia Guidelines; ESVS Mesenteric Arterial/Venous Disease Guidelines; ASH VTE Guidance.

Trauma Surgery.title: Abdominal Trauma and Solid Organ Injury

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Abdominal trauma may cause injury to liver, spleen, kidneys, pancreas, bowel, mesentery, major vessels, and pelvic organs. Injuries may be blunt or penetrating. Internal hemorrhage and hollow-viscus injury can be initially occult.
• Mechanisms: RTCs, falls, blunt impact/crush, stab/firearm, high-energy trauma.
• Abdominal pain, tenderness, distension. Bruising, seat-belt marks, penetrating wounds.
• Hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, altered mental status. Hematuria. Peritonitis or signs of ongoing hemorrhage.
• [color=#991B1B]A normal initial abdominal examination or hemoglobin does not exclude serious injury.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow the trauma ABCDE approach. Control external hemorrhage; protect airway.
• Activate trauma team and major hemorrhage protocol for suspected severe bleeding.
• Establish large-bore IV access or IO access if necessary. Obtain blood samples including type & crossmatch.
• Use bedside eFAST in appropriate trauma patients.
• Perform urgent operative evaluation in hemodynamically unstable patients with suspected intra-abdominal hemorrhage.
• Give tranexamic acid when indicated by major trauma protocol and within recommended time window.
• Prevent hypothermia and correct coagulopathy. Reassess repeatedly.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, blood group & crossmatch, blood gas/lactate, coagulation/fibrinogen, electrolytes/renal function/glucose, urinalysis, pregnancy testing when applicable.

[color=#1E3A8A]eFAST:[/color] Helps identify free intraperitoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, selected thoracic findings. Negative does not exclude bowel, mesenteric, retroperitoneal, or solid-organ injury.

[color=#1E3A8A]CT Abdomen/Pelvis with IV Contrast:[/color] Preferred in hemodynamically stable patients with significant blunt abdominal trauma. Do NOT delay laparotomy for CT in an unstable patient with a clear indication for operative hemorrhage control.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Hemorrhage Resuscitation[/color]
• Use blood products and major hemorrhage protocol when significant ongoing bleeding or hemorrhagic shock suspected.
• Avoid relying on large volumes of crystalloid as sole resuscitation strategy.
• Prevent hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy. Definitive hemorrhage control must occur promptly.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Tranexamic Acid (TXA)[/color]
• For eligible adults with significant traumatic hemorrhage: 1 g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1 g IV over 8 hours.
• Administer as early as possible and within 3 hours of injury.
• [color=#991B1B]Do not administer routinely to every trauma patient. Do not initiate beyond recommended window unless specialist protocol indicates.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia[/color]
• Titrated analgesia according to injury severity and hemodynamic stability.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Nonoperative Management[/color]
• Selected hemodynamically stable patients with solid-organ injuries when: no peritonitis, appropriate monitoring/serial examination available, blood products/IR/emergency surgery accessible if deterioration occurs.

[color=#1E3A8A]Angioembolization[/color]
• May be appropriate for selected solid-organ injuries with active bleeding or vascular injury, particularly in stable patients or selected responders.

[color=#1E3A8A]Operative Management[/color]
• Emergency laparotomy for hemodynamic instability with suspected intra-abdominal bleeding, peritonitis, bowel perforation, or uncontrolled hemorrhage.
• Damage-control surgery may be necessary in profoundly deranged patients.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Hemodynamic instability due to suspected intra-abdominal hemorrhage.
• Generalized peritonitis.
• Suspected hollow-viscus perforation.
• Uncontrolled bleeding not amenable to other definitive methods.
• Clinical deterioration during nonoperative management.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with significant solid-organ injury for appropriate monitoring.
• ICU care for shock, major transfusion, severe associated injuries, or organ dysfunction.
• Discharge only when injury-specific criteria are met and follow-up instructions are clear.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS; WSES Guidelines on blunt/penetrating abdominal trauma; EAST Practice Management Guidelines; NICE Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Penetrating abdominal trauma occurs when an object breaches the abdominal wall, potentially injuring bowel, solid organs, mesentery, major vessels, diaphragm, or retroperitoneal structures.
• Mechanisms: Stab wounds, firearm injuries, impalement, penetrating fragments.
• Abdominal wound with or without visible tissue protrusion. Abdominal pain, tenderness, distension.
• External hemorrhage. Hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, altered mental status.
• Evisceration, peritonitis, or signs of shock.

[color=#991B1B]Red Flags:[/color] Hemodynamic instability, generalized peritonitis, evisceration, impalement with object in place, active hemorrhage, suspected major vascular/hollow-viscus injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate trauma team and perform ABCDE assessment.
• Control external bleeding with direct pressure when appropriate.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT remove an impaled object in the ED; stabilize it and arrange controlled removal.[/color]
• Cover eviscerated abdominal contents with sterile saline-moistened dressings and a protective covering. Do NOT push organs back into the abdomen.
• Keep patient NPO. Establish large-bore IV/IO access. Obtain blood samples and activate major hemorrhage protocol if indicated.
• Prevent hypothermia. Request immediate surgical assessment.
• Administer antibiotics when bowel injury or operative contamination is suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, blood group & crossmatch, blood gas/lactate, coagulation/fibrinogen, electrolytes/renal function, urinalysis.

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color]
• eFAST: useful for rapidly assessing free fluid in selected trauma patients. Negative result does not exclude significant abdominal injury.
• CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast: appropriate for selected hemodynamically stable patients. Helps define trajectory and identify organ, vascular, or bowel injury.
• [color=#991B1B]Imaging must NOT delay laparotomy in an unstable patient with peritonitis or clear evidence of uncontrolled intra-abdominal hemorrhage.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Blood Product Resuscitation[/color]
• Activate local major hemorrhage protocol for significant bleeding or hemorrhagic shock. Use blood components according to clinical status and institutional protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Tranexamic Acid[/color]
• For eligible adults with significant traumatic hemorrhage: 1 g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1 g IV over 8 hours. Administer as early as possible and within 3 hours of injury.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Antibiotics for Suspected Hollow-Viscus Injury[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours.
• Severe contamination, shock, or healthcare-associated infection may require broader coverage.

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
Immediate operative management generally indicated for:
• Hemodynamic instability attributable to abdominal hemorrhage.
• Generalized peritonitis.
• Evisceration with other indications for exploration.
• Uncontrolled bleeding.
• Clear evidence of major hollow-viscus or vascular injury.

Selected stable patients without peritonitis may undergo CT-guided evaluation and selective nonoperative management under experienced trauma surgical supervision.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with suspected significant intra-abdominal injury.
• ICU care for shock, major transfusion, or organ dysfunction.
• Discharge only after an appropriate observation or evaluation pathway establishes that significant injury is unlikely.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS; EAST Guidelines for penetrating abdominal trauma; WSES Guidelines on blunt/penetrating bowel injury.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Chest trauma may cause life-threatening injury to lungs, pleura, heart, great vessels, and chest wall.
A tension pneumothorax occurs when air accumulates under pressure in the pleural space, impairing ventilation and venous return and causing obstructive shock.
• Mechanisms: Blunt chest trauma, penetrating injuries, rib fractures, high-energy RTCs, positive-pressure ventilation in a patient with pneumothorax.
• Chest pain and dyspnea. Tachypnea, hypoxemia, respiratory distress. Reduced/absent breath sounds on affected side. Asymmetric chest movement.
• Hypotension and tachycardia in tension pneumothorax.
• Tracheal deviation may occur late and is not required for diagnosis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment. Administer oxygen for hypoxemia/respiratory distress.
• Expose and inspect chest while preventing hypothermia.
• [color=#991B1B]If tension pneumothorax is clinically suspected in an unstable patient, decompress immediately; do NOT wait for imaging.[/color]
• Arrange definitive pleural drainage after emergency decompression.
• Request urgent trauma and thoracic surgical assessment for major chest injury.
• Evaluate for associated hemothorax, cardiac tamponade, flail chest, and great-vessel injury.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Bedside:[/color] Continuous SpO2 and ECG monitoring. eFAST or lung ultrasound when available. Chest radiograph in stable patients when appropriate.

[color=#1E3A8A]CT Chest:[/color] Consider in stable patients with significant trauma, suspected occult pneumothorax, vascular injury, or complex chest-wall injury.

[color=#991B1B]In a clinically unstable patient with suspected tension pneumothorax, imaging must NOT delay decompression.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Emergency Decompression of Tension Pneumothorax[/color]
• Indication: Suspected tension pneumothorax causing respiratory or hemodynamic compromise.
• Perform immediate decompression using an accepted institutional technique (finger thoracostomy by trained clinician or needle decompression when appropriate).
• In adults, 4th or 5th intercostal space in anterior-to-midaxillary region is commonly used for decompression.
• Follow emergency decompression with definitive tube thoracostomy when indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]This is a lifesaving invasive procedure requiring appropriate training.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Tube Thoracostomy[/color]
• Indications: Significant traumatic pneumothorax, hemothorax, persistent air leak.
• Insert appropriately sized chest drain using institution's trauma procedure. Connect to designated drainage system and verify function.
• [color=#991B1B]Do not clamp a chest drain routinely in a patient with an active air leak.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — ADDITIONAL CHEST TRAUMA MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Open Pneumothorax[/color]
• Apply an appropriate vented chest seal or locally recommended dressing. Monitor for evolving tension physiology. Arrange definitive chest drainage away from the wound.

[color=#1E3A8A]Flail Chest[/color]
• Provide adequate analgesia, oxygen, respiratory monitoring. Escalate ventilatory support for respiratory failure. Consider regional analgesia and specialist assessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Massive Hemothorax[/color]
• Initiate blood product resuscitation and urgent chest drainage. Obtain immediate surgical evaluation for ongoing major intrathoracic bleeding.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients requiring chest drainage or significant respiratory support.
• ICU care for respiratory failure, shock, major chest trauma, or associated organ injury.
• Transfer to trauma center when major thoracic or vascular expertise is unavailable.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS; EAST Guidelines on traumatic hemothorax/pneumothorax; WSES–AAST Thoracic Trauma Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
An open fracture is a fracture associated with a wound that communicates with the fracture or fracture hematoma. Carries risks of contamination, infection, neurovascular injury, and compartment syndrome.
• Open wound near suspected fracture. Visible bone or deep tissue injury. Deformity, swelling, or bleeding.
• Reduced distal pulses or abnormal capillary refill. Sensory loss, weakness, or severe pain. Contamination with soil, water, or foreign material.

[color=#991B1B]Limb-Threatening Features:[/color] Absent distal pulse or acute ischemia, uncontrolled hemorrhage, progressive neurologic deficit, compartment syndrome, extensive soft-tissue destruction.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment and control life-threatening hemorrhage.
• Document mechanism, time of injury, contamination, and neurovascular status.
• Cover wound with sterile dressing. Do NOT repeatedly probe the wound or perform unnecessary bedside exploration.
• Give IV antibiotics as early as possible. Check tetanus immunization status and provide prophylaxis when indicated.
• Immobilize the limb in an appropriate splint. Reassess and document distal pulses, sensation, movement, capillary refill after splinting.
• Request urgent orthopedic and vascular assessment for severe injuries. Arrange urgent operative debridement when indicated.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Plain radiographs including the joint above and below the injury when appropriate.
• CBC and metabolic studies in significant trauma. Group & crossmatch for major bleeding or likely surgery.
• CT angiography when vascular injury suspected and patient stable enough for imaging.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay urgent revascularization or hemorrhage control for imaging when a limb is critically ischemic or the patient is unstable.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Antibiotics[/color]
• Selected adult open fractures: cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g if ≥120 kg per local prophylaxis protocol).
• Additional coverage for severe contamination, high-grade injury, or special exposures per current institutional open-fracture protocol.
• Administer as soon as possible after recognizing open fracture. [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay antibiotics while awaiting radiographs.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Analgesia[/color]
• Titrated IV analgesia according to injury severity and hemodynamic status.
• [color=#991B1B]Severe escalating pain may indicate compartment syndrome and requires urgent reassessment rather than analgesia alone.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Tetanus Prophylaxis[/color]
• Administer tetanus-containing vaccine and, when indicated, tetanus immune globulin according to immunization history and national guidance.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Urgent orthopedic evaluation.
• Operative irrigation and debridement according to injury severity and local guidance.
• Fracture stabilization. Vascular repair or revascularization when required.
• Soft-tissue coverage and reconstruction planning.
• Repeated neurovascular assessment and surveillance for compartment syndrome.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Open fracture requiring operative debridement.
• Vascular compromise or uncontrolled hemorrhage.
• Compartment syndrome.
• Severe contamination, tissue loss, or associated injury requiring specialist intervention.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with significant open fractures.
• Urgent transfer to appropriate trauma center if orthopedic, vascular, or reconstructive expertise unavailable.
• ICU care for major polytrauma, shock, or associated organ failure.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS; BOAST Open Fractures; NICE Guidance on Complex Fractures.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute compartment syndrome occurs when pressure rises within a closed fascial compartment, reducing tissue perfusion and potentially causing irreversible muscle and nerve injury. It is a surgical emergency.
• Causes: Fractures (tibial shaft/forearm), crush injury, reperfusion after prolonged ischemia, tight casts/dressings/external compression, vascular injury, severe burns, bleeding into compartment.
• Severe pain disproportionate to apparent injury. Pain aggravated by passive stretch of affected muscles.
• Increasing swelling or tense compartments. Paresthesia or altered sensation. Weakness or paralysis in advanced disease.
• [color=#991B1B]Normal distal pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome. Pulselessness and paralysis are late findings.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Recognize possibility early and call surgical team immediately.
• Remove or loosen constrictive dressings and casts while maintaining appropriate stabilization.
• Keep limb at heart level rather than markedly elevated above the heart.
• Provide appropriate analgesia without allowing pain relief to delay reassessment.
• Document pain, passive-stretch response, sensation, movement, distal perfusion.
• Obtain urgent surgical assessment for possible fasciotomy.
• Measure compartment pressures when diagnosis uncertain or examination unreliable, provided this does not delay necessary surgery.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Clinical Examination[/color]
• Repeated assessment is essential. Document findings and progression.

[color=#1E3A8A]Compartment Pressure Measurement[/color]
• Consider when examination equivocal, patient unconscious, or reliable assessment impossible. Interpret pressure together with clinical findings.
• Commonly used supportive criterion: differential pressure (diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) ≤ 30 mmHg.

[color=#1E3A8A]Additional Investigations[/color]
• CK, renal function, electrolytes, urinalysis when muscle injury/rhabdomyolysis suspected.
• Imaging may identify associated fractures or vascular injuries but does not diagnose/exclude compartment syndrome reliably.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Immediate Pressure Relief[/color]
• Remove external compression immediately. Maintain limb alignment and reassess perfusion.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay surgical review while waiting for laboratory results or imaging. A normal pulse or temporary improvement in pain does not exclude the diagnosis.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluids when Rhabdomyolysis is Present[/color]
• Give isotonic crystalloid according to perfusion, urine output, renal function, severity of muscle injury.
• Monitor urine output, electrolytes, creatinine, CK, fluid balance.
• [color=#991B1B]Fluid therapy does not replace fasciotomy when compartment syndrome is established.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia[/color]
• Use appropriately titrated analgesia while urgent assessment proceeds.
• [color=#991B1B]Do not attribute escalating pain solely to fracture pain without reassessing for compartment syndrome.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Emergency Fasciotomy[/color]
• Indicated when acute compartment syndrome is diagnosed or strongly suspected.
• All affected compartments must be adequately decompressed.
• Wounds often left open initially and managed with planned reassessment, delayed closure, or skin grafting as appropriate.
• Treat underlying fracture, vascular injury, or cause of bleeding.

sections.heading: 06 — COMPLICATIONS
sections.content:
• Muscle necrosis.
• Permanent nerve injury.
• Contractures.
• Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury.
• Infection and limb loss.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate surgical admission.
• Postoperative monitoring for recurrent compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, renal injury, wound complications.
• ICU care when severe muscle injury, shock, or organ dysfunction present.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline on acute compartment syndrome; BOA Guidance; NICE Guidance.

Trauma Surgery.title: Complex Soft-Tissue Defects and Extensive Skin Loss

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Extensive skin and soft-tissue loss may follow trauma, burns, infection, degloving injury, surgical complications, or tissue necrosis.
• Assess: Defect size, depth, contamination. Exposure of bone, tendon, vessels, nerves, implants. Distal circulation, sensation, motor function. Associated fractures/vascular injury. Evidence of infection/ongoing tissue necrosis.
• Major defects may require staged debridement, temporary wound coverage, skin grafting, or flap reconstruction.
• Exposed critical structures often cannot be managed by simple dressings or skin grafting alone.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Control life-threatening hemorrhage.
• Assess ABCs and associated injuries.
• Examine and document distal neurovascular status before and after any intervention.
• Cover wound with sterile, nonadherent dressing; use saline-moistened dressings when appropriate for exposed viable tissue.
• Prevent hypothermia and treat shock.
• Provide analgesia and assess tetanus immunization status.
• Administer antibiotics for contaminated open injuries or established infection per local guidelines.
• Arrange urgent surgical assessment for exposed vessels, nerves, tendons, bone, implants, or extensive tissue loss.
• Coordinate with plastic surgery, orthopedics, vascular surgery, or other specialties according to injured structures.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, glucose, coagulation when clinically indicated.
• Group-and-crossmatch for major bleeding or extensive operative injury.
• Plain radiographs for suspected fractures or retained foreign bodies.
• CT or CT angiography when deep injury or vascular compromise suspected and imaging will not delay necessary treatment.
• Wound cultures when infection present; routine superficial swabs of clean wounds may be unhelpful.
• Serial neurovascular examinations and documentation of wound progression.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Hemorrhage Control[/color]
• Apply firm direct pressure for external bleeding. Use hemostatic dressings or a tourniquet when indicated and available (for life-threatening extremity hemorrhage when direct pressure ineffective/impractical, following training and local protocols).
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT blindly clamp vessels in a deep wound; adjacent nerves and vessels may be damaged.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics for Contaminated/Infected Wounds[/color]
• Select antibiotics according to mechanism, contamination, anatomical site, allergy, local protocol.
• For major open fractures, follow dedicated open-fracture protocol, including timely antibiotic administration and operative debridement.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics do NOT replace irrigation, removal of devitalized tissue, or surgical source control. Routine prolonged antibiotics NOT indicated for every clean soft-tissue defect.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Wound Coverage and Temporary Management[/color]
• Use sterile dressing, appropriate wound-contact layer, temporary coverage system selected by treating surgical team.
• Keep exposed structures protected and avoid desiccation of viable tissue.
• Negative-pressure wound therapy may be appropriate in selected wounds after adequate debridement and hemostasis.
• [color=#991B1B]Negative-pressure therapy is not a substitute for debridement and is unsuitable in some wounds, including certain wounds with exposed major vessels or uncontrolled bleeding.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Perform timely irrigation and debridement of contaminated or devitalized tissue.
• Reassess tissue viability when injury zone is evolving.
• Restore blood flow when vascular injury present.
• Stabilize associated fractures and protect injured tendons, nerves, vessels.
• Choose definitive coverage according to wound bed and exposed structures:
  - Secondary healing for selected small wounds.
  - Skin grafting for suitable vascularized wound beds.
  - Local or free-flap reconstruction when critical structures exposed or durable tissue coverage needed.
• Plan reconstruction with relevant surgical specialties.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit extensive, contaminated, infected, or complex defects requiring operative treatment.
• Transfer to center with reconstructive expertise when local capability insufficient.
• Arrange follow-up for wound assessment, infection surveillance, rehabilitation, functional recovery.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS; WHO Global Guidelines for Prevention of SSI; Specialist Guidelines for Open Fractures/Complex Wounds.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Hemothorax is blood accumulation in pleural cavity, usually following blunt/penetrating chest trauma. Massive hemothorax can cause hemorrhagic shock and respiratory compromise.
• Suspect in trauma patient with: Hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, altered mental status. Respiratory distress, reduced breath sounds on one side. Dullness to percussion on affected side. Chest wall injury/penetrating trauma.
• Common sources: Intercostal vessels, lung parenchyma, internal mammary vessels, major intrathoracic vessels.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow trauma resuscitation principles; assess ABCs.
• Administer oxygen and support ventilation when required.
• Activate major hemorrhage/massive transfusion protocol when indicated.
• Establish large-bore IV or IO access.
• Begin blood-product resuscitation for major hemorrhage; avoid excessive crystalloid.
• Perform bedside eFAST or chest radiography if no delay to treatment.
• Insert appropriate chest drain when indicated by trained personnel.
• Obtain immediate thoracic/trauma surgical consultation.
• Consider emergency thoracotomy in selected patients with traumatic arrest or profound instability per local protocols.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Bedside eFAST for pleural fluid and associated pericardial/abdominal injury.
• Portable chest radiograph when appropriate.
• CBC, blood gas, lactate, coagulation, fibrinogen, electrolytes, group-and-crossmatch.
• CT chest in sufficiently stable patients to identify vascular/associated injuries.
• Monitor chest-drain output and hemodynamic response.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay drainage or operative hemorrhage control for CT in unstable patient.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Blood-Product Resuscitation[/color]
• Use institutional major hemorrhage protocol for life-threatening bleeding. Balanced component therapy or whole blood may be used per local availability/protocol. Transition to lab/viscoelastic-guided resuscitation as soon as feasible.
• Monitor BP, temperature, Hb, lactate, coagulation, fibrinogen, calcium, ongoing blood loss. Replace calcium when clinically indicated. Prevent hypothermia and correct coagulopathy.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay life-saving blood products in uncontrolled hemorrhagic shock while waiting for Hb result. Avoid relying on large crystalloid volumes in major hemorrhage.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Chest Tube Drainage[/color]
• Prepare sterile chest-drain equipment and appropriate monitoring. Select drain size according to injury, clot burden, local trauma protocol.
• Insert using appropriate technique and confirm effective drainage. Record immediate and ongoing output.
• [color=#991B1B]A chest tube may reveal severity of bleeding but does NOT itself control major vascular injury. Do NOT clamp a chest drain routinely in an actively bleeding patient unless specifically directed.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
Immediate operative assessment required for hemodynamic instability or suspected major intrathoracic bleeding.
Common triggers for considering thoracotomy:
• Initial chest-tube output around 1,500 mL in an adult.
• Ongoing drainage around 200 mL/hour for several hours.
• Persistent shock or transfusion requirement despite drainage.
• Suspected major vascular or cardiac injury.
*(These are guideposts, not absolute thresholds; physiology, bleeding rate, mechanism, local protocols determine urgency).*

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit significant hemothorax for monitored care.
• ICU care required for persistent shock, respiratory failure, major transfusion, or operative management.
• Reassess for retained hemothorax, empyema, persistent air leak, delayed bleeding.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS; EAST Practice Management Guidelines on Hemothorax/Occult Pneumothorax; Western Trauma Association Critical Decisions.

Trauma Surgery.title: Flail Chest and Severe Chest Wall Injury

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Flail chest typically results from multiple adjacent ribs fractured in at least two places, producing a free-floating segment of chest wall.
• Paradoxical movement may be visible, but absence does NOT exclude flail chest.
• Respiratory failure often reflects underlying pulmonary contusion, pain-related hypoventilation, and associated injuries rather than chest-wall instability alone.
