• Look for: Severe chest pain/shallow breathing. Tachypnea, hypoxemia, respiratory fatigue. Reduced breath sounds or associated pneumothorax. Subcutaneous emphysema. Shock suggesting associated bleeding/another major injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow trauma ABCDE approach.
• Administer oxygen and monitor SpO2, ECG, BP.
• Assess for tension pneumothorax or massive hemothorax and treat immediately when suspected.
• Provide effective multimodal analgesia.
• Assess for pulmonary contusion, aspiration, associated abdominal/spinal injuries.
• Obtain chest imaging after immediate life-threatening conditions addressed.
• Use noninvasive or invasive ventilatory support when clinically indicated.
• Involve trauma, thoracic surgery, critical care early for severe injury.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Chest radiograph for initial assessment.
• CT chest in stable patients when defining fracture patterns/associated injuries will alter management.
• Blood gas in respiratory failure/significant hypoxemia.
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, lactate according to injury severity.
• Continuous oxygenation monitoring and repeated respiratory assessment.
• Evaluate for pneumothorax, hemothorax, pulmonary contusion, blunt cardiac injury.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Multimodal Analgesia[/color]
• Patient-specific regimen; options may include paracetamol and carefully titrated opioid analgesia. NSAIDs may be considered when renal function/bleeding risk permit. Regional techniques may be appropriate for selected patients.
• Reassess pain, cough effectiveness, RR, sedation, ability to mobilize. Consider epidural, paravertebral, or fascial-plane blocks per expertise/contraindications.
• [color=#991B1B]Excessive opioid sedation can worsen hypoventilation. Regional anesthesia requires assessment of anticoagulation, hemodynamic status, procedural risks.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Oxygen and Ventilatory Support[/color]
• Titrate oxygen to appropriate target; aim for adequate oxygenation while avoiding unnecessary hyperoxia. Provide positive-pressure support when indicated by respiratory distress/gas-exchange failure.
• Monitor oxygenation, work of breathing, mental status, blood gases, fatigue. Consider NIV only in suitable, cooperative patients without contraindications and with close monitoring.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay intubation in progressive respiratory failure, exhaustion, or inability to protect airway. Positive-pressure ventilation may worsen untreated pneumothorax; assess and treat pneumothorax promptly.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Surgical stabilization of rib fractures may be considered in selected patients with flail chest, ventilator dependence, severe chest-wall deformity, or persistent respiratory compromise despite optimal treatment.
• Chest drainage required for clinically significant pneumothorax/hemothorax when indicated.
• Thoracic surgical intervention may be needed for associated intrathoracic injury.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit flail chest or significant multiple rib fractures for close monitoring.
• ICU admission appropriate for respiratory failure, severe pulmonary contusion, or need for ventilatory support.
• Encourage pulmonary hygiene, mobilization, effective pain control to reduce atelectasis/pneumonia risk.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS; EAST Guidelines on Blunt Thoracic Trauma/Rib Fractures; Chest Wall Injury Society Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Traumatic cardiac tamponade occurs when blood accumulates in pericardial sac and impairs cardiac filling. Common mechanisms: Penetrating chest injury; less commonly blunt cardiac trauma with myocardial/vascular rupture.
• Suspect in trauma patients with: Hypotension, signs of obstructive shock. Tachycardia, elevated JVP, poor perfusion. Penetrating injury in cardiac box. Pericardial fluid on eFAST.
• [color=#991B1B]Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) is often incomplete and should NOT be relied upon to exclude tamponade. Absence of pericardial fluid on limited study does NOT exclude all cardiac injury.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate trauma, cardiothoracic/trauma-surgical, anesthesia, and resuscitation teams.
• Assess ABCs. Give oxygen and establish IV/IO access.
• Perform immediate bedside eFAST when available/appropriate.
• Treat associated life-threatening thoracic injuries.
• Arrange immediate operative management for suspected traumatic tamponade with instability.
• Use blood products when hemorrhage suspected.
• Avoid unnecessary delays for CT/advanced imaging in unstable patient.
• If traumatic cardiac arrest occurs, follow institution's resuscitative thoracotomy and traumatic-arrest protocol.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Bedside eFAST for pericardial fluid.
• ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring.
• CBC, blood gas, lactate, coagulation, electrolytes, group-and-crossmatch.
• Formal echocardiography in stable patients when further assessment needed.
• CT may be appropriate for selected stable patients with suspected blunt cardiac/vascular injury.
• [color=#991B1B]Imaging must NOT delay life-saving intervention when tamponade with shock strongly suspected.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Blood-Product Resuscitation[/color]
• Use major hemorrhage protocol when significant traumatic bleeding suspected. Arrange emergency blood products through local trauma/transfusion protocol.
• Monitor BP, perfusion, lactate, temperature, coagulation, calcium during major transfusion.
• [color=#991B1B]Fluid/blood administration alone cannot definitively relieve mechanical cardiac tamponade.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Emergency Pericardial Decompression[/color]
• Prepare for immediate definitive intervention by appropriately trained trauma/cardiothoracic team.
• In traumatic tamponade with instability, operative management generally preferred (permits control of bleeding source).
• Pericardiocentesis may be considered as temporizing measure in selected circumstances when definitive intervention not immediately available, but may fail when blood is clotted.
• [color=#991B1B]Blind pericardiocentesis can cause serious injury and may not control source of traumatic bleeding. Do NOT delay definitive surgery in unstable patient while repeatedly attempting drainage.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Emergency thoracotomy or sternotomy may be required depending on injury mechanism, location, patient condition.
• Evacuate pericardial blood and control cardiac/vascular bleeding source.
• Repair myocardial injury and address associated thoracic injuries.
• In traumatic cardiac arrest, resuscitative thoracotomy is reserved for appropriately selected patients according to mechanism, signs of life, elapsed time, local protocols.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit survivors to ICU or cardiothoracic surgical critical-care setting.
• Monitor for recurrent tamponade, ongoing hemorrhage, arrhythmias, myocardial dysfunction, coagulopathy.
• Arrange definitive cardiac/vascular evaluation based on injury pattern.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS; AHA Resuscitation/Traumatic Cardiac Arrest Guidance; EAST Emergency Resuscitative Thoracotomy Guidelines; ERC Special Circumstances Guidelines.

Trauma Surgery.title: Acute Surgical Bleeding and Hemorrhagic Shock

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Surgical bleeding may occur after trauma, abdominal/thoracic surgery, vascular procedures, or GI intervention.
• Possible sources: Arterial/venous injury. Postoperative wound/intra-abdominal bleeding. GI hemorrhage. Retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Bleeding related to anticoagulants/coagulopathy.
• Early signs: Tachycardia, pallor, anxiety, cool extremities, delayed capillary refill, reduced urine output.
• [color=#991B1B]Hypotension is often a late sign; a normal initial Hb does NOT exclude major acute blood loss. Consider hemorrhagic shock when unexplained deterioration following surgery or trauma.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate major hemorrhage protocol when life-threatening bleeding suspected.
• Call responsible surgeon, anesthesia team, blood bank, critical-care team.
• Control external bleeding with direct pressure, wound packing, or tourniquet for life-threatening extremity bleeding when indicated.
• Establish two large-bore IV lines or IO access if necessary.
• Obtain CBC, blood gas, lactate, coagulation, fibrinogen, electrolytes, ionized calcium, group-and-crossmatch.
• Begin blood-product resuscitation promptly for severe hemorrhage. Prevent hypothermia, monitor for hypocalcemia/coagulopathy.
• Identify bleeding source using bedside assessment, imaging in stable patients, or immediate operative exploration when indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay definitive hemorrhage control while waiting for lab results.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, blood gas, lactate, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation, fibrinogen, ionized calcium. Type and crossmatch.
• Bedside eFAST for suspected traumatic internal bleeding.
• CT angiography in stable patients when it will help identify source/guide embolization.
• Review anticoagulants, antiplatelet drugs, recent procedures, operative records.
• Repeat lab tests according to ongoing blood loss and resuscitation response.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Blood-Product Resuscitation[/color]
• Use local major hemorrhage protocol for life-threatening bleeding. Balanced component therapy/whole blood may be used per local availability/protocol. Transition to lab/viscoelastic-guided treatment when results available.
• Activate emergency blood-bank support. Use appropriate identification/compatibility/transfusion procedures. Use blood warmer when indicated.
• Monitor BP, perfusion, temperature, lactate, Hb, coagulation, fibrinogen, ionized calcium. Replace calcium when clinically indicated. Monitor for transfusion reactions/complications.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT rely on initial Hb to exclude major acute blood loss. Avoid excessive crystalloid in uncontrolled hemorrhage.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Tranexamic Acid (TXA)[/color]
• For selected adults with significant traumatic hemorrhage: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, followed by 1 g IV over 8 hours, when indicated by trauma protocol. Most beneficial when started early (generally within 3 hours of injury). Do NOT use routinely for every type of postoperative/GI bleeding without specific indication.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid rapid IV injection (can cause hypotension). TXA does NOT replace surgical/endovascular hemorrhage control.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Reversal of Anticoagulation[/color]
• Select reversal according to anticoagulant, time of last dose, renal function, bleeding severity, local protocol. Examples: Vitamin K + 4F-PCC for life-threatening warfarin-associated bleeding; specific reversal strategies for selected DOACs.
• [color=#991B1B]Reversal agents have thrombotic risks and should be used for appropriate indications under emergency protocols.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE HEMORRHAGE CONTROL
sections.content:
• Apply direct surgical hemostasis for accessible bleeding.
• Perform emergency laparotomy or thoracotomy when indicated by bleeding source and patient condition.
• Consider interventional radiology and embolization in selected stable patients.
• Correct coagulopathy and hypothermia while controlling source.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit significant hemorrhage for monitored care.
• ICU admission after major transfusion, persistent shock, emergency surgery, or organ dysfunction.
• Reassess for rebleeding, abdominal compartment syndrome, AKI, transfusion-related complications.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS; European Guideline on Management of Major Bleeding/Coagulopathy Following Trauma; ASH Anticoagulant-Associated Bleeding/Reversal Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Necrotizing soft tissue infection (NSTI) is a rapidly progressive infection involving fascia and subcutaneous tissue, sometimes extending into muscle. Can cause septic shock, multiorgan failure, and death.
• Risk factors: Diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, chronic kidney/liver disease, recent surgery/trauma/injections/skin wounds, peripheral vascular disease. Can occur without recognized risk factors.
• Severe pain disproportionate to visible skin changes. Rapidly spreading swelling or erythema. Edema extending beyond visible erythema.
• Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status. Bullae, ecchymosis, skin anesthesia, or necrosis in advanced disease. Crepitus may occur but is not required.
• [color=#991B1B]Early skin findings may be subtle. A low LRINEC score or nondiagnostic imaging must NOT be used to exclude NSTI when clinical suspicion is high.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment and identify septic shock.
• Request immediate surgical assessment.
• Begin sepsis resuscitation and administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly.
• Keep patient NPO and prepare for urgent operative exploration.
• Obtain blood cultures and tissue cultures when feasible without delaying antibiotics or surgery.
• Check glucose, electrolytes, renal function, lactate, coagulation. Provide analgesia and monitor closely.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay surgery for CT or MRI when clinical diagnosis is strongly suspected.[/color]
• Involve ICU, infectious diseases, and relevant surgical specialists early.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, CRP, glucose, CK (if muscle involvement/rhabdomyolysis), lactate/blood gas, coagulation, blood cultures, deep tissue cultures (obtained during surgery).

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color] CT may show fascial edema, fluid, gas, or deep collections. MRI may define tissue involvement in selected stable patients. [color=#991B1B]Neither test reliably excludes early NSTI.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Example: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV per severe-infection dosing protocol.
• Vancomycin using appropriate weight-based regimen and therapeutic monitoring.
• Clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours may be added when toxin-mediated infection (Group A strep or clostridial) suspected.
• Adjust for renal function, body weight, allergy, microbiology, local resistance.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics alone are inadequate treatment for established NSTI.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• For sepsis-induced hypoperfusion: initial crystalloid bolus, followed by reassessment. Individualize in septic shock using perfusion findings and response to treatment.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Vasopressor Support: Norepinephrine[/color]
• Generally first-line vasopressor in adult septic shock. Start and titrate per institutional protocol, commonly targeting initial MAP ~65 mmHg.
• Continuous BP and ECG monitoring required. Monitor peripheral perfusion, urine output, lactate.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay vasopressor treatment in persistent shock while waiting for central venous access when local protocols permit safe peripheral initiation.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Emergency Exploration and Debridement[/color]
• Immediate operative exploration required when NSTI strongly suspected.
• Remove all clearly necrotic tissue. Obtain deep tissue specimens for microbiology.
• Reassess tissue viability and plan repeat exploration, often within 24 hours or earlier if deterioration.
• Reconstructive surgery and wound closure considered after infection control.

[color=#1E3A8A]Additional Management[/color]
• Control hyperglycemia. Treat organ dysfunction. Consider tetanus prophylaxis for relevant wounds.
• Hyperbaric oxygen is not a substitute for urgent surgery and should never delay debridement.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Strong clinical suspicion of NSTI.
• Rapid progression despite treatment.
• Skin necrosis, bullae, deep fascial involvement, or systemic toxicity.
• Suspected clostridial myonecrosis.
• Failure of initial debridement requiring further source control.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Emergency surgical admission.
• ICU care for shock, organ failure, extensive debridement, or ventilatory support.
• Continue multidisciplinary care until infection controlled and organ function stabilizes.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines; Surviving Sepsis Campaign; WSES Guidance on NSTI.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Fournier gangrene is a rapidly progressive necrotizing infection of the perineal, genital, or perianal fascia. Can spread rapidly and cause septic shock.
• Risk factors: Diabetes, immunosuppression, obesity, CKD, perianal abscess/anorectal infection, genitourinary infection/recent instrumentation, recent perineal surgery/trauma.
• Severe perineal/genital/perianal pain. Swelling and erythema. Pain disproportionate to visible skin findings.
• Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status. Bullae, skin discoloration, necrosis, crepitus in advanced disease.
• [color=#991B1B]Absence of crepitus or gas on imaging does NOT exclude Fournier gangrene.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment and identify septic shock.
• Call general surgery and urology immediately; involve other relevant specialists per suspected source.
• Begin IV fluid resuscitation and sepsis management.
• Administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly.
• Keep patient NPO and prepare for urgent operative debridement.
• Obtain blood cultures and lab tests when feasible without delaying treatment.
• Control hyperglycemia and correct metabolic abnormalities.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay surgery for CT when clinical suspicion is high.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory:[/color] CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, glucose, CRP, lactate/blood gas, coagulation profile, CK (muscle involvement suspected), blood cultures, deep tissue cultures during surgery.

[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging:[/color] CT may help define extent in stable patients. Imaging cannot reliably exclude early disease. Do NOT delay operative source control for imaging in a deteriorating patient.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Example: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV per severe-infection dosing protocol.
• Vancomycin using appropriate weight-based regimen and therapeutic monitoring.
• Clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours may be added when toxin-mediated infection suspected.
• Adjust for renal function, allergy, cultures, local resistance. Narrow when results available.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics do NOT replace urgent surgical debridement.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• Adult sepsis-induced hypoperfusion: begin isotonic crystalloid resuscitation and reassess frequently. Further fluid depends on perfusion, cardiac function, urine output, clinical response.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Vasopressor Support: Norepinephrine[/color]
• First-line vasopressor for adult septic shock when indicated. Titrate per institutional protocol, commonly targeting initial MAP ~65 mmHg.
• Continuous BP and ECG monitoring. Monitor perfusion, urine output, response to source control.
• [color=#991B1B]Vasopressors do NOT replace antibiotics and surgery.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Emergency exploration and extensive debridement of necrotic tissue.
• Drainage of associated abscesses.
• Repeated operative assessment and debridement when necessary.
• Management of underlying anorectal, genitourinary, or skin source.
• Urinary or fecal diversion may be considered selectively according to extent of disease and specialist assessment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Emergency surgical admission.
• ICU care for shock, extensive tissue destruction, organ failure, or repeated operations.
• Continue multidisciplinary care until infection controlled.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines; WSES Guidance on NSTI; EAU Urological Infections Guidance; Surviving Sepsis Campaign.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Descending necrotizing mediastinitis is a rapidly progressive, potentially fatal infection spreading from oropharynx/deep neck spaces into mediastinum.
• Common sources: Deep neck infection, odontogenic infection, peritonsillar/retropharyngeal infection, cervical trauma/postoperative infection.
• Warning signs: Fever, toxic appearance, severe neck/chest pain. Neck swelling, dysphagia, odynophagia, trismus. Dyspnea, tachycardia, hypotension, septic shock. Crepitus/swelling extending into chest.
• Early symptoms may be nonspecific; rapid deterioration should raise suspicion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate ENT, thoracic/cardiothoracic surgery, anesthesia, and critical-care teams.
• Assess airway early; progressive neck swelling may make later intubation difficult.
• Provide O2 and establish IV access with continuous monitoring.
• Obtain blood cultures and lab tests without delaying treatment.
• Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering oral streptococci, anaerobes, other likely pathogens.
• Obtain urgent contrast-enhanced CT of neck/chest when patient stable enough.
• [color=#991B1B]Arrange urgent drainage and debridement; antibiotics alone are inadequate for established necrotizing mediastinal infection.[/color]
• Resuscitate septic shock according to current sepsis protocols.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function, coagulation, blood gas, lactate.
• Blood cultures and operative tissue/fluid cultures.
• Contrast-enhanced CT of neck/chest to identify deep-space infection, mediastinal extension, gas, drainable collections.
• Additional imaging based on suspected pleural, pericardial, or vascular complications.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay emergency source control in rapidly deteriorating patient solely to obtain additional imaging.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Select regimen according to severity, allergy, renal function, local resistance. One possible adult empiric regimen: piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 hours (dosing/infusion adjusted to local protocols).
• Add MRSA coverage (e.g., vancomycin) when epidemiology/clinical risk supports.
• If necrotizing soft-tissue infection or toxin-mediated streptococcal disease suspected, specialist-guided addition of protein-synthesis inhibitor may be appropriate.
• Administer promptly and obtain cultures when no delay to therapy. Monitor renal function, drug toxicity, culture results. Narrow therapy when possible.
• [color=#991B1B]Renal adjustment and local resistance patterns essential. Antibiotics must NOT delay surgical drainage/debridement.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Septic Shock Support[/color]
• Individualized crystalloid resuscitation and norepinephrine when hypotension persists despite appropriate fluid assessment. Typical initial MAP target ~65 mmHg, individualized.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid indiscriminate fluid loading when respiratory compromise or fluid overload developing.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Drain original cervical or odontogenic source.
• Perform surgical drainage and debridement of infected mediastinal compartments.
• Drain pleural collections or empyema when present.
• Repeat operative assessment when infection persists or tissue necrosis progresses.
• Coordinate approach with thoracic surgery based on anatomical extent of infection.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU admission usually required.
• Continue close monitoring for airway compromise, septic shock, pleural infection, pericardial involvement, recurrent mediastinal collections.
• Reassess source control early if fever, vasopressor needs, or organ dysfunction persist.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EACTS Guidance; WSES Guidance on Severe Surgical Infections; Surviving Sepsis Campaign.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
An anastomotic leak occurs when a surgically created connection between GI segments fails, allowing enteric contents to escape. Can cause intra-abdominal infection, peritonitis, septic shock.
• Risk factors: Poor tissue perfusion, malnutrition/hypoalbuminemia, diabetes, smoking, immunosuppression/corticosteroid exposure, emergency surgery/severe contamination, tension on anastomosis, technical/vascular complications.
• Persistent tachycardia. Fever or increasing abdominal pain. Ileus/failure to recover bowel function.
• Purulent or enteric drain output. Increasing inflammatory markers. Hypotension, oliguria, confusion, elevated lactate. Peritonitis in major leak.
• [color=#991B1B]Tachycardia and unexplained clinical deterioration after GI surgery may be early warning signs even before dramatic abdominal findings appear.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment. Notify operating surgeon and general surgery team urgently.
• Keep patient NPO. Establish IV access and obtain blood tests.
• Begin sepsis resuscitation when indicated. Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly when leak-associated infection suspected.
• Obtain blood cultures if no delay. Arrange CT imaging in stable patient when it will help determine source/management.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay operative exploration for imaging when generalized peritonitis or instability strongly suggests an uncontrolled leak.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes/renal function/LFTs/CRP, lactate/blood gas in severe illness, blood cultures when sepsis suspected, culture of drain fluid/operative specimens.
• CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast when appropriate. Water-soluble enteric contrast may be considered according to location/local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]A negative scan does not fully exclude a leak when clinical suspicion remains high.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV per local severe-infection protocol. Alternatives depend on severity, allergy, renal function, local resistance, suspected source.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics alone are not adequate for an uncontrolled leak or generalized peritonitis.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluids and Shock Management[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid for hypoperfusion with repeated reassessment. In adult sepsis-induced hypoperfusion, initial volume approaching 30 mL/kg within 3 hours may be considered, individualized.
• Escalate to vasopressors and ICU support if shock persists despite appropriate resuscitation.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Source Control[/color]
• Options: Percutaneous drainage (localized collection), endoscopic treatment (selected anastomoses), surgical exploration/washout/repair/revision/diversion/takedown.
• Choice depends on hemodynamic stability, degree of contamination, anatomy, operating surgeon's assessment.

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Generalized peritonitis.
• Hemodynamic instability or uncontrolled sepsis.
• Major leak with free contamination.
• Failed percutaneous or endoscopic management.
• Persistent clinical deterioration despite treatment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent admission under surgical team.
• ICU care for shock, respiratory failure, or multiorgan dysfunction.
• Continue reassessment until source control and clinical improvement established.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Surgical Infection Society Guidance; WSES Guidance on Postoperative Intra-abdominal Infection; Surviving Sepsis Campaign.

Postoperative & Perioperative Complicati.title: Postoperative Bowel Obstruction and Prolonged Ileus

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Postoperative ileus is temporary impairment of coordinated GI motility after surgery. Mechanical bowel obstruction is a physical blockage and may require urgent intervention.
• Ileus causes: Major abdominal surgery, opioids/anticholinergics, hypokalemia/electrolyte disturbances, sepsis/inflammation/intra-abdominal collections, excessive fluid administration/severe systemic illness.
• Mechanical obstruction causes: Adhesions, internal/external hernia, anastomotic narrowing, volvulus, early postoperative technical complications.
• Abdominal distension, nausea/vomiting, failure to pass flatus/stool, reduced oral intake, abdominal pain.
• [color=#991B1B]Fever, tachycardia, focal tenderness, guarding, or rising lactate may indicate strangulation, ischemia, leak, or another complication.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform ABCDE assessment. Review operation, postoperative day, medications, bowel-function progression.
• Keep patient NPO if significant obstruction or vomiting suspected.
• Establish IV access and correct fluid/electrolyte deficits. Request surgical review.
• Insert NG tube when persistent vomiting or marked distension warrants decompression.
• Review opioids/anticholinergics and reduce when clinically feasible.
• Assess for anastomotic leak, abscess, ischemia, other postoperative complications.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT assume that all postoperative distension is benign ileus.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, magnesium, CRP when indicated, lactate/blood gas if ischemia/sepsis suspected.
• CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast when appropriate (transition point, closed-loop obstruction, ischemia, collection, leak).
• Plain abdominal radiography may show bowel dilation but is less definitive.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Supportive Management (Uncomplicated Ileus)[/color]
• Correct dehydration/electrolyte abnormalities. Encourage early mobilization when safe.
• Minimize opioids and motility-inhibiting medications when feasible. Provide appropriate analgesia/antiemetics.
• NG decompression for selected patients with significant vomiting/distension. Resume oral intake per clinical recovery/surgical team assessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluids[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid according to volume status/ongoing losses. Replace measured NG losses when clinically indicated. Avoid unmonitored fluid overload.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Antiemetics[/color]
• Select according to age, comorbidities, QT interval risk, other medications. For selected adults, ondansetron 4 mg IV may be used per protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Antiemetics do NOT treat mechanical obstruction and must not delay surgical assessment.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT (MECHANICAL OBSTRUCTION)
sections.content:
• Selected adhesive small-bowel obstructions may be managed nonoperatively under close surgical supervision when no evidence of ischemia, strangulation, or peritonitis.
• Management: Bowel rest, IV fluids, NG decompression, selected contrast protocols.
• Surgery required when obstruction is complicated, fails appropriate conservative management, or results from a cause requiring operative correction.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Peritonitis.
• Suspected strangulation, ischemia, or perforation.
• Closed-loop obstruction.
• Clinical deterioration or persistent obstruction despite an appropriate monitored trial of conservative management.
• Anastomotic or other postoperative complications requiring source control.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with suspected mechanical obstruction or significant postoperative ileus.
• ICU care for shock, organ dysfunction, or major postoperative complications.
• Discharge only after clinical improvement, adequate hydration, appropriate oral-intake plan, and clear follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidance on Adhesive SBO; ERAS Society Recommendations; ACR Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Postoperative hemorrhage is bleeding occurring after surgery. May be external, concealed within a body cavity, or present as a wound/organ-space hematoma. Significant bleeding can rapidly progress to hemorrhagic shock.
• Causes: Inadequate surgical hemostasis, slipped ligature/vascular injury, coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia, anticoagulant/antiplatelet medication, anastomotic bleeding, vascular graft/organ injury, bleeding from drain site/operative wound.
• Persistent tachycardia. Hypotension or narrowing pulse pressure. Pallor, diaphoresis, delayed cap refill.
• Increasing wound/drain blood loss. Abdominal distension or increasing pain. Falling hemoglobin (early Hb may initially remain normal). Oliguria, confusion, elevated lactate in severe hemorrhage.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate local major hemorrhage protocol when significant bleeding suspected.
• Perform ABCDE assessment and provide oxygen when indicated by hypoxemia/critical illness.
• Call operating surgeon and anesthesia/critical care team urgently.
• Establish two large-bore IV lines or appropriate rapid-access alternatives.
• Send CBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, blood gas, lactate, electrolytes, group/crossmatch.
• Apply direct pressure to accessible external bleeding.
• Begin blood component resuscitation when indicated by hemorrhage severity/local protocol.
• Identify anticoagulants and reverse their effects when indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay operative control for imaging in an unstable patient with suspected ongoing internal bleeding.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC with serial hemoglobin. PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, platelet count.
• Blood gas and lactate. Electrolytes, renal function, ionized calcium during major hemorrhage.
• Group and crossmatch. Bedside ultrasound or CT angiography in selected stable patients.
• Evaluate drains, wound sites, abdominal findings, operative records.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Blood Component Resuscitation[/color]
• Indications: Major ongoing hemorrhage or hemorrhagic shock. Use local major hemorrhage protocol when criteria met.
• Monitor temperature, ECG, BP, oxygenation, urine output, hemoglobin, coagulation, fibrinogen, ionized calcium. Warm patient and blood products when appropriate.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT rely on a single hemoglobin value to exclude severe acute blood loss. Avoid excessive crystalloid when blood products and definitive hemorrhage control required.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Tranexamic Acid[/color]
• Consider in selected patients with significant hemorrhage when indicated by bleeding context/local protocol.
• For selected adult trauma with significant bleeding: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, followed by 1 g IV over 8 hours, ideally within 3 hours of injury.
• [color=#991B1B]This trauma regimen should NOT automatically be applied to every postoperative bleed. Avoid rapid IV administration (can cause hypotension). TXA does NOT replace surgical hemostasis.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Anticoagulant Reversal[/color]
• Identify anticoagulant, last dose, renal function, severity of bleeding. Use appropriate reversal strategy per local guidance.
• [color=#991B1B]Reversal carries thrombotic risk; select according to clinical situation and drug involved.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Return to operating room when bleeding ongoing or surgical control needed.
• Interventional radiology embolization may be appropriate for selected arterial bleeding in stable patients.
• Correct hypothermia, acidosis, hypocalcemia, coagulopathy.
• Review anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy after hemostasis achieved.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Hemodynamic instability with suspected ongoing internal bleeding.
• Persistent blood loss despite resuscitation.
• Expanding hematoma causing organ or airway compression.
• Suspected major vascular injury.
• Bleeding requiring direct operative control.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit and monitor patients with significant postoperative bleeding.
• ICU care for shock, massive transfusion, coagulopathy, or organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ESVS/Specialty Guidance on Perioperative Bleeding; European Guideline on Major Bleeding/Coagulopathy; NICE Blood Transfusion Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Wound dehiscence is separation of a surgical wound. Fascial dehiscence is a serious complication because abdominal contents may protrude through the wound. Evisceration is the protrusion of abdominal viscera through a disrupted wound.
• Risk factors: Surgical-site infection, poor nutrition/hypoalbuminemia, obesity, diabetes, smoking, chronic corticosteroid use/immunosuppression, increased intra-abdominal pressure (coughing/vomiting/ileus), poor tissue quality/technical failure.
• Sudden serosanguineous discharge. Feeling of wound opening/tearing sensation. Visible separation of wound edges.
• Protruding bowel or omentum. Abdominal pain, fever, signs of infection.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call operating surgeon immediately.
• Assess ABCDE and treat associated shock/sepsis. Keep patient NPO.
• Position patient comfortably, often supine with knees slightly flexed (reduce abdominal wall tension).
• If viscera exposed, cover with sterile dressings moistened with warm sterile saline.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT push exposed organs back into the abdomen. Avoid pressure on protruding viscera.[/color]
• Establish IV access and prepare for urgent operative management.
• Administer antibiotics when infection, contamination, or emergency surgery warrants them.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes/renal function/glucose, coagulation, group/crossmatch if surgery likely.
• Lactate and blood cultures if sepsis suspected.
• Imaging only when patient stable and diagnosis/associated intra-abdominal complication uncertain.
• [color=#991B1B]Imaging must NOT delay surgery when evisceration or major fascial disruption is evident.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Wound Protection[/color]
• Cover exposed viscera with sterile saline-moistened dressings. Maintain warm environment and minimize contamination.
• Prepare for urgent surgical exploration.
• [color=#991B1B]Never apply dry gauze directly to exposed bowel. Never attempt forceful reduction of eviscerated organs at the bedside.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluids[/color]
• Isotonic crystalloid guided by perfusion and repeated reassessment.
• [color=#991B1B]Escalate to blood products when hemorrhage present; crystalloid alone is inadequate for major blood loss.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Antibiotics when Indicated[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours + Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours (selected contaminated intra-abdominal situations).
• Broader therapy may be required per severity, contamination, healthcare exposure, local resistance.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Urgent operative exploration for fascial dehiscence with evisceration.
• Assess bowel viability and associated intra-abdominal infection.
• Repair fascial disruption when feasible.
• Use individualized closure strategy when contamination/edema/tissue quality prevents safe primary closure.
• Treat associated infection, ileus, or increased intra-abdominal pressure.

sections.heading: 06 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Evisceration.
• Complete fascial disruption.
• Bowel compromise or suspected intra-abdominal infection.
• Wound dehiscence associated with uncontrolled bleeding or sepsis.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent surgical admission.
• ICU care when associated with shock, major contamination, or significant organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidance; ACS Educational Resources; Local Protocols.

Postoperative & Perioperative Complicati.title: Stoma Complications: Ischemia, Retraction, Prolapse, and Obstruction

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
A stoma complication may threaten bowel viability, cause obstruction, impair appliance fitting, or lead to fluid/electrolyte loss.

[color=#1E3A8A]Major complications:[/color]
• Ischemia/Necrosis: Dusky, purple, gray, or black stoma. Loss of normal mucosal appearance. Reduced bleeding on gentle specialist assessment. Associated abdominal pain/systemic deterioration.
• Retraction: Stoma lies below skin level. Leakage and skin irritation. Difficulty maintaining appliance seal.
• Prolapse: Excessive protrusion of bowel through stoma. Edema, appliance difficulty, or obstruction. Darkening/severe pain suggests compromised perfusion.
• Outlet Obstruction: Reduced/absent output. Abdominal distension, cramping, nausea, vomiting.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCDE and identify shock, dehydration, or peritonitis.
• Inspect stoma and surrounding skin. Establish IV access if dehydrated/vomiting/systemically unwell.
• Measure stoma output and replace significant fluid losses.
• Request urgent surgical and stoma-care specialist assessment.
• Keep patient NPO when obstruction, ischemia, or surgery suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT force instruments or tubes through a stoma. Escalate immediately for suspected ischemia, strangulation, perforation, or complete obstruction.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes/urea/creatinine, magnesium (high output/fluid loss).
• Lactate/blood gas if ischemia/shock suspected.
• CT abdomen/pelvis for suspected obstruction, internal hernia, intra-abdominal complication.
• Direct specialist assessment of stoma viability and depth of ischemia.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Fluid and Electrolyte Replacement[/color]
• Indications: High-output ileostomy, vomiting, dehydration, AKI.
• Oral rehydration solution when patient can safely drink; IV isotonic crystalloid for significant dehydration/hypoperfusion with reassessment.
• Monitor BP, pulse, urine output, renal function, Na+, K+, Mg2+.
• [color=#991B1B]High-output stomas can cause rapid sodium/fluid depletion. Replace losses according to measured output and labs.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Stoma Prolapse[/color]
• If viable/uncomplicated, trained clinician may attempt gentle reduction using appropriate technique. Edema reduction measures only under clinical supervision.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT attempt forceful reduction. Painful, irreducible, discolored, or ischemic prolapse requires urgent surgical assessment.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Stoma Ischemia/Necrosis[/color]
• Urgent surgical assessment to determine depth/extent of ischemia. Superficial mucosal discoloration may sometimes be observed under specialist guidance. Deep necrosis extending below fascial level usually requires urgent operative management.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT rely on external color alone when depth of ischemia uncertain.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Deep stoma necrosis.
• Strangulation or compromised bowel viability.
• Complete obstruction or failure of conservative management.
• Irreducible prolapse with ischemia.
• Retraction causing severe dysfunction or complications not manageable conservatively.
• Associated intra-abdominal pathology.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with ischemia, obstruction, severe dehydration, or systemic illness.
• Arrange stoma nurse follow-up for stable appliance or skin problems.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ASCRS Clinical Practice Resources; ACPGBI Guidance; Local Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Suspect postoperative infection in any patient with deterioration after surgery.
• Warning signs: fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria, increasing O2 requirement, abdominal pain, or wound discharge.
• Possible sources: Anastomotic leak/bowel perforation, intra-abdominal abscess, infected wound/deep SSI, infected catheter, pneumonia, UTI.
• Septic shock: sepsis with persistent circulatory failure requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate surgical, anesthesia, and critical-care teams.
• Assess ABCs, mental status, peripheral perfusion. Give O2 when indicated; prepare for ventilatory support.
• Establish two IV lines and monitor ECG, SpO2, BP, temperature, urine output.
• Measure lactate, CBC, renal function, electrolytes, LFTs, coagulation, glucose.
• Obtain blood cultures and source-specific cultures before antibiotics if no meaningful delay.
• Start IV antibiotics promptly (ideally within 1 hour in septic shock).
• Give balanced crystalloid in reassessed boluses (initial target ~30 mL/kg within first 3 hours for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion, individualized).
• [color=#991B1B]Arrange urgent source control; antibiotics alone are insufficient when an uncontrolled surgically correctable source persists.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, LFTs, coagulation, blood gas, lactate.
• Blood cultures and cultures from suspected infected sites. Urinalysis/culture when indicated.
• Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis in sufficiently stable patient when intra-abdominal source suspected.
• Bedside ultrasound for free fluid, collections, or biliary pathology.
• Chest radiograph or CT when thoracic source suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay operative exploration or essential source control for imaging in a patient with an obvious surgical catastrophe or rapidly worsening instability.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics[/color]
• Choose empiric therapy according to suspected source, severity, local resistance, recent antibiotic exposure, allergies, renal function.
• Example for severe intra-abdominal infection: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 hours (adjust for renal function).
• Carbapenem may be appropriate when severe infection with resistant organisms likely; follow local guidelines.

[color=#1E3A8A]IV Crystalloid Resuscitation[/color]
• Reassessed boluses (often 250–500 mL at a time in adults), with repeated assessment. Cumulative initial target near 30 mL/kg may be appropriate for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion, individualized.
• Use balanced crystalloid (Lactated Ringer's or Plasma-Lyte) when appropriate.
• Monitor MAP, capillary refill, lung findings, O2 requirement, urine output, lactate. Avoid continued fluid loading when pulmonary edema or fluid intolerance develops.

[color=#1E3A8A]Norepinephrine[/color]
• Start IV infusion per local protocol (commonly ~0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min), titrate to response. Initial MAP target ~65 mmHg, individualized.
• Central line preferred for ongoing administration, but initiation through suitable monitored peripheral IV may be appropriate while central access arranged. Monitor BP continuously and inspect IV site.
• [color=#991B1B]Extravasation can cause tissue ischemia. Treat suspected extravasation immediately per local protocol.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SOURCE CONTROL
sections.content:
• Drain accessible abscesses percutaneously when suitable.
• Perform urgent surgery for perforation, anastomotic failure, necrotic tissue, uncontrolled contamination, or another source not amenable to less invasive treatment.
• Remove infected devices when indicated.
• Coordinate with interventional radiology and endoscopy when they can provide timely definitive source control.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with organ dysfunction to high-acuity setting; septic shock generally requires ICU care.
• Reassess frequently for ongoing contamination, inadequate source control, worsening lactate, renal injury, respiratory failure.
• Review cultures daily and de-escalate antibiotics when appropriate.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Surviving Sepsis Campaign (2021); WSES Guidelines on Intra-abdominal Infections; Surgical Infection Society Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
• Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH): sustained/repeated intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) ≥12 mmHg.
• Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS): sustained IAP >20 mmHg associated with new organ dysfunction or failure.
• Risk factors: Major abdominal trauma/surgery, massive fluid resuscitation, severe pancreatitis, intra-abdominal bleeding/edema, bowel obstruction/ileus/distension, large-volume ascites or burns.
• Clinical features: Tense/progressively distended abdomen. Increasing airway pressures and worsening ventilation. Oliguria/AKI. Hypotension, reduced venous return, increasing vasopressor requirement. Rising lactate and worsening organ perfusion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Recognize progressive abdominal distension with unexplained respiratory, renal, or circulatory deterioration.
• Call surgical and critical-care teams urgently.
• Assess and support ABCs.
• Measure IAP using standardized bladder-pressure technique. Insert urinary catheter if appropriate and monitor urine output.
• Relieve abdominal distension where possible: decompress stomach with NG tube and colon/rectum when indicated and safe.
• Optimize analgesia and sedation; consider brief neuromuscular blockade in selected patients while definitive management arranged.
• Avoid unnecessary ongoing fluid administration after initial resuscitation; use hemodynamic reassessment to guide further fluids.
• [color=#991B1B]Arrange urgent decompressive laparotomy if ACS persists with organ dysfunction despite appropriate nonoperative measures.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serial IAP measurements.
• CBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, blood gas, lactate.
• Continuous assessment of urine output, airway pressures, hemodynamics.
• Bedside ultrasound or CT to identify ascites, bleeding, obstruction, or another treatable cause when patient stable enough.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay decompression for CT when severe ACS clinically evident and organ failure progressing.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Gastric/Intestinal Decompression[/color]
• Correctly positioned NG tube when gastric distension/ileus contributing. Rectal/colonic decompression selected according to cause and procedural safety.
• Monitor abdominal girth, IAP, ventilatory mechanics, urine output. Confirm tube position before use.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid blind rectal instrumentation when perforation, severe colitis, or another contraindication suspected.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia/Sedation[/color]
• Titrated agents per local ICU protocols and patient physiology. Assess sedation depth, BP, respiratory status, abdominal muscle relaxation.
• [color=#991B1B]Sedation may improve abdominal wall compliance but does NOT replace definitive decompression when ACS persists.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Fluid Strategy[/color]
• Individualize fluids according to perfusion/hemodynamic assessment; avoid fixed additional fluid target once adequate resuscitation achieved.
• Track cumulative fluid balance, lactate, urine output, oxygenation, IAP. Consider specialist-guided fluid removal after hemodynamic stabilization when fluid overload significant.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT compromise organ perfusion through overly aggressive fluid restriction or diuresis in an unstable patient.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Treat underlying cause: hemorrhage, bowel obstruction, ileus, ascites, intra-abdominal infection.
• Consider percutaneous drainage of significant fluid collections when appropriate.
• Urgent decompressive laparotomy indicated for overt ACS with persistent/worsening organ dysfunction despite initial measures.
• Temporary abdominal closure and planned reassessment may be required after decompression.
• Following laparotomy, monitor for recurrent ACS, fluid loss, hypothermia, abdominal wound complications.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Manage suspected/confirmed ACS in ICU or equivalent high-acuity setting.
• Obtain immediate surgical review when organ dysfunction accompanies elevated IAP.
• Repeat pressure measurements after interventions and whenever clinical condition worsens.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSACS Consensus Definitions and Guidelines; WSES Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Consider iatrogenic injury when patient deteriorates during or after operation, endoscopy, or invasive procedure.
• Possible injuries: Bowel perforation, major vascular injury/hemorrhage, bile duct injury, bladder/ureteric injury, pancreatic/solid-organ injury.
• Warning signs: Unexpected hypotension/tachycardia/falling Hb. Severe/increasing abdominal pain, guarding, rigidity.
• Fever, peritonitis, unexplained sepsis. Hematuria, oliguria, rising creatinine, urine leakage. Bile-stained drainage/persistent bilious ascites. Free intraperitoneal air/fluid beyond expected postoperative findings.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Notify operating surgeon and senior surgical team immediately.
• Assess ABCs and signs of hemorrhagic shock or peritonitis.
• Establish IV access and continuous monitoring. Keep patient NPO.
• Send CBC, electrolytes, renal function, blood gas, lactate, coagulation, group-and-crossmatch as indicated.
• Begin resuscitation and blood-product replacement when indicated.
• Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics when bowel perforation or intra-abdominal contamination suspected.
• Review operative note, procedure details, drains, postoperative trend.
• Arrange urgent imaging or operative exploration according to stability and suspected injury.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, renal function, electrolytes, LFTs, coagulation, lactate, blood gas.
• Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis in stable patients with suspected bowel injury/intra-abdominal collection.
• CT urography or other dedicated urinary tract imaging when ureteric injury suspected.
• Retrograde cystography or CT cystography when bladder injury suspected.
• Ultrasound or CT angiography for selected bleeding concerns.
• Cholangiography or other biliary imaging for suspected bile duct injury, in consultation with hepatobiliary team.
• [color=#991B1B]Imaging must NOT delay emergency surgery in an unstable patient with suspected uncontrolled bleeding or generalized peritonitis.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]IV Crystalloid and Blood Products[/color]
• Small, reassessed crystalloid boluses while arranging definitive treatment. Transfuse blood components according to hemorrhage severity, hemodynamics, labs, local massive transfusion protocol.
• Monitor BP, HR, temperature, urine output, lactate, Hb, coagulation, calcium, acid-base. Activate massive transfusion protocol for life-threatening hemorrhage.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid excessive crystalloid in major hemorrhage (worsens dilutional coagulopathy and tissue edema).[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics[/color]
• Select IV regimen appropriate to suspected injury/contamination; piperacillin–tazobactam is one possible adult option for severe intra-abdominal contamination.
• Adjust according to cultures, renal function, operative findings.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics do NOT replace repair, drainage, or control of ongoing contamination.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Bowel Perforation[/color]
• Urgent surgical exploration and repair or resection. Choice depends on site, extent of injury, contamination, tissue viability, patient stability.

[color=#1E3A8A]Vascular Injury/Uncontrolled Bleeding[/color]
• Immediate operative or endovascular control, depending on vessel, available expertise, patient condition.

[color=#1E3A8A]Bile Duct Injury[/color]
• Early specialist hepatobiliary consultation. Drain collections and control sepsis; definitive reconstruction or endoscopic treatment depends on injury type and timing.

[color=#1E3A8A]Bladder/Ureteric Injury[/color]
• Urgent urology consultation. Bladder drainage, repair, ureteric stenting, or reconstruction depends on injury location and severity.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for close monitoring and specialist care.
• Reassess for delayed perforation, ongoing hemorrhage, bile/urine leak, abscess, sepsis.
• Document injury, interventions, follow-up plan clearly.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidelines on Iatrogenic Perforation/Bowel Injury; EAU Guidelines on Urological Trauma; ATLS.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute respiratory deterioration after surgery may result from airway obstruction, residual anesthetic effects, opioid-induced respiratory depression, atelectasis, aspiration, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, PE, pneumothorax, or sepsis.
• Warning signs: Increasing RR/work of breathing. Falling SpO2/increasing O2 requirement. Reduced consciousness, shallow breathing, inability to protect airway. Tachycardia, hypotension, cyanosis, exhaustion.
• Consider PE when hypoxemia/unexplained tachycardia occurs, particularly after major surgery or immobility.
• Consider hemorrhage/intra-abdominal sepsis when respiratory deterioration accompanies hypotension or abdominal findings.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for urgent anesthesia, surgical, and critical-care assessment.
• Assess ABCs and mental status. Open/reposition airway; suction secretions when needed.
• Administer supplemental O2 and monitor SpO2, ECG, BP.
• Assist ventilation with bag-mask device if breathing inadequate.
• Check RR, pupil size, medication history, recent opioids/sedatives/neuromuscular-blocking agents.
• Obtain blood gas when respiratory failure, hypercapnia, or severe hypoxemia suspected.
• Examine for pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, aspiration, signs of hemorrhage/sepsis.
• Arrange urgent definitive airway management if patient cannot protect airway or maintain adequate ventilation.
• Treat underlying cause without delay.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Bedside glucose and blood gas as clinically indicated.
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, lactate when deterioration significant.
• Chest radiograph for suspected atelectasis, aspiration, edema, pneumonia, pneumothorax.
• ECG and troponin when cardiac ischemia/myocardial injury suspected.
• CTPA when PE suspected and patient stable enough.
• Bedside ultrasound/echo when pulmonary edema, cardiac dysfunction, or obstructive shock suspected.
• Review anesthetic records, fluid balance, medication chart, operative findings.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Oxygen and Ventilatory Support[/color]
• Titrate oxygen to patient's condition. Usual target 94–98%; use 88–92% in patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure unless individualized target indicated.
• Select appropriate oxygen device (nasal cannula, face mask, non-rebreather). Prepare bag-mask ventilation and airway equipment when deterioration severe.
• Monitor SpO2, respiratory effort, mental status, blood gas when indicated. Escalate to NIV/invasive ventilation according to cause and clinical response.
• [color=#991B1B]Oxygen alone does NOT correct hypoventilation or airway obstruction. Do NOT delay intubation in patient with worsening consciousness, exhaustion, or refractory hypoxemia.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Naloxone for Suspected Opioid-Induced Respiratory Depression[/color]
• In adults with opioid-induced respiratory depression, titrate IV naloxone in small doses, commonly starting at 0.04 mg and escalating every 2–3 minutes as needed. In apnea/life-threatening deterioration, use emergency protocol for rapid reversal.
• Aim to restore adequate ventilation rather than necessarily causing complete analgesia reversal. Continue respiratory monitoring; provide ventilatory support when necessary.
• [color=#991B1B]Naloxone may precipitate severe pain, agitation, withdrawal, sympathetic activation. Its effect may wear off before opioid; recurrent respiratory depression requires continued observation and sometimes repeat dosing or infusion.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Cause-Directed Treatment[/color]
• Bronchospasm: inhaled bronchodilator per severity. Pulmonary edema: respiratory support and treatment of underlying cause. Pneumothorax: urgent decompression when tension suspected. PE: assess severity, initiate anticoagulation/reperfusion when indicated. Aspiration/pneumonia: supportive care, antibiotics when infection suspected/established. Hemorrhage/sepsis: resuscitation and urgent source control.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with persistent oxygen requirement, hypercapnia, respiratory distress, or identified serious cause.
• ICU care for invasive ventilation, hemodynamic instability, or rapidly progressive respiratory failure.
• Reassess frequently after treatment because postoperative deterioration can recur.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ASA Practice Guidelines for Postanesthetic Care; BTS Oxygen Use Guideline; ERC ALS Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
A retained surgical item may present immediately or months to years after a procedure.
• Possible retained materials: Sponges, instruments, needles, fragments of devices.
• Clinical presentations: Persistent/unexplained postoperative pain. Fever, abscess, recurrent infection. Bowel obstruction, fistula, perforation. Palpable mass or persistent drainage. Unexpected radiographic findings.
• [color=#991B1B]A retained foreign body is NOT the only explanation for postoperative symptoms; evaluate other surgical complications concurrently.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess patient stability and identify any immediate threat from sepsis, hemorrhage, obstruction, perforation.
• Notify responsible surgical team and senior hospital leadership per institutional policy.
• Review operative report, count documentation, implant records, procedure details.
• Perform focused examination and obtain appropriate imaging.
• Start resuscitation and antibiotics when infection/sepsis suspected.
• Obtain urgent surgical review if item causing obstruction, perforation, bleeding, or uncontrolled infection.
• Preserve relevant records and follow institutional patient-safety/disclosure policies.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid blind removal or instrumentation that may worsen injury.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, lactate, blood cultures when infection suspected.
• Plain radiography for radiopaque objects or when radiographic surgical count marker present.
• CT abdomen/pelvis for suspected retained sponge, abscess, obstruction, fistula, perforation.
• Ultrasound may help identify superficial collections or selected foreign bodies.
• [color=#991B1B]Imaging choice depends on material, location, suspected complication; some materials are not readily visible on plain radiographs.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics for Associated Infection[/color]
• Choose antibiotics according to suspected infection, source, severity, renal function, allergies, local resistance. For severe intra-abdominal infection, broad-spectrum IV regimen may be required.
• Obtain cultures when appropriate without delaying urgent treatment. Monitor hemodynamics, renal function, temperature, clinical response.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics do NOT remove the foreign body or replace drainage/definitive source control when required.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Abscess Drainage[/color]
• Arrange image-guided drainage or operative drainage depending on anatomy/clinical condition. Send aspirated material for appropriate microbiology.
• Monitor drain output, fever, inflammatory markers, clinical improvement.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid percutaneous drainage when it is unsafe or unlikely to control the source; obtain surgical consultation.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Remove retained item when clinically indicated, using approach appropriate to its location/associated risks.
• Treat associated abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction, tissue injury.
• Emergency surgery may be necessary for peritonitis, uncontrolled sepsis, or bowel obstruction.
• Document event and management transparently according to local law, hospital policy, patient-safety standards.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with infection, obstruction, perforation, or retained item requiring urgent intervention.
• Arrange follow-up to confirm source control/resolution of complications.
• Conduct structured safety review to identify contributing process failures.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist/Safe Surgery Guidance; ACS Surgical Patient Safety Statements; National Surgical Safety Policies.

Postoperative & Perioperative Complicati.title: Acute Abdominal Compartment Syndrome After Major Resuscitation

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Abdominal compartment syndrome can develop after major trauma, massive fluid resuscitation, severe burns, major abdominal surgery, hemorrhage, or severe pancreatitis. Results from elevated intra-abdominal pressure causing impaired organ perfusion and dysfunction.
• Clinical warning signs: Increasing abdominal distension/tense abdomen. Rising airway pressures/worsening oxygenation. Oliguria/AKI. Hypotension or escalating vasopressor requirements. Rising lactate/worsening metabolic acidosis.
• [color=#991B1B]Diagnosis requires sustained intra-abdominal pressure >20 mmHg associated with new organ dysfunction or failure.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate surgical and critical-care teams urgently.
• Assess ABCs and evidence of progressive organ failure.
• Measure intra-abdominal pressure using standardized bladder-pressure technique.
• Check urine output, ventilatory mechanics, blood gas, lactate, renal function, fluid balance.
• Decompress stomach with NG tube when indicated.
• Treat bowel obstruction, ileus, intra-abdominal bleeding, fluid collections contributing to increased pressure.
• Avoid unnecessary additional fluid loading after adequate resuscitation.
• [color=#991B1B]Arrange urgent decompressive laparotomy if organ dysfunction persists/worsens despite appropriate measures.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serial intra-abdominal pressure measurements.
• Blood gas, lactate, electrolytes, renal function, CBC.
• Continuous monitoring of airway pressures, urine output, hemodynamics.
• Bedside ultrasound or CT when patient stable enough and imaging will clarify treatable cause.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay decompression in deteriorating patient with established ACS.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Gastric Decompression[/color]
• Prepare correctly sized NG tube and appropriate drainage system. Confirm placement per local protocol. Monitor drainage, abdominal distension, IAP, respiratory mechanics.
• [color=#991B1B]Decompression alone is NOT definitive treatment for persistent ACS with organ dysfunction.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Hemodynamic Support[/color]
• Individualize fluid and vasopressor treatment according to perfusion, blood loss, hemodynamic response. Use standardized isotonic fluid/vasopressor preparations.
• Monitor MAP, lactate, urine output, renal function, signs of fluid overload. Consider norepinephrine for persistent hypotension per local shock protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid both under-resuscitation and indiscriminate fluid loading; each can worsen organ injury.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Urgent decompressive laparotomy indicated when overt ACS causes persistent/worsening organ dysfunction despite appropriate initial measures.
• Treat underlying cause (bleeding, bowel obstruction, intra-abdominal infection).
• Temporary abdominal closure may be required.
• Monitor for recurrent compartment syndrome, fluid/protein losses, hypothermia, infection, abdominal wound complications.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Manage confirmed ACS in ICU or equivalent high-acuity care.
• Obtain immediate surgical review for rising IAP accompanied by respiratory, renal, or circulatory deterioration.
• Repeat pressure measurements after interventions and whenever patient's condition changes.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSACS Consensus Definitions/Clinical Practice Guidelines; WSES ACS Guidance; Surviving Sepsis Campaign.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
An anorectal abscess is a localized collection of pus near the anus or rectum. Delayed drainage can lead to sepsis, tissue extension, or fistula formation.
• Types: Perianal, intersphincteric, ischioanal, supralevator.
• Risk factors: Anal gland obstruction/infection, diabetes, Crohn disease, immunosuppression, previous anorectal abscess/fistula.
• Perianal pain (worse sitting/defecating). Localized swelling/erythema/fluctuance. Fever/malaise.
• Deep abscess may cause severe rectal/pelvic pain without obvious external swelling. Urinary retention may occur with deep pelvic inflammation.
• [color=#991B1B]Severe pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading erythema, bullae, or skin necrosis raises concern for necrotizing infection.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCDE and look for sepsis.
• Examine perianal region with appropriate consent, analgesia, and chaperone.
• Obtain urgent surgical assessment.
• Keep patient NPO when urgent drainage/anesthesia likely. Provide analgesia.
• Obtain lab tests in systemic illness, diabetes, or immunocompromise.
• Arrange urgent drainage; antibiotics alone are usually insufficient for a drainable abscess.
• [color=#991B1B]If Fournier gangrene suspected, activate the emergency necrotizing-infection pathway.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC/inflammatory markers when indicated. Glucose/renal function in diabetes/systemic illness.
• Lactate/blood cultures when sepsis suspected.
• CT or MRI for deep, complex, recurrent, or clinically occult abscesses when imaging will guide management.
• Superficial, obvious abscesses usually do not require imaging before drainage.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Analgesia[/color]
• Choose appropriate analgesic based on severity, renal function, allergies, comorbidities.
• [color=#991B1B]Severe or escalating pain may indicate deep collection or necrotizing infection and requires reassessment.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Antibiotics when Indicated[/color]
• Indications: Sepsis/systemic infection, significant surrounding cellulitis, immunocompromise, selected high-risk comorbidities, specific indications determined by surgeon.
• Example: Amoxicillin–clavulanate may be appropriate in selected cases when local guidance supports. IV broad-spectrum needed for severe infection/sepsis per local protocols.
• [color=#991B1B]Routine antibiotics do NOT replace incision and drainage of an established abscess.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Incision and Drainage[/color]
• Drainage is primary treatment for most anorectal abscesses. Approach depends on location/complexity. Deep/complex abscesses may require drainage under anesthesia.
• Monitor pain, fever, drainage, wound healing, recurrence. Consider fistula evaluation if symptoms persist/recur.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid blind probing for a fistula during acute drainage because it can injure the sphincter complex.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Established anorectal abscess requiring drainage.
• Deep collection.
• Sepsis or clinical deterioration.
• Suspected necrotizing infection.
• Failure of initial treatment or recurrent disease.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with sepsis, extensive infection, deep abscess, immunocompromise, or need for operative drainage.
• Outpatient management may be appropriate after drainage in selected stable patients with reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ASCRS Clinical Practice Guidelines on Anorectal Abscess/Fistula; ACPGBI Guidance; IDSA Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Major burns may cause airway injury, capillary leak, hypovolemia, hypothermia, electrolyte disturbances, multi-organ dysfunction.
• Estimate TBSA using Rule of Nines (adults) or Lund–Browder chart (children).
• Include partial-thickness and full-thickness burns in TBSA; do NOT include simple superficial erythema.
• Consider major burn referral for extensive burns, full-thickness burns, burns involving critical areas, suspected inhalation injury, electrical/chemical burns, or burns with significant associated trauma.
• Signs of burn shock: tachycardia, hypotension, poor peripheral perfusion, reduced urine output, rising lactate.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stop burning process and ensure scene safety.
• Remove hot/contaminated clothing and jewelry unless adherent to skin.
• Assess ABCs; consider early airway control if progressive airway edema suspected.
• Give supplemental O2 when indicated.
• Expose patient sufficiently to assess burns, then cover with clean, dry dressings and prevent hypothermia.
• Estimate TBSA and burn depth.
• Establish IV access; obtain CBC, electrolytes, renal function, glucose, blood gas, lactate, group-and-crossmatch for major burns.
• Start warmed isotonic crystalloid for major burns, titrate to perfusion and urine output.
• Give appropriate analgesia and assess for associated trauma.
• Contact burn center early for major burns or complex injuries.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, glucose, blood gas.
• Lactate and carboxyhemoglobin when smoke inhalation or CO exposure suspected.
• ECG and cardiac monitoring for electrical injury.
• Urinalysis and assessment for myoglobinuria in high-voltage injury or suspected rhabdomyolysis.
• Chest imaging when respiratory injury/associated trauma suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]Investigations must NOT delay airway stabilization or resuscitation.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Burn Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• For adults with burns ≥20% TBSA, formal IV fluid resuscitation generally required.
• Commonly used starting estimate: 2 mL × body weight (kg) × %TBSA over first 24 hours (adult thermal burns), consistent with contemporary approaches. Adjust to local burn-center protocol and clinical response.
• Use warmed lactated Ringer's or another protocol-approved isotonic crystalloid. Calculate 24-hour requirement from time of injury, not arrival time.
• Give ~half of calculated volume during first 8 hours after burn and remainder over following 16 hours, continuously adjusting to response. Target adult urine output commonly ~0.5 mL/kg/hour.
• Monitor BP, mental status, peripheral perfusion, urine output, lactate, electrolytes, signs of fluid overload. Reassess frequently and titrate infusion rather than treating calculated volume as fixed prescription.
• [color=#991B1B]Excessive resuscitation can cause pulmonary edema, extremity compartment syndrome, abdominal compartment syndrome. Do NOT delay resuscitation in a shocked patient while calculating exact formula.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Titrate IV opioid analgesia according to pain severity, hemodynamics, respiratory status, local protocol. Reassess pain, respiratory rate, SpO2, BP, sedation level.
• [color=#991B1B]Opioids can cause respiratory depression and hypotension; monitor closely, especially with inhalation injury.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Wound Care and Tetanus Prevention[/color]
• Tetanus prophylaxis depends on vaccination history and wound classification.
• Cover burns with clean, dry dressings during initial stabilization. Arrange wound assessment, debridement, definitive dressing care by trained staff.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT apply ice directly to major burns. Avoid prolonged cooling that can cause hypothermia. Routine systemic antibiotic prophylaxis NOT recommended for uncomplicated burns without specific indication.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Refer major burns early to specialist burn service.
• Assess need for escharotomy when circumferential burns compromise ventilation or distal perfusion.
• Evaluate for associated trauma, rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome.
• Provide nutritional support, wound management, infection surveillance, rehabilitation as appropriate.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit major burns to burn center or ICU according to severity.
• Transfer early when specialist burn care unavailable locally.
• Monitor for airway compromise, shock, hypothermia, renal injury, infection, compartment syndrome.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ABA Guidelines for Burn Patient Referral; ABA Burn Shock Resuscitation Guidelines; ISBI Practice Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Suspect inhalation injury after exposure to fire in enclosed space, smoke, hot gases, or chemical combustion products.
• Warning signs: Facial burns/singed nasal hairs. Soot in mouth/sputum. Hoarseness, stridor, drooling, difficulty swallowing. Progressive facial/oral/neck swelling. Cough, wheeze, hypoxemia, respiratory distress. Confusion, collapse, unexplained lactic acidosis (toxic gas exposure).
• Pulse oximetry can appear reassuring in CO poisoning and cannot exclude it.
• Cyanide toxicity may occur after enclosed-space fires (altered consciousness, cardiovascular instability, severe unexplained lactic acidosis).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Remove patient from exposure; ensure rescuer safety.
• Give 100% O2 immediately when smoke inhalation or CO exposure suspected.
• Assess airway patency and look for progressive edema, stridor, voice change, respiratory fatigue.
