• Arrange early endotracheal intubation when significant progressive airway compromise likely; do NOT wait for complete obstruction.
• Assess breathing/circulation, establish IV access, monitor ECG, BP, oxygenation.
• Obtain blood gas with co-oximetry, lactate, electrolytes, glucose, other tests guided by exposure.
• Evaluate for associated major burns and begin appropriate burn resuscitation.
• Contact critical care, anesthesia, burn center early.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Arterial/venous blood gas with carboxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin when available.
• Lactate and acid-base assessment when cyanide exposure possible.
• Chest radiograph as baseline when indicated; early imaging can be normal despite evolving inhalation injury.
• Bronchoscopy may help diagnose/grade lower-airway injury in selected patients.
• ECG and troponin when significant CO exposure or cardiac symptoms present.
• Consider alternative/coexisting causes of respiratory deterioration (aspiration, bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, trauma).

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]100% Oxygen[/color]
• Deliver highest feasible inspired O2 concentration immediately when CO poisoning or significant smoke inhalation suspected. Use non-rebreather mask with reservoir (spontaneously breathing) or appropriate ventilatory system (intubated).
• Continue O2 while urgently evaluating CO exposure. Follow symptoms, blood gas, carboxyhemoglobin per severity and local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Standard pulse oximetry cannot reliably distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin. A normal SpO2 does NOT exclude CO poisoning.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Endotracheal Intubation[/color]
• Use appropriate rapid-sequence intubation regimen per patient physiology and local airway protocol. Prepare airway equipment, suction, backup devices, rescue plan.
• Intubate early when progressive upper-airway edema, stridor, significant respiratory distress, reduced consciousness, or impending airway obstruction present.
• Confirm tube placement with waveform capnography and clinical assessment. Monitor ventilation, oxygenation, airway pressures, hemodynamics.
• [color=#991B1B]Airway edema can progress rapidly. Delayed intubation may make airway control extremely difficult. Facial burns alone do NOT automatically require intubation; decisions should consider exposure history, symptoms, examination, trajectory.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected Cyanide Toxicity[/color]
• In adults with strong clinical suspicion of severe cyanide poisoning after smoke exposure: hydroxocobalamin commonly 5 g IV; second 5 g dose may be considered per response and local toxicology guidance.
• Monitor hemodynamics, acid-base status, lactate trend, clinical response.
• [color=#991B1B]Hydroxocobalamin can interfere with certain lab tests and may cause red discoloration of skin/urine. Do NOT give antidotes indiscriminately for minor smoke exposure.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Manage significant inhalation injury in ICU or burn center.
• Provide lung-protective ventilation when required.
• Treat bronchospasm with inhaled bronchodilators when indicated.
• Evaluate for CO poisoning and consider hyperbaric O2 consultation for selected severe cases.
• Monitor for delayed pulmonary edema, ARDS, airway casts, secondary infection.
• Avoid routine prophylactic systemic antibiotics or corticosteroids unless another specific indication exists.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with significant inhalation injury, airway symptoms, abnormal gas exchange, toxic exposure, or major associated burns.
• Transfer to specialist center when advanced airway, burn, or critical-care support required.
• Reassess frequently because respiratory findings may worsen over several hours.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ABA Guidelines; CDC CO Poisoning Guidance; WHO Smoke/Toxic Gas Exposure; ISBI Guidelines.

Burns & Environmental.title: Electrical Burns and High-Voltage Electrical Injury

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Electrical injury may cause deep muscle necrosis, vascular injury, arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, and compartment syndrome despite small external burns.
• High-voltage injury generally defined as exposure to ≥1,000 volts.
• Assess for: LOC or cardiac arrest. Entry/exit wounds. Deep tissue injury/progressive swelling. Severe muscle pain, weakness, dark urine. Limb ischemia/compartment syndrome. Associated falls, fractures, spinal injury.
• Lightning injury can cause cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest, burns, neurologic complications.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Ensure electrical source disconnected before touching patient.
• Follow standard resuscitation; initiate CPR and defibrillation when indicated.
• Assess ABCs and possible associated trauma.
• Obtain 12-lead ECG and initiate cardiac monitoring for significant exposure.
• Establish IV access and assess for rhabdomyolysis/major tissue injury.
• Remove jewelry/constrictive items before swelling develops.
• Cover burns with clean, dry dressings and prevent hypothermia.
• Obtain urgent surgical assessment for high-voltage exposure, deep burns, neurovascular compromise, or suspected compartment syndrome.
• Contact burn center early.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• 12-lead ECG; continuous monitoring when indicated by exposure severity or abnormal findings.
• CBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, glucose, blood gas when clinically indicated.
• Creatine kinase (CK), potassium, calcium, phosphate, urinalysis for suspected muscle injury.
• Urine or plasma assessment for myoglobin when available.
• ECG monitoring and troponin when cardiac arrest, chest pain, ECG abnormality, or suspected myocardial injury.
• Imaging for fractures, spinal injury, or other trauma according to examination.
• Serial neurovascular examinations of affected limbs.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]IV Crystalloid for Rhabdomyolysis[/color]
• Individualize according to perfusion, urine output, renal function, extent of muscle injury. In adults with significant rhabdomyolysis, starting rate ~200–500 mL/hour may be considered in selected patients, then titrated to response.
• Commonly used urine-output target in adults with substantial rhabdomyolysis: ~1–3 mL/kg/hour, generally not exceeding 300 mL/hour without specialist direction.
• Monitor urine output, fluid balance, potassium, creatinine, CK, calcium, acid-base. Reassess frequently for pulmonary edema/fluid overload.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT administer large fluid volumes blindly in anuric patients or those with heart failure. Routine bicarbonate/mannitol NOT recommended for every case; use only for specific indication under appropriate protocol.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Hyperkalemia Treatment[/color]
• If severe hyperkalemia or hyperkalemic ECG changes: IV calcium for myocardial stabilization per local emergency protocol. Insulin with dextrose and nebulized beta-2 agonist may be used to shift potassium intracellularly.
• Continuous ECG monitoring. Recheck potassium and glucose after treatment. Arrange urgent renal support when hyperkalemia refractory or associated with severe renal failure.
• [color=#991B1B]IV calcium stabilizes myocardium but does NOT lower serum potassium. Insulin can cause delayed hypoglycemia; establish glucose-monitoring plan.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Urgent fasciotomy for confirmed compartment syndrome with compatible clinical findings.
• Early debridement of nonviable tissue when indicated.
• Escharotomy when circumferential burns compromise perfusion or ventilation.
• Vascular repair or other operative treatment for associated injuries.
• Amputation may be required for irreversible tissue destruction (decisions by experienced multidisciplinary team).

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit high-voltage injuries, significant deep burns, rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmias, neurovascular compromise, or associated major trauma.
• Transfer to burn center when specialist management required.
• Continue serial assessment because muscle necrosis and compartment syndrome may evolve after initial presentation.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ABA Guidelines; AHA ACLS Guidance; ERC ALS Guidelines; ISBI Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Chemical burns can result from acids, alkalis, solvents, cement, phenols, industrial chemicals.
• Alkali injuries can penetrate deeply and continue damaging tissue after initial exposure.
• Important findings: Pain, erythema, blistering, tissue necrosis. Ocular pain, redness, blurred vision, visual loss. Respiratory symptoms following inhalation. Systemic toxicity after absorption of particular chemicals.
• Hydrofluoric acid exposure is particularly dangerous (fluoride can cause severe hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperkalemia, cardiac arrhythmias).
• Dry chemicals may need to be brushed off before irrigation if adding water would trigger hazardous reaction.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Protect staff with appropriate PPE. Remove patient from contaminated environment.
• Remove contaminated clothing, shoes, watches, jewelry.
• Brush off dry chemical powders before irrigation when safe/appropriate.
• Irrigate most skin chemical exposures promptly with copious running water.
• Begin eye irrigation immediately for ocular exposure; do NOT delay while searching for specialized solution.
• Assess airway/breathing after inhalation exposure.
• Check vital signs, pain, burn extent, possible systemic toxicity.
• Contact poison center, toxicologist, or specialist burn service for chemical-specific guidance.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid neutralizing an acid with an alkali or vice versa; reaction can generate heat and worsen injury.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Identify chemical using container, safety data sheet, or workplace information when available.
• Assess burn depth, BSA, involvement of eyes, airway, face.
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, blood gas when significant injury/systemic toxicity suspected.
• ECG and electrolytes (including calcium, magnesium, potassium) after suspected hydrofluoric acid exposure.
• Ocular pH assessment and visual examination after eye exposure.
• Additional investigations according to specific agent and symptoms.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Skin Decontamination[/color]
• No fixed drug dose. Irrigate with copious water for prolonged period, commonly at least 20–30 minutes, and longer when required by chemical/persistent symptoms.
• Use safe source of running water or appropriate emergency irrigation system. Remove contaminated clothing; prevent contaminated runoff from exposing staff/other body areas.
• Begin immediately and continue while checking pain, skin appearance, chemical-specific guidance. Prevent hypothermia during prolonged irrigation.
• [color=#991B1B]Some agents have specific decontamination requirements. Consult poison center/chemical safety guidance for reactive substances (elemental metals, agents that react dangerously with water).[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Ocular Chemical Exposure[/color]
• Immediate, continuous irrigation; no fixed volume applies to all exposures. Use clean tap water, normal saline, or another suitable irrigation fluid immediately available.
• Irrigate continuously and evert eyelids when feasible to remove retained particles. Check ocular pH when available; continue irrigation until pH near physiologic and remains stable after brief pause.
• Arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment for significant exposures.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay irrigation to obtain sterile fluid or measure pH first.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Hydrofluoric Acid Exposure[/color]
• Treat as medical emergency. Calcium gluconate may be used topically, by infiltration, or intravenously according to site/severity and specialist-guided protocol.
• Obtain urgent toxicology or burn-specialist advice. Monitor ECG and serial calcium, magnesium, potassium. Treat systemic electrolyte abnormalities promptly.
• [color=#991B1B]Hydrofluoric acid can cause life-threatening arrhythmias even when skin findings initially appear limited. Avoid blind/excessive local calcium injection (tissue injury).[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Urgent debridement may be required for progressive necrosis or deeply injured tissue.
• Ocular burns require urgent ophthalmic evaluation.
• Compartment syndrome or limb ischemia requires immediate surgical assessment.
• Significant airway injury requires early airway and critical-care involvement.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with extensive burns, deep injury, ocular involvement, systemic toxicity, significant pain requiring monitored treatment, or high-risk chemical exposure.
• Arrange burn-center or specialist transfer when appropriate.
• Provide clear documentation of chemical, decontamination performed, serial findings.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ABA Guidelines; CDC Chemical Emergencies/Decontamination; NIOSH Emergency Response Database.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Empyema is infected purulent material in pleural space, commonly following pneumonia but also possible after thoracic surgery, trauma, or esophageal perforation.
• Suspect in patients with fever, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, persistent sepsis, or failure to improve with antibiotics.
• Complicated parapneumonic effusion suggested by pleural fluid with low pH, low glucose, positive microbiology, or loculations.
• Findings may include reduced breath sounds, dullness to percussion, respiratory distress.
• A pleural collection associated with septic shock or respiratory failure requires urgent specialist assessment.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and oxygenation. Give supplemental O2 if indicated.
• Establish IV access and monitor vital signs.
• Obtain CBC, renal function, electrolytes, blood cultures, lactate if sepsis suspected.
• Perform chest ultrasound to identify and characterize pleural fluid.
• Start appropriate IV antibiotics promptly when bacterial infection or sepsis suspected.
• Arrange diagnostic aspiration and pleural drainage when indicated.
• Involve thoracic surgery early for loculated infection, trapped lung, failure of drainage, or ongoing sepsis.
• If esophageal perforation or postoperative leak suspected, investigate and control underlying source urgently.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Chest radiograph as initial assessment.
• Thoracic ultrasound to assess fluid volume, septations, safe drainage site.
• Contrast-enhanced CT chest when needed to define loculations, pleural thickening, lung abscess, or another source.
• Pleural fluid Gram stain/culture, pH measured appropriately, glucose, LDH, cell count.
• Blood cultures when systemic infection suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid delaying drainage in an unstable patient with an obvious infected pleural collection.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Choose empiric antibiotics based on community-acquired vs hospital-acquired infection, prior procedures, local resistance, allergy, renal function.
• Community-acquired coverage may include beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor; hospital-acquired may require broader Gram-negative and MRSA coverage per local guidance.
• Administer promptly in sepsis. Obtain pleural/blood cultures when feasible. Adjust to microbiology and clinical response.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics alone are often insufficient when established pleural pus or complicated infected effusion requires drainage.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Intercostal Chest Drain[/color]
• Use ultrasound-guided site selection when possible. Select suitable small-bore or larger-bore drain based on fluid characteristics, loculations, local thoracic protocols.
• Insert using appropriate aseptic technique and procedural expertise. Connect to prescribed drainage system.
• Monitor respiratory status, drain output, air leak, pain, imaging response.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid blind insertion when ultrasound guidance available. Drain insertion can cause bleeding, organ injury, malposition; reassess immediately if respiratory/hemodynamic status worsens.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Intrapleural tPA and DNase[/color]
• In selected adults with residual loculated pleural infection despite chest-tube drainage: alteplase (tPA) 10 mg plus DNase 5 mg intrapleurally, twice daily for up to 3 days, following specialist assessment and local protocol.
• Assess bleeding risk and anticoagulant use before treatment.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy as substitute for urgent surgery when patient has uncontrolled sepsis or requires definitive operative management.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — SURGICAL INDICATIONS
sections.content:
• Persistent sepsis or residual collection despite appropriate antibiotics and drainage.
• Extensive loculations not adequately drained.
• Trapped lung or organized pleural peel.
• Failure of less invasive management.
• VATS or open decortication may be required, depending on stage, anatomy, patient fitness.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with empyema for antibiotics, drainage, monitoring.
• ICU care may be required for respiratory failure or septic shock.
• Review imaging, drainage output, cultures, clinical response regularly.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline (2023); AATS Empyema Management Guidelines; CHEST Guidance on Pleural Infection.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Acute infection of the mastoid air cells, usually following acute otitis media. It can progress to bone destruction, subperiosteal abscess, or intracranial complications.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Fever and ear pain.
• Recent or current acute otitis media.
• Postauricular erythema, swelling, and tenderness.
• Protrusion of the pinna.
• Otorrhea or hearing impairment.
• Severe headache, vomiting, meningism, or neurological signs.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs and signs of sepsis.
• Perform otoscopy and examine the postauricular region.
• Obtain urgent ENT assessment.
• Establish IV access and provide analgesia and fluids.
• Admit patients with suspected acute mastoiditis.

sections.heading: 04 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC and CRP.
• Blood cultures if febrile or septic.
• Culture ear discharge when available.
• CT temporal bone if complications or diagnostic uncertainty.
• MRI if intracranial complications suspected.

sections.heading: 05 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IV ANTIBIOTICS[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV every 24 hours (Pediatrics).
• Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV every 24 hours (Adults).
• Adjust antibiotics to culture results and specialist advice.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. SOURCE CONTROL[/color]
• ENT may perform myringotomy or tympanostomy.
• Mastoidectomy or drainage may be required for abscess or failure of medical therapy.

sections.heading: 06 — WARNINGS
sections.content: • Do not delay ENT review when postauricular swelling or pinna displacement is present.

sections.heading: 07 — DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
sections.content:
• Uncomplicated acute otitis media.
• Otitis externa.
• Postauricular cellulitis.

sections.heading: 08 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Hospital admission and urgent ENT involvement.
• ICU or tertiary referral for sepsis or suspected intracranial spread.

sections.heading: 09 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Postauricular swelling and protrusion of the pinna are key findings.
• Meningitis, venous sinus thrombosis, and intracranial abscess are serious complications.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Acute Otitis Media and Mastoiditis.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is a rapid decline in hearing, typically developing within 72 hours. It is an otologic emergency requiring prompt assessment and treatment consideration.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Sudden unilateral hearing loss, sometimes bilateral.
• Tinnitus or a feeling of ear fullness.
• Vertigo may occur.
• Otoscopy may be normal.

[color=#991B1B]RED FLAGS: Hearing loss with facial weakness, diplopia, ataxia, or other focal neurological signs. Bilateral sudden hearing loss.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Establish the onset and progression of hearing loss.
• Perform otoscopy to exclude wax, effusion, and conductive causes.
• Perform bedside hearing assessment and tuning-fork tests.
• Arrange urgent ENT assessment and audiometry.
• Evaluate urgently for stroke if neurological symptoms are present.

sections.heading: 04 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Pure-tone audiometry as soon as possible.
• MRI of internal auditory canals/brain when indicated.
• Routine head CT is not recommended for typical idiopathic SSNHL.

sections.heading: 05 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. CORTICOSTEROIDS[/color]
• Prednisone/prednisolone ~1 mg/kg PO daily (max 60 mg/day) for 7–14 days.
• Consider within 2 weeks of symptom onset.
• Monitor blood glucose, blood pressure, mood, GI symptoms.
• ENT may consider intratympanic steroid therapy if incomplete recovery.

sections.heading: 06 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Treatment benefit is not guaranteed.
• Do not delay urgent ENT referral while waiting for routine investigations.

sections.heading: 07 — DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
sections.content:
• Cerumen impaction.
• Otitis media with effusion.
• Ear trauma or barotrauma.
• Ménière disease.
• Vestibular schwannoma.
• Posterior circulation stroke.

sections.heading: 08 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent ENT assessment, ideally the same day or within 24 hours.
• Emergency neurological assessment for focal deficits.

sections.heading: 09 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• A normal otoscopic examination does not exclude SSNHL.
• Early audiometry and timely treatment assessment are important.
• Routine antivirals, thrombolytics, and head CT are not recommended.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO-HNSF: Clinical Practice Guideline — Sudden Hearing Loss.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Severe, persistent ear pain, often worse at night and disproportionate to routine otitis externa.
• Purulent otorrhea and granulation tissue in the external auditory canal.
• Commonly occurs in older adults with diabetes or in immunocompromised patients.
• Facial nerve palsy, dysphagia, hoarseness, or other cranial neuropathies suggest skull-base involvement.
• Persistent symptoms despite standard topical treatment raise suspicion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess for sepsis, cranial neuropathies, and spread beyond the external auditory canal.
• Obtain urgent ENT review.
• Check glucose and assess diabetes control.
• Obtain appropriate cultures before antibiotics when feasible, provided this does not delay treatment in a severely ill patient.
• Avoid traumatic canal manipulation and repeated blind instrumentation.
• Begin systemic antipseudomonal treatment when invasive disease is suspected, guided by specialist and local resistance patterns.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Ear canal examination and culture of discharge or granulation tissue.
• CBC, CRP/ESR, renal function, and glucose.
• CT of the temporal bone for bony erosion and anatomical assessment.
• MRI when soft-tissue, skull-base, cranial nerve, or intracranial extension is suspected.
• Consider biopsy if malignancy or an alternative diagnosis is possible.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Systemic Antipseudomonal Antibiotics[/color]
• Option A: Cefepime 2 g IV every 8–12 hours (adjust for renal function).
• Option B: Ceftazidime 2 g IV every 8 hours (renal adjustment).
• Option C: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 hours (adjust for renal function).

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed (max daily limit).

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Definitive Management[/color]
• Obtain cultures and tailor systemic antimicrobial therapy.
• Provide careful aural toilet by trained staff.
• Optimize glycemic control and address immunosuppression.
• Imaging and serial clinical assessment guide treatment duration; prolonged systemic therapy is often required.
• Surgery is reserved for selected cases (diagnostic uncertainty, abscess, or non-response).

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Renal impairment increases the risk of cefepime-associated neurotoxicity. Adjust the dose accordingly.
• Select according to local susceptibility data; resistance may make ceftazidime inappropriate.
• Broad-spectrum therapy should be narrowed when cultures permit.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with cranial neuropathy, skull-base involvement, sepsis, severe uncontrolled pain, or inability to manage safely as an outpatient.
• Outpatient treatment may be considered only for selected stable patients with reliable specialist follow-up and a clear antimicrobial plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: UK Specialist Guidance on Necrotizing Otitis Externa; IDSA Guidance; Local Protocols.

Otology (Ear & Hearing).title: Ear Canal Foreign Body and Button Battery

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Ear pain, foreign-body sensation, reduced hearing, bleeding, or otorrhea.
• Visible object in the external auditory canal.
• Button battery may cause rapid tissue necrosis, liquefaction, and perforation.
• Suspect tympanic membrane injury if there is bleeding, severe pain, sudden hearing loss, or vertigo.
• In children, ask about possible insertion of button batteries, paired magnets, or sharp objects.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Identify the object, its location, and the duration of impaction.
• Button battery in the ear: urgent removal is required. Do not wait for symptoms.
• Urgently refer to ENT if a battery, paired magnets, sharp object, deeply impacted object, or object adjacent to the tympanic membrane is present.
• Do not irrigate a button battery, magnet, vegetable matter, or other object that may swell or react with water.
• Avoid repeated blind attempts; stop if the object is pushed deeper, bleeding occurs, or the patient cannot remain still.
• Do not use potentially ototoxic drops if tympanic membrane perforation is suspected unless specifically directed by a clinician.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Otoscopy, ideally documenting the object and canal condition before and after removal.
• Assess hearing symptoms and examine the tympanic membrane after removal when possible.
• Formal hearing assessment if persistent hearing loss, suspected tympanic injury, or other auditory symptoms are present.
• Imaging is not routinely required for a straightforward visible foreign body but may be necessary for suspected complications or an unidentifiable object.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Removal of a Non-Hazardous Foreign Body[/color]
• Select method based on object type, location, shape, and patient cooperation. Options include forceps, a suitable hook, suction, or irrigation only when appropriate.
• Use direct visualization. A single well-planned attempt is preferable to repeated unsuccessful attempts. Re-examine the canal and tympanic membrane after removal.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Button Battery[/color]
• Immediate removal by a clinician with suitable equipment and expertise. Arrange urgent ENT assistance if removal cannot be performed safely.
• After removal, assess canal skin, tympanic membrane integrity, bleeding, hearing, and signs of chemical injury. ENT follow-up may be required even if the battery is removed promptly.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed (max daily limit).

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Never irrigate the ear with a button battery in place. Do not apply ear drops or other substances as a substitute for removal.
• Analgesia must not delay urgent battery removal or ENT referral.
• Avoid irrigation if the tympanic membrane may be perforated, the object is a battery or magnet, or the object is hygroscopic or likely to swell.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate ENT assessment for a button battery, paired magnets, sharp object, tympanic membrane injury, significant bleeding, or failed removal.
• Discharge may be appropriate after uncomplicated removal when the canal and tympanic membrane are satisfactory and no significant symptoms remain.
• Provide clear return precautions for worsening pain, discharge, fever, vertigo, or hearing loss.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO-HNS Ear Foreign-Body Management Principles; Pediatric Button Battery Guidance; Local Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Head trauma followed by bleeding from the ear or hemotympanum.
• Hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, or nystagmus.
• Facial nerve weakness.
• Clear fluid draining from the ear or nose, suggesting possible cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage.
• Battle sign, hemotympanum, or other evidence of skull-base fracture.
• Altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurological deficits may indicate associated intracranial injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow trauma priorities and stabilize airway, breathing, and circulation.
• Assess Glasgow Coma Scale, pupils, cranial nerves, and facial nerve function.
• Protect the cervical spine until injury is excluded according to trauma protocols.
• Do not irrigate the ear or insert instruments into a potentially injured canal.
• If CSF leakage is suspected, avoid nasal instrumentation and unnecessary ear manipulation.
• Obtain urgent trauma and ENT assessment; involve neurosurgery when indicated.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CT head according to head injury criteria.
• High-resolution CT of the temporal bones when fracture characterization will affect management.
• Document facial nerve function as early as possible.
• Audiometry when the patient is stable and able to cooperate.
• Assess suspected CSF leakage with appropriate laboratory testing (e.g., beta-2 transferrin).
• Evaluate for associated vascular injury if indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Initial Trauma Management[/color]
• Oxygen and fluid resuscitation according to the patient's physiological needs and trauma protocol.
• Monitor neurological status, vital signs, and evidence of ongoing bleeding or deterioration.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally or by an appropriate alternative route every 6–8 hours as needed.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Antibiotics[/color]
• Do NOT prescribe routine prophylactic antibiotics solely because a temporal bone fracture or CSF leak is suspected. If meningitis, contaminated open injury, or another infection is suspected, initiate the appropriate emergency protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Definitive Management[/color]
• Most uncomplicated fractures are managed conservatively with observation and follow-up.
• Persistent CSF leakage requires specialist management; selected cases may require surgical repair.
• Facial nerve paralysis requires early ENT evaluation.
• Persistent conductive hearing loss may require later assessment and possible surgery.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid hypotension and hypoxia in traumatic brain injury. Do not delay stabilization for detailed ear examination.
• Analgesia must not obscure serial neurological assessment.
• Routine prophylaxis for a CSF leak is not universally recommended.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit according to head injury severity, neurological findings, CSF leakage, facial nerve dysfunction, and associated injuries.
• Urgent escalation for deteriorating consciousness, new focal deficits, meningism, worsening vertigo, or progressive facial weakness.
• Arrange ENT and audiology follow-up after discharge.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS Principles; NICE Head Injury Guidance; ENT/Skull-Base Trauma Guidance.

Otology (Ear & Hearing).title: Acute Otitis Media with Intracranial Complications

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Ear pain, fever, reduced hearing, and a bulging tympanic membrane may indicate acute otitis media.
• Severe or persistent headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status, or seizures may indicate meningitis.
• Persistent fever, vomiting, focal neurological deficits, or reduced consciousness may indicate intracranial abscess.
• Postauricular swelling, erythema, tenderness, or protrusion of the pinna suggests mastoiditis.
• Papilledema, diplopia, or worsening headache may indicate raised intracranial pressure or venous sinus thrombosis.
• Clinical deterioration despite antibiotics raises concern for an invasive complication.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, neurological status, and sepsis.
• Obtain urgent ENT and appropriate infectious diseases or neurosurgical consultation.
• Establish IV access and obtain blood cultures when feasible without delaying treatment.
• Start emergency IV antibiotics when meningitis, intracranial abscess, or another serious bacterial complication is suspected.
• Perform urgent neuroimaging when indicated; stabilize the patient first if unstable.
• Keep the patient fasting if surgery or drainage may be required.
• Do NOT perform lumbar puncture when contraindicated, including suspected mass effect or significant raised intracranial pressure.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, CRP, renal function, electrolytes, glucose, and blood cultures when systemically unwell.
• Contrast-enhanced CT of the temporal bones and relevant intracranial structures.
• MRI brain with contrast when intracranial abscess, venous sinus thrombosis, or other intracranial extension is suspected.
• CT or MR venography if venous sinus thrombosis is suspected.
• Ear examination and culture of discharge when useful.
• Lumbar puncture only if meningitis is suspected, it is clinically indicated, and there are no contraindications.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Empiric IV Antibiotics for Suspected Bacterial Meningitis[/color]
• Common adult component: ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours. Additional agents (vancomycin, ampicillin) may be required according to local resistance patterns, age, immune status, and suspected source.
• [color=#991B1B]This is not a complete universal regimen. Suspected meningitis or intracranial infection requires immediate clinician-directed treatment; do not delay for imaging or lumbar puncture when unsafe.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Additional Anaerobic Coverage[/color]
• Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours may be used when anaerobic coverage is indicated (e.g., selected intracranial abscess regimens).
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotic combinations depend on suspected pathogen, intracranial complication, and local protocol. Do not use metronidazole automatically for every case of otitis media.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia and Supportive Care[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally or by appropriate alternative route every 6–8 hours as needed.
• [color=#991B1B]Analgesia must not obscure clinical deterioration or delay definitive treatment.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• ENT may perform myringotomy or tympanostomy when indicated for drainage and microbiological sampling.
• Mastoidectomy may be necessary for coalescent mastoiditis or failure of appropriate treatment.
• Intracranial abscess may require neurosurgical drainage.
• Manage venous sinus thrombosis with specialist input; anticoagulation decisions must be individualized.
• Narrow antibiotic therapy according to cultures, imaging, and clinical response.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with suspected intracranial complications.
• ICU care may be required for shock, reduced consciousness, seizures, or respiratory compromise.
• Arrange ENT and infectious diseases follow-up after stabilization.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Otitis Media and Related Infection Guidance; ENT Guidance on Acute Mastoiditis/Intracranial Complications; Local Meningitis/Sepsis Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Blood in the external auditory canal or bleeding from the ear.
• Causes include canal trauma, foreign body injury, tympanic membrane perforation, infection, and temporal bone fracture.
• Ear bleeding after significant head trauma may indicate a skull-base or temporal bone injury.
• Associated hearing loss, vertigo, facial weakness, clear fluid leakage, or neurological deficits increases concern for serious injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and neurological status if trauma is possible.
• Control external bleeding gently without inserting material deeply into the ear canal.
• Do NOT irrigate the ear or perform blind instrumentation.
• Avoid ear drops when tympanic membrane perforation is suspected unless directed by an appropriate clinician.
• Obtain urgent ENT assessment for significant bleeding, hearing loss, vertigo, facial weakness, or suspected skull fracture.
• Follow the local head injury pathway after significant trauma.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Otoscopy when safe and appropriate.
• Neurological examination and assessment of facial nerve function.
• CT head and temporal bone imaging according to trauma severity and suspected fracture.
• Audiometry when the patient is stable and hearing symptoms persist.
• Consider investigation for a coagulation disorder or medication-related bleeding when clinically indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Minor External Canal Injury[/color]
• Apply gentle external pressure only where safe and visible; do not pack the canal blindly.
• [color=#991B1B]Deep packing or blind instrumentation may worsen injury or damage the tympanic membrane.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Suspected Temporal Bone Fracture[/color]
• Follow trauma resuscitation and arrange urgent ENT and trauma assessment.
• [color=#991B1B]Do not irrigate or manipulate the ear in suspected skull-base injury.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally or by appropriate alternative route every 6–8 hours as needed.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid delaying investigation of significant trauma or neurological symptoms while treating pain.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Identify and treat the source of bleeding.
• Manage tympanic membrane perforation, canal laceration, infection, or temporal bone fracture according to ENT findings.
• Consider specialist-selected topical treatment if infection or canal injury requires it.
• Arrange hearing assessment when hearing loss or persistent symptoms are present.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate evaluation for bleeding after significant head trauma, facial nerve weakness, vertigo, CSF leakage, or significant hearing loss.
• Minor superficial injuries may be managed as an outpatient after examination confirms no serious injury.
• Return urgently for recurrent bleeding, worsening pain, fever, dizziness, or new neurological symptoms.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Head Injury Guidance; ENT Guidance on External Auditory Canal/Tympanic Membrane Injury; Local Trauma Protocols.

Otology (Ear & Hearing).title: Acute Vertigo with Neurological Red Flags

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Sudden-onset vertigo, imbalance, nausea, vomiting, or difficulty walking.
• Central warning signs: diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, limb weakness, sensory loss, severe truncal ataxia, or new cranial nerve deficits.
• New severe headache or neck pain may indicate posterior circulation stroke or arterial dissection.
• Sudden hearing loss with acute vestibular symptoms may indicate an inner-ear disorder or a vascular event.
• Continuous acute vestibular symptoms in a patient with vascular risk factors require careful assessment.
• [color=#991B1B]CRITICAL POINT: Posterior circulation stroke may present predominantly with vertigo and imbalance, even without obvious limb weakness.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, and neurological status.
• Establish the exact onset or last-known-well time.
• Activate the local stroke pathway when stroke is suspected.
• Do not assume symptoms are benign because the patient is young or has no obvious limb weakness.
• Avoid walking an unstable patient without assistance.
• Use HINTS examination only in the appropriate patient with an acute vestibular syndrome and only when performed by a trained clinician.
• Do not use a reassuring or incomplete HINTS examination to rule out stroke when examiner expertise is lacking.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Full neurological examination, including eye movements, cranial nerves, coordination, gait when safe, and hearing.
• Point-of-care glucose.
• Brain imaging according to stroke pathway; MRI with DWI is more sensitive than non-contrast CT for many posterior fossa infarctions.
• CT angiography or MR angiography when vertebrobasilar occlusion or arterial dissection is suspected.
• ECG and laboratory investigations according to suspected cause.
• [color=#991B1B]A normal early CT does not reliably exclude posterior circulation ischemic stroke.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Suspected Posterior Circulation Stroke[/color]
• Activate stroke team and arrange urgent imaging and reperfusion eligibility assessment.
• [color=#991B1B]Do not delay stroke evaluation to administer vestibular suppressants or antiemetics. Thrombolysis or thrombectomy eligibility must be determined by the stroke team.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Antiemetic for Severe Nausea or Vomiting[/color]
• Ondansetron 4 mg orally, orally disintegrating, or IV as appropriate; repeat dosing per local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Review QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte abnormalities, and significant cardiac risk. Antiemetics do not treat stroke or establish the cause of vertigo.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Short-Term Vestibular Symptom Relief[/color]
• Medication choice depends on cause and comorbidities; routine prolonged vestibular suppressant treatment is not recommended for every case.
• [color=#991B1B]Sedation can worsen falls and obscure neurological reassessment. Do not let symptom relief delay stroke evaluation.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Treat confirmed stroke according to stroke pathway.
• Peripheral vestibular disorders require cause-specific management (e.g., repositioning maneuvers for confirmed BPPV).
• Consider urgent ENT or audiology assessment for sudden sensorineural hearing loss accompanying vertigo.
• Provide vestibular rehabilitation when appropriate.
• Reassess patients with persistent, progressive, or atypical symptoms.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or manage through stroke pathway when central pathology is suspected.
• Do not discharge a patient with new neurological deficits, inability to walk safely, or unexplained acute vestibular syndrome without adequate evaluation.
• Outpatient care may be appropriate for a confidently diagnosed benign peripheral disorder with no red flags and safe mobility.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA/ASA Acute Ischemic Stroke Guidance; NICE Stroke/TIA Guidance; GRACE-3 Guideline for Acute Dizziness/Vertigo.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Bleeding from the nasal cavity, commonly from the anterior septum (Kiesselbach plexus). Posterior bleeding may be severe and difficult to control.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Visible nasal bleeding.
• Blood dripping into the throat, especially with posterior bleeding.
• Dizziness, pallor, tachycardia, or hypotension in significant hemorrhage.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and hemodynamic stability.
• Sit the patient upright and lean forward.
• Apply firm continuous pressure to the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes.
• Suction blood from the mouth if necessary and safe.
• Establish IV access and obtain CBC, coagulation tests, and blood grouping/crossmatch when bleeding is severe.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. TOPICAL VASOCONSTRICTOR[/color]
• Oxymetazoline 0.05%: 2 sprays into the affected nostril; follow local protocol.
• Apply with nasal compression. Reassess bleeding and vital signs.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. CAUTERIZATION AND NASAL PACKING[/color]
• If bleeding point is visible, topical anesthetic and cauterization by a trained clinician.
• If bleeding persists, anterior nasal packing may be required.
• Suspected posterior epistaxis requires urgent ENT assessment and admission.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Use vasoconstrictors cautiously in patients with significant cardiovascular disease. Avoid prolonged use.
• Avoid blind or traumatic instrumentation.
• Do not remove anticoagulants permanently without assessing indication and bleeding severity.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Discharge if bleeding is controlled and patient is stable.
• Admit or urgently refer for persistent bleeding, posterior epistaxis, significant blood loss, or need for posterior packing.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Lean forward; do not tilt the head backward.
• Persistent bleeding despite appropriate compression requires escalation.
• Recurrent unilateral bleeding warrants ENT assessment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO-HNSF: Nosebleed Clinical Practice Guideline.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: A collection of blood between the nasal septal cartilage and its mucoperichondrium, usually following nasal trauma. Delayed treatment can cause cartilage necrosis, septal abscess, and permanent nasal deformity.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Recent nasal trauma.
• Nasal obstruction, often bilateral.
• Pain and tenderness.
• Soft, boggy swelling of the nasal septum.
• Persistent obstruction despite apparent improvement in external swelling.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Ask about trauma and timing.
• Examine the septum using appropriate illumination.
• Arrange urgent ENT assessment.
• Assess for associated facial fractures, significant bleeding, or head injury.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. URGENT DRAINAGE[/color]
• Prompt incision and drainage by a trained clinician.
• ENT may place a drain, quilting sutures, or packing to prevent re-accumulation.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. ANTIBIOTICS[/color]
• May be prescribed after drainage according to local ENT protocol.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content: • A suspected septal hematoma requires urgent drainage; do not manage it with observation or antibiotics alone.

sections.heading: 06 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical.
• CT is not routinely required for isolated septal hematoma.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent ENT review and drainage.
• Admit or escalate care for septal abscess or associated major facial trauma.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Always inspect the nasal septum after significant nasal trauma.
• Early treatment prevents cartilage necrosis and saddle-nose deformity.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Merck Manual Professional Edition: Nasal Fractures.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Fever, eyelid swelling, erythema, and significant ocular pain.
• Painful or restricted extraocular movements.
• Proptosis, diplopia, or chemosis.
• Reduced visual acuity, impaired color vision, or a relative afferent pupillary defect.
• Recent acute sinusitis, particularly ethmoid sinusitis.
• Severe headache, altered mental status, or cranial nerve abnormalities may indicate intracranial extension.

[color=#991B1B]PRESEPTAL CELLULITIS:[/color] Eyelid inflammation without proptosis, impaired vision, or painful/restricted eye movements.
[color=#991B1B]ORBITAL CELLULITIS:[/color] Infection posterior to the orbital septum; a vision-threatening emergency.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, temperature, mental status, and sepsis indicators.
• Document baseline visual acuity in each eye, pupils, color vision if feasible, ocular movements, and proptosis.
• Obtain immediate ophthalmology and ENT consultation.
• Start IV antibiotics promptly when orbital cellulitis is suspected; do not delay treatment for imaging.
• Keep the patient fasting if urgent surgery is possible.
• Escalate immediately for deteriorating vision, rapidly progressive proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, or neurological abnormalities.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits and paranasal sinuses.
• MRI brain and orbits if intracranial extension, cavernous sinus thrombosis, or another intracranial complication is suspected.
• CBC, CRP, renal function, electrolytes, and blood cultures if febrile or systemically unwell.
• Culture material obtained during surgical drainage when available.
• Consider glucose and HbA1c if diabetes is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Empiric IV Antibiotics — Adults[/color]
• Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours.
• Alternative broad-spectrum: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours (some intracranial infections require 2 g every 12 hours).
• Add Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours when anaerobic coverage is indicated (abscess or intracranial extension).
• Add Vancomycin (weight-based, renal adjusted, therapeutic monitoring) if MRSA coverage is indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Definitive Management[/color]
• Urgent surgical drainage may be necessary for an orbital abscess, visual compromise, deterioration despite antibiotics, or selected large abscesses.
• Drain associated infected sinuses when indicated by ENT.
• Modify antibiotics according to cultures and clinical response.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Adjust dosing in renal impairment. Regimens may be insufficient when MRSA risk or other resistant organisms require additional coverage.
• Ceftriaxone alone does not provide reliable MRSA or anaerobic coverage.
• Rapid vancomycin infusion can cause an infusion reaction. Avoid unmonitored dosing, especially in renal impairment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit all suspected orbital cellulitis cases for urgent specialist assessment and IV treatment.
• Consider a higher-acuity setting for visual deterioration, sepsis, intracranial extension, or rapidly progressive disease.
• Discharge only when a specialist confirms that the condition is preseptal rather than orbital and outpatient treatment is appropriate.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Orbital Cellulitis Guidance; IDSA Guidance; Local ENT/Ophthalmology Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Persistent or worsening nasal obstruction, purulent nasal discharge, facial pain, or fever.
• Severe frontal headache, forehead swelling, or focal frontal bone tenderness.
• Periorbital swelling, proptosis, diplopia, or reduced visual acuity.
• Meningism, altered mental status, focal neurological deficits, or seizures.
• Severe systemic illness or deterioration after initial improvement.

[color=#991B1B]RED FLAGS:[/color] Orbital signs, neurological symptoms, forehead swelling, or suspected intracranial infection require emergency evaluation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, circulation, mental status, visual function, and sepsis.
• Obtain urgent ENT review; involve ophthalmology or neurosurgery if orbital or intracranial complications are suspected.
• Start IV antibiotics promptly when complicated bacterial infection is suspected.
• Do not delay antibiotics in an unstable patient while waiting for imaging or specialist arrival.
• Keep fasting if operative drainage may be required.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses and orbits when orbital complications are suspected.
• Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the brain when intracranial extension is suspected; MRI is particularly useful for intracranial soft-tissue complications.
• CBC, CRP, renal function, electrolytes, and blood cultures in severe systemic illness.
• Obtain cultures from surgically drained collections where feasible.
• Consider glucose testing in severe or recurrent infection.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Empiric IV Antibiotics — Adults[/color]
• Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours.
• Alternative for severe/intracranial: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12–24 hours (meningitis regimen for intracranial infection).
• Add Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours when anaerobic coverage is indicated.
• Add Vancomycin if MRSA coverage is indicated (weight-based, renal adjusted).

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Definitive Management[/color]
• Drain orbital, subperiosteal, or intracranial collections when indicated.
• ENT may perform endoscopic sinus surgery for source control.
• Neurosurgical drainage may be required for selected intracranial abscesses.
• Tailor antimicrobial therapy to cultures, imaging, clinical response, and specialist recommendations.
• Pott's puffy tumor (frontal bone osteomyelitis with forehead swelling) requires urgent specialist management and assessment for intracranial spread.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Consider alternative or additional coverage for resistant organisms, intracranial infection, or specific exposure risks.
• Do not use ceftriaxone alone when anaerobic or MRSA coverage is indicated.
• Intracranial infection requires a dedicated specialist-directed regimen; do not assume every sinusitis case requires metronidazole.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with suspected orbital or intracranial complications.
• Escalate to critical care for shock, airway compromise, or severe neurological deterioration.
• Outpatient treatment is appropriate only for uncomplicated sinusitis after red flags have been excluded.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO-HNS Adult Sinusitis Guidance; IDSA Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis Guidance; Local Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Rapidly progressive facial pain, nasal congestion, fever, or facial swelling.
• Black, pale, or necrotic nasal mucosa may occur but is not always present.
• Facial numbness, palatal necrosis, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, or visual loss.
• Severe headache, altered mental status, or focal neurological findings.
• Major risk factors: uncontrolled diabetes, DKA, neutropenia, hematologic malignancy, transplantation, significant immunosuppression.

[color=#991B1B]CRITICAL POINT:[/color] Early mucosal appearance may be deceptively normal. Do not wait for black eschar before suspecting invasive fungal disease in a high-risk patient.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Treat as a time-critical emergency.
• Contact ENT, infectious diseases, ophthalmology, and the relevant medical team immediately.
• Assess and correct diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperglycemia, neutropenia, and other reversible risk factors.
• Arrange urgent nasal endoscopy and tissue biopsy.
• Start appropriate antifungal treatment when suspicion is high; do not wait for final culture results.
• Arrange urgent surgical debridement when indicated.
• Evaluate for orbital and intracranial extension.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urgent nasal endoscopy with biopsy for histopathology and fungal studies.
• Contrast-enhanced MRI of the face, orbits, and brain where feasible to assess soft-tissue and intracranial involvement.
• CT of the sinuses to evaluate bony anatomy and associated sinus disease.
• CBC with differential, renal function, electrolytes, glucose, ketones, and acid-base status when indicated.
• Blood cultures if febrile or systemically unwell; negative blood cultures do not exclude invasive fungal infection.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Liposomal Amphotericin B[/color]
• Dose: 5 mg/kg IV every 24 hours for mucormycosis; higher dosing (often 10 mg/kg/day) may be considered for CNS involvement under specialist direction.
• Monitor creatinine, potassium, magnesium, fluid status, and liver function. Replace electrolytes when indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Control Underlying Metabolic Abnormalities[/color]
• Follow the relevant DKA or hyperglycemic emergency protocol for insulin, IV fluids, and electrolyte replacement.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Definitive Management[/color]
• Urgent endoscopic surgical debridement of necrotic tissue; repeat procedures may be required.
• Histopathology and culture guide diagnosis and ongoing therapy.
• Reverse immunosuppression when feasible.
• Continue antifungal treatment until clinical and radiological response and reversal of risk factors are achieved.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Formulations are not dose-interchangeable. Amphotericin B can cause nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and infusion reactions.
• Correcting hyperglycemia alone is not adequate treatment for invasive fungal disease.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit urgently; these patients generally require inpatient multidisciplinary care.
• ICU care may be necessary for DKA, sepsis, major neurological involvement, or extensive disease.
• Do not discharge a patient with credible suspicion of acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis for routine outpatient follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ECMM/MSG Global Guideline for Mucormycosis; IDSA Guidance; Local Protocols.

Rhinology (Nose & Sinuses).title: Nasal Foreign Body and Nasal Button Battery

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Unilateral foul-smelling nasal discharge, nasal obstruction, epistaxis, or localized pain, particularly in children.
• Visible foreign body in one nostril.
• Button battery or paired magnets may cause rapid mucosal necrosis, septal perforation, and permanent tissue damage.
• Fever, facial swelling, severe pain, or purulent discharge may indicate secondary infection or tissue injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess breathing and determine whether the object is confined to the nose or may have been aspirated.
• Identify the object, location, duration, and whether paired magnets or a battery may be present.
• A nasal button battery requires immediate removal. Do not delay for routine imaging or outpatient follow-up.
• Obtain urgent ENT assistance for batteries, paired magnets, posteriorly located objects, significant bleeding, or failed removal.
• Do not irrigate the nose or push the object posteriorly.
• Avoid repeated unsuccessful attempts, which may cause bleeding, aspiration, or deeper impaction.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Anterior rhinoscopy or nasal endoscopy when available.
• Imaging is not routinely required for a visible uncomplicated foreign body.
• Consider imaging if the object is not identified, complications are suspected, or an unusual radiopaque object may be present.
• Evaluate for aspiration if there is coughing, choking, wheezing, or respiratory distress.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Removal of a Non-Hazardous Foreign Body[/color]
• A trained clinician may use direct-vision forceps, suction, a suitable hook, or a positive-pressure technique in carefully selected cooperative patients.
• Use direct visualization and an appropriate technique for the object's shape and location. Confirm complete removal and reassess the nasal mucosa.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Nasal Button Battery or Paired Magnets[/color]
• Immediate removal by an appropriately trained clinician; obtain urgent ENT support if safe removal is not straightforward.
• After removal, assess mucosal injury, septal damage, bleeding, and possible retained fragments. Arrange ENT follow-up because tissue injury may progress after removal.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed in adults (max daily limit).

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not irrigate, delay removal, or attempt repeated blind extraction. Button batteries can cause severe injury within a short time.
• Avoid blind instrumentation and repeated attempts. Do not use positive-pressure techniques for a button battery, paired magnets, or an object with a high aspiration risk.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent ENT assessment for batteries, paired magnets, significant injury, or failed removal.
• Discharge after uncomplicated removal may be appropriate when bleeding is controlled and no complication is suspected.
• Return immediately for fever, increasing pain, persistent bleeding, foul discharge, or breathing difficulty.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO-HNS Nasal Foreign-Body Management Principles; Pediatric Button Battery Guidance; Local Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Persistent clear, watery nasal or ear drainage after head trauma or skull-base surgery.
• Drainage may increase with certain positional changes.
• A salty or metallic taste may accompany CSF rhinorrhea.
• Associated skull-base fracture, hemotympanum, or neurological injury increases suspicion.
• Fever, neck stiffness, severe headache, photophobia, or altered mental status may indicate meningitis.

[color=#991B1B]CRITICAL POINT:[/color] Clear drainage is not diagnostic by itself. Confirm the diagnosis with appropriate testing where possible.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess trauma severity, neurological status, and signs of meningitis.
• Contact ENT and neurosurgery when traumatic or postoperative CSF leakage is suspected.
• Avoid nasal packing, nasal instrumentation, and unnecessary manipulation of the ear.
• Advise the patient not to blow the nose forcefully or perform Valsalva maneuvers.
• Elevate the head if clinically appropriate and not contraindicated by other injuries.
• If meningitis is suspected, obtain appropriate cultures promptly when feasible and initiate emergency empiric antimicrobial treatment without unsafe delay.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Beta-2 transferrin or beta-trace protein testing of drainage where available.
• CT of the skull base and relevant sinuses to identify a bony defect.
• MRI or specialized cisternographic imaging when the leak site remains uncertain.
• CT head and broader trauma imaging according to the injury mechanism and clinical findings.
• If meningitis is suspected, perform blood cultures and the appropriate infection work-up. Lumbar puncture must be considered only after assessing contraindications.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Conservative Measures[/color]
• No medication is required solely to stop an uncomplicated CSF leak; management depends on the cause and associated injuries.
• Monitor neurological status, fever, meningism, leak volume, and persistence of drainage.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Suspected Bacterial Meningitis[/color]
• Start the local adult bacterial meningitis regimen immediately when clinically suspected. Common empiric component: ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours; additional agents (vancomycin, ampicillin) may be required depending on resistance patterns, age, immune status, and local guidelines.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Definitive Management[/color]
• Many acute traumatic leaks are initially observed under specialist supervision.
• Persistent leaks, recurrent meningitis, large defects, or selected high-risk injuries may require endoscopic or open surgical repair.
• Antibiotics are used to treat suspected or confirmed infection; routine prophylactic antibiotics for every CSF leak are not universally recommended.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Conservative management is not appropriate for every leak. Deterioration, infection, significant skull-base injury, or persistent leakage requires urgent specialist reassessment.
• This is not a complete universal meningitis regimen. Do not delay treatment for imaging or lumbar puncture when doing so would be unsafe.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Suspected traumatic or postoperative CSF leakage generally requires urgent specialist assessment.
• Admit patients with significant trauma, persistent leakage, neurological abnormalities, fever, or suspected meningitis.
• Escalate immediately for altered mental status, seizures, severe headache, neck stiffness, or haemodynamic instability.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Head Injury Guidance; ENT/Neurosurgical Skull-Base Leak Guidance; Local Protocols.

Rhinology (Nose & Sinuses).title: Severe Epistaxis Refractory to Initial Treatment

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Persistent nasal bleeding despite correct compression and initial treatment.
• Suspected posterior bleeding, especially with blood in the oropharynx and no visible anterior source.
• Haemodynamic instability, syncope, tachycardia, hypotension, or signs of significant blood loss.
• Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, coagulopathy, or significant comorbid disease.
• Airway compromise from heavy bleeding or aspiration.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and haemodynamic stability.
• Sit the patient forward if conscious and appropriate; instruct them to spit out blood rather than swallow it.
• Apply firm continuous compression to the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes without repeatedly releasing pressure to check.
• Use suction when needed to clear blood and allow safe assessment.
• Establish IV access and obtain blood tests when bleeding is severe or the patient is unstable.
• Call ENT urgently for persistent bleeding, suspected posterior epistaxis, or failed initial treatment.
• Protect the airway if bleeding is massive or the patient cannot handle secretions.
• Do not delay resuscitation for local procedures in an unstable patient.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC and platelet count in significant or recurrent bleeding.
• Coagulation studies when anticoagulant use, liver disease, or a bleeding disorder is suspected.
• Group and screen or crossmatch if substantial blood loss or transfusion is possible.
• Review anticoagulants, antiplatelets, hypertension, trauma, and other contributing factors.
• Imaging is not routinely required for uncomplicated epistaxis but may be indicated when a tumor, vascular lesion, or trauma is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Topical Vasoconstrictor[/color]
• A locally approved topical oxymetazoline preparation may be used according to its product instructions and local epistaxis protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid excessive or repeated use. Consider cardiovascular contraindications and local guidance.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Topical Tranexamic Acid[/color]
• Some emergency protocols use topical tranexamic acid, commonly 500 mg in 5 mL applied to the bleeding site using an appropriate delivery method.
• [color=#991B1B]Evidence and practice vary. Topical tranexamic acid must not delay packing, airway management, or definitive ENT treatment when required.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Nasal Packing[/color]
• Indication: Persistent bleeding when a source cannot be controlled with initial measures, or when directed by the treating clinician.
• [color=#991B1B]Posterior packing can cause significant discomfort, hypoxia, and other complications; it generally requires admission and specialist oversight. Do not blindly pack a suspected major facial or skull-base injury.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Resuscitation for Significant Blood Loss[/color]
• Use isotonic crystalloid as an initial bridge when indicated, with blood products for major haemorrhage according to the local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Crystalloid alone is inadequate for uncontrolled major haemorrhage. Prioritize definitive bleeding control and appropriate blood-product resuscitation.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• ENT may perform endoscopic cautery or surgical arterial control.
• Endovascular embolization may be considered when bleeding persists or surgery is unsuitable.
• Correct reversible coagulopathy when clinically indicated.
• Review antithrombotic therapy individually; do not automatically discontinue essential anticoagulants without considering thrombotic risk.
• Identify and treat an underlying cause, including trauma, vascular lesions, or neoplasia when suspected.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with posterior packing, significant blood loss, haemodynamic instability, or ongoing bleeding.
• Escalate to ICU or a high-dependency setting when airway protection, major transfusion, or close haemodynamic monitoring is needed.
• Discharge only when bleeding is controlled, the patient is stable, and follow-up and return precautions are clear.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO-HNS Nosebleed (Epistaxis) Clinical Practice Guideline; NICE Blood Transfusion/Emergency Bleeding Guidance; Local ENT/Major Haemorrhage Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: A collection of pus between the tonsillar capsule and surrounding tissues, usually developing as a complication of tonsillitis.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Severe unilateral sore throat.
• Fever and painful swallowing.
• Trismus.
• Muffled 'hot potato' voice.
• Unilateral peritonsillar swelling and uvular deviation.
• Drooling or inability to swallow in severe cases.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway and ability to handle secretions.
• Keep NPO if drainage or anesthesia may be required.
• Provide analgesia and IV fluids if oral intake is inadequate.
• Obtain urgent ENT assessment.
• Suspected airway compromise requires immediate senior airway support.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. DRAINAGE[/color]
• Needle aspiration or incision and drainage by a trained clinician.
• Obtain pus culture when indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. ANTIBIOTICS[/color]
• Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours.
• Alternative: amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO every 12 hours.
• Penicillin allergy: select alternative per local resistance.
• Cover streptococci and oral anaerobes.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not attempt drainage without appropriate training, equipment, and airway support.
• Antibiotics alone may be insufficient when a drainable abscess is present.

sections.heading: 06 — DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
sections.content:
• Severe tonsillitis.
• Peritonsillar cellulitis.
• Retropharyngeal or parapharyngeal abscess.
• Epiglottitis.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for airway concerns, sepsis, dehydration, inability to swallow, or failed outpatient treatment.
• Discharge after successful treatment when airway is safe and oral intake is adequate.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Trismus and unilateral swelling strongly suggest quinsy.
• Drooling, respiratory distress, or inability to handle secretions are emergency warning signs.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Merck Manual Professional Edition: Peritonsillar Abscess.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: A deep neck space infection involving the retropharyngeal tissues, occurring predominantly in young children but also possible in adults.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Fever and sore throat.
• Dysphagia or drooling.
• Neck stiffness, pain, or limited neck movement.
• Muffled voice.
• Posterior pharyngeal wall swelling.
• Stridor or respiratory distress in severe cases.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway and ability to handle secretions.
• Keep the patient NPO.
• Obtain urgent ENT and pediatric/anesthesia support.
• Establish IV access and provide fluids.
• Avoid unnecessary throat manipulation in a child with airway symptoms.

sections.heading: 04 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC and CRP.
• Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck when stable.
• Blood cultures in suspected sepsis.
• Do not delay airway management for imaging.

sections.heading: 05 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IV ANTIBIOTICS[/color]
• Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours (Adults).
• Ampicillin-sulbactam 50 mg/kg/dose IV every 6 hours (Pediatrics).
• Alternative: Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole.
• Cover streptococci, oral anaerobes, and S. aureus.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. DRAINAGE[/color]
• Indications: Airway compromise, sepsis, large/mature abscess, failure to improve with antibiotics.

sections.heading: 06 — WARNINGS
sections.content: • A threatened airway requires immediate management. Do not wait for antibiotic response.

sections.heading: 07 — DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
sections.content:
• Epiglottitis.
• Peritonsillar abscess.
• Bacterial cervical lymphadenitis.
• Meningitis.
• Foreign body.

sections.heading: 08 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Hospital admission for IV antibiotics and observation.
• ICU care for airway compromise or severe sepsis.

sections.heading: 09 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Neck stiffness with fever and dysphagia in a child is concerning.
• Airway obstruction and mediastinal spread are important complications.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Merck Manual Professional Edition: Deep Neck Infections.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: A rapidly progressive cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, commonly originating from an odontogenic infection. Tongue elevation and floor-of-mouth swelling can cause life-threatening airway obstruction.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Dental pain or recent dental infection.
• Painful, firm swelling beneath the jaw.
• Floor-of-mouth induration and tongue elevation.
• Dysphagia, drooling, and muffled voice.
• Fever and systemic toxicity.
• Respiratory distress or stridor.

[color=#991B1B]RED FLAGS: Rapidly progressive swelling, inability to swallow secretions, tongue elevation, stridor, hypoxemia.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess the airway immediately.
• Call ENT, anesthesia, and oral/maxillofacial surgery urgently.
• Keep NPO and upright if tolerated.
• Provide oxygen and monitoring.
• Establish IV access and initiate sepsis management.
• Prepare for early definitive airway management.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay airway protection for CT imaging.
• Sedation or routine induction in an unstable patient may precipitate complete airway obstruction.

sections.heading: 05 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IV ANTIBIOTICS[/color]
• Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours.
• Alternative: Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole.
• Cover oral streptococci and anaerobes.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. SOURCE CONTROL[/color]
• Drainage of infected spaces when indicated.
• Definitive treatment of the dental source.

sections.heading: 06 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, CRP, renal function, blood cultures.
• Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck in stable patients.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Hospital admission is required.
• ICU care for airway compromise or sepsis.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Ludwig's angina may obstruct the airway before a discrete abscess develops.
• Early airway planning and IV antibiotics are essential.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Merck Manual Professional Edition: Deep Neck Infections.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Fever, severe sore throat, unilateral neck pain, or swelling.
• Trismus, dysphagia, odynophagia, or muffled voice.
• Medial displacement of the tonsil or lateral pharyngeal wall bulging.
• Neck stiffness or painful limitation of movement.
• Stridor, drooling, respiratory distress, or inability to handle secretions indicates possible airway compromise.
• Sepsis, cranial neuropathy, or swelling along the sternocleidomastoid region may indicate vascular or deep-space extension.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, sepsis, and ability to handle secretions.
• Contact ENT and anesthesia urgently if airway compromise is possible.
• Keep the patient fasting.
• Avoid unnecessary pharyngeal examination or sedation in a patient with a threatened airway.
• Establish IV access and start empiric IV antibiotics promptly.
• Obtain urgent imaging in a stable patient; do not delay airway stabilization for CT.
• Consider associated internal jugular vein thrombosis or mediastinal spread if clinically suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck in a stable patient to identify the abscess and its extent.
• CBC, CRP, renal function, electrolytes, and blood cultures if septic or systemically unwell.
• Culture material obtained during drainage.
• CT of the chest if descending mediastinal infection is suspected.
• Additional vascular imaging if internal jugular vein thrombosis or carotid involvement is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Empiric IV Antibiotics — Adults[/color]
• Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours (renal adjusted).
• Alternative: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 hours (adjust for renal function).
• Add Vancomycin if MRSA coverage is indicated (weight-based, therapeutic monitoring).

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Airway Management[/color]
• Prepare suction, oxygen, difficult-airway equipment, and emergency surgical-airway equipment.
• Secure the airway early if obstruction is progressing.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Definitive Management[/color]
