• Drainage is often required for a confirmed abscess, especially when large, associated with airway compromise, or not responding to IV antibiotics.
• ENT determines the safest drainage approach.
• Treat the primary source (tonsillar or dental infection).
• Monitor for internal jugular vein thrombosis, carotid complications, sepsis, and descending mediastinitis.
• Tailor antibiotics to culture results and clinical response.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Broader or alternative coverage may be needed according to local resistance patterns, previous antibiotics, allergy history, or complications.
• Sedation or repeated pharyngeal manipulation may precipitate complete obstruction. Do not delay definitive airway management when indicated.
• Do not add vancomycin routinely without an indication. Adjust for renal impairment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with suspected parapharyngeal abscess for IV therapy and specialist assessment.
• ICU or high-dependency care is appropriate for airway compromise, severe sepsis, or major complications.
• Do not discharge a patient with suspected deep neck-space abscess without an appropriate specialist plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ENT Deep Neck Space Infection Guidance; IDSA Antimicrobial Stewardship Guidance; Local Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Acute inflammation and swelling of the epiglottis and adjacent supraglottic structures, potentially causing rapid, life-threatening airway obstruction.

sections.heading: 02 — CAUSES
sections.content:
• Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib).
• Streptococcus species.
• Other bacterial pathogens.

sections.heading: 03 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Sudden severe sore throat and fever.
• Dysphagia and drooling.
• Muffled voice.
• Stridor and respiratory distress.
• Tripod positioning and toxic appearance.

sections.heading: 04 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Recognize possible impending airway obstruction.
• Keep the patient calm and in their preferred position.
• Call senior anesthesia, ENT, and critical care teams immediately.
• Provide oxygen in the least distressing manner.
• Prepare for controlled airway management in an appropriate setting.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not force the patient supine.
• Do not use a tongue depressor to inspect the throat.
• Do not perform unnecessary procedures that may precipitate complete obstruction.
• Do not delay airway stabilization to obtain imaging, blood tests, or cultures.

sections.heading: 06 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. AIRWAY MANAGEMENT[/color]
• Secure the airway when clinically indicated, with the most experienced clinician.
• Have a difficult-airway and emergency surgical-airway plan.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. IV ANTIBIOTICS[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours (Adults).
• Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV every 24 hours (Pediatrics).
• Obtain cultures when feasible without delaying antibiotics or airway stabilization.

sections.heading: 07 — DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
sections.content:
• Viral croup.
• Bacterial tracheitis.
• Retropharyngeal abscess.
• Foreign body aspiration.
• Angioedema.

sections.heading: 08 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Hospital admission is required.
• ICU-level care is indicated for airway compromise, significant respiratory distress, or need for airway protection.

sections.heading: 09 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Drooling, dysphagia, severe sore throat, and toxic appearance should raise suspicion.
• Stridor may be a late sign of severe obstruction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Merck Manual Professional Edition: Epiglottitis.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Partial or complete airway obstruction caused by an aspirated object. Complete obstruction is immediately life-threatening.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Sudden choking or coughing.
• Inability to speak or cry effectively.
• Weak or absent cough.
• Stridor, wheezing, or reduced air entry.
• Cyanosis or loss of consciousness.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]SEVERE OBSTRUCTION — ADULTS AND CHILDREN >1 YEAR[/color]
• If can cough effectively, encourage coughing.
• If unable to cough/speak/breathe: back blows followed by abdominal thrusts.
• Use chest thrusts in pregnancy or if abdominal not feasible.
• If unresponsive, begin CPR.

[color=#1E3A8A]INFANTS UNDER 1 YEAR[/color]
• 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts.
• Do NOT perform abdominal thrusts in infants.
• If unresponsive, begin infant CPR.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content: • Do not perform blind finger sweeps. Remove an object only when it is visible and safely graspable.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Urgent airway and ENT/anesthesia support for persistent obstruction.
• Direct laryngoscopy or bronchoscopy may be required.

sections.heading: 06 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Imaging depends on suspected object and location.
• A normal chest X-ray does not exclude a radiolucent foreign body.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Emergency resuscitation for severe obstruction.
• Urgent specialist assessment for suspected retained airway foreign bodies.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Sudden choking with unilateral wheeze suggests aspiration.
• Button batteries and sharp objects require urgent specialist assessment.
• Do not delay life-saving airway maneuvers for imaging.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Resuscitation Council UK: Adult and Paediatric BLS Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Blunt or penetrating injury to the anterior neck.
• Hoarseness, dysphonia, aphonia, or painful swallowing.
• Stridor, dyspnea, hemoptysis, or subcutaneous emphysema.
• Neck swelling, tenderness over the larynx, or palpable structural abnormality.
• Respiratory distress or progressive voice change may indicate evolving airway obstruction.

[color=#991B1B]CRITICAL POINT:[/color] A patient who initially appears stable can deteriorate as laryngeal edema and hematoma progress.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow trauma priorities and assess airway, breathing, and circulation.
• Call ENT and anesthesia early if laryngeal injury is suspected.
• Provide oxygen and continuous monitoring.
• Keep the patient fasting and prepare difficult-airway equipment.
• Avoid unnecessary manipulation of the neck and avoid blind airway instrumentation.
• If airway obstruction is imminent, secure the airway with the most appropriate expert-led technique; emergency front-of-neck access may be required.
• Control external bleeding without compromising the airway.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Flexible nasolaryngoscopy in a stable patient when performed by an appropriately trained clinician.
• CT of the neck with contrast in a stable patient when structural injury or associated vascular injury is suspected.
• CT angiography if the mechanism or findings suggest blunt cerebrovascular injury.
• Assess for associated cervical spine, esophageal, tracheal, and vascular injuries.
• Do not send an unstable patient to CT before airway stabilization.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Oxygen and Airway Preparation[/color]
• Provide supplemental oxygen and titrate to maintain adequate oxygenation.
• Ensure oxygen delivery, suction, bag-mask ventilation, difficult-airway equipment, and emergency front-of-neck airway equipment are immediately available.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Airway Intervention[/color]
• Indication: Progressive stridor, respiratory fatigue, severe airway narrowing, rapidly expanding hematoma, or inability to maintain oxygenation.
• ENT and anesthesia should plan the airway according to the injury pattern. Maintain spontaneous ventilation when appropriate and avoid repeated traumatic attempts.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally or by an appropriate non-oral route every 6–8 hours as needed in adults.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude impending upper-airway obstruction.
• Blind intubation or repeated attempts may worsen a disrupted larynx and create a false passage.
• Avoid excessive sedation or analgesia that may obscure deterioration in an evolving airway emergency.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with suspected significant laryngeal injury for specialist observation.
• ICU or high-dependency care is appropriate for airway compromise, progressive edema, significant structural injury, or an artificial airway.
• Discharge only after specialist assessment confirms a low risk of delayed airway deterioration.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS Principles; ENT/Difficult-Airway Management Guidance; Local Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Rapid swelling of the lips, tongue, floor of mouth, soft palate, or pharynx.
• Hoarseness, voice change, dysphagia, drooling, stridor, or respiratory distress.
• Urticaria, itching, wheezing, or hypotension suggest histamine-mediated anaphylaxis.
• ACE inhibitor use or a history of hereditary angioedema may suggest bradykinin-mediated disease.
• [color=#991B1B]Absence of urticaria does not exclude a life-threatening reaction.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and progression of swelling.
• Call anesthesia and ENT early if tongue, floor-of-mouth, or laryngeal involvement is suspected.
• Give IM epinephrine immediately if anaphylaxis is suspected.
• Provide oxygen, monitoring, IV access, and resuscitation as indicated.
• Prepare for early expert airway management if voice changes, stridor, progressive tongue swelling, or respiratory distress develops.
• Stop a suspected causative drug, such as an ACE inhibitor.
• Do not delay airway intervention while waiting for medications to work.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical during the emergency.
• Check glucose and other investigations according to the patient's condition.
• In suspected hereditary or recurrent bradykinin-mediated angioedema, consider C4 and C1-inhibitor testing after stabilization.
• Serum tryptase may help support anaphylaxis retrospectively when obtained at an appropriate time, but treatment must not wait for results.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. IM Epinephrine for Suspected Anaphylaxis[/color]
• Adult dose: 0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL preparation) into anterolateral thigh. Repeat after ~5 minutes if airway, breathing, or circulation problems persist.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT give the 1 mg/mL preparation as an IV bolus for routine anaphylaxis treatment.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Crystalloid for Anaphylactic Shock[/color]
• Adult initial bolus commonly 500–1,000 mL of isotonic crystalloid, reassessing after each bolus; larger volumes may be required.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Antihistamine for Skin Symptoms[/color]
• Cetirizine 10 mg orally in a stable adult who can swallow safely. Use only as an adjunct after immediate airway and circulatory threats are addressed.
• [color=#991B1B]Antihistamines do NOT treat laryngeal edema or shock and must never delay epinephrine in anaphylaxis.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Corticosteroids[/color]
• Steroids are NOT routine first-line treatment for anaphylaxis and do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions. Use only as an adjunct when clinically indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]5. Bradykinin-Mediated Angioedema[/color]
• For suspected hereditary angioedema, use an approved disease-specific treatment where available (e.g., C1-inhibitor concentrate or icatibant) according to local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids may have little or no effect in bradykinin-mediated angioedema. Airway management remains the priority.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Secure the airway early if swelling is progressive or laryngeal involvement is suspected.
• Discontinue the causative ACE inhibitor permanently when implicated.
• Arrange allergy/immunology evaluation for recurrent or unexplained attacks.
• Provide an anaphylaxis action plan and appropriate auto-injector prescription when indicated.
• Refer suspected hereditary angioedema for specialist confirmation and prevention planning.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with tongue, pharyngeal, or laryngeal involvement or any airway symptoms.
• ICU or high-dependency care may be required for progressive edema or an artificial airway.
• Discharge only after appropriate observation and resolution of risk, with clear return precautions and follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance; Resuscitation Council UK Anaphylaxis Guidance; Hereditary Angioedema Specialist Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, voice change, or a barking cough.
• Increased work of breathing, suprasternal retractions, or difficulty speaking.
• Drooling or inability to swallow secretions.
• Causes include anaphylaxis, infection, thermal or chemical injury, post-extubation edema, and laryngeal trauma.
• [color=#991B1B]Agitation, exhaustion, reduced air entry, cyanosis, or altered mental status are signs of impending respiratory failure.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and the severity of obstruction.
• Call anesthesia and ENT urgently for severe or progressive symptoms.
• Keep the patient in the position of comfort; avoid unnecessary agitation.
• Provide oxygen and continuous monitoring.
• Prepare difficult-airway equipment and emergency front-of-neck access equipment.
• Treat the cause immediately, such as IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis.
• Do not delay airway stabilization for imaging or diagnostic procedures in an unstable patient.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Clinical assessment is primary in a threatened airway.
• Flexible nasolaryngoscopy may be useful in a stable patient when performed by a trained clinician.
• Blood gas testing may help assess respiratory failure but must not delay treatment.
• Imaging is considered only when the airway is stable and the result will affect management.
• Investigate the underlying cause after stabilization.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Oxygen and Monitoring[/color]
• Titrate oxygen to clinical need and oxygenation target; use high-concentration oxygen during severe respiratory compromise.
• Monitor respiratory effort, stridor, mental status, heart rate, and oxygen saturation continuously.
• [color=#991B1B]A normal oxygen saturation early in the course does not exclude critical upper-airway obstruction.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Nebulized Epinephrine for Selected Upper-Airway Edema[/color]
• For selected cases of significant upper-airway edema: epinephrine 5 mg nebulized (using appropriate 1 mg/mL solution) under local emergency protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Nebulized epinephrine is a temporizing measure, not a substitute for definitive airway management. If anaphylaxis is suspected, give IM epinephrine as first-line treatment.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Corticosteroids for Selected Inflammatory or Post-Extubation Edema[/color]
• Dose and agent depend on cause and local protocol; steroids are not a universal treatment for all causes of stridor. Do not rely on them to rescue a patient with impending airway obstruction.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Secure the airway with an expert-led plan if obstruction is severe or progressive.
• Use cause-specific treatment for anaphylaxis, infection, trauma, or post-extubation edema.
• Consider heliox only as a temporary adjunct in selected settings; it does not correct a critically narrowed airway.
• Reassess after treatment because edema may recur or progress.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit any patient with persistent stridor, significant laryngeal edema, or a need for nebulized epinephrine and close observation.
• ICU care is indicated for respiratory failure, progressive obstruction, or a secured airway requiring intensive monitoring.
• Discharge only after specialist assessment confirms that the airway is stable and the underlying cause has been addressed.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Difficult Airway Society Emergency Airway Guidance; Resuscitation Council UK Anaphylaxis Guidance; Local ENT/Anesthesia Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: An acute problem involving a tracheostomy tube or stoma, including obstruction, displacement, accidental decannulation, bleeding, or respiratory deterioration.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Respiratory distress or desaturation.
• Difficulty passing a suction catheter.
• Reduced or absent airflow through the tube.
• Absent or abnormal capnography waveform.
• Tube displacement or accidental decannulation.
• Bleeding from the tube or stoma.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call resuscitation team and experienced airway support.
• Apply high-concentration oxygen to both the face AND the tracheostomy stoma.
• Remove any speaking valve or cap.
• Remove a removable inner cannula and check for obstruction.
• Attempt gentle suction if trained.
• If tube is nonfunctional, remove promptly according to emergency algorithm.

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not repeatedly attempt ventilation through a tube confirmed blocked or displaced.
• Avoid blind reinsertion, particularly through an immature stoma.

sections.heading: 05 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. BLOCKED TRACHEOSTOMY[/color]
• Remove inner cannula.
• Attempt suction.
• If obstructed, remove nonfunctional tube.
• Oxygenate through face or stoma.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. DISPLACED TUBE[/color]
• Assess upper airway patency.
• Reinsertion only by trained clinician to avoid false passage.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. BLEEDING[/color]
• Minor bleeding: evaluate for trauma/infection.
• Significant/pulsatile bleeding: major vascular complication, requires immediate surgical management.

sections.heading: 06 — MONITORING
sections.content:
• Continuous SpO2 and cardiorespiratory monitoring.
• Waveform capnography when available.
• Reassess chest movement, airflow, consciousness.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Urgent ICU or specialist airway management for obstruction, displacement, or major bleeding.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Oxygenation takes priority over attempts to save the tube.
• A blocked or displaced tube should not be left in place.
• Total laryngectomy patients must be ventilated through the neck stoma (no connection to upper airway).

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: National Tracheostomy Safety Project (NTSP); OpenAnesthesia.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Respiratory distress, desaturation, increased work of breathing, or inability to pass a suction catheter.
• A blocked tube may present with reduced airflow, high airway pressures, or ineffective ventilation.
• Displacement or accidental decannulation may cause rapid respiratory deterioration.
• Bleeding may be minor or may indicate a life-threatening tracheo-innominate artery fistula.
• Subcutaneous emphysema, neck swelling, or surgical emphysema may suggest false passage or airway injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call for help immediately and identify whether the patient has a tracheostomy or a total laryngectomy.
• Give oxygen to the face and the stoma as appropriate while assessing the patient's anatomy and airflow.
• Remove any speaking valve or cap.
• Remove the inner cannula if present and assess whether airflow improves.
• Attempt suction only if appropriate and do not force a catheter through resistance.
• If the tube is blocked or displaced, follow the local emergency tracheostomy algorithm.
• If the patient is deteriorating and ventilation through the tube is ineffective, trained clinicians may need to remove the tube and provide oxygenation through the appropriate route.
• For a total laryngectomy, the stoma is the only route to the lungs; face-mask ventilation will not oxygenate the patient.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Clinical assessment and immediate response to airway maneuvers take priority.
• Check oxygen saturation, ECG, capnography when available, and respiratory effort.
• Obtain blood gas analysis if respiratory failure is suspected and this will not delay stabilization.
• Chest radiography or bronchoscopy may be needed after stabilization to assess tube position, obstruction, or complications.
• Investigate significant bleeding urgently with ENT and surgical teams.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Blocked Tracheostomy Tube[/color]
• Remove inner cannula if present, assess airflow, and follow emergency tracheostomy algorithm.
• Ensure suction, oxygen, bag-mask equipment, spare tracheostomy tubes (same size and one size smaller), and emergency airway equipment are available.
• [color=#991B1B]Do not repeatedly force a suction catheter or ventilation through a suspected blocked or displaced tube.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Displaced or Accidentally Removed Tracheostomy Tube[/color]
• Call ENT and anesthesia immediately. Management depends on whether the stoma is mature and whether the upper airway is patent.
• [color=#991B1B]Blind reinsertion into an immature or difficult stoma can create a false passage and cause fatal airway obstruction. Do not delay oxygenation while attempting repeated replacement.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Significant Bleeding or Suspected Tracheo-Innominate Fistula[/color]
• Treat brisk or pulsatile bleeding as a life-threatening emergency. Call ENT, anesthesia, and surgical team immediately.
• [color=#991B1B]A small sentinel bleed may precede catastrophic hemorrhage. Do not dismiss new tracheostomy bleeding as minor without urgent assessment.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Correct tube position or replace the tube under appropriate conditions.
• Treat the underlying cause (mucus plugging, infection, airway narrowing).
• Arrange bronchoscopy or surgical assessment when indicated.
• Investigate significant bleeding urgently for vascular injury.
• Review humidification, suctioning, tube care, and emergency equipment after stabilization.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Any significant obstruction, displacement, respiratory compromise, or bleeding requires urgent specialist assessment.
• Admit patients with unresolved complications or a need for airway intervention.
• Ensure caregivers and staff have appropriate training and an emergency tracheostomy plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: National Tracheostomy Safety Project Emergency Algorithms; Difficult Airway Society Guidance; Local Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Sudden dysphagia during a meal, often involving meat or another solid food.
• Sensation of food stuck in the throat or chest.
• Regurgitation, drooling, or inability to swallow saliva.
• Complete obstruction is suggested by inability to handle secretions.
• Stridor, choking, or respiratory distress suggests possible airway involvement or aspiration.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, and ability to manage secretions.
• Keep the patient fasting.
• Obtain urgent gastroenterology or endoscopy consultation.
• Arrange emergent endoscopy when the patient cannot handle secretions or has complete obstruction.
• Do not induce vomiting or blindly push the bolus down.
• Avoid giving oral food, drink, or tablets to a patient with complete obstruction.
• Consider airway protection when aspiration risk is high.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Diagnosis is often clinical.
• Plain radiographs may help when a radiopaque foreign body or perforation is suspected, but a normal radiograph does not exclude food impaction.
• CT is appropriate if perforation, a sharp object, or another complication is suspected.
• Endoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
• After resolution, assess for underlying esophageal disease (stricture, Schatzki ring, eosinophilic esophagitis).

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Endoscopic Removal[/color]
• Indication: Complete obstruction, inability to handle secretions, or persistent impaction.
• Perform urgent endoscopic removal or advancement under direct visualization according to specialist judgment.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay emergency endoscopy in complete obstruction to try medications or imaging.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Glucagon — Selected Cases Only[/color]
• Some protocols use glucagon 1 mg IV once in a stable patient while endoscopy is being arranged.
• [color=#991B1B]Evidence of benefit is limited. Avoid relying on glucagon in complete obstruction, and use caution because it can cause nausea and vomiting, increasing aspiration risk.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Acid Suppression After Assessment[/color]
• A proton pump inhibitor may be prescribed when reflux or esophagitis is suspected after the obstruction is resolved.
• [color=#991B1B]Acid suppression does not remove an impacted bolus and must not delay endoscopy.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Remove or safely advance the bolus endoscopically.
• Assess for mucosal injury and perforation.
• Arrange investigation of underlying esophageal disease, including biopsies for eosinophilic esophagitis when appropriate.
• Provide dietary advice and follow-up according to the identified cause.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or observe patients with complete obstruction, aspiration, significant mucosal injury, or suspected perforation.
• Discharge may be appropriate after successful resolution if the patient can swallow safely and there is no complication.
• Return immediately for chest or neck pain, fever, dyspnea, or inability to swallow.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ASGE Management of Ingested Foreign Bodies and Food Impactions; ESGE Foreign Body and Food Bolus Management Guidance; Local Emergency Endoscopy Protocols.

Head, Neck & Esophageal Emergencies.title: Caustic Injury of the Upper Aerodigestive Tract

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
History of ingestion or exposure to acids, alkalis, or corrosive household or industrial products.
• Oral burns, drooling, dysphagia, odynophagia, vomiting, or chest/abdominal pain.
• Hoarseness, stridor, respiratory distress, or neck swelling may indicate airway injury.
• [color=#991B1B]Severe injury may occur even without obvious oral burns.[/color]
• Hematemesis, severe pain, shock, or signs of perforation suggest a complicated injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and the nature and timing of exposure.
• Contact poison control or a toxicology service where available, along with ENT and gastroenterology.
• Give oxygen and prepare for early expert airway management if edema or respiratory symptoms are progressing.
• Keep the patient fasting.
• Remove contaminated clothing and irrigate exposed skin or eyes with copious water when relevant.
• Do NOT induce vomiting.
• Do NOT attempt chemical neutralization with another substance.
• Do NOT administer activated charcoal routinely for corrosive ingestion.
• Do NOT force oral fluids in a patient with dysphagia, drooling, or possible airway injury.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, blood gas, lactate, and other tests guided by severity.
• Chest and abdominal imaging when perforation or thoracic complications are suspected.
• CT of the neck or chest may be indicated in severe cases or when deep injury is suspected.
• Endoscopy is commonly considered within the first 12–24 hours in patients with significant ingestion, according to specialist assessment and local protocols.
• Avoid endoscopy when suspected perforation or instability makes it unsafe until the specialist team determines the appropriate approach.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Airway Support[/color]
• Oxygen according to the patient's respiratory status and oxygenation target.
• Prepare suction, difficult-airway equipment, and emergency surgical-airway equipment.
• [color=#991B1B]Progressive edema may make later intubation difficult. Seek early expert assistance; do not delay a necessary airway intervention.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Fluids[/color]
• Use isotonic crystalloid according to haemodynamic status; in shock, administer reassessed boluses according to the adult resuscitation protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia[/color]
• Select analgesia according to severity, haemodynamic status, and organ function; paracetamol may be appropriate in selected stable patients.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid oral medications in patients unable to swallow safely. Avoid masking worsening pain without reassessment.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Consult ENT and gastroenterology early for suspected significant injury.
• Manage airway injury and esophageal or gastric injury according to specialist assessment.
• Surgery may be required for perforation, necrosis, or severe transmural injury.
• Steroids and prophylactic antibiotics are NOT routine for every caustic ingestion; use only for a specific indication.
• Arrange nutritional support and follow-up for strictures or delayed complications.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with airway symptoms, significant ingestion, persistent vomiting, severe pain, abnormal investigations, or suspected deep injury.
• ICU care may be needed for airway compromise, shock, or major tissue injury.
• Discharge only after specialist assessment establishes low risk and a safe follow-up plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Esophageal Emergencies Guidance; AACT/Poison-Control Guidance; Local Toxicology/ENT/Gastroenterology Protocols.

Head, Neck & Esophageal Emergencies.title: Facial Nerve Injury in ENT Emergencies

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
New unilateral facial weakness involving the forehead, eye closure, and mouth.
• Facial weakness following temporal bone trauma, otitis media, mastoiditis, or ear surgery.
• Associated hearing loss, vertigo, otorrhea, or severe ear pain.
• Vesicles around the ear or in the external auditory canal may suggest Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
• [color=#991B1B]Forehead sparing, limb weakness, speech disturbance, or other focal neurological findings may indicate a central lesion such as stroke.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Establish the time of onset and assess for stroke symptoms.
• Activate the local stroke pathway when stroke is suspected; do not assume every facial palsy is peripheral.
• Assess airway and swallowing if multiple cranial nerves are involved.
• Examine the ear and document facial nerve function.
• In traumatic cases, follow head injury and cervical spine protocols.
• Protect the cornea immediately if eye closure is incomplete.
• Obtain urgent ENT review for facial weakness associated with trauma, invasive infection, or other otologic disease.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Full neurological examination, including forehead movement, eye closure, and lower facial movement.
• CT head and/or temporal bone imaging when trauma or structural injury is suspected.
• MRI when central pathology, tumor, or selected inflammatory disease is suspected.
• Otoscopy and hearing assessment.
• Glucose testing and other investigations guided by the suspected cause.
• Electrodiagnostic testing may be considered by specialists in selected severe traumatic cases.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Corneal Protection[/color]
• Use preservative-free lubricating eye drops frequently while awake; use lubricating eye ointment at night when needed.
• Ensure the eye remains lubricated and closes safely; consider gentle eyelid taping at night when appropriate.
• [color=#991B1B]Incomplete eye closure can cause corneal abrasion and vision loss. Arrange urgent ophthalmology review for eye pain, redness, photophobia, or visual changes.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Corticosteroids for Eligible Acute Bell's Palsy[/color]
• For adults with clinically diagnosed Bell's palsy: prednisolone 50–60 mg orally once daily for 5 days, then taper over next 5 days, per local guidance. Start early, ideally within 72 hours of onset.
• [color=#991B1B]This regimen is for selected Bell's palsy cases, not a universal treatment for facial weakness caused by trauma, stroke, or invasive ear infection. Exclude serious alternative causes.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Antiviral Therapy in Selected Cases[/color]
• Antivirals may be considered with corticosteroids in severe Bell's palsy or suspected Ramsay Hunt syndrome; drug selection and dosing follow local protocol and renal function.
• [color=#991B1B]Antivirals are not a substitute for corticosteroids in eligible Bell's palsy and should not delay urgent evaluation of other causes.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Treat the underlying cause, including trauma, otologic infection, or herpes zoster when diagnosed.
• Facial palsy after temporal bone trauma requires urgent specialist assessment; management depends on onset, severity, imaging, and nerve function.
• Arrange eye care and facial nerve follow-up.
• Consider facial rehabilitation for persistent weakness.
• Reassess patients with progressive weakness, recurrent palsy, bilateral symptoms, or failure to improve.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or urgently refer patients with traumatic facial palsy, multiple cranial neuropathies, suspected invasive infection, or associated neurological deficits.
• Activate emergency stroke care when central neurological signs are present.
• Stable isolated Bell's palsy may be managed as an outpatient after appropriate assessment, eye protection, and follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO-HNS Bell's Palsy Clinical Practice Guideline; NICE Stroke/TIA Guidance; ENT/Temporal Bone Trauma Protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Ocular injury caused by acids, alkalis, or other chemicals. Alkali injuries can penetrate deeply and cause severe ocular damage.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Severe pain, redness, tearing, and photophobia.
• Blurred vision.
• Conjunctival swelling and corneal opacity.
• Severe cases may show limbal ischemia or extensive tissue damage.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Start copious irrigation immediately with clean water, normal saline, or Ringer's lactate.
• Do not delay irrigation to obtain history, measure visual acuity, or contact ophthalmology.
• Remove contact lenses and accessible particulate material when safe.
• Check ocular surface pH when available; continue irrigation until physiologic pH is achieved.
• Recheck pH after a short pause to detect rebound acidity or alkalinity.
• Arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IRRIGATION[/color]
• Irrigate continuously and abundantly; several liters may be required.
• Evert the eyelids and remove retained particles from the conjunctival fornices when trained and when globe rupture has been excluded.
• Document the chemical, exposure time, irrigation performed, pH, and visual acuity when safely obtainable.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. ADDITIONAL TREATMENT[/color]
• Topical anesthetic may be used by a clinician to facilitate irrigation.
• Ophthalmology may prescribe topical antibiotics, cycloplegics, corticosteroids, or other agents depending on injury severity.
• Severe burns may require admission and surgical treatment.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not attempt chemical neutralization with another acid or alkali.
• If open globe injury is suspected, avoid pressure and obtain immediate specialist guidance regarding decontamination.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Immediate ophthalmology referral for significant chemical burns, corneal opacity, reduced vision, persistent abnormal pH, or suspected limbal injury.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Irrigation is the priority; do not wait for a preferred solution.
• Alkali burns can progress despite initially modest symptoms.
• Avoid topical corticosteroids unless directed by ophthalmology.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO EyeWiki: Chemical Eye Injury.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: A full-thickness wound of the cornea or sclera caused by penetrating trauma or blunt trauma resulting in globe rupture.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Severe pain and reduced vision.
• Irregular or peaked pupil.
• Visible wound or protruding intraocular tissue.
• Hyphema or abnormal anterior chamber depth.
• Positive Seidel sign when tested appropriately.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess general trauma and stabilize airway, breathing, and circulation.
• Place a rigid eye shield without pressure on the globe.
• Keep the patient NPO.
• Provide systemic analgesia and antiemetics as required.
• Obtain immediate ophthalmology consultation.
• Check tetanus immunization status.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. PROTECTION AND PREPARATION[/color]
• Prevent rubbing, compression, and further trauma. Avoid manipulation of the eye.
• Obtain urgent surgical assessment.
• CT orbits may be indicated to assess the injury or identify an intraocular foreign body.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. ANTIBIOTICS[/color]
• Systemic broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are generally indicated (e.g., IV vancomycin plus a 3rd/4th-gen cephalosporin).
• Select exact agents according to local protocols.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not perform tonometry, ocular ultrasound, pressure patching, or forced eyelid examination.
• Do not remove an embedded object.
• Avoid MRI if a metallic foreign body is suspected.
• Do not delay urgent surgical repair to complete investigations or antibiotic administration.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Immediate transfer/admission for ophthalmic surgical management.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• A seemingly small wound may conceal a serious globe injury.
• The shield must not exert pressure.
• Definitive repair is time-critical.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO EyeWiki: Pre-Ophthalmologist Management of Eye Trauma.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
A foreign body may remain on the conjunctiva or corneal surface, become embedded in the cornea, or penetrate the globe and enter the eye.

[color=#1E3A8A]High-risk mechanisms:[/color] Hammering metal on metal, grinding, drilling, explosions, high-velocity projectiles. Sharp objects, glass, penetrating trauma. Organic material (increased infection risk).

Symptoms: Foreign-body sensation, tearing, redness, photophobia, pain. Visible foreign material or corneal rust ring. Reduced vision, irregular pupil, shallow anterior chamber, or suspected entry wound in penetrating injury.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] High-velocity mechanism. Protruding or deeply embedded object. Reduced visual acuity, abnormal pupil, hyphema, or positive Seidel sign. Severe pain or signs of endophthalmitis after penetrating trauma.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess visual acuity without applying pressure to the globe.
• Ask specifically about high-velocity metal work, sharp trauma, and protective eyewear.
• [color=#991B1B]If intraocular foreign body or open-globe injury possible: Do NOT remove object. Do NOT press, patch, or manipulate eye. Do NOT perform tonometry or ocular ultrasound. Place rigid eye shield without pressure. Keep NPO and arrange immediate ophthalmology transfer.[/color]
• Provide analgesia and antiemetic treatment when needed to reduce pain, vomiting, and Valsalva-related pressure.
• Update tetanus prophylaxis when indicated by injury and immunization history.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Visual acuity, pupils, and external examination, provided this does not delay transfer or place pressure on eye.
• Slit-lamp examination for superficial foreign body when penetrating injury has been excluded.
• Non-contrast thin-cut CT of orbits when intraocular foreign body or open-globe injury is suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]MRI is contraindicated until a potentially metallic foreign body has been excluded. Do NOT use ocular ultrasound when open-globe injury is suspected before specialist assessment.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Superficial Corneal Foreign Body[/color]
• Removal may be performed by a trained clinician only after confirming injury is superficial and open-globe injury is not suspected.
• Use appropriate magnification, topical anesthetic for examination/procedure, and sterile instruments per local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT attempt removal of a deeply embedded object or one near the visual axis without appropriate expertise. Never use force or manipulate an object that may penetrate the globe.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Antibiotic Treatment After Superficial Removal[/color]
• Erythromycin ophthalmic ointment 0.5% ~1 cm ribbon four times daily for 3–5 days, or alternative topical antibiotic per local guidance.
• For contact lens-associated injury: select an antipseudomonal ophthalmic antibiotic (e.g., ciprofloxacin 0.3% or ofloxacin 0.3%).

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Suspected Intraocular Foreign Body or Open Globe[/color]
• Immediate ophthalmology consultation and transfer for surgical assessment.
• Systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics generally initiated in hospital per open-globe/IOFB protocol.
• Provide tetanus prophylaxis as indicated.
• Maintain NPO status and avoid pressure on the eye.
• Surgical closure and foreign-body management determined by ophthalmic surgeon.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do NOT prescribe a routine superficial-abrasion treatment plan for a suspected intraocular foreign body.
• A normal-looking external eye or a negative initial scan does not completely exclude serious injury when mechanism and clinical findings remain concerning.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Superficial and uncomplicated: discharge may be appropriate after safe removal, reassuring vision, and clear follow-up instructions.
• Deep, central, difficult-to-remove, or infected: urgent ophthalmology review.
• Possible penetrating or intraocular injury: immediate transfer to an ophthalmic surgical service.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Management of Intraocular Foreign Bodies; AAO Open Globe Injury Assessment and Preoperative Management; Defence Medical Services Globe Injury Guideline.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Blood within the anterior chamber of the eye, usually following blunt trauma that damages iris or ciliary body vessels. It may increase intraocular pressure and threaten vision.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Blurred or reduced vision after eye trauma.
• Visible blood in the anterior chamber.
• Eye pain and photophobia.
• Elevated IOP in some cases.
• Severe hyphema may obscure the pupil.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess visual acuity and associated ocular or head trauma.
• Place a rigid eye shield without pressure.
• Elevate the head approximately 30–45 degrees when medically appropriate.
• Arrange urgent, same-day ophthalmology assessment.
• Avoid strenuous activity and prevent further eye injury.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. SUPPORTIVE MANAGEMENT[/color]
• Protective rigid eye shield.
• Head elevation and restricted physical activity.
• Paracetamol for pain when appropriate.
• Antiemetics if nausea or vomiting could increase pressure.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. OPHTHALMOLOGY-DIRECTED TREATMENT[/color]
• Topical corticosteroids may be prescribed.
• Cycloplegic drops may be used.
• Elevated IOP may require topical pressure-lowering medications.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Exclude open globe injury before measuring IOP.
• Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs for routine analgesia.
• Patients with sickle cell disease or trait require particular caution.

sections.heading: 06 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Visual acuity and pupil examination.
• Slit-lamp examination when available.
• IOP measurement only after open globe injury has been excluded.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Urgent ophthalmology assessment for all traumatic hyphema. Admission may be required for significant bleeding or unreliable follow-up.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Rebleeding often occurs during the first several days.
• A small hyphema can still cause elevated IOP.
• Worsening vision or increasing pain requires immediate reassessment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO EyeWiki: Pre-Ophthalmologist Management of Eye Trauma.

Ocular Trauma & Foreign Bodies.title: Orbital Fracture with Extraocular Muscle Entrapment

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Orbital fractures may trap extraocular muscles or orbital soft tissue, particularly in pediatric 'trapdoor' fractures. Entrapment can cause ischemia and oculocardiac reflexes.
• Periorbital bruising and swelling after facial trauma.
• Diplopia or restricted gaze. Pain on eye movement.
• Nausea or vomiting, particularly with attempted upward gaze.
• Infraorbital numbness may occur with orbital floor fractures.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Bradycardia, nausea, vomiting, or syncope triggered by eye movement. Marked restriction of ocular movement. Reduced vision, relative afferent pupillary defect, or suspected globe injury. Proptosis, tense orbit, or rapidly increasing pain suggesting orbital compartment syndrome.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow trauma assessment priorities and stabilize life-threatening injuries.
• Document visual acuity, pupils, ocular movements, diplopia, and facial sensation.
• Avoid nose blowing and advise patient to sneeze with mouth open.
• Provide analgesia and antiemetic when indicated.
• Obtain urgent ophthalmology and maxillofacial consultation if entrapment suspected.
• Treat suspected orbital compartment syndrome immediately according to its dedicated emergency protocol.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Thin-cut CT of orbits and facial bones.
• CT assessment for muscle or soft-tissue entrapment, fracture displacement, orbital hemorrhage, and associated injuries.
• Formal ophthalmic examination.
• Additional head and cervical spine imaging according to trauma indications.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Initial Supportive Management[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed, within patient-specific limits. Antiemetic may be used when clinically indicated.
• Monitor pain, nausea, heart rate, visual acuity, and ocular movement. Keep patient fasting if urgent surgery likely.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid nose blowing (can introduce air into orbit and worsen orbital emphysema). Do NOT press on globe or attempt to manipulate trapped tissue.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Surgical Management[/color]
• Indications: Suspected muscle entrapment (especially with oculocardiac reflex), significant persistent diplopia with mechanical restriction, pediatric trapdoor fracture with entrapment, selected large fractures or progressive enophthalmos.
• Urgent surgical evaluation and release of entrapped tissue when indicated. Timing depends on clinical findings; true entrapment with oculocardiac reflex requires emergency specialist management.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay surgical consultation in a child with restricted eye movement, nausea/vomiting, and bradycardia after orbital trauma.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Manage fracture and any entrapped muscle or soft tissue.
• Monitor ocular motility, diplopia, visual acuity, and orbital position.
• Provide specialist follow-up for persistent diplopia, enophthalmos, or sensory deficits.
• Antibiotics are not automatically required for every closed orbital fracture; use according to injury, sinus involvement, surgical plan, and local guidance.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate specialist assessment for suspected entrapment or oculocardiac reflex.
• Admit when urgent surgery, significant associated trauma, or serious ocular injury is present.
• Outpatient management only after serious ocular injury and entrapment excluded and follow-up assured.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Orbital Floor Fractures; AO Surgery Reference Orbital Trauma; Pediatric Orbital Fracture and Oculocardiac Reflex Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Eyelid lacerations may involve the eyelid margin, levator muscle, canthal tendons, lacrimal drainage system, or globe. Injuries near the medial canthus may damage the canaliculi.

[color=#1E3A8A]High-risk features:[/color] Laceration through eyelid margin. Wound involving medial canthus or punctum. Visible orbital fat (suggesting septal penetration). Ptosis after trauma (suggesting levator injury). Tissue loss, contaminated wounds, animal bites, or high-velocity trauma.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Suspected open-globe injury. Reduced vision, abnormal pupil, or significant ocular pain. Proptosis or tense orbit. Deep penetrating wound, retained foreign body, or associated facial fracture.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess and document visual acuity, pupils, and ocular motility.
• Exclude open-globe injury before manipulating eyelid.
• Control external bleeding with gentle pressure applied to surrounding soft tissue only when open-globe injury not suspected.
• Cover suspected open globe with a rigid shield without pressure.
• Assess tetanus status and mechanism of injury.
• Arrange urgent ophthalmology or oculoplastic consultation for complex wounds.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Detailed ocular examination.
• CT of orbits when penetrating injury, foreign body, fracture, or deep orbital involvement suspected.
• Imaging should not delay urgent surgical assessment when open-globe injury evident.
• Consider wound cultures only in selected infected or heavily contaminated cases.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Wound Care[/color]
• Clean superficial wounds according to local wound-care protocols.
• Avoid probing a deep wound or blindly exploring a laceration near the globe. Do NOT remove a deeply embedded object before specialist assessment.
• [color=#991B1B]Visible orbital fat, medial canthal injury, eyelid-margin disruption, ptosis, or tissue loss requires specialist repair rather than routine skin closure.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Antibiotics when Indicated[/color]
• Antibiotic choice depends on wound mechanism, contamination, bite exposure, local protocols. For selected contaminated wounds or bites, amoxicillin-clavulanate may be used when appropriate.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics are NOT a substitute for surgical repair of canalicular injury or open-globe trauma. Do NOT prescribe prophylactic antibiotics indiscriminately for every simple, clean eyelid laceration.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Definitive Wound Repair[/color]
• Simple superficial skin wounds may be repaired by a suitably trained clinician after globe injury excluded.
• Injuries involving eyelid margin, canaliculus, levator, canthal tendon, or orbital septum require appropriate specialist repair.
• Canalicular injury may require microsurgical repair and temporary stenting.
• [color=#991B1B]Poor alignment of eyelid margin can cause notching, exposure, and chronic irritation. Delayed recognition of canalicular injury may lead to persistent tearing.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Restore eyelid anatomy and function.
• Repair canalicular and deeper structural injuries as indicated.
• Provide wound care, tetanus prophylaxis, and antibiotics when clinically indicated.
• Arrange follow-up to assess healing, eyelid position, tear drainage, and infection.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate referral for suspected open-globe injury or penetrating trauma.
• Urgent specialist repair for canalicular injury, eyelid-margin involvement, levator injury, or tissue loss.
• Discharge only for uncomplicated superficial wounds after appropriate assessment and follow-up arrangements.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Eyelid Laceration Repair; Merck Manual Professional Edition Eyelid Lacerations; Oculoplastic Trauma Management Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Traumatic lens dislocation or subluxation occurs when lens is displaced due to disruption of supporting zonular fibers. May cause acute visual impairment, inflammation, or secondary glaucoma.
• Blurred vision or monocular diplopia after blunt trauma.
• Visible lens displacement or abnormal anterior chamber.
• Irregular or distorted red reflex. Phacodonesis or iridodonesis may be present.
• Intraocular pressure may be elevated if lens obstructs aqueous outflow.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Sudden severe visual loss. Lens displaced into anterior chamber. Markedly elevated intraocular pressure. Associated hyphema, open-globe injury, retinal injury, or severe inflammation. History suggesting penetrating trauma.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess visual acuity, pupils, and mechanism of injury.
• Exclude open-globe injury before performing tonometry or detailed ocular manipulation.
• If open-globe injury suspected, place rigid eye shield without pressure and arrange immediate ophthalmology transfer.
• Obtain urgent ophthalmology assessment for suspected traumatic lens displacement.
• Control pain and vomiting and avoid pressure on globe.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Slit-lamp examination by a trained clinician.
• Intraocular pressure measurement only when open-globe injury excluded.
• Dilated retinal examination when safe and appropriate.
• CT of orbits when associated fracture, foreign body, or significant trauma suspected.
• Ultrasound or other imaging only when appropriate and after open-globe injury excluded.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Initial Stabilization[/color]
• Protect eye from further trauma. Provide analgesia and antiemetic when indicated. Keep patient fasting if urgent surgery likely. Arrange urgent ophthalmology consultation.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT attempt to reposition lens manually. Do NOT use routine glaucoma drops before specialist assessment if open-globe injury remains possible.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Elevated Intraocular Pressure[/color]
• If lens-related secondary glaucoma suspected, obtain urgent ophthalmology guidance.
• Pressure-lowering therapy may be needed, but drug selection depends on mechanism, lens position, inflammation, associated injuries.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid delaying treatment of acute pressure elevation. Do NOT use miotics or other ocular medication empirically without considering lens position and underlying mechanism.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Definitive Ophthalmic Management[/color]
• Observation may be appropriate for selected stable subluxations with acceptable vision and no complications.
• Surgical intervention may be required for anterior lens dislocation, uncontrolled pressure, severe inflammation, or significant visual impairment.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Determine extent of zonular damage and lens displacement.
• Monitor intraocular pressure, inflammation, corneal health, and retinal status.
• Select observation, lens removal, or other surgery according to ophthalmology assessment.
• Plan visual rehabilitation after acute injury stabilized.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent same-day ophthalmology assessment for suspected traumatic lens displacement.
• Immediate emergency management for anterior chamber lens dislocation, acute glaucoma, open-globe injury, or severe visual loss.
• Admission may be necessary if urgent surgery or intensive monitoring required.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Lens Dislocation and Ocular Trauma; AAO Guidance on Traumatic Cataract and Secondary Glaucoma; Ophthalmic Trauma Management Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Traumatic optic neuropathy is injury to the optic nerve following head or orbital trauma. May occur without obvious injury to external eye.
• Reduced vision following blunt or penetrating trauma.
• Impaired color vision or reduced brightness perception.
• Relative afferent pupillary defect when unilateral or asymmetric.
• Normal-appearing optic disc may be present initially in posterior traumatic optic neuropathy.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Rapidly progressive visual loss. Associated severe head injury, orbital fracture, or intracranial hemorrhage. Proptosis, tense orbit, restricted eye movement, or severe pain suggesting orbital compartment syndrome. Signs of open-globe injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stabilize airway, breathing, circulation; follow trauma protocols.
• Record visual acuity, pupils, color vision if feasible, ocular movements without delaying resuscitation.
• Assess for orbital compartment syndrome (separate time-critical emergency).
• If open-globe injury possible, place rigid eye shield without pressure and avoid tonometry.
• Obtain urgent ophthalmology and trauma/neurosurgical consultation as indicated.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CT of orbits and head when indicated to assess fractures, optic canal injury, foreign bodies, intracranial trauma.
• MRI may be considered later for selected optic nerve or intracranial pathology, once metallic foreign bodies and other contraindications excluded.
• Formal ophthalmic assessment and serial visual examinations.
• Investigate associated head injury according to standard trauma protocols.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Initial Management[/color]
• Treat life-threatening trauma first.
• Maintain adequate oxygenation and perfusion; avoid hypotension, particularly in associated traumatic brain injury.
• Manage orbital compartment syndrome immediately if present, according to its specific emergency protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT confuse traumatic optic neuropathy with orbital compartment syndrome. Orbital compartment syndrome may require immediate decompression without waiting for imaging.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Corticosteroids[/color]
• High-dose systemic corticosteroids are NOT routinely recommended for traumatic optic neuropathy because convincing benefit has not been established and high-dose treatment may cause harm, especially in traumatic brain injury.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT administer megadose methylprednisolone routinely for traumatic optic neuropathy. Decisions about selected interventions require specialist discussion and must consider associated head injury.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Surgical Intervention[/color]
• Optic canal decompression is not routinely indicated for all cases; role is controversial and must be assessed by specialist teams.
• Surgery may be required for other associated injuries (orbital compartment syndrome, compressive lesions, selected fractures).

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Coordinate ophthalmology, trauma, and neurosurgical care.
• Monitor visual function and treat associated orbital or intracranial injuries.
• Provide prognosis counseling and rehabilitation support when visual impairment persists.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent hospital assessment for all suspected traumatic optic neuropathy.
• Admission generally required when significant head injury, progressive visual loss, orbital injury, or other serious trauma present.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Traumatic Optic Neuropathy Clinical Guidance; Brain Trauma Foundation Guidelines for Severe TBI; International Neuro-Ophthalmology Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: A rapid increase in orbital pressure, commonly caused by retrobulbar hemorrhage after trauma or surgery, compromising optic nerve and retinal perfusion.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Acute proptosis and tense eyelids.
• Severe orbital pain.
• Reduced vision or color vision.
• Restricted eye movements.
• Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD).
• Elevated IOP when safely measured.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Recognize the condition clinically.
• Call ophthalmology and experienced emergency/trauma clinicians immediately.
• Assess visual acuity, pupils, eye movements, and IOP if safe.
• Prepare for immediate orbital decompression when indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. EMERGENCY DECOMPRESSION[/color]
• Lateral canthotomy with inferior cantholysis is the emergency decompression procedure.
• It must be performed immediately by a trained clinician when indicated.
• Do not wait for CT or ophthalmology arrival if the diagnosis is clear and vision is threatened.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. ADDITIONAL MANAGEMENT[/color]
• Urgent ophthalmology assessment after decompression.
• Treat the cause, such as retrobulbar hemorrhage.
• Reassess vision, pupils, IOP, and orbital tension.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not perform decompression when open globe injury is suspected without specialist direction.
• Imaging must not delay indicated decompression.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Emergency transfer/admission for ophthalmology and surgical management.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Proptosis, tight lids, visual decline, and restricted movements after trauma strongly suggest this syndrome.
• Time to intervention is critical.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO EyeWiki: Orbital Compartment Syndrome.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Corneal abrasion is a defect in the corneal epithelium, commonly caused by fingernails, dust, foreign bodies, contact lenses, or trauma.
Typical symptoms: Sudden eye pain, foreign-body sensation, tearing, redness, photophobia. Pain may worsen with blinking. Blurred vision if central cornea involved.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Reduced visual acuity. Contact lens use with pain or corneal opacity. White corneal infiltrate, hypopyon, or purulent discharge. Suspected penetrating injury, irregular pupil, or positive Seidel test. Severe pain, marked photophobia, or worsening despite treatment.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess and document visual acuity in each eye separately before treatment, if safe.
• Obtain mechanism of injury, time of onset, contact lens use, chemical exposure, previous ocular disease.
• Examine pupils, eye movements, external eye.
• Use fluorescein staining and blue light to identify epithelial defect, provided open-globe injury is not suspected.
• Evert the upper eyelid when appropriate to look for retained foreign body.
• [color=#991B1B]If open-globe injury suspected: stop manipulation, avoid tonometry and ocular ultrasound, place rigid eye shield without pressure, keep NPO, arrange immediate ophthalmology transfer.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Visual acuity, pupils, and relative afferent pupillary defect assessment.
• Fluorescein staining to identify epithelial defect.
• Slit-lamp examination, if available, to assess defect size, depth, infiltrates, anterior chamber.
• Seidel testing only when clinically appropriate and open-globe injury is not strongly suspected.
• Corneal scraping and microbiological studies are not routinely required for simple abrasion but may be needed if infection/ulceration suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed; max 3,000 mg/day for routine unsupervised adult use.
• Alternatively, ibuprofen 200–400 mg orally every 6–8 hours with food, if no contraindications.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT dispense topical anesthetic drops for unsupervised home use. Prolonged/inappropriate use can damage corneal epithelium and delay healing.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Topical Antibiotic Prophylaxis[/color]
• Erythromycin ophthalmic ointment 0.5%: ~1 cm ribbon to affected eye four times daily for 3–5 days.
• For contact lens-associated abrasions: use appropriate topical antipseudomonal agent (e.g., ciprofloxacin 0.3% or ofloxacin 0.3%) per local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotic selection/duration depend on injury type and local guidance. A painful red eye with corneal infiltrate/opacity should be managed as possible microbial keratitis, not simple abrasion.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Lubrication[/color]
• Preservative-free artificial tears: 1–2 drops as needed, often four to six times daily.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use steroid-containing eye drops unless specifically prescribed by an ophthalmologist.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Most uncomplicated abrasions heal within 24–72 hours.
• Do NOT routinely patch the eye.
• Cycloplegic drops may be considered by a clinician for significant photophobia/ciliary spasm after appropriate assessment.
• Reassess if pain or vision does not improve within 24 hours.
• Urgent ophthalmology assessment required for large/central defects, suspected infection, contact lens-associated defects, recurrent erosions, or any red flags.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Discharge may be appropriate when: Abrasion is uncomplicated. Visual acuity reassuring. No evidence of infection or penetrating injury. Patient can follow treatment and return for review.
• Urgent referral: Reduced vision, corneal infiltrate, suspected ulcer, contact lens-associated painful red eye, persistent symptoms, or suspected open-globe injury.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Corneal and External Disease Guidance; College of Optometrists Corneal Abrasion Guideline; ACEP Consensus Guidance on Topical Anesthetic Use.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Infection of the cornea caused by bacteria, fungi, viruses, or Acanthamoeba. Corneal ulceration can progress rapidly and cause scarring, perforation, and permanent visual loss.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Painful red eye.
• Photophobia and tearing.
• Reduced visual acuity.
• Corneal opacity or infiltrate.
• Fluorescein-positive epithelial defect.
• Contact lens use, ocular trauma, or topical steroid use may be risk factors.

[color=#991B1B]RED FLAGS: Central or large corneal ulcer, rapid progression, reduced vision, corneal thinning, contact lens use with painful red eye.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess and document visual acuity.
• Examine the cornea and perform fluorescein staining when safe.
• Arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment.
• Stop contact lens use.
• Obtain corneal scraping and cultures when indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. TOPICAL ANTIBIOTICS[/color]
• Moxifloxacin 0.5% may be used for selected bacterial ulcers.
• Severe or vision-threatening ulcers may require intensive fortified preparations.
• Adjust treatment according to culture results.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS[/color]
• Fungal keratitis requires specialist-directed antifungal therapy.
• Herpetic keratitis requires appropriate antiviral management.
• Acanthamoeba keratitis requires specialist treatment.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay specialist assessment for a central ulcer or reduced vision.
• Avoid topical corticosteroids unless prescribed by ophthalmology.

sections.heading: 06 — DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
sections.content:
• Corneal abrasion.
• Anterior uveitis.
• Acute angle-closure glaucoma.
• Conjunctivitis.
• Scleritis.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Urgent ophthalmology review. Admit for severe ulcers, corneal thinning, or suspected perforation.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• A corneal infiltrate with an epithelial defect suggests microbial keratitis.
• Contact lens wear is an important risk factor.
• A painful red eye with reduced vision is not simple conjunctivitis.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO: Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute anterior uveitis is inflammation of the iris and ciliary body. May be idiopathic or associated with autoimmune disease, infection, trauma, or other ocular pathology.
• Painful red eye, often with ciliary flush.
• Photophobia, including consensual photophobia when light directed at unaffected eye causes pain in affected eye.
• Blurred vision. Small or irregular pupil may occur.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Markedly reduced vision. Severe pain, corneal opacity, or elevated intraocular pressure. Hypopyon or suspected endophthalmitis. History of ocular surgery, injection, penetrating trauma, or possible herpetic eye disease.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess visual acuity, pupils, and pattern of redness.
• Obtain history of autoimmune disease, inflammatory back pain, previous episodes, trauma, infection, ocular surgery.
• Arrange same-day ophthalmology assessment for suspected acute anterior uveitis.
• Exclude acute angle-closure glaucoma, microbial keratitis, and endophthalmitis.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT start topical corticosteroids without appropriate ophthalmology guidance, especially before excluding corneal infection.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Visual acuity and pupil examination.
• Slit-lamp examination to identify anterior chamber cells and flare, keratic precipitates, posterior synechiae.
• Intraocular pressure measurement only when open-globe injury is not suspected and examination is appropriate.
• Additional laboratory tests/imaging guided by clinical history, recurrence, systemic symptoms, ophthalmologist assessment.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Topical Corticosteroid[/color]
• Prednisolone acetate 1% ophthalmic drops may be prescribed by an ophthalmologist, with frequency determined by inflammatory severity.
• [color=#991B1B]Topical steroids can worsen untreated herpetic or microbial keratitis and may increase intraocular pressure. Do NOT use as empirical treatment for undiagnosed red eye.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Cycloplegic or Mydriatic Drops[/color]
• Cyclopentolate 1%: commonly 1 drop in affected eye, frequency determined by ophthalmologist.
• May relieve ciliary spasm and reduce risk of posterior synechiae.
• [color=#991B1B]Confirm clinical situation is appropriate before using pupil-dilating medication, especially if angle closure is a concern.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed, within appropriate daily maximum.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Treat underlying cause when identified, including infection or systemic inflammatory disease.
• Ophthalmology-directed topical anti-inflammatory treatment and cycloplegia are common for noninfectious anterior uveitis.
• Recurrent or bilateral disease may require systemic evaluation and specialist follow-up.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Same-day ophthalmology assessment generally recommended.
• Immediate emergency referral required for severe visual loss, suspected endophthalmitis, marked pressure elevation, or rapidly progressive symptoms.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO EyeWiki Acute Anterior Uveitis; AAO Guidance on Inflammatory Eye Disease and Topical Corticosteroid Safety.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Scleritis is a potentially sight-threatening inflammation of the sclera. May be associated with systemic autoimmune disease, vasculitis, infection, or previous ocular surgery.
• Severe, deep, boring eye pain, sometimes radiating to face or head. Pain may worsen at night or with eye movement.
• Deep redness with a violaceous hue.
• Possible photophobia, tearing, and reduced vision.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Reduced visual acuity. Severe/rapidly worsening pain. Corneal involvement, scleral thinning, or suspected necrotizing scleritis. Previous eye surgery, trauma, or possible infectious disease. Systemic features of vasculitis (skin lesions, joint symptoms, respiratory symptoms, renal abnormalities).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess visual acuity, pupils, eye movements, pain severity, appearance of sclera.
• Arrange urgent same-day ophthalmology assessment.
• Distinguish scleritis from episcleritis, microbial keratitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, anterior uveitis.
• Ask about rheumatoid arthritis, systemic vasculitis, autoimmune disease, infection, trauma, ocular surgery.
• Do NOT delay referral while attempting empirical topical treatment.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Visual acuity and complete ophthalmic examination.
• Slit-lamp examination to assess scleral inflammation and associated corneal or intraocular disease.
• Additional lab investigations guided by clinical suspicion may include CBC, renal function, urinalysis, inflammatory markers, autoimmune testing.
• Microbiological assessment may be needed when infectious scleritis suspected, particularly after surgery or trauma.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Analgesia and Initial Supportive Care[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed, within patient-specific daily limits.
• [color=#991B1B]Severe pain may indicate deeper inflammation or complications. Do not allow symptom relief to delay assessment.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Systemic Anti-Inflammatory Treatment[/color]
• Oral NSAIDs may be used for selected noninfectious cases under clinician/ophthalmologist direction, provided no contraindications.
• More severe disease may require systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressive therapy prescribed by relevant specialist.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT start systemic corticosteroids before considering infectious scleritis and other important contraindications. Topical corticosteroids alone are often insufficient for significant scleritis and should not be started empirically in undiagnosed painful red eye.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Suspected Infectious Scleritis[/color]
• Urgent ophthalmology assessment and microbiological investigation where indicated.
• Antimicrobial therapy selected according to suspected organism, exposure history, cultures, specialist advice.
• Surgical debridement may be required in selected cases.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Determine whether condition is infectious or noninfectious.
• Treat associated autoimmune or systemic disease where identified.
• Ophthalmology-directed anti-inflammatory or antimicrobial treatment depends on subtype and severity.
• Monitor for corneal complications, scleral thinning, perforation, vision loss.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Same-day ophthalmology assessment required for suspected acute scleritis.
• Emergency referral or admission may be necessary for reduced vision, necrotizing disease, suspected infection, posterior scleritis, or systemic vasculitis.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Scleritis Clinical Guidance; AAO EyeWiki Scleritis; Specialist Ophthalmology Guidance on Infectious/Noninfectious Scleritis.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Corneal graft rejection is an immune response against a transplanted cornea. Early recognition and treatment are important to preserve graft clarity.
• New redness, photophobia, blurred vision, or discomfort in an eye with previous corneal transplant.
• Corneal edema or graft haze.
• An endothelial rejection line may be visible in some cases.
• Symptoms can resemble infection or other postoperative complications.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Rapid reduction in vision. Severe pain, discharge, corneal ulceration, or suspected graft infection. Recent interruption of prescribed topical corticosteroids. Previous graft rejection or high-risk corneal transplant.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Establish date and type of corneal transplant.
• Ask about medication adherence, recent steroid changes, trauma, and contact lens use.
• Document visual acuity and examine cornea if equipment and expertise available.
• Arrange same-day ophthalmology assessment for suspected rejection.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT independently increase or restart intensive steroid treatment without assessment, particularly if infection is possible.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Slit-lamp examination to assess graft clarity, epithelial integrity, edema, and inflammation.
• Intraocular pressure measurement when appropriate.
• Corneal scraping or microbiological tests when infection suspected.
• Additional tests directed by ophthalmologist according to graft type and clinical findings.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Topical Corticosteroids[/color]
• Intensive topical prednisolone acetate 1% may be used for acute rejection, with frequency determined by ophthalmologist and severity of inflammation.
• Initiate or adjust therapy under urgent ophthalmology supervision. Monitor graft clarity, visual acuity, IOP, and signs of infection. Treatment often requires carefully supervised taper.
• [color=#991B1B]Topical steroids may worsen microbial keratitis or other corneal infections. Do NOT delay specialist assessment while attempting empirical treatment.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Additional Treatment[/color]
