• Severe endothelial rejection may require additional specialist-directed treatment, including systemic corticosteroids in selected cases.
• Treat associated infection or raised IOP when present.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Confirm diagnosis and exclude infection.
• Begin appropriate anti-rejection treatment promptly.
• Monitor graft clarity and visual function closely.
• Reinforce adherence to prescribed maintenance drops and long-term corneal follow-up.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Same-day ophthalmology assessment recommended for suspected graft rejection.
• Immediate referral required for rapid visual decline, severe pain, suspected infection, or graft failure.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Corneal Transplantation and Corneal Graft Rejection; AAO EyeWiki Corneal Graft Rejection; Cornea Specialist Clinical Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Hypopyon is the accumulation of inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber. It is a clinical sign rather than a diagnosis and may occur in severe microbial keratitis, endophthalmitis, or severe intraocular inflammation.
• Visible white or yellow fluid level in inferior anterior chamber.
• Redness, photophobia, pain, and blurred vision.
• Corneal ulceration or infiltrate may be present.
• Recent ocular surgery, intravitreal injection, or penetrating trauma increases concern for endophthalmitis.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Rapid visual deterioration. Severe pain, marked redness, or recent ocular surgery/injection. Corneal ulcer with stromal thinning or suspected perforation. Fever, systemic illness, or suspected endogenous infection.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess visual acuity in both eyes and document onset/progression of symptoms.
• Ask about recent eye surgery, injections, trauma, contact lens use, and systemic infection.
• Arrange immediate ophthalmology assessment if endophthalmitis possible.
• Avoid pressure on eye if open-globe injury or corneal perforation suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT start topical corticosteroids empirically before infection has been assessed.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Slit-lamp examination to identify source of hypopyon.
• Assessment of corneal integrity, anterior chamber inflammation, and IOP when appropriate.
• Dilated fundus examination if visualization possible.
• B-scan ultrasonography may be considered by ophthalmology team when fundus obscured, provided open-globe injury excluded.
• Corneal scraping and cultures for suspected microbial keratitis.
• Aqueous or vitreous sampling and systemic investigations may be indicated when endophthalmitis suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Suspected Microbial Keratitis[/color]
• Immediate ophthalmology assessment. Corneal scraping and microbiological sampling when indicated, without unnecessarily delaying treatment.
• Intensive topical antimicrobial therapy selected by ophthalmology team according to ulcer severity and suspected organism.
• [color=#991B1B]A hypopyon with corneal infiltrate may represent a sight-threatening corneal ulcer. Do NOT treat suspected infectious keratitis with topical corticosteroids alone.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Suspected Endophthalmitis[/color]
• Treat as ophthalmic emergency. Immediate retinal/ophthalmic specialist assessment required. Intravitreal antibiotics and possible vitreoretinal surgery determined by ophthalmologist.
• [color=#991B1B]Topical antibiotics alone are inadequate for suspected endophthalmitis. Do NOT delay specialist treatment while waiting for culture results.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Pain Control[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed, within patient-specific daily limits.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Identify and treat underlying cause.
• Microbial keratitis requires organism-appropriate antimicrobial treatment and monitoring for corneal thinning/perforation.
• Endophthalmitis may require intravitreal antimicrobial therapy and surgery.
• Noninfectious uveitis requires specialist-directed anti-inflammatory treatment only after infection appropriately considered.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate ophthalmology assessment for unexplained hypopyon.
• Emergency hospital transfer for suspected endophthalmitis, corneal perforation, or rapidly declining vision.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern; AAO Endophthalmitis Guidance; ESCRS Postoperative Infection Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Acute obstruction of the central retinal artery causing sudden retinal ischemia and usually painless monocular visual loss. It is an ocular and systemic vascular emergency.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye.
• Marked reduction in visual acuity.
• Relative afferent pupillary defect.
• Retinal whitening and a cherry-red spot may be seen on fundus examination.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate an emergency stroke pathway and arrange immediate transfer to a stroke-capable center.
• Establish exact symptom onset or last-known-well time.
• Assess neurological status, vital signs, and blood glucose.
• Obtain urgent ophthalmology and stroke-team consultation.
• Evaluate for carotid, cardiac, and other embolic sources.

sections.heading: 04 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urgent stroke-directed brain and vascular imaging.
• ECG and cardiovascular assessment.
• CBC, glucose, renal function.
• Assess for giant cell arteritis (ESR, CRP, platelets) if age >50 and clinically suspected.

sections.heading: 05 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. STROKE-CENTER MANAGEMENT[/color]
• Consider eligibility for acute reperfusion treatment under the current stroke protocol.
• Address vascular risk factors and secondary stroke prevention.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. SUSPECTED GIANT CELL ARTERITIS[/color]
• Urgent systemic corticosteroid treatment is required to protect the fellow eye.
• Do not delay treatment while waiting for biopsy.

sections.heading: 06 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay transfer for outpatient ophthalmology review.
• Routine ocular massage, anterior chamber paracentesis, and unproven pressure-lowering methods should not delay stroke evaluation.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Immediate stroke-center evaluation and urgent ophthalmology assessment.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Sudden painless monocular visual loss should be treated as a vascular emergency.
• CRAO is associated with increased risk of cerebral and cardiovascular events.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO: Retinal and Ophthalmic Artery Occlusions.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
CRVO is an obstruction of the central retinal vein that causes retinal hemorrhage, venous congestion, and variable visual impairment.
• Sudden, painless blurring or loss of vision in one eye.
• Visual acuity may range from mildly reduced to profound loss.
• Fundoscopy may show dilated tortuous retinal veins, widespread retinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, optic disc swelling.
• Risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, glaucoma, dyslipidemia, increasing age.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Severe visual loss. Suspected associated retinal arterial occlusion or another acute vascular event. Ocular pain or red eye developing later (may indicate neovascular glaucoma). Young patients or atypical cases requiring evaluation for selected systemic or hematologic causes.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Record visual acuity in each eye separately.
• Assess pupils, visual fields, and presence of relative afferent pupillary defect.
• Arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment, preferably same day or within 24 hours depending on severity and local access.
• Check blood pressure and review diabetes, vascular risk factors, glaucoma, medications, previous ocular disease.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT attempt empiric ocular massage, pressure-lowering treatment, or anticoagulation solely to reverse CRVO.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Dilated fundus examination.
• Optical coherence tomography (OCT) to assess macular edema.
• Fluorescein angiography when required to assess retinal perfusion and ischemia.
• Intraocular pressure measurement when appropriate.
• Blood pressure, glucose or HbA1c, lipid profile as clinically indicated.
• Further investigations in younger patients or atypical presentations guided by ophthalmology and suspected underlying cause.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Acute Management[/color]
• There is no established emergency bedside medication that reliably reverses established CRVO.
• Arrange prompt ophthalmology assessment to classify occlusion as ischemic or nonischemic and identify complications.
• Optimize systemic vascular risk factors.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT assume CRVO is harmless because it is painless. Do NOT initiate systemic anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy solely for CRVO unless another indication exists.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Intravitreal Anti-VEGF Therapy[/color]
• Common ophthalmology regimens include ranibizumab 0.5 mg intravitreally or aflibercept 2 mg intravitreally for CRVO-associated macular edema. Exact product, regimen, frequency are specialist-directed.
• Administer only by trained ophthalmologist under sterile intravitreal injection protocols.
• [color=#991B1B]These are NOT bedside or emergency-department injections. New severe pain, redness, photophobia, or worsening vision after injection requires urgent evaluation for endophthalmitis or another complication.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Treat macular edema with ophthalmologist-directed intravitreal therapy when indicated.
• Monitor for retinal neovascularization and neovascular glaucoma.
• Manage coexisting glaucoma and systemic vascular risk factors.
• Ischemic CRVO generally carries a worse visual prognosis and requires close follow-up.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent ophthalmology referral for all suspected acute CRVO.
• Immediate specialist assessment for profound visual loss, ocular pain, or suspected neovascular glaucoma.
• Arrange ongoing retinal follow-up because complications may develop after initial presentation.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Retinal Vein Occlusions Preferred Practice Pattern; Royal College of Ophthalmologists Retinal Vein Occlusion Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium. Delayed treatment may result in permanent visual loss.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Sudden onset of flashes of light.
• New or increasing floaters.
• A curtain or shadow across the visual field.
• Blurred or reduced vision.
• Usually painless.

[color=#991B1B]RISK FACTORS: High myopia, previous cataract/retinal surgery, ocular trauma, previous retinal detachment.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess and document visual acuity in each eye.
• Ask about flashes, floaters, field loss, and symptom onset.
• Arrange immediate or same-day ophthalmology assessment.
• Avoid delays for routine investigations when retinal detachment is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Dilated retinal examination by an appropriately trained clinician.
• Ocular ultrasound may assist when the fundus cannot be visualized (provided open globe excluded).
• OCT or other retinal imaging by ophthalmology.

sections.heading: 05 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT[/color]
• Retinal tears may be treated with laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy.
• Retinal detachment may require pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckling, or vitrectomy.
• Choice of procedure depends on detachment characteristics and specialist assessment.

• Arrange urgent retinal specialist review.
• Provide clear instructions to return immediately if vision deteriorates.

sections.heading: 06 — WARNINGS
sections.content: • Do not reassure patients with a new curtain-like shadow or sudden increase in floaters without adequate retinal assessment.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Urgent ophthalmology referral. Suspected acute retinal detachment requires same-day assessment.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Retinal detachment is usually painless.
• New flashes and floaters may indicate a retinal tear before detachment occurs.
• Early treatment can preserve vision.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NHS: Detached Retina; Merck Manual: Retinal Detachment.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Vitreous hemorrhage is bleeding into the vitreous cavity, often caused by retinal tears, proliferative diabetic retinopathy, retinal vascular disease, trauma, or posterior vitreous detachment.
• Sudden painless floaters, cobwebs, haze, or reddish vision.
• Blurred vision or substantial visual loss.
• Fundus view may be obscured by blood.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] New flashes and floaters, curtain-like visual field defect, or sudden severe visual loss. Recent ocular or head trauma. Suspected retinal tear or detachment. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy or anticoagulant use with significant bleeding.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Document visual acuity in both eyes.
• Ask about flashes, floaters, curtain-like shadow, trauma, diabetes, previous retinal disease, anticoagulants.
• Perform pupil examination and assess for relative afferent pupillary defect.
• Arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment to exclude retinal tear or detachment.
• Avoid pressure on eye if trauma or open-globe injury possible.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Dilated retinal examination if fundus can be visualized.
• B-scan ocular ultrasonography may be required when fundus obscured, provided open-globe injury excluded.
• OCT when appropriate to evaluate associated macular pathology.
• Glucose testing and assessment for diabetic retinopathy when indicated.
• Further evaluation for retinal vascular disease, trauma, or systemic causes according to clinical findings.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Initial Management[/color]
• There is no universal medication that clears vitreous blood immediately.
• Arrange urgent ophthalmology review.
• Advise avoiding strenuous activity until retinal pathology assessed; positioning advice individualized by ophthalmologist.
• Review anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy, but do NOT stop essential medication without assessing indication and bleeding severity.
• [color=#991B1B]A vitreous hemorrhage may conceal a retinal tear or detachment. Do NOT discharge a patient with new unexplained vitreous hemorrhage without appropriate retinal assessment and follow-up plan.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Definitive Treatment[/color]
• Observation may be appropriate for selected cases once retinal tear/detachment excluded and follow-up reliable.
• Retinal tears may require laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy.
• Retinal detachment may require urgent retinal surgery.
• Persistent/recurrent hemorrhage may require vitrectomy.
• Proliferative diabetic retinopathy may require retinal laser treatment, intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy, or surgery depending on findings.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Identify and treat source of bleeding.
• Monitor visual acuity and retinal status until hemorrhage resolves or definitive treatment completed.
• Provide appropriate diabetic and vascular risk-factor management.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent same-day ophthalmology or retinal assessment appropriate for new unexplained vitreous hemorrhage.
• Immediate assessment required if retinal detachment, open-globe injury, or major trauma suspected.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Posterior Vitreous Detachment, Retinal Breaks, and Lattice Degeneration Preferred Practice Pattern; AAO Guidance on Diabetic Retinopathy and Vitreoretinal Disease.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Sudden obstruction of aqueous humor outflow causing a rapid rise in intraocular pressure (IOP), potentially resulting in permanent optic nerve damage.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Severe unilateral eye pain and redness.
• Blurred vision or colored halos around lights.
• Headache, nausea, and vomiting.
• Hazy cornea and a mid-dilated, poorly reactive pupil.
• Markedly elevated IOP.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Arrange immediate ophthalmology consultation.
• Assess visual acuity, pupils, and IOP if safe and appropriately equipped.
• Begin pressure-lowering treatment according to local protocol.
• Check for contraindications to beta-blockers and systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. ACETAZOLAMIDE[/color]
• 500 mg IV or orally as an initial dose, if appropriate.
• Monitor renal function, electrolytes, and clinical response.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. TOPICAL PRESSURE-LOWERING AGENTS[/color]
• Timolol 0.5%: 1 drop in affected eye.
• Brimonidine 0.2%: 1 drop in affected eye.
• Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor may be used.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. DEFINITIVE TREATMENT[/color]
• Laser peripheral iridotomy is commonly the definitive treatment.
• Pilocarpine may be considered after IOP begins to fall.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid Acetazolamide in significant renal disease or severe electrolyte abnormalities.
• Check for asthma, bradycardia, heart block, or decompensated heart failure before timolol.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Emergency ophthalmology management and usually hospital-based treatment until IOP is controlled.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Painful red eye with blurred vision, halos, and vomiting is highly concerning.
• Treatment must not be delayed.
• Definitive treatment is usually procedural.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO: Acute Angle Closure.

Glaucoma & Neuro-Ophthalmology.title: Giant Cell Arteritis with Visual Symptoms

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a large-vessel vasculitis that can cause irreversible visual loss. Predominantly affects adults aged 50 years and older.
• New headache, especially temporal. Scalp tenderness or jaw claudication.
• Transient monocular visual loss, diplopia, or sudden permanent visual loss.
• Constitutional symptoms, polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms, or unexplained fever.
• Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy may be found on examination.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Any new visual symptom in patient with suspected GCA. Transient visual loss (may precede permanent blindness). Bilateral or rapidly progressive visual impairment.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Treat suspected GCA with visual symptoms as medical emergency.
• Obtain urgent ophthalmology and medical/rheumatology input.
• Draw blood for ESR, CRP, full blood count, platelet count as soon as possible, but do NOT delay treatment while awaiting results.
• Assess for jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, headache, constitutional symptoms, polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms.
• Arrange urgent evaluation for other causes of acute visual loss when appropriate.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• ESR and CRP. Full blood count and platelet count.
• Temporal artery ultrasound and/or temporal artery biopsy according to local pathways.
• Additional vascular imaging may be required to evaluate large-vessel involvement.
• Ophthalmic assessment to document type and extent of visual impairment.
• [color=#991B1B]Normal inflammatory markers reduce but do not completely eliminate possibility of GCA when clinical suspicion is high.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Immediate Glucocorticoid Therapy[/color]
• For suspected GCA with acute or threatened visual loss, urgent specialist-directed treatment required.
• Commonly used regimen for threatened or established visual loss: methylprednisolone 500–1,000 mg IV once daily for up to 3 days, followed by high-dose oral glucocorticoid therapy per specialist guidance.
• If IV treatment not immediately available, oral prednisolone (commonly 40–60 mg daily or ~1 mg/kg/day up to locally recommended maximum) should be started promptly under appropriate emergency pathway.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay initial glucocorticoid treatment for temporal artery biopsy or imaging. Suspected GCA with visual symptoms requires immediate treatment because visual loss may become irreversible.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Long-Term Disease Control[/color]
• Rheumatology or specialist medical follow-up required.
• Tocilizumab or other steroid-sparing strategies may be considered in selected patients.
• Bone protection, glucose monitoring, blood pressure control, and infection-risk assessment may be needed during prolonged glucocorticoid treatment.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Confirm diagnosis through temporal artery ultrasound, biopsy, or other appropriate imaging without delaying treatment.
• Assess for systemic and large-vessel involvement.
• Monitor symptoms, inflammatory markers, glucocorticoid adverse effects, and recurrence.
• Provide clear instructions to seek immediate care for new visual symptoms, headache, or jaw claudication.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate hospital assessment and specialist involvement for any suspected GCA with visual symptoms.
• Admission often appropriate when acute visual loss or IV glucocorticoid therapy required.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: BSR Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Giant Cell Arteritis; ACR/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for Management of GCA; AAO Ischemic Optic Neuropathy and GCA Clinical Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Optic neuritis is inflammation of the optic nerve that commonly causes acute or subacute visual loss. May be associated with multiple sclerosis, MOG-antibody-associated disease, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, infection, or other inflammatory conditions.
• Subacute reduction in vision, usually developing over hours to days.
• Pain with eye movement.
• Impaired color vision, especially red desaturation.
• Relative afferent pupillary defect in unilateral or asymmetric disease.
• Optic disc may appear normal in retrobulbar optic neuritis.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Severe bilateral visual loss. Profound or rapidly progressive visual impairment. Marked optic disc swelling, retinal hemorrhage, or atypical fundus findings. Fever, meningism, immunocompromise, or suspected infection. Older age, painless visual loss, or atypical clinical course. Neurological deficits suggesting another CNS disorder.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Document visual acuity, pupils, color vision, and visual fields when feasible.
• Assess for neurological symptoms, pain with eye movement, recent infection, autoimmune disease, previous demyelinating episodes.
• Arrange urgent ophthalmology or neuro-ophthalmology assessment.
• Refer to emergency neurology when severe, atypical, bilateral, or rapidly progressive disease present.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT assume that all acute visual loss with pain is optic neuritis; exclude retinal, vascular, infectious, and compressive causes.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• MRI of brain and orbits with appropriate contrast sequences when indicated.
• Formal ophthalmic examination, including fundus assessment and visual fields.
• OCT may help document retinal nerve fiber and ganglion cell changes.
• Blood testing for MOG-IgG, aquaporin-4 IgG, infectious causes, or systemic inflammatory disorders may be indicated in atypical or severe presentations.
• Further neurological evaluation may be required if multiple sclerosis or another demyelinating disorder suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Corticosteroid Treatment[/color]
• For selected typical acute optic neuritis, IV methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 3 days is a commonly used regimen when accelerated recovery is clinically indicated.
• Other specialist-directed regimens may be used according to severity, underlying cause, and local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Corticosteroids may accelerate visual recovery in typical demyelinating optic neuritis but do not necessarily improve long-term visual outcome. Oral prednisone alone at conventional doses should not be used as a substitute for evidence-based specialist-directed treatment of typical optic neuritis because some regimens have been associated with increased recurrence. Suspected infectious optic neuropathy requires cause-specific management.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Severe or Atypical Optic Neuritis[/color]
• Severe disease, bilateral involvement, or poor response to corticosteroids may require specialist-directed plasma exchange or other immunotherapy.
• Treatment for MOG-associated disease, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, or infectious causes differs from routine typical optic neuritis.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay escalation in severe bilateral or rapidly progressive visual loss.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Identify underlying cause and assess risk of future neurological disease.
• Coordinate ophthalmology and neurology follow-up.
• Monitor visual acuity, color vision, visual fields, and OCT where appropriate.
• Provide disease-specific counseling and treatment if demyelinating or systemic inflammatory disorder diagnosed.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent specialist assessment for suspected acute optic neuritis.
• Hospital evaluation appropriate for severe visual loss, atypical features, bilateral disease, suspected infection, or need for IV treatment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Optic Neuritis Clinical Guidance; Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT); AAN Evidence-Based Guidance on Optic Neuritis and Demyelinating Disease.

Glaucoma & Neuro-Ophthalmology.title: Acute Diplopia and Ocular Motor Cranial Nerve Palsy

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute diplopia is double vision that develops suddenly. May result from ocular misalignment, cranial nerve III/IV/VI palsy, neuromuscular disease, orbital pathology, or brainstem lesion.
• Binocular diplopia that resolves when either eye is covered.
• Abnormal eye alignment or restricted movement.
• Ptosis may occur with third cranial nerve palsy.
• Sixth nerve palsy commonly causes impaired abduction.
• Fourth nerve palsy may cause vertical or torsional diplopia.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Third cranial nerve palsy with dilated or poorly reactive pupil. Sudden severe headache or neck pain. Focal neurological deficits, ataxia, dysarthria, or altered consciousness. Proptosis, fever, painful eye movements, or orbital trauma. New diplopia with visual loss or other evidence of stroke.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Determine whether diplopia is monocular or binocular.
• Document visual acuity, pupils, ptosis, ocular alignment, and extraocular movements.
• Perform focused neurological examination.
• Assess for severe headache, neck pain, vascular risk factors, trauma, and symptoms of myasthenia gravis.
• Activate local stroke/emergency neurovascular pathway when stroke or aneurysm suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT assume an isolated cranial nerve palsy is benign until urgent causes have been considered.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Neurological and ophthalmic examination.
• Urgent CT angiography or MR angiography when aneurysm or other vascular lesion suspected.
• Brain MRI when brainstem lesion, inflammation, demyelination, or other intracranial pathology suspected.
• Glucose, blood pressure, and other lab tests according to clinical context.
• Further evaluation for myasthenia gravis or systemic inflammatory disease when indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Suspected Aneurysmal Third Nerve Palsy or Stroke[/color]
• Immediate emergency department evaluation and neurovascular imaging. Obtain urgent neurology, neurosurgery, or stroke-team consultation as indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]A painful third nerve palsy, particularly with pupillary involvement, is an emergency because of the risk of an intracranial aneurysm. A normal initial non-specialist examination does not reliably exclude a dangerous vascular cause.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Symptomatic Diplopia Management[/color]
• Temporary occlusion of one lens may reduce diplopia while evaluation underway, if appropriate. Avoid driving or hazardous activities while diplopia persists.
• [color=#991B1B]Symptom relief must NOT delay urgent investigation.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Suspected Myasthenia Gravis[/color]
• Assess for fluctuating ptosis, fatigable weakness, dysphagia, dysarthria, and respiratory symptoms.
• Respiratory or bulbar weakness requires emergency assessment for myasthenic crisis.
• Arrange neurology review and disease-specific testing.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Treat underlying vascular, neurological, neuromuscular, orbital, or systemic condition.
• Monitor ocular alignment, visual function, and neurological progression.
• Arrange specialist follow-up even when isolated palsy initially thought to be microvascular.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate emergency evaluation for pupil-involving third nerve palsy, severe headache, focal neurological deficits, orbital infection, trauma, or respiratory/bulbar weakness.
• Urgent specialist assessment for all new unexplained binocular diplopia.
• Outpatient follow-up only after dangerous causes excluded and safe plan documented.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Diplopia and Ocular Motility Disorders; AHA/ASA Acute Stroke Guidance; Neuro-Ophthalmology Clinical Guidance on Ocular Motor Cranial Nerve Palsies.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: A potentially sight- and life-threatening infection of the orbital tissues posterior to the orbital septum, often associated with sinusitis.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Fever and eyelid swelling.
• Proptosis.
• Painful or restricted eye movements.
• Reduced visual acuity or color vision.
• Diplopia.
• RAPD or neurological signs in severe cases.

[color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Preseptal cellulitis usually does not cause proptosis, restricted eye movements, or visual impairment.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess visual acuity, pupils, color vision, and eye movements.
• Check vital signs and signs of sepsis.
• Obtain urgent ophthalmology and ENT consultation.
• Admit the patient and keep NPO until the need for surgery is clarified.
• Arrange contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits and sinuses when indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IV ANTIBIOTICS[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV every 24 hours (Pediatrics).
• Third-generation cephalosporin-based regimen (Adults).
• Add MRSA coverage (e.g., vancomycin) if suspected.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. SURGICAL MANAGEMENT[/color]
• Drainage may be required for an orbital or subperiosteal abscess, visual compromise, or failure to respond to IV antibiotics.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not use outpatient oral antibiotics alone for suspected orbital cellulitis.
• Do not delay treatment in an unstable patient for imaging.

sections.heading: 06 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, CRP, blood cultures when indicated.
• Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits and sinuses; MRI if intracranial involvement suspected.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Hospital admission is required. ICU care or tertiary transfer may be necessary for visual compromise or intracranial complications.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Painful or restricted eye movements and proptosis are important warning signs.
• Orbital cellulitis can lead to blindness, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, or intracranial abscess.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Preseptal cellulitis is an infection of the eyelid and periocular tissues anterior to the orbital septum. It must be distinguished from orbital cellulitis, which can threaten vision and life.
• Eyelid erythema, swelling, warmth, and tenderness.
• Visual acuity usually remains normal.
• Extraocular movements are full and generally painless.
• No proptosis or relative afferent pupillary defect attributable to orbital involvement.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags suggesting orbital cellulitis:[/color] Pain with eye movement or restricted ocular motility. Proptosis or diplopia. Reduced vision or abnormal pupillary response. Severe headache, neurological signs, or systemic toxicity.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Document visual acuity, pupils, ocular motility, and proptosis.
• Check vital signs and assess for fever or sepsis.
• Identify potential sources (skin trauma, insect bites, sinusitis, eyelid infection).
• If eye cannot be adequately examined because of swelling, or orbital involvement cannot be excluded, arrange urgent hospital assessment and imaging as appropriate.
• Do NOT delay treatment while waiting for imaging when orbital cellulitis or sepsis is strongly suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• No routine imaging is required for clearly uncomplicated preseptal cellulitis with a reliable examination.
• CBC, CRP, and blood cultures may be indicated in severe illness or hospitalized patients.
• Contrast-enhanced CT of orbits and sinuses is appropriate when orbital cellulitis, abscess, sinus complications, or inadequate examination is a concern.
• Culture any drainable collection when feasible.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Oral Antibiotics for Selected Adults[/color]
• Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally every 12 hours, or 500/125 mg every 8 hours, according to local guidelines and patient factors.
• Review within 24–48 hours to ensure improvement. Adjust therapy for allergy history, renal impairment, likely source, local resistance.
• [color=#991B1B]The correct regimen depends on whether infection is related to sinusitis, skin trauma, animal/human bite, or another source. Suspected MRSA infection may require additional or alternative coverage per local guidelines.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Antibiotics for Severe Disease[/color]
• IV ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g every 6 hours is one commonly used adult regimen when admission or IV treatment is required.
• Broader therapy may be necessary in severe infection, immunocompromise, or suspected orbital involvement.
• [color=#991B1B]If orbital cellulitis cannot be excluded, manage the patient through an orbital infection pathway rather than as uncomplicated preseptal cellulitis.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Treat infection and its source.
• Drain a skin or eyelid abscess when clinically indicated.
• Manage associated sinusitis or other underlying infection.
• Reassess promptly for progression to orbital cellulitis.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Outpatient treatment may be appropriate for mild disease when eye can be examined reliably, patient is systemically well, and follow-up is assured.
• Admit children with significant systemic illness, very young infants, immunocompromised patients, or those unable to take oral medication, per local pediatric guidance.
• Immediate escalation required for any orbital red flag, worsening vision, or deterioration despite treatment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Preseptal and Orbital Cellulitis; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Periorbital/Orbital Cellulitis Guideline; Local Antimicrobial Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute dacryocystitis is an infection of the lacrimal sac, usually caused by obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct.
• Painful, red swelling near the medial canthus, usually below the medial canthal tendon.
• Tearing and tenderness over the lacrimal sac.
• Purulent discharge may be expressed through the puncta.
• Fever or malaise may occur.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, or reduced vision. Rapidly spreading erythema, severe systemic illness, or immunocompromise. Suspected orbital cellulitis, abscess, or sepsis. Neonatal infection or suspected congenital lacrimal obstruction with systemic illness.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs and screen for sepsis.
• Document visual acuity, pupils, eye movements, and extent of periocular swelling.
• Determine whether infection is confined to lacrimal sac or has spread into orbit.
• Avoid forceful pressure or repeated manipulation of a severely inflamed lacrimal sac.
• Arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment for severe infection, systemic symptoms, abscess, or suspected orbital involvement.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Clinical diagnosis is often sufficient in uncomplicated cases.
• CBC, CRP, renal function, and blood cultures may be indicated in systemic illness or hospitalized patients.
• Culture purulent material when feasible in severe, recurrent, atypical, or treatment-resistant infection.
• Contrast-enhanced CT of orbits and sinuses when orbital cellulitis, abscess, or another deep infection is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Oral Antibiotics for Selected Uncomplicated Cases[/color]
• Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally every 12 hours, or 500/125 mg every 8 hours, for a commonly used 5–7-day course, adjusted to clinical response and local guidance.
• Assess response within 24–48 hours. Review allergy history, renal function, and risk factors for resistant organisms.
• [color=#991B1B]This regimen is for selected adults with uncomplicated disease who can take oral medication and have no orbital or systemic complications.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. IV Antibiotics for Severe Infection[/color]
• IV ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g every 6 hours is a commonly used adult regimen when broader treatment is required.
• Alternative regimens should follow local orbital/facial infection protocol, with additional MRSA coverage when indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]Suspected orbital cellulitis, sepsis, or abscess requires hospital management and urgent specialist assessment.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed, within patient-specific daily limits.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Treat acute infection and identify underlying lacrimal drainage obstruction.
• Drain an abscess when indicated by ophthalmology.
• Definitive dacryocystorhinostomy may be considered after acute inflammation has settled, depending on cause and recurrence.
• Recurrent or atypical swelling may require investigation for other lacrimal sac pathology.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Outpatient treatment may be appropriate for carefully selected uncomplicated cases with reliable follow-up.
• Admit or arrange urgent specialist evaluation for systemic illness, abscess, rapid progression, immunocompromise, or suspected orbital involvement.
• Any visual impairment or painful/restricted eye movement warrants emergency reassessment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Lacrimal Drainage System Disease; Merck Manual Professional Edition Dacryocystitis; Local Antimicrobial Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — DEFINITION
sections.content: Severe intraocular infection involving the vitreous and/or aqueous, commonly following eye surgery, intravitreal injection, penetrating trauma, or hematogenous spread.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL PRESENTATION
sections.content:
• Severe eye pain and redness.
• Rapidly declining vision.
• Photophobia.
• Hypopyon.
• Marked intraocular inflammation.
• Recent eye surgery, injection, or penetrating injury.

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Obtain immediate ophthalmology consultation.
• Assess visual acuity and recent ocular procedures or trauma.
• Arrange urgent ophthalmic examination and intraocular sampling when indicated.
• Do not delay definitive treatment for routine laboratory investigations.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. INTRAVITREAL ANTIBIOTICS[/color]
• Vancomycin 1 mg/0.1 mL intravitreal.
• Plus ceftazidime 2.25 mg/0.1 mL intravitreal.
• Administered by an appropriately trained ophthalmologist.
• Severe cases may require urgent vitrectomy.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. SYSTEMIC TREATMENT[/color]
• Consider systemic antibiotics when endogenous endophthalmitis is suspected.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content: • Intravitreal medications require exact preparation and specialist administration. Incorrect concentration may cause severe ocular injury.

sections.heading: 06 — DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
sections.content:
• Severe postoperative inflammation.
• Toxic anterior segment syndrome.
• Acute uveitis.
• Severe microbial keratitis.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Immediate ophthalmic surgical assessment; hospital admission is commonly required.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Pain and rapidly worsening vision after eye surgery or injection are major warning signs.
• Treatment delay can cause irreversible blindness.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO: AWaRe Antibiotic Book; AAO EyeWiki.

Orbit, Adnexa & Ocular Infections.title: Postoperative Eye Emergency and Suspected Endophthalmitis

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Postoperative eye emergencies may include endophthalmitis, wound leak, raised intraocular pressure, retinal detachment, hemorrhage, or corneal complications. Acute endophthalmitis is a severe intraocular infection that may occur after surgery or intravitreal injection.
• Increasing eye pain, redness, or blurred vision after ocular procedure.
• Photophobia and reduced visual acuity.
• Hypopyon or marked intraocular inflammation may be present.
• Some patients with endophthalmitis have relatively little pain.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Rapid visual deterioration after surgery or injection. Hypopyon, severe inflammation, or suspected wound leak. Proptosis, severe pain, or neurological symptoms. Recent penetrating trauma or signs of open globe.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Record visual acuity and exact procedure and date.
• Contact operating ophthalmologist or emergency ophthalmology service immediately.
• Do NOT delay assessment for routine outpatient follow-up.
• Avoid pressure on eye if wound leak or open-globe injury suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT patch tightly, manipulate surgical wound, or start steroid drops without specialist advice.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urgent slit-lamp examination.
• Assessment of surgical wound, anterior chamber, IOP when safe, and posterior segment.
• Dilated fundus examination when visualization permits.
• B-scan ultrasound when posterior visualization limited and open-globe injury excluded.
• Aqueous or vitreous sampling for microbiology when indicated by ophthalmologist.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Suspected Acute Postoperative Endophthalmitis[/color]
• Immediate ophthalmology/vitreoretinal consultation. Intraocular sampling and intravitreal antibiotics commonly required. Decision between intravitreal treatment alone and urgent vitrectomy depends on visual acuity, clinical severity, and specialist assessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Common Intravitreal Regimens (Ophthalmologist-Administered):[/color]
• Vancomycin 1 mg/0.1 mL intravitreally.
• Ceftazidime 2.25 mg/0.1 mL intravitreally.
• [color=#991B1B]These are specialist intravitreal preparations requiring strict aseptic technique, correct dilution, and verification of final concentration by trained ophthalmic personnel. Intravitreal dosing is NOT interchangeable with systemic dosing. Preparation errors can cause severe retinal toxicity. Do NOT attempt preparation or injection in an unequipped emergency department.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Other Postoperative Complications[/color]
• Raised IOP, wound leak, retinal detachment, and suprachoroidal hemorrhage require diagnosis-specific urgent ophthalmic treatment.
• Do NOT assume all postoperative pain or reduced vision represents infection.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Treat identified complication promptly.
• Arrange repeated examinations and microbiological follow-up when endophthalmitis suspected.
• Review postoperative medications with operating ophthalmologist.
• Document visual acuity and all changes carefully.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate transfer or direct assessment by ophthalmic surgical team.
• Do NOT discharge a patient with suspected postoperative endophthalmitis without specialist evaluation.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Endophthalmitis Clinical Guidance; Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study; ESCRS Prevention and Management of Postoperative Endophthalmitis.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) occurs when varicella-zoster virus reactivates in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1).
• Unilateral painful vesicular rash involving forehead, scalp, or upper eyelid.
• Burning, tingling, or neuropathic pain.
• Red eye, tearing, photophobia, or blurred vision if ocular structures involved.
• Vesicles on tip or side of nose (Hutchinson sign) increase concern for ocular involvement.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Reduced vision, severe eye pain, photophobia, or corneal changes. Immunocompromised status or disseminated rash. Ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, severe headache, confusion, or other neurological signs. Suspected keratitis, uveitis, retinitis, or optic nerve involvement.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess visual acuity, pupils, eye movements, and distribution of rash.
• Begin systemic antiviral treatment promptly when HZO suspected; most effective when started within 72 hours of rash onset.
• Arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment, especially if ocular symptoms or signs present.
• Provide appropriate analgesia and advise against touching/scratching lesions.
• Use standard infection-control precautions and cover lesions when feasible.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Clinical diagnosis is often sufficient for typical cases.
• Visual acuity and ocular examination are essential.
• Slit-lamp examination and fluorescein staining indicated when ocular involvement suspected.
• Renal function should be assessed when clinically indicated to guide antiviral dosing.
• Atypical, disseminated, or immunocompromised cases may require additional investigations and specialist input.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Oral Antiviral Therapy — Adults[/color]
• Valacyclovir 1,000 mg orally three times daily for 7 days.
• Alternatives: Acyclovir 800 mg orally five times daily for 7–10 days or Famciclovir 500 mg orally three times daily for 7 days.
• Start as early as possible, ideally within 72 hours of rash onset.
• [color=#991B1B]Severe disease, disseminated infection, immunocompromise, or neurological involvement may require hospital admission and IV therapy.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Intravenous Antiviral Therapy for Severe Disease[/color]
• IV acyclovir may be indicated for severe, disseminated, neurological, or selected immunocompromised cases. Common adult regimen: 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours, adjusted for renal function.
• [color=#991B1B]IV acyclovir can cause crystal-associated kidney injury and neurotoxicity, particularly when renal dosing or hydration is inadequate. Involve specialist for severe disease.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Ocular Treatment[/color]
• Preservative-free lubricants may help surface discomfort.
• Specific antiviral eye treatment, topical corticosteroids, and IOP-lowering medication depend on ocular complication and should be directed by ophthalmology.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT initiate topical corticosteroids without ophthalmology supervision.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Pain Control[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed, subject to patient-specific maximum limits.
• Neuropathic pain treatment may be considered when indicated, according to local guidance.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Complete indicated systemic antiviral course.
• Treat keratitis, uveitis, retinitis, or raised intraocular pressure under ophthalmology guidance.
• Monitor for delayed ocular complications and postherpetic neuralgia.
• Consider specialist input for immunocompromised patients or suspected neurological involvement.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Same-day ophthalmology review recommended when ocular involvement suspected.
• Admit or arrange urgent specialist assessment for severe ocular disease, disseminated infection, neurological signs, or inability to take oral treatment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus; NIH Clinical Guidelines Varicella-Zoster Virus Disease; CMAJ Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus.

General Ophthalmic Emergencies.title: Acute Painful Red Eye — Emergency Differential Diagnosis

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
A painful red eye may be caused by minor surface disease or a vision-threatening emergency. Priority is to identify conditions requiring immediate treatment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Important differential diagnoses:[/color] Acute angle-closure glaucoma. Microbial keratitis and corneal ulcer. Anterior uveitis. Scleritis. Endophthalmitis. Chemical injury. Open-globe injury. Severe conjunctivitis or episcleritis.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Reduced visual acuity. Severe pain or marked photophobia. Corneal opacity or infiltrate. Fixed or mid-dilated pupil. Halos around lights, headache, nausea, or vomiting. Hypopyon, proptosis, or restricted eye movements. Recent ocular surgery, injection, trauma, or chemical exposure.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and systemic illness when indicated.
• Measure visual acuity in each eye separately if safe.
• Examine pupils, ocular movements, cornea, and pattern of redness.
• Ask about contact lenses, trauma, chemical exposure, previous glaucoma, recent procedures, and medication use.
• Suspected chemical injury requires immediate copious irrigation before detailed examination.
• Suspected open-globe injury requires rigid shield without pressure and immediate ophthalmology transfer.
• Arrange urgent specialist assessment for any red flag or uncertain diagnosis.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Visual acuity and pupil examination.
• Fluorescein staining when appropriate and open-globe injury not suspected.
• Slit-lamp examination when available.
• Intraocular pressure measurement only when open-globe injury excluded and measurement appropriate.
• Additional tests depend on suspected diagnosis.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma[/color]
• Immediate emergency ophthalmology consultation. Initiate pressure-lowering therapy per dedicated acute angle-closure glaucoma protocol. Definitive treatment usually involves laser peripheral iridotomy.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay treatment for severe ocular pain, reduced vision, halos, headache, nausea, and a mid-dilated pupil.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Microbial Keratitis[/color]
• Urgent ophthalmology assessment. Corneal scraping when indicated. Intensive topical antimicrobial therapy directed by severity and likely organism.
• [color=#991B1B]Contact lens-associated painful red eye is particularly concerning for microbial keratitis.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Anterior Uveitis or Scleritis[/color]
• Urgent ophthalmology assessment. Cycloplegic and anti-inflammatory therapy may be required after diagnosis. Suspected infectious causes must be considered before initiating corticosteroids.

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Suspected Endophthalmitis[/color]
• Immediate ophthalmology/vitreoretinal assessment. Intraocular antimicrobial therapy may be required urgently.

[color=#1E3A8A]5. Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed, within patient-specific limits.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Identify underlying cause and follow relevant disease-specific protocol.
• Reassess visual acuity and clinical findings after initial treatment.
• Provide explicit return precautions and arrange specialist follow-up.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Immediate emergency ophthalmology assessment: Reduced vision, severe pain, corneal opacity, abnormal pupil, hypopyon, recent eye surgery or injection, suspected open-globe injury, or suspected acute angle closure.
• Possible outpatient management: Only when a benign diagnosis is established, visual acuity is reassuring, dangerous causes excluded, and follow-up is reliable.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAO Red Eye and Emergency Ophthalmology Guidance; Merck Manual Professional Edition Red Eye; Emergency Ophthalmology Clinical Assessment Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
An open fracture is a fracture associated with a wound communicating with the fracture or fracture hematoma. Even a small wound may represent an open fracture.

[color=#1E3A8A]Assess:[/color]
• Wound location, contamination, tissue loss, and exposed bone.
• Mechanism and energy of injury.
• Distal pulses, capillary refill, temperature, sensation, and motor function.
• Associated vascular injury, compartment syndrome, and systemic trauma.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform the trauma primary survey and control life-threatening hemorrhage.
• Contact orthopedics immediately; involve vascular or plastic surgery when indicated.
• Cover the wound with sterile saline-moistened gauze and an appropriate sterile dressing.
• Do not repeatedly probe the wound or attempt definitive wound cleaning in the ED.
• Realign and splint the limb when appropriate; document neurovascular status before and after manipulation.
• Administer IV antibiotics as early as possible, ideally within one hour.
• Assess tetanus immunization and provide prophylaxis.
• Keep the patient fasting if surgery is likely.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Radiographs including the joint above and below the fracture.
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation profile, and type and crossmatch according to injury severity.
• CTA or urgent vascular assessment if vascular injury is suspected; do not delay revascularization for imaging when hard signs are present.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics (Adult examples):[/color]
• Lower-grade: cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours (local protocols may differ).
• Severe contamination/high-grade: protocol-specific broader regimen.
• Pediatric example: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV per dose, commonly every 8 hours.

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration:[/color]
• Give antibiotics promptly and document administration time.
• Duration depends on fracture grade, operative findings, contamination, and local protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Surgical management:[/color]
• Urgent operative irrigation and debridement.
• Stabilization of the fracture.
• Early definitive soft-tissue coverage.
• Vascular repair or shunting if limb perfusion is compromised.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Antibiotics do not replace operative debridement.
• Do not delay antibiotics while waiting for radiographs or an orthopedic review.
• Do not push exposed bone back into the wound.
• Suspected arterial injury requires urgent specialist management.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit for urgent orthopedic management. High-energy, contaminated, vascularly compromised injuries require a trauma center.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Any wound near a fracture should be treated as potentially communicating until assessed.
• Record neurovascular status before and after splinting or reduction.
• Tetanus prophylaxis depends on immunization history and wound characteristics.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE, Fractures (Complex): Assessment and Management; NICE, Major Trauma.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Complete or partial traumatic separation of finger, hand, foot, or limb. Severe bleeding, contamination, crush injury, or associated fractures.
• Assess for shock and additional injuries.
• A partially attached part may retain some circulation; do not complete amputation at bedside.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow ABCDE and control life-threatening hemorrhage.
• Apply firm direct pressure and pressure dressing. Use tourniquet for life-threatening extremity hemorrhage not rapidly controlled with direct pressure, per trauma protocol. Record tourniquet application time and keep visible.
• Do not clamp vessels blindly.
• Cover stump with sterile dressing and provide analgesia.
• Contact orthopedic, vascular, and microsurgical/replantation services early when available.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, blood group and crossmatch, coagulation, electrolytes, blood gas/lactate when indicated.
• Radiographs of residual limb and amputated part when they will guide management and will not delay resuscitation.
• Assess for crush syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, other traumatic injuries in severe crush or prolonged entrapment.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Hemorrhage Control[/color]
• Blood products and resuscitation fluids guided by hemodynamic status and major hemorrhage protocol. Tranexamic acid may be considered for significant traumatic hemorrhage when indicated and within early treatment window.

[color=#1E3A8A]Stump and Amputated-Part Care[/color]
• Administer IV antibiotics according to contamination/tissue damage/open-fracture status/allergies/local protocol. Give tetanus prophylaxis as indicated.
• Cover stump with sterile dressing after bleeding control. Wrap amputated part in sterile gauze lightly moistened with saline, place in sealed waterproof bag, place that bag in second container with ice and water. Keep tissue cool but do not place directly on ice or immerse directly in water. Label part and send with patient.
• Do not freeze part, scrub it, or apply antiseptic directly to it.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay life-saving hemorrhage control to preserve amputated part.
• A tourniquet must not be intermittently loosened outside a trained, protocol-directed setting.
• Replantation suitability depends on mechanism, ischemia time, tissue condition, patient stability, specialist assessment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Emergency transfer or admission required for complete amputation, major bleeding, significant crush injury, or possible replantation.
• Any unstable patient requires resuscitation and definitive hemorrhage control before nonessential procedures.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS; Stop the Bleed; AAOS Limb Salvage/Amputation Resources; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Prolonged compression of muscle after entrapment, building collapse, industrial injury, or severe limb trauma. Muscle pain, swelling, weakness, or dark urine may occur.
• Systemic complications: rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury, metabolic acidosis, shock. Hyperkalemia can cause fatal dysrhythmias.
• Crush syndrome may develop even when external injuries appear limited.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow trauma ABCDE approach and activate appropriate rescue/trauma teams.
• Establish IV access and cardiac monitoring as early as feasible.
• Obtain urgent blood tests, including potassium, creatinine, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, creatine kinase. Check ECG promptly when hyperkalemia possible.
• Begin isotonic crystalloid resuscitation when indicated, individualized to hemodynamics, urine output, renal function, risk of fluid overload.
• Seek urgent critical-care, trauma, and surgical advice.
• Do not delay lifesaving rescue or hemorrhage control for laboratory testing.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serial potassium, renal function, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, creatine kinase.
• Blood gas and lactate when shock or metabolic disturbance suspected.
• Urinalysis; heme-positive urine with few red cells may suggest myoglobinuria.
• ECG monitoring for hyperkalemic changes.
• Assess for associated fractures, vascular injury, compartment syndrome.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• Use isotonic crystalloid according to perfusion, hemodynamic status, urine output, renal function, local crush-injury protocol. Do not apply fixed high-volume regimen to every patient, particularly when renal failure or cardiac dysfunction present.
• Reassess BP, HR, lung examination, peripheral perfusion, urine output, electrolytes, renal function. Insert urinary catheter when clinically indicated for accurate output monitoring. In adults, urine output targets may be individualized; avoid pursuing target with escalating fluid when patient anuric or developing pulmonary edema.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hyperkalemia Management[/color]
• If hyperkalemia causes ECG changes or is severe, treat immediately per emergency hyperkalemia protocol. IV calcium used to stabilize myocardium when indicated; insulin with glucose and inhaled beta-agonist may be used to shift potassium intracellularly. Select drug doses according to age, renal function, ECG findings, local protocol.
• Continuous ECG monitoring required for severe hyperkalemia. Recheck potassium after treatment and monitor glucose frequently after insulin. Arrange definitive potassium removal and renal replacement therapy when indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]Limb Assessment and Surgical Management[/color]
• Perform serial examinations for compartment syndrome and vascular compromise. Fasciotomy indicated when compartment syndrome diagnosed after urgent surgical assessment; not routinely indicated solely because crush injury occurred.
• Debridement or amputation may be necessary for nonviable tissue, uncontrollable infection, or unsalvageable limb. Dialysis may be required for refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, fluid overload, or other standard indications for renal replacement therapy.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Excessive fluid administration can cause life-threatening overload.
• Routine bicarbonate or mannitol is not recommended for every case of rhabdomyolysis; use only for specific indications under appropriate protocol.
• Calcium stabilizes myocardium but does not lower serum potassium. Hyperkalemia treatment is temporizing; potassium must be monitored and definitive management arranged.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with suspected crush syndrome for serial laboratory testing and monitoring.
• Critical-care admission for shock, severe electrolyte disturbance, dysrhythmias, respiratory compromise, or renal failure.
• Arrange urgent nephrology and orthopedic/surgical involvement when indicated.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAST Rhabdomyolysis Consensus; KDIGO AKI Guideline; Local trauma/hyperkalemia protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — GENERAL SAFETY CHECKLIST
sections.content:
For all orthopedic emergencies:

• Complete the trauma primary survey before focusing on the fracture.
• Document neurovascular status before and after reduction, splinting, or casting.
• Escalate immediately for an absent pulse, a cold or pale limb, progressive neurological deficit, severe disproportionate pain, or uncontrolled bleeding.
• Do not delay time-critical surgery or revascularization for unnecessary imaging.
• Confirm allergies, weight-based dosing, renal function, pregnancy status when relevant, and local antimicrobial protocols.
• Record consultation, decisions, reassessments, and transfer arrangements clearly.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Supracondylar fracture is a common pediatric elbow injury. Displaced fractures may injure the brachial artery, median/anterior interosseous nerve, radial nerve, or ulnar nerve.

[color=#1E3A8A]Assess:[/color]
• Swelling, deformity, skin tenting, and open wounds.
• Radial pulse, capillary refill, hand temperature, and color.
• Median/anterior interosseous, radial, and ulnar nerve function.
• Pain, passive-stretch pain, and compartment syndrome signs.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Provide age- and weight-appropriate analgesia.
• Contact orthopedics urgently for displaced fractures or any neurovascular abnormality.
• Document neurovascular status before and after splinting or reduction.
• Immobilize in an above-elbow backslab; avoid excessive elbow flexion.
• Obtain AP and lateral radiographs of the distal humerus.
• Urgent reduction and fixation are needed for displaced fractures, vascular compromise, open injury, or threatened skin.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP and lateral radiographs of the distal humerus.
• Repeat neurovascular examination after any intervention.
• Doppler or vascular imaging only as directed by the specialist.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia:[/color]
• Paracetamol: 15 mg/kg orally per dose, every 4–6 hours as needed.
• Ibuprofen: 10 mg/kg orally per dose every 6–8 hours (if appropriate).
• IV analgesia may be needed for severe pain.

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Orthopedic reduction and percutaneous pin fixation may be required.
• A child with a pulseless, poorly perfused hand needs emergency orthopedic and vascular assessment.
• A pulseless but warm, well-perfused hand after reduction may be observed in selected cases under close specialist supervision.
• Monitor for compartment syndrome and evolving nerve dysfunction.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not dismiss a pulseless hand.
• Do not apply a tight circumferential cast to a swollen elbow.
• Avoid prolonged flexion in a tense, swollen limb.
• A normal capillary refill alone does not exclude vascular injury.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Undisplaced fractures may be managed with immobilization and planned follow-up. Displaced fractures, open fractures, vascular compromise, or suspected compartment syndrome require urgent specialist care and often admission.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Assess the anterior interosseous nerve by asking the child to make an 'OK' sign.
• Record pulse, perfusion, and nerve function before and after splinting.
• Reassess swelling and pain frequently.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital, Supracondylar Fracture of the Humerus; NICE, Fractures (Complex).

Upper Limb Injuries.title: Pediatric Forearm Fracture with Neurovascular Compromise

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Forearm pain, deformity, swelling, reduced use of affected arm. Assess radial and ulnar pulses, capillary refill, hand temperature, finger movement. Test median, anterior interosseous, ulnar, and radial nerve function as age/cooperation allow.
• A pale, cold, poorly perfused hand or progressive neurological deficit is an emergency.
• Severe pain, tense swelling, pain with passive finger stretch may indicate compartment syndrome.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow trauma stabilization principles.
• Provide age- and weight-appropriate analgesia. Remove rings or constrictive items.
• Document neurovascular examination before and after any manipulation.
• Obtain urgent orthopedic assistance for vascular compromise, open fracture, severe deformity, or suspected compartment syndrome.
• If circulation threatened, urgent reduction by trained clinician should not be delayed for routine imaging.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP and lateral radiographs of forearm, including wrist and elbow as appropriate.
• CBC and other tests only when indicated by major trauma, bleeding, or planned intervention.
• Vascular imaging or specialist vascular assessment when arterial injury remains suspected after reduction.
• Repeat neurovascular examinations and document changes.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Reduction and Immobilization[/color]
• Use appropriate pediatric analgesic regimen based on weight and contraindications. Procedural sedation or anesthesia may be required for reduction and must follow pediatric sedation protocols.
• Calculate all medication doses from child's current weight. Verify maximum doses and concentrations. Prepare appropriate pediatric monitoring, oxygen, suction, airway equipment if sedation planned.
• Immobilize fracture with appropriately padded splint. If reduction required, perform under suitable analgesia or anesthesia by trained clinician. Reassess circulation, sensation, motor function immediately after reduction and immobilization. Obtain post-reduction radiographs.

[color=#1E3A8A]Open Fracture Management[/color]
• Cover wound with sterile dressing. Administer IV antibiotics promptly according to pediatric open-fracture protocol. Give tetanus prophylaxis when indicated. Arrange urgent orthopedic assessment and operative management when required.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• A normal pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome or evolving vascular injury.
• Increasing pain, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, or progressive sensory/motor loss requires immediate reassessment.
• Do not delay emergency orthopedic intervention for a persistently ischemic hand.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or transfer for neurovascular compromise, open fracture, suspected compartment syndrome, unstable reduction, or need for urgent surgery.
• Outpatient care only for selected stable fractures with intact perfusion, adequate immobilization, pain control, reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: BOAST Fractures in Children; NICE Non-Complex Fractures; AO Pediatric Resources; Local protocols.

Upper Limb Injuries.title: Humeral Shaft Fracture with Radial Nerve Injury

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Upper-arm pain, swelling, bruising, deformity, and reduced arm function after trauma.
• Radial nerve injury may cause wrist drop, weak finger extension, and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand near the first web space.
• Assess brachial artery perfusion, distal pulses, capillary refill, and hand temperature.
• Open fracture, vascular injury, and progressive neurological deficits require urgent specialist assessment.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow the trauma ABCDE approach when indicated.
• Provide analgesia and support the arm in a suitable splint.
• Document radial, median, and ulnar nerve function before and after immobilization.
• Assess distal perfusion and document pulses.
• Cover open wounds with a sterile dressing and initiate the open-fracture protocol.
• Arrange orthopedic consultation for displaced fractures, open injuries, vascular compromise, or worsening neurological findings.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP and lateral radiographs of the humerus, including the shoulder and elbow as appropriate.
• Vascular imaging if arterial injury is suspected.
• CBC and blood group/crossmatch if significant bleeding or surgery is anticipated.
• Repeat neurological examination and document the findings clearly.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Immobilization and Analgesia[/color]
• Use paracetamol or other appropriate analgesia according to age, weight, renal and hepatic function, and local protocol. Titrated opioid analgesia may be required for severe pain.
• Prepare a suitable coaptation splint or other immobilization device.
• Immobilize the arm and support it in a sling when appropriate. Reassess skin condition, distal perfusion, sensation, and motor function after splinting.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Many closed humeral shaft fractures can be treated with functional bracing or other nonoperative methods.
• Operative fixation may be required for open fractures, vascular injury, unstable fracture patterns, polytrauma, or selected cases of nonunion.
• A primary radial nerve palsy associated with a closed fracture does not automatically require immediate nerve exploration; the decision depends on fracture pattern, associated injuries, and specialist assessment.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not apply a tight circumferential cast to a markedly swollen arm.
• New or progressive neurological deficits or impaired perfusion require urgent reassessment.
• Open injury, suspected nerve transection, or new neurological deficit after manipulation or fixation requires urgent specialist review.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Refer to orthopedics for definitive fracture management.
• Admit or transfer for open injury, vascular compromise, unstable polytrauma, or other urgent surgical indications.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AO Surgery Reference; AAOS Humeral Shaft Fractures; Local protocols.

Upper Limb Injuries.title: Clavicle Fracture with Skin or Neurovascular Compromise

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Shoulder pain, swelling, bruising, and tenderness over the clavicle.
• Displacement may cause skin tenting, blanching, or threatened skin breakdown.
• Assess for associated rib fractures, pneumothorax, and chest injury.
• Check distal perfusion and brachial plexus function.
• Open fracture, skin compromise, or suspected subclavian vessel injury is an emergency.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, and circulation, especially after high-energy trauma.
• Inspect the skin carefully over the fracture.
• Provide analgesia and support the arm in a sling.
• Document distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation, and motor function.
• Obtain urgent orthopedic consultation for open fracture, threatened skin, vascular injury, or severe displacement.
• Do not repeatedly manipulate the fracture in the emergency department.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Clavicle radiographs.
• Chest radiograph or CT according to trauma mechanism and suspected associated injury.
• CT angiography when subclavian or other major vascular injury is suspected and the patient is sufficiently stable.
• Additional imaging for suspected pneumothorax, rib fractures, or scapular injury.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia and Support[/color]
• Use appropriate analgesia based on age, weight, renal and hepatic function, and contraindications.
• Prepare a correctly fitted sling that supports the arm without excessive pressure.
• Support the arm and reassess pain, skin condition, and distal neurovascular status.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Most uncomplicated clavicle fractures can be treated nonoperatively with a sling and gradual rehabilitation.
• Surgery may be indicated for open fracture, threatened skin, neurovascular injury, selected markedly displaced fractures, or associated shoulder-girdle instability.
• Associated chest injuries must be evaluated and treated independently.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Skin blanching or severe tenting over a displaced fracture requires urgent orthopedic assessment.
• A normal distal pulse does not exclude subclavian vascular injury.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent orthopedic review for skin compromise, open injury, marked displacement, or neurovascular abnormality.
• Admit or transfer for major associated trauma or suspected vascular injury.
• Discharge is appropriate for selected uncomplicated fractures with adequate pain control and follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAOS Clavicle Fractures; NICE Non-Complex Fractures; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Fracture of proximal ulna associated with dislocation of radial head.
• Pain, swelling, deformity, reduced movement of elbow and forearm.
• Radial head dislocation can be missed if elbow not adequately imaged.
• Assess posterior interosseous nerve function (finger and thumb extension).
• Pediatric cases may have subtle radiographic findings and require careful assessment.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Provide analgesia and support arm.
• Document distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation, motor function.
• Obtain radiographs of entire forearm, including elbow and wrist.
• Apply well-padded splint and avoid repeated manipulation.
• Arrange urgent orthopedic assessment.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP and lateral radiographs of forearm, elbow, wrist as indicated.
• Confirm alignment of radiocapitellar joint on appropriate views.
• CT may be needed for complex fractures or uncertain joint alignment.
• Repeat neurovascular examination after splinting or reduction.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Immobilization and Reduction[/color]
• Provide age- and weight-appropriate analgesia. Procedural sedation or anesthesia may be required for reduction, particularly in children.
• Immobilize forearm and arrange prompt orthopedic reduction/stabilization. Reassess radial nerve function, distal perfusion, sensation after any intervention. Obtain post-reduction imaging to confirm restoration of radial head alignment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
