• In adults, operative stabilization of ulna commonly required to restore radial head alignment.
• In children, management depends on fracture pattern, displacement, stability; many require reduction and close specialist follow-up.
• Persistent radial head dislocation requires urgent reassessment.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Failure to recognize radial head dislocation can lead to chronic disability.
• Do not repeatedly attempt reduction without appropriate expertise and imaging.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent orthopedic referral or admission generally required.
• Transfer to center with pediatric or upper-limb expertise if appropriate treatment unavailable locally.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AO Surgery Reference; BOAST Fractures in Children; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Fracture of radial shaft, typically distal third, associated with disruption of distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ).
• Forearm pain, wrist pain, swelling, restricted pronation/supination. DRUJ instability may be subtle.
• Check for ulnar nerve symptoms and distal neurovascular compromise.
• In children, related injury may involve distal radial fracture with distal ulnar physeal injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Provide analgesia and immobilize forearm. Document distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation, finger movement.
• Obtain radiographs of entire forearm, including wrist and elbow.
• Seek urgent orthopedic assessment, especially for deformity, open injury, or neurovascular abnormalities.
• Cover open wounds with sterile dressing and initiate open-fracture care.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP and lateral forearm radiographs including wrist and elbow.
• Assess DRUJ alignment and compare with opposite side when necessary.
• CT may help evaluate complex DRUJ injury or uncertain alignment.
• Post-reduction or postoperative imaging should confirm restoration of alignment.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Immobilization and Pain Control[/color]
• Use appropriate analgesia based on age, weight, renal function, contraindications. Procedural sedation or anesthesia may be needed for selected reductions.
• Immobilize limb and avoid forceful forearm rotation. Reassess distal perfusion, sensation, motor function after splinting. Arrange urgent orthopedic management.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Adult Galeazzi fractures commonly require operative fixation of radius and assessment of DRUJ stability. Additional stabilization may be needed if DRUJ remains unstable after fixation.
• Pediatric management depends on specific fracture pattern and stability.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• A radial shaft fracture with DRUJ disruption can be missed if wrist not examined and imaged.
• Do not assume injury is stable solely because radial fracture appears minimally displaced.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent orthopedic referral and usually hospital-based definitive management.
• Admit or transfer for open fracture, neurovascular compromise, unstable joint alignment, or need for surgery.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AO Surgery Reference; NICE Complex Fractures; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Severe elbow pain, deformity, swelling, restricted movement after trauma. Posterior dislocation common.
• Assess brachial artery and distal perfusion. Check median, ulnar, and radial nerve function.
• Consider associated radial head, coronoid, or distal humeral fractures.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Provide analgesia and support arm.
• Document pulses, capillary refill, hand temperature, sensation, motor function before reduction.
• Obtain radiographs before reduction if no urgent neurovascular/skin threat and imaging immediately available.
• Urgent reduction required when vascular compromise or severe skin tension present.
• Seek orthopedic help for complex dislocation, associated fracture, open injury, or failed reduction.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP and lateral elbow radiographs.
• Post-reduction radiographs to confirm alignment and identify fractures.
• CT when associated fracture or complex injury suspected.
• Vascular imaging and urgent vascular consultation when arterial injury suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Reduction and Analgesia[/color]
• Select procedural sedation or appropriate regional/local anesthetic technique according to patient condition/expertise/protocol. Sedative and analgesic doses must be individualized.
• Prepare cardiorespiratory monitoring, oxygen, suction, airway equipment, resuscitation supplies before procedural sedation. Ensure trained personnel available.
• Reduction by trained clinician gently. Reassess neurovascular function immediately after. Immobilize elbow in appropriate splint. Obtain post-reduction imaging and assess joint stability.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Simple stable dislocations may be managed with brief immobilization followed by supervised early mobilization. Associated fractures, instability, open dislocation, or vascular injury may require surgery.
• Avoid unnecessarily prolonged immobilization because elbow stiffness can develop rapidly.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not make repeated forceful attempts.
• Persistent absent pulse, expanding hematoma, progressive neurological deficit, or irreducibility requires urgent specialist intervention.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent orthopedic assessment for all confirmed dislocations.
• Admission or transfer for complex injuries, neurovascular compromise, open injury, or unstable reduction.
• Discharge only after satisfactory reduction, imaging, neurovascular reassessment, clear follow-up plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AO Surgery Reference; NICE Complex Fractures; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute shoulder pain, deformity, restricted movement, inability to use arm. Anterior dislocation common; posterior dislocation may follow seizures/electrical injury and can be missed on single AP radiograph.
• Assess axillary nerve function (sensation over lateral deltoid, deltoid contraction when feasible).
• Check radial pulse, capillary refill, hand sensation, distal motor function.
• Consider associated proximal humerus fracture, brachial plexus injury, or vascular injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Provide analgesia and support arm in comfortable position.
• Document neurovascular status before any reduction attempt.
• Obtain appropriate radiographs before reduction when fracture suspected and patient neurovascularly intact.
• Urgent reduction needed when vascular compromise suspected, under appropriately trained clinician and local emergency protocol.
• Avoid repeated or forceful reduction attempts.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Shoulder radiographs, including views that assess alignment and help identify associated fractures.
• Additional imaging if posterior dislocation suspected or radiographs inconclusive.
• Vascular imaging and urgent specialist consultation if arterial injury suspected.
• Repeat neurovascular examination after reduction.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia and Reduction[/color]
• Use analgesia and, where appropriate, procedural sedation or intra-articular local anesthetic per local protocol and patient factors.
• If procedural sedation planned, prepare monitoring, oxygen, suction, airway equipment, resuscitation supplies. If intra-articular anesthesia selected, use approved sterile technique and verify maximum safe local-anesthetic dose.
• Reduction by trained clinician using gentle, appropriate technique. Stop if unexpected resistance, worsening pain, or concern for fracture.
• Reassess distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation, motor function immediately after reduction. Obtain post-reduction radiographs and immobilize shoulder.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not attempt routine manipulation when associated fracture or complex injury makes it unsafe.
• Persistent absent pulse, expanding hematoma, or progressive neurological deficit requires urgent specialist assessment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Discharge may be considered after successful reduction, satisfactory post-reduction imaging, intact/evaluated neurovascular status, safe follow-up plan.
• Admit or transfer for fracture-dislocation, vascular injury, irreducibility, or unresolved neurological deficit.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAOS Shoulder Dislocation; NICE Complex Fractures; Local protocols.

Upper Limb Injuries.title: Acute Rotator Cuff Tear After Trauma

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Sudden shoulder pain and weakness following a fall, traction injury, or shoulder dislocation.
• Inability to actively elevate the arm despite relatively preserved passive movement.
• Weakness may be more prominent than pain after initial analgesia.
• Consider associated proximal humerus fracture, dislocation, and axillary nerve injury.
• Older adults may develop an acute tear after relatively minor trauma.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess for fracture, dislocation, and neurovascular injury.
• Provide analgesia and support the arm in a sling for comfort.
• Document active and passive shoulder movement when safe.
• Assess axillary nerve sensation over the lateral shoulder and distal upper-limb neurological function.
• Arrange urgent orthopedic assessment if there is marked weakness, inability to elevate the arm, or suspected acute full-thickness tear.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Shoulder radiographs to exclude fracture or dislocation.
• Ultrasound or MRI when a significant rotator cuff tear is suspected.
• Additional imaging if nerve injury or other structural injury is suspected.
• Document the degree of weakness and functional limitation.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia and Support[/color]
• Use appropriate analgesia according to age, comorbidities, renal function, and contraindications.
• Prepare a sling that supports the arm without unnecessary prolonged immobilization.
• Provide analgesia and reassess shoulder function. Encourage gentle movement of unaffected joints.
• Avoid forceful shoulder exercises until fracture, dislocation, and major tendon injury have been assessed.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Treatment depends on tear size, tendon involvement, functional requirements, and patient factors.
• Early specialist assessment is important for suspected acute traumatic full-thickness tears because selected patients may benefit from timely repair.
• Rehabilitation is guided by the final diagnosis and specialist plan.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Persistent inability to actively elevate the arm after trauma warrants further evaluation even when radiographs are normal.
• Do not attribute all weakness to pain without reassessment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent orthopedic or shoulder-specialist follow-up for substantial weakness or suspected full-thickness tear.
• Emergency referral is required for associated dislocation, fracture, vascular compromise, or progressive neurological deficit.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAOS Management of Rotator Cuff Injuries; NICE Non-Complex Fractures; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Wrist pain after fall on outstretched hand. Tenderness in anatomical snuffbox or over scaphoid tubercle. Pain with axial loading of thumb or wrist movement.
• Initial radiographs may be normal despite clinically significant fracture.
• Proximal pole fractures have increased risk of avascular necrosis due to scaphoid's blood supply.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Remove rings and assess swelling. Document distal perfusion, sensation, motor function.
• Immobilize wrist in thumb-spica splint when scaphoid fracture suspected.
• Avoid forceful wrist movement and weight-bearing through affected hand.
• Arrange timely fracture-clinic or orthopedic assessment.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Scaphoid-specific wrist radiographs.
• If initial radiographs negative but clinical suspicion remains: arrange MRI where available; CT may be used according to local pathways. Repeat radiographs may be considered if advanced imaging unavailable, but should not replace appropriate follow-up.
• Reassess for associated distal radius or other carpal fractures.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Immobilization and Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol according to age, weight, liver function, local guidance. NSAID may be considered when appropriate after assessing renal function, GI risk, contraindications.
• Immobilize wrist with well-padded wrist splint that protects suspected fracture. Provide clear instructions to keep splint dry/intact. Reassess swelling, sensation, skin condition, distal perfusion. Arrange definitive imaging and follow-up.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Nondisplaced fractures may be treated with immobilization under specialist guidance. Displaced fractures, proximal pole fractures, instability, or nonunion may require surgical fixation. Follow-up imaging important to confirm healing.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not dismiss persistent anatomical snuffbox tenderness because initial radiographs are normal.
• Increasing pain, numbness, or cold/pale hand requires urgent reassessment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Discharge may be appropriate with immobilization, adequate analgesia, reliable follow-up.
• Refer urgently if neurovascular compromise, open injury, or significant associated trauma.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Non-Complex Fractures; BSSH Scaphoid Fractures; AO Surgery Reference.

Wrist & Hand Injuries.title: Distal Radius Fracture with Neurovascular Compromise

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Wrist pain, swelling, deformity, reduced hand function after fall.
• Check radial pulse, capillary refill, hand temperature, finger movement.
• Assess median nerve function (sensation in thumb/index/middle fingers, thumb opposition when possible).
• Severe pain, progressive median nerve symptoms, or tense wrist may indicate acute carpal tunnel syndrome.
• Open fractures and marked deformity require urgent assessment.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Remove rings and constrictive items. Document neurovascular examination before manipulation.
• Provide analgesia and elevate limb if appropriate.
• Obtain wrist radiographs if this does not delay treatment of threatened circulation or skin.
• Urgent reduction required for markedly displaced fracture with threatened skin or compromised circulation.
• Seek urgent orthopedic assistance for persistent ischemia, progressive neurological deficits, open injury, or suspected acute carpal tunnel syndrome.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP and lateral wrist radiographs. Include forearm imaging if injury extends proximally or additional fracture suspected.
• Post-reduction radiographs to confirm alignment.
• CT may be required for complex intra-articular fractures and operative planning.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Reduction and Immobilization[/color]
• Use appropriate analgesia, regional anesthesia, or procedural sedation according to patient condition/local protocol.
• Perform reduction using appropriate technique by trained clinician. Apply well-padded splint that accommodates swelling. Repeat neurovascular examination immediately after reduction/immobilization. Obtain post-reduction radiographs.

[color=#1E3A8A]Open Fracture Management[/color]
• Cover wound with sterile dressing. Administer IV antibiotics promptly per open-fracture protocol. Assess tetanus immunization status and provide prophylaxis when indicated. Arrange urgent operative assessment when required.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Stable fractures may be managed with immobilization and scheduled radiographic follow-up. Unstable, significantly displaced, or intra-articular fractures may require operative fixation. Acute carpal tunnel syndrome caused by fracture may require urgent decompression.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not apply a tight circumferential cast to a markedly swollen limb.
• Persistent vascular compromise or progressive median nerve deficit after reduction requires immediate orthopedic reassessment.
• A palpable pulse does not exclude acute carpal tunnel syndrome.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent orthopedic review for neurovascular compromise, open fracture, unstable reduction, or progressive median nerve symptoms.
• Outpatient management appropriate only when alignment, perfusion, pain control, follow-up arrangements satisfactory.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Non-Complex Fractures; AAOS/ASSH Distal Radius Fractures; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
High-energy wrist injury, commonly following a fall on an outstretched hand.
• Severe wrist pain, swelling, and reduced movement.
• Median nerve compression may cause numbness or tingling in the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger.
• Carpal alignment may be abnormal on lateral radiographs.
• Perilunate dislocation may be associated with scaphoid fracture, creating a perilunate fracture-dislocation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess distal perfusion and document median, ulnar, and radial nerve function.
• Provide analgesia and immobilize the wrist.
• Obtain urgent radiographs and orthopedic or hand-surgery consultation.
• If there is acute median nerve compression or threatened circulation, arrange immediate specialist-led reduction without unnecessary delay.
• Avoid repeated forceful reduction attempts.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP, lateral, and appropriate additional wrist radiographs.
• Carefully assess carpal alignment on the lateral view.
• CT may be required to define associated carpal fractures.
• Repeat neurovascular examination after reduction.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Urgent Reduction and Immobilization[/color]
• Use appropriate analgesia, regional anesthesia, or procedural sedation according to patient condition and local protocol.
• Prepare monitoring, oxygen, suction, airway equipment, and resuscitation supplies if procedural sedation is planned.
• Reduction should be performed by a trained clinician with urgent specialist involvement. Immobilize the wrist after reduction.
• Reassess median nerve function, distal perfusion, sensation, and movement. Obtain post-reduction radiographs and arrange CT if indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Most perilunate dislocations and fracture-dislocations require urgent operative management.
• Surgery may involve reduction, ligament repair, and fixation of associated fractures.
• Monitor for acute carpal tunnel syndrome, avascular necrosis, stiffness, and post-traumatic arthritis.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Perilunate dislocation is a time-sensitive injury because of the risk of median nerve injury and long-term carpal dysfunction.
• Persistent median nerve symptoms, vascular compromise, or failed reduction requires immediate hand-surgery review.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent admission or transfer to a center with orthopedic or hand-surgery capability.
• Do not discharge a patient with an unreduced perilunate dislocation.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AO Surgery Reference; BSSH Wrist Injury Resources; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Severe, progressive hand pain following crush injury, fracture, reperfusion, or tight circumferential dressing. Tense swelling of hand or individual compartments. Pain on passive stretch of fingers.
• Paresthesia or progressive sensory/motor deficits may occur.
• Pallor and absent pulses are late findings; normal pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Obtain immediate orthopedic or hand-surgery consultation.
• Remove or split constrictive dressings, casts, bandages promptly.
• Keep hand approximately at heart level rather than excessively elevated when compartment syndrome suspected.
• Document pain, swelling, sensation, motor function, perfusion.
• Do not delay urgent surgical assessment for imaging when clinical diagnosis clear.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Diagnosis is primarily clinical.
• Measure compartment pressures when examination unreliable or diagnosis remains uncertain.
• Check for associated fractures, crush injury, vascular injury, rhabdomyolysis.
• Obtain electrolytes, renal function, creatine kinase in significant crush injuries.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Emergency Decompression[/color]
• Analgesia should be titrated to patient's condition. Definitive treatment is urgent surgical decompression when acute compartment syndrome diagnosed.
• Arrange immediate hand-surgery or orthopedic assessment and prepare for operative fasciotomy. Obtain urgent anesthesia and operating-room support. Perform necessary laboratory testing without delaying decompression.
• Maintain appropriate hemodynamic support and reassess hand frequently. Proceed to fasciotomy when indicated by surgical team. Reassess muscle viability, perfusion, neurological function after decompression.
• Manage associated fractures, vascular injuries, rhabdomyolysis.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not wait for pulselessness before acting.
• Analgesia, elevation, or dressing release alone is not definitive treatment when compartment syndrome persists.
• Delayed decompression can result in permanent nerve and muscle damage.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Emergency admission and operative management.
• Postoperative monitoring and repeat debridement may be required depending on muscle viability and wound condition.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: BOA Compartment Syndrome Guidance; AAOS Acute Compartment Syndrome Guidance; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
High-energy trauma, commonly road traffic collisions or falls from height. Severe thigh pain, swelling, deformity, inability to bear weight. Affected limb may appear shortened or externally rotated.
• Significant occult blood loss can occur into the thigh, causing hemorrhagic shock.
• Assess for associated pelvic, chest, abdominal, and other long-bone injuries.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow trauma ABCDE approach.
• Control external bleeding and establish IV access when indicated.
• Assess distal pulses, capillary refill, skin temperature, sensation, and motor function before and after splinting.
• Apply a suitable long-leg splint. Traction splint may be considered for isolated femoral shaft fracture when pelvic/ipsilateral knee injury and other contraindications excluded.
• Provide titrated analgesia and monitor vital signs.
• Activate major hemorrhage protocol if shock or significant ongoing bleeding suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP and lateral radiographs of entire femur, including hip and knee.
• Trauma imaging according to mechanism and hemodynamic stability.
• CBC, blood group and crossmatch, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation when clinically indicated.
• Repeat neurovascular examination and document findings.
• Consider associated femoral neck fracture, especially after high-energy trauma.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• IV morphine: commonly 0.05–0.1 mg/kg in carefully titrated doses. IV paracetamol may be used as adjunct.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hemorrhage Management[/color]
• Give isotonic crystalloid judiciously while arranging blood products when major hemorrhage suspected. Use blood-component therapy per institutional major hemorrhage protocol. Consider tranexamic acid for significant traumatic bleeding when indicated and within recommended early treatment window.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Fracture Management[/color]
• Urgent orthopedic consultation. Most adult femoral shaft fractures require operative stabilization, commonly intramedullary nailing. Temporary external fixation may be required in selected patients with severe physiological instability or major soft-tissue injury.
• Provide tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics if open fracture, following open-fracture protocol.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Reduce or carefully titrate opioids in patients with shock, respiratory compromise, or reduced consciousness.
• Do not assume that a femoral fracture is the only source of shock. Search for associated thoracic, abdominal, pelvic, and other bleeding.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit under orthopedics, with trauma or critical-care involvement when indicated.
• Escalate urgently for hemodynamic instability, suspected associated vascular injury, open fracture, or evolving compartment syndrome.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: ATLS; AO Surgery Reference; Local trauma/orthopedic protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Common in older adults after a low-energy fall; may occur in younger patients after high-energy trauma.
• Groin or hip pain, inability to bear weight, pain with passive hip movement.
• Affected limb may be shortened and externally rotated in a displaced fracture.
• Occult fractures may occur despite initially normal radiographs.
• Assess for head injury, other fractures, anticoagulant use, and causes of the fall.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCDE if major trauma suspected.
• Provide timely analgesia and support the affected limb.
• Avoid unnecessary movement and repeated attempts to mobilize the patient.
• Assess distal neurovascular status.
• Obtain urgent orthopedic consultation.
• Review anticoagulants, baseline mobility, cognition, frailty, and relevant comorbidities.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP pelvis and lateral hip radiographs.
• MRI when clinical suspicion remains high despite negative radiographs; CT may be considered if MRI unavailable/contraindicated.
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation tests when indicated, blood group/crossmatch if surgery anticipated.
• ECG and additional preoperative investigations according to clinical status.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol according to age, weight, liver function, local protocol. Carefully titrated opioid analgesia may be required for severe pain. A fascia iliaca or other appropriate regional nerve block may reduce opioid requirements when performed by a trained clinician.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Most confirmed femoral neck fractures require surgical management. Options include internal fixation, hemiarthroplasty, or total hip arthroplasty depending on fracture displacement, patient function, and overall condition.
• Optimize dehydration, anemia, electrolyte abnormalities, anticoagulation, and other reversible medical problems without unnecessary surgical delay.
• Provide VTE prophylaxis according to bleeding risk and local protocol.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• NSAIDs may be unsuitable in some older adults due to renal impairment, GI bleeding risk, or anticoagulant use.
• Do not delay analgesia while waiting for imaging.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for orthopedic management and coordinated medical assessment.
• Aim for surgery on the day of or the day after admission when medically appropriate.
• Begin postoperative mobilization and rehabilitation as soon as clinically safe.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Hip Fracture Management; AAOS Hip Fractures in Older Adults; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Hip dislocation is an orthopedic emergency because prolonged displacement increases the risk of femoral-head osteonecrosis.

[color=#1E3A8A]Posterior dislocation:[/color]
• Usually follows high-energy trauma.
• Hip is often flexed, adducted, and internally rotated.
• The limb may appear shortened.

[color=#1E3A8A]Anterior dislocation:[/color]
• Hip may be abducted and externally rotated.

Assess sciatic nerve function, distal perfusion, associated fractures, and other injuries.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform trauma assessment and treat life-threatening injuries first.
• Document distal pulses, capillary refill, foot sensation, ankle dorsiflexion, and plantarflexion.
• Obtain urgent orthopedic consultation.
• Provide analgesia and prepare for controlled reduction with appropriate sedation or anesthesia.
• Aim for reduction as soon as safely possible, preferably within six hours.
• Obtain pre-reduction radiographs unless an immediately threatened limb requires an exception.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP pelvis and appropriate hip radiographs.
• CT after reduction to identify occult fractures, intra-articular fragments, or acetabular injury.
• Repeat neurovascular examination after reduction.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Dose:[/color]
• Ketamine may be used for procedural sedation. A commonly used IV dissociative dose is 1–1.5 mg/kg, with additional titrated doses according to protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]How to prepare:[/color]
• Ensure oxygen, suction, bag-mask ventilation, monitoring, IV access, and resuscitation equipment are available before sedation.
• Prepare reduction equipment and post-reduction immobilization.

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Reduction should be performed by a trained clinician with adequate sedation and muscular relaxation.
• Monitor ECG, SpO2, BP, respiratory status, and level of consciousness.
• Repeat and document the full neurovascular examination immediately after reduction.
• Confirm reduction radiographically and arrange CT when indicated.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not attempt repeated forceful reductions.
• A suspected associated fracture may change the reduction plan; involve orthopedics urgently.
• Persistent sciatic nerve deficit or vascular compromise requires immediate reassessment.
• Do not discharge before confirming reduction, assessing associated injury, and establishing an orthopedic plan.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Urgent orthopedic admission or specialist-directed management is generally required. Associated fractures, instability, or failed reduction require operative assessment.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• The sciatic nerve is particularly vulnerable in posterior dislocation.
• Reduction timing matters; do not allow avoidable delays.
• A post-reduction CT may identify injuries missed on plain radiographs.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Emergency Care Institute NSW, Hip Dislocation; NICE, Fractures (Complex).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Severe hip pain and inability to move or bear weight after high-energy trauma.
• Posterior dislocation commonly presents with a shortened, flexed, adducted, internally rotated limb.
• Anterior dislocation may present with limb externally rotated and abducted.
• Assess sciatic nerve function (ankle dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, sensation over foot).
• Associated acetabular or femoral head fractures may complicate reduction.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow trauma ABCDE approach.
• Document distal pulses, perfusion, and neurological function before intervention.
• Provide analgesia and arrange urgent orthopedic consultation.
• Obtain pre-reduction radiographs unless immediate limb-threatening emergency requires action without delay.
• Arrange urgent reduction by trained clinician, usually under procedural sedation or anesthesia.
• Avoid repeated forceful reduction attempts, particularly when associated fracture suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP pelvis and appropriate hip radiographs.
• CT after reduction to assess acetabular and femoral head fractures or loose intra-articular fragments.
• Additional trauma imaging according to mechanism and clinical findings.
• Repeat neurovascular examination after reduction.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Urgent Reduction[/color]
• Select procedural sedation or general anesthesia according to patient stability, injury complexity, local protocol. No single sedation regimen is appropriate for every patient.
• Perform reduction using appropriate technique by experienced clinician. Reassess neurovascular status immediately after reduction.
• Obtain post-reduction radiographs and CT when indicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Simple dislocations may be managed with protected mobilization under orthopedic direction. Associated acetabular or femoral head fractures may require operative fixation.
• Evaluate for sciatic nerve injury and persistent instability.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Hip dislocation is time-critical because delayed reduction increases risk of femoral head avascular necrosis.
• Vascular compromise, irreducibility, or suspected fracture-dislocation requires urgent specialist management.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or transfer for orthopedic management.
• Discharge only after successful reduction, satisfactory imaging, stable neurovascular findings, and documented orthopedic plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AO Surgery Reference; NICE Complex Fractures; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Pelvic fractures may cause life-threatening retroperitoneal hemorrhage, especially after high-energy trauma.

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspect significant pelvic injury with:[/color]
• Hemodynamic instability after blunt trauma.
• Pelvic, groin, hip, or lower-back pain.
• Perineal bruising, pelvic deformity, or associated lower-limb injuries.

[color=#991B1B]Do not repeatedly compress or 'spring' the pelvis to test stability.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate the major trauma and hemorrhage protocols.
• Follow ABCDE; control external bleeding and establish large-bore IV or intraosseous access.
• Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters when an unstable pelvic fracture is suspected.
• Activate massive transfusion when indicated; use blood products rather than excessive crystalloid.
• Keep the patient warm and correct hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy.
• Contact trauma surgery, orthopedics, interventional radiology, and urology.
• Do not delay hemorrhage control for CT in a persistently unstable patient.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, blood gas/lactate, electrolytes, coagulation profile, fibrinogen, and type and crossmatch.
• FAST/eFAST as part of the trauma assessment.
• Pelvic radiograph if needed in an unstable patient.
• CT with contrast in patients sufficiently stable for imaging.
• Assess for associated abdominal, urinary tract, rectal, and vascular injury.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Hemorrhage control:[/color]
• Pelvic binder at the greater trochanters.
• Blood component therapy according to the massive transfusion protocol.
• Early tranexamic acid (TXA) may be considered for significant traumatic bleeding within 3 hours: adult dose 1 g IV over 10 minutes, followed by 1 g IV over 8 hours.
• Urgent pelvic packing, external fixation, angioembolization, or other operative intervention.

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Continuous ECG, BP, SpO2, temperature, urine output, and repeated assessment of perfusion.
• Repeat blood gas/lactate, hemoglobin, coagulation studies, and fibrinogen.
• Reassess binder position and the need for definitive stabilization.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not repeatedly manipulate the pelvis.
• Do not place the binder over the iliac crests; it should be centered over the greater trochanters.
• A normal initial hemoglobin does not exclude major acute hemorrhage.
• Avoid routine large-volume crystalloid resuscitation.
• Tranexamic acid is not a substitute for hemorrhage control.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Immediate trauma-center management, usually ICU. Persistent shock requires immediate definitive hemorrhage control.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• The binder is a temporary stabilization measure, not definitive treatment.
• A patient who remains unstable needs a rapid hemorrhage-control pathway.
• Consider non-pelvic sources of bleeding even when a pelvic fracture is present.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE, Fractures (Complex); Royal Children's Hospital, Pelvic Injury.

Lower Limb Injuries.title: Knee Dislocation and Popliteal Artery Injury

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Knee dislocation may spontaneously reduce before arrival. Severe ligament injury, deformity, or a high-energy mechanism should raise suspicion even if the knee appears aligned.

[color=#991B1B]Critical risk: Popliteal artery injury can cause limb-threatening ischemia.[/color]

Assess:
• Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses.
• Limb temperature, capillary refill, skin color, and Doppler signals.
• Common peroneal nerve function (ankle dorsiflexion, sensation over dorsum of foot).
• ABI when appropriate.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate orthopedic and vascular consultation early.
• Document neurovascular status before reduction.
• Perform urgent reduction of a dislocated knee by a trained clinician.
• Repeat neurovascular examination immediately after reduction.
• If hard signs of vascular injury persist, proceed to immediate vascular surgical intervention; do not delay for angiography.
• If vascular injury remains possible, obtain urgent CTA.
• Immobilize the reduced knee and arrange admission.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Knee radiographs before and after reduction when feasible.
• ABI and Doppler examination.
• CTA for suspected popliteal artery injury when stable.
• Serial vascular examinations even when initial findings appear reassuring.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Reduction and stabilization:[/color]
• Urgent closed reduction with appropriate analgesia or sedation.
• Splint the knee after reduction, commonly in slight flexion.
• Vascular repair, thrombectomy, bypass, or temporary shunting may be necessary.

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Record pulses, Doppler signals, skin temperature, capillary refill, sensation, and motor function before and after reduction.
• Continue serial vascular examinations and monitor for reperfusion injury and compartment syndrome.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Palpable pulses alone do not reliably exclude arterial injury.
• A normal-looking knee does not rule out a spontaneously reduced dislocation.
• Do not delay revascularization for imaging when there are persistent hard signs of arterial injury.
• Watch for compartment syndrome after revascularization.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit for orthopedic management and appropriate vascular observation or intervention. Confirmed or suspected popliteal artery injury requires urgent vascular surgical management.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• A knee dislocation is a vascular emergency until assessed adequately.
• Document all pre- and post-reduction findings.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE, Fractures (Complex); StatPearls, Knee Dislocation.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Knee pain, swelling, inability to bear weight after fall, direct impact, or twisting injury. Large knee effusion or hemarthrosis may be present.
• Assess for associated ligament injury, meniscal injury, neurovascular compromise.
• High-energy injuries may cause significant soft-tissue damage and acute compartment syndrome.
• Consider associated knee dislocation even if joint appears aligned at presentation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow trauma ABCDE approach when injury high energy.
• Provide analgesia and immobilize knee in comfortable position. Keep patient non-weight-bearing.
• Assess and document distal pulses, capillary refill, foot temperature, sensation, ankle/toe movement.
• Perform serial examinations for compartment syndrome.
• Obtain urgent orthopedic consultation for displaced fractures, skin compromise, open injury, or neurovascular abnormalities.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP and lateral knee radiographs.
• CT of knee for fracture configuration and operative planning when indicated.
• CT angiography if vascular injury suspected; do not delay emergency vascular management in critically ischemic limb.
• CBC, renal function, other trauma investigations according to injury severity.
• Repeat neurovascular examination after splinting and any manipulation.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Immobilization and Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol may be used as adjunct according to age/weight/liver function/local protocol. Opioid analgesia may be required for severe pain, titrated to clinical response.
• Apply well-padded knee immobilizer or splint without excessive pressure. Reassess distal perfusion, sensation, movement after immobilization.
• Monitor pain, swelling, compartment-syndrome warning signs.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Fracture Management[/color]
• Nonoperative treatment may be suitable for selected stable, minimally displaced fractures after orthopedic assessment. Displaced, unstable, depressed, or intra-articular fractures may require operative fixation.
• Open fractures require urgent open-fracture management, including antibiotics, wound coverage, and surgical assessment.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Increasing pain, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, or new neurological deficits require immediate reassessment.
• Normal distal pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or urgently refer for displaced fracture, significant swelling, open injury, suspected compartment syndrome, vascular concern, or inability to ensure safe outpatient management.
• Maintain non-weight-bearing status until definitive plan established.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AO Surgery Reference; NICE Complex Fractures; Local orthopedic trauma protocols.

Lower Limb Injuries.title: Patellar Fracture and Extensor Mechanism Disruption

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Anterior knee pain and swelling after direct blow or sudden quadriceps contraction. Hemarthrosis and focal patellar tenderness may be present.
• Inability to perform straight-leg raise suggests disruption of extensor mechanism, although pain can also limit examination.
• Open fractures may communicate with knee joint. Consider associated quadriceps tendon or patellar tendon rupture.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess skin integrity and distal neurovascular status.
• Provide analgesia and apply knee immobilizer with knee in extension if appropriate.
• Keep patient protected from weight-bearing until fracture assessed.
• Obtain urgent orthopedic consultation for open fracture, extensor mechanism disruption, or significant displacement.
• Cover open wounds with sterile dressing and initiate open-fracture management.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP and lateral knee radiographs; additional views may be useful when tolerated.
• CT for complex or comminuted fractures when needed for operative planning.
• Ultrasound or MRI may be considered if tendon injury remains uncertain.
• CBC and other tests according to trauma severity and operative requirements.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Immobilization and Analgesia[/color]
• Use age- and weight-appropriate analgesia based on comorbidities and contraindications. Titrated opioid analgesia may be required for severe pain.
• Immobilize knee in extension when appropriate. Reassess skin, swelling, distal perfusion, sensation, pain. Document ability to perform straight-leg raise when pain control permits.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Nondisplaced fractures with intact extensor mechanism may be treated with immobilization and close orthopedic follow-up. Displaced fractures, open fractures, or loss of extensor mechanism commonly require operative treatment.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not allow an unassessed patient with suspected extensor mechanism disruption to walk unsupported.
• Increasing pain or tense swelling requires reassessment for associated compartment syndrome or other injury.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent orthopedic review for displaced fracture, open injury, or inability to extend knee.
• Discharge only for selected stable injuries with secure immobilization plan and reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAOS Patellar Fractures; AO Surgery Reference; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Sudden anterior knee pain after jumping, falling, or forceful quadriceps contraction.
• Inability to actively extend the knee or perform a straight-leg raise.
• Patella alta may suggest patellar tendon rupture; patella baja may suggest quadriceps tendon rupture.
• A palpable tendon defect may be present.
• Risk factors include older age, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and previous tendon disease.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Provide analgesia and immobilize the knee in extension when appropriate.
• Document distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation, and motor function.
• Assess skin integrity and associated fractures.
• Obtain urgent orthopedic consultation when the extensor mechanism is disrupted.
• Avoid unsupported weight-bearing.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP and lateral knee radiographs to assess patellar position and associated fractures.
• Ultrasound or MRI when the diagnosis is uncertain.
• Check for associated patellar fracture or other traumatic injury.
• Additional laboratory testing is guided by comorbidities and planned surgery.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Immobilization and Pain Control[/color]
• Use appropriate analgesia according to age, weight, renal and hepatic function, and contraindications.
• Prepare a well-fitted knee immobilizer or extension splint.
• Immobilize the knee in extension when indicated. Reassess pain, swelling, skin condition, and distal neurovascular status. Arrange prompt orthopedic evaluation.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Complete quadriceps or patellar tendon ruptures usually require surgical repair.
• Partial tears with preserved extensor function may be treated nonoperatively under specialist supervision.
• Rehabilitation and progressive mobilization must follow the treating orthopedic team's protocol.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not assume that inability to extend the knee is caused only by pain.
• Delayed diagnosis of complete tendon rupture can impair functional recovery.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent orthopedic assessment for suspected complete rupture.
• Admit or arrange expedited specialist management when surgery is indicated or the patient cannot mobilize safely.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAOS Quadriceps Tendon Tear; AAOS Patellar Tendon Tear; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Severe ankle pain, swelling, deformity, or inability to bear weight. Skin tenting, blanching, open wounds, or threatened skin from displaced bone.
• Distal pulse reduction, delayed capillary refill, numbness, or weakness may indicate neurovascular compromise.
• Look for associated proximal fibular tenderness suggesting Maisonneuve injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess and document distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation, and motor function.
• Remove constrictive footwear and assess skin.
• Provide analgesia and elevate limb if this does not delay urgent reduction.
• Obtain radiographs before reduction if limb is neurovascularly intact and imaging immediately available.
• If threatened skin, severe deformity, or neurovascular compromise: perform urgent reduction without delaying for radiographs.
• Cover any open wound with sterile dressing and follow open-fracture pathway.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• AP, lateral, and mortise ankle radiographs when safe and feasible. Examine entire fibula and proximal leg.
• CT may be required for complex fractures or operative planning after stabilization.
• Repeat and document neurovascular findings after reduction.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Closed Reduction[/color]
• Procedural sedation or regional anesthesia selected according to patient condition/expertise/protocol. Ensure monitoring, oxygen, suction, airway equipment, resuscitation drugs available before sedation.
• Perform gentle reduction using appropriate technique by trained clinician. Reassess distal perfusion, sensation, movement immediately afterward. Apply well-padded splint. Obtain post-reduction radiographs and repeat neurovascular examinations.

[color=#1E3A8A]Open Fracture Management[/color]
• Administer IV antibiotics as soon as possible per open-fracture protocol. Give tetanus prophylaxis per immunization history. Cover wound with sterile dressing. Arrange urgent orthopedic assessment and operative debridement when indicated.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not repeatedly attempt forceful reduction.
• Persistent vascular compromise, irreducibility, or threatened skin requires immediate orthopedic escalation.
• Do not probe wound or perform repeated bedside wound manipulation.
• Do not delay antibiotics while waiting for imaging or definitive surgery.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or arrange urgent orthopedic management for fracture-dislocation, open injury, unstable reduction, or neurovascular concern.
• Discharge only for selected stable injuries after assessment, with safe immobilization and reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Complex Fractures; BOAST Ankle Fractures; AO Surgery Reference.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Heel pain and swelling after fall from height or axial loading injury. Bruising around heel and plantar surface may be prominent. Patient may be unable to bear weight.
• Assess skin tension and posterior heel skin viability.
• Consider associated thoracolumbar spine fractures and other injuries from same mechanism.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess for additional injuries using trauma approach when indicated.
• Keep patient non-weight-bearing. Elevate limb and apply well-padded splint.
• Perform and document neurovascular assessment.
• Urgently refer if open fracture, threatened skin, severe deformity, or neurovascular compromise.
• Avoid tight circumferential casts in markedly swollen limb.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Lateral and axial calcaneal radiographs when appropriate.
• CT for intra-articular fractures and operative planning.
• Examine spine and other regions injured by axial loading. Assess for associated foot fractures and soft-tissue injury.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Pain Control and Immobilization[/color]
• Use age- and weight-appropriate analgesia. Titrate opioid analgesia when required for severe pain, following local protocol.
• Apply well-padded posterior splint or other suitable immobilization. Elevate limb and monitor swelling, skin condition, pain, distal neurovascular status.
• Maintain strict non-weight-bearing.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Management depends on fracture displacement, joint involvement, soft-tissue condition, patient factors. Selected fractures may be managed nonoperatively. Displaced intra-articular fractures or fractures with threatened skin may require urgent specialist intervention.
• Delay definitive fixation when necessary to allow soft-tissue swelling to improve, provided limb remains safe.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Blanching, pressure necrosis, or skin tenting over heel requires urgent orthopedic assessment.
• Do not delay referral when skin is threatened.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Urgent orthopedic referral for displaced, open, or skin-threatening injuries.
• Assess for spinal injury and arrange further imaging when indicated.
• Discharge only when injury stable, pain controlled, non-weight-bearing feasible, follow-up reliable.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AO Surgery Reference; NICE Complex Fractures; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Sudden posterior ankle pain, often described as being kicked in the back of the leg. A snapping sensation during running, jumping, or sudden acceleration.
• Difficulty pushing off or standing on tiptoe.
• Palpable tendon gap may be present. Thompson calf-squeeze test may be abnormal, with reduced/absent plantarflexion.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Provide analgesia and avoid forced ankle dorsiflexion.
• Immobilize ankle in plantarflexion to reduce tension on tendon.
• Provide crutches and protect limb from unsupported weight-bearing.
• Arrange timely orthopedic assessment. Check skin condition and distal neurovascular status.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Diagnosis is often clinical.
• Ultrasound can help when examination findings equivocal.
• MRI reserved for selected uncertain or complex cases.
• Radiographs may be indicated if associated avulsion fracture or other bony injury suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Immobilization and Pain Control[/color]
• Paracetamol or another appropriate analgesic according to patient factors and local guidance.
• Maintain ankle in plantarflexion using appropriate splint or functional boot. Check skin pressure areas, distal circulation, sensation, comfort. Arrange prompt specialist review to select functional rehabilitation pathway.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Both nonoperative functional rehabilitation and surgical repair may be appropriate, depending on patient factors, tendon gap, activity requirements, specialist assessment. Rehabilitation requires structured protocol with gradual progression of ankle movement/loading.
• Assess VTE risk and consider prophylaxis per individual risk and local policy.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not force ankle into neutral dorsiflexion during initial immobilization.
• Avoid unsupported walking until appropriate protection plan in place.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Arrange timely orthopedic or specialist musculoskeletal follow-up.
• Urgent referral required for open injury, suspected neurovascular compromise, or associated fracture.
• Provide clear instructions on immobilization, mobility aids, return precautions.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAOS Achilles Tendon Rupture; NICE VTE Prevention; Local protocols.

Lower Limb Injuries.title: Acute Achilles Tendon Avulsion or Insertional Rupture

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Sudden posterior heel pain following forced dorsiflexion or powerful calf contraction.
• Tenderness at the Achilles insertion or a palpable defect near the heel.
• Weak plantarflexion and difficulty pushing off during walking.
• Insertional avulsion may be associated with a calcaneal fracture.
• Consider open injury, skin compromise, and associated neurovascular abnormalities.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess skin integrity and distal neurovascular status.
• Provide analgesia and immobilize the ankle in plantarflexion.
• Avoid stretching the tendon or forcing the ankle into dorsiflexion.
• Keep the patient protected from unsupported weight-bearing.
• Arrange prompt orthopedic assessment, especially when an avulsion fracture or open injury is suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Lateral ankle and calcaneal radiographs if an avulsion fracture is suspected.
• Ultrasound may help assess tendon continuity.
• MRI may be useful in complex or uncertain injuries.
• Additional imaging depends on the mechanism and suspected associated fractures.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Immobilization and Analgesia[/color]
• Use appropriate analgesia based on age, weight, renal function, hepatic function, and contraindications.
• Prepare a well-padded splint or boot that maintains plantarflexion.
• Immobilize the ankle and avoid tendon stretch. Reassess skin pressure points, pain, sensation, and distal perfusion.
• Arrange timely specialist assessment to determine the definitive treatment pathway.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Treatment may include functional rehabilitation or surgical repair, depending on rupture location, displacement, tissue condition, and patient factors.
• Displaced calcaneal avulsion fractures may require urgent operative management.
• Rehabilitation should follow a structured specialist protocol.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not force the ankle into neutral position when acute Achilles rupture is suspected.
• Open injuries or threatened skin require urgent surgical assessment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Arrange prompt orthopedic review.
• Admit or transfer for open injury, displaced avulsion fracture, threatened skin, or neurovascular compromise.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAOS Achilles Tendon Rupture; AO Surgery Reference; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Neck pain or midline cervical tenderness after trauma. High-risk mechanisms include road traffic collisions, falls from height, diving injuries, and axial loading.
• Neurological symptoms may include limb weakness, numbness, paresthesia, or respiratory difficulty.
• Altered consciousness, intoxication, distracting injury, or inability to communicate reliably may prevent clinical clearance.
• Absence of neck pain does not exclude cervical spine injury in an unreliable examination.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow the trauma ABCDE approach while maintaining spinal motion restriction.
• Maintain the airway with appropriate cervical spine precautions.
• Avoid unnecessary neck movement and manual manipulation.
• Assess limb power, sensation, respiratory function, and sphincter-related symptoms when feasible.
• Obtain urgent trauma and spinal specialist consultation for suspected unstable injury or neurological deficit.
• Treat associated hypoxia and hypotension promptly.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CT cervical spine is generally the first-line imaging test for significant suspected cervical spine trauma in adults.
• MRI is indicated when spinal cord, ligamentous, or other soft-tissue injury is suspected, particularly with neurological abnormalities not explained by CT.
• Additional spine imaging depends on the mechanism, examination, and local trauma protocol.
• Document the neurological examination before and after transfers or interventions.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Spinal Motion Restriction and Stabilization[/color]
• No medication reverses mechanical spinal instability. Analgesia should be individualized according to pain, hemodynamic status, and respiratory function.
• Prepare an appropriately fitted cervical collar when indicated. Ensure trained personnel and suitable equipment are available for transfers and airway management.
• Maintain spinal precautions until the injury is assessed and the spine is appropriately cleared. Reassess airway patency, breathing, circulation, and neurological status frequently.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hemodynamic and Neurological Management[/color]
• Treat hypoxia and hypotension promptly to reduce secondary spinal cord injury.
• If neurogenic shock is suspected, assess for concurrent hemorrhage before attributing hypotension to spinal cord injury.
• High-dose corticosteroids are not routinely recommended as standard treatment for acute traumatic spinal cord injury.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid routine prolonged rigid-collar use without reassessment; collars can cause pressure injury and other complications.
• Do not perform unsupervised neck manipulation or traction.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or transfer urgently for suspected unstable fracture, neurological deficit, or spinal cord injury.
• Do not discharge until the cervical spine has been appropriately assessed and cleared under an accepted protocol.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Spinal Injury; ACS Best Practices Spine Injury; AO Spine Cervical Injury Management.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Back pain and focal tenderness following high-energy trauma or a fall. Axial loading injuries may cause vertebral compression, burst fractures, or fracture-dislocation.
• Neurological findings may include lower-limb weakness, sensory loss, saddle anesthesia, or bladder and bowel dysfunction.
• Older adults and patients with osteoporosis may sustain fractures after relatively minor trauma.
• Associated abdominal, pelvic, and chest injuries must be considered.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCDE and treat life-threatening injuries first.
• Maintain spinal motion restriction when an unstable injury is suspected.
• Assess lower-limb power, sensation, and sphincter-related symptoms.
• Provide analgesia and avoid unnecessary spinal manipulation.
• Seek urgent spinal consultation for neurological deficit, suspected instability, or significant fracture.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CT of the relevant spinal region is generally preferred for significant traumatic injury.
• MRI is indicated when spinal cord, cauda equina, ligamentous injury, or neural compression is suspected.
• Evaluate for associated abdominal, chest, and pelvic trauma.
• Obtain laboratory testing based on associated injuries and planned intervention.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Stabilization and Analgesia[/color]
• Use appropriate analgesia based on age, weight, renal function, respiratory status, and contraindications. Opioids may be required for severe pain but should be carefully titrated.
• Maintain spinal precautions until stability is determined. Monitor vital signs, pain, limb power, sensation, and bladder function when relevant.
• Reassess neurological status after transfers and interventions.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Stable fractures without neurological compromise may be treated nonoperatively with appropriate mobilization and follow-up.
• Unstable fractures, progressive deformity, or neural compression may require surgical stabilization or decompression.
• Bracing is selected according to fracture pattern and specialist advice rather than used automatically in every case.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• New weakness, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, or bowel dysfunction requires immediate reassessment for neural compression.
• Do not delay urgent specialist assessment while awaiting nonessential tests.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or transfer for unstable fracture, neurological deficit, inability to mobilize safely, or associated major trauma.
• Discharge only after appropriate imaging, stability assessment, pain control, and a documented follow-up plan.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Spinal Injury; ACR Acute Spinal Trauma Criteria; AO Spine Thoracolumbar Injury Management.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Acute traumatic spinal cord injury may cause weakness or paralysis, sensory loss, respiratory impairment, autonomic dysfunction, and neurogenic shock.

[color=#1E3A8A]Assess:[/color]
• Mechanism and spinal pain.
• Motor function and sensation in all limbs.
• Respiratory effort, cough strength, and diaphragmatic function.
• Blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, and signs of neurogenic shock.
• Associated head, chest, abdominal, and pelvic injuries.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow ABCDE and control catastrophic hemorrhage.
• Maintain spinal motion restriction and manual in-line stabilization during airway procedures.
• Prevent hypoxemia and hypotension.
• Activate trauma, spinal surgery/neurosurgery, and ICU teams.
• Perform and document a structured neurological examination.
• Obtain urgent CT; perform MRI after CT when neurological abnormalities suggest injury.
• Arrange early transfer to a specialist trauma/spinal center.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CT of the relevant spinal region; whole-body CT when indicated.
• MRI when spinal cord, ligament, disc, or epidural pathology is suspected.
• CBC, electrolytes, blood gas, lactate, coagulation profile, and type and crossmatch.
• ECG and cardiac monitoring if neurogenic shock is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Airway and circulation:[/color]
• Provide oxygen and ventilatory support as required.
• Treat hemorrhagic shock by controlling bleeding.
• If neurogenic shock is suspected after hemorrhage is assessed, use specialist-guided vasopressor support.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hemodynamic management:[/color]
• A 2024 AO Spine/Praxis guideline suggests augmenting MAP to at least 75–80 mmHg, avoiding active augmentation above 90–95 mmHg, for approximately 3–7 days.

[color=#1E3A8A]Dose:[/color]
• Norepinephrine may be used in monitored critical care, titrated to the agreed MAP target.
• Do not use high-dose methylprednisolone routinely.

[color=#1E3A8A]Monitoring:[/color]
• Continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring; arterial line where appropriate.
• Frequent neurological reassessment and monitoring of respiratory function, temperature, urine output, and electrolytes.
• Decompression within 24 hours is recommended when medically feasible.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Avoid hypotension and hypoxia.
• Do not attribute hypotension to neurogenic shock until hemorrhage and other causes have been assessed.
• Avoid unnecessary spinal movement; do not delay life-saving airway or hemorrhage interventions.
• Routine high-dose corticosteroids are not recommended.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit to a trauma center, usually ICU or a specialist spinal unit.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Neurological deficits can progress due to secondary injury.
• Document motor and sensory findings before and after interventions.
• Early specialist involvement is essential.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE, Spinal Injury; AO Spine/Praxis, Acute Spinal Cord Injury Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Cauda equina syndrome is compression or dysfunction of lumbosacral nerve roots and is a time-critical neurological emergency.

[color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color]
• New urinary retention, difficulty initiating urination, or loss of awareness of bladder filling.
• Saddle or perineal sensory disturbance.
• New bowel dysfunction or sexual dysfunction.
• Bilateral sciatica or progressive bilateral leg weakness.
• Reduced anal tone may occur, but a normal examination does not exclude the diagnosis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Obtain immediate spinal/neurosurgical consultation.
• Arrange emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine.
• Document the time of symptom onset, bladder/bowel symptoms, perineal sensation, and lower-limb motor/sensory findings.
• Perform bladder scan and measure post-void residual when available.
• Keep the patient fasting if urgent surgery is possible.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Emergency MRI is the preferred investigation.
• Bladder scan/post-void residual as an adjunct.
• CBC, CRP/ESR, blood cultures if infection or malignancy suspected.
• CT may identify bony injury but does not reliably exclude neural compression.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive treatment:[/color]
• Emergency surgical decompression when compressive pathology is confirmed and indicated.
• Treat the underlying cause (disc herniation, epidural abscess, hematoma, or tumor).

[color=#1E3A8A]Dose & Administration:[/color]
• Analgesia according to local protocol.
• If epidural abscess is suspected, obtain blood cultures if this does not delay care; initiate urgent empiric IV antibiotics for sepsis or neurological deterioration.
• Prepare for urgent MRI and possible transfer to a center with spinal surgical capability.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay MRI because symptoms are incomplete or the patient can still walk.
• A normal rectal examination or low post-void residual does not safely exclude the syndrome.
• Do not discharge a patient with unresolved clinical suspicion without an appropriate definitive assessment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Emergency spinal/neurosurgical evaluation. Admit or transfer urgently when MRI or specialist treatment is unavailable locally.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• New urinary dysfunction plus saddle sensory changes is a major warning pattern.
• Early recognition and decompression may reduce permanent deficits.
• Document findings clearly and time-stamp changes.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE, Suspected Neurological Conditions; NICE, Spinal Injury.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Severe low-back pain with new urinary retention, altered urinary sensation, or overflow incontinence.
• Saddle or perineal sensory loss.
• New bowel dysfunction or sexual dysfunction.
• Bilateral sciatica, progressive lower-limb weakness, or sensory changes may occur.
• Symptoms can be incomplete or evolve over time; a normal single examination does not reliably exclude the syndrome.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Treat as a time-critical spinal emergency.
• Obtain urgent spinal surgical consultation.
• Perform and document a focused lower-limb neurological examination.
• Ask specifically about urinary sensation, ability to initiate urination, saddle sensation, and bowel function.
• Arrange emergency MRI as soon as possible according to the local pathway.
• Assess bladder retention with a bladder scan when available, without delaying definitive assessment.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Emergency MRI of the lumbar spine is the preferred investigation for suspected cauda equina compression.
• Bladder scan and post-void residual measurement may provide useful supporting information but cannot independently exclude the diagnosis.
• Additional investigations depend on suspected causes such as tumor, infection, hemorrhage, or fracture.
• Check anticoagulant use and relevant infection or malignancy history.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Emergency Assessment and Supportive Care[/color]
• Provide appropriate analgesia according to clinical status and local protocol. No analgesic regimen substitutes for urgent diagnosis and decompression when indicated.
• Arrange MRI, specialist consultation, and transfer to a center capable of urgent spinal intervention if necessary.
• Prepare a bladder catheter when retention is present and catheterization is clinically appropriate.
• Record bladder symptoms, neurological findings, symptom onset, and progression.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• MRI-confirmed compressive pathology requires urgent spinal surgical assessment.
• Emergency decompression may be required depending on the cause and neurological findings.
• Treat the underlying cause, such as a large disc herniation, epidural hematoma, tumor, or infection.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay MRI or specialist referral because symptoms are incomplete or because a bladder scan appears reassuring.
• Do not rely on digital rectal tone alone to exclude cauda equina syndrome.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Emergency hospital assessment and specialist management are required.
• Do not discharge a patient with suspected cauda equina syndrome without appropriate definitive assessment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Suspected Neurological Conditions/Spinal Injury; BASS Cauda Equina Resources; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Sudden focal back pain after minor fall, lifting, coughing, or spontaneous onset in patient with osteoporosis. Localized spinal tenderness and pain worsened by movement.
• Consider vertebral fracture in older adults and patients with long-term corticosteroid exposure.
• [color=#991B1B]Red flags:[/color] Progressive weakness, sensory changes, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, fecal incontinence, fever, cancer history, significant trauma.
• Severe trauma, neurological deficits, or suspected spinal instability requires emergency evaluation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCDE if significant trauma suspected.
• Perform focused neurological examination of lower-limb power, sensation, reflexes, sphincter-related symptoms.
• Use spinal precautions when instability suspected after trauma.
• Provide analgesia and assist safe movement without unnecessary prolonged bed rest.
• Obtain urgent spinal or orthopedic consultation for neurological deficit, suspected instability, or cauda equina symptoms.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Spine radiographs or CT depending on mechanism, severity, suspected fracture.
• MRI when neurological deficits, concern for spinal cord/nerve compression, suspected malignancy/infection, or uncertainty about fracture acuity.
• CBC, renal function, calcium, other tests when secondary causes or alternative diagnoses suspected.
• Evaluate bone health and secondary osteoporosis after acute stabilization.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia and Supportive Care[/color]
• Paracetamol when appropriate. Short-term opioid analgesia may be considered for severe pain, with cautious titration. Avoid routine prolonged opioid treatment.
• Encourage safe mobilization as tolerated after stability assessed. Use brace only when recommended for appropriate indication; prolonged immobilization may worsen deconditioning.

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Most uncomplicated compression fractures managed nonoperatively with analgesia, gradual mobilization, osteoporosis treatment.
• Specialist evaluation needed for persistent severe pain, progressive deformity, instability, or neurological compromise. Vertebral augmentation procedures reserved for selected patients after specialist assessment.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• New weakness, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, or bowel dysfunction requires immediate reassessment for neural compression.
• Do not attribute severe back pain automatically to osteoporosis without considering malignancy, infection, other serious causes.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or urgently refer for neurological deficits, unstable fracture, uncontrolled pain, inability to mobilize safely, or suspicion of malignancy/infection.
• Arrange follow-up for fracture healing, falls prevention, osteoporosis evaluation.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE Spinal Injury; ACR Appropriateness Criteria; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Acute compartment syndrome (ACS) is a surgical emergency caused by increased pressure within a closed fascial compartment, compromising tissue perfusion and potentially causing irreversible muscle and nerve necrosis.

[color=#1E3A8A]Common causes:[/color]
• Tibial shaft fractures and forearm fractures.
• Crush injuries, reperfusion after ischemia, and major soft-tissue trauma.
• Tight casts, dressings, or circumferential burns.
• Bleeding in patients receiving anticoagulants.

sections.heading: 02 — CLINICAL FEATURES
sections.content:
• Severe pain disproportionate to the injury.
• Pain on passive stretch of muscles within the affected compartment.
• Tense swelling and increasing analgesic requirements.
• Paresthesia, reduced sensation, or weakness are concerning later findings.

[color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Normal distal pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome. Pallor, paralysis, and pulselessness are late signs.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call orthopedics immediately; notify anesthesia and the operating theatre.
• Remove or fully release constrictive dressings, casts, and bandages.
• Keep the limb at approximately heart level; avoid excessive elevation that may reduce perfusion.
• Maintain systemic blood pressure and correct hypotension.
• Provide appropriate analgesia without allowing pain relief to replace serial examinations.
• Document pain, passive-stretch pain, sensation, motor function, capillary refill, pulses, and Doppler findings.
• Prepare for urgent fasciotomy if clinically indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Clinical examination is central; do not delay surgery for tests when the diagnosis is clear.
• Measure compartment pressures when the examination is equivocal or unreliable (e.g., unconscious/sedated patient).
