• A diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure (delta pressure) of ≤30 mmHg is concerning and supports the diagnosis.
• CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, CK, urinalysis for myoglobin, and blood gas/lactate when significant muscle injury or rhabdomyolysis is suspected.
• Radiographs for associated fractures.

sections.heading: 05 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive treatment:[/color] Emergency surgical fasciotomy with complete decompression of all involved compartments.

[color=#1E3A8A]Dose:[/color]
• There is no medication that reverses established acute compartment syndrome.
• Give analgesia according to the local trauma protocol (e.g., IV morphine titrated in small doses, such as 2–4 mg in an adult, with reassessment).

[color=#1E3A8A]How to prepare:[/color]
• Prepare for operative decompression, blood tests, IV access, and possible fracture stabilization.
• Treat rhabdomyolysis and electrolyte abnormalities when present.

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Repeat and document neurovascular examinations frequently.
• Monitor urine output, creatinine, potassium, CK, and acid-base status.
• Continue surveillance after fasciotomy; wound management and delayed closure may be necessary.

sections.heading: 06 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not wait for pulselessness or paralysis.
• Do not use a normal pulse or a single normal pressure measurement to rule out evolving disease.
• Avoid neuraxial or regional techniques that obscure assessment.
• Late presentations with irreversible tissue damage require senior surgical assessment; fasciotomy is not automatically beneficial in every late case.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit urgently under orthopedics. Confirmed or strongly suspected ACS requires emergency surgical management and postoperative monitoring.

sections.heading: 08 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are key early clues.
• Repeat examinations are essential because findings evolve.
• Compartment pressure measurements support, but do not replace, clinical judgment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AAOS, Management of Acute Compartment Syndrome, 2025; BOAST.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Acute limb ischemia is a sudden reduction in arterial perfusion, generally with symptoms lasting less than two weeks. It threatens limb viability and requires emergency vascular assessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]The six Ps:[/color]
• Pain.
• Pallor.
• Pulselessness.
• Paresthesia.
• Paralysis.
• Poikilothermia (cold limb).

[color=#991B1B]Motor or sensory deficits suggest a threatened limb and increase urgency.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call vascular surgery immediately.
• Rapidly assess limb viability and document sensory and motor function.
• Assess arterial and venous Doppler signals.
• Establish IV access, provide analgesia, and obtain blood tests.
• Start IV unfractionated heparin promptly unless contraindicated.
• Do not delay intervention for CTA or other imaging when the limb is immediately threatened.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation profile, blood group, and crossmatch.
• ECG and assessment for atrial fibrillation or another embolic source.
• Bedside Doppler examination.
• CTA or duplex ultrasound when appropriate.
• Assess for rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, and acidosis.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Anticoagulation:[/color]
• IV unfractionated heparin is commonly used (e.g., 70–80 units/kg IV bolus followed by approximately 15–18 units/kg/hour, adjusted to aPTT or anti-Xa).

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Monitor aPTT, hemoglobin, platelets, bleeding, and clinical perfusion.
• Definitive treatment may include embolectomy, thrombectomy, bypass, or catheter-directed therapy.
• Monitor after reperfusion for compartment syndrome, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and renal injury.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not anticoagulate automatically when major bleeding or aortic dissection is suspected.
• A threatened limb with motor deficit requires immediate revascularization planning.
• Do not delay revascularization for imaging when this would jeopardize limb salvage.
• Do not assume a palpable pulse excludes evolving ischemia.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Emergency vascular admission or immediate transfer to a facility capable of revascularization.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Neurological deficits indicate a more advanced ischemic threat.
• Document the time of onset and serial neurovascular findings.
• Reperfusion can itself cause compartment syndrome and systemic metabolic complications.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: 2024 ACC/AHA Guideline for Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease; NICE, Fractures (Complex).

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Septic arthritis is infection within a joint that can rapidly destroy cartilage and cause sepsis.

[color=#1E3A8A]Features:[/color]
• Acute painful, swollen, warm joint with restricted movement.
• Fever may be absent, particularly in older or immunocompromised patients.
• Risk factors: prosthetic joints, recent surgery/injection, bacteremia, diabetes, immunosuppression, skin infection.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Urgent orthopedic consultation.
• Assess for sepsis and begin resuscitation when indicated.
• Obtain urgent joint aspiration for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystals.
• Obtain blood cultures when febrile or systemically unwell.
• In a stable patient, obtain synovial fluid and blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible.
• If septic shock is present, do not delay antibiotics for aspiration.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Joint aspiration: appearance, leukocyte count/differential, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis.
• CBC, CRP/ESR, renal function, blood cultures, and lactate.
• Ultrasound for effusion and aspiration guidance.
• X-ray for baseline assessment; MRI when osteomyelitis or deep infection is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric antibiotics (Adult examples):[/color]
• Vancomycin IV (15–20 mg/kg) when MRSA coverage is indicated.
• Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for Gram-negative coverage.
• Adjust therapy to culture results and local guidelines.

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Urgent joint drainage is required in many cases (aspiration, arthroscopy, or open surgery).
• Monitor temperature, hemodynamics, pain, range of motion, CRP, renal function, and cultures.
• Narrow antibiotics when microbiology results become available.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay antibiotics in sepsis or septic shock.
• Crystals in synovial fluid do not exclude concomitant septic arthritis.
• A negative Gram stain does not rule out infection.
• Prosthetic-joint infection requires urgent specialist management.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit for urgent orthopedic assessment, drainage planning, and IV antimicrobial therapy. Sepsis requires an appropriate high-acuity pathway.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Aspiration is central to diagnosis.
• The absence of fever does not exclude septic arthritis.
• Antibiotics alone are often insufficient without adequate source control.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: SANJO Guideline, Septic Arthritis in Native Joints; NICE, Sepsis.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Fever, focal bone pain, tenderness, reduced use of affected limb. Children may present with refusal to walk, limp, or refusal to move arm/leg.
• Early radiographs may be normal.
• Consider associated septic arthritis, especially when pain centered on joint or passive movement severely restricted.
• Suspect severe infection in patients with systemic toxicity, hypotension, altered mental status.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess for sepsis and initiate local sepsis pathway when indicated.
• Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics if this can be done promptly without delaying treatment.
• Arrange urgent orthopedic and pediatric/infectious-disease consultation as appropriate.
• Provide analgesia and avoid unnecessary weight-bearing on affected limb.
• If unstable or septic, start empiric IV antibiotics promptly after cultures when feasible.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, CRP, ESR, renal function, blood cultures.
• Plain radiographs to assess for fracture/alternative diagnoses (early osteomyelitis may not be visible).
• MRI generally preferred when diagnosis uncertain or extent must be assessed.
• Ultrasound may identify joint effusion/superficial collection but does not exclude bone infection.
• Aspirate or obtain tissue for culture when feasible, especially if drainage/debridement required.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric Antimicrobial Therapy[/color]
• Empiric IV antibiotic choice must cover likely pathogens, particularly Staphylococcus aureus. Add MRSA coverage when local prevalence/patient risk factors/severity/previous colonization warrants.
• Pediatric and adult regimens differ; select using age, weight, renal function, allergy history, local resistance, institutional osteomyelitis guideline.

[color=#1E3A8A]Drainage and Source Control[/color]
• Antibiotics alone may be insufficient when drainable abscess, infected joint, or necrotic tissue present.
• Urgent surgical drainage/debridement indicated for selected patients with abscess formation, associated septic arthritis, necrotic bone, or failure to respond to appropriate antimicrobial treatment.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay antibiotics in unstable patient to obtain MRI or invasive specimen.
• In clinically stable patient, specialist-directed sampling before antibiotics may improve microbiological diagnosis when it can be performed safely and promptly.
• A suspected associated septic joint requires urgent evaluation because delayed drainage can cause rapid joint damage.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with systemic toxicity, suspected abscess, inability to tolerate treatment, uncertain diagnosis requiring urgent investigation, or need for IV therapy/surgery.
• Selected stable patients may transition to appropriate oral regimen after specialist review and clinical improvement, with reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: PIDS/IDSA Pediatric Osteomyelitis Guideline; IDSA Infectious Diseases Guidelines; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Localized swelling, warmth, tenderness, and erythema over a superficial bursa, commonly the olecranon or prepatellar bursa.
• Fever may be absent, especially in older or immunocompromised patients.
• Skin abrasions, penetrating injury, diabetes, and immunosuppression increase infection risk.
• Differentiate from septic arthritis, cellulitis, gout, and traumatic bursitis.
• Severe pain with passive joint movement or a joint effusion should raise concern for septic arthritis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs and screen for sepsis.
• Examine the skin for wounds, fluctuance, spreading cellulitis, and drainage. Mark the extent of erythema when appropriate.
• Obtain urgent specialist assessment if septic arthritis, deep infection, or systemic toxicity is suspected.
• If sepsis is present, obtain blood cultures when feasible and start prompt empiric antimicrobial therapy.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, CRP, and other tests according to clinical severity.
• Aspirate bursal fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis when indicated and safe.
• Blood cultures for systemic illness, fever, or suspected bacteremia.
• Ultrasound may help identify a fluid collection.
• Imaging is indicated if foreign body, osteomyelitis, or another deep process is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric Antimicrobial Therapy[/color]
• Select empiric antibiotics to cover likely Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci. Include MRSA coverage when severity, local prevalence, prior colonization, or other risk factors warrant it.
• Start IV therapy for severe infection, systemic toxicity, or circumstances requiring inpatient management. Oral therapy may be suitable for selected stable patients after clinical assessment.
• Review culture results and narrow therapy when appropriate.

[color=#1E3A8A]Drainage and Supportive Care[/color]
• Aspiration or incision and drainage may be needed for a significant infected collection or failure of medical treatment.
• Elevate and protect the affected area. Provide analgesia and review tetanus status if there is an associated wound.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay antibiotics in an unstable or septic patient while waiting for aspiration.
• Avoid aspirating through infected skin when an alternative safe approach is available.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for sepsis, rapidly progressive infection, suspected septic arthritis, immunocompromise with severe infection, or need for operative drainage.
• Outpatient treatment may be appropriate for selected stable patients with reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines; AFP Common Superficial Bursitis; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord, compromising testicular blood flow. It is a time-critical surgical emergency.

[color=#1E3A8A]Clinical features:[/color]
• Sudden, severe unilateral scrotal pain.
• Nausea and vomiting.
• High-riding or horizontally oriented testis.
• Swelling and testicular tenderness.
• Absent cremasteric reflex may be present.

[color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Torsion can occur in neonates, children, adolescents, and adults. A preserved cremasteric reflex or atypical presentation does not reliably exclude torsion.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Request immediate urological or surgical review.
• Keep the patient nil by mouth.
• Establish IV access and provide analgesia.
• Document symptom onset, testicular position, swelling, and examination findings.
• Prepare for emergency scrotal exploration.
• Do not delay surgery for imaging when clinical suspicion is high.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Clinical examination.
• Doppler ultrasound if immediately available and diagnosis remains uncertain, provided it does not delay surgical assessment.
• Urinalysis when alternative diagnoses are considered; a normal urinalysis does not exclude torsion.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive treatment:[/color] Emergency surgical exploration, detorsion, assessment of viability, and orchidopexy. The contralateral testis is generally fixed during the same operation.

[color=#1E3A8A]Dose:[/color]
• Paracetamol: 1 g orally or IV in an adult, usually every 6 hours as needed.
• Severe pain may require titrated IV opioid analgesia under appropriate monitoring.

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Monitor pain, vital signs, and response to analgesia.
• Keep the patient fasting and document the time of symptom onset and referral.
• Manual detorsion may be attempted by a trained clinician if surgery is delayed, but it must never delay definitive surgery.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not wait for the testis to become discolored or for the ultrasound result if suspicion is high.
• Testicular salvage is best when treatment occurs within approximately 4–6 hours, but late presentation is still an emergency.
• Pain relief after manual detorsion does not eliminate the need for surgery.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Immediate surgical management. Admit for operative treatment and postoperative assessment.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Time is testicular tissue.
• Differential diagnosis includes epididymo-orchitis, torsion of the appendix testis, incarcerated hernia, and testicular trauma.
• A normal Doppler study should not override strong clinical suspicion.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology, Acute Scrotum; Royal Children's Hospital.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Testicular rupture is disruption of the tunica albuginea after blunt or penetrating scrotal trauma. Delayed treatment can lead to testicular loss.

[color=#1E3A8A]Clinical features:[/color]
• Severe scrotal pain after trauma.
• Rapid swelling and bruising.
• Nausea or vomiting.
• Difficulty palpating the testis due to swelling.
• Hematocele or abnormal testicular contour.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess trauma mechanism and associated injuries.
• Provide analgesia and scrotal support.
• Request urgent urological assessment.
• Obtain urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler.
• Keep the patient fasting if surgical exploration is likely.
• Do not delay exploration when rupture is strongly suspected or imaging is inconclusive.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler.
• CBC and other trauma investigations.
• Assess testicular perfusion and contour.
• Evaluate for associated penile, urethral, pelvic, or abdominal injury.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive treatment:[/color]
• Urgent surgical exploration when rupture is diagnosed or strongly suspected.
• Debridement of nonviable tissue and repair of the tunica albuginea.
• Orchiectomy may be necessary if the testis is nonviable.

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Prepare for urgent surgery and anesthesia assessment.
• Maintain scrotal support while awaiting definitive care.
• Monitor pain, swelling, skin condition, and vital signs.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not assume that severe scrotal swelling is only a hematoma.
• A negative or equivocal ultrasound does not exclude rupture when clinical suspicion remains high.
• Do not delay surgical review while waiting for repeat imaging if the testis may be threatened.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Urgent urological management. Confirmed rupture generally requires operative exploration and admission.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Early repair improves the chance of testicular preservation.
• Ultrasound is useful, but clinical judgment and specialist assessment remain essential.
• Consider safeguarding concerns in children when the injury mechanism is unclear.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Guidelines on Urological Trauma; AUA Urotrauma Guideline.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute scrotal pain is a time-sensitive presentation. Testicular torsion must be considered first because delayed treatment can result in testicular loss.
Important differential diagnoses include:
• Testicular torsion.
• Epididymitis and epididymo-orchitis.
• Testicular rupture or blunt scrotal trauma.
• Incarcerated or strangulated inguinal hernia.
• Testicular appendage torsion.
• Scrotal abscess or severe soft-tissue infection.
• Referred pain from ureteric stones or other abdominal pathology.

Clinical clues:
• Sudden severe unilateral pain, nausea, vomiting, or a high-riding testis suggests torsion.
• Gradually progressive pain, epididymal tenderness, dysuria, or fever may suggest epididymitis.
• Trauma with marked swelling, bruising, or an abnormal testicular contour raises concern for rupture.
• An irreducible painful groin mass with vomiting suggests an incarcerated or strangulated hernia.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs, pain severity, and signs of shock or systemic infection.
• Obtain a focused abdominal, inguinal, and genital examination with consent and a chaperone.
• Establish the time of symptom onset and ask about trauma, urinary symptoms, sexual history when relevant, and previous episodes.
• Provide prompt analgesia.
• Request immediate urological or surgical assessment if torsion, testicular rupture, strangulated hernia, or a necrotizing infection is suspected.
• Arrange Doppler ultrasound if the diagnosis is uncertain and imaging will not delay urgent surgical management.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Scrotal ultrasound with color Doppler when clinically appropriate.
• Urinalysis and urine culture if urinary infection is suspected.
• STI nucleic acid amplification testing when epididymitis due to a sexually transmitted infection is possible.
• CBC, renal function, inflammatory markers, and blood cultures when systemic infection or significant trauma is suspected.
• Additional abdominal or pelvic imaging if a referred cause or associated injury is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Select age-appropriate analgesic according to pain severity, contraindications, renal function, and local protocol.
• Provide prompt pain relief without delaying surgical assessment.
• Reassess pain, vital signs, and response to treatment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected Testicular Torsion[/color]
• Treat as surgical emergency.
• Obtain immediate urological consultation and prepare for surgical exploration when indicated.
• Do not wait for laboratory results or ultrasound if clinical suspicion is high.
• Manual detorsion may be attempted by a trained clinician while arranging surgery, but it must not delay operative management.

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected Epididymo-Orchitis[/color]
• Obtain appropriate urine and STI testing.
• Start empiric antibiotics according to suspected pathogen and local guidelines.
• Reassess if diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms fail to improve.

[color=#1E3A8A]Suspected Traumatic Testicular Injury[/color]
• Provide analgesia and scrotal support.
• Obtain urgent Doppler ultrasound if this does not delay necessary surgery.
• Suspected testicular rupture requires urgent urological assessment and often surgical exploration.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content: • A normal or equivocal ultrasound does not reliably exclude torsion when clinical suspicion remains high. Preserve the testis by prioritizing timely surgical assessment.

sections.heading: 06 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Torsion: urgent surgical detorsion and orchiopexy, with management of the contralateral testis according to surgical practice.
• Rupture: surgical exploration and repair when indicated.
• Epididymo-orchitis: pathogen-directed antimicrobial therapy and follow-up.
• Hernia: urgent surgical management if incarcerated or strangulated.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Any patient with suspected torsion, rupture, strangulated hernia, or necrotizing infection requires immediate specialist evaluation.
• Discharge only after time-critical diagnoses reasonably excluded and clear treatment/follow-up plan established.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Paediatric Urology/Urological Infections Guidelines; AUA Acute Scrotum Resources; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Unilateral scrotal pain and swelling, often developing over hours or days. Epididymal tenderness, scrotal erythema, possible fever.
• Dysuria, urinary frequency, urethral discharge, or recent urinary instrumentation may be present.
• Consider sexually transmitted pathogens in sexually active patients; urinary pathogens in older patients or those with urinary tract abnormalities.
• [color=#991B1B]Testicular torsion must be excluded urgently[/color], especially with sudden severe pain, nausea, vomiting, high-riding testis, or absent cremasteric reflex.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs, pain severity, systemic toxicity.
• Perform focused abdominal, inguinal, genital, scrotal examination with appropriate consent and chaperone.
• [color=#991B1B]If torsion strongly suspected: obtain immediate urological/surgical assessment; do NOT delay exploration for imaging.[/color]
• Provide analgesia and scrotal support.
• Obtain urine testing and STI testing when indicated.
• Arrange urgent ultrasound with Doppler when diagnosis uncertain and imaging will not delay necessary intervention.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urinalysis and urine culture.
• First-catch urine NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae when STI possible.
• CBC and inflammatory markers when systemic infection suspected.
• Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler when torsion, abscess, or uncertain diagnosis remains a concern.
• Evaluate for urinary obstruction or structural urinary disease when suggested.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive Care[/color]
• Rest and scrotal elevation/support. Wrapped cold packs intermittently if helpful (avoid direct ice contact). Appropriate analgesia. Encourage hydration according to status.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotic Therapy[/color]
• Select treatment according to likely pathogen, STI risk, local resistance, allergies, local guidelines.
• Example (Suspected STI): Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once + Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days. For patients ≥150 kg, some guidelines recommend ceftriaxone 1 g IM once.
• Obtain appropriate STI specimens without unnecessarily delaying treatment. Counsel regarding adherence, adverse effects, partner evaluation, temporary abstinence from sexual activity until treatment completed and partners treated, per local guidance. Reassess if no improvement within 72 hours.
• [color=#991B1B]This regimen is NOT suitable for every cause. Suspected enteric pathogens, gonorrhea resistance, severe infection, and local recommendations may require a different regimen.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content: • Tailor antimicrobial treatment to culture/STI results. Evaluate sexual partners and arrange testing/treatment when STI identified/suspected. Consider abscess, infarction, torsion, or another diagnosis when clinical course atypical. Persistent swelling after treatment requires reassessment.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit or obtain urgent specialist review for severe systemic illness, abscess, suspected infarction, inability to tolerate oral therapy, immunocompromise with significant infection, or unresolved concern for torsion.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines—Epididymitis; EAU Urological Infections Guidelines; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Ischemic priapism is a painful, prolonged erection caused by impaired venous outflow and trapped blood within the corpora cavernosa. It is a urological emergency (risk of permanent erectile dysfunction).

[color=#1E3A8A]Clinical features:[/color]
• Erection lasting four hours or longer.
• Painful, rigid corpora cavernosa.
• The glans may remain relatively soft.
• History of sickle cell disease, hematologic malignancy, or causative drugs.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Obtain immediate urological consultation.
• Establish IV access and provide analgesia.
• Record duration, pain, relevant medications, and medical history.
• Do not delay definitive treatment while attempting oral remedies.
• Assess for sickle cell disease or another underlying cause without delaying penile treatment.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Clinical assessment.
• Cavernosal blood gas when diagnosis is uncertain (ischemic shows hypoxic, hypercarbic, acidotic blood).
• CBC and targeted investigations for sickle cell disease or other causes.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive initial treatment:[/color]
• Corporal aspiration (with or without saline irrigation), followed by intracavernosal phenylephrine.
• Surgical shunting may be required if conservative treatment fails.

[color=#1E3A8A]Phenylephrine — specialist-administered:[/color]
• Concentration: 100–500 micrograms/mL.
• Typical adult dose: 100–500 micrograms injected intracavernosally, repeated every 3–5 minutes.
• Max total dose of 1 mg within one hour (follow local protocol).

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Must be performed by a trained clinician.
• Monitor BP, heart rate, and ECG.
• Reassess penile rigidity and pain after each step.
• Escalate to surgical management promptly if erection persists.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Oral medication or observation alone is not adequate.
• Phenylephrine can cause severe hypertension, arrhythmias, and cardiovascular complications.
• Dilution errors can cause serious cardiovascular harm. Never inject undiluted concentrate.
• Do not delay urology consultation.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Urgent urological treatment and observation until detumescence and clinical stability. Admit when ongoing treatment or complications are suspected.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Ischemic priapism is usually painful with rigid corpora.
• Non-ischemic priapism is often less painful and follows trauma.
• The longer ischemia persists, the greater the risk of erectile dysfunction.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AUA/SMSNA, Diagnosis and Management of Priapism.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Paraphimosis occurs when a retracted foreskin becomes trapped behind the glans penis, producing a constricting ring and progressive edema. It can compromise blood flow and cause tissue necrosis.

[color=#1E3A8A]Clinical features:[/color]
• Retracted foreskin that cannot be brought forward.
• Painful swelling of the glans and foreskin.
• A tight constricting band behind the glans.
• Dusky or dark discoloration in severe cases.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess glans color, sensation, swelling, and perfusion.
• Provide analgesia and explain the procedure.
• Obtain urgent urological help if reduction is difficult or ischemia is suspected.
• Attempt prompt manual reduction if appropriate and performed by a trained clinician.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Manual reduction:[/color]
• Apply gentle, sustained compression to reduce edema, then move the foreskin forward over the glans.
• Provide adequate analgesia; local anesthesia or penile block may be considered.

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Reassess pain, swelling, color, and perfusion after reduction.
• If manual reduction fails, urgent surgical intervention may be needed (dorsal slit or circumcision).

sections.heading: 04 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not delay reduction when perfusion is threatened.
• Avoid repeated forceful attempts that may cause tissue injury.
• Dusky, blue, or black discoloration, severe pain, or impaired perfusion requires immediate urological intervention.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Discharge may be appropriate after successful reduction if glans is well perfused, pain is controlled, and follow-up is arranged. Failed reduction or ischemia requires specialist care.

sections.heading: 06 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Always return the foreskin to its normal position after examination or catheterization.
• Explain recurrence prevention and the need for urological follow-up if phimosis is present.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology; NHS.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Penile fracture is rupture of the tunica albuginea of an erect corpus cavernosum, usually due to bending trauma during sexual activity.

[color=#1E3A8A]Typical features:[/color]
• Sudden cracking or popping sound.
• Immediate loss of erection.
• Acute penile pain.
• Rapid swelling and bruising.
• Penile deviation or deformity.

[color=#1E3A8A]Associated urethral injury may present with:[/color] Blood at meatus, gross hematuria, difficulty urinating.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Contact urology urgently.
• Keep the patient nil by mouth.
• Provide analgesia.
• Document mechanism, timing, swelling, deformity, and urinary symptoms.
• Assess for associated urethral injury.
• Prepare for prompt surgical exploration and repair.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Clinical diagnosis is often sufficient when history and findings are typical.
• Ultrasound or MRI may be considered when diagnosis is uncertain.
• Retrograde urethrography or urethroscopy may be required if urethral injury is suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive treatment:[/color]
• Prompt surgical exploration and repair of the tunica albuginea.
• Evaluate and manage associated urethral injury during the operative assessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Monitoring:[/color]
• Monitor pain, swelling, urinary function, and vital signs.
• Postoperative follow-up should assess healing, penile curvature, erectile function, and urethral symptoms.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do not manage a convincing penile fracture with ice and observation alone.
• Do not delay surgical consultation for imaging when the clinical diagnosis is clear.
• Blood at the meatus, hematuria, or urinary retention increases concern for urethral injury.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Urgent urological admission or operative management. Prompt repair, ideally within 24 hours, reduces the risk of long-term complications.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• A sudden pop followed by immediate detumescence and bruising is highly suggestive.
• Early repair is associated with better functional outcomes.
• Exclude associated urethral injury.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Guidelines on Urological Trauma; British Association of Urological Surgeons.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Acute urinary retention is the sudden inability to empty the bladder, often with painful bladder distension.

[color=#1E3A8A]Common causes:[/color] Benign prostatic enlargement, urethral stricture, stones/clots, medications (anticholinergics/opioids), constipation, postoperative retention, neurological disease.

[color=#1E3A8A]Clinical features:[/color] Inability to pass urine, suprapubic pain, palpable/ultrasound-confirmed distended bladder, overflow dribbling.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs and abdominal findings.
• Perform a bladder scan when available.
• Relieve retention by urethral catheterization if there is no suspicion of urethral injury.
• If catheterization fails, stop repeated traumatic attempts and seek urological assistance.
• Investigate the cause and assess renal function, infection, and post-obstructive diuresis risk.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Bladder scan and post-void residual.
• Urinalysis and urine culture if infection suspected.
• Creatinine, electrolytes, and glucose.
• Renal/bladder ultrasound if renal impairment suspected.
• Neurological examination if spinal cord/cauda equina pathology is possible.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Bladder drainage:[/color]
• Insert an appropriately sized urethral catheter using aseptic technique.
• If contraindicated/unsuccessful, urgent urological assessment for alternative drainage (e.g., suprapubic catheter).

[color=#1E3A8A]Medication:[/color]
• For BPH: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg orally once daily may be initiated.
• A trial without catheter may be considered after at least 3 days of alpha-blocker therapy.

[color=#1E3A8A]Monitoring:[/color]
• Record volume and appearance of drained urine.
• Monitor urine output, fluid balance, BP, renal function, and electrolytes.
• Watch for post-obstructive diuresis.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Blood at the urethral meatus after trauma, perineal bruising, or suspected urethral disruption requires evaluation before blind catheterization.
• Do not force a catheter against resistance.
• Sudden decompression is generally acceptable; monitor for hematuria, hypotension, and post-obstructive diuresis.
• New urinary retention with saddle anesthesia or leg weakness is a possible cauda equina emergency.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Depends on cause, renal function, infection, and follow-up safety. Admit for sepsis, AKI, significant electrolyte abnormalities, suspected neurological disease.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Relieving the obstruction is the first priority.
• Alpha-blockers improve the chance of a successful trial without catheter in BPH.
• Persistent retention requires evaluation of the underlying cause.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: American Urological Association, BPH Guideline.

Urinary Retention & Obstruction.title: Acute Urinary Retention with High-Risk Complications

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Sudden inability to void, often with suprapubic pain and palpable/ultrasound-confirmed distended bladder.
• Overflow incontinence may occur, particularly in chronic retention.
• Causes: benign prostatic enlargement, urethral stricture, medications, constipation, neurological disease, postoperative retention.
• [color=#991B1B]High-risk features: fever/sepsis, AKI, hydronephrosis, gross hematuria with clots, neurological deficits, suspected urethral injury.[/color]
• New saddle anesthesia, bilateral leg weakness, or bowel dysfunction raises concern for cauda equina syndrome and requires emergency spinal assessment.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs, pain, bladder distension, neurological symptoms.
• Confirm retention with bladder scan/ultrasound when available.
• Obtain renal function and electrolytes when retention prolonged, severe, recurrent, or associated with systemic illness.
• Relieve retention promptly when safe.
• [color=#991B1B]If urethral injury suspected, do NOT perform blind urethral catheterization; seek urgent specialist evaluation.[/color]
• Monitor urine output and hemodynamic status after decompression, particularly in chronic or high-volume retention.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Bladder scan and post-void residual measurement when relevant.
• Creatinine, urea, electrolytes, urinalysis. Urine culture if infection suspected.
• Renal ultrasound when renal impairment, hydronephrosis, or chronic high-volume retention suspected.
• Neurological examination and urgent spinal imaging when cauda equina syndrome or other compressive neurological cause suspected.
• Review medications that can contribute to retention (anticholinergics, opioids, sympathomimetics).

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Bladder Decompression[/color]
• Urethral catheterization commonly initial approach when no contraindication. Use sterile technique and appropriate catheter selection.
• If catheterization difficult, stop repeated traumatic attempts and obtain experienced assistance.
• Suprapubic catheterization may be required when urethral access unsafe/unsuccessful, according to specialist assessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Monitoring After Decompression[/color]
• Record initial drained volume and monitor subsequent urine output. Watch for post-obstructive diuresis, hypotension, hematuria, electrolyte abnormalities.
• Check renal function/electrolytes when retention prolonged, high-volume, or associated with complications.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT routinely clamp catheter simply because a large volume drains; manage drainage and monitoring according to clinical status and local protocol.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Alpha-Blocker Therapy[/color]
• Example: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg orally once daily may be used in selected adult men with suspected prostatic outlet obstruction, per local guidance.
• Review BP, dizziness, falls risk, interactions, contraindications. Consider as part of plan for supervised trial without catheter, NOT substitute for urgent decompression.
• [color=#991B1B]Tamsulosin does NOT provide immediate relief of acute retention. It may cause orthostatic hypotension and dizziness.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Identify and treat underlying cause. Arrange trial without catheter when clinically appropriate and follow local urology guidance.
• Investigate recurrent retention, renal impairment, hydronephrosis, or suspected neurological disease. Review and adjust causative medications when appropriate.
• Refer for definitive management of prostatic enlargement, urethral stricture, or other structural obstruction.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or obtain urgent specialist management for AKI, significant electrolyte disturbance, sepsis, hydronephrosis with complications, suspected neurological compression, traumatic urethral injury, or failed drainage.
• Stable patients may be discharged with catheter only when appropriate follow-up plan, catheter-care instructions, and return precautions in place.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Male LUTS Guidelines; NICE LUTS in Men; KDIGO AKI Guideline; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Obstruction of urine flow at kidney, ureter, bladder outlet, or urethra.
• Flank pain, reduced urine output, urinary retention, or anuria.
• Bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a solitary functioning kidney can rapidly impair renal function.
• Causes: stones, prostatic enlargement, urethral stricture, tumors, blood clots, external compression.
• Fever, rigors, hypotension, or confusion in an obstructed patient suggests infected urinary system and requires emergency management.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess hemodynamic stability, pain, fever, urine output, signs of sepsis.
• Measure bladder volume when lower urinary tract obstruction possible.
• Obtain IV access and blood tests if severe obstruction, dehydration, infection, or AKI suspected. Record fluid intake and urine output.
• Arrange urgent imaging and urology consultation for anuria, bilateral obstruction, solitary kidney obstruction, deteriorating renal function, or suspected infected obstruction.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay drainage of an infected obstructed system while waiting for definitive stone treatment.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urea, creatinine, electrolytes, glucose. CBC and inflammatory markers when infection suspected. Urinalysis and urine culture.
• Renal and bladder ultrasound to identify hydronephrosis and retention.
• CT imaging when needed to identify site and cause of obstruction.
• ECG when severe hyperkalemia suspected/confirmed.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Lower Urinary Tract Obstruction[/color]
• Bladder decompression usually required when acute urinary retention confirmed. Use urethral catheterization only when safe; suspected urethral injury requires specialist assessment. If urethral catheterization fails/contraindicated: urgent urological assessment for alternative drainage.

[color=#1E3A8A]Upper Urinary Tract Obstruction[/color]
• Arrange urgent urological drainage when obstruction threatens renal function, causes anuria, or is associated with infection.
• Options: ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, selected according to anatomy, availability, clinical circumstances. Definitive treatment of stones/tumors/strictures follows stabilization and appropriate assessment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hyperkalemia[/color]
• For confirmed/strongly suspected clinically significant hyperkalemia, particularly with ECG changes. Obtain ECG and urgent potassium when possible without delaying treatment of life-threatening arrhythmia.
• Give IV calcium for cardiac membrane stabilization when indicated by ECG changes/severe hyperkalemia, per local emergency protocol. Use insulin with glucose and other potassium-lowering measures per institutional pathway. Monitor glucose, potassium, ECG, renal function. Obtain urgent nephrology/critical care input for refractory hyperkalemia or severe renal failure.
• [color=#991B1B]Calcium stabilizes myocardium but does NOT remove potassium from body. Repeat potassium and glucose measurements are essential.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content: • Relieve obstruction. Treat underlying cause. Monitor renal recovery and complications. Consider nephrology input if renal impairment persists after drainage or if dialysis indications develop.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit patients with anuria, bilateral obstruction, obstruction of solitary functioning kidney, AKI, significant electrolyte disturbance, infected obstruction, or need for urgent intervention.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Urolithiasis/Urological Infections Guidelines; NICE AKI Guidance; KDIGO AKI Guideline; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
High urine output after relief of urinary obstruction, commonly after catheterization for prolonged retention or drainage of bilateral obstruction.
• Commonly used clinical definition: urine output >200 mL/hour for two consecutive hours or >3 L in 24 hours.
• Patient may develop thirst, dizziness, hypotension, dehydration, weakness.
• Electrolyte abnormalities may include hypokalemia, sodium disturbances, magnesium abnormalities.
• Distinguish transient physiologic diuresis from persistent pathologic diuresis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Measure and document urine output hourly in high-risk patients. Record fluid intake, vital signs, clinical volume status.
• Obtain serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, urea, creatinine, magnesium when significant diuresis present.
• Assess for orthostatic symptoms, hypotension, dehydration.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT automatically clamp urinary catheter or stop bladder drainage solely because large volume has drained.[/color]
• Admit or closely observe patients with persistent high output, significant electrolyte abnormalities, renal impairment, or hemodynamic instability.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serial electrolytes and renal function; frequency depends on urine output/clinical severity.
• Urine osmolality and urine electrolytes may help evaluate persistent/unexplained diuresis.
• ECG if significant potassium abnormalities suspected.
• Monitor daily weight and fluid balance in patients with ongoing diuresis.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Fluid Replacement[/color]
• Principle: Replace losses according to hemodynamic status, oral tolerance, laboratory findings, ongoing urine output rather than fixed volume for every patient.
• Encourage oral fluids when patient alert, stable, able to drink safely. Use IV crystalloid when oral intake inadequate or significant hypovolemia present.
• In stable patient with ongoing post-obstructive diuresis, commonly used starting strategy: replace approximately 50–75% of preceding urine output, then adjust according to volume status and electrolytes.
• [color=#991B1B]This is NOT a universal formula; avoid both inadequate replacement and excessive fluid administration. In shock, follow resuscitation protocol rather than routine post-obstructive replacement strategy.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Electrolyte Correction[/color]
• Replace potassium, magnesium, other electrolytes according to measured deficits and local protocols. Correct sodium abnormalities carefully, following established limits for rate of correction.
• Reassess electrolytes frequently when losses substantial or replacement being given.
• [color=#991B1B]Excessive replacement can perpetuate diuresis and cause fluid overload. Inadequate replacement can lead to hypovolemia, hypotension, and AKI.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content: • Continue monitoring until urine output declines and volume status/electrolytes stabilize. Investigate persistent diuresis for ongoing tubular dysfunction or another cause. Plan trial without catheter or definitive management of underlying obstruction only when clinically appropriate.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Patients with persistent marked diuresis, hypotension, significant sodium/potassium abnormalities, or impaired renal function require hospital observation or admission.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: NICE AKI Guidance; KDIGO AKI Guideline; Standard urology/nephrology references; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Inability to pass a urinary catheter despite appropriate initial attempts. Resistance, severe pain, urethral bleeding, or catheter coiling.
• Potential causes: prostatic enlargement, urethral stricture, bladder-neck contracture, false passage, previous urethral surgery, urethral trauma.
• [color=#991B1B]Repeated unsuccessful attempts increase risk of urethral injury, bleeding, and false passage formation.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Confirm indication for catheterization; consider whether catheter necessary.
• Assess for urinary retention using bladder examination/ultrasound.
• Ask about previous urethral stricture, prostate surgery, difficult catheterization, recent trauma.
• [color=#991B1B]If pelvic trauma, blood at urethral meatus, perineal bruising, or suspected urethral injury: STOP blind catheterization and obtain urgent urological assessment.[/color]
• Use adequate analgesia, appropriate positioning, sterile technique, generous sterile lubricant/anesthetic gel when suitable.
• Stop if significant resistance or bleeding occurs; do NOT force catheter.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Bladder scan to confirm retention and estimate bladder volume.
• Renal function and electrolytes when retention prolonged/severe/associated with suspected renal impairment.
• Retrograde urethrography when urethral injury suspected.
• Flexible cystoscopy or specialist-directed imaging may be needed to assess strictures/other anatomical obstruction.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Initial Catheterization Attempt[/color]
• Use appropriately sized catheter selected according to anatomy/clinical indication. Ensure adequate lubrication and gentle technique.
• Experienced clinician may consider different catheter type when prostatic obstruction/stricture suspected, provided urethral injury not suspected. Do NOT repeatedly attempt different catheters without clear plan.

[color=#1E3A8A]Local Anesthetic Gel[/color]
• Example: Lidocaine urethral gel, using product-specific adult dose and maximum allowable amount. Check concentration, dose, allergy history, product instructions. Use sterile single-use gel when available.
• Instill gently according to product instructions and allow sufficient time for local anesthesia. Observe for discomfort, bleeding, or signs of local injury.
• [color=#991B1B]Lidocaine toxicity is possible with excessive dosing/absorption. Account for other lidocaine products already administered.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Failed Catheterization[/color]
• Stop further blind attempts after persistent resistance, significant pain, or bleeding.
• Obtain urgent urological assistance for guidewire-assisted placement or flexible cystoscopic catheterization.
• If urgent bladder drainage essential and urethral access unsafe/impossible: suprapubic catheterization may be required by trained clinician after assessment of contraindications/anatomy.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Treat underlying cause (urethral stricture, prostatic obstruction, bladder-neck contracture).
• Document attempts, catheter type/size, resistance encountered, bleeding, and final drainage method.
• Arrange follow-up when stricture or other structural abnormality suspected.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Patients with persistent retention, renal impairment, infection, urethral injury, or failed drainage need urgent specialist assessment.
• Discharge with catheter should include documented drainage plan, catheter-care instructions, and follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Urological Trauma/Male LUTS Guidelines; AUA Urethral Stricture Guideline; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute rise in serum creatinine due to impaired urinary drainage.
• Oliguria or anuria may occur, but urine output can remain relatively preserved in partial obstruction.
• Bilateral obstruction, bladder outlet obstruction, or obstruction of a solitary functioning kidney is particularly concerning.
• Symptoms may include suprapubic fullness, flank pain, urinary hesitancy, weak stream, or overflow incontinence.
• Hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, pulmonary edema, confusion, or uremic symptoms may indicate severe complications.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, vital signs, volume status.
• Measure urine output and obtain urgent bladder scan when lower urinary tract obstruction possible.
• Obtain blood tests: creatinine, urea, sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, glucose.
• Obtain ECG urgently if hyperkalemia suspected/confirmed.
• Review nephrotoxic medications and temporarily withhold relevant agents when clinically appropriate.
• Arrange urgent urinary decompression when obstruction confirmed/strongly suspected and threatening renal function.
• Seek urgent nephrology or critical care input for severe hyperkalemia, refractory acidosis, pulmonary edema, or other indications for renal replacement therapy.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serial creatinine and electrolytes.
• Urinalysis and urine culture if infection suspected.
• Bladder scan and renal ultrasound to assess retention and hydronephrosis.
• CT imaging when cause/level of obstruction remains unclear.
• ECG for significant potassium abnormalities. Blood gas when severe acidosis/critical illness suspected.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Relieve the Obstruction[/color]
• Bladder outlet obstruction may require catheter drainage when urethral catheterization safe. Suspected urethral injury or failed catheterization requires specialist assessment.
• Upper tract obstruction may require ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy.
• Infected obstruction requires antibiotics and urgent drainage.

[color=#1E3A8A]Hyperkalemia Management[/color]
• For severe hyperkalemia or hyperkalemia with ECG changes: emergency treatment. Give IV calcium for cardiac membrane stabilization when indicated. Administer insulin with glucose and other potassium-shifting/removal therapies per local emergency protocol.
• Monitor ECG, glucose, potassium, renal function, response to treatment. Consider dialysis for refractory hyperkalemia or other established indications.
• [color=#991B1B]Calcium does NOT lower serum potassium. Insulin can cause delayed hypoglycemia, so glucose monitoring is essential.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Fluid and Electrolyte Management[/color]
• Correct hypovolemia if present, but do NOT give routine large-volume fluids to an oliguric patient without assessing volume status. Treat pulmonary edema and electrolyte disturbances per standard emergency protocols.
• Monitor fluid balance closely after decompression because post-obstructive diuresis may develop.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Identify and treat underlying cause (stones, prostatic obstruction, stricture, clot retention, malignancy).
• Monitor for renal recovery after drainage. Seek nephrology input if kidney function does not improve or complications persist.
• Review medications and arrange follow-up renal function testing.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admission generally indicated for significant postrenal AKI, bilateral obstruction, solitary kidney obstruction, anuria, hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, infection, or need for urgent drainage.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: KDIGO AKI Guideline; NICE AKI Guidance; EAU Urolithiasis/Male LUTS Guidelines; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Suspected UTI with systemic illness or organ dysfunction. Fever/hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, confusion, oliguria, mottled skin.
• Flank pain, dysuria, urinary frequency, suprapubic pain, CVA tenderness may be present. Older adults/immunocompromised may have few local urinary symptoms.
• Consider obstructing ureteric stones, hydronephrosis, urinary retention, infected catheters, renal/perinephric abscess, recent urological procedures.
• Septic shock suggested by persistent circulatory failure despite initial fluid resuscitation and may require vasopressors.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate local sepsis pathway; assess ABCDE. Give oxygen when hypoxemic; support ventilation as required.
• Establish IV access; monitor BP, HR, RR, SpO2, temperature, mental status, urine output. Measure serum lactate when sepsis with hypoperfusion/shock suspected.
• Obtain blood cultures and urine culture before antibiotics when no clinically significant delay.
• [color=#991B1B]Start empiric IV antibiotics promptly, ideally within 1 hour for septic shock or high likelihood of sepsis, per local protocol.[/color]
• Assess urgently for urinary obstruction and other sources requiring source control.
• Request early critical care and urology input in shock, organ dysfunction, or suspected obstructed infection.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, LFTs, glucose.
• Serum lactate with repeat measurement when initially elevated or perfusion remains impaired.
• Blood cultures and urine culture. Urinalysis. Coagulation when indicated.
• Renal and bladder ultrasound to identify hydronephrosis/retention.
• CT abdomen/pelvis when needed to assess stones, obstruction, abscess, emphysematous infection, or another complicated source.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Selection depends on severity, likely source, prior cultures, recent antibiotic exposure, healthcare-associated infection, renal function, allergies, local resistance, risk of resistant organisms.
• Example: Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV every 24 hours for susceptible community-acquired urinary infection; severe sepsis may require upper end of range per local guidance.
• [color=#991B1B]Ceftriaxone alone may be inadequate in healthcare-associated infection, suspected Pseudomonas, resistant organisms, or certain complicated infections. Select broader therapy when clinically indicated per local protocols.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]IV Fluid Resuscitation[/color]
• For sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock: balanced crystalloid or 0.9% NaCl per protocol. Initial volume ~30 mL/kg within first 3 hours is guideline-based starting point, NOT inflexible requirement.
• Give fluid in reassessed boluses, particularly in HF, renal failure, or risk of fluid overload. Reassess BP, capillary refill, mental status, lung findings, urine output. Stop/reduce fluids if overload develops.

[color=#1E3A8A]Vasopressor: Norepinephrine[/color]
• For persistent hypotension despite appropriate initial fluid resuscitation, or earlier when profound shock requires it.
• Start per local critical-care protocol, commonly 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min IV, titrate to perfusion targets. Prefer central venous catheter for ongoing infusion, but well-sited peripheral IV may be used temporarily in emergency with frequent site checks per local protocol.
• Titrate to MAP target ~65 mmHg in most adults, individualized. Monitor BP continuously, rhythm, peripheral perfusion, urine output, lactate trend, IV site for extravasation.
• [color=#991B1B]Norepinephrine is a high-alert medication. Verify concentration, dose units, and pump settings independently per local safety policy.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Source Control: Obstructed Infected Urinary System[/color]
• Infected obstruction requires urgent drainage (ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy). Antibiotics alone NOT sufficient when infected collecting system remains obstructed. Coordinate urgent decompression with urology/IR. Delay definitive stone removal until infection adequately controlled.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content: • Tailor antimicrobial therapy to cultures, susceptibility, source, renal function, clinical response. Remove/replace infected urinary catheter when indicated. Drain obstructed systems/abscesses when required. Assess for additional sources/complications. Review antimicrobial duration and step-down therapy based on source control and response.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU or high-dependency care for: Persistent hypotension/vasopressor requirement. Altered mental status/respiratory failure. Rising lactate/persistent hypoperfusion. Significant AKI/other organ dysfunction. Need for urgent source control with ongoing instability.
• [color=#991B1B]Patients with uncomplicated infection should NOT be labeled as having sepsis solely because of fever or positive urine test; diagnosis depends on overall clinical assessment and evidence of organ dysfunction.[/color]

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Surviving Sepsis Campaign (2021); EAU Urological Infections/Urolithiasis Guidelines; SCCM Sepsis Resources; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Fever, rigors, flank pain, CVA tenderness, nausea, vomiting. Dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency may accompany upper urinary tract symptoms.
• Complicated infection more likely with urinary obstruction, stones, structural abnormalities, pregnancy, immunosuppression, diabetes, renal impairment, or recent instrumentation.
• Persistent fever or clinical deterioration despite appropriate antibiotics raises concern for renal abscess, perinephric abscess, obstruction, or resistant pathogens.
• Confusion, hypotension, tachypnea, oliguria, or elevated lactate may indicate sepsis.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess for sepsis, shock, dehydration, AKI.
• Obtain IV access and start resuscitation when clinically indicated.
• Obtain urinalysis and urine culture before antibiotics when this does not significantly delay treatment.
• Obtain blood cultures when sepsis, severe systemic illness, or bacteremia suspected.
• Start empiric antibiotics promptly, guided by severity, prior microbiology, allergies, renal function, local resistance patterns.
• Assess for obstruction and arrange urgent imaging when clinically indicated.
• Seek urgent urology input if infected obstruction or drainable abscess suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urinalysis and urine culture with susceptibility testing.
• CBC, renal function, electrolytes, inflammatory markers.
• Blood cultures and lactate in suspected sepsis.
• Renal ultrasound to assess hydronephrosis/obstruction.
• CT abdomen/pelvis when complicated infection, abscess, emphysematous infection, obstruction, or poor response to treatment suspected.
• In pregnancy, choose imaging and antibiotics according to pregnancy-specific guidance.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric Antibiotic Therapy[/color]
• Choose according to illness severity, local antibiograms, prior cultures, recent antibiotic use, allergy history, pregnancy status, renal function.
• Example: Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV every 24 hours for appropriate susceptible infections; severe illness may require regimen selected under local sepsis guidance.
• [color=#991B1B]Ceftriaxone may not provide adequate coverage for all resistant/healthcare-associated pathogens. Critically ill patients may require broader empiric therapy selected according to local guidance.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive Care[/color]
• Appropriate analgesia and antiemetics. Replace fluids according to clinical volume status. Monitor urine output and renal function. Avoid nephrotoxic medications where possible in AKI.

[color=#1E3A8A]Renal or Perinephric Abscess[/color]
• Obtain specialist assessment and appropriate imaging. Continue antibiotics directed by likely pathogens and culture results. Drainage may be required depending on abscess size, location, clinical response, patient stability.

[color=#1E3A8A]Infected Obstruction[/color]
• Treat as emergency requiring antibiotics and urgent urinary drainage. Ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy may be needed. Antibiotics alone NOT sufficient when infected collecting system remains obstructed.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content: • Adjust antibiotics according to cultures, clinical response, renal function. Identify and correct urinary obstruction when present. Evaluate for abscess or resistant organisms if patient fails to improve as expected. Determine duration/route of antibiotic treatment according to pathogen, severity, source control, local guidelines.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit for sepsis, hemodynamic instability, persistent vomiting, significant dehydration, AKI, pregnancy with systemic illness, suspected obstruction/abscess, or inability to take oral medication.
• Outpatient management appropriate only for selected stable patients who can tolerate oral treatment and have reliable follow-up and clear return precautions.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Urological Infections Guidelines; NICE Pyelonephritis; Surviving Sepsis Campaign; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Severe upper urinary tract infection associated with gas within renal parenchyma or surrounding tissues.
• Most commonly associated with diabetes mellitus or urinary obstruction.
• Fever, flank pain, vomiting, confusion, hypotension, signs of sepsis may occur.
• Presentation may be nonspecific, particularly in patients with diabetes or impaired immunity.
• Severe disease can progress rapidly to shock, AKI, multiorgan dysfunction.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Activate sepsis pathway and assess airway, breathing, circulation, organ dysfunction.
• Obtain IV access, CBC, renal function, electrolytes, lactate when indicated, blood cultures, urine culture.
• Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly according to local resistance patterns and severity.
• Begin hemodynamic resuscitation with reassessment of fluid responsiveness and signs of overload.
• Arrange urgent CT imaging when patient stable enough; CT important for defining gas distribution and associated obstruction.
• Request urgent urology and critical care assessment.
• Identify and relieve urinary obstruction when present.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, renal function, electrolytes, glucose, lactate.
• Blood cultures and urine culture. Urinalysis.
• CT abdomen/pelvis to assess gas within kidney, perinephric tissues, collecting system, and to identify obstruction or abscess.
• Monitor urine output, BP, lactate, renal function.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Broad-Spectrum IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Choose therapy based on severity, likely pathogens, local resistance, previous cultures, allergy, renal function. Severe disease may require antipseudomonal beta-lactam or another broad-spectrum regimen under local sepsis protocol. Consider resistant organisms based on prior healthcare exposure, antibiotic use, local epidemiology.
• Adjust doses for renal function where necessary. Review cultures and de-escalate when clinically appropriate.

[color=#1E3A8A]Resuscitation and Organ Support[/color]
• Give IV crystalloid for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion, reassessing frequently. Use vasopressors when hypotension persists despite appropriate resuscitation, following critical-care protocol. Monitor oxygenation, mental status, urine output, lactate, electrolytes. Provide glucose management and support other failing organs.

[color=#1E3A8A]Source Control[/color]
• Arrange urgent decompression of obstructed collecting system. Percutaneous drainage may be required for drainable collection or selected cases of extensive infection.
• Nephrectomy may be necessary in selected patients with uncontrolled infection or deterioration despite appropriate treatment and less invasive measures; decision requires specialist assessment.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• This is a life-threatening infection, NOT a routine outpatient UTI.
• Do NOT delay antibiotics or source control in a deteriorating patient.
• Imaging and procedures must NOT delay immediate resuscitation in an unstable patient.

sections.heading: 06 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Combine effective antimicrobial therapy, correction of obstruction, and drainage or surgery when indicated.
• Use CT findings, clinical status, renal function, response to treatment to guide further intervention.
• Arrange follow-up for renal recovery and control of contributing conditions.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• All suspected/confirmed cases require hospital admission.
• Patients with shock, organ dysfunction, or need for vasopressor support should be managed in critical care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Urological Infections Guidelines; Surviving Sepsis Campaign; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Persistent fever, flank pain, and malaise despite treatment for urinary infection.
• Nausea, vomiting, CVA tenderness, or systemic toxicity.
• Risk factors: diabetes, urinary obstruction, stones, immunosuppression, recent urinary instrumentation.
• Renal abscess involves renal parenchyma; perinephric abscess extends into surrounding space.
• Severe cases may progress to sepsis or septic shock.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs and sepsis-related organ dysfunction.
• Establish IV access and obtain CBC, renal function, electrolytes, lactate when indicated, blood cultures, urine culture.
• Start empiric IV antibiotics promptly when severe infection suspected.
• Assess for urinary obstruction and arrange urgent imaging.
• Consult urology and interventional radiology early if collection requiring drainage suspected.
• Provide fluids according to volume status and monitor urine output.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urinalysis and urine culture. Blood cultures in systemic illness.
• CBC, renal function, electrolytes, inflammatory markers.
• Contrast-enhanced CT is often most informative imaging test for renal/perinephric abscess when clinically appropriate.
• Ultrasound may identify collection but can be less sensitive for defining extent.
• Obtain cultures from drained material when drainage performed.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Choose therapy according to severity, likely organisms, prior cultures, recent antibiotic exposure, local resistance, allergy, renal function. Ceftriaxone may be suitable for selected community-acquired infections; severe illness or resistant-organism risk may require broader therapy per local guidance.
• Adjust treatment according to culture results and clinical response. Monitor temperature, hemodynamics, renal function, inflammatory markers, clinical improvement. Reassess promptly if fever or systemic illness persists.

[color=#1E3A8A]Drainage[/color]
• Indications may include: Large/enlarging abscess. Persistent sepsis or failure to improve with appropriate antibiotics. Obstructed infected urinary system. Collection accessible and judged likely to benefit from drainage.
• Procedure: Arrange image-guided percutaneous drainage when appropriate. Surgical drainage or other interventions may be required in selected complex cases. Treat any associated urinary obstruction.
• [color=#991B1B]There is NO single abscess-size threshold that determines drainage for every patient. Decisions depend on clinical stability, collection characteristics, response to antibiotics, and specialist assessment.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Tailor antibiotics to cultures and susceptibility. Drain collections when indicated. Relieve associated obstruction.
• Repeat imaging when clinical course suggests persistent/recurrent infection. Address contributing factors (stones, diabetes, urinary tract abnormalities).

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Hospital admission generally required for confirmed renal/perinephric abscess.
• Patients with sepsis, obstruction, or need for drainage require urgent specialist management and may need critical care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Urological Infections Guidelines; Surviving Sepsis Campaign; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Acute fever, chills, malaise, dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency. Pelvic, perineal, rectal, or lower back pain.
• A tender prostate may be found on gentle rectal examination when clinically appropriate.
• Acute urinary retention can occur.
• Severe disease may progress to bacteremia, sepsis, or prostatic abscess.
• Risk factors: urinary instrumentation, bladder outlet obstruction, recent catheterization, UTI.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs, sepsis features, hydration, ability to pass urine.
• Obtain urinalysis and urine culture before antibiotics when feasible without delaying treatment.
• Obtain blood cultures when febrile with systemic illness or suspected sepsis.
• Check renal function and electrolytes if retention, dehydration, or severe illness present.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid vigorous prostate massage because it can precipitate bacteremia.[/color]
• Assess urgently for urinary retention and obtain urology input if drainage needed.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urinalysis and urine culture.
• CBC, renal function, electrolytes, inflammatory markers when indicated.
• Blood cultures if systemic infection suspected.
• Bladder scan if retention suspected.
• Imaging with CT, MRI, or transrectal ultrasound may be needed if prostatic abscess suspected or patient fails to improve.
• [color=#991B1B]PSA is NOT useful for diagnosing acute bacterial prostatitis because it may be transiently elevated during acute inflammation.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotic Therapy[/color]
• Select according to illness severity, likely organisms, previous cultures, local resistance, allergy, renal function.
• Stable patient suitable for oral treatment: Use appropriate oral antibiotic with prostatic penetration, per local guidelines and culture results. Fluoroquinolones or trimethoprim-based regimens may be options in selected patients when susceptibility and safety considerations support use.
• Severely ill patient or suspected sepsis: Start IV antibiotics promptly per local severe urinary infection or sepsis guidance. Examples include ceftriaxone or broader-spectrum beta-lactams when indicated by severity and local resistance.
• Review culture results and de-escalate when appropriate. Monitor temperature, symptoms, renal function, signs of complications. Duration commonly measured in weeks per local guidance.
• [color=#991B1B]Fluoroquinolones have important potential adverse effects and resistance limitations. Do NOT prescribe empirically without considering local guidance, patient-specific contraindications, and susceptibility data.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia and Supportive Care[/color]
• Appropriate analgesia and antipyretics. Maintain hydration according to volume status. Avoid unnecessary urethral instrumentation.

[color=#1E3A8A]Acute Urinary Retention[/color]
• Obtain urgent urological advice regarding bladder drainage.
• Urethral catheterization may be difficult or undesirable in some cases; route should be selected by experienced clinician. Suprapubic drainage may be considered when urethral catheterization unsuitable or unsafe.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Tailor antimicrobial therapy to microbiology and response.
• Evaluate persistent fever or symptoms for abscess or obstruction.
• Drain prostatic abscess when indicated.
• Address associated bladder outlet obstruction after acute infection controlled.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit patients with sepsis, hypotension, significant dehydration, urinary retention requiring complex drainage, vomiting preventing oral treatment, suspected abscess, or major comorbidity requiring inpatient care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Urological Infections Guidelines; NICE Prostatitis (Acute); Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
An infected, obstructed urinary collecting system (Obstructive Pyelonephritis / Infected Hydronephrosis) is a urological emergency. It may progress rapidly to urosepsis, septic shock, and acute kidney injury.

[color=#1E3A8A]Clinical features:[/color]
• Fever, chills, flank pain, or costovertebral-angle tenderness.
• Dysuria or urinary frequency may be present.
• Nausea and vomiting.
• Hypotension, tachycardia, confusion, or oliguria in severe infection.
• Risk increased with ureteric stones, strictures, tumors, pregnancy.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call urology immediately.
• Assess for sepsis and initiate resuscitation when indicated.
• Obtain urine and blood cultures when feasible.
• Start IV antibiotics promptly.
• Arrange urgent decompression with a ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy.
• Do not delay drainage in a septic/deteriorating patient while waiting for definitive stone treatment.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urinalysis and urine culture.
• CBC, creatinine, electrolytes, lactate, and blood cultures.
• Renal ultrasound to identify hydronephrosis.
• Non-contrast CT for suspected ureteric stone when appropriate.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Antibiotics (Adult examples):[/color]
• Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV every 24 hours.
• Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 hours for severe infection or broader coverage.
• Adjust dosing for renal impairment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Monitor BP, urine output, lactate, renal function, and response.
• Arrange urgent ureteric stenting or nephrostomy for decompression.
• Delay definitive stone removal until sepsis has resolved and infection is controlled.
