sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Antibiotics alone cannot reliably treat infection behind a persistent obstruction.
• Do not discharge a patient with sepsis and an obstructed collecting system.
• Anuria, bilateral obstruction, or obstruction of a solitary functioning kidney requires urgent specialist intervention.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit urgently. Septic patients may require ICU care. Transfer to a center capable of urgent urinary drainage if unavailable locally.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Sepsis plus obstruction requires antibiotics AND source control.
• Ureteric stenting and nephrostomy are accepted decompression methods.
• Reassess renal function after drainage.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Guidelines on Urolithiasis; EAU Guidelines on Urological Infections.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Flank pain or renal colic with fever, rigors, or systemic illness.
• Urinalysis may show pyuria, bacteriuria, or hematuria.
• Hydronephrosis may be present on ultrasound or CT.
• Hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status, oliguria, or elevated lactate suggests severe infection or sepsis.
• A patient may have significant obstruction even if urine output is initially preserved.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess for sepsis and hemodynamic instability.
• Establish IV access and obtain CBC, renal function, electrolytes, lactate when indicated, blood cultures, and urine culture.
• Start empiric IV antibiotics promptly according to local resistance patterns and sepsis guidance.
• Provide analgesia and appropriate fluid resuscitation based on clinical status.
• Arrange urgent urology consultation for drainage.
• Do not delay source control while waiting for definitive stone treatment or for a complete diagnostic workup in an unstable patient.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urinalysis and urine culture.
• Blood cultures in patients with systemic illness or suspected sepsis.
• CBC, creatinine, urea, electrolytes, and lactate when indicated.
• Renal ultrasound to identify hydronephrosis.
• Non-contrast CT kidneys/ureters/bladder in suitable patients to define stone location and size; contrast-enhanced imaging may be needed when complications or alternative diagnoses suspected.
• Monitor urine output and renal function.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric IV Antibiotics[/color]
• Choose treatment according to severity, likely organisms, previous cultures, recent antibiotic exposure, allergy history, renal function, and local resistance patterns.
• Example: Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV every 24 hours for susceptible infections, according to local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Ceftriaxone may be inadequate for resistant or healthcare-associated pathogens. Severe sepsis may require broader empiric coverage based on local antibiogram.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Urgent Urinary Drainage[/color]
• Indication: Infected obstructed collecting system.
• Options: Retrograde ureteric stent. Percutaneous nephrostomy.
• Arrange urgent decompression by urology or interventional radiology. Monitor hemodynamics, urine output, renal function, response to antibiotics. Obtain cultures from drained system when appropriate.
• [color=#991B1B]Antibiotics alone are NOT adequate source control for an infected obstructed kidney.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Use appropriate analgesic based on pain severity, renal function, contraindications. Avoid NSAIDs or use cautiously when significant AKI or dehydration present.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Stabilize the infection and achieve drainage first.
• Delay definitive ureteroscopy or other stone-removal procedures until infection is controlled.
• Tailor antibiotics to culture results and clinical response.
• Establish a plan for subsequent stone removal and assessment of underlying cause.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admission required for infected obstruction, systemic illness, AKI, or need for urgent drainage.
• Patients with shock or organ dysfunction may require critical care.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Urolithiasis/Urological Infections Guidelines; Surviving Sepsis Campaign; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Sudden severe unilateral flank pain, often radiating to groin. Restlessness, nausea, vomiting, microscopic or visible hematuria. Patients may be unable to find a comfortable position.
• Fever, rigors, hypotension, or systemic toxicity suggest infection and possible obstructed infected urinary system.
• Reduced urine output, anuria, solitary kidney, bilateral obstruction, pregnancy, or known renal impairment increases urgency.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs, pain severity, hydration, and evidence of sepsis.
• Provide prompt analgesia and antiemetic therapy when indicated.
• Obtain urinalysis, renal function, electrolytes, and pregnancy testing when relevant. Obtain urine culture if infection suspected.
• Assess for red flags: fever, sepsis, anuria, AKI, solitary kidney, bilateral obstruction, uncontrolled pain/vomiting.
• Arrange urgent urology assessment for infected obstruction, anuria, deteriorating renal function, or refractory symptoms.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urinalysis (blood, leukocytes, nitrites). Urine culture when infection suspected.
• Creatinine, urea, electrolytes. CBC and inflammatory markers when infection/complications suspected.
• Non-contrast CT kidneys/ureters/bladder is highly accurate in most nonpregnant adults when imaging indicated.
• Ultrasound preferred initially in pregnancy; may be appropriate in selected younger patients or when radiation avoidance important.
• Evaluate for alternative diagnoses if presentation atypical.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]First-Line Analgesia: NSAID[/color]
• Example: Diclofenac 50 mg orally or 75 mg IM when appropriate; follow formulation-specific max dose and local protocol.
• Avoid or use specialist guidance in significant renal impairment, active GI bleeding/ulceration, severe dehydration, NSAID allergy, relevant pregnancy stages.
• Do NOT combine multiple NSAIDs. [color=#991B1B]NSAIDs may worsen kidney injury in dehydration or obstructive renal impairment. Select alternative when contraindicated.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Alternative Analgesia: Paracetamol[/color]
• Adults commonly 500–1,000 mg orally or IV per formulation/local protocol. Respect maximum daily dose (lower limit in liver disease, low body weight, malnutrition, heavy alcohol use).

[color=#1E3A8A]Antiemetic Treatment[/color]
• For persistent nausea/vomiting. Select agent/dose according to age, pregnancy status, QT risk, concurrent meds, local protocol.

[color=#1E3A8A]Medical Expulsive Therapy[/color]
• Example: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg orally once daily in selected adults. Consider primarily for appropriately selected distal ureteric stones when stone size/location make spontaneous passage less likely but conservative management remains safe.
• [color=#991B1B]Not a substitute for urgent decompression of infected obstruction or threatened renal function. Counsel about dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, possible ejaculatory adverse effects.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Infected Obstructed System[/color]
• Treat as urological emergency. Start appropriate IV antibiotics promptly per local resistance patterns and sepsis protocols. Arrange urgent decompression with ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy. Definitive stone removal generally delayed until infection controlled.

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Base management on stone size, location, obstruction, symptoms, renal function, likelihood of spontaneous passage.
• Options: observation, medical expulsive therapy in selected cases, ureteroscopy, shock-wave lithotripsy, percutaneous procedures.
• Provide clear follow-up to confirm stone passage/resolution of obstruction. Analyze retrieved stones when appropriate and assess recurrent stone risk.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or arrange urgent urology management if: Fever/sepsis with suspected obstruction. Anuria, bilateral obstruction, solitary kidney with obstruction, or AKI. Pain/vomiting uncontrolled. Significant dehydration or inability to maintain oral intake. Pregnancy with concerning symptoms or complicated obstruction.
• Discharge may be appropriate for stable patients with controlled symptoms, preserved renal function, no evidence of infection/high-risk obstruction, and reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Urolithiasis Guidelines; NICE Renal and Ureteric Stones; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Flank pain, often radiating toward groin, with nausea or vomiting.
• Hematuria may occur but its absence does not exclude a stone.
• Physiological hydronephrosis of pregnancy can complicate ultrasound interpretation.
• Fever, rigors, hypotension, or systemic illness may indicate infected obstructed system.
• Differential diagnoses: pyelonephritis, obstetric emergencies, appendicitis, ovarian pathology, musculoskeletal pain.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess maternal vital signs, pain, hydration, sepsis features.
• Assess gestational age and involve obstetric care when clinically indicated.
• Obtain urinalysis, urine culture, CBC, renal function, electrolytes.
• Provide pregnancy-appropriate analgesia and antiemetics.
• Arrange renal and bladder ultrasound as first-line imaging.
• Obtain urgent urology and obstetric input if infection, renal impairment, persistent pain, vomiting, or suspected obstruction.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urinalysis and urine culture. CBC, creatinine, electrolytes.
• Renal and bladder ultrasound; Doppler or transvaginal ultrasound may be helpful in selected cases.
• MRI without gadolinium may be considered when ultrasound inconclusive and additional imaging needed.
• Low-dose non-contrast CT may occasionally be justified when diagnosis remains uncertain and result will materially change management; requires individualized risk-benefit assessment and specialist input.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Analgesia[/color]
• Paracetamol generally preferred initial analgesic when appropriate. Severe pain may require short course of opioid under supervised care.
• [color=#991B1B]NSAIDs should generally be avoided during pregnancy unless specialist determines use appropriate; particularly problematic from 20 weeks onward and contraindicated in third trimester under standard regulatory guidance.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Hydration and Antiemetics[/color]
• Correct dehydration if present; forced fluid loading does not reliably expel a stone and may worsen discomfort. Select antiemetics using pregnancy-specific guidance and consider QT risk and concurrent medication.

[color=#1E3A8A]Infected Obstruction or Threatened Renal Function[/color]
• Start pregnancy-appropriate IV antibiotics promptly when infection suspected. Arrange urgent urinary drainage by ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy when indicated. Coordinate care among urology, obstetrics, anesthesia, radiology.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay necessary source control because of pregnancy.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Many uncomplicated stones can initially be managed conservatively with close monitoring. Persistent obstruction, uncontrolled symptoms, or complications may require ureteroscopy or temporary drainage.
• Select procedures and imaging according to gestational age, clinical urgency, local expertise.

sections.heading: 06 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Fever or sepsis with urinary obstruction is an emergency.
• Do NOT assume hydronephrosis is caused by a stone; physiological dilatation is common during pregnancy.
• Avoid medications with pregnancy-related risks unless clinical benefit and safety assessed.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with infection, AKI, uncontrolled pain/vomiting, significant obstruction, or obstetric concerns.
• Outpatient care requires stable maternal status, controlled symptoms, no evidence of infection/threatened renal function, and reliable follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Urolithiasis Guidelines; ACOG Diagnostic Imaging During Pregnancy; NICE Renal/Ureteric Stones; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Visible blood in urine, sometimes with large clots. Suprapubic pain, bladder distension, urgency, or inability to pass urine. Reduced urine output despite a distended bladder.
• Tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, or syncope may indicate significant blood loss.
• Causes: bladder/renal tumors, stones, infection, trauma, anticoagulants, recent urological procedures, radiation cystitis.
• [color=#991B1B]Red urine is not always hematuria; consider hemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, medication-related discoloration.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, mental status, and hemodynamic stability.
• Establish IV access; use two large-bore IV cannulas if significant bleeding or shock suspected.
• Monitor BP, HR, SpO2, urine output, mental status.
• Obtain CBC, renal function, electrolytes, coagulation when indicated, and group/type and screen or crossmatch if significant bleeding.
• Assess for bladder distension and clot retention using examination and bladder ultrasound.
• Obtain urgent urology consultation for clot retention, ongoing heavy bleeding, hemodynamic instability, or suspected malignancy/trauma.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC (Hb and platelets), urea, creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis, urine culture.
• PT/INR and aPTT when anticoagulation/coagulopathy relevant.
• Bladder ultrasound or bladder scan to assess retention.
• CT urography or other upper tract imaging after stabilization, depending on renal function and suspected cause.
• Cystoscopy may be required for persistent bleeding, clot evacuation, diagnosis, or definitive treatment.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Bladder Decompression and Clot Evacuation[/color]
• Indication: Significant clot retention or inability to drain bladder.
• Equipment: Large-bore three-way urinary catheter (commonly 22–24 Fr in adults), sterile irrigation fluid, closed continuous bladder irrigation system.
• If urethral injury suspected: do NOT attempt blind catheterization; obtain urgent specialist assessment.
• If no urethral injury: insert large-bore three-way catheter. Gently irrigate with sterile 0.9% NaCl to remove clots. Start continuous bladder irrigation once cleared, adjusted to maintain light-pink urine.
• Record irrigation input and actual urine output separately. Net urine output = total drainage minus irrigation volume.
• [color=#991B1B]Never force irrigation against resistance or continue when outflow is blocked; excessive pressure may injure bladder.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Hemodynamic Support[/color]
• If shock present: follow local hemorrhage/resuscitation protocol. Give IV isotonic crystalloid judiciously; transfuse blood products per clinical status, Hb, ongoing bleeding, comorbidities, local guidance.
• Review anticoagulants/antiplatelet agents. Reversal only when clinically indicated, considering drug, indication, severity, thrombotic risk.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT routinely use tranexamic acid for undifferentiated gross hematuria without specialist guidance (urinary tract clot obstruction may worsen).[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Definitive Management[/color]
• Identify and treat underlying cause. Cystoscopic clot evacuation and endoscopic control of bleeding may be necessary. Arrange appropriate evaluation for malignancy when indicated. Treat infection when confirmed/strongly suspected. Coordinate anticoagulation management with prescribing team.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content: • If catheter cannot be inserted safely, irrigation does not restore drainage, or bleeding remains severe → urgent urological intervention may be required for cystoscopic clot evacuation and hemostasis.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit or arrange urgent specialist management if: Clot retention/inability to maintain catheter drainage. Hemodynamic instability, significant anemia, or ongoing heavy bleeding. AKI, suspected obstruction, or significant infection. Recent significant urinary tract trauma/procedure with ongoing bleeding.
• Discharge only after bleeding and drainage adequately controlled, patient stable, and timely follow-up/return precautions established.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Guidelines on Urological Trauma and Non-neurogenic Male LUTS; AUA Hematuria Resources; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Visible blood in urine, with or without dysuria, flank pain, or urinary frequency.
• Possible causes: UTI, stones, malignancy, renal disease, trauma, recent instrumentation, anticoagulant-associated bleeding.
• [color=#991B1B]Painless visible hematuria, especially in older adults or smokers, requires evaluation for urinary tract malignancy.[/color]
• Clots, reduced urine output, suprapubic distension, or inability to void suggest evolving clot retention.
• Hypotension, tachycardia, syncope, or pallor may indicate significant blood loss.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess vital signs, hemodynamic stability, urine output, presence of clots or retention.
• Establish IV access if bleeding heavy or patient unstable.
• Obtain CBC, renal function, electrolytes, urinalysis, urine culture when infection suspected.
• Check coagulation studies when anticoagulation, liver disease, or bleeding disorder relevant.
• Obtain blood group and crossmatch if significant bleeding or transfusion may be required.
• Seek urgent urological assessment for persistent heavy bleeding, falling hemoglobin, obstruction, trauma, or suspected malignancy.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Urinalysis with microscopy to confirm red blood cells and assess proteinuria or infection.
• Urine culture if infection suspected.
• CBC and serial hemoglobin when ongoing bleeding significant.
• Creatinine and electrolytes. Coagulation studies when indicated.
• Renal and bladder ultrasound or CT imaging according to suspected cause and clinical stability.
• Cystoscopy and upper urinary tract evaluation are often required for unexplained visible hematuria, even if bleeding resolves.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Initial Management[/color]
• Provide analgesia when required. Treat confirmed/strongly suspected infection per local guidelines. Correct clinically significant coagulopathy when indicated.
• Review anticoagulants/antiplatelet agents with prescribing team; interruption/reversal depends on bleeding severity, drug, indication, thrombotic risk.
• Monitor urine output and watch for clot formation/retention.

[color=#1E3A8A]Significant Ongoing Bleeding[/color]
• Resuscitate patients with hemodynamic instability per local hemorrhage protocol. Transfuse according to clinical status, Hb, ongoing blood loss, local transfusion guidance.
• If clots develop with impaired drainage, follow emergency pathway for clot retention and urgent urological management.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do NOT attribute visible hematuria solely to anticoagulant use without evaluating for underlying urinary tract cause.
• Do NOT delay resuscitation in patient with hemorrhagic shock.
• Avoid routine tranexamic acid for undifferentiated urinary bleeding without specialist guidance (urinary clot obstruction may occur).

sections.heading: 06 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Identify and treat underlying cause. Arrange urological assessment for unexplained visible hematuria.
• Consider nephrology assessment if findings suggest glomerular disease (significant proteinuria, dysmorphic red cells, red-cell casts).

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with hemodynamic instability, significant anemia, ongoing heavy bleeding, AKI, clot retention, or suspected serious underlying pathology.
• Stable patients may be discharged only with reliable and timely investigation plan and clear return precautions.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AUA Hematuria Resources; EAU Urological Cancers/Urolithiasis Guidelines; NICE Suspected Cancer Referral; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Blunt or penetrating trauma to the flank, abdomen, lower chest, or back.
• Hematuria may be present but its absence does NOT exclude serious renal injury.
• Flank tenderness, bruising, abdominal pain, or penetrating wound along renal trajectory.
• Hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, or altered mental status may indicate major hemorrhage.
• Associated injuries to liver, spleen, bowel, pancreas, ribs, or spine are common in high-energy trauma.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow the trauma primary survey: ABCDE. Control external hemorrhage and initiate appropriate resuscitation.
• Obtain large-bore IV access and blood samples (CBC, renal function, electrolytes, urinalysis, type and crossmatch when indicated).
• Activate major hemorrhage protocol if severe bleeding or shock suspected.
• Assess for associated abdominal, thoracic, pelvic, and spinal injuries.
• Contact trauma surgery and urology early for suspected high-grade injury, ongoing bleeding, urinary extravasation, or a solitary functioning kidney.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Imaging[/color]
• Stable/stabilized patient: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis with appropriate delayed/excretory phase when renal collecting-system or ureteric injury suspected.
• CT findings may include renal contusion, laceration, hematoma, devascularization, active contrast extravasation, collecting-system injury, or vascular injury.
• Unstable patient: Do NOT delay life-saving hemorrhage control to obtain CT. Use bedside trauma ultrasound as adjunct; negative FAST does NOT exclude retroperitoneal renal injury.

[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory[/color]
• CBC and serial Hb when bleeding suspected. Creatinine and electrolytes. Urinalysis. Coagulation studies and blood group/crossmatch when indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Hemorrhage and Resuscitation[/color]
• Use trauma resuscitation principles and blood products when clinically indicated. Avoid delaying definitive hemorrhage control in persistent shock.

[color=#1E3A8A]Nonoperative Management[/color]
• Indication: Most blunt renal injuries in hemodynamically stable patients, depending on CT grade and associated injuries. Admit for observation. Serial abdominal exams, vital signs, Hb. Monitor urine output, renal function. Analgesia. Avoid unnecessary nephrotoxic medications. Bed rest/activity restrictions individualized according to injury grade/clinical course.

[color=#1E3A8A]Angioembolization[/color]
• Indication: Selected stable/stabilized patients with active arterial bleeding, pseudoaneurysm, or AV fistula. Arrange urgent IR assessment. Selective angioembolization can control bleeding while preserving viable renal tissue.

[color=#1E3A8A]Operative Management[/color]
• Indication: Persistent hemodynamic instability attributable to renal bleeding, major vascular injury, or injuries requiring operative exploration. Urgent trauma and urological surgical management required. Nephrectomy may occasionally be necessary for uncontrollable life-threatening hemorrhage; renal preservation preferred when safely achievable.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Do NOT use presence/absence of hematuria alone to determine injury severity.
• A normal initial Hb does not exclude acute major hemorrhage.
• A negative FAST does not exclude retroperitoneal bleeding.
• Avoid delaying intervention for CT in persistently unstable patient.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Unstable patients require immediate trauma-level resuscitation and hemorrhage control.
• High-grade injuries generally require admission and specialist monitoring.
• Discharge after minor injury requires stable observations, controlled pain, adequate oral intake, clear follow-up/return precautions.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AUA Urotrauma Guideline; EAU Urological Trauma Guidelines; ATLS.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Pelvic fracture, blunt lower abdominal trauma, penetrating injury, or trauma with a full bladder.
• Gross hematuria, suprapubic pain, abdominal distension, or inability to void. Reduced urine output despite adequate fluid administration.
• Urinary ascites, unexplained elevation of serum creatinine, or peritonitis may occur with intraperitoneal rupture.
• Consider iatrogenic injury after pelvic surgery or instrumentation.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Follow trauma primary survey and treat shock immediately.
• Assess for pelvic fracture, abdominal injury, and associated urethral injury.
• Obtain CBC, renal function, electrolytes, urinalysis, and blood group/crossmatch when indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid blind urethral catheterization if urethral injury is suspected.[/color]
• Contact trauma surgery and urology early when bladder rupture suspected.
• Arrange appropriate bladder imaging after stabilization.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]CT Cystography or Conventional Retrograde Cystography[/color]
• Properly performed retrograde cystography is the key diagnostic test when bladder rupture suspected. CT cystography commonly used in trauma centers.
• Bladder must be adequately filled retrogradely with contrast per radiology protocol; routine IV contrast CT alone may miss a bladder rupture.
• Gross hematuria with pelvic fracture is a major indication for bladder imaging.
• Additional indications: gross hematuria after trauma without pelvic fracture, inability to void, or other strong clinical evidence.

[color=#1E3A8A]Laboratory[/color]
• CBC, creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis. Monitor serial Hb and renal function.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Extraperitoneal Bladder Rupture[/color]
• Many uncomplicated extraperitoneal ruptures can be managed with continuous bladder drainage.
• Insert urethral catheter only when urethral injury excluded or safe placement confirmed by experienced clinician.
• Maintain closed urinary drainage per urology instructions. Monitor urine output, hematuria, infection, abdominal findings, renal function.
• Follow-up cystography generally performed before catheter removal.
• Consider surgery when: bladder-neck involvement, bone fragments penetrating bladder, associated rectal/vaginal injury, bladder-wall entrapment or another indication for abdominal surgery, or complicated/failing rupture.

[color=#1E3A8A]Intraperitoneal Bladder Rupture[/color]
• Usually requires urgent surgical repair. Arrange urgent urological and trauma surgical management. Provide resuscitation, analgesia, perioperative antibiotics per local protocol. Repair bladder defect and establish postoperative urinary drainage. Assess associated intra-abdominal injuries.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Intraperitoneal bladder rupture can cause urinary peritonitis, sepsis, and metabolic abnormalities.
• Do NOT assume that a pelvic fracture alone proves bladder rupture.
• Do NOT rely on routine IV contrast CT without appropriate cystographic bladder filling to exclude rupture.
• Avoid blind catheterization when urethral injury suspected.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Suspected/confirmed rupture requires urgent urological assessment and usually hospital admission.
• Discharge with a catheter should occur only under documented specialist plan with catheter-care instructions and follow-up.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AUA Urotrauma Guideline; EAU Urological Trauma Guidelines; ATLS.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Urethral injury may occur after pelvic fractures, straddle injuries, penetrating trauma, or instrumentation. Failure to recognize it can worsen damage (strictures, incontinence).

[color=#991B1B]Warning features:[/color]
• Blood at the urethral meatus.
• Inability to urinate after trauma.
• Perineal or scrotal bruising.
• Pelvic fracture with urinary symptoms.
• Difficulty passing a catheter after traumatic injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Perform the trauma primary survey and control life-threatening bleeding.
• Contact urology or trauma surgery urgently.
• If urethral injury is suspected, avoid blind urethral catheterization.
• Perform retrograde urethrography in appropriate patients.
• Arrange bladder drainage through a specialist-directed approach if required.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Retrograde urethrogram in suspected urethral injury.
• CT and other trauma imaging based on associated injuries.
• Urinalysis and renal function.
• Assess for associated bladder, pelvic, rectal, and vascular injuries.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Initial management:[/color]
• Stabilize associated injuries.
• Avoid repeated attempts at urethral catheterization.
• Urinary diversion may require a suprapubic catheter placed by a trained clinician.
• Selected partial injuries may be managed with specialist-directed catheter placement or endoscopic realignment.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Blood at the meatus after pelvic trauma is a major warning sign.
• Do not blindly pass a Foley catheter when urethral disruption is suspected.
• In life-threatening circumstances, urinary drainage decisions must be made urgently without delaying resuscitation.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Admit or transfer for specialist evaluation. Pelvic fracture-associated injury generally requires coordinated trauma and urology care.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Urethral injury should be considered in pelvic fractures with blood at the meatus or inability to void.
• A single traumatic catheterization attempt may worsen a partial injury.
• Long-term follow-up is important because strictures may develop later.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: AUA Urotrauma Guideline; EAU Guidelines on Urological Trauma.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Possible injury after pelvic, colorectal, gynecological, vascular, or urological surgery.
• Unexplained flank pain, fever, ileus, abdominal distension, or sepsis after an operation.
• Urinary leakage from a surgical drain or wound.
• Hydronephrosis, urinoma, reduced renal function, or persistent urinary leak.
• Injury may be recognized during surgery or present hours to days later.
• [color=#991B1B]Hematuria may be absent, so its absence does not exclude ureteric injury.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess hemodynamic stability, abdominal findings, urine output, evidence of sepsis.
• Review operative report and timing of symptoms.
• Obtain CBC, renal function, electrolytes, urine studies when indicated.
• Contact operating surgical team and urology promptly.
• Treat sepsis and resuscitate if clinically indicated.
• Arrange appropriate imaging to identify site and extent of injury.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CT urography with delayed excretory-phase imaging when patient stable and contrast imaging appropriate.
• Retrograde pyelography may be used by urology to define injury and facilitate stent placement.
• Ultrasound can identify hydronephrosis or fluid collection but may not fully characterize injury.
• Check creatinine and monitor urine output.
• Analyze drained fluid for creatinine when urinary leakage suspected and this will help establish diagnosis.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Urinary Diversion[/color]
• Options: Retrograde ureteric stenting, percutaneous nephrostomy, or another specialist-selected drainage strategy.
• Indication: Obstruction, urinary leakage, or ureteric injury requiring diversion.
• Arrange urgent urology and, when necessary, interventional radiology involvement. Monitor temperature, urine output, renal function, signs of infection. Drain significant infected/symptomatic urinoma when indicated. Start antibiotics when infection suspected/confirmed per local protocols.

[color=#1E3A8A]Operative Repair[/color]
• Indication: Complete transection, major devascularization, uncontrolled leakage, or injury not amenable to endoscopic/percutaneous management.
• Repair depends on injury location, extent, tissue viability, patient's condition. Options include ureteric reimplantation, ureteroureterostomy, or more complex reconstruction.
• In unstable patients, initial drainage and stabilization may precede definitive reconstruction.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Delayed diagnosis can result in urinoma, sepsis, fistula, obstruction, and loss of renal function.
• Normal urine output does NOT exclude unilateral ureteric injury.
• Do NOT rely on routine abdominal CT without appropriate delayed excretory imaging when ureteric injury suspected.

sections.heading: 06 — DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Establish urinary drainage and control infection. Perform definitive repair/reconstruction when appropriate.
• Arrange follow-up imaging and renal function assessment to identify persistent obstruction or stricture.

sections.heading: 07 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Suspected iatrogenic ureteric injury requires urgent specialist assessment.
• Patients with sepsis, major urinary leakage, obstruction, or significant renal impairment generally require admission.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Urological Trauma Guidelines; AUA Urotrauma Guideline; Local protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNITION
sections.content:
Fournier's gangrene is a rapidly progressive necrotizing infection of the perineum, perianal region, and external genitalia. It may cause septic shock and death.

[color=#1E3A8A]Risk factors:[/color] Diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, recent urological procedures, perianal/urinary/genital infections.

[color=#1E3A8A]Clinical features:[/color]
• Severe genital or perineal pain (sometimes disproportionate to visible findings).
• Swelling, erythema, dusky discoloration, or skin necrosis.
• Crepitus or foul-smelling discharge in advanced disease.
• Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, or altered mental status.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Call urology and general surgery immediately.
• Activate the sepsis pathway and assess for shock.
• Establish IV access, obtain cultures when feasible, and begin broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly.
• Resuscitate with appropriate IV fluids and vasopressors when indicated.
• Arrange emergency operative debridement.
• Involve ICU, anesthesia, and other surgical teams as required.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, glucose, blood gas, lactate, coagulation profile, and blood cultures.
• Cultures from operative tissue and drainage.
• CT may help define extent in a stable patient, but imaging must not delay surgery.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Empiric adult antibiotic example:[/color]
• Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 hours.
• Add vancomycin when MRSA coverage is indicated (15–20 mg/kg IV initial dose).
• Add clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours when toxin suppression is indicated.
*(These are example components, not a universal regimen).*

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and monitoring:[/color]
• Give antibiotics immediately and document administration time.
• Monitor BP, lactate, urine output, renal function, glucose, and resuscitation response.
• Perform urgent surgical debridement; repeated debridement may be required.

sections.heading: 05 — WARNINGS
sections.content:
• Antibiotics alone are insufficient.
• Do not delay surgery for CT, laboratory scores, or complete culture results.
• Visible skin changes may underestimate deep tissue destruction.
• Avoid relying on the absence of fever or crepitus to exclude the diagnosis.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content: • Emergency surgery and hospital admission. ICU care is required for shock, organ dysfunction, or severe disease.

sections.heading: 07 — CLINICAL PEARLS
sections.content:
• Severe pain with subtle genital or perineal skin findings should raise suspicion.
• Early source control is critical.
• Assess for urinary, anorectal, and cutaneous sources.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EAU Guidelines on Urological Infections; Emergency Care Institute NSW.

sections.heading: 01 — GENERAL UROLOGICAL EMERGENCY SAFETY CHECKLIST
sections.content:
• Identify time-critical diagnoses early: testicular torsion, Fournier’s gangrene, infected urinary obstruction, ischemic priapism, and traumatic urinary tract injuries.
• Contact urology or surgery early and document the time of referral.
• Do not delay surgery, drainage, or revascularization for unnecessary imaging.
• In suspected urethral trauma, avoid blind catheterization.
• Verify medication allergies, weight-based dosing, renal adjustment, and drug concentrations.
• Reassess vital signs, urine output, pain, perfusion, and response to treatment.
• Arrange appropriate admission, transfer, and follow-up.

A. General Toxicology.title: Initial Assessment of the Poisoned Patient

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Suspect poisoning in patients presenting with:
• Unexplained altered mental status, coma, or agitation.
• Seizures, unexplained metabolic acidosis, or elevated lactate.
• Respiratory depression, hypoxemia, or unexplained respiratory failure.
• Hypotension, shock, bradycardia, tachycardia, or dysrhythmias.
• Abnormal pupils, excessive secretions, diaphoresis, dry skin, or hyperthermia.
• A known or possible medication overdose, chemical exposure, or intentional ingestion.

[color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: A normal initial examination does not exclude serious poisoning. Modified-release preparations and some cardiotoxic agents can cause delayed deterioration.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Scene Safety and Decontamination[/color]
• Identify suspected agent and route of exposure.
• Use appropriate PPE. Avoid direct contact with contaminated clothing, vomitus, powders, or liquids.
• Remove contaminated clothing and irrigate exposed skin or eyes when indicated.
• Prevent secondary contamination of healthcare staff.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT enter a contaminated environment without appropriate PPE and training.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Airway and Breathing[/color]
• Assess airway patency, respiratory rate, SpO2, and ventilation.
• Provide oxygen for hypoxemia and bag-mask ventilation for inadequate ventilation.
• Intubate when airway protection or ventilation cannot be maintained.
• Consider capnography in respiratory depressant poisoning and ventilated patients.
• [color=#991B1B]In salicylate poisoning, intubation can worsen toxicity if adequate compensatory hyperventilation is not maintained. Avoid intubation unless necessary; if required, manage ventilation carefully.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Circulation[/color]
• Establish IV access and continuous cardiac monitoring. Obtain 12-lead ECG.
• Assess BP, peripheral perfusion, signs of shock.
• Give isotonic crystalloid when clinically indicated, reassessing after each bolus.
• Use vasopressors and toxin-specific therapy when shock persists, according to suspected mechanism.

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Disability[/color]
• Assess GCS, pupils, and seizure activity.
• Check bedside glucose immediately. Treat hypoglycemia promptly.
• Treat toxicologic seizures initially with benzodiazepines and appropriate airway support.

sections.heading: 03 — INITIAL INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Core tests in significant or uncertain poisoning:[/color]
• Bedside glucose.
• Electrolytes, bicarbonate, urea, creatinine.
• Blood gas and lactate in critically ill patients.
• 12-lead ECG.
• Acetaminophen concentration when indicated.
• Salicylate concentration when suspected or history unclear.

[color=#1E3A8A]Additional tests when indicated:[/color]
• Liver function tests. Measured serum osmolality and calculated osmolar gap.
• Pregnancy test when clinically relevant. Specific drug concentrations.
• Co-oximetry for suspected CO or methemoglobinemia.
• CK and urinalysis in prolonged seizures, hyperthermia, or suspected rhabdomyolysis.

[color=#991B1B]Routine urine drug screens have limitations. A negative screen does not exclude poisoning, and a positive result does not establish current toxicity or its severity.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Supportive Care[/color]
• Maintain oxygenation, ventilation, and perfusion.
• Correct clinically significant glucose and electrolyte abnormalities.
• Treat seizures, hyperthermia, hypothermia, and dysrhythmias.
• Avoid drugs that may worsen the suspected toxidrome or ECG abnormality.
• Reassess frequently for delayed deterioration.

[color=#1E3A8A]Antidote Strategy[/color]
• Identify likely toxin and determine whether a specific antidote is indicated.
• Do not delay resuscitation while awaiting confirmatory testing.
• Follow toxin-specific protocol and monitor for treatment complications.
• Consult a poison center or clinical toxicologist whenever available.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]ICU or high-acuity admission:[/color]
• Respiratory failure, shock, significant dysrhythmias, recurrent seizures, severe acidosis, or anticipated life-threatening delayed toxicity.

[color=#1E3A8A]Monitored admission:[/color]
• Persistent symptoms, abnormal ECG or laboratory results, or an agent requiring prolonged observation.

[color=#1E3A8A]Discharge:[/color]
• Only after the appropriate observation period, resolution of concerning clinical findings, and assessment of intentional self-harm and safeguarding risks.

sections.heading: 06 — REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA 2025 Guidelines: Special Circumstances of Resuscitation; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Poisoning Guidance; Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content: A toxidrome is a recognizable pattern of clinical findings suggesting a particular toxin class. It supports early treatment but does not replace history, ECG, laboratory assessment, or consideration of mixed poisoning.

sections.heading: 02 — COMMON TOXIDROMES
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Opioid Toxidrome[/color]
• Respiratory depression. Reduced consciousness. Miosis (not always pinpoint). Bradycardia/hypotension in severe cases.
• Agents: Morphine, heroin, fentanyl, methadone, other opioids.
• Action: Support ventilation; administer naloxone when opioid toxicity suspected.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Sympathomimetic Toxidrome[/color]
• Agitation, anxiety, psychosis. Tachycardia and hypertension. Mydriasis. Diaphoresis and hyperthermia. Tremor, seizures, chest pain.
• Agents: Amphetamines, cocaine, other stimulants.
• Action: Reduce stimulation; treat agitation with benzodiazepines; monitor temperature/ECG; manage hyperthermia promptly.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Anticholinergic Toxidrome[/color]
• Delirium and agitation. Mydriasis and blurred vision. Dry skin and mucous membranes. Tachycardia and hyperthermia. Urinary retention and reduced bowel sounds.
• Agents: Atropine, diphenhydramine, TCAs, other antimuscarinics.
• Action: Supportive care, temperature control, ECG assessment, benzodiazepines for severe agitation/seizures.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use physostigmine empirically in undifferentiated poisoning. Avoid in suspected TCA toxicity or significant conduction abnormalities.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Cholinergic Toxidrome[/color]
• Salivation, lacrimation, sweating. Bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, respiratory distress. Vomiting, diarrhea, urinary incontinence. Miosis. Bradycardia, fasciculations, muscle weakness/paralysis.
• Agents: Organophosphates, carbamates, cholinergic medications.
• Action: Protect staff, remove contamination, support ventilation, give atropine promptly. Consider pralidoxime for significant organophosphate poisoning.

[color=#1E3A8A]5. Sedative-Hypnotic Toxidrome[/color]
• Drowsiness, ataxia, slurred speech. Reduced consciousness. Respiratory depression (especially with co-ingestants). Hypotension in severe poisoning.
• Agents: Benzodiazepines, barbiturates, alcohol, other sedatives.
• Action: Airway/ventilatory support, glucose assessment, ECG, evaluation for co-ingestion.
• [color=#991B1B]Flumazenil is NOT routinely recommended in undifferentiated overdose (may precipitate seizures or withdrawal).[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]6. Serotonin Toxicity[/color]
• Agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia. Inducible/spontaneous clonus. Hyperreflexia (often greater in lower limbs). Tremor, autonomic instability.
• Agents: Serotonergic antidepressants, drug combinations, recreational substances.
• Action: Stop serotonergic agents, supportive care, benzodiazepines for agitation, urgently manage severe hyperthermia.

[color=#1E3A8A]7. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome[/color]
• Hyperthermia. Generalized rigidity. Altered mental status. Autonomic instability. Elevated CK may occur.
• Agents: Dopamine-blocking medications or abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy.
• Action: Stop causative agent, supportive care, temperature control, assess renal function and CK, critical care for severe cases.

[color=#1E3A8A]8. Toxic Alcohol Pattern[/color]
• Altered consciousness, vomiting, unexplained metabolic acidosis. Elevated osmolar gap may be present early.
• Visual disturbance suggests methanol. AKI or hypocalcemia may suggest ethylene glycol.
• Action: Obtain blood gas, electrolytes, measured osmolality, specific levels. Contact toxicology early; do not delay antidotal treatment.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• ECG for suspected cardiotoxic agents.
• Blood glucose, electrolytes, bicarbonate, renal function.
• Blood gas and lactate in severe illness.
• CK in rigidity, hyperthermia, prolonged seizures, or suspected rhabdomyolysis.
• Specific drug levels and toxic alcohol studies when indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT PRINCIPLES
sections.content:
• Treat the patient, not the toxidrome label alone.
• Mixed ingestions can produce overlapping or contradictory findings.
• Give specific antidotes only when the clinical indication is appropriate.
• Use continuous monitoring in severe or evolving toxicity.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with respiratory compromise, seizures, severe hyperthermia, significant ECG abnormalities, hemodynamic instability, or persistent altered mental status.
• Discharge only when toxicity has resolved and the required observation period is complete.

sections.heading: 06 — REFERENCES
sections.content: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies; AHA 2025 Guidelines; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Consider GI decontamination only after a potentially toxic ingestion and when expected benefit outweighs risk.
Decision depends on:
• Substance and estimated amount. Time since ingestion.
• Immediate-release vs modified-release formulation. Risk of ongoing absorption.
• Airway protection and aspiration risk.
• Presence of GI obstruction or perforation risk.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stabilize airway, breathing, circulation first.
• Identify product, strength, formulation, maximum possible dose.
• Determine time of ingestion and co-ingestants.
• Contact poison center/clinical toxicologist for serious or uncertain exposures.
• Do NOT induce vomiting.
• Do NOT administer food, milk, neutralizing agents, or home remedies as substitute for medical assessment.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT OPTIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Single-Dose Activated Charcoal[/color]
• Indications: Potentially toxic ingestion of a substance adsorbed by charcoal. Greatest benefit when given early (generally within ~1 hour). Selected later presentations may benefit when absorption is delayed.
• Dose: 1 g/kg orally or via gastric tube. Adult max typically 50 g per local protocol.
• Use commercial activated charcoal suspension. Administer orally only when patient is cooperative with safe airway. Use gastric tube only when justified and airway protected. Monitor for vomiting, aspiration, deterioration.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid in unprotected airway or substantial aspiration risk. Do NOT use routinely after corrosive ingestion, hydrocarbon ingestion with aspiration risk, or poorly adsorbed substances. Does NOT effectively adsorb many metals (iron) or alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol).[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Multiple-Dose Activated Charcoal[/color]
• Potential indications: Selected life-threatening ingestions of carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine, or theophylline.
• Dose: Initial 1 g/kg, followed by repeated doses per poison-center protocol. Adult regimens often 25–50 g every 4–6 hours.
• Monitor bowel function, vomiting, aspiration risk, fluid balance, electrolytes.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use routinely for all overdoses. Avoid with bowel obstruction, ileus, or unprotected airway. Requires specialist guidance.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Whole-Bowel Irrigation[/color]
• Potential indications: Selected sustained-release/enteric-coated ingestions, iron/lithium/other poorly adsorbed substances, body-packing cases (specialist management).
• Use appropriate PEG-electrolyte solution. Adult regimens may use ~1.5–2 L/hour, adjusted to tolerance. Continue until rectal effluent is clear.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use with bowel obstruction, ileus, perforation, hemodynamic instability, or unprotected airway. Do not delay resuscitation or essential antidotal therapy.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Gastric Lavage[/color]
• NOT routine. Consider only in exceptional, potentially life-threatening ingestions with very short interval.
• [color=#991B1B]Risks: aspiration, hypoxia, laryngospasm, GI perforation. Never perform routinely or in corrosive/hydrocarbon ingestion.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Induced Emesis[/color]
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT induce vomiting with ipecac or other methods. Does not reliably improve outcomes and may increase complications.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Patients requiring decontamination should remain under observation appropriate to the substance and exposure.
• Admit patients with significant symptoms, high-risk ingestion, abnormal ECG/labs, or risk of delayed toxicity.

sections.heading: 05 — REFERENCES
sections.content: AACT/EAPCCT Position Statements on Activated Charcoal and GI Decontamination; Goldfrank's; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Enhanced elimination may be considered when a toxin can be removed effectively and clinical severity justifies the procedure.

[color=#1E3A8A]Potential modalities:[/color]
• Intermittent hemodialysis. Continuous kidney replacement therapy.
• Multiple-dose activated charcoal. Urinary alkalinization for selected substances.

Decision must consider toxin characteristics, severity, renal function, clinical trajectory, and availability of specialist services.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stabilize airway, breathing, circulation.
• Identify suspected toxin and obtain relevant concentrations when available.
• Check electrolytes, renal function, blood gas, ECG.
• Contact clinical toxicologist and nephrology team early when severe poisoning may require extracorporeal treatment.
• Do NOT delay essential antidotes or supportive care while arranging dialysis.

sections.heading: 03 — HEMODIALYSIS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Indications (Severe Poisoning):[/color]
• Methanol with severe clinical toxicity or significant acidosis.
• Ethylene glycol with severe metabolic abnormalities, organ injury, or significant toxic burden.
• Salicylate poisoning with severe toxicity, neurologic manifestations, pulmonary edema, renal impairment, or failure of medical treatment.
• Lithium poisoning with severe neurologic/cardiac toxicity, impaired clearance, or markedly elevated concentrations.
• Severe metformin-associated lactic acidosis.
• Selected severe valproate, theophylline, or other dialyzable poisonings.

[color=#1E3A8A]Preparation and Monitoring:[/color]
• Arrange nephrology and toxicology consultation. Confirm toxin and relevant labs.
• Prepare vascular access and dialysis equipment per institutional policy.
• Review electrolyte abnormalities, hemodynamic status, antidote dosing.
• Intermittent hemodialysis preferred when rapid clearance required and patient can tolerate.
• CRRT may be used when intermittent unavailable or poorly tolerated.
• Monitor BP, ECG, electrolytes, blood gas, renal function, toxin concentrations.
• Repeat toxin levels after dialysis when indicated to detect rebound.
• Continue/adjust antidotes during/after dialysis (extracorporeal treatment may remove antidote).
• [color=#991B1B]Dialysis decisions are toxin-specific and should not be based solely on an elevated osmolar gap or an isolated lab result. Monitor for post-dialysis rebound, ongoing absorption, delayed organ injury. Consult poison center/toxicologist for specific thresholds.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — URINARY ALKALINIZATION
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]Indication:[/color] Clinically significant salicylate poisoning when appropriate and not contraindicated.

[color=#1E3A8A]Dose and Preparation:[/color]
• Commonly: Sodium bicarbonate 150 mEq added to 1 L D5W per local protocol.
• Potassium supplementation may be required based on serum K+, renal function, urine output.
• [color=#991B1B]The formulation and potassium content must be individualized. Do NOT add potassium automatically in renal impairment, hyperkalemia, or oliguria.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]Administration and Monitoring:[/color]
• Administer by IV infusion under continuous clinical supervision.
• Common target: urine pH 7.5–8.0.
• Monitor urine pH, serum pH, K+, Na+, renal function, fluid balance, clinical status.
• Correct hypokalemia (can prevent effective alkalinization).
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid uncontrolled alkalinization producing severe alkalemia, hypernatremia, or fluid overload. Must not delay hemodialysis when severe salicylate poisoning meets dialysis criteria.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — MULTIPLE-DOSE ACTIVATED CHARCOAL
sections.content: May enhance elimination of selected drugs through interruption of enterohepatic circulation or enhanced GI clearance. Use only for toxin-specific indications under appropriate protocol. Refer to Topic 03 for dosing, contraindications, monitoring.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Patients undergoing enhanced elimination generally require admission to a monitored setting.
• ICU care appropriate for severe acidosis, neurologic deterioration, respiratory failure, shock, or major electrolyte abnormalities.

sections.heading: 07 — REFERENCES
sections.content: EXTRIP Workgroup Recommendations; Goldfrank's; American College of Medical Toxicology.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Consider a specific antidote when exposure history, toxidrome, ECG, laboratory findings, or clinical presentation supports a treatable toxic mechanism.

[color=#1E3A8A]Core principle:[/color] Antidotes complement, rather than replace, airway management, ventilation, circulatory support, and other resuscitative measures.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stabilize airway, breathing, circulation.
• Check bedside glucose and obtain ECG in significant or uncertain poisoning.
• Identify agent, formulation, amount, time of exposure.
• Contact poison center/clinical toxicologist for severe or uncertain cases.
• Obtain relevant toxin concentrations when indicated, without delaying time-critical treatment.

sections.heading: 03 — COMMON ANTIDOTES
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Naloxone — Opioid Toxicity[/color]
• For suspected opioid-induced respiratory depression: titrate IV naloxone to restore adequate ventilation.
• Common initial IV dose: 0.04 mg in patients with opioid dependence, followed by escalating doses (0.1, 0.2, 0.4 mg).
• In apnea/severe hypoxia: use larger initial dose and prioritize ventilation.
• No IV access: use approved intranasal or IM product per label.
• Titrate to adequate respiratory effort rather than full wakefulness. Repeat as required. Consider infusion for recurrent depression.
• [color=#991B1B]Naloxone may wear off before the opioid (especially methadone or modified-release). Continue observation and provide ventilatory support.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) — Paracetamol Poisoning[/color]
• Indication: Potentially toxic ingestion per timed concentration and applicable protocol. Unknown time with detectable paracetamol or evidence of hepatotoxicity may also require treatment.
• Common IV regimen: Total 300 mg/kg over ~20–21 hours (divided into protocol-specific infusions).
• Start promptly when indicated; do not delay for results in high-risk presentation.
• Monitor paracetamol concentration, AST/ALT, INR, renal function, clinical status.
• Reassess whether treatment should continue beyond initial regimen using accepted stopping criteria.
• [color=#991B1B]Early concentration may be misleading if obtained before 4 hours after single acute ingestion. Use Rumack–Matthew nomogram only for appropriate single acute ingestion with known time. Monitor for anaphylactoid reactions.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Atropine — Cholinergic Toxicity[/color]
• Indication: Clinically significant bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, respiratory compromise, or bradycardia due to cholinergic poisoning.
• Severe organophosphate poisoning: Common adult initial IV dose 1–3 mg, followed by rapid reassessment and repeated doubling every few minutes until secretions/ventilation improve.
• Titrate to improvement in bronchial secretions, bronchospasm, oxygenation, ventilation.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use pupil size or heart rate alone as endpoint. Atropine does not reverse nicotinic muscle weakness; respiratory support may still be necessary.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]4. Pralidoxime — Organophosphate Poisoning[/color]
• Indication: Significant organophosphate poisoning (especially with muscle weakness, fasciculations, respiratory compromise).
• Common adult regimen: 1–2 g IV over ~15–30 minutes, followed by repeat dosing or infusion when indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay atropine or respiratory support while preparing pralidoxime. Benefit depends on agent, timing, clinical circumstances.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]5. Sodium Bicarbonate — Selected Sodium-Channel Blocker Toxicity[/color]
• Indication: TCA poisoning or other sodium-channel blocker toxicity with QRS widening, ventricular dysrhythmias, or hemodynamic compromise.
• Common adult initial dose: 1–2 mEq/kg IV. Repeat per ECG/hemodynamic response and institutional protocol.
• Administer IV with continuous ECG monitoring. Follow QRS duration, BP, rhythm, blood gas, Na+, K+.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid excessive alkalemia and hypernatremia. Do NOT use bicarbonate routinely for every overdose or metabolic acidosis; treatment must match the mechanism.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]6. Digoxin Immune Fab — Severe Digoxin Toxicity[/color]
• Indication: Life-threatening dysrhythmias, severe hyperkalemia from acute digoxin poisoning, or other accepted indications.
• Calculate using product information, estimated ingested dose, or serum digoxin concentration when appropriate.
• [color=#991B1B]Hypokalemia can occur after successful treatment; monitor K+ closely. Do NOT delay life-saving treatment in critically unstable patient while waiting for confirmatory level.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]7. Fomepizole — Methanol or Ethylene Glycol[/color]
• Indication: Suspected/confirmed toxic alcohol poisoning meeting accepted treatment criteria.
• Common initial adult dose: 15 mg/kg IV. Subsequent doses/intervals depend on protocol, treatment duration, and whether hemodialysis is being performed.
• Coordinate dosing with dialysis team (fomepizole dosing may require adjustment during extracorporeal treatment).
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay indicated treatment while awaiting toxic alcohol levels when clinical suspicion is high. Contact toxicology and nephrology early.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — GENERAL ANTIDOTE SAFETY
sections.content:
• Confirm correct antidote, concentration, route, dose, infusion rate.
• Check contraindications, interactions, required monitoring.
• Use weight-based calculations carefully, especially in children.
• Verify high-alert medications and infusion preparations independently when possible.
• Document indication, dose, time, response, adverse effects.
• Contact poison center/toxicologist for complex cases.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Patients receiving antidotes for life-threatening poisoning require observation appropriate to the toxin and risk of recurrent toxicity.
• ICU admission indicated for respiratory failure, shock, serious dysrhythmias, severe metabolic abnormalities, or recurrent toxicity.

sections.heading: 06 — REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA 2025 Guidelines; Goldfrank's; EXTRIP Workgroup; Product prescribing information and local poison-center protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Paracetamol poisoning may initially be asymptomatic despite potentially severe delayed hepatic injury.

[color=#1E3A8A]Early phase (0–24 hours):[/color] Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, diaphoresis. Patient may appear clinically well. Labs may initially be normal.

[color=#1E3A8A]Intermediate phase (24–72 hours):[/color] RUQ discomfort. Rising AST/ALT. Increasing INR and possible renal impairment.

[color=#1E3A8A]Severe phase (72–96 hours and later):[/color] Acute liver failure, coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, encephalopathy, multiorgan dysfunction.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, bedside glucose.
• Establish IV access in significant poisoning.
• Determine time, amount, formulation, pattern of ingestion.
• Identify combination products containing paracetamol.
• Obtain serum paracetamol concentration at 4 hours or later after single acute ingestion with known time.
• If presentation delayed, ingestion time unknown, or liver injury suspected: obtain relevant tests immediately.
• Contact poison center/toxicologist for uncertain, massive, or complicated ingestions.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serum paracetamol concentration.
• AST, ALT, INR/PT. Electrolytes, urea, creatinine, glucose.
• Blood gas and lactate in severe poisoning.
• Bilirubin and additional acute liver failure investigations when indicated.
• Pregnancy test when clinically relevant.

[color=#1E3A8A]Interpretation of Paracetamol Concentration:[/color]
• For single acute ingestion with reliably known time: plot concentration on locally accepted Rumack–Matthew nomogram (generally used for concentrations obtained 4–24 hours after ingestion).
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use nomogram for repeated supratherapeutic ingestion, unknown ingestion time, or presentations outside validated circumstances. If time unknown or hepatic injury suspected, treatment decisions based on history, concentration, labs, toxicology advice.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. N-Acetylcysteine (NAC)[/color]
NAC replenishes glutathione and reduces risk of hepatic injury. Benefit greatest when started early, but remains indicated in many late presentations.
• Indications: Concentration at/above treatment line on appropriate nomogram. Suspected potentially toxic ingestion when concentration result delayed beyond treatment window. Unknown time with detectable concentration concerning for toxicity. Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion with concerning concentration or abnormal liver tests. Suspected paracetamol-related liver injury per specialist guidance.
• Common IV regimen: Total 300 mg/kg over ~20–21 hours. One traditional three-infusion regimen: 150 mg/kg over 1 hour; 50 mg/kg over 4 hours; 100 mg/kg over 16 hours. Follow locally approved protocol (two-bag regimens also used). Check maximum dosing weight and infusion volumes.
• Start promptly when indicated. Monitor for nausea, vomiting, flushing, rash, wheezing, hypotension, other infusion reactions.
• Recheck paracetamol concentration, AST/ALT, INR, creatinine, relevant prognostic markers before planned end of treatment.
• Continue NAC beyond initial course if paracetamol remains detectable, hepatic injury worsening, INR remains significantly abnormal, or prognostic markers not improving.
• Stop only when accepted clinical and laboratory stopping criteria are met, with toxicology input for complicated cases.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT stop NAC automatically when initial infusion schedule finishes. Early concentration obtained before 4 hours after single acute ingestion cannot reliably exclude toxicity. Massive ingestion may require modified treatment. Early consultation with liver transplant center essential when acute liver failure develops.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Activated Charcoal[/color]
• Dose: Commonly 1 g/kg orally, usually up to 50 g in adults.
• Consider early after potentially toxic ingestion when airway protected and aspiration risk acceptable. Later use may be appropriate in selected massive or delayed-absorption ingestions after specialist consultation.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT give to patient with unprotected airway or substantial aspiration risk.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with hepatotoxicity, coagulopathy, significant metabolic abnormalities, or other evidence of severe poisoning.
• ICU care indicated for acute liver failure, encephalopathy, shock, severe acidosis, or hypoglycemia requiring intensive support.
• Consider early transfer to liver transplant center when acute liver failure develops.

sections.heading: 06 — REFERENCES
sections.content: ACMT Practice Statement: Duration of IV NAC Therapy (2026 update); Goldfrank's; Local poison-center paracetamol protocol.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Salicylate poisoning can cause severe acid-base disturbances, hyperthermia, neurologic toxicity, pulmonary edema, and death.

• Tinnitus or hearing changes. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort.
• Tachypnea and hyperventilation. Sweating, fever, dehydration.
• Agitation, confusion, seizures, coma.
• Pulmonary edema and respiratory failure in severe cases.

[color=#1E3A8A]Characteristic Acid-Base Pattern:[/color]
• Early respiratory alkalosis (direct stimulation of respiratory center).
• Anion-gap metabolic acidosis (organic acid accumulation, impaired metabolism).
• Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis is common.
• [color=#991B1B]A normal or near-normal pH does NOT exclude severe poisoning because simultaneous respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis may coexist.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, temperature, mental status.
• Obtain IV access and continuous monitoring. Check bedside glucose and ECG.
• Obtain blood gas, electrolytes, renal function, serum salicylate concentration.
• Assess volume status and urine output.
• Begin treatment promptly when clinical suspicion is significant.
• Contact toxicology and nephrology early in severe poisoning.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid suppressing compensatory hyperventilation unnecessarily. Sedation, paralysis, or intubation can precipitate rapid deterioration if ventilation not carefully maintained.[/color]

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serial salicylate concentrations until clear decline and clinical improvement established.
• Blood gas, bicarbonate, anion gap, electrolytes.
• Potassium, glucose, urea, creatinine.
• Lactate and liver tests when indicated.
• Chest imaging for suspected pulmonary edema.
• Co-ingestant testing when appropriate.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Sodium Bicarbonate and Urinary Alkalinization[/color]
• Indication: Clinically significant salicylate poisoning when urinary alkalinization appropriate.
• Common approach: Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg IV as initial bolus when indicated, followed by alkalinizing infusion. Commonly used adult infusion: 150 mEq sodium bicarbonate in 1 L D5W, with potassium supplementation individualized to labs/renal function.
• Aim for urine pH ~7.5–8.0. Maintain adequate circulating volume without fluid overload.
• Monitor urine pH, serum pH, Na+, K+, bicarbonate, creatinine, fluid balance.
• Reassess salicylate concentrations and clinical status frequently. Correct hypokalemia (can make alkalinization difficult).
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid severe alkalemia, hypernatremia, fluid overload. Urinary alkalinization does NOT replace hemodialysis in severe poisoning. Clinical deterioration despite treatment requires urgent reassessment.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Hemodialysis[/color]
• Indications: Altered mental status or seizures. New hypoxemia or pulmonary edema. Severe acidemia (particularly pH ≤ 7.20). Renal impairment with significant toxicity. Failure of standard therapy. Very high salicylate concentrations.
• EXTRIP recommends extracorporeal treatment for severe poisoning. Intermittent hemodialysis preferred when available.
• Continue supportive care and bicarbonate therapy while arranging dialysis. Monitor ECG, BP, electrolytes, blood gas, serial salicylate concentrations. Reassess after dialysis for clinical improvement and rebound.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use serum concentration alone to determine severity, especially in chronic poisoning or delayed presentation.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Activated Charcoal[/color]
• Dose: Commonly 1 g/kg orally, up to 50 g in adults, when indicated.
• Consider in selected early presentations with protected airway. Repeated-dose charcoal may be considered in selected serious cases with specialist guidance.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid aspiration risk. Do NOT delay resuscitation or alkalinization.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit symptomatic patients and patients with abnormal acid-base status or rising concentrations.
• ICU admission indicated for neurologic toxicity, pulmonary edema, severe acidemia, seizures, or hemodynamic instability.
• Transfer to facility capable of urgent hemodialysis when severe toxicity present and local dialysis unavailable.

sections.heading: 06 — REFERENCES
sections.content: EXTRIP Salicylates Recommendations; ACMT Guidance Document: Salicylate Toxicity; Goldfrank's.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Opioid toxicity is a potentially fatal cause of respiratory depression and altered consciousness.

[color=#1E3A8A]Classic Findings:[/color]
• Reduced respiratory rate or inadequate ventilation.
• Reduced consciousness.
• Miosis (pupils may not always be pinpoint).
• Hypoxemia or hypercapnia.
• Bradycardia and hypotension in severe cases.

[color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Respiratory depression is the key immediate threat. Do NOT delay ventilation while waiting for naloxone.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, level of consciousness.
• Open airway and provide bag-mask ventilation when ventilation inadequate.
• Administer oxygen as indicated.
• Obtain bedside glucose.
• Establish IV or other appropriate access.
• Apply continuous SpO2 monitoring and consider capnography.
• Administer naloxone when opioid toxicity suspected and respiratory depression clinically significant.
• Assess for co-ingestants, trauma, other causes of coma.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Bedside glucose.
• ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring in significant toxicity.
• Blood gas if respiratory failure or persistent altered consciousness.
• Electrolytes and renal function when clinically indicated.
• CK, renal function, urinalysis if prolonged immobilization or rhabdomyolysis suspected.
• Co-ingestant testing based on clinical context.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Naloxone[/color]
• Indication: Suspected opioid-induced respiratory depression or life-threatening opioid toxicity.
• Dose: For adult with suspected opioid dependence and spontaneous circulation: titrated IV approach may begin at 0.04 mg, followed by escalating doses according to response. For apnea/severe hypoxia/life-threatening respiratory depression: use appropriate larger initial dose or approved intranasal/IM product without delaying ventilation. Repeat doses as required.
• Prioritize restoration of adequate breathing rather than complete wakefulness. Continue bag-mask ventilation as needed.
• Reassess respiratory rate, oxygenation, mental status, BP, recurrence of symptoms.
• Consider naloxone infusion if repeated boluses needed, particularly with long-acting opioids. Commonly used infusion: approximately two-thirds of effective reversal dose per hour, adjusted to clinical response and local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, causing recurrent respiratory depression. Precipitated withdrawal may cause agitation, vomiting, occasionally severe complications. Patients exposed to long-acting opioids, methadone, or modified-release preparations may require prolonged observation or admission.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Supportive Care[/color]
• Maintain ventilation and oxygenation. Treat hypoglycemia and other reversible causes. Evaluate for aspiration, pulmonary edema, trauma, co-ingestants. Monitor temperature, ECG, hemodynamics when indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]A response to naloxone supports opioid involvement but does NOT exclude mixed poisoning or another concurrent diagnosis.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with recurrent respiratory depression, persistent hypoxia, aspiration, pulmonary edema, long-acting opioid exposure, or significant co-ingestants.
• ICU care appropriate for respiratory failure, severe complications, or ongoing ventilatory support.
• Discharge only after appropriate observation period, stable vital signs, adequate ambulation and mentation, and assessment of recurrence risk.

sections.heading: 06 — REFERENCES
sections.content: AHA 2025 Guidelines; WHO Community Management of Opioid Overdose; Goldfrank's.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Benzodiazepine overdose commonly causes CNS depression. Severe respiratory or cardiovascular compromise is more likely with large exposures, older or medically vulnerable patients, and co-ingestion of opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives.

• Drowsiness and reduced consciousness. Slurred speech and ataxia.
• Poor coordination and confusion.
• Respiratory depression (especially in mixed ingestion).
• Hypotension in severe cases.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, GCS.
• Check bedside glucose.
• Support airway and ventilation as required.
• Establish IV access in significant poisoning.
• Obtain ECG in suspected mixed or intentional overdose.
• Determine whether opioids, alcohol, antidepressants, or other drugs may have been co-ingested.
• Avoid routine flumazenil in undifferentiated poisoning.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Bedside glucose.
• ECG when significant overdose or co-ingestion suspected.
• Blood gas for respiratory failure or persistent altered consciousness.
• Electrolytes and renal function when indicated.
• Acetaminophen and salicylate concentrations in appropriate intentional or uncertain ingestion cases.
• Additional tests based on clinical presentation.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Supportive Care[/color]
• No specific antidote routinely required for isolated benzodiazepine overdose.
• Maintain airway patency and ventilation. Use positioning and suction when appropriate. Provide bag-mask ventilation or intubation if required.
• Monitor SpO2, respiratory rate, BP, level of consciousness. Evaluate for aspiration, trauma, co-ingestants.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT assume that all coma is caused by benzodiazepines, even when history suggests ingestion.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Flumazenil[/color]
• Indication: Consider only in carefully selected cases (known iatrogenic benzodiazepine oversedation or selected isolated benzodiazepine exposures) after assessing seizure and dependence risks.
• Common adult IV starting dose: 0.2 mg over ~15 seconds. Further doses per product label and institutional protocol.
• Ensure resuscitation equipment and seizure treatment immediately available. Administer slowly under continuous monitoring.
• Reassess consciousness, ventilation, vital signs. Monitor for resedation (flumazenil may wear off before benzodiazepine). Observe for seizures and withdrawal symptoms.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT routinely use flumazenil in: Unknown/mixed overdose, chronic benzodiazepine dependence, seizure disorder or high seizure risk, suspected TCA or other proconvulsant co-ingestion, ECG findings suggestive of sodium-channel blockade. Flumazenil can precipitate seizures or acute withdrawal and may be more dangerous than supportive care in many overdose presentations.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with respiratory failure, persistent altered consciousness, aspiration, significant co-ingestion, or recurrent sedation.
• ICU admission indicated for severe respiratory or cardiovascular compromise.
• Discharge only after adequate clinical recovery and appropriate observation period based on agent, formulation, and co-ingestants.

sections.heading: 06 — REFERENCES
sections.content: Goldfrank's; Product prescribing information for flumazenil; Local poison-center guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
TCA poisoning can deteriorate rapidly and cause seizures, hypotension, and fatal ventricular dysrhythmias. Common agents include amitriptyline, imipramine, and clomipramine.

• Altered consciousness, agitation, coma.
• Anticholinergic features: dry skin, mydriasis, tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperthermia.
• Seizures. Hypotension. QRS widening and ventricular dysrhythmias.

[color=#1E3A8A]ECG Findings:[/color]
• QRS widening, particularly > 100 ms.
• Terminal R wave in lead aVR or increased R/S ratio in aVR.
• QT prolongation. Ventricular dysrhythmias in severe poisoning.
• [color=#991B1B]QRS widening and hemodynamic instability are key triggers for urgent sodium bicarbonate therapy.[/color]
