sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Initiate ABC resuscitation and continuous cardiac monitoring.
• Obtain 12-lead ECG immediately and repeat frequently.
• Establish IV access.
• Check bedside glucose, blood gas, electrolytes, potassium, renal function.
• Treat hypotension and seizures promptly.
• Contact critical care and toxicology early for significant poisoning.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Sodium Bicarbonate[/color]
• Indications: QRS widening (commonly 100–110 ms or greater depending on protocol). Ventricular dysrhythmias. Hypotension attributable to TCA cardiotoxicity. Significant sodium-channel blockade with clinical instability.
• Dose: 1–2 mEq/kg IV initial bolus. Repeat boluses according to ECG and hemodynamic response and local protocol. Titrate to QRS narrowing and clinical improvement. Common target pH ~7.50–7.55; avoid excessive alkalemia.
• [color=#1E3A8A]Preparation:[/color] Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% contains 1 mEq/mL. Calculate dose using body weight. Verify concentration and total dose before administration.
• Administer IV bolus under continuous ECG monitoring. Reassess QRS duration, rhythm, BP, perfusion after each dose. Monitor blood gas, Na+, K+, pH.
• [color=#991B1B]Monitor for hypernatremia, hypokalemia, fluid overload, excessive alkalemia. Avoid class IA and IC antiarrhythmics in TCA-related sodium-channel blockade. Do NOT use physostigmine in suspected TCA poisoning. If intubation necessary, prevent peri-intubation acidosis and maintain adequate ventilation.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Seizure Management[/color]
• Benzodiazepines are first-line for toxicologic seizures. Common adult option: Lorazepam 2–4 mg IV, repeated according to response and local seizure protocol.
• Administer IV with airway and respiratory monitoring. Correct hypoglycemia and clinically significant metabolic abnormalities. Escalate promptly for persistent seizures or status epilepticus.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid phenytoin for TCA-induced seizures (can worsen cardiac conduction toxicity). Refractory seizures require critical care and specialist-guided treatment.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Hypotension[/color]
• Give isotonic crystalloid when appropriate, reassessing after each bolus. Use sodium bicarbonate when hypotension associated with sodium-channel blockade. If hypotension persists, norepinephrine may be required under critical care guidance.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid excessive fluid administration in patients who develop pulmonary edema or have impaired cardiac function.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Activated Charcoal[/color]
• Indication: Selected potentially serious ingestions when presentation early and airway protected.
• Dose: Commonly 1 g/kg orally or via gastric tube, up to 50 g in adults, according to protocol.
• Consider only after resuscitation and assessment of aspiration risk.
• [color=#991B1B]Never give charcoal to patient with unprotected airway or delay essential resuscitation to administer it.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serial 12-lead ECGs.
• Blood gas and pH.
• Electrolytes, especially potassium and sodium.
• Glucose and renal function.
• Acetaminophen and salicylate concentrations when intentional or uncertain ingestion warrants testing.
• Additional tests according to presentation and suspected co-ingestants.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with symptoms, ECG abnormalities, seizures, hypotension, or significant suspected ingestion.
• ICU admission indicated for QRS widening with instability, ventricular dysrhythmias, recurrent seizures, severe altered consciousness, or vasopressor requirement.
• Selected asymptomatic patients may be considered for discharge only after appropriate observation period, normal ECG, and specialist or local protocol clearance.

sections.heading: 06 — REFERENCES
sections.content: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne TCA Poisoning Guideline; Goldfrank's; Queensland Poisons Information Centre Sodium Bicarbonate Guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Beta-blocker overdose can cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, myocardial depression, conduction abnormalities, and cardiogenic shock.
• Common Agents: Propranolol, Metoprolol, Atenolol, Bisoprolol, Carvedilol, Sotalol.
• Bradycardia and hypotension. Dizziness, syncope, altered mental status. Cardiogenic shock and poor peripheral perfusion.
• Hypoglycemia, particularly in children. Bronchospasm, especially with nonselective agents.
• Seizures and QRS widening with propranolol toxicity. QT prolongation and torsades de pointes with sotalol toxicity.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Propranolol is highly lipophilic and may cause seizures and sodium-channel blockade. Atenolol and sotalol toxicity may be complicated by renal impairment.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation. Establish IV access and continuous cardiac monitoring.
• Obtain 12-lead ECG. Check bedside glucose immediately.
• Measure electrolytes, renal function, blood gas, lactate in significant poisoning.
• Treat symptomatic bradycardia and shock promptly.
• Contact poison center, clinical toxicologist, and critical care team early.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serial ECGs. Glucose and electrolytes (including potassium and magnesium).
• Renal function. Blood gas and lactate in shock.
• Echocardiography when cardiogenic shock or myocardial dysfunction suspected.
• Additional investigations guided by co-ingestants and clinical findings.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Initial Hemodynamic Support[/color]
• If hypotension and fluid administration appropriate: isotonic crystalloid bolus, commonly 250–500 mL in adult, then reassess. Use smaller aliquots when pulmonary edema or cardiac dysfunction suspected.
• Vasopressors may be required for persistent shock.
• [color=#991B1B]Excessive fluid administration may worsen pulmonary edema. Standard bradycardia treatment alone may be insufficient in severe beta-blocker poisoning.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Glucagon[/color]
• Indication: Significant beta-blocker-associated bradycardia or hypotension, particularly when initial supportive measures insufficient.
• Adult initial dose: 3–5 mg IV over approximately 1–2 minutes. If inadequate response, repeat or increase dose per local toxicology protocol. Continuous infusion may be considered after response to bolus.
• [color=#991B1B]Vomiting is common and may be severe. Glucagon may have limited/transient effect and must not delay other therapies for shock.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. High-Dose Insulin Euglycemia Therapy (HIET)[/color]
• Indication: Severe beta-blocker toxicity with myocardial dysfunction or shock refractory to initial treatment.
• Regular insulin: commonly 1 unit/kg IV bolus, then infusion at approximately 1 unit/kg/hour. Titrate per hemodynamic response and protocol; substantially higher doses may be required in refractory poisoning under specialist supervision.
• Check glucose and potassium before treatment. Monitor glucose every 15–30 minutes initially. Monitor potassium frequently and replace when clinically indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]HIET is a high-risk therapy requiring ICU-level monitoring and experienced staff. Hypoglycemia and hypokalemia are major complications. Insulin dosing must be prescribed in units, not milliliters; confirm concentration before administration.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Vasopressors[/color]
• Norepinephrine may be useful for vasodilatory shock. Epinephrine may be considered when significant myocardial depression and bradycardia coexist.
• Select and titrate therapy according to hemodynamic phenotype and specialist advice.
• [color=#991B1B]No single vasopressor is optimal for every beta-blocker overdose. Escalate early when shock persists.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]E. Sodium Bicarbonate[/color]
• Indication: QRS widening or ventricular dysrhythmias associated with sodium-channel blockade, particularly in propranolol poisoning.
• Common initial adult dose: 1–2 mEq/kg IV. Repeat according to ECG response and local toxicology protocol.
• Monitor QRS duration, rhythm, blood gas, sodium, potassium. Avoid excessive alkalemia and hypernatremia.

[color=#1E3A8A]Refractory Shock[/color]
• Specialist-directed options: HIET escalation, lipid emulsion in selected cases (severe propranolol toxicity), temporary pacing for selected conduction abnormalities, VA-ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock/cardiac arrest.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit significant symptomatic overdoses for continuous monitoring.
• ICU admission indicated for hypotension, significant bradycardia, conduction abnormalities, seizures, myocardial dysfunction, or need for antidotal infusions.
• Consider prolonged observation for sustained-release preparations and agents with delayed toxicity.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies; AHA 2025 Guidelines; Poison-center protocols for beta-blocker overdose and high-dose insulin therapy.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Calcium channel blocker (CCB) overdose may cause profound vasodilation, bradycardia, myocardial depression, and shock. Verapamil and diltiazem frequently produce marked cardiac toxicity, while dihydropyridines such as amlodipine may initially cause prominent vasodilatory shock.
• Common Agents: Amlodipine, Nifedipine, Verapamil, Diltiazem.
• Hypotension and shock. Bradycardia or AV block.
• Hyperglycemia due to impaired insulin secretion and utilization. Altered mental status and elevated lactate. Pulmonary edema in severe cases.
• [color=#991B1B]Hyperglycemia may support diagnosis of significant CCB toxicity but is not diagnostic by itself.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Initiate ABC resuscitation. Establish IV access and continuous ECG monitoring.
• Obtain 12-lead ECG. Check bedside glucose immediately.
• Measure electrolytes, renal function, blood gas, lactate.
• Consider bedside echocardiography in shock.
• Contact toxicology and critical care early.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IV Calcium[/color]
• Indication: Significant CCB-associated hypotension, bradycardia, or myocardial dysfunction.
• One commonly used adult regimen: Calcium chloride 10%: 10–20 mL IV, OR Calcium gluconate 10%: 30–60 mL IV. Repeat doses may be required according to clinical response, ECG, and ionized calcium.
• [color=#991B1B]Verify exact calcium salt and concentration. Calcium chloride 10% contains approximately three times as much elemental calcium per mL as calcium gluconate 10%. Use secure IV line; central access preferred for calcium chloride when feasible. Do NOT substitute equal volumes of calcium chloride and calcium gluconate. Calcium chloride extravasation can cause severe tissue injury. Avoid excessive hypercalcemia.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. High-Dose Insulin Euglycemia Therapy (HIET)[/color]
• Indication: Significant CCB-associated shock or myocardial dysfunction, especially when initial therapy inadequate.
• Regular insulin: commonly 1 unit/kg IV bolus, then infusion at approximately 1 unit/kg/hour. Titrate to clinical response under high-dose insulin protocol; higher doses may be required in severe refractory poisoning.
• Check glucose and potassium before treatment. Monitor glucose every 15–30 minutes during initiation and dose changes, then at protocol-defined intervals once stable.
• [color=#991B1B]HIET is a high-risk ICU therapy. Hypoglycemia and hypokalemia can be life-threatening. Use a dedicated protocol and independent dose verification.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Vasopressors[/color]
• Norepinephrine commonly used for significant vasodilatory shock. Epinephrine may be useful when myocardial depression or bradycardia prominent. Combined vasopressor therapy may be required in severe poisoning.
• Titrate to adequate perfusion and institution's blood pressure target.
• [color=#991B1B]Vasopressors may not adequately correct myocardial depression without adjunctive therapy.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Additional Therapies[/color]
• Consider glucagon in selected cases (evidence and response variable).
• Consider lipid emulsion only in selected refractory cases after specialist consultation.
• Consider VA-ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock or cardiac arrest where available.
• Do NOT delay escalation when shock is worsening.

sections.heading: 04 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serial ECGs. Glucose and electrolytes.
• Ionized calcium during IV calcium treatment.
• Renal function. Blood gas and lactate.
• Echocardiography when myocardial dysfunction suspected.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit significant overdoses for continuous cardiac and hemodynamic monitoring.
• ICU admission indicated for hypotension, bradycardia, AV block, hyperglycemia with systemic toxicity, myocardial dysfunction, or need for HIET or vasopressors.
• Sustained-release preparations may require prolonged observation.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies; AHA 2025 Guidelines; Poison-center protocols for calcium channel blocker toxicity and high-dose insulin therapy.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Digoxin toxicity may result from acute overdose, chronic accumulation, renal impairment, or interactions with other medications.
• Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, abdominal discomfort. Weakness, confusion, visual disturbances.
• Bradycardia and AV block. Atrial tachycardia with block. Ventricular ectopy or ventricular dysrhythmias. Hyperkalemia in severe acute poisoning.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Digoxin toxicity can occur at concentrations that overlap with therapeutic ranges. Clinical findings, renal function, ECG, potassium, and timing of last dose are essential to interpretation.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs and establish IV access.
• Obtain 12-lead ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring.
• Check potassium, magnesium, calcium, renal function, glucose.
• Obtain serum digoxin concentration when indicated.
• Determine timing of last dose and whether exposure was acute or chronic.
• Contact toxicology and cardiology early for significant toxicity.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• ECG and continuous rhythm monitoring. Serum potassium and magnesium. Urea and creatinine.
• Serum digoxin concentration. Blood gas and lactate if unstable.
• Additional tests for possible co-ingestants.
• [color=#991B1B]A digoxin level obtained too soon after ingestion may not reflect tissue distribution. When feasible, measure at least 6 hours after last dose, but do NOT delay emergency treatment in unstable patient.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Digoxin Immune Fab[/color]
• Indications: Life-threatening toxicity (ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation, severe symptomatic bradycardia or high-grade AV block not responding to appropriate measures, significant hyperkalemia attributable to acute digoxin poisoning, hemodynamic instability, large acute ingestion meeting accepted criteria).
• Dose: Use product-specific calculation based on estimated ingested dose or serum digoxin concentration when reliable. In immediately life-threatening toxicity, follow emergency institutional protocol and consult toxicology urgently.
• [color=#991B1B]Potassium can fall rapidly after successful Fab treatment; monitor closely. Hypersensitivity reactions can occur. Do NOT delay Fab in life-threatening poisoning while waiting for confirmatory serum concentration.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Electrolyte Management[/color]
• Correct hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia carefully when present. Treat clinically significant hyperkalemia according to severity and mechanism. In severe acute digoxin toxicity, Fab is preferred specific therapy for digoxin-mediated hyperkalemia.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Bradyarrhythmias[/color]
• Atropine may be used for symptomatic bradycardia while preparing definitive treatment. Temporary pacing may be necessary in selected unstable cases but requires expert management. Avoid provoking ventricular dysrhythmias during emergency procedures.
• [color=#991B1B]Fab is definitive specific treatment for life-threatening digoxin toxicity. Routine electrical cardioversion can precipitate serious dysrhythmias in digoxin-toxic patients; reserve for situations in which necessary and manage with expert input.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with clinically significant toxicity, ECG abnormalities, electrolyte disturbances, or suspected acute overdose.
• ICU admission indicated for ventricular dysrhythmias, high-grade AV block, severe hyperkalemia, or hemodynamic instability.
• Observation duration should account for renal function, formulation, exposure pattern, and recurrence risk.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Goldfrank's; Digoxin Immune Fab product prescribing information; Poison-center and cardiology protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Insulin and sulfonylurea overdose can cause profound, recurrent, and prolonged hypoglycemia.
• Common Causes: Excess insulin administration, accidental administration of another patient's insulin, intentional insulin overdose, sulfonylurea ingestion (glibenclamide/glyburide, glimepiride, gliclazide), medication errors, reduced food intake after glucose-lowering therapy.
• Sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger. Confusion, behavioral changes, reduced consciousness. Seizures or coma. Persistent or recurrent hypoglycemia. Hypokalemia, particularly after substantial insulin exposure.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Check bedside glucose immediately. Treat hypoglycemia without delay.
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, neurologic status. Establish IV access.
• Identify exact insulin or sulfonylurea, dose, formulation, time of exposure.
• Obtain ECG and electrolytes in significant poisoning.
• Contact toxicology early for long-acting insulin or sulfonylurea exposure.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Frequent bedside glucose measurements.
• Serum potassium, magnesium, phosphate, renal function when indicated.
• ECG in significant poisoning or electrolyte abnormalities.
• Additional investigations if cause of hypoglycemia unclear.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IV Dextrose for Acute Hypoglycemia[/color]
• Indication: Symptomatic or clinically significant hypoglycemia, especially altered consciousness or seizures.
• Adults: commonly 10–25 g IV dextrose, titrated to glucose response (e.g., 100–250 mL of 10% dextrose for 10–25 g). In severe hypoglycemia, use locally approved concentration and dose. Pediatric dosing must be weight-based.
• Recheck glucose promptly after treatment, commonly within 10–15 minutes. Repeat if hypoglycemia persists. Once consciousness restored, provide oral carbohydrate when safe.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid unnecessary large glucose loads that produce extreme hyperglycemia. Do NOT delay IV treatment in severe symptomatic hypoglycemia.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Continuous Dextrose Infusion for Insulin Overdose[/color]
• Indication: Recurrent hypoglycemia or large insulin exposure requiring sustained glucose support.
• Select concentration and infusion rate according to serial glucose measurements and ongoing insulin effect. No single fixed infusion rate suitable for every insulin overdose.
• Titrate to maintain glucose within institution's target range. Monitor glucose frequently during initiation and rate changes. Monitor potassium, magnesium, phosphate, fluid balance.
• [color=#991B1B]Long-acting insulin and large subcutaneous injections can produce prolonged toxicity. Avoid excessive fluid administration; more concentrated glucose solution may be needed under appropriate protocols.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Octreotide for Sulfonylurea-Induced Hypoglycemia[/color]
• Indication: Recurrent or persistent hypoglycemia after sulfonylurea ingestion, particularly when dextrose treatment alone leads to repeated episodes.
• Commonly used adult regimen: octreotide 50–100 micrograms SC every 6 hours. IV administration or infusion may be used under specialist protocol for severe cases. Pediatric dosing requires toxicology guidance and weight-based protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Octreotide suppresses insulin release but does NOT replace immediate glucose correction. Sulfonylurea toxicity may recur after initial improvement; prolonged observation often required.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Glucagon[/color]
• Indication: Temporary treatment for hypoglycemia when IV access not immediately available, depending on clinical setting and product.
• Adult emergency dosing is product-specific; common preparations use 1 mg IM or SC.
• [color=#991B1B]Glucagon may be ineffective when hepatic glycogen stores depleted. It is NOT definitive treatment for sulfonylurea poisoning and may be followed by recurrent hypoglycemia.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — ADDITIONAL MANAGEMENT
sections.content:
• Correct potassium, magnesium, or phosphate abnormalities when indicated.
• Consult toxicology regarding large or long-acting insulin exposures.
• Consider critical care setting for recurrent hypoglycemia, seizures, or high glucose-infusion requirements.
• Evaluate for intentional self-harm and medication-safety issues.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with recurrent hypoglycemia or significant insulin or sulfonylurea exposure.
• ICU care indicated for severe neurologic manifestations, recurrent seizures, hemodynamic instability, or intensive glucose support.
• Observation must be prolonged when agent or formulation can cause delayed or recurrent hypoglycemia.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Goldfrank's; Poison-center protocols for sulfonylurea and insulin overdose; Local emergency hypoglycemia protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Organophosphates and carbamates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, producing excessive acetylcholine activity at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors and within the CNS.

[color=#1E3A8A]Common Exposure Sources:[/color] Agricultural insecticides, household pesticides, occupational exposure, intentional ingestion.

[color=#1E3A8A]Muscarinic Features:[/color] Salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, sweating, miosis, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramping, bradycardia, urinary incontinence.

[color=#1E3A8A]Nicotinic Features:[/color] Fasciculations, muscle weakness, paralysis, respiratory muscle failure. Tachycardia or hypertension may also occur.

[color=#1E3A8A]CNS Features:[/color] Anxiety, agitation, confusion, seizures, coma, respiratory depression.

[color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Respiratory failure may result from bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, central respiratory depression, and respiratory muscle weakness simultaneously.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Protect Staff[/color]
• Use appropriate PPE. Avoid direct contact with contaminated clothing, vomitus, or skin. Remove contaminated clothing carefully and isolate it. Wash exposed skin with soap and water. Prevent secondary contamination.

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Airway and Breathing[/color]
• Suction secretions and provide oxygen. Use bag-mask ventilation and intubation when required. Anticipate prolonged ventilatory support.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid succinylcholine when possible because cholinesterase inhibition may prolong its paralytic effect; choose an alternative neuromuscular blocker under the airway protocol.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Circulation and Monitoring[/color]
• Establish IV access. Apply continuous ECG and SpO2 monitoring. Check glucose, electrolytes, blood gas, renal function. Obtain chest imaging if aspiration/pulmonary edema suspected.

sections.heading: 03 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Atropine[/color]
• Indication: Clinically significant cholinergic toxicity, especially bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, respiratory compromise, or bradycardia.
• Adults: commonly 1–3 mg IV initially. In severe poisoning, rapidly reassess and double the dose every 3–5 minutes until respiratory secretions and ventilation improve. Very large cumulative doses may be required.
• [color=#1E3A8A]Monitoring:[/color] Titrate to improvement in bronchial secretions, bronchospasm, oxygenation, ventilation. Once adequate atropinization achieved, continuous infusion may be used in severe cases; common starting approach: 10–20% of total loading dose per hour, adjusted to clinical response.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use pupil size or heart rate alone as endpoint. Persistent muscle weakness may continue despite adequate atropine. Recurrent bronchorrhea may require additional boluses or infusion adjustment.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Pralidoxime (2-PAM)[/color]
• Indication: Significant organophosphate poisoning, particularly with fasciculations, weakness, respiratory muscle involvement, or severe systemic toxicity.
• Adult loading dose commonly 1–2 g IV over approximately 15–30 minutes. Continuous infusion or repeat dosing may follow per specific product and local toxicology protocol. Pediatric doses weight-based.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay atropine or airway support while preparing pralidoxime. Efficacy varies with compound, time since exposure, and whether enzyme has undergone aging. Carbamate poisoning differs from organophosphate poisoning; consult toxicology regarding oxime use when agent uncertain.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Seizure Management[/color]
• Benzodiazepines first-line. Common adult option: lorazepam 2–4 mg IV, repeated according to response and status epilepticus protocol. Provide airway support and monitor oxygenation. Escalate promptly for persistent seizures.

sections.heading: 04 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Cholinesterase activity may support diagnosis but should NOT delay treatment. Plasma butyrylcholinesterase and red-cell acetylcholinesterase may be useful where available.
• ECG and continuous rhythm monitoring. Blood gas, electrolytes, glucose, renal function.
• Chest imaging when aspiration or pulmonary complications suspected. CK and renal function when prolonged seizures or muscle injury occur.

sections.heading: 05 — COMPLICATIONS
sections.content:
• Respiratory failure. Aspiration pneumonitis.
• Intermediate syndrome with delayed muscle weakness. Recurrent cholinergic symptoms.
• Delayed neuropathy with certain organophosphates. Hypoxic brain injury after severe respiratory compromise.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU admission indicated for respiratory compromise, significant bronchorrhea, muscle weakness, altered consciousness, seizures, or ongoing atropine infusion.
• Patients may require prolonged observation after initial improvement because respiratory muscle weakness or recurrent toxicity can develop later.
• Discharge requires stable respiratory function, no recurrent cholinergic signs, and an appropriate observation period.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WHO Clinical Management of Acute Pesticide Intoxication; Goldfrank's; Local poison-center and organophosphate poisoning protocols.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Methanol is a toxic alcohol found in some solvents, fuels, and adulterated alcoholic products. Toxicity is caused primarily by formate, which produces metabolic acidosis and optic nerve injury.
• Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache. Visual blurring, photophobia, altered color perception, or visual loss. Tachypnea due to metabolic acidosis. Confusion, seizures, coma in severe cases.
• High anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Elevated osmolar gap may occur, particularly early.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Symptoms may be delayed for several hours. Absence of visual symptoms or a normal early osmolar gap does NOT exclude methanol poisoning.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, neurologic status. Obtain IV access and continuous monitoring.
• Check bedside glucose immediately.
• Obtain blood gas, electrolytes, bicarbonate, anion gap, renal function, measured serum osmolality.
• Send methanol concentration if available.
• Contact toxicology and nephrology urgently.
• Start antidotal treatment promptly when clinical suspicion and exposure history justify it; do NOT wait for confirmatory levels in high-risk patient.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Blood gas, pH, bicarbonate, anion gap. Measured serum osmolality and calculated osmolar gap.
• Serum methanol concentration when available. Electrolytes, glucose, urea, creatinine.
• Lactate and ketones when clinically indicated. Visual acuity, pupils, neurologic examination. ECG in significant poisoning.
• [color=#991B1B]Interpretation: The osmolar gap can be elevated early and decrease as methanol is metabolized, while the anion-gap metabolic acidosis becomes more prominent. Neither gap alone can reliably exclude poisoning.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Fomepizole[/color]
• Indication: Suspected or confirmed methanol poisoning meeting accepted treatment criteria.
• Commonly used adult and pediatric regimen: Loading dose 15 mg/kg IV. Doses 2–5: 10 mg/kg IV every 12 hours. Subsequent doses: increase to 15 mg/kg every 12 hours because of enzyme autoinduction. During hemodialysis, dosing intervals must be shortened because fomepizole is dialyzable.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay treatment in strongly suspected, clinically significant exposure while waiting for methanol level. Fomepizole prevents further toxic metabolite formation but does NOT remove formate already present or correct severe acidosis by itself.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Sodium Bicarbonate[/color]
• Indication: Significant metabolic acidemia.
• Individualize according to pH, clinical status, sodium concentration, institutional toxicology protocol. No single fixed dose appropriate for all poisonings.
• [color=#991B1B]Bicarbonate is supportive treatment, NOT a substitute for fomepizole or hemodialysis when indicated.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Hemodialysis[/color]
• Indications: Visual impairment attributable to methanol. Severe metabolic acidosis. Coma, seizures, significant neurologic abnormalities. Renal impairment or other severe clinical manifestations. High methanol concentration meeting accepted extracorporeal treatment criteria. Persistent acidosis or clinical deterioration despite treatment.
• Continue fomepizole during dialysis, adjusting dose and interval. Monitor blood gas, electrolytes, methanol concentration, clinical status. Reassess for rebound or ongoing absorption.
• [color=#991B1B]Dialysis decisions should follow current EXTRIP recommendations and specialist advice, considering methanol concentration, acid-base status, clinical findings, availability of antidote.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU admission for severe acidosis, visual symptoms, seizures, coma, or hemodynamic instability.
• Urgent transfer to dialysis-capable facility when indicated.
• Arrange ophthalmology assessment for visual symptoms and follow-up for potential permanent visual impairment.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EXTRIP Workgroup Methanol Recommendations; Fomepizole product prescribing information; Goldfrank's.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Ethylene glycol is commonly found in antifreeze and some industrial fluids. Its toxic metabolites cause metabolic acidosis, neurologic toxicity, and acute kidney injury.

[color=#1E3A8A]Early phase:[/color] Intoxication-like behavior, dizziness, nausea, vomiting. Ataxia or altered mental status.

[color=#1E3A8A]Intermediate phase:[/color] Tachypnea and high anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Tachycardia and cardiovascular instability in severe cases.

[color=#1E3A8A]Later phase:[/color] Acute kidney injury, flank pain, oliguria, or anuria. Hypocalcemia and possible calcium oxalate crystalluria. Seizures or coma in severe poisoning.
• [color=#991B1B]Absence of calcium oxalate crystals does NOT exclude ethylene glycol poisoning.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stabilize airway, breathing, circulation. Obtain IV access and continuous monitoring.
• Check bedside glucose.
• Obtain blood gas, electrolytes, bicarbonate, anion gap, renal function, calcium, measured osmolality.
• Send ethylene glycol concentration when available.
• Contact toxicology and nephrology urgently.
• Begin fomepizole promptly when indicated without waiting for confirmatory testing.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Blood gas, pH, bicarbonate, anion gap. Measured serum osmolality and calculated osmolar gap.
• Ethylene glycol concentration, if available. Electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal function.
• Urinalysis and microscopy. Lactate, glucose, ECG as clinically indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]Interpretation: Early poisoning may produce elevated osmolar gap before severe acidosis develops. As ethylene glycol is metabolized, osmolar gap may decline while anion gap increases.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Fomepizole[/color]
• Indication: Suspected or confirmed ethylene glycol poisoning meeting accepted treatment criteria.
• Commonly used regimen: Loading dose 15 mg/kg IV. Doses 2–5: 10 mg/kg IV every 12 hours. Subsequent doses: 15 mg/kg IV every 12 hours. During hemodialysis, adjust dose interval per product label and protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay antidotal therapy when suspicion is high and consequences of delay are significant. Fomepizole prevents formation of additional toxic metabolites but does NOT directly reverse established kidney injury.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Sodium Bicarbonate[/color]
• Indication: Significant metabolic acidemia. Individualize according to degree of acidemia and clinical condition.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid excessive alkalemia and fluid overload.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Thiamine and Pyridoxine[/color]
• May be considered as adjuncts in selected cases per institutional toxicology protocol. Must never delay fomepizole or indicated hemodialysis.

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Hemodialysis[/color]
• Indications: Severe metabolic acidosis. Significant acute kidney injury. Coma, seizures, other severe clinical manifestations. High ethylene glycol burden or anion-gap abnormalities meeting accepted EXTRIP criteria. Deterioration despite appropriate treatment.
• Continue fomepizole with dialysis-adjusted dosing. Monitor pH, electrolytes, renal function, toxin concentrations. Reassess need for continued treatment after dialysis.
• [color=#991B1B]Use current EXTRIP criteria and toxicology/nephrology advice. Do NOT base dialysis decision on osmolar gap alone.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU admission for severe acidosis, seizures, coma, shock, or major electrolyte abnormalities.
• Urgent transfer to dialysis-capable facility when indicated.
• Monitor renal function and urine output for evolving kidney injury.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EXTRIP Workgroup Ethylene Glycol Recommendations; Fomepizole product prescribing information; Goldfrank's.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas produced by incomplete combustion. It reduces oxygen delivery and interferes with cellular oxygen utilization.

[color=#1E3A8A]Common Sources:[/color] Generators used indoors or near windows. Charcoal or fuel-burning heaters in poorly ventilated rooms. Vehicle exhaust. Fires and faulty combustion appliances.

• Headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting. Confusion, ataxia, syncope.
• Chest pain, arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia. Seizures or coma in severe poisoning. Fetal distress in pregnant patients.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: A normal conventional pulse oximeter reading does NOT exclude carbon monoxide poisoning.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Remove patient from exposure to safe environment without exposing rescuers.
• Administer 100% oxygen immediately.
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, neurologic status, glucose.
• Obtain IV access and ECG monitoring in significant cases.
• Request blood co-oximetry for carboxyhemoglobin (COHb).
• Assess for smoke inhalation, trauma, possible cyanide co-poisoning in fire victims.
• Contact hyperbaric oxygen service or toxicology specialist for severe presentations.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Blood co-oximetry for COHb. Blood gas and lactate in significant poisoning.
• ECG and cardiac troponin for chest pain, significant exposure, or cardiac risk.
• Neurologic assessment. Pregnancy assessment when relevant.
• Additional evaluation for airway injury or associated toxic exposures.
• [color=#991B1B]COHb concentration may fall after oxygen treatment and may underestimate peak exposure. COHb concentration does NOT correlate reliably with clinical severity or long-term neurologic outcomes. Interpret results alongside exposure history, symptoms, timing, and treatment already given.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. High-Concentration Oxygen[/color]
• Indication: Suspected or confirmed CO poisoning.
• Administer 100% oxygen using non-rebreather mask with adequate flow, or 100% oxygen through advanced airway when clinically indicated.
• Start immediately and continue until symptoms resolve and specialist-guided clinical criteria met. Monitor mental status, vital signs, ECG, clinical response. Repeat COHb testing when it will assist management, without delaying treatment.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use a normal pulse oximeter reading to rule out CO poisoning. Do NOT withhold oxygen while waiting for laboratory confirmation.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Hyperbaric Oxygen Consultation[/color]
• Consider urgent consultation when: Loss of consciousness or persistent neurologic impairment. Cardiac ischemia, significant myocardial injury, serious dysrhythmia. Severe metabolic acidosis. Significant COHb elevation in appropriate clinical context. Pregnancy with significant exposure or concerning maternal/fetal findings.
• [color=#991B1B]There is no single COHb threshold that determines every hyperbaric treatment decision. Hyperbaric oxygen availability should NOT delay initial high-concentration oxygen or essential resuscitation.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Supportive Care[/color]
• Treat seizures and shock per emergency protocols. Assess myocardial injury and manage complications. In smoke inhalation, evaluate for concomitant cyanide poisoning when clinically indicated.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with persistent neurologic symptoms, syncope, myocardial injury, severe acidosis, pregnancy-related concerns, or significant ongoing symptoms.
• ICU care appropriate for coma, seizures, hemodynamic instability, or respiratory failure.
• Provide discharge instructions about delayed neurologic symptoms and arrange follow-up when indicated.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: CDC Clinical Guidance for Carbon Monoxide Poisoning; Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society Indications; Goldfrank's.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Cyanide inhibits cellular oxygen utilization and can cause rapid cardiovascular collapse. Severe poisoning may occur after exposure to certain industrial chemicals, smoke from enclosed-space fires, or other cyanide-containing materials.
• Sudden altered consciousness, seizures, coma. Hypotension, shock, cardiac arrest.
• Severe metabolic acidosis. Markedly elevated lactate. Respiratory distress.
• Possible soot, airway injury, or smoke exposure in fire victims.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: No single clinical sign or lactate value definitively diagnoses cyanide poisoning. Interpret findings in context of exposure and clinical presentation.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Ensure scene safety and appropriate responder PPE. Remove patient from exposure when safe.
• Initiate ABC resuscitation and high-concentration oxygen.
• Establish IV or intraosseous access.
• Treat seizures, shock, cardiac arrest per resuscitation protocols.
• Obtain blood gas, lactate, electrolytes, ECG.
• Administer appropriate antidote promptly when severe cyanide poisoning strongly suspected. Do NOT delay treatment for cyanide concentration.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Blood gas and lactate. Electrolytes, glucose, renal function. ECG and cardiac monitoring.
• Co-oximetry and carboxyhemoglobin when smoke inhalation suspected.
• Cyanide concentration if available, recognizing results generally not fast enough to guide initial resuscitation.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Hydroxocobalamin[/color]
• Indication: Suspected severe cyanide poisoning, particularly with cardiovascular instability, severe lactic acidosis, seizures, or collapse following compatible exposure.
• Adults: 5 g IV over approximately 15 minutes. A second 5 g dose may be administered according to clinical severity and response, following product label and emergency protocol. Pediatric dosing weight-based.
• [color=#991B1B]Hydroxocobalamin commonly causes red discoloration of skin and urine. It can interfere with laboratory assays and some dialysis blood-leak detection systems. Hypersensitivity reactions and hypertension may occur. Do NOT delay administration in critically ill patient with strongly compatible exposure.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Sodium Nitrite and Sodium Thiosulfate[/color]
• Alternatives in selected circumstances when hydroxocobalamin unavailable or when specialist protocol supports use.
• [color=#991B1B]Sodium nitrite can cause methemoglobinemia and hypotension. It may be particularly hazardous when carbon monoxide poisoning or severe anemia also suspected. In smoke-inhalation victims with possible combined CO and cyanide exposure, hydroxocobalamin generally preferred when available.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Supportive Care[/color]
• Provide high-concentration oxygen. Maintain ventilation and circulation. Treat seizures with benzodiazepines. Treat shock with appropriate resuscitation and vasopressors. Manage cardiac arrest using standard protocols while treating suspected toxic cause.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU admission indicated for significant suspected cyanide poisoning, antidote administration with ongoing symptoms, severe acidosis, shock, seizures, or respiratory failure.
• Evaluate smoke-inhalation victims for coexisting carbon monoxide exposure and airway injury.
• Monitor for recurrent or persistent metabolic abnormalities and organ injury.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Cyanokit (hydroxocobalamin) prescribing information; AHA 2025 Guidelines; Goldfrank's.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Corrosive ingestion can cause chemical burns of the mouth, pharynx, esophagus, and stomach. Severe cases may lead to airway edema, perforation, mediastinitis, peritonitis, and later esophageal strictures.

[color=#1E3A8A]Common Agents:[/color] Strong acids, strong alkalis (drain/oven cleaners), industrial cleaning agents, concentrated household chemicals.

• Oral burns, drooling, painful swallowing. Dysphagia or inability to swallow secretions.
• Hoarseness, stridor, respiratory distress. Chest or abdominal pain. Vomiting or hematemesis. Signs of shock, perforation, or peritonitis in severe cases.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Absence of visible oral burns does NOT exclude serious esophageal or gastric injury.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]1. Airway[/color]
• Assess voice, swallowing, drooling, stridor, respiratory effort.
• Obtain early anesthesia and ENT support if airway edema suspected. Consider early controlled intubation when progressive airway compromise likely. Prepare for difficult airway and surgical airway rescue.
• [color=#991B1B]Delayed intubation can become extremely difficult as edema progresses.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]2. Circulation and Stabilization[/color]
• Establish IV access. Monitor vital signs and SpO2. Give IV fluids for shock according to clinical condition.
• Keep patient nil by mouth until evaluated. Contact gastroenterology, surgery, and toxicology as appropriate.

[color=#1E3A8A]3. Exposure History[/color]
• Identify product, concentration, amount, time of ingestion. Determine whether acid, alkali, or other corrosive. Assess accidental vs intentional. Bring product container or photograph of label when safe.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, blood gas in significant cases. Lactate when shock or tissue injury suspected.
• Chest and abdominal imaging when perforation or aspiration suspected.
• CT of neck, chest, and/or abdomen when significant transmural injury or perforation suspected.
• Upper GI endoscopy in appropriate patients, generally within 12–24 hours when indicated and after stabilization.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT perform endoscopy in suspected perforation or when procedure otherwise contraindicated. Timing and need for endoscopy or CT should be decided with specialist team.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Airway and Supportive Care[/color]
• No universal medication dose applies to all corrosive ingestions. Treat hypoxemia, shock, and airway compromise per standard emergency protocols.
• Prepare suction, oxygen, airway equipment, and IV access. Arrange advanced airway support early when edema or stridor developing.
• Monitor airway patency, respiratory effort, oxygenation, hemodynamics, signs of perforation. Keep patient nil by mouth. Provide analgesia and antiemetics when appropriate.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT induce vomiting. Do NOT attempt chemical neutralization. Do NOT give activated charcoal. Do NOT perform routine gastric lavage.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Oral Dilution[/color]
• Do NOT routinely give large volumes of water or milk. Small amounts may be considered only immediately after certain exposures if patient fully alert, able to swallow normally, and poison center or product-specific protocol recommends it.
• [color=#991B1B]Never give anything by mouth to patient with drooling, dysphagia, vomiting, reduced consciousness, airway compromise, or suspected perforation. Do NOT delay emergency evaluation to attempt dilution.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Endoscopy and Surgical Assessment[/color]
• Indications: Symptoms suggesting significant esophageal or gastric injury. Intentional ingestion. Known ingestion of highly concentrated corrosive. Concerning clinical findings despite relatively normal oral examination.
• Perform endoscopy only after stabilization and specialist assessment, usually within first 12–24 hours when appropriate. Use CT and surgical assessment when transmural necrosis or perforation suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]Avoid blind nasogastric tube placement in significant corrosive injury unless directed by specialist team. Routine corticosteroids and prophylactic antibiotics are NOT recommended for every corrosive ingestion; use only for specific indications decided by treating team.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — COMPLICATIONS
sections.content:
• Airway edema and respiratory failure. Esophageal or gastric perforation.
• Mediastinitis or peritonitis. Hemorrhage and shock.
• Esophageal stricture developing weeks or months later.

sections.heading: 06 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with symptoms, significant exposure, abnormal imaging, or suspected GI injury.
• ICU care indicated for airway compromise, shock, perforation, severe acidosis, or major organ injury.
• Discharge only after appropriate specialist evaluation and determination that significant injury is unlikely.
• Arrange follow-up for dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, or other symptoms suggesting delayed stricture.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: WSES Guidelines on Esophageal Emergencies; Goldfrank's; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Corrosives Guideline.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Iron poisoning typically follows ingestion of iron-containing tablets (ferrous sulfate, fumarate, gluconate). Toxicity depends on the amount of elemental iron ingested, not total tablet weight.

[color=#1E3A8A]Stage 1 — GI phase:[/color] Vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea. Hematemesis or GI bleeding. Dehydration/volume depletion.
[color=#1E3A8A]Stage 2 — Apparent improvement:[/color] Symptoms may temporarily improve despite ongoing systemic toxicity.
[color=#1E3A8A]Stage 3 — Systemic toxicity:[/color] Severe metabolic acidosis. Hypotension/shock. Altered mental status, seizures, coma. Hepatic injury, coagulopathy, multiorgan failure.
[color=#1E3A8A]Stage 4 — Hepatic injury:[/color] Elevated aminotransferases, hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, possible hepatic failure.
[color=#1E3A8A]Late complication:[/color] GI scarring/obstruction may develop after severe injury.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status.
• Establish IV access and continuous monitoring. Check bedside glucose.
• Obtain blood gas, electrolytes, renal function, liver function, coagulation, CBC.
• Obtain serum iron concentration at appropriate time and repeat when indicated.
• Identify formulation, number of tablets, time of ingestion, estimated elemental iron dose.
• Contact toxicology early for significant/uncertain exposures.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serum iron concentration, commonly measured around 4–6 hours after ingestion for immediate-release preparations. Earlier and serial measurements may be required for modified-release preparations or uncertain timing.
• Blood gas, bicarbonate, anion gap, lactate.
• Glucose, electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, coagulation profile.
• Abdominal radiograph may show radiopaque tablets but normal image does NOT exclude ingestion.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: A single serum iron measurement can be misleading if obtained too early or after peak concentration. Interpret with formulation, timing, symptoms, and serial results.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Gastrointestinal Decontamination[/color]
• Indication: Whole-bowel irrigation may be considered for significant tablet ingestion, especially when numerous radiopaque tablets are visible or sustained-release tablets were ingested.
• [color=#991B1B]Activated charcoal does NOT effectively bind iron. Do NOT perform routine induced emesis or gastric lavage. Avoid whole-bowel irrigation in bowel obstruction, ileus, perforation, hemodynamic instability, or unprotected airway.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Deferoxamine[/color]
• Indication: Consider IV deferoxamine for severe iron poisoning, particularly with shock, severe metabolic acidosis, altered mental status, significant hepatic injury, or markedly elevated serum iron in appropriate context.
• Commonly used IV infusion rate: 15 mg/kg/hour initially, with dose and duration determined by severity and specialist guidance. Do NOT exceed maximum rate/total dose per product label and local protocol.
• [color=#991B1B]Rapid infusion may cause hypotension. Prolonged/high-dose treatment can cause serious adverse effects, including pulmonary toxicity. Severe cases require ICU care and toxicology consultation.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit symptomatic patients and patients with significant or uncertain ingestion.
• ICU care indicated for shock, severe acidosis, altered consciousness, or hepatic failure.
• Arrange follow-up for complications after significant GI injury.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Goldfrank's; Deferoxamine product prescribing information; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Iron Poisoning Guideline.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Lithium toxicity may be acute, acute-on-chronic, or chronic. Chronic toxicity can cause severe neurologic manifestations even when measured serum concentration is not extremely high.

[color=#1E3A8A]Risk Factors:[/color] Dehydration/sodium depletion. Acute kidney injury or CKD. Interactions with NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, thiazides. Recent dose changes/overdose. Reduced oral intake, vomiting, diarrhea.

[color=#1E3A8A]Clinical Features:[/color] GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea. Neurologic: coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, agitation, lethargy, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, seizures, coma. Other: renal impairment, ECG changes/dysrhythmias, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess ABCs, mental status, bedside glucose.
• Establish IV access and cardiac monitoring.
• Obtain serum lithium concentration, electrolytes, renal function, glucose.
• Obtain ECG. Review timing of last dose, formulation, chronic dose, interacting medicines.
• Contact toxicology and nephrology early for significant toxicity.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serum lithium concentration. Serial lithium concentrations until clear downward trend and appropriate clinical improvement established.
• Creatinine, urea, sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, other electrolytes. ECG.
• Additional testing based on altered consciousness, seizures, suspected co-ingestion.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Interpret lithium concentrations in relation to timing of ingestion, formulation, renal function, clinical status. A single level does NOT reliably establish severity in every case.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. IV Isotonic Fluids[/color]
• Indication: Volume depletion/dehydration when no contraindication.
• Give 0.9% sodium chloride according to degree of volume depletion, BP, urine output, cardiac/renal function.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT use forced diuresis or large fluid volumes solely to accelerate lithium elimination. Patients with heart failure or renal impairment require individualized fluid management.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Gastrointestinal Decontamination[/color]
• Whole-bowel irrigation may be considered after significant ingestion of sustained-release lithium tablets, following toxicology advice.
• [color=#991B1B]Activated charcoal does NOT meaningfully bind lithium. Do NOT perform GI decontamination in unprotected airway or patients with ileus, obstruction, hemodynamic instability.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Hemodialysis[/color]
• Indication (per EXTRIP): Impaired kidney function with markedly elevated lithium concentrations. Decreased consciousness, seizures, life-threatening dysrhythmias regardless of concentration. Severe clinical toxicity or concentrations remaining high despite appropriate treatment. Predicted time to safe lithium clearance prolonged.
• Intermittent hemodialysis generally preferred when feasible. Continue serial lithium measurements during and after dialysis. Monitor for rebound due to redistribution. Repeat dialysis when indicated by rebound levels or persistent toxicity.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT make dialysis decisions based on lithium concentration alone. Chronic toxicity can produce severe neurologic injury at lower concentrations than acute ingestion. Consult nephrology and toxicology promptly.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with significant symptoms, renal impairment, rising levels, or suspected chronic toxicity.
• ICU care indicated for seizures, coma, severe dysrhythmias, or hemodynamic instability.
• Monitor for persistent neurologic sequelae after severe poisoning.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EXTRIP Workgroup Lithium Recommendations; Goldfrank's; Lithium product prescribing information.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Valproate overdose can cause CNS depression, metabolic abnormalities, hyperammonemia, and in severe cases, cerebral edema and cardiovascular instability.
• Nausea/vomiting. Drowsiness, confusion, ataxia. Respiratory depression/coma. Hypotension in severe poisoning.
• Hyperammonemia with or without marked liver enzyme elevation. Metabolic acidosis and electrolyte abnormalities. Cerebral edema in severe cases.
• Delayed toxicity can occur after ingestion of enteric-coated or extended-release preparations.

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status. Check bedside glucose.
• Establish IV access and continuous monitoring.
• Obtain serum valproate concentration, electrolytes, renal function, liver function, blood gas, ammonia.
• Consider acetaminophen level and other tests if intentional/mixed overdose suspected.
• Contact toxicology early in severe poisoning.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Serial serum valproate concentrations. Ammonia concentration.
• Blood gas, electrolytes, glucose, renal function. Liver enzymes and coagulation studies in significant poisoning. ECG.
• Neuroimaging when cerebral edema or another intracranial complication suspected.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Clinical deterioration can occur despite initially reassuring valproate concentration, particularly with delayed-release products. Repeat levels when indicated.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Airway and Supportive Care[/color]
• Provide airway protection and ventilatory support when necessary. Treat hypotension with IV fluids and vasopressors if indicated. Correct glucose/electrolyte abnormalities. Monitor neurologic status and respiratory function.

[color=#1E3A8A]B. L-Carnitine[/color]
• Indication: Consider IV L-carnitine in severe valproate poisoning, especially with significant altered consciousness, hyperammonemia, hepatotoxicity, or metabolic complications. Seek toxicology guidance.
• Commonly used regimen: Loading dose 100 mg/kg IV (max 6 g). Maintenance: 50 mg/kg IV every 8 hours (max 3 g per dose). Optimal regimen/duration vary; follow institutional protocol and toxicology advice.
• [color=#991B1B]L-carnitine is an adjunct, not a substitute for airway support or indicated extracorporeal treatment. Do NOT delay stabilization while obtaining medication.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Hemodialysis[/color]
• Indications: Very high serum valproate concentrations. Shock or cerebral edema. Coma or respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Severe metabolic acidosis. Acute hyperammonemia associated with severe clinical toxicity.
• EXTRIP provides concentration-based and clinical criteria. Decisions should be made with toxicology and nephrology specialists.
• [color=#991B1B]Severe hyperammonemia can occur even when liver enzymes are not markedly elevated. Consider cerebral edema in a deteriorating patient with severe poisoning.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit symptomatic patients and those with significant or rising concentrations.
• ICU care indicated for coma, respiratory failure, shock, severe acidosis, or cerebral edema.
• Continue monitoring for delayed toxicity with extended-release products.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: EXTRIP Workgroup Valproic Acid Recommendations; Goldfrank's; L-carnitine product information.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Isoniazid (INH), used in TB treatment, can cause severe and rapidly developing seizures by interfering with pyridoxine-dependent GABA synthesis. Refractory seizures and profound metabolic acidosis may occur.
• Recurrent or refractory generalized seizures. Altered consciousness or coma.
• Severe metabolic acidosis, often with elevated lactate. Vomiting and agitation. Respiratory depression and hemodynamic instability in severe poisoning.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Standard anticonvulsants may be insufficient if pyridoxine deficiency caused by isoniazid remains untreated.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Protect airway and support ventilation. Check bedside glucose immediately.
• Establish IV or intraosseous access. Treat seizures promptly.
• Obtain blood gas, electrolytes, lactate, renal function, liver function.
• Identify estimated amount and time of ingestion.
• Obtain pyridoxine urgently and contact toxicology.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Blood gas, pH, bicarbonate, anion gap, lactate. Glucose and electrolytes.
• Renal and liver function. ECG.
• Evaluation for co-ingestants when appropriate.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay pyridoxine while waiting for confirmatory toxicology testing.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)[/color]
• Indication: Suspected significant isoniazid overdose, particularly with seizures or severe metabolic acidosis.
• Dose: If amount of isoniazid ingested known: give pyridoxine gram-for-gram relative to estimated amount of isoniazid ingested. If amount unknown in adult with severe suspected poisoning: commonly used initial dose is 5 g IV. In children: weight-based regimen, commonly 70 mg/kg IV, up to adult maximum of 5 g per initial administration. Additional doses may be required if seizures or severe toxicity persist.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT delay pyridoxine in a patient with severe compatible poisoning. Dose may be large; independently verify calculation, especially in children. Do NOT assume that seizure cessation alone excludes ongoing toxicity.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Benzodiazepines[/color]
• Indication: Immediate seizure control while pyridoxine is prepared and administered.
• Use established IV benzodiazepine seizure protocol (e.g., lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV, max 4 mg per dose, with repeat dosing according to status epilepticus protocol).
• [color=#991B1B]Benzodiazepines alone may NOT control seizures caused by isoniazid toxicity. Avoid delaying pyridoxine while repeatedly administering anticonvulsants.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Metabolic Acidosis and Supportive Care[/color]
• Restore adequate ventilation and circulation. Treat underlying seizure activity and toxic exposure. Consider bicarbonate only for selected severe acidemia or specific indications, with toxicology guidance. Monitor potassium and other electrolytes during correction of severe acidosis.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• ICU admission indicated for seizures, severe acidosis, coma, respiratory failure, or hemodynamic instability.
• Continue neurologic and metabolic monitoring after seizure control.
• Evaluate for aspiration, rhabdomyolysis, and complications of prolonged seizures.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Goldfrank's; AHA Guidelines for Seizures and Emergency Cardiovascular Care; Poison center and institutional protocols for isoniazid overdose.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Methemoglobinemia occurs when hemoglobin iron is oxidized from ferrous (Fe²⁺) to ferric (Fe³⁺) state, reducing oxygen delivery to tissues.

[color=#1E3A8A]Common Causes:[/color] Benzocaine and prilocaine. Dapsone. Nitrates and nitrites. Aniline dyes and other oxidizing chemicals. Certain medication overdoses.

• Cyanosis that may not improve with oxygen alone. Headache, dizziness, fatigue, dyspnea.
• Chocolate-brown or dark blood. Tachycardia and confusion. Seizures, dysrhythmias, coma, or shock in severe cases.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Conventional pulse oximetry may remain near 85% and may not accurately reflect oxygenation. Confirm suspected methemoglobinemia with blood co-oximetry.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Stop exposure to suspected oxidizing agent.
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status. Administer oxygen while evaluating patient.
• Obtain IV access and continuous monitoring.
• Send blood gas with co-oximetry and relevant lab tests.
• Identify causative substance and assess for G6PD deficiency and serotonergic medication use.
• Contact toxicology for significant or uncertain cases.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Blood co-oximetry for methemoglobin concentration. Blood gas and lactate.
• CBC and renal function. ECG in symptomatic or severe cases. Hemolysis investigations when indicated.
• Review of medications, chemical exposures, possible inherited causes.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: A calculated arterial oxygen saturation from a standard blood gas may be misleading. Use direct co-oximetry when available.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Methylene Blue[/color]
• Indication: Symptomatic acquired methemoglobinemia or clinically significant methemoglobin elevation, interpreted in context of symptoms, comorbidities, and oxygen-delivery risk.
• Initial dose: 1–2 mg/kg IV over approximately 5 minutes per product instructions. If significant symptoms persist or methemoglobin remains elevated, further dose may be considered after 30–60 minutes under specialist guidance. Do NOT continue repeated dosing without reassessment and toxicology advice.
• [color=#991B1B]Methylene blue may be ineffective and can cause severe hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency. It can precipitate serotonin syndrome in patients taking serotonergic medicines (SSRIs, SNRIs, others). Use specialist guidance in pregnancy and significant renal impairment. Methylene blue can interfere with pulse oximetry and some laboratory measurements.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Alternative Management[/color]
• When methylene blue is contraindicated, ineffective, or inappropriate: stop causative agent, supportive oxygen therapy, consult toxicology/hematology urgently. Consider ascorbic acid in selected cases (effect slow, not adequate substitute for urgent definitive therapy in severe cases). Exchange transfusion or hyperbaric oxygen may be considered for severe refractory poisoning in selected patients with specialist input.

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Supportive Care[/color]
• Maintain airway and circulation. Treat seizures and dysrhythmias per emergency protocols. Evaluate for hemolysis and renal injury. Provide advanced support in severe tissue hypoxia.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with significant symptoms, high methemoglobin levels, ongoing exposure, hemolysis, or need for antidotal treatment and observation.
• ICU care indicated for seizures, coma, shock, severe hypoxia, or refractory methemoglobinemia.
• Monitor for rebound toxicity after agents with prolonged absorption or activity.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Methylene blue injection prescribing information; Goldfrank's; Clinical toxicology guidance on acquired methemoglobinemia.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Hydrocarbons include kerosene, gasoline, lamp oil, lighter fluid, industrial solvents. Major immediate danger after ingestion is aspiration into lungs, causing chemical pneumonitis.
• Respiratory: Coughing/choking during or after ingestion. Tachypnea, wheezing, hypoxemia. Increased work of breathing. Chemical pneumonitis and, in severe cases, respiratory failure.
• Neurologic: Dizziness, drowsiness, confusion, seizures after significant exposure.
• Other: Nausea/vomiting. Cardiac dysrhythmias after exposure to certain hydrocarbons (particularly some halogenated solvents).

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status.
• Remove patient from exposure and ensure adequate ventilation.
• Give oxygen if hypoxemia or respiratory distress present. Establish IV access if clinically indicated.
• Identify substance, route, amount, time of exposure. Assess for aspiration, altered consciousness, co-ingestants.
• Contact toxicology for significant exposure or uncertain product.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• Continuous SpO2 monitoring in symptomatic patients.
• Chest radiograph for respiratory symptoms or suspected aspiration. Blood gas when respiratory failure or significant hypoxemia suspected.
• ECG and cardiac monitoring for significant solvent exposure.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Respiratory symptoms and radiographic abnormalities may develop after initially reassuring examination. A normal early chest radiograph does NOT exclude subsequent pneumonitis.[/color]

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Supportive Respiratory Care[/color]
• Oxygen therapy titrated to patient's oxygenation and clinical condition. No specific antidote exists for most hydrocarbon exposures.
• Monitor respiratory rate, oxygenation, work of breathing, mental status. Provide bronchodilators for clinically significant bronchospasm. Consider noninvasive or invasive ventilatory support when indicated.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT intubate solely because ingestion occurred; base airway intervention on clinical indications. Avoid unnecessary procedures that increase aspiration risk.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Gastrointestinal Decontamination[/color]
• Do NOT induce vomiting. Do NOT perform routine gastric lavage.
• Do NOT routinely administer activated charcoal (binds many hydrocarbons poorly, may increase aspiration risk).
• Do NOT give oral liquids to patient with respiratory symptoms, reduced consciousness, or swallowing difficulty.
• [color=#991B1B]GI decontamination generally avoided because aspiration can be more dangerous than GI absorption.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Antibiotics and Corticosteroids[/color]
• Do NOT routinely administer prophylactic antibiotics for chemical pneumonitis. Do NOT routinely use corticosteroids for uncomplicated hydrocarbon aspiration. Treat documented bacterial infection or another specific indication.

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Observe asymptomatic patients for appropriate period per product, route, local toxicology protocol.
• Admit patients with persistent cough, hypoxemia, abnormal respiratory examination, radiographic injury, or neurologic symptoms.
• ICU care indicated for respiratory failure, severe hypoxemia, seizures, or hemodynamic instability.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: Goldfrank's; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Hydrocarbon Poisoning Guideline; ATSDR Medical Management Guidelines.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
This topic covers pesticide poisoning other than organophosphate and carbamate poisoning (addressed separately).

[color=#1E3A8A]Important agents:[/color] Pyrethroids/pyrethrins. Paraquat and other toxic herbicides. Glyphosate-containing herbicide formulations. Rodenticides, including anticoagulant products. Other agricultural chemicals with product-specific toxicity.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Management depends on exact active ingredient and formulation. The word 'pesticide' alone is insufficient to select an antidote.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Protect healthcare staff from secondary contamination. Use appropriate PPE.
• Remove contaminated clothing and bag safely. Wash exposed skin thoroughly with soap and water. Irrigate exposed eyes with clean water or saline.
• Assess ABCs, mental status, glucose, vital signs.
• Identify product from label or container.
• Contact toxicology early in significant or uncertain exposures.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC, electrolytes, renal function, liver function. Blood gas and lactate in significant poisoning.
• ECG for systemic toxicity or suspected cardiotoxicity.
• Coagulation profile for suspected anticoagulant rodenticide ingestion.
• Serial renal function and respiratory assessment in paraquat poisoning.
• Additional agent-specific testing as indicated.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Pyrethroid Poisoning[/color]
• Commonly cause skin irritation, paresthesia, nausea, vomiting, tremor, seizures in severe cases.
• No specific antidote routinely available. Treat seizures with standard benzodiazepine protocols.
• [color=#991B1B]Some products contain additional solvents/active ingredients that may produce more severe toxicity than pyrethroid itself. Do NOT assume all pesticide-associated cholinergic symptoms are caused by organophosphates; confirm likely agent and clinical syndrome.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Paraquat Poisoning[/color]
• Can cause severe GI injury, acute kidney/liver injury, delayed pulmonary fibrosis.
• Immediate actions: prevent further exposure, decontaminate skin/eyes, urgent hospital evaluation, contact toxicology immediately, assess renal/liver/acid-base/respiratory status.
• GI decontamination: Activated charcoal or Fuller's earth may be considered after ingestion under product-specific toxicology protocol, provided airway protected and no contraindications.
• [color=#991B1B]There is NO established specific antidote that reliably reverses paraquat poisoning. Do NOT administer high-concentration oxygen routinely to patient who is not hypoxemic. However, never withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic patient; titrate respiratory support to clinical need. Avoid delaying decontamination or specialist consultation.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]C. Anticoagulant Rodenticide Poisoning[/color]
• Some rodenticides interfere with vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors. Others have different toxic mechanisms.
• Investigations: PT/INR and baseline coagulation profile. Repeat coagulation tests per product, exposure time, toxicology advice. Assess for bleeding, anemia, hemodynamic instability.
• Treatment: Vitamin K1 (Phytonadione). Indication: confirmed or strongly suspected clinically significant anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning with coagulopathy, or another specific indication identified by toxicology. Dose/route depend on product, degree of coagulopathy, bleeding severity, whether long-acting anticoagulant involved. Use product-specific toxicology protocol. IV vitamin K1 must be administered with particular caution because severe infusion reactions can occur.
• [color=#991B1B]Do NOT administer vitamin K routinely for every rodenticide exposure. Do NOT assume all rodenticides are anticoagulants; identify active ingredient.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]D. Glyphosate-Containing Formulations[/color]
• Severe poisoning can produce GI irritation, hypotension, metabolic abnormalities, renal injury, respiratory complications.
• Provide supportive care and hemodynamic monitoring. Assess for shock, electrolyte disturbances, renal injury. Treat complications per standard critical care protocols.
• [color=#991B1B]The formulation and surfactants may contribute substantially to toxicity. There is NO universally effective specific antidote.[/color]

sections.heading: 05 — DISPOSITION
sections.content:
• Admit patients with systemic symptoms, abnormal coagulation, respiratory symptoms, significant paraquat exposure, or organ injury.
• ICU care appropriate for shock, seizures, respiratory failure, severe acidosis, or evolving multiorgan dysfunction.
• Arrange follow-up laboratory testing when delayed toxicity possible.

sections.heading: REFERENCES
sections.content: CDC Paraquat Chemical Emergencies; Goldfrank's; WHO Clinical Management of Pesticide Poisoning; Product-specific toxicology guidance.

sections.heading: 01 — RECOGNIZE
sections.content:
Snake envenomation may cause neurotoxicity, coagulopathy, hemorrhage, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, shock, and local tissue destruction. Clinical effects vary by snake species and geographic region. Do NOT rely solely on visual identification of the snake.

[color=#1E3A8A]Local:[/color] Pain, swelling, bruising, blistering. Progressive swelling extending along limb. Local tissue necrosis in some species.
[color=#1E3A8A]Systemic:[/color] Ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar weakness, respiratory paralysis. Spontaneous bleeding or abnormal coagulation. Hypotension or shock. Dark urine from hemoglobinuria/myoglobinuria. Oliguria or acute kidney injury. Nausea, vomiting, collapse.
• [color=#991B1B]IMPORTANT: Some neurotoxic bites may produce severe paralysis with little local swelling.[/color]

sections.heading: 02 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
sections.content:
• Ensure scene safety and move away from snake.
• Reassure patient and minimize movement. Immobilize affected limb with a splint.
• Remove rings, watches, tight clothing before swelling progresses.
• Arrange urgent transport to facility capable of monitoring and administering appropriate antivenom.
• Assess ABCs, especially bulbar function and respiratory effort. Establish IV access and monitor vital signs.
• Mark leading edge of swelling and record time.

[color=#1E3A8A]Do NOT:[/color]
• Apply a tight arterial tourniquet.
• Cut, suck, burn, or electrically treat the bite.
• Apply ice or unproven herbal preparations.
• Attempt to catch or kill the snake.
• Delay transfer to identify the species.
• Pressure-immobilization techniques are appropriate only for selected snake species and regional protocols; do not apply indiscriminately.

sections.heading: 03 — INVESTIGATIONS
sections.content:
• CBC and platelet count. PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen when available.
• Creatinine, urea, electrolytes, urine output. Urinalysis for blood or myoglobin.
• Blood group and crossmatch in significant bleeding or severe envenomation.
• ECG and blood gas when clinically indicated.
• Serial assessment of swelling, neurologic function, coagulation.
• Where locally validated, standardized 20-minute whole-blood clotting test may help identify venom-induced coagulopathy when lab coagulation testing unavailable.

sections.heading: 04 — TREATMENT
sections.content:
[color=#1E3A8A]A. Snake Antivenom[/color]
• Indication: Give appropriate region- and species-specific antivenom when there is evidence of clinically significant envenomation, including neurotoxicity/progressive paralysis, coagulopathy or spontaneous systemic bleeding, shock/cardiovascular instability, acute kidney injury or significant hemoglobinuria/myoglobinuria, rapidly progressive local swelling meeting regional criteria, other established indications in relevant regional protocol. A bite without evidence of envenomation does NOT automatically require antivenom.
• Dose: Use product-specific dose recommended for implicated species or regional envenomation syndrome. Dose is NOT reliably determined by patient weight alone; children generally require same venom-neutralizing dose as adults for same degree of envenomation. Do NOT use a universal vial count across different antivenoms.
• [color=#991B1B]Antivenom can cause severe acute hypersensitivity reactions. Should be administered in setting equipped to recognize and treat anaphylaxis. Do NOT delay appropriate antivenom in patient with life-threatening envenomation while waiting for snake identification. Unnecessary antivenom exposes patients to risk without assured benefit.[/color]

[color=#1E3A8A]B. Anaphylaxis During Antivenom Administration[/color]
• Epinephrine (adrenaline) IM: 0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL solution, max 0.5 mg per dose in adults. Repeat every 5–15 minutes if required per anaphylaxis protocol.
